Mr. BEATTIE: On this Appropriation
Bill, of which each and everyone knows
the purport, I think the time has arrived
when we should make our comment in a
way which is likely to express the declared
opinion of the public at large. There is
no one in this House who has greater
authority for doing so than I have. I
can claim to represent at least half of
Belfast officially. I represent the East
and I represent the West. It is not just
as Kipling has said, for the East and
West have met, and there they intend to
remain. And the North and South
would be an easier proposition. In say
ing that, I wish to convey to the House
that my voice when heard here is not the
voice of an isolationist. It is not a voice
without any backing. It is the voice of
authority from the people of Belfast. It
is the voice of authority known as the
official Labour party with 90 per cent. of
the trade unionists attached. I hope
right hon. Gentlemen will realise that,
and I hope every Member of this House
will realise that, when casting insults and
rebukes at me. It does not matter to me
personally, but they must remember that
the bigger thing has got to be considered
and respected. I hope that will be borne.
in mind by every Member of this House
in future.
The first point I wish to raise on this
Bill is on an Imperial service, but I do
this by way of directing attention to the
authority who is acting as agent for the
Imperial Service in the position of Coal
Controller of Northern Ireland. I want
to ask what is this professional ramp that
the
is taking place at the moment among
suppliers of the small householders in
receiving their ration of coal. It is quite
true I had a letter from the right hon.
Gentleman this morning in which he was
able, I believe, to put right a very
difficult case. That is only one among
many I received. I would like to draw
his attention to it because it is a burning
question, but it is a question that does
not affect very much the middle class or
well-to-do who can buy a half a ton or a
ton or two tons if the merchant allows
that. It affects the very poor who can
buy only by the stone or bag or whatever
the purchasing power of their home
warrants them in purchasing.
I have one case where only sixpence
was in the home and the medical officer
gave a line for an emergency coal ration
and they applied to the right hon.
Gentleman's Department to see what
could be done, and the Department gave
them an intimation that they would phone
to the firm concerned, Wallace's, of
Newry, and have the ration of coal

immediately sent on the medical line. The
right hon. Gentleman, I know, cannot
just have his finger on every unit of his
Department. There was an emergency
case and a certificate by a doctor and the
coal did not arrive until the fourth day
after the line had been sent in. The
fault may be with the merchant or with
the right hon. Gentleman's Department.
That is one of the emergency cases to
which my attention has been directed.
There are numerous cases where the
merchant has refused to supply bellmen.
I feel some sympathy with the bellman
who has customers and cannot get his
merchant to give him his supply. Bellmen are traders just the same as anyone
else and their trade is going to be lost if
they cannot provide the goods for the
customers.
I am told that the larger purchasersthose men who can order a ton or over it
-are receiving preferential treatment. I
am not suggesting that you would agree
with that at all, but I am told that that
is the case. If we are getting our quota
of coal from Britain, as I believe we are
-I have made inquiries and I find we are
getting a very generous quota of coal for
the consumption needs both of the householder and of industry-then I say we
should have an ample supply of coal to
meet the rationed conditions of the coal
consumers in Northern Ireland and I
want to know why the very poorest people
are being denied their ration of coal.
raise that for the purpose of giving the
right hon. Gentleman an opportunity of
trying to bring some pressure on
the coal authority in his Department,
to see that these people get what
they are entitled to under the regulations
and not as a complaint against any
member of the coal department.
I
The next thing I want to bring to the
notice of the right hon. Gentleman is this.
We had the question of the health of the
people and the question of how we are
going to maintain the population of
Northern Ireland if marriages are going
to be stopped to the extent they are at
the present moment. There is a ban
occasioned by the lack of housing accommodation, but whether that ban is going
to be justified in the future is another
matter. I know hundreds of young men
and young women who are anxious to get
married, but owing to the cost they cannot do so at present. There are houses
for sale. There are houses that are empty,
but when you go to look about them you
are told that they are not to be let, but
are for sale. If you wish to have one of
those houses a hire-purchase agreement
will be drawn up for you under which
the amount agreed to can be paid off in
rent. The first guarantee that you must
give is a substantial deposit, and that is
based not on the real value of the house,
but on an inflated value. A house that
cost £600 in the market two years ago
is now being sold at from £900 to £1,000.
To ask for a deposit on a £550 or a £600
house on a basis of £1,000 is to ask for
too high a figure, one that is not within
the buying power of the industrial classes
at the moment.
I want the right hon. Gentleman, as
Prime Minister, to consider whether it is
in the interests of the Six Counties to
keep on this prohibition of marriage until
the war is over, or whether he thinks it
would be fit and proper to apply for the
same right to build houses that has been
given in England and Scotland. There
they have not stopped building completely. They are building hundreds of
homes for agricultural labourers throughout the country. They have got that
charter, and only the week before last
they got authority to increase the number
because the original number was insufficient to meet the needs and requirements
of the country. I should like that aspect
of the health of the people to be taken
up. At least permission should be sought
to proceed with the erection of the necessary homes for the people who have not
the money to buy the houses now available
because of the exploitation of the property
market.
Then there is another thing to which
I wish to draw the attention of the right
hon. Gentleman. I think that the new
Government which was to clean up
Unionist politics has begun well. Almost
its first act has been to perpetrate one of
the worst pieces of jobbery ever perpetrated by any group calling itself a Government. If that is to be its policy I think
that its career will be shorter than I
prophesied it would be. The job hunters
are on the rampage once more. When the
manager of a firm is sacked he does not
go to the back door of that firm asking for
a job as message boy. I have never heard
of it happening in any instance, but that
is what has happened here in connection
U

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
with this Government. The only explanation that I can come to for the dismissal
of the old firm is incompetence. The whole
trend of the argument of the right hon.
Gentleman was that they were out of touch
with the people, and were not modernised
sufficiently to meet the political thought
that was going to overthrow the Tory
party. He has endeavoured to combine a
number of units to challenge the political
thought of the present and the rising
generation. If he thinks that that line of
thought is going to be successful he is
making a sad mistake, because no man
who has been dismissed for being incompetent will be accepted into the same firm
again to fill an important position and to
carry a very heavy responsibility.
I say that because I believe that since
the right hon. Gentleman came into this
House, and that is some time ago, I can
place the creation of more jobs to his
account than to the account of any other
Minister. No Department developed so
fast and furious as the Ministry of Agriculture during his time as Minister. We
wondered where the masses of the people
were actually employed, and we found
that his new ideas, the new orientation
he was devising for the coming generation, and the new thought that inspired
him to lead the rebels, were going to be
very costly. I wonder if all this has been
justified. Are all the huge sums of money
that have been spent really bringing all
that we expected and hoped they would
bring? What do I find here at the present
time? There are jobs under the milk
scheme, in the Pigs Boards, and other
activities of the Ministry.
Only last night I was at a meeting of
the milk distributors, in connection
with the very thing the hon. lady Member and I have been trying to push forward, and the very thing that young life
is clamouring to receive-free milk and
free food for the children-I find there is
a very great waste of milk, skimmed and
otherwise. This is actually causing
damage in the rivers into which it is being
poured. This is not my own story, it is
a story told to me by those who know.
Thousands and thousands of gallons of
skim-milk are being poured into the
rivers, so much so that the owners of the
lands and of the fishery rights have complained to the Ministry in regard to the
great disaster that is taking place owing
to this wilful waste of one of the essential
foodstuffs of this country.
I want the right hon. Gentleman
clearly to understand that if he has any
skim-milk or other product of that kind
there are thousands of housewives
anxious and willing to buy it for
the purpose of baking bread. When
I was young, soda bread and potato
bread were every-day articles of diet
in my home, but they are now passing
away from the tables of the working class
owing to the scarcity of the necessary
material for baking. When I was informed by this company, who should be
an authority, of the thousands of gallons
being poured into the rivers Ĭ
horrified and shocked, and I said that I
would take the earliest opportunity of
directing the attention of some sympathetic person in the Cabinet to the
matter.
was
I come to the question of labour, but
if I have omitted any point I wished to
bring before the right hon. Gentleman,
the Prime Minister, I hope you will give
me an opportunity of going back. He is
a dual Minister, being Prime Minister
and Minister of Commerce, but my questions are 'directed to him as Prime
Minister. I have accepted this House as
being the medium to express the views
held by the public outside. Coming to
the question of the control of rubber and
petrol of which we hear so much, there is,
in my opinion, great waste of these in
connection with the reorganisation of the
milk collections. Retailers who previously
had their supplies on the County Down
side have now been directed to make
their collections on the County Antrim
side, and it takes anything from three to
four times more petrol and an increased
wastage of from 20 per cent. to 25 per
cent. of rubber
than the old
system.
more
Why this change has been made I do
not know. As it was put to me last
night, it is like a Chinese puzzle. The
man on this side goes to the farthest point
on the other side, and the man there to
the farthest point on this side. That
scheme brings about what is exactly the
opposite of the desire of the Minister of
Fuel in Great Britain. It is a wastage
of rubber, petrol, and oil, the very thing
which we in this part of the world and
they in Great Britain are trying to
avoid. I am not the authority on the
Appropriation Bill-

scheme; I am only the mouthpiece to
direct your attention to it in the hope
that you will examine it and see what
improvements can be brought about by a
further reorganisation in which rubber,
petrol and oil can be saved and perhaps
efficiency in the milk trade be maintained.
As I said, I would come to labour. In
connection with the Ministry of Labour
there is very much that I want to say,
and, in saying it, I am going to make my
point very clear. What I am about to
say, I say with no personal feeling
against any man either inside this House
or outside of it. I say it with a public
responsibility towards the betterment of
the administration of labour and the
betterment of the relationship between
this part of the world and the Minister
of Labour on the other side.
I find that the Minister of Labour has
been a hindrance in regard to one or two
cases, particularly as to the fitting in of
the voluntary worker to useful employment in Britain. I have never agreed,
and never intend to agree, with compulsory recruitment for industrial positions
in Great Britain. I always contended
that if men or women want to go to
Britain they should go there, and if they
can serve the interests of Britain in the
winning of the war, they have my best
wishes. I am going to quote two cases
whereby Britain has been rather handicapped by the failure of the administration on this side of the water to recognise
what their responsibilities are in regard
to the parity agreement under the Unemployment Insurance Acts. As some.
Members are aware, there was a call from
the armed Forces to the industrial field.
Large numbers of airmen, groundmen,
soldiers and other technicians were called
back into the industrial area to perform
work. One of these was a member of
the R.A.F. ground staff. He was asked
to go to a firm in England-the de Haviland Co. I will try to inform the right
hon. Gentleman in the man's own words
what took place:
I came home on sick leave from the
de Haviland Co. about the 6th April.
One month later I reported to the
labour exchange for permission to return to de Haviland's. One week later
a reply came, and I was told I was not
known. The exchange promised to
write again. Ten days elapsed, when
a reply arrived stating there was no
vacancy. No reasons were given for
this, and I made. an appointment to see
the manager, Mr. Hamilton, to clear
matters up.
In case there may be any misunderstanding, let me say that Mr. Hamilton
is well known to me. There is no officer
in the labour exchange more fitted for his
position than Mr. Hamilton, and I hope
the right hon. Gentleman will clearly
recognise that point. This man
tinues:
con-
Mr. Hamilton informed me he would
look into things and he would most
probably have me reinstated, and following that get me a permit to obtain
my position. In the meantime, a
letter had arrived from the former shop
steward in the works, who has been
looking after things on my behalf.
This stated he had seen the works
superintendent, Mr. Brown, and was
informed that my release had been
signed at my own wish, and that a
letter from the labour exchange had
stated I did not wish to return.
Here is the point. This man was not
signing at the exchange in Corporation
Street. He was released from de Haviland's in Bolton because of sickness. The
labour exchange immediately asked the
de Haviland Co. for his unemployment
and national health insurance cards.
What authority or right had they to do
that in regard to an unregistered person,
a man on the R.A.F. ground staff, who
was released to go on war work? I have
a copy of the letter, and I fail to find
any justification for that representation
being made on this man's behalf. He
was so annoyed and worried about this
that he wrote a letter saying that he had
never asked for his release, but wished to
get back to his work, and he asked them
to give him a permit. He got a telegram
which was headed, "On His Majesty's
Service, saying:
Kelly, Orby Drive, Belfast. Work
not available for you.-De Haviland,
Bolton.
If the Minister wishes to see this I can
hand it to him afterwards. That was

rather startling to this man.
sent

That is dated the 21st. Thinking there
was
some misunderstanding about the
name he went to the labour exchange
and showed this telegram to Mr. Hamilton. He asked him to get him a permit
to enable him to go back to his employment, but he was refused a further opportunity of taking the job. I have often
heard the remark that there is something
wrong in the state of Denmark. Surely
there is something wrong in that. I am
asking the right hon. Gentleman to make
inquiries into the matter and get the
position clarified. This man is not a
civilian; he is a soldier. He is released
and is liable to be picked up as a deserter
if he does not return to the employment
for which he was released. He is here
still and cannot get away because he
cannot get the necessary permit.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): He is still in the service?
Mr. BEATTIE: He is released, but
he requires a permit from the labour
exchange to proceed to work in Great
Britain under the release scheme. I am
not going to develop that case. There is
much more in this than I have said. I
do not wish to be charged with making a
mountain out of a molehill. I wish to
give the Minister an opportunity of
examining the case and finding out why
this man was humbugged so much.
We have heard so much about agricultural labour that I have got rather shy
of taking any notice of statements. We
are told we are going to have a gang of
industrial workers placed on agricultural
work. Just to-day I had a deputation
from Kircubbin requesting me to go to
the court of referees with them this afternoon. That was something I could not
do, because I had other matters to deal
with. They told me there were numbers
of highly efficient agricultural workers
unemployed in that area, and they could
not get any opportunity for taking up
work. One of these highly efficient agricultural workers was sent yesterday to the
medical referee in Kircubbin for a job
across the water. He has been 20 miles
away from his home looking for employment in the occupation he follows. He
was late in arriving at the doctor's residence. The result was that the doctor,
who was the medical referee, refused to
examine him, and he got a paper this
morning disallowing him for six weeks
for failure to comply with the request as
to suitable employment. There is something I want the right hon. Gentleman
to look into and find out if the management of all these departments is being
carried out in the way he would desire.
I have a great liking for the administration of the Ministry of Labour.
branch of the services comes into more
personal contact with the public than this
Ministry. Therefore I have sympathy
for the Department, as a whole, in my
criticisms on various matters that come
before the House.
No
With regard to the question of old-age
pensions, there was a hint in the King's
Speech in the British House that something would be done, but there was a
division of opinion as to how it should be
done. I wonder has the Minister thought
of doing anything or is he going to wait
until something is done in Great Britain.
We have a free hand on the question of
old-age pensions. We are not tied by
any agreement or any step-by-step policy..
I believe that the basic pension rate of
10s is too low. No one on that side will,
I am sure, disagree with that. It is all
very well to say you can have a supplementary pension, but a supplementation
of the low basic rate does not bring the
amount up to the standard necessary to

have to say. There is, I understand,
rule in the Ministry of Education that an
average attendance of 95 must be maintained in a school before three teachers
can be available in that school. Now I
have in my own mind to-day a school in
Northern Ireland where the average, unfortunately, has fallen, say, to about 90;
but on many days there are not only 90,
but there are 100 pupils in that school
and still the education committee are not
allowed by the Ministry of Education to
appoint a third teacher. Now that is
neither fair to the teachers nor to the
scholars. These boys and girls being
educated in these schools are to be the
men and women who are to build this
new Jerusalem for us. If they are going
to build the new Jerusalem for us they
ought at least to be educated in a way to
qualify them for such an important office.
The Ministry of Education have already
agreed with the Ministry of Agriculture
that school-children are going to be
allowed to help agriculturists, and because
of the fact that they have been allowed
to do that-and I do not object-on good
days when the farmers are busy and the
children are not allowed to attend school
when they have to help at home-and I
am not objecting to that-the Ministry
acquiescing in that agreement to allow
children to stay away a few days in the
week to help in putting in or harvesting
the crop at the same time are going
to punish them because they are not going
to allow three teachers unless there is an
average of 95 maintained.
In the case in point there are 100 pupils
in the school-room and there are only
two teachers to look after them. It is
not fair to the teachers and it is not fair
to the pupils. I think something ought
to be done to make the rule a little more
elastic than it is and in a case where
they are genuinely employed in agriculture to help to save the harvest or put in
the crop, something ought to be done to
meet that case. The next item is education
again, religious instruction. I referred
to it before; I only want to say to-day
Appropriation Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Elliott]
that I am afraid the case is no better than

It is all wrong.
I am hoping that the new Minister of

Another matter on which I would like
to speak has been referred to by the
Member for Pottinger. It is in connection with the wastage of milk. I told
the right hon. Gentleman yesterday that
I proposed to raise this question to-day
in connection with the new milk factories.
I am not passing one word of condemnation on the new milk factories, but I say
that it is a shame in these days when
every ounce of food, whether it be milk,
potatoes, or any other class of food,
should be saved, to think that in Northern Ireland thousands of gallons of skimmilk are being poured down the drain at
these milk factories. I think it is a
shame and a scandal, but I am not blaming the right hon. Gentleman the
Minister of Agriculture who had nothing
to do with the establishment of these
factories. I would rather be inclined to
blame the hon. and gallant Member for
Iveagh, who formerly represented the
Ministry of Agriculture in this House,
but is now Parliamentary Secretary of the
Ministry of Commerce. I am not sure
whether his war service of six weeks
entitles him to the distinction, but he had
on the King's uniform for that time, and
so I may style him the hon. and gallant
Member for Iveagh.
I think he had more to do with the
building of these factories than the present Minister of Agriculture, but I can
take the right hon. Gentleman to one
factory in South Derry on the border of
County Tyrone, and there every day on
which milk is delivered to the factory he
will find that a huge quantity of skimmilk is poured down the drain.
I am
informed that that is so, but I have not
seen it myself. This skim-milk would be
very gladly used by many people in Northern Ireland for baking bread and other
household purposes. Surely there ought
to be some means by which this milk
could be saved and utilised with great
advantage by the poor people, and others
perhaps, in Northern Ireland.
I understand that this whole milk
question is being operated by a gentleman
in the Ministry of Agriculture called
Mr. Cope. When I think that this might
perhaps be the same gentleman who
operated the Pigs Marketing Board, I
am not surprised that he has rather made
a mess of it. However, be that as it may,
the hon. and gallant Member is probably
directing the Minister now on that very
important question, and so we may have
some light upon that subject later on.
I want to say that unless something is
done, and done very soon, there will be
an outcry in Northern Ireland by the
farmers, by the people who require this
milk, and by the people who are prepared to pay for this milk. That is as
far as Dunman is concerned.
Coming to Cullybackey, I am informed
by the people there that so much skimmilk was being put into the river that
the works in Cullybackey objected to it,
as it was doing harm to their products,
and not only did they object to it, but
the Fishery Board also objected. What
has happened is that the milk instead of
being drained into the River Main is
diverted into some bog. Those are the
facts that I have been given. I hope
they are not correct. If they are not
right the Minister of Agriculture or his
very distinguished companion, the hon.
and gallant Member for Iveagh, will, I
am sure, be able to put me right on that
matter.
This skim-milk would have been very
useful to the farmers if the Ministry of
Agriculture had not adopted their very
foolish policy of allowing young calves to
be slaughtered in all directions. Practically no calves have been reared in my
own district, but if the Ministry of
Agriculture had taken thought for the

Northern Ireland a great many calves
which could have been fed on this milk
which has gone down the drain. I hope

men and you are going to pay them 50s
3d per week. Are you not going to raise

Then I want to know when four workers

are

going to get more money than the men

In my district and county we have men

It is all to the good that labour is going

say
quantity of the. harvest lost in my district was infinitesimal. I hope that this

and who is going to revolutionise

In order to give him the opportunity

I want to make an appeal to him to-day,
and that is to gather up the scrap metal
that is lying all round Northern Ireland.
This, I am told, is the pigeon of the
Ministry of Commerce. We have the
Ministry of Finance officials with welders
and acetylene lamps of one kind and
another going round and taking away the
railings and gates of the people of Northern Ireland. I do not believe that any
resident in the Province, who has either
gates or railings, will quarrel with their
taking these away if they were assured
that all the scrap metal in Northern Ireland was being utilised as it ought to be
utilised. I want to tell the hon. and
gallant Gentleman that I know a man in
my constituency who has 60 tons of scrap
lying available, and although he has tried
time after time to get it collected it has
never been collected yet. I know other
places where there are dumps of scrap
lying and not collected. I know places
where wastepaper is lying and never
collected, and where bones are lying and
never collected.
All these things are going on. The
only thing the Ministry of Finance or the
Ministry of Commerce can see are the
railings and gates round the private
residences of the people. They never even
saw the gates on this estate of Stormont
until I drew attention to the matter
yesterday; at last we are told with much
reluctance that these gates at Stormont
are going to be taken. Surely the Government should give a lead in the matter.
They should not ask private individuals
to give up their gates and their railings
until they have set a good example by
giving up the gates and railings at
Stormont, precious though they be. If
the people thought the Government were
sincere in their attempt to gather all the
scrap there would be far less talk amongst
the people about giving up their gates and
railings.
Are we going to have all this scrap
which we are told is necessary collected or
are we not? Is the Ministry of Commerce
going to stand by and say, "We will not
bother our heads. Save paper, save
bones, save scrap, gather them into dumps
and let them lie there." That must not
be allowed to happen.. I have great
faith in this superman, this man who has
stemmed the tide of the aggressor, and
but for whose military services we might
be under the domination of a Hitlerite
Government. I have faith in this man.
I hope he will rise to the occasion and
will do something more than he has yet
done to save us from the domination of
Hitler and all he stands for.

going to suggest to the Prime

Let them come and stay in Armagh, because their duty is to look after the wellbeing of the people and the administration of local government.
Coming to the Ministry of Labour, we

register. It is a sad feature of the life

I have had many problems solved for

of unemployment, and the future
prospects of the workers of Northern
Ireland. Post-war planning schemes and
post-war reconstruction are all right, but
you must look at realities. You must
look back to the period before the war,
and to the position in the provincial areas
where there is no work, and then decide
what your intentions are when the war is
over. The Government should make an
honest declaration of policy as to what
they intend to do with the workers, and
whether they can give them any degree
of security.
Many anomalies are still in existence
as regards old-age pensions. There is a
means test, and our blind pensioners
have a means test. There is still a means
test for supplementary pensions, and for
unemployment assistance, and I am informed that at the present time those who
own a little farm and are in receipt of
an old-age pension are having their cases
reviewed by certain officials in the
Ministry of Labour. Their pensions may
be reduced, because there may have been
some small increase in their incomes from
the sale of the produce of their farms.
Before the Ministry take such a step they
should look back and consider the plight
of the small farmer prior to 1938.
I should like to mention the case of an
old-age pensioner whose book was taken
from him in the month of January last,
and after it had been reviewed his pension was reinstated only this month,
although he received his back pay. That
causes a certain amount of inconvenience
to the pensioner. He is under the impression that he has done wrong, and it
meant that he had a journey from the
farthest corner of South Armagh to visit
me to ask if I could do anything. I knew
that if a pension could be granted it
would be granted by the Department, but
there should not be so much delay. It
does not help. I know the present
Minister of Labour believes in higher
pensions than 10s a week. I think I am
right in saying he has advocated higher
pensions in this House, and I hope he wil
be an advocate for the removal of the
means test. It is not fair.
You can retire from the highest post
in the Government, or in the Police
Force, or any of the other services, and
your pension is paid without fear or
favour and without a quibble. There is
no investigating officer to ask you how
much so and so is earning. I think there
is a little bit of class distinction attached
to these various classes of pensions. The
higher you are in the world the bigger
the pension, and there is no question of
a means test. In view of what we are
fighting for, the right to live, freedom,
and democracy, and all that is enshrined
in the Atlantic Charter, I hope the day
of the means test is almost gone.

I know there are people in Ormeau

it often, but there is no use in preaching

We come now to the question of education. I feel sometimes that while
preach the gospel of following step by
step we are a long way behind. It is a
feature of education in Great Britain that
the children attending schools there do
not have to buy their books. We have
been trying to influence the local authorities to do something about it, but nothing
has been done. I feel the Ministry has
a certain amount of responsibility. They
should try to remind local education
authorities that they should do these
things. Even the question of meals has
been neglected by the education authority.
They are talking about appointing somebody to look after the distribution of
meals. That is all right. But there is
no use in talking about it. I would ask
the Minister of Education to go into this
question.
A particular case came my way last
year.
It was a question of a scholarship
gained by a student in Dungannon under
the Dungannon Regional Committee. Now
that boy desired if it was possible that
his scholarship should be changed to
Maynooth. What I would like to know
is this: Is it the custom of other
regional committees to allow a scholarship
which has been won, say, for Queen's
University to be transferred to Trinity in
Dublin. I took a particular interest in
these cases; I just wanted to see how far
it would go.
But in this particular case
the decision of the particular committee
must stand. I do not mention any
names. The Parliamentary Secretary is
conversant with the case I have mentioned. I think when we find education
committees dealing with matters in such
a manner, the Minister and the department should take notice. It is a serious
state of affairs. As a member of an
education committee myself, I would
have spoken very strongly on such a

to my information, our committee is

to any place outside Northern Ireland

committees who are not prepared to do
that, and I do not want to suggest why.
Now I come to the question of agricul
ture. The new Minister himself had

But the fact of the matter is this: the

and the strong views expressed as to

for this country if they did. When we

of New Zealand, we must take notice of

We find, even in England to-day, that
the farm workers are looking for something better than what they are getting.
They want a 52-hour week in the summer
and a 48-hour week in winter. I hope
there will not be the same delay in
Northern Ireland as there was in the

which took then 14 years. If it takes

never get it. The farm workers of
Northern Ireland are
as good as the
workers anywhere. They perform very
useful service.
I have asked the. Ministry many times
here for the intervention of the Ministry
on behalf of the people living in certain

of this. Some little consideration should

season, and have a point allotted for the

and I hope the Government will occasionally consider what we suggest on this
side of the House. We come down here

We
want to see peace, harmony, and more

I would ask those who represent the

In the name of the constituency which

just answered in this way. A wealthy

have been returned, and if a survey is

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): I want to say a
word in reply to this question that has
been raised about the waste of skim-milk.
There were quite a number of other points
raised relating to my Ministry, but as the
hon. Members who raised them have all
disappeared I do not know that they are
very deeply concerned about them. I do
not want it to go out in the way in which
it has been presented to the House that
there is a wanton waste of a valuable food.
That is not to say that I am getting up to
deny that a certain amount of skim-milk
is at the moment being destroyed.
In a time of war a certain amount of
waste is inevitable. That is one of the
tragedies of war, and we cannot help
noticing it in various directions. Since
the war began there has been a complete
revolution in the arrangements for the
control of milk and for its production in
Northern Ireland, and we have been
blamed as a Ministry for the changes that
we have made. One of those changes has
been the replacement of creameries by
factories for condensing whole milk. Points
have been put up, even here to-day, that
we have been unfair to the creameries and
unfair to certain people who had vested
interests in connection with the running
of the creameries. That, on the other
hand, is the problem that is tossed up to
the Ministry.
I merely wanted to say that if we had
listened to the criticisms of the people
who objected, and who still object to the
erection and running of these condensing
factories, instead of comparatively small
quantities of skim-milk being wasted we
would have had in the Omagh district
another 19,000 gallons a day going down
the drains, and we would have had in the
Ballymoney district another 6,000 gallons
a day going down the drains. We have
tried to get the farmers to accept this
surplus skim-milk. We have been told
to-day that it should be used for pig
Appropriation Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Rev. Robert Moore]
feeding and for the rearing of calves,
and that sort of thing, but the farmers
simply decline to take it.
We are using every means we can use
to dry every gallon possible. Still
further factories would have been in
operation by this time for the condensing
of more and more of the whole milk and
thereby cutting skim-milk out of the
process altogether, but we have been held
up by difficulties in getting the necessary
plant. We are pushing that matter with
all the energy of which we are capable,
and we hope, and have good reason to
believe, that in another four to six weeks
will
we
have sufficient condensing
capacity to deal with all this milk.
The problem is a war problem, and has
arisen mainly owing to the drastic changes
that have taken place in connection with
the pig industry. As I mentioned when
speaking in support of the Estimates for
my Ministry, there has been a very steep
decline in the pig population in the Six
Counties, and that is due to the fact that
other foods could not be obtained to mix
with the skim-milk, so as to make a
balanced ration for the pigs.
Skim-milk
is quite a good food, but you cannot rear
pigs on skim-milk alone; but the other
constituents cannot be got, and therefore
the pigs have gone and the skim-milk has
remained.
Just look at what the picture would
have been like if the Ministry had been
content to take the advice of their critics
and had left the creameries in sole possession of the field. We would to-day
have had to pour another 25,000 gallons
of good food down the drains every day.
I do not think that I need at this late
hour take up the time. of the House replying to any of the other points, as they
are only comparatively small points, but
I do not wish it to go out to the general
public that there was a wanton and deliberate waste of food. We only ask ląd
a gallon for the skim-milk, and whatever
surplus is available at the creameries can
be had so long as the farmer and producer is not willing to take it.
Mr. HENDERSON: It was not my intention to take part in the debate this
afternoon. It is quite true to say that I
have attended the House very irregularly
for some time past, owing to the fact that
I was asked by the Prime Minister and
Minister of Production to try to do something to increase salvage in Belfast. I
will say this, that never was more done
to ruin a Government than was done by
the non-attendance of the. Members who
were responsible for driving the last
Government out of office.
I say quite frankly that it is about a
50 per cent. worse Cabinet than the one
we had previously. In view of the importance of this measure, I think the
Prime Minister might have had the
courtesy to remain in the House to reply
to the criticisms made from this side. No
doubt he has some able, leaders beside him
on the Front Bench, but he might have
had the decency to be present. Some
important matters were raised, and I suggest that, whenever replying, the Prime
Minister should agree that the Government will go to the country. If ever
there was justification for going to the
country, it is now. There was no mandate from the electors that the Government should be constituted as it is to-day.
It is not a Unionist Government. When
the old Government was returned to
power through the efforts of the Ulster
Unionist Council, it was 100 per cent.
Unionist. That is all changed.
What is being done by the Cabinet.
Judging by what I see in the Estimates,
I find it is the most costly little Government to be found in the whole universe.
I know that Members want to get away.
I want to leave myself, as I have a garden
party to attend. I prefer going to that
party rather than waste my time making
a speech to which no attention will be
paid. I am not going to excel the long
speech I made on the Estimates on one
occasion. I will not attempt that. The
amount of money asked for in the Estimates is startling. Indeed, I am getting
alarmed at what I see in the Estimates.
There is one matter I want to bring before
the Minister of Home Affairs, and that is
the question of housing. In Belfast
4,000 people have put down their names
for houses. No more names are now
being taken. If they had taken any
more they could easily have 4,000 additional names. Over and above that, you
have at least 6,000 slums in Belfast. Dr.
Carnwath's report would startle anybody. That report showed that the
Government and Corporation have
neglected their duty so far as houses are
concerned. Owing to the air raids, three

and four families are living in the one
house.
There is not the equal of some of the
homes in the city in any other country.
If you go north, south, east or west you
find terrible conditions prevailing. If we
had the least spark of Christianity we
would have many of these houses demolished or some steps taken immediately
to have structures put up so that the
houses could be rebuilt in a modern way.
It is because of the alarming situation
that I want to focus the attention of the
Government on this important matter.
What I have said not only applies to
Belfast, but to Derry where housing conditions are appalling. The only strong
thing about Derry is Derry's walls. I
hope they will remain strong for the next
ten thousand years. We cannot do without Derry's walls. What would we do
at election times without them? While
I am proud of the historic walls of Derry
and the guns that adorn them, I am not
proud of the housing conditions that
prevail there.
Did the Members of the entire Cabinet
on the day that the ex-Prime Minister
received the Freedom of the City visit
the slums in Derry? They went there not
to celebrate the closing of the gates, but
to join the festive board when the late
Prime Minister, who had received the
order of the boot, was being honoured.
I like sincerity, but some of the men who
went to Derry on that occasion were the

sit at the same table with you and drink

every constituency. In Duncairn, for

rebuild them. Many of those people are

The Minister of Home Affairs will tell
us that we cannot build houses during the
war. We have thousands of skilled,
semi-skilled, and unskilled men whose

building houses. We have an ample
supply of cement, stones, sand and water.
We can put fabricated doors, windows
and floors in the houses so that people
can live in common decency. It has been
argued that no houses are being built in

are. Houses have been erected in
Glasgow and Coventry to accommodate
the people.
In any case, I am not concerned with
what they do in cities on the other side.
I am concerned with Northern Ireland
where we have an ample supply of skilled
craftsmen, and hundreds of joiners and
bricklayers, as well a number of
plasterers.

skilled men running about doing nothing.
They could be utilised for the purpose of

no place to lay their heads. I know that

of guineas.

made homeless

I see that the Minister of Finance is

because he lacks knowledge of financial
He knows practically nothing
matters.
about finance; he has been pitch-forked

The people

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 20th November, 1934.
The Second Session of the Fourth Parliament of Northern Ireland appointed
to meet 20th November, 1934, in the
Twenty-fifth year of the Reign of King
George V, was opened by the Governor
(His Grace the Duke of Abercorn,
K.G., K.P.) in person.
The House met at Five Minutes before
Twelve of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER
(Right Hon. H. G. H. Mulholland, M.P)
in the Chair.
Mr. SPEAKER: It will be a matter
of great convenience if, on entering the
Senate, right hon. and hon. Members
will take up their positions behind me
in formation on a front of four or five.
This will enable Members of the House
of Commons to fit in comfortably when
the door is shut, and guests of the
Senate to see the proceedings.
On coming out of the Senate, I might
suggest that those hon. Members who
are nearest the door would perhaps move
out towards the Lobby, in order to allow
right hon. and hon. Members to return
on a front of two.
I will give hon. Members plenty of
time to get into that formation.
The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod
(Major T. Dalby Hackett, D.S.O.) was
announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Gentleman Usher said:
His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the
Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
The Sitting was suspended until Three
of the Clock, and then resumed.

misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in
any case before this House or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary do take
care that, during the Session of Parliament the passages through the streets
leading to this House be kept free and
open, and that no obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members
to and from this House, and that no
disorder be allowed in the precincts of or
in the passages leading to this House,
during the Sitting of Parliament, and
that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts; and that the Serjeant-at-
Arms attending this House do communicate this Order to the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS, AND
RECORDS.
Ordered: That the Votes, Proceedings,
and Records of this House be printed,
being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and
that he do appoint the printing thereof;
and that no person but such as he shall
appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered: That a Committee of Privileges be appointed.

KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report that
the House has this day attended in the
Senate to hear his Grace's Speech on behalf of His Majesty to both Houses of
Parliament, of which I have for greater
accuracy obtained a copy. The speech is
as follows:-
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
In addressing you at the opening of
the Second Session of this Parliament
it is a matter of great satisfaction to
me to learn that, although there have
been fluctuations in the number of
persons out of work who are registered
at the employment exchanges, the
improvement in employment which
began in 1933 has been sustained.
During the last twenty-one months the
Register has shown a rise in only six
of the months. For fifteen of the
months a fall has been recorded, and
in October of this year the figure was
over 14,000 less than in January,
1933. During the twelve months that
ended in October, 1934, more than
26,000 persons have found employment through the agency of the employment exchanges. I trust that our
industries will continue to provide
substantial employment for our workers
during the coming years.
It is a matter of gratification to
know that active steps are being
taken to bring into operation the
comprehensive scheme of unemployment assistance that was authorised by
the Unemployment Act of 1934, and

As regards the Unemployment Act, 1934,

distressed areas as it affected Northern
Ireland. We here have no large distressed areas but we have small scattered
pockets where work once available has left
that area.
There is such a pocket one
and a half miles from my own door, where
owing to a mill having been closed down
some 350 people have not worked at their
trade for 4 years. My point in May
last was, and still is, that these areas require special attention and consideration.
The problem is not one to be dealt with
by the normal procedure under the
Unemployment Acts. Public
relief works-and there are one or two
utility
being carried out in that area-while

Imperial Government found they could
not wait for the Unemployment

Reference is made to one of the most

This co-ordination is urgent and necessary

this House can build up suitable legislation which will restore transport
to normal conditions. The recent statement by the Government that the Transport Board to be set up will be a public
one and not subject to any of the existing
owners of transport should
should inspire

the transport authorities in Great Britain

May I say here that last Session certain
Bills were brought before this House and
pushed through by the Government with
what appeared to some Members to be

without undue haste. Undue haste not

The Bill dealing with the powers of the
magistrates will give rise to much discussion. It has given rise to much discussion
outside this House. I hope it will be a
wise Measure of reform, for there is room
for reform; that it will maintain intact
the independence of the administration of
justice, free of the political executive or
permanent bureaucracy, and that there

As regards the development of the pig
and bacon industry, the whole basis of
the marketing scheme was to secure a
market for home suppliers by putting
imports under a quota and so
secure a
price to the producer based on the cost
of production. In the past nine months
the imports of bacon from abroad have
exceeded the quota by 7 per cent., and
there has been an increase in the imports
of frozen pork from America by over 80
per cent.
Farmers have responded to the
scheme by increasing their production
but this is useless if the market in which
the curers have to sell the finished product is to be weakened by excess imports.
All this is reflected by the legislation
passed in Great Britain to fill contracts
for the next twelve months; in fact as
most people know the closing date for
contracts, which was the 14th November,
has had to be extended. The success of
the scheme rests on the manner in which
the quota imports are controlled. Here I
would like to link what I have said about
distressed areas with the proposals for a
development board to expand the pig and
bacon industry, and to suggest there is a
fine chance for the various Ministries to
work together to see if this can be applied
to places where mills are closed down.

The PRIME MINISTER: In the
first instance I would like to say how
honoured we all feel to-day that the
mover of the Address in Reply to the
Gracious Speech was our old friend who,
as Minister of Agriculture for so many
years, assisted his fellow countrymen in
Ulster. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I think it is an absolutely unique
occasion for a member of the Privy
Council and an ex-Cabinet Minister to
come down and take the position of
moving the Address, and I, personally,
as a humble Member of the House, beg
to thank him. With regard to the hon.
and gallant Member (Lieut.-Colonel
Gordon), it gives me special pleasure that
he should have the honour of seconding
it, because he sits for a constituency for
which I sat for many years before this
Parliament was established.
There is really very little for me to
refer to arising out of what has already
been said, but I would like the right hon.
Gentleman (Sir Edward Archdale) to
rest quite assured that the new Transport
Bill will not in any way whatever affect
the right of private lorry owners
carrying their Own goods, whether
agricultural or otherwise. They will
be able to carry on in future as they
carried on in the past. What the Government have at the back of their mind
is not to interfere with private lorries,
but to try to save the whole system in
Ulster from the breakdown which, it
must be obvious to anyone who has
studied transport during the past number of years, is bound to occur unless
steps are taken. I can assure the
House that these steps will be taken
cautiously in a way, and yet they will
be enough to solve the problem, which
must be solved, without dire consequences to any citizen we represent.
With regard to some remarks made by
the hon. and gallant Member (Lieut.-
Colonel Gordon) in which he suggested
that hasty legislation led afterwards to
difficulties arising, I would only like to
say that the worst instance I can call
to mind was the Milk Bill. I sympathise with everybody, but that Bill
had to be put through with some
rapidity. I would ask the House quietly
to consider what would have been the
effect if that Bill had not been put on
the Statute Book as rapidly as possible.
It would have meant in those areas
where creameries exist, especially Tyrone
and Fermanagh, that they would have
had to wait during six months before
they could have received the relief which
I am sure all who know the subject will
agree saved them practically
practically from
disaster. Therefore, there was an excuse in that case. If there were any
other instance of such a thing happening I can only say that the Government
take all the pains they possibly can in
order to give the House as long time to
consider Bills as possible, and I hope to
be able in a minute or two to assure them
that, in regard to the important matters

I am sorry I had to change my mind at

was taken converted me entirely from the

I would like to say, in regard to that
Bill, that we have been charged in the
country on various occasions with getting
out of step with Great Britain in the
matter. This is not, of course, the
moment to discuss any of the details of
the Bill, but I would just like to say that
there must not be too narrow a meaning
read into the words "step by step with
Great Britain." The phrase was coined
in reference to the social services, that
is to say, unemployment relief and all the
analagous Acts that have been passed for
the people who were responsible for saving
Ulster in the first instance, and who, as a
reward, were assured that there would be
no differentiation between them and their
fellow citizens in Great Britain in consequence of Ulster having accepted the
responsibility of its own Constitution and
its own Parliament. Those undertakings
which were given at this box fourteen
years ago in 1921, have been fully fulfilled, and in regard to all the social
services, over which my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews),
has presided to his own credit and for the
benefit of the people as a whole, those
steps have always been measured, just
right and left, with what has taken place
in legislation and administration on the
other side; and as long as I have the
honour to be in the position in which I
am that will be carried out most faith-
But when it comes to talking
fully.
about step by step in some other matters
it is really hardly fair for anyone to read
into the words more than there actually
lies in them.
Might I just take two very concrete
instances that have happened in the past
few years.
One of them was the
Licensing Act. The Licensing Acts of
Ulster are based on an entirely different
basis to those in Great Britain, and I
venture to say that our Licensing Acts
are infinitely preferable to those that
exist in England, Scotland, and Wales.
In fact, I would say that up to the
present they have borne such fruit that
even the most extreme opponents of the
Act in the first instance are now satisfied-I observe the hon. and learned
Member (Mr. Campbell) shaking his
head, and I will just answer one of the
questions he put to us in a moment-that
everybody, who really sits down and considers the situation in Ulster to-day and
compares it with what it was twenty-five
or thirty years ago, must inevitably come
to the conclusion that we are infinitely
better off than we were then; and, in
addition-and this is answering the hon.
and learned Member's question-it has
done no harm whatever in connection
with the tourist traffic to our shores.
Each year, as we have gone along, we
have been able to multiply the number
of visitors who come from abroad and
from Great Britain, in spite of all the
warnings that we were given by hon.
Members opposite that our licensing laws
would kill the whole thing. It is open
for anyone to read.
That is one case where we branched
away from Great Britain in legislation.
Another case, which I think I am right
in calling to mind, was in connection with
the Betting Act. The Chancellor of the
Exchequer in Great Britain brought in a
Bill imposing a tax upon betting, 1
the Government here said, "We w

Mr. NIXON: And the motor duties.
The PRIME MINISTER: So far as
the motor duties are concerned they do
not arise on the King's Speech to-day,
but if the hon. Member for Woodvale

prove that, owing to the excessive number
of roads that we have here compared
with Great Britain, and also owing to the
fact that our roads, in the first instance,
were not nearly so well bottomed as they
were on the other side of the Channel,
it meant that, if we were to make good
here, we were bound to put all our
energies into making our roads-firstclass, second-class, third-class roads-no
worse, at all events, than they are on the
other side. I think everybody who
motors through our countryside now will
admit that we stand unashamed in regard
to the roads we are able to provide for
visitors with motor-cars to the Ulster
area. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) And
I should say, since the question has been
raised, that our grateful thanks are due
to the various county authorities and to
the county surveyors for the extraordinary
way in which, in these few years, they
have revolutionised roads which we can
all remember in a miserable condition and
which we are now able to compare with
the very best arterial roads in England.
I remember quite well, and I am sure
other hon. Members will remember, what
the Lisburn Road was like. At any rate
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Commerce (Mr. Barbour) can tell the
House what it was like, what Lisburn
town itself was like even a few years ago
so far as roads were concerned. Therefore, I do not think the hon. Member
need twit the Government with having,
in the meantime, put charges upon
mechanically driven vehicles slightly
higher than on the other side, if they
are slightly higher. I think, on the
average, there is not really very much.
to quarrel about.
Mr. NIXON: Some other time.
The PRIME MINISTER: Some other
time I am ready to cross swords with the
hon. Member, not only on that, but on
a great many other questions. The other
question that has been raised is with
regard to the Summary Jurisdiction Bill.
I will only say this. It is the intention
of the Government to produce a Bill
which will be of benefit to the citizens of
Northern Ireland. We are not bringing
in the Bill with any mischievous intent.
We are not bringing in the Bill casually
or thoughtlessly. We propose to place
upon the Statute Book an Act which will
compare favourably with the law of any
other country in the world. I want to
say here and now that some Measures are
rather difficult to understand at the first
blush, but, when people absorb them and
take time to think, they realise afterwards what a great thing has been done
to help everybody-no special class, but
everybody-in the Ulster area. Nobody
need be in the slightest degree perturbed
that we are out to do harm. We are out
to do good. We are out to make Ulster
the model State that I always have before
me, and that I hope every hon. Member
in the House has before him, so that we
may be the envy of the world for our
judicial, social, and Parliamentary
services. There is no reason why, in this
area of ours, we should not take the lead
in every direction for the benefit of our
citizens.
With regard to the new system which is
to be inaugurated under the Unemployment Assistance Board, I would like to
say that I think not only the Government
but the whole House would be desirous
that a very cordial vote of thanks should

advice and of all the help they could get.
I wish to pay a tribute to the public
assistance committees, which arose out of
that. I wish to pay that tribute, not only
to the committees as a whole and
collectively, but individually. I had the

Debate on the Address
Sir ROBERT LYNN: We always do.
I believe that the Government has been
lax in this respect. In one of last Sunday's papers a great English writer stated
as far as Sunday was concerned Ulster was
like a province of the dead. I felt
inclined to refute that, but in many
respects there is truth in it. What
attractions are there to induce tourists to
come here?
Mr. ELLIOTT: The scenery.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Do you want to
keep them away?
Mr. HENDERSON: I admit that the
scenery is the finest to be found in any
part of the world. But what are the
facts? Hon. Members on the opposite
side of the House and their friends are
not satisfied to come to Northern Ireland
to see the loveliest scenery in the world;
they go to foreign countries. I try to
bring as many English and Scottish
visitors to Northern Ireland as I can, and
I always find that when they come over
here for one season they come back again.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) But if
you look at the recent statements made,
even by the Bangor Urban Council, you
will see that everything of an attractive
nature to make tourists enjoy themselves
is going to be taken away. I suggest to
the Prime Minister that he should take
this matter up in a far more serious
manner in the future than he has done
in the past, because I feel that more
could be done to encourage tourists to
come to Northern Ireland, and, as far as
the Government are concerned, they have
done practically nothing to advertise
Northern Ireland. I do not know
whether I am in order in saying this or
not, but I would have thought that legislation would have been introduced during
'this Session to let the English people
know that Ulster is still part and parcel
of the British Empire. That is not done
in the way it ought to be done.
Mr. ELLIOTT: It is done all right.
Mr. HENDERSON: Not at all. The
hon. Member for South Tyrone knows
nothing at all about that, for he is one
of those who are not in the know. When
the Prime Minister and the Members of
his Cabinet go across the water why do
they not tell the people at these large
Unionist demonstrations that Ulster is
part and parcel of the British Empire?
Mr. HENDERSON: Well, none of the
English papers ever take any notice of it
in your speeches for they never put it in.
I suggest that more could be done by
the Government to encourage local
authorities throughout Northern Ireland
to construct better roads and more roads
than we have at the present time. It is
quite true that many of the roads in
Northern Ireland have been reconstructed
in concrete, but a large percentage of
those roads have no footpaths at all. The
construction of those footpaths would give
a considerable amount of work. I am
sure the Minister of Agriculture or the
Minister of Home Affairs will tell us
what the Government are going to do,
seeing that the Prime Minister is going
away now. In this Gracious Speech from
the Throne is there a solitary line that is
going to be of any benefit to the people
of this country? Not at all. Not a
solitary line in this Gracious Speech is
going to do anything towards bettering
the conditions of the people in the
country. I would have thought that
drastic measures would have been introduced for the relief of unemployment.
Hon. Members on this side of the House
have harped continually at right hon.
Gentlemen to do something to relieve the
distress that exists not only in Belfast but
throughout the length and breadth of
Northern Ireland. There is not a solitary
line to say that anything is going to be
done for the thousands and thousands of
single men, some of whom have not
worked for the past twenty years. Is it
not deplorable to think that in a country
which the Prime Minister says is a
paradise there are young men who have
not done a solitary day's work since the
war finished? I am rather surprised that
the Ulster loyalist, about whom you
always speak but for whom you do
nothing, is as loyal as he is. You cannot
expect loyalists to be always loyal.
Mr. ELLIOTT : You can.
Mr. HENDERSON: No, because the
lip service of the Government and their
friends is not going to fill the stomachs of
the wives and children of the loyalists of
Northern Ireland. I cannot understand
the apathy of the Government towards
the single men in Northern Ireland in
the matter of finding them employment.

are suffering. We should try to face the
facts and the realities of the situation in
Northern Ireland. It is no pleasure to
me to have to get up in this House and
tell you that there are young men in
starvation or that there are young women
in utter destitution. Let the hon. and
gallant Member come out with me any
time he likes on the streets of Belfast and
I will show him dozens and dozens of men
in utter destitution, and if he has anything to give away I will show him the
proper ones to give it to, men who are
loyal.
Again, I cannot understand why, in
view of the fact that you have from
20,000 to 25,000 children leaving school,
absolutely nothing is being done, good,
bad, or indifferent, to introduce legislation to create new industries in Northern
Ireland. There is not a solitary line here
about new industries, and the only hope
of making any country prosperous is by
creating new industries. Will the
Minister of Agriculture or the Minister
of Home Affairs tell me what is going to
be done to absorb these young persons in
employment? It states here that under
the system adopted by the Minister of
Labour 26,000 persons have found
employment.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Mr. HENDERSON: There is nothing
much to "Hear, hear" about.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I think there is.
Mr. HENDERSON: Would it surprise
the hon. Member to know that many of
those 26,000 people have been sent to
employers who have given them the handsome sum of five bob a week?
Sir ROBERT LYNN: It would.
Mr. HENDERSON: I can take you to
dozens of them. Would it surprise the
hon. Member to know that in the great
city of Belfast there are hundreds who
are only getting from 5s. to 6s. a week?
Those are people sent out by the Ministry
of Labour. I would have thought that
the Minister of Labour would have
been careful when he sent these people
out, because many of these people who
are asked to work for from 5s. to 8s. a
week would have far more money if they
were drawing unemployment benefit.
What is the system adopted by the
Minister of Labour, or someone acting on
his behalf, in the exchanges? When
some employer sends in and says, "I want
a couple of persons to perform some
manual labour," those people are sent
from the exchange without any inquiry
from the Ministry of Labour as to whether
that employer pays a fair rate of wages
for services rendered. You should be
introducing legislation here to compel
such employers to pay those people a wage
that would at least enable them to exist.
But that is not done. When these persons who are sent through the exchanges
'find out that the employer to whom they
are sent is offering them a ridiculous
wage they refuse to take it, and then
they are disqualified, automatically struck
off, and receive no benefit for at least six
weeks. That should not be done at all.
I am sorry that I have to protest against
such a ridiculous and outrageous system
in the year 1934.
As far as the unemployed of Ulster are
concerned there is no reason for hope that
they are going to receive anything from
this Government. I see no hope at all.
You have between fifty and seventy
thousand people unemployed. Even in
the City of Derry, which the hon. and
learned Member (Mr. Murphy) represents, hundreds and hundreds of girls are
out of work because of the competition
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
20 NOVEMBER 1934
which the Derry shirt factories have to
meet, not only in Great Britain but all
over the world. What has been done to
try to get those girls in the Maiden City
into employment? Practically nothing.
The same applies to the 60,000 people who
are unemployed. I would have thought
that at least some effort of a concrete
nature would have been made during this
Session to provide work for the unemployed industrial worker. But no;
nothing is going to be done. The 50,000
men who are signing at the labour
exchanges, the 20,000 children leaving
school every year, the thousands and
thousands of single men
and young
women who do not sign at the exchanges
because they know it is hopeless, are still
going to carry on in the same manner,
wanting and starving, and nothing is
going to be done for them.
We will have an opportunity later on
to go into the Estimates, but for the
moment we will take the marketing scheme
for pigs and bacon. The Minister
of Agriculture may tell us that he
has done a great deal of good, but once
again before I sit down I want to protest
against the fact that no protection is being
given to the consumer. I protest that in
this Speech there is nothing to give one
ray of hope to the unemployed workers of
Northern Ireland. The only thing I can
see in it is a reference to legislation that
is going to increase the cost of living for
every solitary citizen of the country. I
shall avail myself of the earliest opportunity to draw the attention of the House
to the conditions of slavery that exist in
this country. I say there is nothing in
this Speech that is going to help the poor
people.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: May I be
allowed to join with the other right hon.
and hon. Gentlemen who have congratulated the mover and seconder of
the Address in Reply to the Gracious
Speech from the Throne? I have
been associated with the mover of
the Address, the Father of this House,
for many years in the Imperial Parliament, and I am sure we are all delighted
to find him in the full vigour of health
and strength. The seconder also put his
points with great clearness, and with
that ability that we usually expect from
him. I am glad the Minister of Agriculture is here, for there are two points
to which I should like briefly to draw his
attention. I hope the fact that the
Leaseholders' Bill is not mentioned in
the Gracious Speech does not mean that
the Government have dropped that subject, and that they are not going to deal
with it during the present Session. I
most earnestly and anxiously appeal to
the
Government to deal with this
question. This subject has been hanging much too long, and I know that
there is a strong feeling that the time is
more than ripe for legislation in regard
to it.
Mr. SPEAKER: I hope that the hon.
Gentleman is content to have got in so
much as he has on this point.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I am delighted
that you have allowed me to get in so
much as that, and I will leave the point.
I have listened to the vigorous speech of
the hon. Member for Shankill, but
among all the chaff it contained I was
not able to find a single grain of wheat.
He spent all his time abusing not only
the Government but the Members on this
side of the House for doing nothing, and
after a lengthy speech he sat down without making a single practical suggestion
in regard to anything that ought to be
done. He talked about slavery. I
should
say that the hon. Member for
Shankill is a champion in the matter of
rendering lip service Ulster and
nothing else.
to
He talked about the question of
bringing visitors to Ulster. I am glad
to say that the number of visitors to
Ulster in the last ten or twelve years has
increased yearly. As I listened to the
hon. Member for Shankill, I thought he
was going to make some suggestion that
would help us to get more British people
to come here to spend their holidays.
But he did not make a single suggestion
that would bring a single visitor to
Northern Ireland. On the contrary, he
has drawn a false picture of Northern
Ireland that, if I were a Britisher instead of an Ulsterman, would keep me
away from the Province altogether. We
hear about the terribly bad roads, about
slavery, and all sorts of things. I know
that the hon. Gentleman does not mean
what he says, but the speeches he makes
are calculated to keep people out of
Northern Ireland, and, as one who
knows something of the mentality of the
British people, I warn him that he is

[Sir Robert Lynn]

by the speech to which we have just

The King's Speech shows that this is
going to be one of the most important
Sessions that I think we have ever had
since this House was established in 1921.
I am
not like the hon. Member for
Shankill. I do not say that all the wisdom, all the loyalty, and all the
patriotism is on one side of the House
only. There are hon. Gentlemen on the
other side who are just as anxious as I
am to do what they can to make this
Province a better and happier place to
live in.
Mr. HENDERSON: Why do you not
live in it?
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I live in it as
much as I can. I am very sorry if I
have to live out of it even for a single
week, but that is not my fault; it is
my misfortune. The time that the hon.
Gentleman spends in it in the way I
have described I spend
greater
advantage to the people of Ulster.
to
The programme outlined in the
Gracious Speech is, in my judgment, one
of the most important that has been
before this House since 1921, and I do
appeal to Members on all sides of the
House to approach these important
questions with a clear mind, without
prejudice, without trying to damage this
party or that party, and without trying
to damage the Government. After all,
Governments come and go, Parliaments
come and go, but Ulster will remain
and the people of Ulster will remain.
We have an opportunity this Session of
passing legislation that may have a most.
beneficial effect on this Province. Therefore I appeal to Members on all sides of
the House to exercise wisdom and to keep
clear of the rancour of party politics
which has never been advantageous in
debates, even in this House. I think the
hon. Member for Shankill was quite
wrong in saying that there was nothing
in the Gracious Speech that was going to
help the unemployed. I should like him.
to tell me of any other country in the
world where so much has been done for
the unemployed as has been done in
Northern Ireland.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I will tell you.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I should like
my hon. Friend, the Member for Dock,
to tell me if there is any other country
doing more for the unemployed than
Northern Ireland is doing.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I will tell you that
when I get you in a corner.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I do not like
these whispers. I would rather have the
statement made in public. I should like
the hon. Member for Shankill and the
hon. Member for Dock to tell me of anything that is being done in any other
country that is not being done in Norther Ireland. I know that the hon.
Member for Dock thinks that this Parliament should be abolished, and that
we should amalgamate with the Free
State, but if he would only look at the
unemployment figures for the Free State
he will find that they are proportionately
higher than they are here, and that
while our figures are growing less the
figures there are growing greater and
greater. It is no pleasure to me to introduce these things, but justice ought to
be done to the people who are grappling
with this terrible problem. If a wealthy
country like Great Britain does no more
for the unemployed than we do here,
surely we are justified in the course we
have taken?
I congratulate the Minister of Labour
on what he has done to alleviate distress,
and I know that if he were able to do
more to help the unemployed there is no
Member on this side of the House who
would not respond and help. I do appeal
to Members not to imagine that they can
create a new heaven and a new earth by
making speeches or passing Bills. What
they have got to do is to re-establish
confidence and to restore trade to this
country. The Government that does
those two things does far more for the
peace, order, goodwill and happiness of
the country than all the speechmakers in
this House or out of it.
Mr. HEALY: I beg to move,
the Debate be now adjourned."

Mr. MIDGLEY: I rise on a point of
order to protest against any arrangement
whereby this Debate can be adjourned
this afternoon without a representative of
the working classes being heard, with the
possible exception of one speaker.
Mr. SPEAKER: As regards the point
of order, it is customary for the Government to come to an arrangement through
the usual channels with the largest party
on the Opposition side of the House as to
the procedure to be adopted. I am given
to understand that on this occasion it was
arranged that a certain number of
speeches would be made on the Main
Question, and that an hon. Member
belonging to the Nationalist Party would
move the Adjournment of the Debate.
The Amendment of which notice has been
given will, of course, be discussed
to-morrow, and the second Amendment of
which notice has also been given, will be
taken as soon as the first is disposed of.
Then we will come back to the main
Question, and any hon. Member who has
not already spoken on the main Question
or who has not moved an Amendment to
it will be allowed to develop his views.
Mr. MIDGLEY: On a point of order.
What I object to is this. I object to an
arrangement being concluded between
representatives of the Government and
representatives of the largest Opposition
party without regard to the feelings or
aspirations or desires of other sections of
the Opposition. That is what I object to.
Mr. SPEAKER: The only duty I have
to do is to safeguard the interests of the
minority. So long as the minority are
able to discuss the Amendment which
they have put on the Order Paper, or
are allowed to debate the main Question
when we come back to it, I think no
injustice is being done, and I can only
give effect to the arrangement come to in
accordance with the usual procedure of
Parliament.
Mr. HEALY: If the hon. Member for
Dock feels that he has a grievance I am
quite prepared to withdraw the Motion I
have made in regard to the Adjournment
of the Debate, and allow him to proceed.
Captain DIXON: We have followed the
ordinary custom of the House. Always
the Opposition have desired time to study
the King's Speech in order to work out a
reasoned Amendment, and they speak
upon that Amendment on the following
day. That has been the custom in this
House. To-day, as usual, I went round to
see if this course would be agreed to. I
saw representatives of the Nationalist
Party, and they said it suited them very
well. Naturally they have not had the
King's Speech in their hands, and it was
not fair to expect them to make any
pronouncement until they had had an
opportunity of studying it and preparing
their Amendment. There was no other
Member of the Opposition in the House
except the hon. and learned Gentleman
who represents the University (Mr.
McNeill). He was the sole representative
of the minority in the House outside the
Nationalist Party. I went to him and
told him of the usual custom of the House
and what the Nationalist Party had
agreed to. He said that the course
suggested was agreeable to him, and, so
far as he knew, would be agreeable to all
sections of the Opposition. Had my hon.
Friend the Member for Dock been here,
or any other hon. Member of the
Minority, I should certainly have been
very glad to discuss this question with
him. This has always been the custom
of the House, and it has been brought
about because it seems much more fair
to the Opposition to give them time to
look at the King's Speech and reasonable
time to consider it and prepare any
Amendments they may wish to put on
the Paper. Personally it is a matter of
indifference to me.
Mr. NIXON: You will recollect that
the Prime Minister stated in his speech
that if any Member had any real
grievance he should trot it out now, or
words to that effect, and that if it was not
trotted out to-day it would take from the
effect of it. Only one Member on this
side of the House spoke. The Chief Whip

in my opinion, there never will be. At
any rate, there is no such thing now, and
I think the hon. and gallant Member for
Dock (Mr. Midgley) should be allowed
to reply to the speeches made on the other
side of the House.
Mr. SPEAKER: The only hon. Member who is affected is the hon. Member

a certificate that the Regulations embodied in the Resolution of the House of
Commons of the eighteenth day of

Summary Jurisdiction and Criminal
Justice Bill,
"to amend the law relating to the powers
and duties of justices of the peace in

of those powers and duties to resident
