provision with respect to petty sessions
districts and the appointment of clerks
of petty sessions; to amend the law relating to the powers and procedure of
courts of summary jurisdiction in criminal and civil matters, and appeals from
such courts; and to provide for purposes
connected with the matters aforesaid,"

provision for the inspection of dairy

supported by Sir Dawson Bates; to be
read a Second time and to be printed.
(Bill 2).
Agricultural Marketing (Pig Industry)
Bill,
"to provide for the regulation of the

Debate on Question (20th November):
"That an humble Address be presented to His Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland, as follows:
:-
"Your Grace,
"We, His Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland, in Parliament assembled,
beg leave to offer our humble thanks to
Your Grace for the Speech which Your
Grace has addressed to both Houses of
Parliament."-(Sir Edward Archdale).
Question again proposed.
Mr. SPEAKER: Before we go on I
would like the House to observe that
there are two Amendments on the Order
Paper. There is a common factor linking the two, that is the question of unemployment. Therefore, if that question
is to be discussed at all it must be discussed on the first Amendment only and
cannot be discussed on the second
Amendment. I want to make that clear
so that right hon. and hon. Members
may know the position.
Mr. HEALY: When the Prime
Minister was making his speech yesterday on behalf of the Government he
used a phrase-one of those old phrases
used from time to time-to describe the
work of the Government, namely, that
he was out to make Ulster a model
State.
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
21 NOVEMBER 1934
Mr. SPEAKER: Will the hon. Member allow me? The first Amendment
stands in his name. It will be necessary
to move that before he can go on talking.
He cannot talk on the main Question.
Mr. HEALY: I beg formally to move
the Amendment standing in my name:
As an Amendment to the Address at
the end to add the words:-"But
humbly regrets that no mention is made
of any steps to secure to the minority
the rights guaranteed to them under the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, and
further regrets the absence of measures
to mitigate the prevailing unemployment and provide houses for the more
poorly paid working classes and expresses
concern that boards established under
Acts of the past Session have been constituted on a sectarian basis."
As I was saying, the Prime Minister
described Northern Ireland yesterday as
a model State. My reply to that would
be to quote not my own opinion or the
opinion of anybody on this side of the
House, but the opinion of a friend and
a very close follower of the Northern
Ireland administration-Mr. Gallagher,
who addressed a public meeting in the
Ulster Hall last week. He said:
Orange sashes frequently cover empty
stomachs.
That is more descriptive, perhaps, than
polite, but I think on the balance it is
likely to represent the facts of the situation much more adequately than the
Prime Minister. After all, that comes
from a man who is of the people and who
would be more likely to realise the condition of affairs amongst the democracy
than the Prime Minister would, living at
Stormont.
If the Prime Minister's statement were
correct it would indicate too, I think,
that he is largely ignorant of the position
of the administration. Therefore, I can
only conclude that he was endeavouring
to make the best possible case he could
of very bad material. We who know the
Prime Minister in this House and elsewhere know there is no one can make
better use of slender materials than he
can. When we raised this question of
administration partially in April I gave
many concrete instances. The reply of
the Prime Minister was given somewhat
later on the Twelfth of July-and he
referred not to the specific instances of
injustice that we had given, but to something wholly different, namely, gunrunning at Larne, which had nothing
whatever to do with the case we made.
At all events, I suppose the Prime
Minister felt that it was the most
efficacious and most striking reply he
could make to the audience he was
addressing.
I would like, at the outset, to draw
the Prime Minister's attention to the
Act of 1920, which I may describe as the
Constitution of this Parliament. The
Act of 1920 was passed by the Imperial
Government at a time when there was
no one representing Ireland, North or
South, in the Imperial Parliament. It
was passed by people who knew the situation that was likely to be. It was passed
by friends of the Prime Minister, who
understood the mentality of his party
and also their record in certain ways in
the past.
The 1920 Act, which the
Prime Minister and his friends accepted
and loyally agreed to carry out, contained
a proviso in Article 5, which said that:
The Parliament of Northern Ireland
shall not make a law so as either
directly or indirectly to establish or
endow any religion, or prohibit or restrict the free exercise thereof, or give
a preference, privilege, or advantage,
or impose any disability or disadvantage on account of religious belief or
ecclesiastical status.
I shall have a good deal to say later
on about the manner in which the Government have discharged their duty in respect
of that obligation, but for the moment
I want just to refer in passing to a Bill
known as the Magistrates Bill, which is
mentioned in the King's Speech. We,
on this side of the House, have no special
reason for regarding with affection the
present magistrates. They are recruited
from our opponents. Since this administration came into power they have made
appointments to the magistracy almost a
test of political and religious belief with
very few exceptions, so that to-day you
find the magistrates of Northern Ireland,
who ought to be in the position of holding
the scales fairly, as between one class and
another of the community, almost of the
one political and religious creed. That
cannot be good for any community where
the great proportion of the people feel
that they are not likely, in certain cases,
to have justice administered.
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Healy]
When the Government felt it necessary
to make the change from what I may
decribe as an unpaid to a paid magistracy,
which is contemplated in this Bill, I
should have thought that they would
have been very careful to see that they
did not incorporate in the present system
a good many of the evils of the old; but,
perhaps, they have gone further than
that, because the Measure purposes, I
take it, to displace unpaid justices by
resident magistrates. We may take it
that if the Government policy be in the
immediate present as it has been in the
past, what we are likely to have in
Northern Ireland will be the appointment
of a number of paid camp-followers of
the Government to these positions. I am
not going to ask you to take my view
with regard to that.
I will quote from a pamphlet issued
recently by an ex-resident magistrate,
who describes the position of gentlemen
holding that post. He says they are
entirely dependent upon the goodwill of
the Home Office, and that their position.
is so insecure that occasionally a clerk in
the Home Office will address an admonition to the resident magistrate. A clerk
who has heard nothing of the evidence,
has not observed the demeanour of the
witness, and knows nothing of the case,
will tell the resident magistrate, "I am
very much surprised at the method you
adopted in handling a particular case.
Fancy a man in the position of a judge
receiving an admonition of that kind
from a clerk in the Home Office. Is it
not likely to sap the whole independence
of the man and his sense of right and
wrong and drive him to give decisions that
will be more in conformity with the views
of the Home Office than the strict
administration of justice?
""
I have often wondered why it was that
resident magistrates invariably were out
for the maximum penalty and were out
in all cases to find the defendant guilty.
I do not marvel at it any longer. The
resident magistrate is obliged to do that
in order to retain his position. The
Home Office might tell him his period of
usefulness had come to an end, or that
he was no longer capable of administering
the various Acts in conformity with the
wishes of the Home Office. Under those
conditions Northern Ireland will not be a
model State, but will be one of the most
extraordinary States in the world.
There will be inspectors inspecting
almost every activity that a man in a
shop, or farm, or factory can engage in.
There will be an inspector at his elbow
night, noon, and morning. It may be
weeds, potatoes, flax, oats, milk, beef or
bacon. There will be inspectors for
inspecting all those things, and if the
farmer does not carry out exactly the
wishes of the inspector he will be
hauled before the resident magistrate,
and the resident magistrate will be
obliged, in order to retain his position, to
impose the maximum penalty. That is a
nice prospect for the independent citizens
of Northern Ireland, this extraordinary
model State the Prime Minister spoke of
yesterday. A resident magistrate cannot
call his soul his own, and he will, in a
short while, reduce the community to a
similar pitiable plight.
The Government appoints all the magistrates, and I have no doubt that in this
matter they will follow the well-known
and established precedent of appointing
their own friends-people of one political
view and one religious faith-and that
when that has been achieved the minority
will be in a more helpless and hopeless
position than they are at this moment.
I said at the beginning that we do not
regard the administration of justice by
the present magistrates as being altogether
free from bias, but, at all events, these
people live in the community, they understand the people, and they are more
likely to administer justice in ordinary
cases than this struggling fellow, who is
dependent for his bite and sup on the
goodwill of the Minister of Home Affairs
and the Parliamentary Secretary. Much
as we dislike many of the magistrates and
much as we doubt their decisions in many
cases, we have no doubt whatever that
they are infinitely preferable to the
people who are going to take their place.
Mr. McElroy, who had some experience of the position of resident magistrate,
described the condition of the law in
Northern Ireland in a few words so much
more graphic and concise than I could
use that I will quote them. He said:
"I assert that the British Constitution is not now in force in this country.
It has not been in force since 1922,
when the Civil Authorities (Special
Powers) Act was passed. He (the
Debate on the Address

21 NOVEMBER 1934
Debate on the Address
Minister of Home Affairs) has long
since put the Constitution in pawn and
shows no sign that he wishes to redeem
it."
That is a description by a man who did
not owe his appointment to the present
Administration, and who was absolutely
independent during the time he occupied
it, of this model State in June last, when
he relinquished his judicial office. There
is not the least excuse for the Government, as they could have found a model
for their new judiciary by merely looking
across the Border. I suppose they would
not adopt anything from the twenty-six
counties. Execpt on that principle I do
not know why, when they were setting up
a new order of justices in this country,
as they are so intimately connected with
the lives and interests of the people, they
did not take as a model the district
justices of the Free State. There the
district justices are in the same position
as judges of the High Court. They are
not dependent upon the goodwill of the
Home Office or the Government. Here
the resident magistrate will know that if
his decisions are not favourable to the
Home Office the Members of this House
down the country and the political
friends of the Ministry will be able to
make representation in the right quarter
and his position may be very seriously
jeopardised. His whole career and the
outlook for his family may be altered.
In those circumstances it is impossible,
humanly speaking, for any man to discharge his duties with only one object
in view, the administration of justice.
He would be thinking all the time that
"So-and-so will be complaining to the
Prime Minister or the Minister of Home
Affairs, who is a great friend of his." I
recently heard of a resident magistrate
who was told by a local politician that if
he did not cease to impose such heavy
fines in police cases he would soon hear
more about it. That is merely the
beginning; it is not going to be the end
of it. Surely the Government have
sufficient control of the country through
the police and inspectors without putting
people, who are compelled to resort to
the law, in the position of imagining that
the decision given is not on the merits of
the case but in the fear of the resident
magistrate as to what the personal consequences to himself may be.
The 1920 Act is very specific that the
Government must not give a preference
or advantage to anyone on account of
religion. Is it a mere coincidence that
every resident magistrate in the North,
as well as the judiciary, are non-Catholics?
(Hon. Members: No, no.) Is it a mere
accident that nearly all the inspectors
appointed in recent times are of the same
creed and class?
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Wrong again.
Mr. HEALY: No, I am not wrong.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am afraid the
hon. Member opposite entirely forgets
that one of the resident magistrates in
the city of Belfast one of the most.
important positions-is a co-religionist of
his own.
-
Mr. HEALY: I know that as well as
the right hon. Gentleman. I said that
as to recent appointments, not only of
resident magistrates but of clerks of the
Crown and peace and inspectors in the
Ministry of Agriculture and other departments, every one was recruited on the
basis of religion and politics, notwithstanding the fact that this State adopted
the Act of 1920, which expressly forbade
them giving any advantage or preference
on account of religion. I want to know
what the cry is in this case. When the
Prime Minister is speaking to his English
friends he says, "We administer the law
fairly between one class and another,”
and when he is speaking to the people on
this side he says, "We want a Protestant
State for a Protestant people." There
are the two voices. I want to know which
of those represents the policy of the
Government to-day, the voice in England
or the voice at Larne?
But even in connection with this, and
apart from the religious aspect, there is
a very serious matter which affects the
whole of the residents of Northern
Ireland. The Minister of Finance has
told us that we have reached the peak
with regard to expenditure. I ask you
to-day where are we going to find the
money to pay these new resident magistrates. There is only one source from
which it can come, and that is from
additional fines, heavier fines and more
fines. That is a nice prospect for the
resident magistrates of Northern Ireland,
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Healy]
that they are going to be forced gradually
by one Ministry or another to see that
maximum fines are imposed in future. I
can imagine the Minister of Home Affairs
giving a kind of blackboard demonstration to these new resident magistrates and
saying to them,
them, "You are costing
£35,000 or £36,000, and the Ministry of
Finance is kicking up a terrible row
about it. The difference between the
fines you have imposed and the salaries
you are going to receive is a certain
amount. You will really have to be very
much more energetic and conscious of the
fact that you are supposed to represent
the Government point of view on the
bench, and you must, in future, see that
as far as possible maximum instead of
minimum fines are inflicted." That is
going to be the outcome of this change in
the magistracy. In the Free State, on
the other hand, it would not matter one
penny to a district justice. If the Parliamentary Secretary asked him to come up
he could be as independent with him as
with his fellow district justices. But it
is not so here. The magistrates enjoy
no security at all. They are going to be
creatures of the administration, subject
not merely to the Ministry but to the
friends of the Ministry in the country as
well.
Now I will pass from the magistrates
and will come to another matter in which
I think the Government have seriously
departed from the underlying principles
of the Government of Ireland Act of
1920. That is, with regard to
to the
abolition of Proportional Representation. When the Government took office
in 1921 that system of voting was in
force here. It was put into force because
the British Government wanted to ensure
that minorities would have due representation in proportion to their numbers.
You knew and they knew the difficulties
in Ireland. They knew that there was a
minority of seven per cent. in the South,
and that there was a very much larger
minority in the North, amounting to
over 33 per cent. They put this Clause
5 into the 1920 Act expressly to preclude the Government from doing what
they thought they might do, having in
view their record and their experience.
They knew that the Unionist party had
made certain speeches and had done.
certain things for years, and, therefore,
is Clause 5 was put in expressly to
provide security for the minority which
would be left here.
There was security under Proportional
Representation not only in Parliamentary elections, but in local government elections. But at the very earliest
moment-and this shows that at any
time their talk was mere lip service to
goodwill on the part of the Government
-almost before they had formed their
administration, their friends in the
country began to form schemes for the
gerrymandering which was to take place
simultaneously with the abolition of
Proportional Representation, and which
was designed to drive the Nationalists
out of the positions they held in Fermanagh, Tyrone, the City of Derry,
South Armagh, South Down, Magherafelt, and even in Downpatrick, which is
a good bit further away.
Without the abolition of Proportional
Representation the Government could
never have hoped to have got complete
control of the county councils in Northern Ireland, and that would have meant
that they never could have passed the
Education Act. To work the Education
Act it was absolutely necessary that the
friends of the Ministry must control
these county councils. There is no
doubt that the Government had made up
their minds before they were more than
a few days in office that they would,
firstly by abolishing Proportional Representation, and secondly by gerrymandering the constituencies, no matter what
the number of electors might be,
get that control. It was a negation of
all democracy. You might as well have
no franchise at all so far as the majority
are concerned. I was speaking a moment
ago about minorities, but in the case of
the Border areas I am speaking about
majorities.
It is true that there was some pretence early in 1922 at holding an inquiry,
but that inquiry only gave the minority
two weeks in which to prepare their
counter case. Mr. Miller, a late Member of this House, speaking at Fintona
on the 12th July, 1922, said that they
had been preparing schemes for two
years and now they were going to see
their fruition. On a previous occasion
the Prime Minister twitted me with not
having come in and prepared a counter
claim. I ask any man seriously how was
it possible at two weeks' notice to pre-

pare a counter claim with all the intricacies and difficulties it involved, when
it took the Government schemers two
years to prepare their claim. It was
impossible. I suggest that when you
sent down Mr. Leech, whose political
and religious views were well known, and
when the spokesmen of the Government
said in this House that the object was
to equalise population and valuation,
Mr. Leech knew very well what he was
going to do, because at the very first
sitting he held in Omagh he said: "I am
going to take equal regard to population
and valuation." What did that mean?
The Nationalists had been driven from
their homes to the bogs in the days of
the Ulster Plantation and were not
likely to be occupying the best land in
the country. Your representatives took
care of that. Before Mr. Leech sat at
all to hear evidence he established a
basis on which he was going to
proceed, a basis which made it impossible for any other conclusion to be
arrived at, than the one at which he
ultimately arrived. It is well known that
in County Fermanagh, County Tyrone,
the City of Derry, South Armagh, South
Down, Magherafelt, and Downpatrick
there were Nationalist majorities.
Mrs. PARKER: May I just ask the
hon. Member a question? Is he quite

District?
Mr. HEALY: I am speaking of the

Mrs. PARKER: The Rural District
and the Board of Guardians. Is he quite

Mr. HEALY: I am quite certain that

Mrs. PARKER: I am quite certain
that the hon. Member is incorrect in

Mr. HEALY: The Census is in the
Library and it will not be very difficult
when you come to speak to give the
correct figures. The Government believed that so long as Fermanagh and
Tyrone maintained the attitude that they
had adopted-and the attitude of the
majority is to-day exactly the same as it
was then; notwithstanding the constituencies and all the disabilities you
have imposed on them you have not
changed the views of the people in the
least until they got control of these two
Councils the Education Act that they
were then inaugurating could not possibly
be put into operation. It would have
meant that in those areas the regional
committees administering the schools
would have been Nationalist, which was
unthinkable from the point of view of
the Government. Therefore, you see the
farseeing nature of the scheme which was
prepared at the beginning of 1921, almost
before the Government had begun to
function. They had made up their minds
that the minority were going to take control of the county councils, and not only
of the county councils but of practically
every other public body.
Let me give you an instance-for these
are facts-of how the abolition of Proportional Representation worked in Fermanagh, Tyrone, and Derry. I will just
take the county council areas and the
county borough of Derry. Under Proportional Representation when an area
with a small population is merged with
an area with a large population you get
a certain uniformity; that was the main
concern of Proportional Representation.
The hon. Member for South Derry (Mrs.
Parker), who interrupted me a moment
ago, once quoted instances of one or two
isolated areas, but my point now is
that when you amalgamate these areas
with larger areas you get a certain
uniformity that enables the people of
the whole to elect the board or the
council to which their numbers entitle
them. Now, in Derry the Nationalists
had 21 members to the Unionists' 19 on
the Derry Corporation. That is mathematically correct according to the numbers on the register. Fermanagh had 11
Nationalists to the Unionists' 9, which
is equally correct and equally fair, and
Tyrone had 11 to 9, which is also right.
Immediately the change over came,
immediately the Government had had the
opportunity of gerrymandering and of
abolishing Proportional Representation,
taking the two together this was the net
result: Instead of having 21 in the Derry
Corporation we had 16 and the Unionists,
instead of having 19, had 24. In Fermanagh the Unionists, instead of having

Mr. HEALY: Taking these totals

defy anyone on the Government side or

believe in doing justice to minorities and
that your talk about accepting the obligations of the 1920 Act was all eye-wash.
You never really meant to carry them
out. If I were to tell you of some of
the difficulties that this scheme of gerrymandering has meant for us they would
astonish you. People in many instances
are obliged to walk 20 miles to poll, and
to pass two other polling stations on the
way. They have to cross mountains;
people on one side of the mountain have
no connection with the people on the
other side. It was necessary for the
friends of the Minister of Home Affairs
to do that sort of thing; otherwise they
could not have managed to carry out the
schemes for which I have given the
figures.
More than that, if you take the
Parliamentary constituency of South Fermanagh you will find the most extraordinary type of gerrymandering that it
is possible for me to describe. It is a
constituency which is 40 miles long. It
crosses Lough Erne, so that the people
on one side of the lake have no connection with the people on the other side.
It goes over to Cavan and Leitrim and
extends to the end of Donegal. That was
done in order to give two seats to the
minority and one to the majority. I say
it is a dirty trick, and the Government
or any Member of the Government who
tries to justify it is bound to fail.
What took place in the Union of Downpatrick, which is nearer than Fermanagh?
Downpatrick Union had a majority of

not been able to drive them out-not
yet but I have no doubt that if the

the hon. and learned Member for Derry
City, have sufficient time they probably
will be able to achieve that. What
Cromwell did not succeed in doing they
hope to do. In the Union of Downpatrick
was

another type. They did not change the

I want to put it another way.

say that on the current register in Derry,
the 1933 register, the Nationalists have
a majority of 1,742, yet they can only
elect 16 members of the Corporation,
while the Unionists have 24.
Come to the County of Antrim, which
is still nearer, and you get a gross injustice done there to the minority, with
no effort on the part of the Government
to redress it. Under Proportional
Representation the Nationalists had one
member, and sufficient voters for one and
a half, almost two members, yet they have
been left by the Government without a
representative at all. That is how the
Catholic minority in the County of
Antrim has been treated. That is not
generous, that is not just; that could not
be justified by anyone. If you come to
the constituency in Derry which is represented by my hon. Friend, the Member
for Foyle (Mr. McCarroll), you will find
that he represents twice as many people
as the hon. and learned Member for
Derry City (Mr. Murphy). In other
words, taking the city of Derry as a
whole, there are a great many more
Nationalists than Unionists, yet the
Nationalists have only one representative.
Come nearer home to the constituency
of Ballynafeigh, and you find it has a
very small electorate compared with the
constituencies of Falls and Central.
Gerrymandering has been carried out not
only in Fermanagh and Tyrone, but it
has been done in Belfast. Every single
constituency that has been fixed up has
been gerrymandered in order to carry out
the will of the Government and give the
maximum amount of representation to
the Unionists and the minimum to the
Nationalists. If we had in this House
the number of members to which we are
entitled we would have 17 Members
instead of the number we have, and even
assuming that Labour would have certain
representatives we would have at least 14
Members. That is a clear demonstration
of the fact that Proportional Representation never got a fair trial in the North,
and that the Government have never made
any effort to be just to the minority under
their jurisdiction.
If we have a grievance in that respect,
we have a grievance also in regard to
appointments. I have said already that
we believe that most public appointments
are made on a sectarian and religious
basis, with very little regard to the men.
When the former Minister of Agriculture
came to Enniskillen in 1921 he had to
make an apology for the fact that out of
109 of his officials four happened to be
Catholics, and he explained that with
such a large proportion of Catholics he
had been obliged to take over three of
those. He had appointed only one
Catholic in 109. The penal laws have
been enforced in this area in a way that
they never were in the days of O'Connell. If the former Minister of Agriculture appointed only one Catholic on his
staff, how many members does anyone
seriously think the present Minister of
Agriculture would appoint? We know
that he has made a public declaration
that he would not employ Catholics, and
is he likely to practise something in
Belfast that he would not practise in
Fermanagh? I do not think so. I take
it for granted he is consistent. Therefore, the rule in the Ministry of Agriculture is that no Catholic will be
employed.
Then, in regard to Catholic schools, the
1920 Act operates too. Catholics and
Nationalists pay their proportion of rates
and taxes, and from the point of view of
efficiency the public records show that the
pupils turned out by the Catholic schools
are just as efficient as those turned out
by your schools. The percentage of
passes and of honours that they receive
is as
high as yours, and yet you
impose discrimination, and you try
to humiliate them-it is nothing else.
We are not the minority in this matter;
we
are the majority. We have the
largest number of children attending the
public elementary schools of Northern
Ireland-not the Presbyterians, the
Methodists, the Church of Ireland, or any
other denomination, but the Catholics,
and yet we are the people who have made
the most sacrifices for education, not only

people were too proud to interest themselves in education.
We made great sacrifices to give the
best possible education to our children,
and we are the only people whom you have
proscribed. You began with secular
education. We protested against it. It
was not very long until the Protestant
Churches were shouting too, and then you
immediately succumbed. Immediately
the Orange Order spoke you had to do
something. The Prime Minister said

So, I think it is a remarkable fact that

boundary line had been overstepped in

The PRIME MINISTER: The hon.
Member's memory is conveniently short.
The Act of 1920 gave us the power to
abolish Proportional Representation at
the end of three years. As a matter of
fact the Government here did not abolish
Proportional Representation for this
House at the end of three years. I am
ready to be corrected by anyone in the
House; I am speaking from memory,
but
what happened was this. We saw very
early on the disadvantage it was to the
people to carry on elections for either the
local authorities or Parliament under the
system of P.R. The question has been
argued ad nauseam, and I think it was a
general expression-even by people who
imagined it was the panacea for all ills
and who came round afterwards strongly
to the opinion that it did not work out as
they expected it would-" Let us get rid
of P.R."
Mr. HEALY: You got rid of P.R. all
right.
The PRIME MINISTER: It worked
out here all right possibly in isolated
cases, but taking it as a policy for the
country I say it is unworkable, it is
unfair, and full of so many objections
that really the old-fashioned British.
system of single-member constituencies is
infinitely better than any of these foreign
innovations. What happened when it was
discovered it was a bad system? We had
thought if we were to change to single
member constituencies that it would be
very difficult for anyone in carving out
seats to know how many would naturally
go to the Opposition which we always
thought should have a fair share in the
country where they represent roughly
speaking one-third of the population.
Therefore, in order to be punctilious in
the matter we not only had the original
election under P.R., which gave the
Nationalist Party, if I remember right,
twelve seats, but we actually carried out
at the end of the four years term of that
Parliament the next election under P.R.,
and for the second time this wonderfully
accurate system did work out exactly the
same as before-gave the Nationalists
eleven or twelve seats.
Mr. HEALY: Twelve.
The PRIME MINISTER: Yes, twelve.
On two occasions the Nationalists got
twelve seats. In the third election
which was held under the single member
constituency system the Nationalists got
twelve seats. How many more do they
want or how many more could they get
even if they went under Proportional
Representation? They would get exactly
the same.
Mr. HEALY: We got eleven.
The PRIME MINISTER: If you look
back all the records you will find there
were only eleven sitting in the House. I
doubt if there are twelve sitting here
to-day.
Mr. BEATTIE: There is a Republican.
The PRIME MINISTER: We do not
want any Republicans.
Mr. BEATTIE: He got a seat.
He may

have got a seat outside but not inside. I
hope we will never be troubled by them in

The county electoral divisions shall

are

Having dealt with those two points, I

those who acquiesce in the policy of the
hon. Members opposite, of endeavouring
to break down the machinery of government given to us by the British people?
Surely nothing could be clearer than that.
If a man is a Roman Catholic, if he is
fitted for the job, provided he is loyal to
the core, he has as good a chance of
appointment as anybody else; and if a
Protestant is not loyal to the core he has
no more chance than a similar Roman
Catholic.
Mr. O'NEILL: How do you test their
loyalty?
The PRIME MINISTER: There are
ways of finding that out. The hon.
Member knows just as well as I do there
are ways of discovering whether a man is
heart and soul in carrying out the intention of the Act of 1920, which was given
to the Ulster people in order to save them
from being swallowed up in a Dublin
Parliament. Therefore, it is undoubtedly
our duty and our privilege, and always
will be, to see that those appointed by
us possess the most unimpeachable loyalty
to the King and Constitution. That is
my whole object in carrying on a
Protestant Government for a Protestant
people. I repeat it in this House.
In this connection I would like to say
how gratified I am that the two hon.
Members who spoke have raised no
objections on personal grounds to any of
the appointments that have been made.
I am glad of that at any rate, because
I think it is a tribute to my right hon.
Friends and the various departments who
are appointing boards, committees, and
so on, that no one can find any exception
to the personnel of those bodies, some of
the members being paid officials and
others voluntarily carrying on the duties
as loyal citizens.
Mr. HEALY: Surely the Prime
Minister would not expect me to indulge.
in personalities.
The PRIME MINISTER: No, I
would not expect it. I am sure if the
hon. Member searches his heart he will
admit that the administration all through
is pure, clean, honest, and straight.
You cannot have more than that.
Another point I would like to make with
regard to his remarks is this. He
said that we had never considered them
in any way with regard to appointments.
Does the hon. Member bear in mind that
when we established our Administration
here one of the most important of all
appointments that could be made was
that of the police for maintaining law
and order, because without good
administration of law and order any
State is bound to collapse. We
appointed at that time a Committee of
this House, I rather think quite free
from the Government. There may be
some hon. Members here who can correct
me if I am wrong. My recollection is
that there were no Members of the Government on that Committee.
They produced a report, which is open
to any hon. Member, stating that in
their opinion the force necessary for the
preservation of law and order in Ulster
should be 3,000 police, and they said
that in view of the fact that roughly
one-third of the population were Roman
Catholics, one-third of the places in
the police should be kept open for men
of that denomination. What happened?
There, again, there was a boycott. They
were given orders they were not to join,
and very few dared to disobey those
orders, but later there was a slight revulsion of feeling and, I think, permission was given. And because in the
period in between it was found necessary
to fill up their places with others, hon.
Members opposite complain from then to
now that we have not played fair in
carrying out the recommendations of
that Committee. That is another very
false charge, and one that should not he
made, because the Government let it be
known very widely that there were these
places for them, but they said no. Very
often I have noticed, not only here but
in the Imperial House, that the
Nationalist party live, thrive, and have
their being more on grievances than on
having their grievances remedied. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
There is very little more that I can
deal with, except to refer to what is in

phraseology of the Amendment is-
"but regrets the absence of Measures
to... provide houses for the more
poorly paid working classes."
That has not been developed very much,
and I will, therefore, only make a com-

I wish to turn the attention of the
House to the acreage under flax in Northern Ireland. Up to 1900-34 years agoover 50,000 acres of flax were grown, and
that was a very valuable supply for our
local industry. We were not altogether
dependent upon the supply from abroad.
As we are all well aware, during the war
the acreage under flax was largely increased, because this was the only
area available at that time for
flax production for war material.
Russian flax was not available. Belgium
and Northern France were occupied by
the Germans, and the production of
Northern Ireland was all that was left to
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
21 NOVEMBER 1934
supply the Allies. Consequently, there
was a greatly increased acreage, and for
some years afterwards that was maintained
until Russia came into the market with
flax, which was sold at a price with which
nobody in Germany, Belgium, France,
Holland or Poland could compete. In
fact, it was sold at a less price than the
cost of production, so that our growers
were forced out of growing flax. Consequently, the acreage of flax in the whole
of Ireland fell from 60,000 in 1924 to
8,000 in 1931, and to 6,000 in 1932. In
1933 it went up again to 10,000 acres.
The governments of France, Belgium and
other Continental countries, seeing the
danger of the State being entirely dependent on foreign supplies, commenced to
subsidise their growers, and they have
continued to do so up to the present, so
that in Northern France, in Belgium, and
in other Continental countries there is still
a considerable quantity of flax grown; but
here in Northern Ireland we are dependent upon foreign countries for 90 per
cent. of our flax supplies. That is a very
dangerous position for the trade to be in.
I venture, therefore, to call the attention
of the Government to the serious state of
affairs that prevails, and to ask them what
they intend to do. This is a matter
entirely for the Minister of Agriculture.
I know perfectly well that the Minister of
Agriculture is very much interested in
pigs, and I am quite certain that he knows
all about the merits of pigs' feet. He will
soon be immersed in milk. At the same
time, I am quite certain that he should
not ignore this great question of the supply
of home-grown flax for the mills of
Northern Ireland. We alone, of all the
governments and research departments,
have produced a better class of flax fibre.
for our people to sow, and I am at a loss
to know why the Government here will
not encourage the growing of this pedigree
flax, which is the best in the world, and
which ought to be sold in sufficient quantities to enable the linen trade to be no
longer in danger in regard to its supplies.

know about that, but it certainly does
not come within the scope of this
Amendment.
Mr. CAMPBELL: The Member for
North Antrim (Sir Robert Lynn) referred to the occupying leaseholders of
business premises in Northern Ireland.
The Member for North Antrim, who
speaks with a still small voice from the
Government side, used to be much more
strident in his criticism of the Government. He is much more amenable to
reason now. I have in my mind's eye
another Member on the Government
benches who in the old days was a big
opponent of the Government, and made
many eloquent speeches vindicating the
rights of these occupying leaseholders.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: I am
afraid the hon. and learned Member is
again out of order. I can discover no
reference to leaseholders in this
Amendment.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Of course, I will
bow to your ruling. I apologise to the
House for the time I have occupied, and
I certainly hope I have not offended the
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
21 NOVEMBER 1934
feelings of the House, although I have
spoken strongly in vindication of our
position. I commend the Amendment
to your consideration.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: May I assure
my hon. and learned Friend what
he probably knows already—that during
the whole course of history the still small
voice has always been the most powerful
voice. Therefore I am glad he has
referred to mine in that term. In all
the debates I have listened to, I
have never listened to a more futile
subject than the subject we have
been discussing to-day. Indeed, I
should have thought that we would have
been more at home in the sixteenth
century than here almost in the middle
of the twentieth century, dealing with
questions of religious beliefs and
appointments, and suggesting that the
real object of the Government should be
to appoint people either because they are
Protestants or Roman Catholics. Whatever my failings may be, and they are
many, I have never a feeling of bigotry
or intolerance towards my fellow countrymen. I have always adopted the
attitude that they are just as much
entitled as I am to all their views, and
I think that is the only way a community can get along satisfactorily.
The Member for South Fermanagh has
covered an enormous piece of ground, and
if we were guilty of half the offences he has
laid to our charge, we ought not to be
allowed to have anything to do with responsible government. First, he spoke of
the Civil Service. Might I point out to
him that when this Parliament was set
up the Civil Servants who were then
in Dublin were allowed to select which
Parliament they would serve, the Parliament of Northern Ireland or the Parliament of Southern Ireland. A great many
of the hon. Member's co-religionists
elected to come here and serve, and are
serving in the Government of Northern
Ireland. The Member for South Fermanagh, and the hon. and learned
Member who has just sat down, made
great play of the fact that you must be
loyal. Would the hon. Members, in their
private capacity, appoint a man to serve
in a community or a State if he was not
loyal to that community or that State. I
put it to them that the Government is
entitled, indeed its first duty is to defend
itself, and people who are openly disloyal
to a State cannot be expected to be
appointed by that State to its service. I
say, and I am particularly anxious to say
it, that if we are to pull together better
in the future than we have done in the
past it will be well to get rid of all those
things that have caused so much friction
and trouble in the past and work together
in the interests of the community at
large.
But we cannot do that as long as hon.
Members on the other side of the House
are openly advocating the destruction of
the State for which we stand. If they
want to co-operate with us, their business
is to recognise the hard fact that Northern
Ireland has been set up as a State, and
that it is going to remain a State, and
that there is not the slightest intention in
the world of it ever being merged in the
Irish Free State. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) If hon. Members opposite
will only recognise that fact, and then sit
down to business and clear away all
religious bitterness, it will be good for
Northern Ireland, good for Protestants,
and good for Roman Catholics.
The Member for South Fermanagh
dealt with this question as if we were
terrible sinners, and the people in the
Free State were really the most tolerant
on the face of the earth. The hon. and
learned Member for Central (Mr. Campbell) also emphasised that point. May I
point out, not as a matter of controversy
but as a clear statement of fact, that in
the Free State there is not a single Protestant District Judge.
Mr. McCARROLL: That is not true.
Read to-day's Press.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Very well, I
will accept the hon. Member's statement,
because he is always very accurate with
regard to his facts, and if there is one I
am glad to know it. But when this
Parliament was set up, of the six Clerks
of the Crown and Peace in Northern
Ireland, five were Roman Catholics, and
even to-day three of them belong to the
faith of the hon. Member opposite.
Mr. HEALY: Who appointed them?
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I cannot tell you
at the moment who appointed them. I
am only pointing out that fact. Now I
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Robert Lynn]
come to a question the Member for South
Fermanagh stressed, namely, the Royal
Ulster Constabulary. As the Prime
Minister has already pointed out, the
committee that was appointed to set up
the Royal Ulster Constabulary recommended that one-third of the members of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary should be
of the Roman Catholic faith. What
happened was simply this, that owing to
the pressure of influential politicians, of
whom the Member for South Fermanagh
was one, the Roman Catholics were not
allowed to join the Royal Ulster Constabulary in 1921. They were prevented
from doing so for years afterwards, and
now that the ranks have been filled they
come along and make a grievance out of
what they have really brought into being
themselves.
Again, in Belfast they have got two
Resident Magistrates. One of them, who
happens to be a very old friend of mine,
belongs to the faith of the Member for
South Fermanagh. If we were merely
making appointments on purely religious
grounds would not a Protestant have been
appointed instead. I say that in that
particular case a very excellent man was
appointed. Therefore, I think there has
been no bigotry whatever. Further, I
would point out that as regards the Constabulary in the two greatest counties in
Ulster-Antrim and Down-the County
Inspector of Antrim and the County
Inspector of Down belong to the Roman
Catholic faith, and they are excellent
officers and loyal men who have served
their country well.
Mr. HEALY: Is it not true that
these men
were transferred from the
Royal Irish Constabulary, and you had
no choice in the matter at all.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: That is not a
fact, as I happen to know. They were
both junior officers at the time this Parliament was set up, and they were promoted.
I would also draw the hon. Member's
attention to a statement made by a
prelate to whom he pays some attention
and respect, as I hope we all do Cardinal
MacRory. He went down to Ballymena,
which is often abused in this House, to
open a Roman Catholic bazaar. In the
course of his speech he pointed out that
the success of the bazaar was due in a
large measure to the amount of support
they had got from the Protestant community. He also pointed out that during
all the troublous times in Ireland no
Catholic was ever interfered with in
Ballymena. I hope hon. Members
opposite will remember that fact when
they are inclined to abuse Ballymena, because this City of the Seven Towers has
shown a tolerance that might well be
followed by hon. Members on the other
side of the House.
Then we were told that the Free State
is a perfect Paradise. Well, I am not
going to say a single word about the Free
State except this: that while I would be
very sorry to lose some of my political
opponents and friends I would not for a
moment think of confining them in
Northern Ireland if they want to go into
the Free State. If they think it is a
better place than Northern Ireland then
the remedy is in their own hands. As
regards local government affairs, the
Member for South Fermanagh forgets to
point out that when this Parliament was
established the majority of its Nationalist
Councils simply set out to defy the
Government and make it impossible to
carry out the law. If they were suppressed it was due to their own foolishness.
There is one other point I desire to
refer to before I sit down, and that is
the question of Proportional Representation. Proportional Representation, as
the hon. and learned Member for Central
pointed out, was in operation when this
Parliament was set up, but what has been
the result of the abolition of P.R.? It is
that under single Member constituencies,
which I myself think were far the best,
the hon. Member's party has got as much
representation in this House as it had
under P.R.
Of course if the Nationalist Members in
this House go out to preach Socialism as
they do sometimes, and for political purposes save two seats to the Socialist party,
they have no right to blame us. I hope
we have heard the last of this talk about
bigotry. Let us sit down to our own
practical work. Let us eliminate as far
as humanly possible those things that
divide and separate and let each one of us
work for the good of Northern Ireland
and not for any sectarian or political
party.

Mr. LEEKE: The hon. Member (Sir
Robert Lynn) in his speech said you would

think that the penal days would be much

deprived of any representation, conveniently forgetting that the County of
Antrim had been deprived of a Nationalist representative. There is a big section

Mr. ELLIOTT: On both sides.
Mr. LEEKE: Oh, no.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Oh. yes.

Mr. LEEKE: I mean the High Court
Judges. But even the Tyrone County
Court Judge was appointed by the British
Government and not by this Government. Then you cannot defend the
Education Act as it stands, because
Catholics are penalised on account of
their religion. They will not accept the

allowed the same benefits and privileges
as Protestants.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Certainly they are.
Mr. LEEKE: That cannot be denied.
You are going further, because you are
going to penalise the schools. I know
a young priest in County Derry who today at a cost of £2 brings children to a
Catholic school because there is no school
near them. He brings 20 children to
school in the morning and leaves them
home in the evening. Is that fair? I
also heard the hon. Member for North
Antrim say it was necessary for the Government of a State to maintain law and order.
How could you maintain law when an hon.
Member comes along and apologises for
not being able to curse the Pope at
Stormont, but says that he can, thank
God, do so at a meeting in Antrim.
Mr. MINFORD: It was not the
Member for Antrim.
Mr. LEEKE: It was the Member for
Bann Side. It is not an offence for a

but if it were some poor fellow outside he

out of eleven representatives only one,

we consider that fair. To my mind, it is

always be so because you will be returned
to power.
That is because you are
Protestant and Orange. I hope that you
will see our point of view in the future
and do something. We are only demanding fair play. On the question of unemployment, there is a big industry for which.
something could be done-the fishing industry. If action had been taken in this
connection a good deal of employment
would have been afforded.
Mr. POLLOCK: Where is the market
for the fish?

Mr. LEEKE: I could get you hundreds of markets.

Mr. GAMBLE: I rise to take part in
this debate with great interest. I think
it has devolved into a debate as to the

would have expected that when such a
Amendment was tabled you would have

minority in Northern Ireland. The
mover of the Amendment travelled over a
very wide field. He began with the

the magistrates were of the faith to which

would be better than the persons appointed under the new Measure. I do not
know whether that is so or not.
A good deal of the blame lies with his

Majesty's Lieutenant for the County of

That is a word often used in connection
with Tyrone County Council and Fermanagh County Council. I happen to be a
member of the Tyrone County Council, and
we get on very agreeably. We have
people of his side of the House sitting

If he took their opinions he would

He never mentioned a word about the
amount of money which the Unionist
ratepayers pay, or of the agreement which
was entered into, under which regard was
to be had both to valuation and population. He mentioned the poulation part
and quietly left out the valuation side of
it altogether. I think that we on the
Unionist side of this House are entitled
to a little consideration for the amount
of property we hold. He talked about

It is also the case in my constituency.
There are a good many farmers of his

and who are quite satisfied to remain
in the Six Counties under the present
Government. They are not at all ready
to fly over the Border, where it is
supposed they would be received with
such open arms. I think there is no
one very anxious to get away from the

Mr. BYRNE: We on this side regret very
much that it is necessary to bring forward
such an Amendment as this. I think,
after the statements made by the hon.
Member for South Fermanagh, Members
on both sides of the House can see that
we are labouring under many grievances.
The hon. Member for North Antrim said
he would like to see this matter of bigotry
and religion wiped away.
We on this
side wish to God that they could be wiped
away. When we get justice and fair play
you will find no trouble from this side.
Many matters were mentioned to which I
would like to refer. As representing a
working-class constituency I
say the
Government have not done a lot for
housing and unemployment. Those are
great grievances that we labour under at
the present time. Thousands of people
are unemployed to-day, and in my
opinion one of the first duties of the
Government is to look after them. At
present at least 7,000 or 8,000 houses are
needed in the City of Belfast, and in some

looking for each. In my opinion the
Government should give a great deal more

subsidy for housing, building would have.
gone on and would have been an asset to

Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Byrne]
To-day a very bad state of affairs
exists in the City of Belfast. We have
thousands of people who are getting outdoor or distress relief and 90 per cent. of
them would rather be working and
earning the money they are getting. It
was a great mistake and a great financial
loss that the Government did not continue
to give the assistance they formerly gave
in order to carry out works and to give
employment to our people. You are
largely responsible for those people.
getting into bad habits, for a very large
number of them would rather be working
than drawing this money for doing
nothing. The Government have made a
great mistake in that direction, and they
should at the earliest possible moment
introduce some scheme whereby they
could get these people into work.
It is
their responsibility as well as the responsibility of the Corporation to look after
these people, and if you gave the Corporation any encouragement there are many
schemes that could be put into operation
in a very short time which would give
employment at a not very large cost. For
instance, there is the reclamation of the
foreshore in County Antrim. For not
much money you could convert that big
space of useless land into something that
might become very valuable.
As far as other matters are concerned,
it is my duty as one of those representing
the Catholic community to renew my
protest against what I consider the most
unfair and unjust action of the Government with regard to education. We have
said over and over again, and I repeat it
here on behalf of the Catholic community,
that we will never hand over our schools
to any public authority. Why continue
to penalise us? We are going to educate
our children under our bishops and our
priests. We are not going to surrender
our schools. If you want to do justice
and fair play to our people give us the
money to erect schools. In several
districts in this city our Catholic schools
are in a very bad condition, and we have
great difficulty in raising money to erect
schools. You are the biggest section of
the community, you can afford it better
than we can, and it is only just and fair
that we should get the same treatment
as is meted out to people of other
religions. You may say it is in our
power to get the full grants if we like,
but, as I say, we will never accept the
control of any public authority over our
schools. The Protestant community can
conscientiously and without any disagreement with their faith hand over their
schools and have them controlled by other
authorities, but we, as Catholics cannot
and will not hand them over. Therefore,
I renew my protest and say that it is only
right and just that you should give us
the full cost of our schools. Give us that,
give us our fair share of the appointments
you have in your power, give us a fair
share of these positions and we will not
complain, but if we do not get justice and
fair play it will be our duty as long as we
are here to make this claim on behalf of
the people we represent.

Mr. BEATTIE: I should like to ask
the Parliamentary Secretary of the
Ministry of Education a question of which
I have given him private notice, that is,
whether the 29th day of November,
which, as I understand, is to be a general
school holiday in Northern Ireland for
the purpose of celebrating a Royal
wedding, is to be an additional day outside of the 50 recognised school holidays
which the teachers of Northern Ireland
are guaranteed; and if so, does it apply
to all national teachers and other teachers
in Northern Ireland?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb):
In every
case in which the manager of the school,
with whom the decision lies, grants a
holiday on that particular day, it will be
a gift--an extra day.

Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am not yet
in a position to give the final results of

MILK FOR SCHOOL CHILDREN.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he is
aware of the following resolution passed
by the Education Authority for County
Down-"That the Ministry of Education
be asked to state whether, in conjunction
with the Ministry of Agriculture, it is
prepared to consider the framing of a
scheme for the provision of milk for
school children on the lines of the scheme
at present in operation in England," and
whether the Joint Milk Council would
undertake to operate such a scheme early
in 1935.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): My Department is at present engaged in preparing
a scheme for the supply of graded milk
to school children at a reduced rate. I
attach the greatest importance to it and
intend to introduce a scheme for this
purpose at the earliest possible moment.
As the hon. and gallant Member is
aware, the provisions of the Milk and
Milk Products Act, relating to the sale
of graded milk to the public will not
come into operation for a few weeks. I
am most anxious that the milk to be
supplied to school children shall be of
the best grade and quality procurable and
as soon as the provisions of the Act with
regard to the grading of the liquid milk
supply become operative, I shall take
steps to put into operation a scheme for
supplying school children. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

PRICE FOR FAT CATTLE.
3. Mr. CHRISTIE asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he is prepared to
fix a minimum price per cwt. to be paid
to the farmer for fat cattle which have
been passed by his inspectors at the
weighing centres; and also whether he is
satisfied that the farmers are receiving
the full benefit of the 5/- per cwt. bounty
paid by the Government.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I have no
authority to fix a minimum price per
cwt. to be paid to farmers for fat cattle,
nor would such a proposal be practicable
without similar action in Great Britain.
With regard to the latter part of the
question, I am satisfied that the beef subsidy scheme has conferred very substantial benefits on the farmers of Northern Ireland. For example, up to the
middle of November no less than 17,798
animals had been certified as eligible for
the subsidy, entitling our farmers to receive in hard cash about £40,000. As to
whether the farmers receive the full benefit of the 5/- per cwt. subsidy, this is
largely a matter in which farmers must
help themselves. The most generous
facilities have been provided to enable
all farmers to have their beef cattle certified and the subsidy paid direct to them
by cheque. If, however, farmers choose
to sell their cattle to dealers before
getting them
them certified no legislative
machinery can ensure that the whole
benefits of the subsidy accrue to them.
I would, however, point out that
average prices at sales in Northern Ireland are now practically the same as at
this time last year but, in addition, the
farmer now receives the subsidy, amounting to from £2 to £2 10s per animal.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
With regard to
to the beef subsidy
generally, I think it right to remind
the hon. Member that the general

principles on which this subsidy is
to be administered are laid down bv
the Cattle Committee for the whole of
the United Kingdom and that the
function of my Ministry is to operate

Committee, on which the Ministry is
represented.
Lieut. Colonel GORDON: May I ask is
the Minister satisfied that all the cattle
passed by his inspectors are fit for killing

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I think that

children leaving school during the twelve

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-

In the year 1933, 22,953 pupils left

number who entered outside employment
was 1,131 more in 1933 than in the previous calendar year, and the number who
were reported as being employed at home
was 287 more in 1933 than in 1932.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.

round it, and on the Northern Irish

Under Section 24 of the same Act

provided at British Government expense

paid over to this Government a sum of
£400,000 so as to enable Northern Ireland to provide itself with buildings such.
as a police depot, State
depot, State training
colleges, convict prison and agricultural
institutions equivalent to those which were
physically situated in Southern Ireland.
The greater part of this money has
already been applied to similar purposes
in Northern Ireland with the statutory
approval of this House.
There are one or two small items of
expenditure of this nature which still
remain to be settled with the Imperial
Government, totalling in all only a few
thousand pounds.

GRANT OF RELIEF TO JAMES
GLASS.
12. Mr. MIDGLEY (for Mr. Nixon)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he can state the grounds on which
the Belfast Board of Guardians refused
to grant relief to James Glass, 28 Cornea
Street; whether he would state the income
of this man's home; and whether the
refusal to grant relief is a breach of the
agreement made between the guardians
and the unemployed and approved by the
Government some years ago.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have caused
enquiries to be made into this case, and
I understand that the Board of Guardians
refused to grant outdoor relief to this
man on the ground that he was not a fit
person for such relief.
During the last ten years he has worked
on ordinary employment for about only
a year and a half. He had been for some
time on unemployment relief work under
the auspices of the Belfast Corporation,
but in May, 1932, he met with a slight
accident to his hand, which disabled him
for some time. He was placed on halfpay by the Corporation until the 23rd
June of that year and was then employed
as a watchman by the Corporation at the
rate of £2 10s a week. It is understood
that this employment ceased on the 6th
December, 1933, as he was instituting proceedings against the Corporation under
the Workman's Compensation Act.
The case was heard by the Recorder on
the 8th February, 1934, when his claim
was dismissed, the Recorder holding that,
on the evidence put before him, he had
no doubt that the injury to his hand was
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
caused by the applicant himself, and that
the condition of his arm was not due to
the accident which had occurred in 1932.
He subsequently was in receipt of
health insurance benefit and unemployment relief for certain periods, but his
case was finally disposed of by the umpire,
whose general opinion on the case, I
understand, was to the effect that the man
was more anxious to secure compensation
or benefit than to secure employment.
In the meantime he had been receiving
provisional outdoor relief from the Board
of Guardians pending the hearing of his
appeal by the umpire, but in view of the
circumstances referred to above, the
Board of Guardians decided that his was
not a proper case for outdoor relief.
The income of the family, as disclosed,
by the information accorded to me, is
17s 6d a week.
I have no jurisdiction to question the
course of action adopted by the Board of
Guardians in this particular case, and I
would once again point out that the suggestion that there is anything in the
nature of an agreement between the
Board of Guardians and any section of
the community in regard to the granting
of outdoor relief is unfounded. The
question of granting any form of relief is
entirely a matter within the discretion
of the Board of Guardians, having regard
to all the circumstances of each case
coming before them.

at a recent parade of Girl Guides to

Sir DAWSON BATES: It is incorrect
to suggest that the sergeant of police referred to ordered the lady in question not
to display the Union Jack on the particular occasion referred to.
The facts of the case are as follow:-
On the date referred to the lady in
question, in charge of a detachment of
Girl Guides, was about to proceed to a
church parade, and in order to reach the
place of parade it was necessary for her
to pass through a Roman Catholic
quarter. The sergeant of police advised
the lady that it might be better if the
Union Jack were furled while the Guides
were passing through the locality referred.
Miss Musgrave consented to adopt
this advice and there was no question of
any protection being asked for or given
on the occasion.

Sir DAWSON BATES: The expression

Rural District Council some months ago,

In this particular instance, the Coleraine Rural District Council advertised
for a properly qualified engineer to act

in another rural district in Northern

Mr. McCARROLL: When this debate
was interrupted by the adjournment of
the House last night there were just one
or two matters to which I thought it well
to refer. It occurred to me that yesterday's debate was remarkable for two
statements. One was the statement made
by the hon. and learned Member for the
University (Mr. McNeill), and the other
was that remarkable declaration by the
Prime Minister, which pinned him, and
pinned his Government, definitely down
to the position that this is a Protestant
Government for a Protestant people.
That, I think, is the most remarkable
thing disclosed in the debate, and with
your permission I propose to deal with
it a
little later. But I was rather
amazed at the attitude adopted by the
hon. and learned Member for the
University, who took occasion to attack
us, as he alleged, for the introduction

It
and continual putting forward of sectarian
questions in this House. My attitude to
that is one of more than amazement.
is one of resentment, for any imputation
against us of maintaining sectarian issues
in this House is unjustified and unfair.
I do not think it lies in the mouth of the
hon. and learned Member for the
University, or of any hon. Member on
any side of the House, to impute to us
that our purpose
here is to maintain
sectarian issues and to keep this question
of religious differences continually boiling
up and obtruding itself in our affairs
here. That is not our purpose, and if the
Government of this area kept the religious
question out I can assure you and I
think I am speaking absolutely for every
Member on this side of the House-that
we would never raise it. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Our only excuse, and
not merely our excuse, but our justification for introducing it here, is that it is
put up to us daily, and we would be the
merest poltroons if we did not face to
the situation that is presented to us by
the Government, the leader of which proclaims that this is a Protestant Government for a Protestant people.
up
The hon. and learned Member for the
University paid a tribute to my hon.
Friend (Mr. Healy) from South
Fermanagh for his interest in Celtic
tradition and in all those things which
are entirely divorced from religious feeling and animosity. We all know that my
hon. Friend has interests other than that,
and that there is nothing more repugnant
to him or to any of us, than to have to
come here to introduce the religious
question in this way. And just let me
say that no one knows better than the
hon. and learned Member for the
University that the whole tradition of
Irish nationalism is opposed to the question of sectarianism. As a matter of fact
the fathers of Irish nationalism were non-
Catholics. It was they who kept the
spirit of Irish nationalism alive, but, notwithstanding the knowledge the hon. and
learned Member for the University has of
that, he comes along and, because we are
put into the position of defending ourselves against the introduction of these
sectarian issues, he puts us into the dock,
so to speak, and says we are perpetuating
these issues and keeping them alive. Our
attitude all along has been one of protestation against and repudiation of
sectarianism. We do not want the issue
raised, and there is nothing more
grievously wrong than for the Prime
Minister or any Member of this House
to say that we depend for our political
existence on keeping this question to the
forefront in this area. Nothing of the
sort. If there is any party in Ireland
which depends for its political existence
upon the maintenance of sectarian issues
it is those who occupy the benches
opposite and not we. As I said the
leaders of Irish nationalism at all times
have repudiated sectarianism and have
stood for absolute equality for all the
people, irrespective of the altar at which
they worship.
But there is one other aspect of the
question as referred to by the hon. and
learned Member for the University which,
to my mind, rather puts him out of court
in his indictment of us.
Less than a year
has elapsed since there was an election in
the University. Although yesterday in
indicting us
he said he was an
independent, if I recollect aright he did.
not stand in that election as an independent but as an unofficial Unionist, and at
the declaration of the poll there was a
statement made by his opponent which
puts a different complexion entirely on
the position he presented to this House in
criticism of us yesterday. Dr. McSorley
was a candidate in that election, and on
the conclusion of the declaration of the

I do believe that we use wrong terms
in this House. For example, the terms
"Catholic" and "Protestant" have been
bandied about from one side of the House
to the other since yesterday afternoon.
I say that these words are not synonymous with religion. I say that any man
who acts unjustly, deals dishonourably,
or uses a foul expression towards other
people's religion, that man, no matter
what he may call himself, is not a Protestant, and is not doing Protestantism a
good service. I was brought up to worship God as the Heavenly Father of the
whole human race. I was also taught
as an integral part of my Protestantism
to respect the rights of all sections of the
community to worship God in whatever
way they liked.
We have heard during the last two
days in this House that Protestantism
means this and Catholicism means that.
I think they are wrong. What we ought
to say is that misguided people, in the
name of religious fanaticism, do things
which, if they were educated or if they
reflected upon the matter they would not
do at all. I do know that in Northern
Ireland it is quite true to say that actions
have been done, not only in the Parliamentary sphere but in the sphere of local
government, that were based upon
religious intolerance. There is not the
shadow of doubt about that. The
sooner you face up to it the better, and
the sooner you realise that you cannot
run a community on these lines the better
for all concerned.
That is what makes me a representative of the party to which I belong. I
know that so long as you proceed to

stand for-religious

The working classes are herded together
in rather worse conditions than those
others, and their mentality is not so keen.
Two or three nights after the report of
the debate appears a band goes through
a district playing a sectarian tune and a
crowd of people congregate. A sectarian
clash takes place, a number of people are
injured and grave anxiety and unrest prevails throughout the city. Surely to
goodness we want to see the end of that.
That is why I regret the aspects of this
Amendment dealing with unemployment
and housing were not stressed more than
they were in this House, when such an
unique opportunity presented itself on
the debate on the King's Speech. It
seems to me, as regards the question of
unemployment, that it is the opinion of
some Members that things are now in
a condition which would warrant them
claiming that a return of prosperity is at
hand.
I recall when I was fighting my first
Parliamentary election in 1923 in West
Belfast that the Prime Minister, who was
speaking in opposition to my candidature,
said that no matter what happened in
Great Britain he would solve the problem
in Northern Ireland. That has been repeated so often it has become objectionable. but I want to base my argument on
it. The position in regard to unemployment at that time was that we had
42,000 unemployed in Northern Ireland.
To-day, in the year 1934, we have
approximately speaking, 61,000 registered
unemployed. Why? Because of the
economic forces that are at work. We
have passed through a world crisis of
tremendous magnitude in that time. The
year 1929, which was regarded as the peak
year of prosperity, was followed by a year
which knocked the bottom out of the
thing. The man who said eleven years
ago, regardless of what happened in Great
Britain, he would solve the problem here,
was speaking without due regard to the
economic factors in affairs throughout the
world. In other words, he was claiming
to do something he could not do. It was
not because his inclination was worse than
that of any other person, and it was not
because he did not desire to see it solved,
but because it is not within the wit of
man, within certain systems or elements
in society, to solve that problem. You
have to dig deeper and get at the fundamentals.
In my hand here I have got a great
deal of collected information from Great
Britain with regard to what are known
as derelict areas. The hon. and gallant
Member (Lieut.-Colonel Gordon) referred
to an area not far from his home which
he designated as a derelict area. I had
the privilege of being there once, and I
agree with him. That is not the only
derelict area. Take Belfast, at the
present time there must be something like
35,000 registered unemployed.. Although
Belfast could not be designated a derelict
area yet, within Belfast itself, there are
sections of the population who are
becoming derelict, and that is a very big
thing from the humanitarian point of
view. What is going to be done under
the new Unemployment Act? I know
you have kindly feelings, and certain
things are going to work all right, but
that Act is not going to solve the problem
of unemployment. It was never designed
to do that.
What are you going to do from a constructive point of view in regard to unemployment? There are various phases
of activity which might be explored.
Could better use not be made of the land
than is made at the present time? I
looked
up the
census regarding the

small farmers-as there are farm

been tried in certain districts in England,

is closed against these people.

The scheme should be spread over ten,

I believe a long-term programme is

At present in the city of Belfast there

the whole of Northern Ireland. Even

employed and, later on, if it is a passenger

before the War, during the War, or even

I cannot for the life of me see what
inequities the Roman Catholics suffer
under the Education Act which they will
not adopt. If they adopt the Act they
will get exactly the same treatment as
Protestants get. Why should they
demand any preferential treatment as
compared with Protestants who will not
transfer their schools? Let them adopt
the Education Act, and they will find
they will get absolutely fair play. They
know perfectly well that no regional committee would attempt to foist a Protestant
teacher on a Roman Catholic school. To
start with, no Protestant teacher would
attempt to take employment in a Roman
Catholic school, and further, no regional
committee would ever attempt to appoint
a Protestant teacher to a Roman Catholic
school. There is no reason under heaven
why the Roman Catholic Church should
try to get preference to which we as
Protestants are not entitled. The real
difference between Roman Catholics and
Protestants is that from time immemorial

around the world at the present time
and consider the position of members of

elsewhere, they will have to admit that

places.

Debate on the Address
