HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
I am certain that those 60,000 people
are not concerned with the debate that
has taken place here to-day and yesterday.
They are more concerned with their livelihood, and they are more concerned with
an income sufficient to give decency and
comfort to their respective homes. Therefore, I am not going to enter into the
debate that has taken place on the basis
of the religious persuasion of one side of
the House or the religious persuasion of
the other side of the House. I certainly
deplore the statements made in the name
of Protestantism. Perhaps some Members of this House will say that I am not
a Protestant, being a Presbyterian.
Mr. ELLIOTT: That is the best kind
of Protestant.
Mr. BEATTIE: If you read the
history of the Presbyterian Church in
Ireland you will get something to think
about. That is all I want to say on
that subject. But I want to say that
the bigger question of unemployment is
looming in front of me to such an extent
that I feel this House is not competent
to deal with it. No matter what efforts
have been made in the past ten years,
they have not been sufficient to get back
into employment those who have been
unemployed for periods of from one year
to five, and the duty of the Government
should be to find ways and means whereby
this evil in our midst should be abolished.
I believe we have Members of the Government who are sincere when they speak on
the question of unemployment, but I
believe there are diehards also in the
Government who believe that unemployment is a necessity within this State, and
that unemployment must be maintained.
I am one of those who realise that the
two staple industries of Northern Ireland
are passing away. Shipbuilding cannot
give the continuity of employment that
it gave up to the year 1919. The linen
industry is in danger of collapsing, owing
to insufficient supplies of raw material.
If those two industries fade out of existence, then this House also fades out of
existence, and then only will you realise
that your time in this House was spent
on things that do not matter, and that
you neglected the things that do matter.
The question of unemployment, and how
to deal with it, should be the uppermost
estion throughout the whole of this
Session of Parliament. Twenty-three
thousand children left school in 1933, and
22,000 children left school in 1932. Taking
those two years together, does this House
fully realise that a very large percentage
of those young people failed to find
employment of any kind? Is that not
the experience of the rising generation?
Last year alone 40 per cent. of 23,000
children failed to find employment of any
kind; 27 per cent. found employment, and
that 27 per cent. are subject to a percentage employment until they are 16
years of age. At the age of 16 years
a certain percentage will go out of employment, not through being unfit to continue
but because they have attained an age
when the insurance payment must be
made. These figures denote a serious
aspect of the unemployment situation.
They show that with the unemployment
figure of 35,000 to 40,000 in Belfast and
with the increased figure coming from the
juvenile end we are going to have a
permanent figure of 50,000 unemployed
in this particular area. I made a suggestion years ago as to how this matter could
be dealt with. I got sympathy from the
Government side, but the sympathy was
not strong enough to compel the Government to do as I asked. I ask the Government to seriously consider what the local
authorities are doing in Great Britain.
There they are educating the parents of
the children, and making them understand that their continuance at school
until 15 is part of the solution of the
problem. It will also give an additional
year's equipment to the children, so that
they can fight the strenuous battle that
has to be met in the world's affairs. I
ask the Minister of Finance not to raise
the bogey of "This will cost more. This
will bring into employment redundant
teachers.

scales of salary may be found in the
Estimate, which is in the hands of hon.
Members.

The conditions under which many people
in this Province have to live
regrettable. Some of the homes not only
in Belfast but throughout Northern Ireland, are a disgrace to civilisation. It
is true to say that if 5,000 houses were
built in the city of Belfast to-day there
would be 5,000 people ready to occupy
them inside a fortnight or three weeks.
My contention is that the Government
have failed miserably in the way of providing houses for the working people.
The same thing applies to the agricultural
districts. The Member for Mid Antrim
(Mr. Crawford) shakes his head. I am
sure the hon. Member has gone round
all the roads in County Antrim and has
seen the old dilapidated houses with
earthenware floors and no sanitation.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Earthenware?
Mr. HENDERSON No, if they were
earthenware floors they would be sanitary
in a way, but I mean earth floors which
contain matter which is detrimental to
the health of the people. You know
what it is to live in an agricultural area.
Many of the people keep fowl in the
kitchen. I cannot understand the
mentality of the people in returning some
of the Members who sit on the opposite
side, because no attempt is made by them
to see that the people residing in agricultural areas are provided with proper
houses to live in. You do not look to the
people, and only talk to them when an
election comes on.
Mrs. PARKER: Hundreds of houses
have been provided.
Mr. HENDERSON: It is thousands
of houses that are wanted throughout the
whole area.
No one realises that better
than the hon. Lady, who represents an
agricultural area, but hon. Members are
not concerned. If they were concerned
they would demand from the Government,
for these people, the rights that they enjoy themselves. As I said, the houses in
agricultural areas are in a deplorable
condition. There is no water supply.
The people in some cases have to travel
500 or 600 yards before they get ordinary
water to satisfy nature. There is no
sanitation. I want to show that there is
ample scope for the Government to provide employment for the people. I
understand a petition has been placed
with the members of the Newtownards
Rural District Council. Even in Newtownards the condition under which the
people are living is a disgrace to
civilisation.
But I am going to speak of a seaside
resort in Northern Ireland where there
is no water supply-I refer to Millisle.
Many Members have.
gone through
Millisle when going to make speeches at
Portavogie. I want to draw attention to
what you pass when going through
Millisle. You pass a village which is
progressing very rapidly. There is an
old mill there. I have often spoken to
the Minister of Home Affairs about that
old mill. It is in rack and ruin, and is
the only dumping place the people have.
It is a bed of disease. I do not think
you could find the equal of that old mill
as far as smell is concerned in any part
of the world. It is a danger to life, and
is a menace to the health of the
inhabitants of Millisle. You know what
is thrown there, I need not tell you,
because the people have not been supplied with the ordinary sanitary conveniences you have got yourselves.
Then the only source of drinking water
is two pumps. They supply not only the
visitors who come to this very popular
seaside resort but the villagers with water.

When the Unionists controlled the

1920 they made, in spite of the cry of

Report, 22nd November, 1934, Vol.

I have here a correct list of appointments
made in County Tyrone in the year 1920
when it was controlled by the Unionist
councils. In the county of Tyrone there
were something like 63 Protestants
employed. They drew salaries amounting
to £6,800. There were nine Catholics
and they got in salaries £1,200. The
hon. Lady referred to the appointment of
the county court judge and the county
court registrar. The county court judge,
as all hon. Members know, was in those
days a British appointment, and the
county court registrar was appointed by
the county court judge. Therefore, the
fact that we had a county court judge and
a county court registrar was in no way
due to the tolerance of the Unionists who
then controlled the county council.
The hon. Member also referred to the
appointment of tuberculosis officer, and I
have a distinct recollection of what
happened on that occasion. The tuberculosis officer was appointed because he
was the only applicant who had the necessary qualifications. The same applied to
the appointment of matron of the sanatorium. I would like to point out to the
Member for South Derry that when we
got control of the county council in 1921,
not alone in this House but on several
platforms it was stated that we did not
make a single Protestant appointment.
As a matter of fact, when we got control
of the county council and any other
councils we did get control of in the
county what did we find? We found that
from the days of the Grand Jury, notwithstanding that we have a great
Catholic majority, both in population and
votes, by a system over which we had no
control these councils were controlled by
Unionists who invariably gave their
appointments to non-Catholics. When
we got control we started to level up, and
immediately we started to level up the
cry went forth of intolerance by the most
intolerant reactionaries probably in the
world, the Unionists of Tyrone. When I
read speeches from gentlemen dependent
for their livelihood on our Catholic people
in which charges are made of intolerance
I begin to think we must be very soft
people if we swallow the dope these gentlemen would like us to digest.
In the City of Belfast in 1920-that is
when the Unionists had control and
before we got control-there were 475
Protestants employed. They drew in
salaries £138,197. There were 35
Catholics employed and they drew in
salaries £6,243. Then in Derry, where
we should have control, and where, please
God, we will have control-

These figures which I have given you

Counties. This is the month in which we

those who went out to fight for what they

What is the position in my county in

sure, but there is a member of the County
Council here this afternoon and I am sure

The advertisement was issued and the
applicants came before the Council.
There was one applicant whose qualifications were equal to, if not better than, the
qualifications of any other applicant. He
was the one applicant who had gone forth
and served his King and country. When
it came to vote that applicant was turned

and the only reason he was turned down

no question or doubt about that.
The Dungannon Board of Guardians,
of which I am a member, a few years ago
advertised for a dispensary nurse for the
town of Coalisland. Coalisland has been
mentioned here in this House, but for the

exclusively Catholic centre. An advertisement was issued for a nurse for this
Catholic centre controlled by the Dungannon Board of Guardians. One of the
qualifications in the advertisement was
that, as well as maternity training, the
nurse should have general training. I
may say that I was quite agreeable to that

married woman whose husand was a bricklayer. The other application came from
a lady who resided in the district of
Coalisland. She had something like ten

thought when her application came before
the board that, in view of the protestations of loyalty, to which I am so sick
listening at all these public boards, there
would be no doubt about this lady being
appointed. I was at the board meeting.
Some time prior to that board meeting I

I leave that altogether, and now come

Guarantee Acts many ships were built in

breach. We can all see the result of the

Harland & Wolff are certainly reaping

opportunity of criticising the Government
on this question of loans guarantee. As

employment. We all realise that everything that can be done has been done, and

has not been done, simply because it has

One of the earlier speakers this afternoon mentioned that nearly every country
that used to be a customer of ours is a
competitor of ours now in some line or
other in various forms of industry. One
way in which our social system operates
at the present time to produce poverty is
this, that having reached a certain saturation point in production of goods for the
home market they begin to produce
capital goods for export. Capital goods
produced in this country for export to
another country are goods which are going
to be used for industrial capital in
another country for the manufacture of
the very things you are manufacturing in
your own country at the present time.
We know that in Belfast and the North
of Ireland-not only do we know this
but we can prove it by a Member of this
House certain firms have manufactured
capital goods for export to other countries,
and these capital goods in turn have been
used for the manufacture of certain textile
articles that were formerly the monopoly
of the Northern Ireland textile industry.
The words used by the Member for Bann
Side to-day prove that, because a fortnight ago, when I went to a textile conference and quoted all those figures, that
were quoted by the hon. Member for
Bann Side, and other statistics relating
to the linen industry, what did I find?
I found the employers themselves
argued that those very figures proved their
case that there was a diminution in trade,
because just as the export of linen piece
goods, that is linen in the piece, went up,
so the export of fancy linens and handkerchiefs diminished. The diminution of
one was pro rata to the increase of the
other. I claim, therefore, that when you
export capital goods to China, Japan, the
United States, Italy, Switzerland,
Australia, New Zealand, or any other
part of the globe, as they have been exported from Northern Ireland, and when
you find that some linen merchants in
Northern Ireland, including one who is
a Member of this House, are liquidating
capital in order to establish factories and
warehouses in other parts of the world to
exploit the cheap labour of the citizens of
those parts, you find it inexorably working out that our present social order produces poverty because it creates industries
in other countries for the satisfaction of
the physical requirements of the people
of those countries, and just as that growth
takes place in other countries there is a
diminution in productive industry here.
The reason there is diminution here is
that the industry is carried on on the
basis of profit. I claim that 99 per
cent. of the poverty which confronts
humanity to-day is inherent in the
present order of society in which you
have some people very rich, some fairly
rich, and the majority very poor. That
is what I mean by economic inequality.
I claim that because of the inevitable
working out of the industrial elements
in our present social order, we are going
to have a continuance of this economic
inequality. One of the reasons is the
development of the system itself. We do
know that the ordinary and natural
working of the present order of society
is that the workers are never paid back
as much as they produce, or they are
never paid back sufficient to purchase back
that which they produce. Hence there
is always a surplus on the market.
can
Then after the wealthiest class of the
community have done what they possibly
not only in satisfaction of their
legitimate requirements but in furtherance of their recreational and social
enjoyment, even after they have done all
they possibly can to absorb as much of

of.
In bygone days that surplus was
disposed of by Great Britain and Ireland
because of their preponderance within
the industrial system. Because they
foresaw more quickly than any other
country in Western Europe the advantage of applying steam to industry as a
motive power, because we led the way in
the industrial revolution we were practically able to control the world's markets
and to disgorge our surpluses to the far
ends of the earth. But in process of
time the facts of the industrial revolution began to be acquired by other
countries, and due to the development
of that principle, plus the coming of
the war, which augmented or accelerated
that development, we find ourselves today confronted with a situation in which

I remember the time when it was the
proud boast of the city of Belfast that

country in the world. I have

I have spoken. To-day those nations are
doing those things for themselves. China,
Japan, Italy, Switzerland, various parts

Zealand, and Australia are all to-day

which, in the first place, was operated by

Ministers. That brings another question.
Is it right for any man to have £5 a week
while another man has 35/- a week.
Should it not be a basic principle of any
civilised community to ensure that before
anyone has too much everybody should
have enough. I read from ancient literary
resources that amongst primitive communities throughout the world there is a
cardinal principle operating all the time,
and that cardinal principle is that before
one member of a primitive community can
have more than he requires at least they
endeavour to secure that every person

Christian community are in receipt of less

the whole history of mankind since mankind first stood erect on two feet. Every
other period of the world's history

of society when things are produced for
profit and not for use is wrong.
claim that before you can solve these

"That an humble Address be pre--
sented to His Grace the Governor of

Which Amendment was: At the end
to add the words: "But regrets the

Question again proposed, "That the

Mr. BEATTIE: I formally seconded
this Amendment last night, and I wish
now to present to the Government in
justification of the Amendment the
claims of that section of the community
which we on this side of the House represent. This section is one which we believe would be a great asset to the Government if they only had the power to
give that service which is necessary for
making the wheels of industry revolve
fast enough to bring into proper use all
those units which are now displaced. The
first part of the Amendmentregrets the Government's failure to
move in harmony with Great Britain
in the matter of restoring cuts enforced
by the Government in the name of
economy.
That part of the Amendment is one of
great importance to Northern Ireland as
a whole. In the year 1931 we were
called upon during what was described
as a national crisis, to make sacrifices
on behalf of the country so that we would
be able to bring the trade of the country
back to a state which would result in the
provision of work for those people who
were unemployed.
I think every section in Northern Ireland responded to that call without offering any of the criticism usually made when
cuts are asked for, but no section of the
community responded to that call with
more loyalty than the teaching pro-
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
28 NOVEMBER 1934
fession. The teaching profession entered
into an agreement on the 29th November, 1920. This is the 28th November,
1934, and it may be a coincidence that
on the 29th November, 1920, a solemn
covenant was entered into by the British
Treasury, the National Commissioners,
and the Irish National Teachers' Organisation. That solemn covenant, which
favoured the Irish national teachers,
was given over by the British Government into the custody of the Northern
Government to preserve and hold intact
in accordance with the conditions there
set out. The Northern Government
duly responded to the wishes of the
British Government in so far as that
agreement was concerned for a period of
three years.
We have heard in the
debate on the previous Amendment
reference to minority rights. I claim
that if ever a minority was imposed on,
it is the minority whom the Amendment
covers in regard to the cuts that have
taken place, although signed and sealed
documents were there to protect it.
That agreement of the 29th November,
1920, was the termination of a long
drawn out battle, a battle that lasted for
67 years, a battle that was in the forefront of the Irish National Teachers'
Organisation at every Easter congress,
and a battle that was recognised by the
Ulster Members of Parliament in the Imperial House before the establishment of
the Northern Government. Every representative in the Imperial House agreed
that the claim of the Irish national
teachers was a just one and that they
would press it on the British Government.
Then at the end of that 67 years they
got this solemn declaration, which was
signed and sealed by the British Treasury.
Yet to-day, we find it has been violated,
and not only has it been violated but the
administration has been curbed to such
an extent that the actual face value of
the reduction is not placed on the papers
which one can look upon. I claim, as
regards the last 7 per cent. taken off,
that the national crisis has now passed
away. When the cause of the cut has
passed away there is only one thing left
to do, and that is to restore into their
former position those units that were disturbed at that period.
I am proud to say that in Great Britain
they are righting that position as fast as
possible. Although the Government in
Northern Ireland have extended conditions of restoration to certain units they
have failed to live up to their obligations
to the teachers. Hence my reason for
specially mentioning their position. The
Civil Service have got a percentage on
the cost of living restored. The police
have got a percentage restored as regards
pensions. There is only one other unit
in this Province that has not been considered, and that is the unit which I am
speaking of at the moment. All those
who have followed the history relating to
the teachers' position prior to 1920 are
well aware of the struggles and trials that
the profession had to undergo. From
1920 to 1922, when the full effects of that
agreement became operative, we were all
saying that the future generation of
Northern Ireland would be in a position
to have the best equipped tutors it was
possible for any nation to possess. Those
statements of responsible persons at that
time have been borne out in actual
practice.
I believe that our education system in
the North of Ireland is one of the best,
and that its fruits will be worthy of the
efforts put forth in 1920. I do not want
anything to happen to retard the progress
of education in this Province, I want it to
get the support and assistance from the
inside of fully-equipped, mentally sound,
and contented persons, so that we will be
able to say we have done everything
possible in providing for the child all
we think necessary to equip it for the
battle of life. But I fear that if the 7
per cent. is retained we will undo the
good work carried out since the establishment of this scale. By retaining the 7
per cent. the Minister of Finance is
bringing the profession back into such a
position that the type of entrants we
require will have no incentive now to
come along and take upon themselves the
duties of teachers.
You may say that is not correct, but
as other professions provide better and
safer investments you will find that what
I am saying is actually the case. We have
patted ourselves on the back, and have
been told by responsible educationists,
and I may say by Ministers of the
Government, that the phenomenal
advance of the past ten years, as represented by palatial schools, is almost
entirely due to the sacrifices the teachers
were called upon to make. To my mind

that is a statement a responsible Minister

in Northern Ireland means that the

where is the money to
come from?
Because it was given on loan. He may

this instance. That was a loan from the

and the date for payment is now due.
We are determined to uphold the position
created by the British Treasury in 1920.
We are not unmindful of the great

to the teaching profession in Northern
Ireland, and we do hope they are not
going to destroy their good work by retaining the 73 per cent. which the teachers are
now entitled to receive.
That, in my opinion, is a short survey
of one unit in Northern Ireland that has
suffered, but there are other units. One
has had a partial restoration based on the

ask for a full restoration in their case

Ireland Civil Service. I ask the Minister
of Finance to give the same consideration to the members of the Northern Ireland Civil Service as has been given by
the British Treasury to the British Civil
Service. Those are two units that
cannot be ignored, the teachers and the
Civil Service.
Then we have the other unit, the protectors of the public, those who preserve
the peace-the police. I admitted in my

They also had a scale of salary or wages,
whichever you call it, drawn up and

it. Although perhaps one of the rejected

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I am glad to feel that the
hon. Member for Dock and I have one
aim in common at any rate. I think he
will agree that we each desire to help in
every way possible those of our fellow
countrymen who suffer from poverty and
distress, no matter how caused. There,
however, our roads cross and part. He
desires to pull up our present social
system by the roots. He wishes, somehow, some day, to reconstruct society on
a different basis altogether.
He is prepared to take a great gamble. My
colleagues and I consider it a wiser policy
to continue to pursue the much safer
course of assisting in every way possible
within the present social system those who
need help, especially where the need is
caused by unemployment, widowhood,
sickness, or old age. And I am in a
position to prove that during the last
thirteen years this Government have done
more to help in that direction than any
other Government, ably helped, as we
have been, by every Member who sits on
this side of the House. The difference
between our party and the Socialist party
is that they desire to pull down from the
top while we desire to build up from the
bottom.
In proposing this Amendment to the
Address the hon. Member for Dock spoke
for almost an hour and referred at great
length to the economic inequalities which
exist, and I think he holds the view that
labour produces all wealth. I disagree.
Brains and organising power are required
as well as hands and labour.
Mr. MIDGLEY: But those are labour.
Mr. ANDREWS: If the hon. Member
hold that those are labour then I am glad
to think that he and I agree on two
points.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Yes, that labour
creates all wealth.
Mr. ANDREWS: But there must be
inequalities, mental and physical as well
as economic, under any system, as I think
I will be able to show to-day. It was
rather strange that the hon. Member,
notwithstanding the fact that he spoke at
considerable length, never gave us any
details, or any general information even,
as to the scheme which he proposes to put
in place of our present system. Does he
agree with and does he desire to establish
the system of Socialism that was
advocated by Lord Snowden and is still
advocated by Sir Stafford Cripps, or is it

28 NOVEMBER 1934
the Socialism of Mr. Lansbury or Mr.
Maxton with which he agrees. Their
forms of Socialism differ very widely, and
I think we should like to know which of
these systems the hon. Member for Dock
supports. Again he did not say how he
proposes to establish his system or his
scheme of Socialism. Is it by revolution
and confiscation, as was done in Russia,
or is it by compensation? The hon.
Member for Dock is a rather reasonable
sort of Socialist, and possibly he would
like to pay for what he took. I observe
that the Socialist
Socialist party
party in Great
Britain are divided on this matter
at the present time. The difficulty
of Socialists is this if the Socialists
decide upon compensation it obviously
means that they are going to create
inequalities in their new system, because
the change will simply be this, that
instead of fixed assets such as mills and
factories those from whom these instruments of production are taken will receive
cash payments which they may be able to
invest in this country or which they may
have to invest in some other land.
It was
also rather strange that the hon. Member
never mentioned Russia yesterday. I
always notice that when I mention Russia
Socialists hang their heads-
Mr. MIDGLEY: Not at all.
Mr. ANDREWS- -and do not look
particularly happy. The reason is this.
I know no country to which hon. Members who believe in Socialism can point
that has been a success under a socialistic
scheme. I have read a good deal about
Socialism, and about Russia in particular,
in the last few years, and I have listened
to a large number of men who have
examined Russia on the spot I also had
the advantage a few weeks ago of talking
to a British workingman who had just
returned from Russia after working there
for a considerable time. He did not know
me, he certainly was not speaking with a
desire to please me, and I believe he was
speaking quite honestly. He seemed to
be a very intelligent, fair-minded man.
He told me that in Moscow and in
Petrograd you could see very little
difference except that most of the
churches have been turned into public
halls and boarding establishments. But,
he said, when you went to the smaller
provincial towns and to the country districts the position was simply appalling,
and the people were starving in millions.
He went further. He said that no
Russian worker ever saw the coin of the
realm, that when wages day came round
the workmen were paid by chits not on
account of the work done or the number
of hours worked, but because of the need
of the families to which they belonged.
That is quite contrary to our whole trade
union system here, because it simply
means this that two men working at the
same bench, at the same work, for the
same number of hours, in the same week,
would be paid different sums for what
they had done. I do not think that even
the Socialist Members opposite would
desire to see that system established here,
and yet it is established and is in practice
in that great country of Russia.
My view is this, that you really cannot
abolish a capitalist system. A capitalist
system must remain under any social
system. The question really is-and if I
can I want to be clear and perfectly frank
-who are to be the guardians of the
capital? Is it to be the private
individual who has been trained in
industry, who carries out the work of the
concern of which he is the head, with
which he is connected, and in which he
has a personal interest, or is it to be the
Government of the day acting for the
community at large? I have never heard
my two hon. Friends express a great deal
of confidence in any Government. They
certainly never have expressed any confidence in this Government.
Mr. MIDGLEY: That is right.
Mr. ANDREWS: They have never
expressed any degree of confidence in the
National Government.
Mr. MIDGLEY: That is right.
Mr. ANDREWS: And I really cannot
remember that they ever expressed any
confidence in the Socialist Government
when it was in power. Therefore, we
agree that in no government have they
expressed their confidence at all, and yet
the remarkable thing is that they propose
to hand over the capital of the country
to the government, whatever government
it may be. But, then, of course, what
they really aim at is to replace this
Government by a Government of themselves.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Campbell]
Let us look at one aspect of the case.
Will any man stand up as an apologist
for the existing order, if you look at
that one aspect. Think of the thousands
of children in this area of Northern Ireland and the 2,000,000 children of Great
Britain living in wretched habitations
into which no ray of sunlight ever enters
from year's end to year's end. There
are people there who live splendid
honourable lives, and we can only bow
our heads in reverence to them, because
we can realise how heroic the struggle
must be against conditions which tend
to sap, disintegrate, and destroy family
life, conditions which are absolutely inseparable from the surroundings in which
they are placed.
What has been the reaction of our own
Government to the injustices of the
social order? It can be summed up in
two words-preventably tragic. I read
some time ago of one remedy. One of
the leading Members on the opposite side
of the House said what Ulster wanted
was more drums. That will waken some
people up. Nero's fiddling while Rome
was burning affords a parallel to the
inanities of the Ministers on that point.
The peculiarity is that our own Government is becoming rapidly socialistic in
many ways itself. It is socialistic in the
control of beef, in the control of bacon,
and in the control, I think, of milk, and
soon, probably, in the control of transport. Where are you going to end?
The Minister of Labour says the way
of Socialism is the primrose path. I
very much fear he is treading that path,
and treading it with a light foot and a
lighter heart. I would ask the Minister
of Labour to remember that these results
of our social order referred to in this
Amendment, these slums, these depressed
areas, this huddling of vast masses of
people into town for the purpose of mass
production-all these things had their
genesis and origin in the industrial
revolution in this country, and the industrial revolution dates back to 1688,
the year of another revolution.
Hon.
Members know perfectly well what revolution I refer to. Since that, England

majority by the small minority.

Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
They were concerned solely with the
interests of the Province, and had their
relationship to the income and expenditure of the Province solely. The British
Government, some months after our
action, found it necessary, in the interests
of the United Kingdom, to follow the
course adopted by our Government and
Parliament here, and now that the
British Government has found that it is
in a position to restore 50 per cent. of
these cuts it does not necessarily follow
that we are under any obligation to
adopt the same course as the British
Government.
It was in the month of May, when I
presented my Budget, that this question.
came up for discussion, and that, if I
may say so incidentally, is the proper
time for such a discussion. Even if it
was my desire, or if it were necessary, I
could not restore these cuts in the middle
of the financial year. Six months have
passed since I made the statement, which
I can repeat to-day :-
"I will only go so far as to say that
the door is not shut, but that nothing
more definite can be said until next
year, when the whole matter will be
brought under careful review by the
Government."-(Official Report, 16th
May, 1934, Vol. XVI, Col. 1638.)
As I have said, six months of that
period have passed, and I have no more
information to guide me on the subject
of the restoration of these cuts than I
had then. Therefore, we will rule out
altogether an affirmative reply to the
question asked by the hon. Member for
Pottinger.
A great many statements were made in

Ulster. I do not believe, for a single
moment, that the cuts to which they were
subjected has had the slightest effect upon
the enthusiasm with which they carry on
their work for education in this Province
of Ulster.

Diseases of Animals (Dairy Cattle) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): This Bill is a natural
consequence of the Milk and Milk
Products Act which was before the House
last Session. The main purposes of the
Bill are first, to amend the existing
Animal Diseases Act so as to bring it into
conformity with the provisions of the
Milk and Milk Products Act; secondly,
to eliminate the duplication of services
which at present exist; and thirdly, to
provide the Province with an efficient
whole-time Veterinary Service, a need
which has long been clamant and which I
am now happy to think we have a unique
opportunity of meeting.
Hon. Members will remember that
under the Milk and Milk Products Act
the sale by a producer of milk for other
than manufacturing purposes is prohibited unless the producer possesses a
licence from the Ministry. Such a licence
amongst other factors can only be granted
if the cows have been inspected by the
Ministry's veterinary officers and
found to be normal healthy animals.
This provision in the Milk and Milk
Products Act has the effect of transferring
to the Ministry in respect of liquid milk
producers the duties hitherto imposed
upon the local authorities by the Dairies
and Cowsheds Order and by the Bovine
Tuberculosis Order.
are
It is agreed on all sides that these two
Orders have been largely ineffective, and
that the only real effective part of them
has been the expenditure incurred through
them. The reason has undoubtedly been
the fact that it has been necessary to
administer them through part-time local
veterinary surgeons whose main income is
derived from private practice. It followed
as a consequence that the more faithfully
they carried out the provisions of the two
Orders the more they prejudiced their
private practice. The part-time local
veterinary officers have been placed in an
impossible position. Some of them,
owing to particular circumstances, have
been able to surmount these difficulties to
a truly remarkable extent.
In many
instances the problem has been accentuated by the fact that many rural
councils consist mainly of milk producers,
who desire to hear as little as possible
about activities under the two Orders in
question, and the veterinary officers have
thus been deprived of the essential local
backing.
Inasmuch as the Ministry is now responsible for the veterinary inspection of all
cows and byres where milk is produced
for liquid consumption, the existing overlapping of services will be still further
complicated, and it is, therefore, proposed
to withdraw the Bovine Tuberculosis
Order, amend the Dairies and Cowsheds
Order, and to substitute in their place
veterinary inspection
inspection by whole-time
officers of the Ministry.
And now may I make it perfectly clear
to the House that we do not propose to
interfere in any way with the existing
powers of medical officers of health. They
will remain, as at present, the final
authority within their area as to the
suitability of the milk supply from a
public health point of view.
The withdrawal of those sections of the
Dairies and Cowsheds Order relating to
the veterinary inspection of cows and
byres would leave the producers of milk
sent to creameries or otherwise used for
manufacturing purposes free from any
type of inspection. This is clearly
undesirable, and I feel very strongly that
it is desirable that the milk which is sent
to our creameries should be produced
from sound healthy cows. The Bill,
therefore, seeks to empower the Ministry
to extend veterinary inspection to all producers of milk whether for liquid consumption or manufacturing purposes. Up
to the present time it has not been
possible to take any steps to eradicate
Diseases of Animals Bill-
Second Reading
28 NOVEMBER 1934
diseased cows and prevent the spread of
infantile tuberculosis in those rural areas
where the producer utilises his milk solely
for the purpose of consumption at home
or for the manufacture of farm butter.
This has been a great source of weakness
as clearly diseased cows tended to congregate on such farms, with obvious
unfortunate results to the health of the
community in those areas.
I feel sure that it is unnecessary to
stress the desirability of bringing such
herds under effective veterinary inspection,
and of taking all practical steps to ensure
a disease-free supply of farm butter and
butter-milk.
There is one other feature of the Bill
which calls for special comment and
that is the financial provision. I know
that many hon. Members are anxious to
avoid as far as possible the putting of
burdens on to local rates. The whole
of the reform will be carried out without any additional cost to the local
authorities as a whole. The Ministry
already has power to increase the existing d rate for animal diseases to d.
It is proposed to do so, and the Bill gives
the Ministry power to use the proceeds of
the additional d for the purposes of
veterinary inspection under the Milk and
Milk Products Act. This additional
farthing rate will yield no more than
local authorities are at present spending
on their part-time veterinary services;
and as they will be relieved of such expenditure they will clearly be involved
in no additional charge.
It has been possible to carry through
the reform without calling upon the local
authorities for any additional contribution, owing to the fact that the whole of
the extra cost involved will be borne by
the Milk Fund. Hon. Members are no
doubt aware that in England and Scotland it is proposed to place the whole of
the additional cost not only of
veterinary inspection but also of
bacteriological examination under the
Milk Scheme upon local authorities, and
I am glad to think that our proposals
will enable us to carry through this much
needed reform without placing a single
additional burden upon local authorities.
I am, moreover, happy to be able to
inform the House that in spite of the
obvious difficulties of such comprehensive reorganisation the Bill has received
all but unanimous support from the
parties concerned.
I have discussed the provisions with
the Veterinary Medical Association,
many of the members of which will lose
their part-time employment by local
authorities, and I should like to pay a
tribute to the Northern Ireland branch
of the Veterinary Medical Association
for the public spirited manner in which
they have faced the issues involved. The
Veterinary Medical Association is at one
with me in the view that if we are to
make real headway with the problem of
eradicating animal diseases, and, in particular, to maintain healthy herds of dairy
cows it can only be done by providing
a whole-time State Veterinary Service
acting under one authority and direction. In order, therefore, that the
change over may be carried into effect
with the minimum of hardship I am
arranging that the additional whole-time
veterinary officers who will be required
shall be recruited as far as possible from
the existing veterinary surgeons
in
Northern Ireland who desire to enter the
service. I have also agreed that the
present age limits for recruitment to and
retirement from the veterinary service
shall not operate in this case. Those
who remain in private practice will benefit from the withdrawal of others into
the service, and the consequent broadening of their sphere of private practice.
I have also discussed these proposals
with the county councils and with representatives of the rural and urban
councils and have their full support.
The proposals will cost the local authorities no more than they are at present
spending on part-time veterinary services and there will be an immense gain
to the Province in efficiency. The whole
of the additional cost will be borne by
the Milk Fund established under the
Milk and Milk Products Act.
I realise that in this work the Ministry has much to gain from the close and
active co-operation of local authorities.
and I am most anxious that this cooperation and help should be continued.
I, therefore, propose to arrange for the
Ministry's area veterinary officer to make
a practice of attending from time to time.
the meetings of local authorities within
his area in order that the local authorities may be kept in touch with the work
generally and may have an opportunity

be. I beg to move.

Mr. MIDGLEY: I did not expect this
matter to come on this afternoon. I was
less optimistic than some of the members
of the Government are with regard to the
facility with which business would be
done, and consequently I have more or
less been caught napping. That is not
the first time to-day, by the way. I want
to say that the closing remarks of the
Minister's speech bring me to the point
on which I wish to address the House,
and that is in regard to the attitude of
the Belfast Corporation. I can speak as a
member of the Public Health Committee
of the Belfast Corporation. I wish to
say, before going into detail with regard
to the Corporation's attitude on this
matter, that, personally, I appreciate and
approve of the principle enunciated by
the Minister as to the co-ordination
of veterinary inspection throughout
Northern Ireland. I think, generally
speaking, that principle is approved of
by the members of the Public Health
Committee and by the civic authority
generally. The public health authority
of Belfast has always carried out its
duties in regard to pure milk to a far
greater extent than any other local
authority in Northern Ireland.
I make that statement in its most
challenging fashion-that the Belfast
Public Health Committee has always
carried out its work in regard to milk
inspection more efficiently and more
thoroughly than any other local authority
in Northern Ireland. For ten years past
we have been impressing on the Government the necessity of taking this step.
We found many times in Belfast that
disease had its origin in milk which was
imported into the city. In this connection it is important to point out that out
of about 27,500 gallons of milk distributed
daily in Belfast only 2,000 gallons are
actually produced in the city-a little over
7 per cent. The bulk of the milk distributed in Belfast comes from country
districts, and invariably we have found
in cases of contaminated milk that the
origin of the disease has been in areas
outside the city, where we have every
reason to believe there was no veterinary
inspection. The Minister, in more
polished and more technical language
than it is necessary for me to employ, has
told the House why veterinary inspection
was not carried out as efficiently as it
ought to be. You cannot expect a parttime veterinary inspector in a country
district, where his clients are milk producers and where he is in business in a
private way, to be as efficient from the
public point of view as a full-time
veterinary officer. We are in the happy
position in Belfast that we have got one
of the most efficient services in the
country with regard to inspection as prescribed under the Act.
The Corporation object to the establishment of a principle for which they are
going to be asked to pay. The Corporation are going to be asked to pay at the
present time a sum equal to d. in the £
on the rates for this additional inspection.
They have pleaded for this for years, but
they did not think during that period
that when the principle was finally
established they were going to have to
pay for the establishment, in part
at any rate, of what is obviously a
State responsibility. The Belfast Corporation claim, and I think on the ground
of equity this claim is fairly well
established, that if they have exercised
their responsibilities under existing Acts
of Parliament and met all the obligations
required of them by statute, if they have
fulfilled and discharged their respon-

The average price of milk arrived at
by the Ministry under Section 11 (3) (a)
of the Milk and Milk Products Act is
the average price per gallon paid by
creameries for milk delivered at their

IMPORTS OF PIG PRODUCTS.
4. Mr. GAMBLE asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether it is a fact that
imports of pig products during the past
twelve months have already exceeded the
quota, and, if so, whether steps will be
taken to bring this matter before the
Imperial Government with a view to
strict adherence to the quota arrangement.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Imports of
bacon and hams from foreign countries
during the period 1st March (when the
present quota period commenced) until
the 23rd October, 1934, were about 7
per cent. in excess of the proportionate
part of the allocation for the period
March-December, 1934. The attention
of certain foreign Governments has, I
understand, recently been drawn to their
obligations to keep their exports of
bacon to the United Kingdom within
the prescribed limits, and I believe that
we may anticipate closer adherence to
quota allocations in the future. Since
this matter is already receiving the
attention of the Imperial Government, I
do not think the necessity arises for the
action suggested by the hon. Member in
the latter part of his question.

-
DEDUCTION BY

Mr. ELLIOTT (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Agriculture
whether he can give the House any
further information in regard to the
charge of 1/- per pig carcase which is
at present deducted by curers in respect
of each pig carcase bought by them from
producers and for the purpose of defraying the expenses of the buyer and to
ensure the buyer against loss in the event
of subsequent condemnation of the carcase, and whether there is any likelihood of this charge being reduced in the
near future.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am pleased
to be able to inform the hon. Member,
who I know is much interested in this
matter, that I have been able to make
an arrangement with the curers that the
sum of 1/- which is at present being
deducted by curers from producers in
respect of losses incurred through the
condemnation of pig carcases will be reduced to sixpence. This arrangement
will operate for the next six months,
when the whole question will again be
reviewed. The lower figure of sixpence
will apply to all pigs purchased by curers
on and after 1st December.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Agricultural Marketing (Pig Industry)
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: When the
various Bills relating to agricultural
marketing schemes were before the House
I took the opportunity of emphasising the
fact that they were, to some extent, of an
experimental character, that it was
impossible to foresee the trend of events
and the difficulties that were likely to
arise, and that, therefore, they would
require to be amended from time to time
in the light of events and the experience
gained.
The pigs and bacon marketing
schemes have been in operation for over
a year, and he would be a bold man who
would deny the great advantage it has
been to the Province as a whole, despite
the many difficulties that have been encountered. It is within the knowledge
of the House that preparations for the
inauguration of
of the pigs and bacon
marketing schemes were being made in
the early days of 1932, and I am sure it
will be of interest to the House to know
that since 1932 our population of breed-
289 Agricultural Marketing Bill— 29 NOVEMBER 1934

Second Reading
ing pigs has been increased by 102 per
cent. between June, 1932, and June of
this year. The production of Northern
Ireland pigs for curing purposes in 1932
was approximately 270,000, and for the
coming year, 1935, our production is
estimated at 542,000. I feel sure I do
not need to emphasise the great benefit
such a development has been to Northern
Ireland. The benefit is not confined to
farmers, it is one which is reflected in
many trading concerns such as the feeding
stuffs trade, the transport companies,
and general argricultural merchants.
CO-
Perhaps I can best illustrate this by an
example drawn from a farmers'
operative store which has no connection
with a creamery. I think the figures
which I am quoting can be related not
only to the Pigs Marketing Scheme but
various other marketing schemes. During
the period from October, 1933, to
October, 1934, in this particular store,
where the turnover was about £20,000 a
year, the amount has increased by no less
than £1,000. There was a profit of
something over £200. The cash in bank
and hand amounted to £1,209, which is
an increase of £240. In addition, outstanding debts show a reduction of £200,
when more credit would be expected on a
larger turnover. I am authorised to say
that 75 per cent. of the trade of this concern is done in the city of Belfast.
quote these figures as it is only right that
those Members who are not agricultural
Members should realise that when the
country is prospering we can also anticipate prosperity in the towns.
I
I have made it my business to make
enquiries as far as possible amongst agricultural and general merchants without
creating the impression that I was an
income tax enquirer and, as a result, I
find the same story-an increased business
turnover, less difficulty in collecting
accounts, and a resultant better bank
balance. Perhaps the most important
factor which has contributed to the rapid
expansion of our pig industry is the
relative stability of price to the producer.
I use the term relative because I am fully
conscious that we have not yet succeeded
in accomplishing our aim fully. But we
have gone a long way, and the producer
does at least know what he will get for his
pigs a month ahead, and is able to make
his arrangements accordingly.
The immediate reason for the Bill which
is now before you is a serious difficulty
which arose a few weeks ago and which
necessitated immediate action and protection for the future. For reasons which
I need not go into in the interests of the
smooth working of the schemes, the
Bacon Marketing Board failed to
implement its agency agreement to hand
over to the Pigs Marketing Board the
Pigs Board levies which curers had
deducted from producers. The Bacon
Board was several thousand pounds in
arrears, and it was clear that the Bacon
Marketing Board was not in a position to
control its own constituents. The outstanding levies have now been paid in
full, but I have come to the conclusion
that the machinery for collection must
be put on a secure footing, and one of
the proposals of this Bill is to make it a
statutory obligation on all licensed curers
to transmit to the Ministry all contributions or levies made by the Pigs Board,
and for the Ministry to transmit the sums
so collected to the Pigs Board. The Ministry requires no additional facilities for
this purpose, as under the Agricultural
Produce (Meat Regulation) Act, 1930,
the Ministry already collects a levy in
respect of veterinary inspection of all
pigs entering curing establishments in
Northern Ireland.
As immediate legislation was necessary
for the purpose, I am taking the opportunity thus afforded of bringing the two
schemes in line with recent developments
and of making such improvements in their
structure as experience has shown to be
necessary.
Clause 1 of the Bill transfers from the
Bacon Board to the Ministry the duty of
allocating the bacon quota to individual
curers. So far the home producer has
been allowed unlimited and uncontrolled
expansion in the home market. It is
now, however, necessary to estimate production ahead, as foreign countries must
be told in advance, and for a period of a
year, what supplies of bacon and hams
they will be permitted to send to the
United Kingdom market. It is important, therefore, that the home output,
which will allow for expansion, should be
adhered to if the market conditions are
not to be upset. It is, moreover,
essential that the increasing home production should be spread as far as practicable over the whole year and not concen-
291 Agricultural Marketing Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Sir Basil Brooke]
trated in the autumn months, leaving
shortages at other periods. This can most
readily be done by means of control of the
output of bacon.
Since the coming into operation of the
Pigs and Bacon Marketing Schemes I
have, from time to time, received representations from the Bacon Marketing
Board as to the necessity and desirability
of introducing a licensing scheme for new
bacon factories. One of the difficulties in
securing efficiency in the industry is the
large number of small curers, and it is
clearly not in the interests of the industry
or of the Province, as a whole, that there
should be unlimited expansion of curing
establishments, many of which, in the
course of time, would be operating at half
capacity or less.
It is, therefore, proposed to set up a
Pig Industry Council, consisting of three
members, nominated by each of the two
Boards, and three independent members,
nominated by myself, and one of the
duties of the Council will be to advise the
Ministry as to the licensing of new
factories and the conditions, if any, which
shall be attached to such licences.
As hon. Members are aware, the price
to the producer is a problem which has
given rise to many difficulties since the
start, and although the existing scheme.
has given a far greater measure of
stability and security than has ever
existed in the past, experience has shown.
it to be capable of considerable improvement. The Pigs Marketing Board, which
has the ultimate say with regard to prices
to the producer, has had a most difficult
and thorny problem to solve, and I should
like to pay a very sincere tribute to the
Pigs Board for the exceedingly able and
faithful manner in which they have
tackled their problems. Hon. Members
will remember the chaotic conditions
which existed in the pork markets last
year when curing establishments were
glutted and buying was limited. By
taking over the live pig trade and giving
to producers a price comparable to that
agreed upon for pork carcases, the Pigs
Board has been able to secure the orderly
marketing of many more thousands of
pigs than for the corresponding period
last year, and to secure for the producers
the maintenance of the standard price.
Although, as I have indicated, the
power to fix prices rests with the Pigs
Marketing Board, it has been the practice
of the Pigs Board to negotiate with the
Bacon Board and agree to a formula
which is subject to periodic review and
adjustment. There has been no serious.
difficulty in such negotiations but, unhave
fortunately, there
been
many
instances of individual curers and groups
of curers breaking away from the agreement.
Unfortunately the Bacon Marketing
Board has not been able to see its way
to accept the power to prosecute those of
its constituents who fail to adhere to
the price bargain. I can understand and
appreciate the reasons which make that
Board reluctant to accept and operate
the power of prosecution, but I am faced
with the position that the Bacon Board,
while making a bargain with the Pigs
Board with regard to prices, is not prepared, or able, to enforce its bargain
upon its own curer constituents.
At the same time, the Bacon Marketing Board is most anxious that it should
play a part in price determinations, and
the Bill, therefore, proposes to vest in
the Pig Industry Council, on which both
parties are represented in equal force,
together with independent members, the
duty of fixing prices for the various
grades of pigs and to give to the Ministry
the unpleasant task of prosecuting any
curer or pig producer who fails to adhere
to the price determination.
The problem of prices to the producer
is one which has given me much anxiety.
Owing to the special organisation of our
trade the standard prices to our producers have been in the neighbourhood of
10s a cwt. less than in Great Britain.
This is a position which it will not be
possible to remedy completely as long as
we are exporting pigs for curing in Great
Britain, but it is one to which the operation of the Pig Industry Council and other
factors, which are coming into play, will
bring a satisfactory solution in a short
time.
Although the two schemes have been
in force for a period of 14 months, it has
only now been possible to agree upon a
system of pig grading, and in this respect.
we are a year behind Great Britain. The
two Boards have agreed upon a grading
scheme and as to their respective contributions towards the cost and to the operating of the scheme by the Ministry. The
Bill provides for the making of this pig
293 Agricultural Marketing Bill- 29 NOVEMBER 1934

Second Reading
grading scheme compulsory and for the
powers necessary to operate it. The Bill
also provides for the compulsory grading
of bacon, but it is not the intention of
the Ministry to institute a bacon grading
scheme in the immediate future.
In moving the Second Reading of this
Bill I should like the House to know that
I have, to-day, received intimation that
it has the unanimous support of the Pigs
Marketing Board. I am conscious of the
fact that in the Pigs and Bacon Marketing Scheme we have set our hand to a big
task, on which there can be no going back.
I hope and trust that inasmuch as I have
endeavoured to meet and provide the
means of overcoming the difficulties experienced by both parties, that this
Measure, when it becomes law, will be
instrumental, not alone in consolidating
the truly remarkable expansion of our
trade which has been made, but in securing its orderly development and expansion in the future. But I shall not
hesitate to come to this House and claim
the support of all parties should circumstances make it desirable to modify or
augment the provisions already made or
proposed in this Bill. I beg to move.

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: In dealing
with the Bill now before the House I do
not propose to enter into or to discuss the
various boards, or the working of the
various boards, which already exist, that
is the Pigs Marketing Board and the
Bacon Board, nor am I in a position to

arisen between them. But I would like
to repeat what I said in seconding the
Address in Reply to the King's Speech.
I said that I hoped these boards would
not consider their actions in the nature of
an America's Cup race, and that if the
Minister of Agriculture were introducing
a Bill to deal with those boards he would
provide that both should sail in the same
ship. By that I meant that both boards
should work together for the prosperity
of the industry as a whole.
I will say no more about the boards
but will proceed to deal with the Bill.
The Bill to my mind is divided into two
distinct parts. The first part places the
bacon industry under the control of the
Government, and the second part sets up
a Pigs Industry Council. Before I deal
with the first part of the Bill I am going
to quote what was said in this House
yesterday from the Government Benches
in reply to the speech made by the hon.
Member for Dock (Mr. Midgley). The
Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews) said
this:
"Did the hon. Member for Dock want
the Government of the day to undertake to control industry?"
And then he went on to say:
"Did the hon. Member really think
that if he sat on the Government
Benches the prosperity of industry
would be furthered by a Socialistic
State or would more looms be brought
into work, more orders be created, or
more work given by Government or
State control of industry?"
I intend to apply those words to this Bill.
In Clause 1 certain powers, which this
House in setting up the pigs and bacon
schemes gave to the bacon trade, are
going to pass to the Ministry. As I said
that is State control of the bacon
industry.
Here I would like to call the attention
of the House to the fact that on the back
of this Bill there is the name of the
Minister of Commerce (Mr. Barbour). I
would ask him to listen to me while I
paraphrase this Clause as if in fact these
boards were Flax Boards and the industry
to be controlled the linen industry. It
would read like this:
"The Ministry of Agriculture shall
have power to regulate the production
of linen by determining from time to
time the quantity of linen, or of any
description thereof, which may be
produced by a licensed linen
merchant..
""
That shows how far State Control is
creeping into industry. I very much
doubt if we would see a Clause like that
in the Bill if it were to have the effect
that the linen merchants were to be controlled by the Minister of Agriculture. I
will say no more on that. I just want to
call attention plainly and clearly to the
fact that the Government have now
decided to take control and to say what
can be produced by the bacon industry,
how much a curer is to cure, what he can
cure, and so on.

The Pigs Marketing Board have been

a good demand, and we, in the Pigs

that in a short time we shall have

Northern Ireland, producing the proper
type of goods, to absorb every pig in
Northern Ireland.
We recognise that the only hope of
success for the whole scheme is to absorb
every pig produced here. Success will
only come when we are able to do that,
and when the amount of money
necessarily lost in sending pigs to the
British market is saved by the absorption
in Northern Ireland of all pigs produced
here. That will provide more employment, a fact which will please every
Member of this House. We have been
faced with a great deal of difficulty. Some
hon. Members have referred to the taking

say that I, for one, was opposed to that

now more than ever convinced that the
Pigs Marketing Board never did a better
day's work for the industry than when
they decided unanimously to take over
the live pig business. I must confess that
in taking it over we were not, perhaps,
fully alive to the fact that some of the

of pigs they did get, and perhaps we
fixed their commission too high. There
is no truth in the statement made by the
hon. and gallant Member for East Down
that it amounted to £200 a week, but we
found out that the number of pigs sent
to the Board did not warrant us paying
that particular rate of commission, and
we have accordingly taken steps whereby
that commission is reduced by at least 50
per cent., and something more.. We
learn only by experience, and I am here
to say that we, on the Pigs Marketing
Board, are doing our very best in the
interests of the industry as a whole.

When you are faced with a situation
like that, and when you find bacon curers
going out and taking from a man 6s or
7s a cwt. off his two or three pigs, is it
any wonder we come to the Ministry and
ask them to help us out of this terrible
position in which we find ourselves placed
by the bacon curers. We are glad the
Minister has listened to our appeal, and
this Bill will make it possible for us to
carry on our work in the interests of the
producers. The Member for North
Tyrone (Mr. Gamble), in stating that the
levy on pigs at the moment is 7s, was
rather misstating the facts. The present
levy on dead pigs is 4s, and the meat
inspection charge is 1s, which, I am glad,
is going to be reduced by 50 per cent.
That was a charge over which the Pigs

Marketing Board had no control whatever. If you take a levy of 4s on a pig
weighing lcwt. 3qrs. 14lbs. it represents
a price of about 54s per cwt. When the
pig producers of Northern Ireland look
across the Border and see that pigs of the
same quality and weight are only producing something like 40s to 42s per cwt. I
think they will agree that on this side of
the Border they are getting very fair
treatment. It is all very well to say
curers would not take pigs from the Free
State. We could hardly expect the curers
of Northern Ireland to pay us 57s 4d per
cwt. for our pork if they could go across
the Border and get it for 40s or 42s a cwt.
I am glad to say that through a suggestion put forward by the Pigs Marketing Board the Ministry of Agriculture
were able to induce the British Minister
of Agriculture and his colleagues in the
Cabinet to curtail the supply of Free
State pork to this side of the Border. To
those people who say the Board should be
wiped out, I would reply that I would
be prepared to wipe out the Board provided we retained all the restrictions we
have at the moment, but to wipe out the
Board without retaining the quota would
place us in a far worse position than we
are in to-day. One reason why to-day
this levy of 4s is not less is the fact that
last autumn, during the glut period,
when the Pigs Marketing Board were in
harness only a short time and had no
machinery to deal with the situation, they
were faced with an increase of pork to
the extent of about 73 per cent. Pig producers all over Northern Ireland could
get no market for their pork. These
public benefactors we hear so much about
would not take in the pork, and pig producers were at their wits' end to know
what to do with their pigs. A few
markets were cleared by the Pigs Marketing Board, and I again say "thank you"
to those bacon curers who rose to the
occasion and helped the Board to clear
those markets. But they could not do
that continuously, so on several occasions
the Pigs Marketing Board had to take
over dead pigs from different country
markets and put them in cold storage,
and they made a very heavy loss on them.
However, they paid the producers in full
and, in my opinion, it was the proper
thing to do. Then the Pigs Marketing
Board said to the curers, "Can we not
come to some arrangement with you
whereby we can indemnify you against
loss and allow you to clear the markets.'
The curers agreed to do so, with the result
that the pig industry is faced to-day with
a bill for £27,000, which the curers have
got to receive from the pig producers.
One shilling of that levy is going now to
help to raise a fund to pay that idemnity
to the curers. If the curers lost £27,000
-and I have to believe they did those
of us who reside in the country know there
are plenty of pig producers who lost
money as well. If the bacon curers lost
£27,000 during that glut period it would
be no exaggeration if I said that the pig
producers lost £27,000 too. If the
industry lost £54,000 last autumn, and
the Pigs Marketing Board this year was
able to handle the pigs and pay the
producers the full standard price, whether
they sold pigs dead or alive, with a loss
to the industry of less than 7 per cent.,
surely they did good business for the
industry when they kept in the pockets of
those engaged in it more than £40,000. I
am one of those who congratulate the
Pigs Marketing Board-and in doing so
I congratulate myself-on the way we
were able to bring the pig producers
through this glut period.
Now we are faced with other difficulties.
One difficulty is that our production is not
a level production, that we have glut
periods every autumn, and what we are
trying to do at the moment is to get our
pig producers to put on the market a
stated supply of bacon products, so that
we shall be able to ask the British Minister of Agriculture, and those associated
with him, to strictly adhere to the quotas.
We cannot expect that our pig producers
will send us in the last three months of
the year more than 33 per cent. of the
total yearly output, and we cannot expect
that the market in great Britain, which
has been open to us, will be kept open if
we do not supply it. So we decided to
make those people who produce pigs at
the time of year which causes the glut
pay a 2s levy to recoup ourselves in the
only way we, as a board, can recoup ourselves, that is, by a direct levy. We did
that in order that the people who produced pigs in the glut period would pay
for the glut that they themselves caused.
I hope that very soon after New Year's
Day we, as a Pigs Board, will be able,
not only to reduce the levy, but at least
to take off that 2s which we had to put on
to recoup
our losses. The total levy
would have been reduced by another 1s

I am sure the pig producers realise that it
is an unpleasant duty which the Pigs
Marketing Board have had to discharge,
and, except in so far as I am responsible
for these marketing schemes, it is not for
me to defend the Board, because no
defence is necessary. Although it may
appear unpleasant that the producer of
pigs has at the present moment to pay a
levy of some 5/-, the fact remains that for
every shilling he spends on levy he would
have lost three shillings if it had not been
for the action of the Pigs Marketing
Board. This is not the time to go into
the details of these levies, but the Pigs
Marketing Board have taken the only
action they could take to safeguard the
producers of this country. I feel confident that this Bill will facilitate the
general working of the scheme. As I said
at the beginning, I know that these
schemes are always subject to criticism.
Everybody can criticise them, but we

do not work I am prepared to introduce

trade shall prosper with it.

IRISH IN ELEMENTARY AND
SECONDARY SCHOOLS.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he can state the number of pupils learning Irish in elementary
schools and in secondary schools
spectively, on 31st December, 1933.
re-
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The number
of pupils of public elementary schools
who were learning Irish on 31st December, 1933, was 10,602. The number in
secondary schools is not known, but of
the 3,732 pupils whose names appeared
on the entry forms for the Secondary
School Certificate Examinations in 1934,
1,225 or 32.8 per cent.-were marked
as intending candidates in Irish.
SCALES OF TRANSITIONAL
PAYMENTS.
2. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour if he can state whether Public
Assistance Committees in the urban and
rural districts have laid down scales of
transitional payments in their areas, and,
if so, can he give details of these scales.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) The Public Assistance Committees have complete discretion in
fixing the amounts they allow to persons.
applying for transitional payments, as
long as they do not exceed the ordinary
rates of unemployment benefit and give
to applicants the benefit of the allowances
laid down by the Transitional Payments
(Determination of Need) Act, 1932.
I believe that some committees lay
down scales for the guidance of their
staffs, but, for the reason I have
mentioned, these scales are not submitted to my Department for approval,
and it is within the discretion of the
Public Assistance Committees themselves
to vary them at any time as they think
fit.
It is anticipated that transitional payments will be superseded next month by
the new Unemployment Assistance
Scheme, when Public Assistance Committees will cease to function.
ANTRIM MENTAL HOSPITAL-
TENDERS FOR COMMODITIES.
3. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware that
considerable apprehension exists in
Antrim as to the method of accepting
tenders for commodities required by the
Mental Hospital; whether it is a fact
that the principle of the lowest tender
does not necessarily apply; and whether
he will cause an investigation to be made
with a view to ascertaining the facts.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): I
have been asked by my right hon.
Friend to reply.
I have no information which would
lead me to think that any irregularities
exist in connection with the acceptance
of tenders by the Antrim Mental Hospital Committee.
The question of the acceptance of
tenders by the committee is a matter
within the discretion of the committee,
subject always to the committee being in
a position to satisfy the Local Government Auditor as to the propriety of their
action in the event of their accepting a
tender other than the lowest.

I wish to state that the public health
authority of the Borough of Belfast have
had repeated conversations with representatives of the Ministry in this connectior and they have put their point of
view forward, certainly with emphasis.
I want to say, speaking individually, that

So far as I am concerned, and I think
I speak for the majority of the Public
Health Committee, we thoroughly
approve of the principles of co-ordination
embodied in this Bill. There can be no
doubt about that. What the Public
Health Committee want to emphasise is
that for ten years they have been trying
to get the Government to embark upon
a certain policy in regard to the veterinary
inspection of milk. We have felt that
Belfast has been under a considerable
handicap and has encountered many
obstacles because of lack of proper supervision in the outside areas. I do not
want any hon. Member to imagine that
we make the claim that Belfast is 100
per cent. perfection and that all the outside authorities fall far below that, but
the truth does remain that Belfast did
more, so far as the supervision of milk
is concerned, than any other county
borough or rural or urban district in the
North of Ireland.
We set up certain services years ago,
including medical inspection and bacteriological examination, and we feel that, as
we have provided the machinery which
already is in operation, and will be
utilised by the Minister and his Department, as they recognise it is an efficient
machine, as far as Belfast is concerned
it must be used in conjunction with the
national scheme propounded in this Bill.
The Belfast Corporation, therefore,
should not be called upon to pay for the
continuance of machinery which, but for
the fact that the Corporation provided it,
would have to be provided by the Minister
and his Department under this Bill. At
the present time we are providing services
in the city of Belfast which amount
roughly to £1,143.
The yield of 1d rate under this Bill will
amount to £1,990, or in round figures
£2,000. At the present time we are expending upon this essentially national
service the sum of £1,143, made up as
follows:-In connection with the Diseases
of Animals Act, £550; in connection with
the inspection of milk shops, £93; under
the heading inspection of cowsheds, to

con-
In recent years, as proof of that, the
incidence of disease arising from contaminated or impure milk has been,
generally speaking, traced to milk supplies which came from outside Belfast.
I am only speaking from memory when
say that 80 per cent. or 85 per cent. of
the total milk consumption in the city of
Belfast comes from outside. We have
proved over a period of years that our
expenditure in regard to inspection,
bacteriological tests, and the rest of it,
has been increased as the result of the
lack of supervision and co-ordination
outside.
Having moved the Amendment I do not

manner.
As an individual corporator, I

tribute for this advanced and progressive
step which they are taking at the present
time in order to ensure for the public a
pure milk supply.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am unable to
accept this Amendment. The hon. and

which are collected and, if this is to be

There are other and equally weighty
considerations which make it impossible
for me to accept this Amendment. The
secretary of the Council must be a man of
very considerable experience and knowledge of affairs. The Council will only
meet at intervals and the post will be a
