Public Rights of Way Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I beg to move,
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time." This is a non-contentious and
necessary Bill. It has been treated as a
non-contentious matter at Westminster.
Before a similar Bill was put in the
Statute Book for England in 1932 it had
been read a Second time in the House
of Commons on five occasions and had
twice passed through all its stages in the
House of Lords. Nowhere did it meet
with opposition. Though supported by
Members of all parties, by every Government since 1907, by every law officer
during that period, and by Law Lords
in their legislative capacity it failed to
pass owing to the slow grinding of the
Parliamentary mill. The Bill deals only
with public rights of way; it is in no
way concerned with private rights. That
is a fact that should be distinctly borne
in mind.
The object of the Bill is to assimilate
the law of public rights of way to the law
of private rights of way. At present
this branch of the law is a complex
medley. It ought to be simple and
plain to the unlettered, and I submit
this Bill will put it upon a clear, intelligent and rational basis. Two classes
of rights of way exist, private and
public. A private right of way is the
right of an owner of land to pass and
repass for the purpose of his land over
the land of somebody else. A public
right of way is the right of everyone to
pass and
repass without let or hindrance
over the public highways. They are two
distinct as they are two entirely
separate and independent rights. One
is private and the other is public, and
that is a distinction that ought to be
carefully borne in mind.
A private right of way can arise only
by grant, or by long user which presumes
Rights of Way Bill-
Second Reading
4 DECEMBER 1934
grant. It never did arise by grant. By
a legal fiction the courts assumed that a
grant had been made where a private
right of way had been exercised for a
period beyond which the memory of man
ran not to the contrary. The memory of
man was fixed as not running beyond the
first years of the reign of Richard I—
the year 1189. This led to difficulty and
confusion in the courts. An Act was
passed in 1832, by which, if you could
prove that if a private right of way had been
enjoyed uninterruptedly, and as a right
for 20 years it should not be defeated
merely by proof that the right had arisen
at an earlier date. If you could prove
40 years user your right was absolute. A
public right of way was deemed to arise
from dedication to the public by the
owner of the land over which the right
of way ran. The dedication could only
be made by an absolute, out-and-out
owner.
As the law stands, there is no fixed
period of public use which is accepted as
proof of dedication. Much reliance is
put on the memory of the oldest inhabitant. This has caused no end of confusion. In one case an 18 months' user
was held sufficient to establish dedication.
In another an uninterrupted user for 85
years was of no avail, and in yet another
it was said 1,000 years user would have
to be proved in order to presume dedication. Public rights were jeopardised
often through this uncertainty.
This Bill will not, and it is not intended
to, throw open a single new right of way
in the sense of giving people leave to
walk where they are not now allowed, but
it will simplify the proof that footpaths
continuously and openly in public use for
years were, in truth, trod by the people
as of right and not merely by leave and
licence. The Bill will reduce greatly the
costs of litigating such rights. The costs
were crushing in fought-out lawsuits of
this class and inflicted an almost unbearable burden on litigants. The expense of
one such action in England not long ago
is said to have amounted to £16,000. A
score or two of witnesses, pro and con,
were not an unusual array at a trial, in
the forefront among them being octogenarians and nonogenarians, who crept to
the witness box to testify in "childish
treble" to the user of far-off days. The
oldest inhabitant was never more in
honour and request.
The Bill will make it easier for the
public to maintain existing ways, and also
easier for landowners to prevent the
acquisition of new rights of way against
their will. Clause 1 (1) provides :
Where a way, other than a way user
whereof by the public could not give
rise at common law to a presumption of
dedication, upon or over any land, has
been actually enjoyed by the public as
of right and without interruption for a
full period of twenty years, such way
shall be deemed to have been dedicated
as a highway unless there is sufficient
evidence that there was no intention
during that period to dedicate such
way, or unless during such period of
twenty years there was not at any time
any person in possession of such land
capable of dedicating such way.
Sub-section 2 of Clause 1 provides that:
Where any such way has been
enjoyed as aforesaid for a full period of
forty years, such way shall be deemed
conclusively to have been dedicated as
a highway unless there is sufficient
evidence that there was no intention
during that period to dedicate such
way.
Sub-section 3 provides that a landlord
who allows people to walk through his
grounds can put up a notice that dedication is not intended-a right he has not
now, and this will prevent a right of way
arising. I submit to the House that this
Bill, short and simple as it is, will in no
way harass landlords or trench on privacy
but will be an effective safeguard to their
interests as well as to the rights of the
public.
Clause 1 renders public use of a way
for a full period of 20 years proof of
dedication as a highway unless there is
sufficient evidence that there is no intention to dedicate, or unless during
those 20 years there was not any owner
in possession capable of dedicating such
way. After forty years use the latter
hurdle has not to be jumped and the way
is deemed conclusively to have been dedicated as a highway unless there is
sufficient evidence that there was no intention to dedicate. Subclauses (3) and
(4) of this Clause relate to notices by
owners of land and are submitted as wise
and salutary. Clause (3) relaxes the strict
rules of evidence necessary in disputes of
this kind and enables a court to look

There is no doubt that this reform,

Before the war it passed through all its
stages in the House of Lords without
ever reaching the Statute Book. It
eventually received the Royal Assent on
12th July, 1932, and came into operation
on 1st January, 1934, after a very long
and arduous passage through the two
Houses at Westminster.
From that it does not appear to be a
Measure which commanded immediate
approval even across the water. Accordingly, when one comes to examine it from
the point of view of its application here
one is naturally a little bit careful about
it. Of course, this branch of the law is
highly technical, but although it is
highly technical I think it is pretty well
understood because generations of lawyers.
have had to deal with it; and, therefore,
I should say, speaking as a lawyer, that
unless there is some very special reason
for altering the law here it would be
better to leave it as it is, and I propose
to examine the Bill upon that basis.
This English Act was passed mainly at
the instigation of societies, one especially,
which was founded for the purpose of
preserving to the public their rights of
way over feudal England.
a
There are
many Members of this House, and some

Berkshire Downs, with which I have
some personal acquaintance. Hon.
Members on both sides of the House will
be able to think of other places.
The law was in such a condition of
confusion as to the rights of the public
upon these bridle paths, especially in
modern days when the population are
going back again to walking exercises,
that these societies were established for
the purpose of preserving the rights of
the public, but that condition of affairs
is quite different from anything we have
here. When that Bill was ultimately

United Association of English County

Councils and of the Rural District

4 DECEMBER 1934
Labourers' Cottages.
Mr. LEEKE: I beg to move,
That in the opinion of this House
legislation should be introduced to
enable occupiers of labourers' cottages
to buy out their holdings by a system
of State aided payments of terminable
annuities.
I feel that there is a clamant demand
for a scheme of this kind, and that 95 per
cent. of the occupants of these cottages
are anxious, and indeed enthusiastic,
about facilities to purchase their homes.
If any agricultural representative cares to
go down to the constituency from which
he comes, and if he ascertains that there
is not this demand, then I will say I was
wrong in bringing forward this Motion.
The House will understand the importance
of keeping the people on the land. We
hear complaints everywhere about the
tendency of the people to rush from the
country to the towns, and you can help
to keep them in the rural areas by giving
them security of tenure in their homes.
After all is said and done, the agricultural labourer is equal in importance to
the farmer. Their interests are identical,
and if anything can be done to encourage
the people to stay on the land and to
acquire their own holdings it will be for
the good of Northern Ireland.
This House might usefully apply itself
to legislation of this kind instead of to
some of the legislation with which our
time has been occupied here. At the
present time the occupant of a labourer's
cottage is only a tenant at will. He can
be put out if a public body wishes to
remove him. He has no security of
tenure. If he were enabled to purchase
his own home, he would be encouraged to
do many things. He could grow more
food, he could plant trees and help to
beautify the landscape, and he would have
employment for himself and his family
when, perhaps, no other work was available. The rents in many cases at present
are too high, and the cost of repairs far
exceeds what is reasonable. If the
tenant is enabled to buy out under a
terminable land annuity scheme he would.
then have to do his own repairs, and he
would do so in a manner worthy of the
country.
""
The Minister of Finance will say,
Where is the money to come from?
That is always his first question. He was
able to find six millions for the building
of ships in Belfast. That was very useful
work, I agree, whether the money will
ever be repaid or not.
Mr. POLLOCK: We did not give any
money.
Mr. LEEKE: The Government guaranteed money. They can guarantee this
scheme. They can float a loan in London.
You have said that Ulster credit stands
very high in the London market. That
is largely due to your diplomatic finance.
As it stands high, the right hon. Gentleman will have no trouble in raising the
money to do this useful work in the rural
areas. We know that agriculture is the
paramount industry. If the Government
adopt this suggestion, they will remove
the financial responsibility from the local
bodies. That will be one advantage, and
there will be no further complaints.
There will be a lot of other objections,
I am sure, to this Motion. The Irish
Land Commission was set up to carry out
the transfer of the land from the landlords to the tenants. The same people
could control this scheme and collect the
annuities. Nobody in this House with
experience of the land question will deny
that the land legislation was the best
series of Measures passed for the benefit
of Irish farmers. The Government should
give a lead in this direction for the agricultural labourers. There are a good
many agricultural representatives in this
House, and if they do not support this
Motion they may be asked some very
awkward questions during the next few
weeks. I would suggest to the Leader of
the House that he will agree to a free
vote of the House and thereby test what
is the opinion of the agricultural representatives, clear of party politics. If they
do that I am sure they will get their eyes
opened. They could then concentrate on
working out some scheme whereby this
legislation might be passed with advantage
to the Northern Ireland agricultural
labourer. There has been very little
done for him. If he gets security of
tenure it will be some compensation and
some incentive to remain in this part of
the country. I think it is an obligation
on you people to-day to investigate the
matter. I am not going to say you are
to bring it in immediately. I want it
investigated. I do not want a commission.
I know the few commissions I have seen

Mr. CAMPBELL: I beg to second the
Motion of the hon. Member. As I was

am sure that expression of opinion will

has been the settled policy of all parties
in the State for many years to root the
farmer on the soil, and why there should
be any difference in principle with regard
to rooting the rural labourers on the soil
also. It has been a matter of public
policy that the farmers should be made

to these terminable annuities paid to the
State. That is pursuing a wise and well
considered policy, and I cannot see why
in principle the same procedure and the
same methods and the same machinery
should not be applied in the case of the
agricultural labourers. They are a
thrifty class and a law-abiding class and
they have difficulties to struggle against.
They are doing their best and they have
not fixity of tenure on the soil. They
have no real interest in the land they
cultivate.
I thoroughly approve of what has been
done in regard to the farmers, and I
cannot see why in principle there should
be any differentiation between their case
and the case of the agricultural
labourer living side by side with the
farming community. The only objection.
to my mind at the moment can be one of
money. I do not know how that may

Mr. MINFORD: I rise to support this
Motion. I think the time has now come
when the Minister responsible should give
some assurance that something will be done
by the Government to enable the farm
labourer to purchase his own house.
Speaking now as an agriculturist, we got
the benefit of the Land Purchase Act, and
I would not deny my workers the right to
participate in the benefits of a similar
Act. The life of the agricultural labourer
is a hard and a dull life, and there is
nothing makes a man so contented and
loyal as having a house and a patch of
land of his own.
Mr. MIDGLEY: It generally makes
him a Tory.
Mr. MINFORD: It makes him a good
man, at any rate. I believe that in Northern Ireland we have the very best type
of agricultural labourer, and that there
are none better anywhere. They work
hard and they work well, and I agree with
the Member for North Antrim (Sir
Robert Lynn) that from this House we
should send a message to our agricultural
labourers that we are not forgetting them.
They work pretty long hours, and it is
unfortunate that the state of agriculture
at the present time does not permit the
farmer paying his men the wages he would
like to pay them. I know that the financial difficulties will be put forward by the
Minister of Finance, but it would be
quite easy for the Minister to lengthen the
number of years over which the purchase
price was repayable. As an individual, I
like a house of my own, and I agree that
the time has arrived when we should take
steps to secure for the agricultural
labourer the cottage he lives in. In the
County of Antrim there are agricultural
labourers who have paid in rent double
the value of the house they live in.
You will find in County Antrim
cottages and plots that one could not help
feeling proud of, and when you give the
occupier of such a cottage a stake in his
country by making him the owner you
make him a satisfied and contented man.
If he has a house of his own in which to
bring up his family he is almost sure to
try to get them work in his own district.
Although farming at the moment is not a
very paying industry, yet I hope the time
is not far distant when we will see our
countryside dotted with these labourers'
cottages. It would entail no hardship on
the community if these labourers were
enabled to purchase their houses. They
were built by the local authorities, and I
am sure they would not stand in the way.
It is not beyond the power of the Ministry
of Finance to find the necessary money to
buy out these cottages. When the farmer
was enabled to buy out his land he had
not to find the money.
Where did he get

suggestion of hon. Members, and deal
with the matter in a very quiet and
sympathetic way. Indeed, nearly every
hon. Member who has spoken has at one
time in his remarks answered the Motion.
The question I would like to ask hon.
Members to consider is this: Do they
want to put an end for all time to the
beneficent and benevolent proposals in the
Labourers Acts? If the House adopted
this Resolution as it stands now, and if
legalisation was brought in to carry out
the terms of this Motion, I put it to
hon. Members that there would not ever
again be another labourer's cottage built
in Northern Ireland. Would the ratepayers in any part of Northern Ireland
build houses at a cost of, say, £250 to
£300 a house, and then make a present
to some person who had become the
occupier of one-half of that money? Dare
any member of the urban or rural council
propose anything of that sort, or dare we?
There has been a great call for more
and more labourers' cottages. Unfortunately the circumstances were such that
the Government in the last two or three
years were not able to offer to rural
district councils that practical help and
assistance that they required if they were
to build more, but I am glad to be able
to suggest the possibility of being in a
position before long to take up a scheme
of building more labourers' cottages.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I want to
assure the House that every member of
the Government is perfectly sympathetic
in so far as doing everything that lies
in their power to make the lot of the
agricultural labourer and other labourers
as comfortable as it is within their power
and means to do so, but it would be
unfair if we attempted to hold out any
hope that such a scheme as is suggested
could be favourably considered. Suggestions have been made that the Minister
of Finance could find the money. It is
not a question of the Government finding
the money in connection with this proposal. It is a pure question of the
labourer finding the money. Who is to
redeem the liability? These houses belong
to the rural district council; they do not
belong to the Government. Such money
as is got from the labourers who occupy
these houses goes in relief of the rates.
Mr. LEEKE: You say the cottages
are the property of the rural council?
Mr. HANNA: Yes.

Progress of Agricultural Marketing

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I wish to
raise the question of the manner in which
this Agricultural Marketing (Pig Industry) Bill is being rushed. When the
House adjourned on Thursday last, we
were told that the business to-day would
be the Supplementary Estimates of the
Ministry of Labour. I had in my mind
two Amendments to the Agricultural
Marketing (Pig Industry) Bill, which
took considerable consideration, and reference to other people outside who are
interested in this Bill. This morning I
had to telephone those two Amendments.
They did not appear on the Order
Paper. When I came to the House I
found that I had made a mistake in one
of those Amendments, and it had to be
altered. On the Order Paper which I
received there were various Amendments,
and there was one which I never received
at all, put down by the hon. Member for
South Tyrone, and of which I would not
have known if the hon. Member concerned
had not called my attention to it.
All this is most unfair to the private
Member who tries to do his best to bring
forward such Amendments as he considers
right and just, and it also places him at a
very grave disadvantage when he comes
forward with an Amendment which is not
on the Order Paper. The other Members
do not know what he is talking about. It
puts a Member with such an Amendment
in a very invidious position, as he has to
explain to the House the terms of his
Amendment, and very often the House
cannot follow him. I do say this is not
fair to Members who come to this House.
I had the honour to second the Address in
reply to the King's Speech, and in doing
so I referred to the fact that last Session
certain Bills were pushed through with
undue haste. Here we are back at the old
rush again. I do not want an answer from
the Government. I want the Government
to think about this. I do not know
whether it is the Chief Whip or the
Minister of Agriculture who is responsible
for this, but I do know that it places the
private Member at a very great disadvantage.
Captain DIXON: As one who has the
unfortunate responsibility of looking after
the general working of the House, I should
like to say that I fully appreciate the
remarks which the hon, and gallant
Member has made. He has my real
sympathy in this matter for I know he
takes a great deal of trouble about these
Amendments. I should like to tell him
that this is not a case either of my office
or of the Ministry of Agriculture trying
to rush the business of the House. The
fact of the matter is it is owing to the
difficulty of getting these small Bills forward to the Senate, so that they can be
got through in time for the New Year
when they actually have to come into
operation. That is the only reason for the
apparent speed with which we have had
to put these Measures through. They
are not Measures of first-class importance.
The principle of these Measures has
already been decided by the House. They
are Bills which are important, but which
deal merely with detail. I can assure the
hon. and gallant Gentleman that so far
as I can facilitate his work in this matter
I shall be only too glad to do so.

Supplementary Estimates
Mr. ELLIOTT: The purpose of the
Amendment which stands in my name is
to meet certain difficulties which have
been experienced by the Pigs Marketing
Board in carrying out their functions
under the Pigs Marketing Scheme. The
Board have found that the powers
of inspection under the Agricultural
Marketing Act, which was passed in
1933 and under which the Pigs
Marketing Scheme has been framed, are
hardly adequate to enable the Board to
carry out its functions properly.
With the object of maintaining the
price for dead pigs, the Board has recently required all live pigs of bacon
weight to be sold only to it. At present,
the Board is making a heavy loss on
purchases of these live pigs, but in this
way it is maintaining the price of dead
pigs and is preventing the dead pig price
being undercut. It may happen that in
future there will be short periods during
which live pig prices will be above the
corresponding dead pig prices,
as
occurred for a week or two last spring.
A temporary rise in the price of live
pigs may be due to exceptional circumstances and may not reflect the proper
trend of the market. If such a rise
occurred, however, many farmers might
be tempted to sell their pigs otherwise
than to the Pigs Marketing Board and
the dead pig price might be broken. As
the Minister of Agriculture has said,
however, a breach of the standard price
in an upward direction may be just as
serious and just as objectionable as a
breach of the price in downward
direction.
a
At present an officer of the Ministry
of Agriculture may enter and inspect
any land or premises used for the purpose of selling pigs, but there is
no power to enable that officer to examine
and weigh pigs found on those premises.
Since only certain classes of pigs are
required to be sold to the Pigs Marketing Board, it is clear that unless the
inspector has the right to examine and
weigh pigs which are being disposed of
it is impossible for him to decide whether
these pigs are in fact pigs which should
be sold to the Board or not.
Under Section 15, sub-section (2), of
the Act of 1933, the Ministry of Agriculture may require any person carrying
on business as a dealer in a regulated
product, which in the case of the Pigs
Marketing Scheme is, of course, pigs, to
supply returns as to his purchases and
sales of the regulated product. This subsection, however, does not at present
include auctioneers, through whose
agency a very large number of pigs are
disposed of. The Amendment which
stands in my name seeks to bring
auctioneers into the same position as
ordinary dealers in pigs and will enable
information to be obtained as to the disposal of pigs through auction yards.
The third paragraph of the proposed
New Clause extends to the additional information, which it is proposed to collect,
the same restriction on the disclosure of
that information to any unathorised person or for any unauthorised reason
applies in respect of information collected under the principal Act.
as
I trust that the Minister will be prepared to accept this Amendment, which
is desired by the Pigs Marketing Board
in order to strengthen the administrative machinery which exists for carrying
out the inmportant functions which have
been entrusted to it. I beg to move.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am prepared
to accept this New Clause.
Question put, and agreed to.
Clause, accordingly, read a Second
time, and added to the Bill.
Title agreed to.
Bill reported; as amended to be considered to-morrow.

Mr. GORDON: The net supplementary amount for which it is necessary
to ask under this Vote is a
sum of
£186,000. This is arrived at as follows:
On Sub-head A (Contribution to the Unemployment Fund) there is an estimated

Supplementary Estimates-
Unemployment Insurance
5 DECEMBER 1934
total

a net deficiency on the Vote of £186,000.
When the main Estimate for this
service was framed early this year, the
igures adopted were based on a rather
more favourable expectation of the unemployment situation than events have
proved to have warranted. The Committee will, however, realise the difficulties which confront us in framing these
Estimates. Every slackening of the
world's rate of progress causes unemployment in trades producing for export, and
a few weeks' slump in the linen industry
is enough to throw us out by thousands
of pounds.
But there are other factors as well as
trade fluctuations which have made it
necessary for me to ask for additional provision this year. Hon. Members will
recollect that in the Unemployment Act
passed last session it was provided that
the rates of unemployment benefit should
be restored to the level obtaining before
the passing of the Economy Act. This
concession was not budgeted for in our
original Estimate, and has resulted in an
added expenditure on insurance benefit
alone of approximately £100,000. Moreover, the cost of providing our Fund
with its parity proportion of the
surplus in the British Fund under the
Re-insurance Agreement, has also proved
higher than was estimated, by approximately £20,000.
In addition to the cost of restoring the
cuts in the rates of benefit, the amounts
paid out in insurance benefit have
exceeded estimate not only on account
of the expected percentage of unemployment being exceeded, but also because a
larger proportion of the cost of unemployment during the year has fallen on insurance benefit (and smaller amount
transitional payments) than was
anticipated.
on
a
These various factors taken together
make up the additional sum of £282,000,
for which I am asking under the head of
equalisation payment.
The savings of £108,000 on transitional
payments arise from two main sources.
First, the net effect of the consequential
saving on transitional payments through
a larger part of the cost of unemployment
falling on insurance benefit than was
estimated, and, secondly, owing to the
fact that we estimate that it will now be
necessary to provide for the cost of transitional payments for 48 weeks instead
of 52 during the current financial year.
This latter circumstance is the result of
the passing over to the Unemployment
Assistance Fund of the cost of allowances
to persons now entitled to transitional
payment, with effect from the second
appointed day, which will, I expect, be
the 1st of March, 1935. The four weeks'
saving referred to will, I estimate,
amount to about £55,000.
The income of the Unemployment Fund
during the year has proved higher than
estimate. This, at first sight, may seem

estimate. The apparent inconsistency

Ireland, amounting to the considerable

I feel that I ought to warn the Committee that even this Supplementary

year. However, I am hopeful that it

Motion made, and Question proposed,

defray the sum required in the year

Board, and the remuneration, salaries,
and allowances of the members, officers,
and servants of the appeal tribunals

Mr. GORDON: This Estimate is the
first of its class to be presented to Parliament. It makes provision for the charge
that will fall during the current financial
year for the salaries of the staff of the
Unemployment Assistance Board which
was established by the Unemployment
Assistance Act of 1934 to undertake the
administration, within the limits laid
down by the Act of Parliament, of the
new scheme of unemployment assistance.
Hon. Members will recollect that the
members of the Board are appointed by
His Grace the Governor, and their salaries
are borne upon the Consolidated Fund of
Northern Ireland.
This Estimate is concerned only with
the staff appointed to discharge, under
the Board's direction, the functions
allotted to the Board, and also with the cost
of the appeal tribunals established under
the Act as part of the machinery for the
determination of claims for unemployment assistance allowances. In the initial
stages of its career, the Board will be
concerned mainly with the granting of
allowances to persons within the scope of
the unemployment assistance scheme,
who satisfy certain simple statutory conwho
ditions, and
are in need of
assistance.

Mr. GORDON: If the decision of the

established under the Fifth Schedule to

Supplementary Estimates-
Unemployment Assistance
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gordon]
with the leave of the chairman, and the
statutory provisions of the scheme imply
that the cases which reach appeal
tribunals will be cases where there is
reason to doubt that there has been a
proper assessment, or where other special
circumstances exist.
When the claim for assistance has been
determined in the manner I have
indicated, the area office of the Board will
despatch to the local office of the Ministry
of Labour at which the claim was made,
and at which the claimant will have continued to register for employment, a
notice informing the manager of the
Employment Exchange of the weekly
amount of allowance which should be paid
to the claimant. The weekly payment
will continue until varied or revoked by
the Board. Changes in the applicant's
circumstances, or in the circumstances of
members of his household, will necessitate periodical re-investigations and
reviews by the Board, and as, frequently,
these alterations in circumstances will be
reported by the claimant when he attends
for payment at the local office of the
Ministry of Labour, it will be realised by
the Committee that in the day-to-day
administration of the scheme it will be
essential that the closest possible touch
should be maintained between the
Employment Exchanges and the area
offices of the Board.
The duties under the scheme which
will devolve on the Board's local staff will,
therefore, be, in general, investigation
and determination of claims, and on the
local staff of the Ministry of Labour will
fall the duties of registration of claimants,
payment of cash allowances, and placing
in employment. The Board proposes to
establish area offices at nine centres in
Northern Ireland, namely, Belfast,
Portadown, Londonderry, Ballymena,
Newry, Dungannon, Downpatrick, Coleraine and Enniskillen. Each area office
will be under the control of a manager.
He will have a staff of outdoor officers for
investigating work, and of indoor officers
to assist in the work of determination and
to discharge the usual clerical duties. The
number of staff in an area office will,
obviously, depend on the traffic with
which the office will be called on to deal.
The total number of staff in the nine
area offices of the Board is shown in
Section (2) of Sub-head A of this
Estimate. The headquarters' staff of the
Board is shown in Section (1) of Subhead A. Under the Fourth Schedule to
the Act the Board appoints such staff
and pays to them such salaries as the
Board, after consultation with the Minister of Labour and with the consent of
the Ministry of Finance, may determine.
It has been the desire of the Minister and
the desire of my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Finance-as I am sure it is
the desire also of the Committee-that the
additional staff required for this new
service should be kept at the lowest
consistent
possible figure
with the
efficiency of the service. In particular,
we have been reluctant to embark upon
large commitments for further permanent
posts until we have some experience of
the probable demands of the work. It
was, therefore, our aim to maintain at
the outset a substantial reserve of
temporary staff within which retrenchment might be effected if it should prove
necessary. I am glad to say that in
securing these ends we have had the
fullest co-operation of the Board, and the
establishment proposals contained in this
Estimate represent what all concerned
agree to be a reasonable staff provision,
having regard to the probable traffic with
which the Board will be called on to deal.
Part of the duties to be assumed by the
Board will comprise those functions which
are now discharged by public assistance
committees. These committees will go
out of existence as statutory bodies on the
first appointed day, and I should like
to take this opportunity, on behalf of the
Government, of paying a public tribute
to the ungrudging, voluntary services
they have discharged during the transitional period between the passing of the
Economy Act in 1931 and the commencement of the new scheme. As regards the
staffs now employed by those committees,
I am glad to be able to inform hon.
Members that it is the intention of the
Unemployment Assistance Board to afford
an opportunity of employment in a
temporary capacity to persons at present
in full-time employment on the work of
the public assistance committees, whom
the Board consider to be suitable.
Hon. Members will recollect that the
new unemployment assistance scheme will
come into operation in two stages. These
stages will be marked by the fixing of two
appointed days, which are to be fixed by

the Minister of Labour in a statutory
order. It is our intention that the two
appointed days in Northern Ireland
shall coincide with those in Great
Britain, and although no final dates have
yet been fixed it is probable that the first
appointed day will be the 7th of January,
1935, and that the second will be the 1st
of March, 1935. On the first appointed
day the Board takes control of the scheme
in so far as it includes within its scope
persons who are now within the transitional payments scheme. On the second
appointed day the remaining classes come
under the Board's care. The money provision contained in this Estimate takes
account of those considerations.
With regard to appeal tribunals, the
constitution of these bodies is set out in
the Fifth Schedule to the Act. They will
consist each of a chairman-
Mr. BEATTIE: What class of chairman?
Mr. GORDON: Similar to the chairman of a court of referees.
Mr. BEATTIE: A legal gentleman?
Mr. GORDON: Not necessarily.
Mr. BEATTIE: You have always had
a legal gentleman.
Mr. GORDON: Not always. They
will each consist of a chairman, to be
appointed by the Minister of Labour, and
of two other members, one of whom will
be nominated by the Board to represent
the Board, and the other chosen from a
panel of persons nominated by the Minister to represent workpeople. The chairman will be paid such remuneration as
may be fixed under the same safeguards
as apply to salaries of the Board's staff.
Definite arrangements have not yet been
made, but the remuneration of the chairman of these bodies will probably be fixed
so as to bear some relation to the fees at
present payable to chairman of courts of
referees. There is also authority in the
statute to pay travelling expenses and
compensation for loss of remunerative
time to the members of tribunals. A sum
of £500 is included in Sub-head B of the
Estimate for the fees and allowances of
chairmen and members of these bodies
during the current financial year.
The Board has been provided with an
exceedingly able secretary, interested in
work of this character, and has the assistance of a very efficient staff. I ask the
House to be moderate but helpful in their
criticism. Every person in this Committee is interested in the involuntarily
idle workman, and, I am sure, anxious
for the smooth functioning of the new
system now brought into being. I beg to
move.

MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £10 be granted to His Majesty to
defray the amount required in the year
ending 31st March, 1935, to defray the
salaries and expenses of the Ministry of
Agriculture (15 and 16 Geo. V., c. 3, s. 4
(N.I.); 16 Geo. V., c. 4 (N.I.) ).”
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The purpose of
this Supplementary Estimate is to show
the administrative cost of various new
services undertaken by the Ministry since
the original Estimate for the year was
prepared. The greater part of the
expenditure, of course, arises from the
various schemes such as the Milk Marketing and Pig Marketing schemes. The
balance represents expenditure proposed
to be incurred by the Ministry in the
capacity of agent for the British Government in the administration of the Cattle
Industry (Emergency Provisions) Act,
1934. With regard to the Milk Scheme,
it is quite obvious in a new scheme such
as has been lately introduced, and is
working satisfactorily, a large increase in
the clerical staff is necessary.
In undertaking the first part of the
scheme, which, I am glad to say, has been
in operation for some time and has given
general satisfaction, namely, the equalisation payments to creameries in respect of
the price of milk during the winter and
summer which is 6d. and 5d. respectively,
it is quite natural that a large staff is
required to audit the accounts of the
creameries and for other matters of that
sort and computing bonuses.
The Estimate also provides for the
assessment and collection of fees based
on sales of milk for the liquid market,
the determination of bonus payments to
licensed producers in respect of milk
delivered to creameries. The liquid side
of the Milk Scheme, I am glad to say,
has now the prices fixed for quality, and
an arrangement has been come to for it
to come in on 16th December. I should
like here to say that as Minister I can
only express the very greatest satisfaction
that the Board which was set up composed of representatives of producers,
consumers, and distributors, and three
members appointed by myself has been
able to come to a unanimous opinion.
Of course closely allied to the Milk
Scheme are the provisions for the inspection of cow byres and such like buildings.
That again requires an increased staff,
and I am sure the House will remember
that under the Diseases of Animals Act
which has just gone through all its stages
the veterinary services have been coordinated under the Ministry, instead of
as heretofore run by the local authorities
with part-time veterinary officers. That
entails an increase in the number of
whole-time officers, and, therefore, an
increase in the amount of money which
has to be paid to them. There is no
charge on the Northern Ireland
Exchequer, because the actual amount
will be recovered from the farthing rate
which the local authorities have heretofore been charging for the purpose of paying the part-time veterinary officer. That
extra farthing will be paid into the

arranged a rate of 5s a cwt. is paid for
animals who kill out at 52 per cent. live
weight. The actual subsidy is being disbursed directly by the Cattle Committee
set up under the Act. Of course it will
entail-it has entailed-an increase in
the veterinary officers who have to attend
for the convenience of producers at
various fairs and markets, and in view of
the fact that records have to be kept there
is an increase in the clerical staff. But
there again no charge falls on the
Exchequer, because the levy of 6d
per head on each animal will go to
defray the cost; and in the event of that
proving insufficient there is an appropriation in aid from the Cattle Fund set up
by the Imperial Government.
Finally, the only other matter which
comes under this Estimate is the question
of grading of pork. Hitherto the only
actual grading of pork has consisted in
the weight of the pig. The intention
under the new scheme, which has the
approval of the two marketing boards and
of my Ministry, is that quality should
relate to weight, and that producers who
see that the animal kills out at high
quality should get in proportion a higher
sum.
Any outlay which will be incurred
through the increase in the veterinary
staff a lot of the veterinary officers will
be carrying out duties under the Act, and
their salaries will be divided up according to the various duties they are performing-but any additional charge will be
repaid from the Pig Industry Fund.
There, again, that means that the finances
of this country will not be involved. I
am asking the House for a token Vote of
£10.
Mr. MINFORD: I rise not to criticise

staff is not too highly paid and that the
staff gives the farmers satisfaction.

MILK AND MILK PRODUCTS
BILL-COUNTY DONEGAL
REPRESENTATIONS.
1. Mr. McCARROLL asked the Minister of Agriculture whether he can state
the nature of the representations made to
his Ministry by milk vendors in County
Donegal concerning the effects of the
Milk and Milk Products Act, and the
response which these overtures elicited;
and when it is proposed to put the Act
into operation.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): I have
received representations from persons
resident in County Donegal, who at
present sell milk in Londonderry alleging that they would suffer loss if it were
made impossible for them to continue
their milk business in Londonderry.
I have informed these persons that I
have given very careful and most sympathetic consideration to their representations and have come to the conclusion
that it would be quite impracticable for
my Department to authorise the sale of
liquid milk in Northern Ireland, where
such milk had been produced upon
premises over which this Government had
no jurisdiction.
I am aware that hardship will result
in a number of cases, and regret that no
other decision is in the circumstances possible for me.
I have appointed Sunday, the 16th of
December, 1934, as the date for the
coming into operation of the provisions
of the Act relating to the sale of milk
according to the grades of quality and in
accordance with licences issued under the
Act.
COUNTY DONEGAL INHABITANTS
AND REVISION OF THE
BOUNDARY.
2. Mr. McCARROLL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether his attention
has been called to the existence of a
petition purporting to have been signed
by certain inhabitants of County Donegal praying for revision of the boundary
between the severed portions of Ulster
and the Irish Free State; if he can state
whether a copy of the petition, as transmitted to the Imperial Government, has
been received by the Government of
Northern Ireland; and, if so, what reply
has been given, or what action the Government propose to take; and whether
the document will be laid on the Table
of the House.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The Government is
not prepared to give any information on
this subject, but if the hon. Member will
furnish me with the names of any members of that section of the community
which he represents who are anxious to
emigrate to the Free State, the Government of Northern Ireland will willingly
assist in every way in its power to
arrange an exchange of holdings with
loyalists of Donegal who may wish for a
transfer to Northern Ireland. In view
of the speeches of the hon. Member and
his Parliamentary colleagues, I fully
anticipate that the number of his friends
desirous of entering the jurisdiction of
the Free State will be amply sufficient
to make room not only for the loyalists
of Donegal, but for others in the South
who would like once more to reside under
the sheltering folds of the Union Jack.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. McCARROLL: Will the right
hon. Gentleman say whether he received
the petition or not?

UNEMPLOYMENT ASSISTANCE
BOARD.
3. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the date,
or dates, upon which the Unemployment
Assistance Board will begin to function;
what is the total number of persons who
will pass under the administration of the
Board; and whether there will remain a
substantial section of the population, not
under the control of the Board, which
will be dealt with by Poor Law administration.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The Unemployment Assistance
Board was established on 7th July, 1934.
Since that date it has been engaged in
setting up the organisation necessary to
discharge the work which will fall on it
with effect from the two Appointed Days.
The first of these Appointed Days has
been provisionally fixed for 7th January,
1935, and the second Appointed Day for
the 1st March, 1935.
The persons who will come within the
scope of the Unemployment Assistance
Scheme are those between the ages of 16
and 65 who are insured under the Contributory Pensions Acts and who satisfy
the conditions laid down in Section 31 of
the Unemployment Assistance Act, 1934.
These number approximately 360,000.
It is anticipated that comparatively
few of the able-bodied industrial population will be left to be covered by the
Poor Law.

AND SHRIGLEY.
3. Mr. CHRISTIE (for Lieut.-Colonel
Gordon) asked the Minister of Labour
whether he can state the number of unemployed in Killyleagh and Shrigley due
to the Shrigley Mill being closed down
four years ago; the number of these
people who have had no work at their
trade for this period; the number who
have exhausted all benefits under the
Unemployment Insurance Acts; and the
number who have been given temporary
employment by the Killyleagh Waterworks Scheme.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The number of persons who
were thrown out of employment by the
closing of the Shrigley Mills was 440.

at their trale, while about 350 of them
have exhausted their benefit rights
under the Unemployment Insurance
Acts. Thirty-two of them have obtained
employment on the Killyleagh Water
Scheme.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Summary Jurisdiction and Criminal
Justice Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In moving the
Second Reading of this Bill, I would like
first of all to endeavour, if possible, to
remove any misunderstanding that may
exist in the minds of individuals as to
the motives which have impelled the
Government to introduce this Bill and
their intentions as embodied in the Bill.
I would like also, if possible, to allay
any feelings that may exist among members of the lay bench that this is in any
sense a personal attack by the Government on the lay magistracy as a whole.
Any individuals who may have that impression cannot fully realise what the
Government realise and what, I think,
the vast bulk of the community and the
majority of lay magistrates realise the
vital necessity of having a good judicial
system in all its branches. This Bill,
therefore, is an attempt to reform one of
its most important branches.
We have in our High Courts and in
our county courts judicial systems of
which we in Northern Ireland are justly
proud. Can we conscientiously express
the same opinion regarding our summary
jurisdiction courts courts which, though
sometimes referred to as the lower courts,
are no less important by reason of their
wider application and appeal to the "Man
in the street?"
But
When one realises that our petty
sessions system has existed in its present
form without alteration since the Act
of 1851, even the most severe critic of
the Bill must admit that in bringing
forward this scheme of reform we have
not acted either hastily or rashly.
it must be obvious to hon. Members that
a system which has been in existence for
nearly a hundred years, and which was
designed in those old days to cope with
the social condition of affairs that then
existed, cannot be regarded as suitable in
the light of modern progress and
development.
The necessity and the demand for
reform which have existed for years past
are proved by the representations which
I have received from local authorities,
from organisations representing the business community, from those organisations
which are particularly interested in
social reform, and from individual members of the public.
This House, for years past, with the
general approval of the community at
large, has again and again recognised
that the existing machinery of summary
jurisdiction is not fitted to administer
properly many of the enactments passed
by Parliament.
469 Summary Jurisdiction Bill-

11 DECEMBER 1934
Second Reading
Take, for example, the Intoxicating
Liquor Acts. At the initial stages in
our Parliamentary existence it became
necessary to amend the licensing laws,
but, having regard to the grave abuses
that had existed for years on the magisterial bench in connection with the
administration of the licensing laws, it
was speedily recognised on all sides by
those who were engaged in the trade,
by those interested in temperance and
social reform, and by the public
generally, that it would be utterly useless to bring in any amending Acts dealing with this matter unless the
administration of the Acts was handed
over to trained lawyers-men of independence, men who would administer the
law strictly on the evidence brought
forward and without regard either to
personal feelings, personal inclinations,
or to pressure by interested parties. And
so it was that this Parliament, in its
wisdom, transferred the administration
of those Acts to resident magistrates.
Similarly, take the Game Preservation
Act, the Illegitimate Children (Affiliation Order) Act, the Marketing of Eggs
Acts, the Fishery Acts, the Midwives
Act, the Street Trading Act, the Personation Act, and finally, the Motor
Acts. Here again, there was universal
support for the principle contained in
these Acts that they should be administered by resident magistrates.
May I say in passing that the principle is by no means new? It has been
long recognised in England, where
stipendiary magistrates are employed in
the London Metropolitan Area and in
other cities, and it has also for a very
considerable time been in operation in
the case of courts of quarter sessions in
county boroughs, where the recorders are
the sole judges?
Is it not somewhat astounding to find
certain members of the lay magistracy
who took an active part in bringing about
and supporting these reforms, coming forward now and complaining that the Government in promoting the present
Measure are not only insulting the
magistrates but are attempting to violate
the constitutional rights of the subject.
I cannot recall any references to the constitutional rights of the subject when the
Intoxicating Liquor Acts, and the other
Acts referred to by me, were under consideration in this House.
What has led to the change of opinion
of those who welcomed that principle?
How can it now be contended that the
logical development of that principle is
an insult and reproach to the lay bench
and a violation of the constitutional
rights of the subject? But what are the
constitutional rights of the subject that
we are now accused of violating? Is it
not the inherent right of every British
subject to have recourse to courts presided over by men skilled in law and of
strict impartiality and independence?
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
This Bill, I submit, will achieve this
object and secure for the lower or poor
man's court the same respect and confidence which 'our other courts So
deservedly enjoy to-day in Northern
Ireland. I confidently say that the
transfer of the judicial administration of
the Acts I have referred to, to resident
magistrates has given satisfaction to the
vast majority of the community.
At the same time, attacks have been
made by certain individuals on resident
magistrates, and I would, at this early
stage in my remarks, like to pay a
tribute to these gentlemen for the fearless, competent, and impartial manner in
which they have carried out their duties
since the transfer of services to the Government of Northern Ireland. These
duties are at all times onerous, often
unpleasant, and at times even dangerous.
The experience which this Province has
had of the manner in which resident
magistrates have discharged their duties
in the past should be an assurance to
the whole community that the additional
duties which will be entrusted to them
will be carried out to the satisfaction of
all, both rich and poor.
In this connection I would like to
refer to the unfounded statements that

suggesting that the principal object of
this Bill is to extend what is known as
"bureaucratic government." It has
been stated that the Home Office, as
representing the Government, regard
resident magistrates as their officials,
who, as such, are compelled to administer the law in such manner as the Ministry of Home Affairs would wish.
repudiate that suggestion in the strongest
possible manner. It is wholly unfounded. To my mind, a Minister of the
Crown who would in any way seek to

influence a resident magistrate in

Resident magistrates are appointed by
His Grace the Governor on the advice of
the Minister of Home Affairs, who is
responsible to Parliament. They are entirely independent of the Government,
and once appointed are as free from
pressure or interference on the part of
the Ministry of Home Affairs, or any
other Department of the Government, as
a judge of the High Court or county
court is. These facts are universally
understood and appreciated, and I cannot but believe that even those persons
who have made these unfounded allegations know them to have no foundation
in fact.
It is of the utmost importance that the
independence of resident magistrates
should be assured, and I am at present
considering a form of amendment to be
introduced by me during Committee
stage ensuring that they can be removable from office only with the express
approval of both Houses of Parliament.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
We have been told that the Government intends to let loose a "horde of

I have quoted only a few cases
indicative of the general feelings of representative bodies regarding the machinery
of petty sessions administration. I would
now like to give a few extracts from
representations which I have received
from public bodies regarding the necessity
for increasing the powers of summary
jurisdiction courts.
We have, in Northern Ireland, an
Association of Chambers of Commerce.
To that body are affiliated the various local
Chambers of Commerce, and, therefore,
we have a right to assume that their
opinion largely reflects the mind of the
trading community. In 1931 my right
hon. and learned Friend the Attorney-
General, and I received a deputation representing that body. In a very succinct
way they impressed on the Government the importance of increasing the
jurisdiction of summary courts in connection with such matters as the recovery
of small debts, etcetera. They also
stated that it would be advisable that
the proposed extended jurisdiction should
be confined to resident magistrates.
A similar resolution was passed by the
Portadown Chamber of Commerce, and
this was the subject of a Parliamentary
question in the House by the hon. Member for Mid Tyrone (Mr. McAleer).
The Portadown Chamber of Commerce
also urged upon the Government the
desirability of increasing the jurisdiction
of petty sessions courts in connection with
ejectment proceedings, representing that
the present system of instituting proceedings in the county court in cases above
a certain limit was both slow and
expensive and imposed a hardship on
litigants. A similar recommendation was
made by the Landlord and Tenant
Commission.
Similar representations have been made
on behalf of tenants, property owners,
and estate agents, so that, in this particular aspect of the question, there
appears to be complete unanimity as to
the desirability of extending the jurisdiction of petty sessions courts.
But apart altogether from these more
or less formal representations made by
public bodies and authorities, we have
received, from time to time, and are constantly receiving, numerous representations from individuals pointing out the
desirability and necessity of extending the
jurisdiction of summary courts in various
respects.
I think, therefore, from what I have
said, it is apparent that there has been
for some time past a deep-rooted conviction throughout the whole community in
favour of extending the jurisdiction of
our summary courts. I may say that
this conviction was shared to the fullest
extent by the Government, but it has
always been felt, as I have already
indicated, that it would be impossible to
grant further powers to the petty sessions
courts constituted as they are at present,
and that such additional powers could
only be granted simultaneously with the

reorganisation of the constitution of the
courts on the lines which this Bill proposes. In other words, if we are to
grant these additional powers they can
only be granted to magistrates fully
qualified to exercise them in every respect
that is to say, to men with practical
legal training, standing, experience, and,
last but not least, impartiality.
Therefore, in considering this important matter, we are faced with certain
alternatives. One alternative is to
restore the powers already taken away
from the lay magistrates and confer upon
them the additional powers sought to be
imposed on the petty sessions courts by
this Bill. The other alternative is to
adopt the present Measure. There is no
middle course, unless we are prepared to
acquiesce in the continuance of the existing system, considered on all sides as unsatisfactory. The present system of
divided jurisdiction has always been
recognised as a necessary makeshift. It
is illogical, inconvenient, and cumbersome, and cannot be allowed to continue.
This Parliament has now to decide in its
wisdom which is the better alternative in
the interests, not of a limited class, but
of the community at large. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
We have two magistrates' associations
in the Province holding different views on
certain matters, but apparently united in
opposing this Measure. They have
asserted that all the trouble arises from
improper appointments to the lay
magistracy, and that individuals are
appointed entirely on their political views,
but I fancy they differ in their views as
to what are suitable and proper appointments. I, on the other hand, differ from
both of them for the simple reason that it
has been the invariable rule, since the
establishment of the Government of
Northern Ireland, that all these appointments should, following the practice that
prevailed in the past, be made on
the recommendation of His Majesty's
Lieutenant for the county or city, as the
case may be. But in saying that members of the lay magistracy are recommended by His Majesty's Lieutenant for
the respective counties and cities I do not
in any sense absolve myself, if it is
necessary to do so, from my responsibility
in regard to these appointments.
After all, lay magistrates are only
human. They may be country gentlemen
owning lands, they may be manufacturers, they may be farmers, they may
be professional men, they may be storekeepers, they may be members of trade
unions, but very few of them can claim
to have any knowledge of the practice of
law, and, a whole, they cannot
possibly, by reason of that lack of legal
training, command the general confidence
of the public in dealing with complicated
and difficult cases, involving not only
questions of fact but also of law which
are now entrusted to the magisterial
bench.
as
Lay magistrates might be divided into
several categories. We have some who,
leaving out the question of their legal
qualifications, endeavour to carry out
their duties impartially and courageously,
and for the valuable services which they
have rendered to the public they are entitled to the esteem and appreciation of
the whole community.
Then we have another class-a very
large class of men who would be equally
suitable but who, for reasons best known
to themselves-it may be that they have
not the time to devote to the duties of
their office or that they do not wish to
incur the odium of giving unpopular
decisions but, whatever the cause is,
refrain from attending the bench.
I find that during the year 1933, out of
a total of 181 magistrates in the city of
Belfast, no fewer than 119-that is to
say, almost two-thirds of the whole did
not attend any of the 311 sittings of the
courts, while of the rest 29 attended
fewer than five times, 10 attended more
than five and fewer than ten times, 8
attended more than ten and fewer than
twenty-five times, while only 15-or less
than 10 per cent. of the whole-attended
more than 25 times out of a total of 311
sittings. Some of these gentlemen have
never attended since they were sworn in
many years ago.
From such statistics as I have been
able to obtain, the position in the country
is very little better. Even there I find
that at least 30 per cent. of the total
country magistrates never attend at all,
while of the remainder, a substantial percentage only attend on very rare
occasions.

There is another type of magistratethe individual, well-intentioned, who cannot realise that his duty is to administer
the law as he finds it, but who administers
the law as he thinks it should be. As a
result, he disregards the evidence and expresses disapproval of the law which he
is called upon to administer. My attention was drawn to one case in the country
in which two magistrates adjudicated and
decided to fine a bookmaker £50. They
then thought the matter over and reduced
the fine from £50 to one penny. I am
not here to say whether the betting laws
are right or wrong. My point is that
as long as there is a law on the Statute
Book magistrates are bound to carry out
the law.
Before I proceed to deal with the
additional powers, duties, and responsibilities which the Bill proposes to impose
on the petty sessions courts, I feel it
necessary to remind the House that while
under the Bill the lay magistrates will
not be called upon in future to exercise
jurisdiction in petty sessions, at the same
time it will be observed from Clause 3
of the Bill that the justices of the peace
will, in future, be entrusted with duties
of a most important character in relation
to the preservation of law and order and
the keeping of the peace.
In fact, it would not be far wrong to
say that the justices of the peace will,
in future, have entrusted to them the
duties and functions which were contemplated as being appropriate to be carried
out by them when the system was first
initiated.
in certain
It has been suggested in
quarters that the Bill proposes to deprive
justices of the peace of all their functions,
but if any Member reads the duties that
are prescribed in section (2) of Clause 3
-I do not think it necessary to read them
now he must feel convinced that in
future justices of the peace will have entrusted to them most important duties
and valuable services, while, at the same
time, they will not be called upon, as at
present, to undertake the public, onerous,
unpleasant, and even embarrassing duties
which under modern conditions more than
often involve them with their neighbours
and co-equals.
I am also considering the question of
introducing an Amendment in Committee
stage enabling the magistrates out of
petty sessions to deal with juvenile
offenders, and thereby obviating what we
are all desirous of avoiding-the exposing
of children to the criminal taint associated
with the courts.
Although many bitter things have been
said by thoughtless and interested persons
in regard to the proposals in this Bill, I
have endeavoured, and I hope succeeded,
in avoiding any unpleasant note in this
speech, but I think that the office of
justice of the peace, for reasons which I
need not enter into, has not been accorded
the respect and esteem which such a high
office should carry with it. I am satisfied
that, with the change now proposed, the
office will be sought after by men of standing and repute in the community, and I
am glad to feel that in Northern Ireland
we have always available, perhaps in a
greater degree than in many other
countries, a body of public-spirited men
and women who are prepared to give
their services, their time, their experience, and their wisdom to the service of
the community and in preservation of the
King's Peace.
I have no doubt, therefore, but that
in the fullness of time there will be
established in Northern Ireland an
eminent body of justices of the peace,
composed of men and women commanding
the highest respect in the community.
Now, I will turn to the other side of
the picture. These courts of summary
jurisdiction, as I have stated, are in the
future to be constituted by resident
magistrates sitting alone.
The qualification of resident magistrates will be that they must be either
practising barristers or practising solicitors of at least six years' standing. Hon.
Members of the House are aware that in
the old régime there was no such qualification, and possibly there was at that
time no undue necessity for legal experience and training as a necessary qualification for a resident magistrate, but
immediately after the inauguration of the
Government of Northern Ireland I
realised the growing complexities and
difficulties of summary jurisdiction, and
laid down a departmental rule that in no
circumstances should anyone be appointed
to fill the position of resident magistrate
unless he were a practising barrister or
solicitor of six years' standing at least.

This rule has been invariably observed
ever since, even though it was not a
statutory provision but only a departmental rule. However, as from the passing of this Bill, this rule will become
statutory.
Under existing conditions it is necessary
to allocate two resident magistrates to sit
and hear cases coming under certain Acts,
such as the Intoxicating Liquor Acts.
This is an expensive and cumbersome
system which the present Bill proposes to
abolish save in respect of Crimes Act and
Civil Authorities Act cases.
This provision will relieve resident magistrates
from much unnecessary duty and so
enable them to undertake the additional
responsibilities and functions which the
Bill imposes on them.
I have dwelt at very considerable
length on the subject of the reconstitution of our summary courts, mainly
because public attention has been
focussed on this aspect of the Bill and has
not appreciated the other valuable
features in the Bill regarding the
increased jurisdiction of the courts,
which, in my opinion, constitutes not the
least important part of the Bill.
I have already alluded briefly to the
necessity and origin of these provisions
in the Bill, and I will now indicate
shortly the effect of the provisions in the
Bill dealing with the increased jurisdiction proposed to be accorded to summary
jurisdiction courts. These provisions will
be found in Parts III, IV and V of the
Bill.
Part III deals with indictable offences,
and it will be observed from Clause 12
that, whereas in the past the jurisdiction.
of summary jurisdiction courts was
limited to the case of simple larceny
where the value of the property involved
did not exceed 5s, in future the summary
jurisdiction courts will be empowered to
deal with a larger variety of cases coming
within the wider definition of "larceny"
up to a property limit value of £10.
Similarly, the summary jurisdiction
courts will be empowered to deal with
indictable offences under the Malicious
Damage Act of 1861 in all cases where
the damage does not exceed £20-a substantial departure from the existing procedure, which limited the jurisdiction of
the summary jurisdiction courts to cases
involving damage not exceeding £5.
It would not be out of place for me at
this stage to state that the principles embodied in this Clause have been in operation for many years in England. These
proposals in effect will avoid the necessity
for sending forward for trial to the High
Court and County Court persons charged
with these offences, provided they have
expressed their willingness to be dealt
with summarily. What is equally
important is that it will ensure for the
accused persons a prompt and inexpensive
trial. It sometimes happens that poor
persons charged with such offences cannot get bail, and it is essential that as
far as possible the trials of custody cases
should be expedited.
In this connection, also, I think it
right to point out that we are not only
preserving the right of appeal to the
county court judge, so far as it existsand it exists to a limited extent only
--but we are going further. Under the
Bill it is proposed to extend the right of
appeal to all cases, but I would like to
emphasise the fact that the Bill does not
confer any fresh right of appeal on the
Crown.
Where a right of appeal exists to-day
the procedure is very complicated, and
under the Bill we have endeavoured to
cheapen and simplify the procedure by
having one common form regardless of
the Act under which the proceedings may
have been taken.
Surely these extended rights of appeal
should once and for all end the scandalous
suggestion that one of the objects of the
Bill is to secure Governmental or Departmental control of the petty sessions
courts.
The new provisions regarding ejectments will be found in Part IV of the
Bill. I have already referred to the
representations which have been made to
the Government from all sections of the
community for amendment of the law in
this respect, with the object of simplifying and cheapening the procedure and
avoiding the delays and consequent hardship on litigants which the present system
necessarily involves.
The provisions incorporated in the Bill
follow closely the recommendations in
this respect made by the Departmental
Committee on the law of landlord and
tenant.

At present, the principal statute under
which action is taken in such cases is the
Summary Jurisdiction Act of 1851, which
deals with houses let on a basis not
exceeding a monthly tenancy, at rents not
exceeding £1 a month. There is also the
procedure prescribed by the Cottier
Tenant Act of 1856, which applies to
certain premises where the rent is not
more than 12s. a month, and finally,
there is the procedure under the Landlord
and Tenant Act, 1860, which applies to
certain premises where the rent does not
exceed £5 per annum.
The Bill repeals the above provisions
and prescribes a common procedure
applying to cases where the rent does not
exceed £26 a year in the case of houses
and premises held under monthly or
shorter tenancies. It is hoped that this
provision will prove to be expeditious,
convenient, and economical to all parties.
As the law now stands, courts of
summary jurisdiction in ejectment cases
have no discretion in connection with
suspending the execution of warrants and
postponing the dates on which possession
of houses is to be given. This Bill confers
these rights on the courts and removes
what I regard as a hardship, especially on
the working classes.
Part V of the Bill deals with the
summary recovery of debts, and has been
included with the object of meeting the
representations which I have already
referred to. Under existing conditions,
the jurisdiction of the summary jurisdiction courts in respect of the recovery of
debts is limited to cases where the amount
involved does not exceed £2. This jurisdiction is conferred by the Manor Courts
Abolition Act, 1859, an Act which is
more popularly known as the Small Debts
Act, and hon. Members will appreciate
that a Measure passed in 1859 dealing
with the recovery of debts is not suited
to modern economic conditions.
The Bill repeals the Act of 1859 and
re-enacts its provisions in an improved.
form with the important addition that
the jurisdiction of the petty sessions
courts will in future extend to cases where
the amount involved is not more than £5.
This provision will be welcomed by all
classes of the community.
Part VI of the Bill relates to appeals
to quarter sessions, and in this connection
I have already explained that under the
new régime a common form of appeal will
be prescribed to meet all cases.
Part VII of the Bill brings the law in
Northern Ireland generally into line with
that which obtains in Great Britain in
connection with cases stated by courts of
quarter sessions on appeal from summary
jurisdiction courts.
At the present time such rights as do
exist are of such a complicated nature as
to be in effect inoperative, the result
being that litigants in cases originating
in summary courts cannot, without
involving themselves in expensive litigation, obtain the benefit of the opinion of
the High Court on matters which, however trivial they may appear, are
regarded by the parties as of vital
importance.
The only point of interest in Part VIII
to which I wish to draw attention at the
moment is the provision which enables a
summons to be served and a warrant to
be executed anywhere in Northern Ireland. As the House is aware, under
existing conditions the summons issued
in a county can only be served in that
county or an adjoining county, and it is
obvious that under modern conditions
this mode of procedure is unsuitable and
inconvenient.
I will not delay the House with anything in the nature of a detailed explanation of the provisions contained in
Part IX of the Bill, which deals with
bail and recognisances, but I would draw
attention to Clause 37 which enables
police officers to release on bail persons
arrested without a warrant. This principle already obtains in Great Britain and
it is one that will obviously make for
convenience and tend to prevent hardship, doing away, as it will, with the
practice which at present exists under
which persons arrested for comparatively
trivial offences are unable to get bail
until they are brought before a magistrate.
In Part XI which is also of a more or
less general and technical character, the
two most important provisions are those
relating to vagrancy and to the impounding of animals. As hon. Members are
aware, the law regarding vagrancy is a
very old one and dates from 1824, and
its most salient point is that any person
convicted under it is liable to imprisonment without the option of a fine. This

Under modern traffic conditions it is

should be strictly enforced, and it is now

At present the maximum penalty for

40s.

the Measure. That opposition has been

opposition, so far as it is sincere or disinterested, is, I am satisfied, due to

There is one rooted objection I have to

promised, but we must read the text as

not hold office at the pleasure of the
Executive Council. They have a guarantee of office, they have security of
tenure, they are placed in a position of
independence, and they can be removed
only on certificate signed by the
Attorney-General and the Chief Justice.

of County Court judges, but I do not

Mr. POLLOCK : The answer being
somewhat lengthy and involved, I propose, with the hon. Member's concurrence,
to circulate it in the Official Report.
The following is the answer referred to:
As the hon. Member is doubtless aware,
the Northern Government assumed
control of the different services transferred from the Imperial Government at
varying dates, the majority of the Departments not beginning to function until
after the 31st December, 1921. A statement of the number of Civil Servants
employed by the Departments at that date
would therefore have little significance
even for the purposes of comparison.
Some time ago, however, I had a return
prepared to give me a comparison such
as that desired by the hon. Member,
between the staff members soon after our
Government had taken over its functions,
i.e., in 1923, and in September, 1933;
and as there is no material difference
between the figures in September, 1933,
and December, 1933, I think that I can
serve the purpose of the hon. Member
by supplying the information disclosed in
the return to which I have referred.
The number of Civil Servants in
September, 1923, was 1,617, exclusive of
labourers, cleaners, industrial staff and
part-time employees. Since then, the
Departments have taken over from the
Imperial Government and have had
assigned to them, under legislation, many
new duties, the results of which, in regard
to increases of staff, is largely indicated.

Also, the number of temporary staff
required by the Ministry of Labour varies.
with the amount of unemployment, and
this circumstance accounts for 76
additional heads of staff between 1923
and 1933.
These additions brought the total
number of Civil Servants up to 2,151.
Besides, some increases were necessitated
by normal expansion in existing duties,
but as the demands on this account were
met to a very considerable extent by a
policy of retrenching posts, where feasible,
the increase was less than it otherwise
would have been, so that the 1933 total
became 2,179. This number includes
some 750 officers employed on a temporary
basis.
It is regretted that in the time at my
disposal, it has not been possible to compute the total salaries and allowances
payable to the staff in post on the 31st
December, 1921, and 31st December,
1933, respectively; but full information
as to salaries, etc., can be obtained by the
hon. Member from the appropriate
volumes of the Estimates. He will not
fail to note that a considerable proportion
of staff costs is recouped by way of
Appropriations-in-Aid.
UNEMPLOYMENT ACT.
3. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state if, in the
assessment of assistance under the Unemployment Act, Trade Union benefits or
disability pensions will be taken into
account.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
Section 33 of the Unemployment Act,
1934, provides that the need of an
applicant for an unemployment assistance
allowance shall be determined and that
his needs shall be assessed in accordance
with regulations to be made under
Part II of the Act, and that such regulations shall among other things provide
that in computing the resources of the
applicant and of the members of his
household, the first 5s. a week of any sick
pay from a friendly society and the first
£1 a week of any wounds or disability
pension shall be disregarded.
The hon. Member is, of course, aware
that the regulations to be made for the
purpose of this section will be laid before
Parliament.
