That was in 1910, so that from the
time of Shakespeare down through some
centuries to 1910 you find the same complaint against some, but not all of the
magistrates.
When statutes began to be frequent,
imposing liabilities on members of the
public who committed offences, it
was found necessary to have legal
tribunals that could decide cases
quickly and cheaply. Accordingly courts
of petty sessions were set up, and
they were made use of for the trial of
simple offences. It was discovered at an
early period that some classes of cases
were not suitable for trial by these courts,
and resident magistrates were appointed
and were given exclusive jurisdiction in
certain cases. From that time on Act
after Act has been passed limiting the
powers of the ordinary justices.
In his very clear statement the Minister
of Home Affairs has shown the necessity
for a change in the law. Various stories
are told about magistrates sitting with
the county court judge at quarter sessions.
When the evidence is concluded the
county court judge takes the opinion of
all the magistrates, and announces the
judgment of the court according to the
majority. One story is that as a county
court judge was going round the magistrates he came to one man, who said, "I
am not on this case." He had been
brought there for another one. Another

Mrs. PARKER: We are dealing with
an office which has stood the test of
centuries. When we once begin to pull
down buildings which are cemented and
embodied in our national life it seems to
me that you never can tell where the
destruction is going to end. If you pull
down those buildings you never
what wall will be the next to crumble,
and what building will be the next to be
pulled down. I quite realise that in the
march of civilisation, and in time, alterations in the fabric must be inevitable.
Abuses creep in and abuses must be done
away with. But I want to take this
opportunity of saying that to me it seems.
there is very great danger in reforms too
rapidly inaugurated, and that the great
danger is that you should bring discontent to those who are unable to keep
mental pace with the pioneers. I believe
that public opinion must be guided and
not coerced. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Wherever reforms, even the most
necessary and most elementary, have been
undertaken all those reforms if they are
undertaken too rapidly have come to an
end, temporarily at any rate, because of
the downfall of those who had in their
zeal set too hard a pace.
Having said that I want to make it
clear that to my mind this would apply to
a situation even where a really good case
has been made out for the abolition of
something or for some reform. But has
such a case been made out here to-day
or yesterday? If such a case were made
out I do not believe we would be justified

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: In rising to
speak on this Bill may I say that I consider it one of the most far-reaching
Measures that have ever been brought
before this Parliament since it came into
existence. It practically abolishes the
administration of justice as we know it
in our day and generation. I personally
feel a very great and grave responsibility in coming to a right decision in
this matter. It is one's duty to ensure
that justice is administered free of
favour, fear, partiality, or affection, and
above all, that no suspicion may lurk or
rest in the minds of anyone that justice
is or can be controlled by the executive.
In coming to a decision I have asked myself three questions. The first is, is the
reform of the judicial system necessary?
The answer, I think, is not disputed and
it is that reform is necessary. To my
mind no good purpose is to be served by
laying the blame on anyone or at any
particular door, but the fact remains
that reform is essential. The next
question I put to myself is this. Does
this Bill provide the best means for that
reform? That is a very wide and deep
question. To my mind it is not practical
politics for this House to tell the Government, as has been suggested outside, that
magistrates should all be dismissed and
then a new selection made and somebody
appointed. To my mind that is quite
impossible.
The next suggestion put forward is
that a rota system should be established.
That was mentioned just now by the
Member for North Derry (Mrs. Parker).
I have considered that suggestion and I
do not think that, in country districts
especially, it would be either workable
or practicable. We have then to consider, what can we do to make the reform
of summary jurisdiction in Northern
Ireland practicable and workable. The
Bill now before the House applies this
reform by setting up resident magistrates
supreme in the petty sessions courts, and
as far as I can see this reform will hold
the field until someone else puts forward
a better suggestion.
During the debate on the King's
Speech I said I hoped there would still
be scope for men and women of integrity
and public spirit throughout the country
under this Bill. May I explain to the
House why I used those words, and I
might refer to the system of government and the system of justice as we
know it in the United Kingdom. The
system of government is based on beginning at the bottom. We have first the
guardians, who deal with poor law
administration. Then we come to
district councils, a grade higher, and
then urban district councils, county
councils, city corporation and borough
councils, and Houses of Parliament. In
the same way justice begins at the
bottom with the justices of the peace.
Then we
come to the petty sessions,
quarter sessions, county courts, and
High Courts of Justice, and I hold that
it is an essential part of our British
system of justice and government that
it should be based on
a very broad
principle, and that you should begin at
the bottom and build upwards.
I ask how can we apply this to the

successfully into law in a form which is
of a satisfactory drafting nature will be
of great assistance in the administration
of justice in Northern Ireland.
Now practically the whole Second Reading debate has ranged round the first
part of the Bill, the part of the Bill
which proposes shortly to take away the
greater part of the judicial functions of
what we call the lay magistrates. Now,
considering whether such a proposal as
this should recommend itself to the House,
I think there is one simple test which
can be applied. That test is whether the
carrying out of the proposals made by the
Government will tend to better administration of justice in Northern Ireland,
and perhaps a second and scarcely less
important test that the carrying out of
such proposals in the opinion of the people
of Northern Ireland does better the
administration of justice here. These
are the cardinal tests.
What is
What are the arguments used against
the Government proposals? The first is
the historical argument, first introduced
in this debate by my fine old conservative
friend the Member for Central.
the historical argument? The historical
argument is surely this. Justices of the
peace are an old institution. The world
may be changing round, is rapidly changing, has rapidly changed, but they should
be allowed to stand firm, the
unchanging institution in this rapidly
changing world.
one
Mr. CAMPBELL: You are not changed.
Mr. BLACK: When one comes to
examine a proposition of this kind one
inquires whether the administration of
justice throughout English history was
unchanged as suggested here. From the
first examination one sees that that is not
the case. The old local courts have gave
way to the feudal courts. The old feudal
courts in their turn gave way to the
King's courts. And why? Because a
better constitution was gradually being
evolved as social conditions and even
physical conditions were changed, and
when these changes took place it was seen
that a
better administration of justice
was demanded. No one to-day would
wish to go back from the King's courts
to the old local courts of Saxon times.
With regard to justices of the peace not
only legal changes have taken place. It
569 Summary Jurisdiction Bill-

12 DECEMBER 1934
Second Reading
used to be that the office was held by one
class, the country gentleman class. That
is not so now. A change has taken place
in that. Does the hon. Gentleman who
represents Central suggest going back to
those old times and that these changes
ought not to have been made?
Not only has that change taken place,
but through a great part of England
justices of the peace have been supplanted
by stipendiary magistrates. In courts of
petty sessions we have stipendiary justices
all over London and in many of the great
boroughs. Right through England in
practically every borough in England
criminal jurisdiction, which was formerly
exercised at quarter sessions, is not now
exercised by unpaid justices but is exercised by a professional man, the Recorder.
In that respect things have changed.
And as I have said there are reasons for
the change. When one looks back at the
middle ages one sees that the administration of justice by local justices was
convenient thing. The country was
sparsely populated, and the means of communication were far different from what
they are to-day. It was a most convenient thing to have someone in each
district to administer justice in regard to
petty matters. The obvious man was the
man who had some education, the country
gentleman. He administered justice and
administered it well, because the matters
dealt with in those times were simple
matters such as ordinary assault and the
ordinary little disputes.
a
If one looks at the statutes at large one
sees right to the seventeenth century the
whole statutes of England could be compressed into one single volume. There was
very little law to learn-very little statute
law. Look at the vast bulk of the statutes
at the present time, and see the duty that
lies before one about to administer justice.
It is a far different task. Nowadays for
a man to qualify himself for the administration of justice he has to make a study
of a very complex body of statute law. We
have heard to-day of how justices in
country districts-apparently there is
agreement that the people of Belfast are
unsatisfactory-but in country districts
they are paragons of virtue and knowledge. I wonder how many justices of
the peace in any district which hon.
Gentlemen represent have seriously sat
down to any elementary textbook and
made themselves familiar with it, so as
to be ready to pass an examination on
the duties which they have taken upon
themselves to perform. I venture to say
none. I wonder if the hon. Member for
Antrim would undertake to sit for an
examination on the first or second volumes
of O'Connor's Justices of the Peace.
Mr. CRAWFORD: I have read it.
Mr. BLACK: I wonder if the hon.
Gentleman has read it forward or backward.
Mr. CAMPBELL: How many resident
magistrates could sit for an examination?
Mr. BLACK: The hon. Member for
Central suggests the resident magistrates
might not pass an examination. My
answer is that any one appointed by the
Ministry has a duty to make himself
acquainted with, and any man who fails
to make himself acquainted with it is
guilty of a grave dereliction of duty. So
much for the historical argument.
The next argument is that the Bill
proposes something in the nature of a
bureaucratic system. I do not wish to
repeat what was said so well by the hon.
and learned Member for the City of
Derry who preceded me, but when one
complains of the resident magistrate being
something in the nature of a bureaucratic
institution subject to the control of the
Ministry of Home Affairs one asks the
simple question the hon. and learned Member
for Derry City asked, can anyone point to
any occasion since this Government was
set up where a resident magistrate has
been controlled by the Ministry of Home
Affairs. Surely the most emphatic
certificate of the entire absence of that
control is the pronouncement a resident
magistrate lately retired has issued
against the proposal.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Have you read his
book?
Mr. BLACK: I have read his book
and read it with care. But one thing
does emerge in regard to that gentleman.
The fact that he should make such a pronouncement as that proves conclusively
how little the resident magistrate is under
the thumb of the Executive. It should
be made clear that they are not. I for
one, for that reason, greatly welcome the

The next objection taken to the Bill

who have spoken on this side of the

and wisdom in the plain man. The

profession are fit to deal with affairs of
men, and how can it be suggested that

while these magistrates moved about and

not understand. As the hon. Member
for Central put it it was quite an
attractive proposition, but as put on this
side it becomes rather a different proposition. It becomes a proposition that this
plain wisdom should over-ride all law,
Any judicial person coming to administer
justice takes a judicial oath to administer
justice according to the law. Here it
is claimed that magistrates should
administer, not the same justice, but
some justice superior to the law of the
land.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I did not say that.
Mr. BLACK: The hon. and learned
Member did not say that, but following
on what he did say it has been suggested
on
•
this side of the House of some
Recorder of London, now deceased but
not named, that his virtue was not that
he administered the law but that he
administered some wisdom of his own
which was superior to the law. The
function of a justice in Northern Ireland
is to preserve the judicial oath and
administer the law of Northern Ireland,
and it is not his privilege to administer
some fanciful justice of his own like a
Cadi sitting under a palm tree in the

throughout the country districts is that

should be supplanted by a body of men
who will administer the law according to

The final suggestion of those who
oppose this Measure was that it amounts
to a withdrawal of a privilege enjoyed
by a privileged class. I am acquainted
with a good number of justices of the
peace in Belfast, and I must say that I
have never heard such an argument put
forward by them. It is a very petty
mind that takes the view that "I am
being deprived of a privilege and a high
rank and, therefore, I say that the reform
is no reform and should be opposed." As
time goes on in the development of the
institutions of the country certain
privileges have to be taken away from
those who enjoy them. Up to 1898 grand
jurors enjoyed the honour and privilege
of administering the local government of
the county. That privilege was taken
away in 1898, and their jurisdiction given
to the county councils. Would it not
have been a sign of a weak mind on the
part of grand jurors to have opposed this
reform on the ground that it was taking
away some special privilege, and it is
equally a sign of a mean and shallow
mind to oppose this Bill on the ground
that it is taking away a privilege either
from an individual or a class.
To go back again to Shakespeare and
Mr. Justice Shallow, not in Henry IV,
but in the opening scene of the first Act
of "The Merry Wives of Windsor,"
where Mr. Justice Shallow displays himself with all his privileges and all his
prerogatives as "Justice of Peace and
'Corum'," and "Ay, cousin Slender, and
'Custalorum'." One can almost hear
that note in some of the resolutions that
have been passed by country benches of
justices. "We are great people. We are
not as other men are. We are the
Palladium of the town, and it is we who
are attacked." There is no commonsense in that. We come back again to
the one question which I suggest is the
primary question, will this reform conduce to the better administration of
justice? An attack has been made on
the justices in Belfast. I have not had
experience of petty sessions courts, but
I am well acquainted with many persons

A man living in one street possibly does

There is another reason why the reform

ordinary justices, however honest and

course, when you have so many justices

This being admitted, and there having

necessary to recollect that there has

courts, since 1851 than there was from

There certainly has been more change in
our summary jurisdiction courts since
the war than there was between 1851 and
1914. Therefore, while there has been
a progressive change in our summary
jurisdiction law, making it more complicated and more difficult, and entering
more closely into the life of the people,
there has, on the other hand, at the same
time been a progressive dilution of the
bench which has weakened it and has
caused it to lose the confidence of the
public. I think there is no doubt that,
to a very great extent, the magistracy has
lost the confidence of the public. That
being the case, when I first occupied the
office which I have the honour still to
occupy a number of representations were
made, from time to time, both to the

department, asking that certain changes
should be made in summary jurisdiction.
Some of those representations were made
by resident magistrates, who found flaws
in the law. Other difficulties arose owing
to the fact that changes were made in
England, which were found to work well,
and the question arose whether they
should be applied here.
Then we had a number of representations, some of which were referred to by
the Minister in his speech yesterday,
from various bodies and associations, asking for changes in the law to bring it up
to modern requirements. That file has
been on my table off and on for the last
eight or nine years. All these various
reforms were considered from time to
time by my Department in conjunction
with members of the public, and with the
assistance of the officers of the Ministry
of Home Affairs. They were all tabulated out from the very earliest stage,
and it was obvious to anyone who had
any knowledge of the administration of
justice, that a great number of these reforms could not be embarked on while the
bench remained in its present condition.
That was not only the opinion of the
lawyers, it was the opinion of the persons
who made these representations to the
Government from outside, and certainly,
when I came to look into them, I was
fully of the same opinion. Therefore,
when the Government came to consider
the reform of summary jurisdiction they
found the reform of the magistracy was
mixed up with it in such a way that they
could not deal with one without dealing
with the other.
The question arose, what was to be
done? It was admitted on all hands that
the bench was in an unsatisfactory condition, and the question arose as to how
it was to be reformed. It is hardly
necessary to go into that matter to any
great detail, because it has been discussed by Members on both sides. So far
as I followed the debate the various
alternatives have all been negatived.
The first one which was suggested was

all the

All these matters were considered most

court and, therefore, that possible way
out was rejected.
The only other suggestion that I heard

that is that a resident magistrate, with
legal qualifications, should sit with a lay
magistrate as assessor. I considered that
at a very early stage in this controversy, but I do not think it would work,
in fact I am certain it would not work.
It is quite a different proposition when a
judge sits with a jury, because the judge
directs the jury as to law, and the jury
finds the facts, but you cannot divorce
law from facts in a summary jurisdiction.
court.

the case of the Elder Brethren of
Trinity House, you have them sitting
with a judge during cases. The

The Minister in his speech said it would
require no further resident magistrates to

done by the whole of these 1,500 unpaid
magistrates who at present hold the commission of the peace. Therefore the
proposition presented itself in that way.
You have a necessary reform to carry out.
You have no alternative of a satisfactory
nature other than to commit this jurisdiction to the resident magistrates. You
find when you come to investigate it that
the resident magistrates are easily able to
do this work without any increased
expense. The Minister having considered
this matter has now promised in order to
allay this bogey-that resident magistrates are subject to the control of his
Department-that they shall have the
same right and tenure as county court
judges. When that is said there is no
possible objection to the terms of this Bill.
I have not gone into matters in the
Bill itself. If hon. Members will look
through the Bill carefully they will see
there are a great number of requirements
in it. A great many motives have been
ascribed to the Government for bringing
in this Bill. I have a great many years
experience of summary jurisdiction, and
also so far as the Minister and the
Government are concerned, and I can
assure Members that this Bill is a genuine
attempt to improve the administration of
justice in Northern Ireland, and I ask the
House to give it a Second Reading. I
am quite satisfied when it becomes law it
will effect the great improvements the
Government expect.

LEGISLATION FOR DISTRESSED

2. Mr. GRANT (for Lieut.-Colonel
Gordon) asked the Minister of Labour
whether he can state if, in view of the
very grave distress which exists in the
village of Shrigley as disclosed by his
answer on the 11th December, the Government does not consider that legislation is required for the distressed areas
in Northern Ireland similar to that now
before the Imperial Parliament.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The Bill at present under
consideration at Westminster is designed
merely to permit experiments of methods
of helping unemployed persons to be
carried out in certain extensive areas in
Great Britain. A small district like
Shrigley does not fall within the category
of those regions, but I shall watch closely
the result of the Commissioners' experiments.
Meantime, the Unemployment Assistance Board which has been established
in Northern Ireland possesses statutory
powers which, in my opinion, will be of
considerable assistance in helping the unemployed in Shrigley, with whom I have
much sympathy. Besides I have approved
a further relief scheme in the district,
to be commenced when the present relief
scheme is completed, which will give a
substantial amount of employment.

in wages to the Northern Ireland farm
labourers.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): It is true
that agricultural labourers' wages are
somewhat lower in Northern Ireland than
in England. So are the profits of
farmers and for that reason it would not
be desirable at the present time to set up
any kind of wage-fixing machinery.
The object of such machinery is to
secure to the labourer not an arbitrarily
fixed standard of living, but a just and
reasonable share of the product of the
industry.
Now, I believe that although the wage
level is lower here than in England, the
Northern Ireland labourer's share of the
net agricultural income is at least as
great as, if not greater than, that of the
English labourer. Of course, to make
this comparison between England, where
family labour is negligible, and Northern
Ireland, where it predominates, those
'sons and daughters who work on the farm
must be included in the labouring class.
But even if only one family labourer is
included for every hired labourer, the
Northern Ireland labourers as a class are
still in a better position vis-à-vis the
farmer, than their English fellows.
Hence, any attempt to fix a higher
level of wages than rules at present would
result in further unemployment. Farms
are run for the most part by a combination of hired and family labour; instead
of paying the increased price for hired
labour, the farmer would dispense with
some of it and either get more out of
his family or decrease production.
On the other hand, if, as we believe,
the Government's marketing schemes lead
to greater returns from agriculture, this
improvement will be reflected automatically in better conditions for agricultural
labourers.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: May I ask if it
is not a fact that the low wages of agricultural labourers is chiefly due to the
dumping of foreign produce into this.
country, and further, if the right hon.
Gentleman is aware that dumping is one
of the principal planks in the platform
of the Socialist Party.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I agree that
the low wages paid in agriculture at the
present time are a reflection of the depressed state of the industry which has
been largely caused by the competition of
cheap food supplies from abroad. It has
been the object of the National Government to revive prosperity in agriculture
by means of the regulation of imports of
agricultural produce, coupled with the
orderly marketing of home produce
through the agency of the various marketing schemes which have been established.
I trust that the labourers in Northern Ireland will, in future, share in the benefits
of this improvement in the prosperity of
the agricultural community.
If, as the hon. Member suggests, the
encouragement of foreign dumping is a
principal plank in the British Socialists
programme, I am glad, for in that case
their prospects at the next election are
blacker than even I had dared to hope.

TRADE OF NORTHERN IRELAND.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he can state the
industries most adversely affected by the
fall in the trade of Northern Ireland from
£135,000,000 in the year 1924 to
£107,000,000 in the year 1930, and to
£72,000,000 (exclusive of trade with
the Irish Free State) in the year 1933;
and what administrative measures the
Government propose to take to check this
decline.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): In the absence of my right
hon. Friend, I am taking this question.
The hon. and learned Member has
asked for particulars of a fall in trade
which has, in fact, not taken place.
Whilst. as was shown by the figures
which I furnished in reply to a previous
question by him on the same subject, the
sterling value of Northern Ireland's trade
in 1933 was less than that for 1930, and
for the latter year less than the value
for 1924, the volume of trade has shown
remarkably little variation.
But I may say that the best available
index we have of the volume of Ulster
trade is to be found in the returns of
the Belfast Harbour Commissioners.
Taking 1929 as the peak year before
the collapse of trade took place, the total
volume of goods passing through the port
amounted to 3,362,084 tons. For the
eleven months of the present year,
the figures are 3,110,264 tons, and, adding an estimate for the present month of
December, we reach a total trade for the
present year of 3,370,000 tons, which is
365,000 tons more than last year, and
may be regarded as a record.
This furnishes indubitable evidence of
the progress of the Province, notwithstanding the vast contraction of world
trade, as may be realised when I refer
the hon. and learned Member to the
published statistics, which show that
trade, taking that of the year 1929 as 100,
was only-81 in 1930, 58 in 1931, 39 in
1932, and 35 in 1933.
These figures imply that the trading
between all the different countries of the
world has fallen away in value by 65
per cent. surely an enormous drop
within a comparatively short period.
We have, therefore, reason to congratulate ourselves that the volume of our
provincial trade has been so well maintained.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Is it not a
fact that, if the hon. and learned Member for Central were able to enforce his
policy of incorporating Northern Ireland
as part of the Irish Free State the result
would be a total loss of our free markets
in the United Kingdom, the bankruptcy
of the farming community, and widespread distress and unemployment?
Mr. CAMPBELL: In view of the
nature of the answer to this question, I
give notice that I will raise the matter
spread distress and unemployment?

violation of the fair wages clause, this
firm should be permitted to shelter behind a public utility service which is
financed by the people of Northern Ireland; and whether he will take steps to
end this condition of affairs.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) As a result of inquiries which
I have made, I think this is a matter,
in the first instance, at any rate, for
the Electricity Board, to whom representations should be addressed.

5. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the total
number of persons in receipt of 65 pensions and those in receipt of 70 pensions;
and the number of persons over 60 years
of age in Northern Ireland.
Mr. ANDREWS: On 30th September,
1934, which is the latest date for which
figures are available, 13,847 persons between the ages of 65 and 70, and 18,762
persons aged 70 or over were in receipt
of old-age pensions under the Contributory Pensions Act. In addition, 33,369

Old Age Pensions Acts.
As regards the latter part of the hon.
Member's question, it is estimated that
there are approximately 150,000 persons
in Northern Ireland aged 60 or over.

and thus add to the cost of production
you make it more difficult for employers
to compete in the neutral markets of the
world. Therefore I would say again, as
I have said before, that I would like to
see the strong influence of the trade union
Members on the opposite side of the
House brought to bear during the next
few years on other countries-and if I
might mention one country more than
another in this respect it would be Japan
-so that we could compete fairly and
squarely in the neutral markets and thus
get back to that state of prosperity which
will enable us to consider reasonably such
schemes as that of a pension of £1 a
week. Then only would I be prepared
to support such a Motion as that before
the House.
In the meantime I feel it is in the
interests of the Province that we should
carry on in the future as in the past,
which I think has been reasonably
generous, having regard to the fact that
such a large sum as I have mentioned,
namely, £500,000,000 per annum, is
being spent on social services. I notice
that Sir George Newman, in his report on
the health of the people issued the other
day, states that the health and nutrition
of the poor, in spite of the slump, has
never been better than it is at the present
moment. In addition to that we find that
the savings of the poor have, even during
the slump, been increasing by leaps and
bounds. For these reasons I have every
confidence in supporting the Amendment.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) I rise at this stage because I
feel that hon. Members opposite are entitled to have a considered answer to the
various important matters which they
have dealt with. I would like to make
it quite clear at the beginning of my
remarks, as I have done at other times,
that hon. Members on this side of the
House are just as anxious for the welfare
of our people of all classes as are hon.
Members opposite, but there is a great
difference between our positions. Hon.
Members on the opposite side of the
House, or some of them at any rate, can
go about at election times and advocate
the expenditure of huge sums of public
money, and between election times, in
public halls and in the streets, they can
spend vast sums in their imaginations at
the expense of the State.
Then again, they can put down Motions
time after time in this House, urging that
large sums be spent in all directions.
They never tell us how these vast sums
are to be raised. But the position of the
Government is very different. We have
to make sure, before we make promises,
675 Widows' and Old Age Pensions HOUSE OF COMMONS
Widows' and Old Age Pensions 676
[Mr. Andrews]
that we can fulfil them, and I would like
to say, for the reasons that I have already
mentioned, that the Opposition in this
House is the more free from fetters than
any Opposition probably in the world,
because they know quite well that the
day of reckoning will never come when
they will have to foot the bill.
I think I am entitled to refer to the
fact, just to show what has been done
in the last ten years in the direction of
helping those who are temporarily passing
through a period of adversity, that when
the same question is raised again and
again on the opposite side of the House
it requires to be answered in the same
way, and, therefore, if my answers are
somewhat similar to what they have been
before it is due to the fact that the story
is just the same.
I would ask the Member for Dock to remain quite quiet. I
listened to him with attention, and now
I want to give him a considered answer
if he wants to hear it. The position ten
years ago was this. My Department was
spending in benefits £3,000,000 per
annum. Now the Department is spending £5,000,000 per annum, notwithstanding the fact that unemployment has
fallen by approximately one half.
The Member for Dock proposes that an
inquiry should be held in order that this
matter should be looked into. I do not
think an inquiry is necessary, because the
real difficulty is not that we would not
like to do better than we are doing, but
it is to find the money to do it.
Mr. MIDGLEY: The money is there
all right.
Mr. ANDREWS: Would the hon.
Member please stop buzzing like a bee,
because it is rather disconcerting, and it
is not particularly helpful. Now the
hon. Member for Pottinger and the hon.
Member for Dock are not quite agreed
in their views in regard to this matter,
although one moved the Motion and the
other seconded it. The hon. Member for
Dock said he would be satisfied with an
inquiry that is rather reasonable-but
the hon. Member for Pottinger on Thursday last said that he would prefer no
inquiry but would like the thing done at
once.
Mr. MIDGLEY: So would I.
Mr. ANDREWS: I am glad they are
in agreement now if they were not in
agreement on Thursday. It rathers clears
the position. One of the reasons for
putting this Motion forward is that it
will be a cure for unemployment; in other
words, that the people would get adequate
pensions of £1 a week, as was suggested
in the first instance, and therefore they
would cease to work. I do not think the
hon. Members were entitled to assume
that at all. Many people who receive a
pension of 10s. a week continue to work.
I know people doing very faithful work
and they are over 70 years of age. They
are getting the wages they got before.
They never were in as good a position as
they are now because they have 10s. a
week in addition. I feel quite positive
that a great many under the voluntary
system would simply accept the pension of
£1 a week and continue to work.
fore, it would not go any way towards a
solution of the unemployment situation,
nor would it help to get work for the
younger men.
There-

Mr. ANDREWS: They are prepared

Mr. MIDGLEY: Certainly.

As regards the cost of the proposals,

has dealt with the matter, but may I

old-age and widows' pensions were
increased to £1 a week, and if the
qualifying age was reduced to 60 it
would mean that the total cost of the
pensions would be £8,600,000. The existing cost is £2,210,000. If we assumed
there would be a saving in the Unemployment Fund of £300,000 there would
then be £2,510,000 to take from the new
cost of £8,600,000, leaving an additional
cost of over £6,000,000. Then if we take
the other view the hon. Member for Dock
has put forward and give a pension to
all on the basis of the average of what
they are at present receiving it would
mean that the cost would be £17,000,000,
and if we deduct two and a half millions
from the present cost, we find the
additional cost would be about
£15,000,000. The thing is absurd. When
you think that the revenue of Northern

Tuesday, 6th
March, 1934, provided always that if it
appears to the satisfaction of Mr. Speaker,
after consultation with the Government,
that the public interest requires that the
House should meet at an earlier time,
during the Adjournment Mr. Speaker
may give notice that he is so satisfied and
thereupon the House shall meet at the
time stated in such notice and shall transact its business as if it had been duly
adjourned to that date."-(The Prime
Minister.)
Mr. BEATTIE: I think that this
House requires from the Government
some justification for the Motion on the
Order Paper. We came back to the
House on the 18th December, after an
absence of two months, and now the
Prime Minister desires that the House
close down from to-day until the 6th
Parker, Mrs. Dehra
[3-30 p.m.
Pollock, Rt. Hon. Hugh MacDowell
Robb, John Hanna
Shillington, Major David Graham
Wilson, John Charles
Young, George Charles Gillespie
TELLER FOR THE AYES-
Captain Dixon.
TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Mr. Henderson
March. If the Prime Minister had done
what he should have done for the people
of Northern Ireland, he could have had a
very good holiday on the Continent, but
in view of the apathy of the Government
and the carelessness of the Government's
supporters in other public boards, I think
this House would be neglecting its duty.
in not opposing an adjournment for such
a lengthy period. To-day the Minister of
Labour gave the figures showing the total
unemployed in Northern Ireland, and in
view of the position, I think the House
should re-assemble in the second week in
January, with a view to co-ordinating the
services of the Members of this House and
getting an immediate start of those works
which are required to absorb into employment all those who desire work of this
kind.
It seems to me that the Prime Minister
is always on the "Wait, wait, waiting'
policy, just as the Minister of Finance has
proved himself to be in the case of the
Dundonald sewerage scheme. Twelve
months ago it was stated in this House
Adjournment of the House 144
Adjournment of the House
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
that that scheme was to be started, and I
lived in the expectation that the Government would have started last summer.
I am told to-day that the inquiry will be
held only in January, or in the New Year,
and to the Government that means any
time between January and December. I
say that carelessness of that kind is an
outrage upon the decencies of any community. Every Member on this side of
the House is anxious to do his part in the
alleviation of the distress which prevails
in Northern Ireland. .
I want to tell the Prime Minister that if
he is prepared to re-assemble the House
in January, I and other representatives on
this side of the House are willing to proceed with him to London to ask his friends
for a percentage of the shipbuilding programme of the Admiralty for the Belfast
shipyards. I make that suggestion on
this ground, that we are paying our share
of the taxation which goes to the building
of those ships in the Admiralty programme, and I feel inclinded to say that
we are entitled to our share of the work.
Under the Admiralty's programme several
million pounds are to be spent in shipbuilding, and not the smallest contract
has been placed with the Belfast shipyards.
a
the juveniles would become an asset to
the State in which they reside, instead of
being a hindrance through force of circumstances which may eventually result
in their being shipped off to Canada out
of the road.
Another reason why we should not
adjourn until 6th March is that the new
Unemployment Bill is coming, and I
should like to be kept in close touch with
the working of that Measure as it proceeds through the British Parliament. If
I have not an opportunity in this House
of keeping in close touch with the
progress of that Bill, then you are preventing me from doing justice to it when
it comes before this House. I feel that
it is the duty of the Government to give
us the opportunity of watching carefully
the interests of the unemployed of Northern Ireland.
The third point I wish to mention is
that the Government do not seem to
realise that there are many thousands of
widows, with small families in Northern
Ireland who have been denied the right
to widows' and orphans' pensions, through
circumstances over which they had no
control. And there are many unemployed persons who have lost their right
to the 65 pension, because, owing to circumstances over which they had no
control, they have been placed outside the
Act of Parliament. Whether the Government like it or not, I feel that it is my
duty to express the view that they will
have to make provision for those widows
and orphans by bringing forward a special
Measure to include them within the
The fact that
their claims have been disallowed is not
due to the fault of their husbands. I feel
that on these grounds I am justified in
moving that the House should re-assemble
in the second week in January instead of
on the 6th March.
We are told by the Members on the
other side of the House that we are the
most loyal people in the world. If that
is the position, then Great Britain is not
showing much loyalty to us in return
for our loyalty. I am in favour of
a reciprocal arrangement with the other
side, and as
paying community which contributes
to the building of Admiralty ships,
I contend that we have the right to a
percentage of work for the Belfast shipyards. I think a good mission could be
undertaken with that object in view, if
we met in the second week in January and
made our representations as a combined
body to the British Treasury for the work
which is required in our area.
provisions of the Act.

Further, if we met in the second week
in January we could devise ways and
means to provide some form of work for the
large number of juveniles who are now
roaming about Northern Ireland falling
into blind alleys. I think we could reorganise a scheme suitable for the juvenile
population, whereby benefit would accrue
to the State in the future as a whole, and
Mr. HENDERSON: I have great
pleasure in supporting the Amendment of
the hon. Member for Pottinger. The
Government have come here from the
electorate, and it has been the Prime

If you love Ulster you should work for
Ulster. I can understand what has happened. It is all very well for the Prime
Minister, the Minister of Labour, and the
Minister of Finance to go to the Willowfield Unionist Club, or to Glengall Street,
or to the North Belfast Memorial Hall,
and to an audience of about twenty-three
make bloodthirsty speeches about the
invasion of Ulster.
The men of Ulster will never permit
invasion of this Province, but if the
Prime Minister wants to make loyal subjects he must have the people properly
housed and fed, so that they will be
physically fit to resist invasion from any
source. It is only by feeding and
housing the people of Ulster that you will
be able to render them fit to defend their
own homes. At the present time their
plight is terrible. I wonder if the Prime
Minister ever thinks about these people.
I have them at my door, because, unfortunately, I live next door to the poorhouse. Is it fair that I, as the representative of a very honoured citizen who
lived on the Shankill Road, and who has
had to leave his home and go into the
poorhouse, should not be allowed to come
to this House to tell his troubles to the
Prime Minister and the Members of this
House, who are the only people who can
do anything for him.
Do you realise that there are hundreds
of married men who have had to give up
their homes in many parts of Belfast and
seek the shelter of the poorhouse. What
do you care. Sooner or later these
people and their sons and daughters will
turn against this Government; in fact, I
think the Prime Minister must have got
a warning prior to the last election,
because he took good care to have the
election on the old register, otherwise
there might have been a different result
to-day. I am altogether dissatisfied with
the tactics adopted by this Government
during the past twelve and a half years.
We meet for only six or eight weeks in the
year. Is that fair to the taxpayers of
Northern Ireland, who have to pay our
salaries. Would the Minister of Labour
or the Minister of Finance be prepared
to pay their employees fifty-two weeks
wages for working six or eight weeks in
the year. Not at all. What you
would do to your own workers you should
apply to yourselves. The country is in
such a state of destitution that it requires
you to work for fifty-two weeks in the
year. Destitution is rampant in Northern
Ireland, and we want to put a stop to the
exploitation of the poverty of the people.
The Minister of Finance exploited ex-
Servicemen when he appointed rangers
on the Stormont estate at a wage of 35s
a week, but he is not so bad as some employers who are employing men at 16s a
week, and some even pay their workers
only 10s a week.
Why should you get any more holidays
than a shipyard worker. He gets only
Christmas Day, Boxing Day, and the day
after, and he does not receive payment
for those days. Yet after sitting for
only ten and a half hours we are proposing to adjourn until 6th March. I do
not know what you think of yourselves.
I know the Prime Minister loves this
House so much that he would not care
if he never saw it open at all, but he
should remember that, notwithstanding
all the slanders and statements made,
especially against the Independent Members, during the last election, we were
sent here to see that you do your duty to
the people, not only the people who voted
for us, but those who voted against us.
I always look forward to coming to this
House. Someone asked me the other
day, "Why are you so anxious to get
to this House," and I replied, "It is the
only House I get an opportunity of talking in." (Laughter.) Therefore, I
have a great inducement to come here,
and I love to come here. I do not like
to come here and see hon. Members
asleep. I like to se them lively, like
the Prime Minister is to-day. I want
to see the Prime Minister having a happy
Christmas, but I also want to see every
citizen in Northern Ireland having a

where there will not even be a fire on

that affect the well-being of the people.
I do not wish to take up the time of the
House. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
If you say "Hear, hear," I will go on

20 DECEMBER 1933
Adjournment of the House
There are two schools of thought even
in Northern Ireland. One school of
thought is that the more seldom Parliament meets the more business will be done
and the more efficiently it will be done.
The other school of thought believes that
Parliament ought to meet as often as possible in order to survey the economic and
industrial development of this portion of
our country. I am on the democratic side.
I believe in our Parliamentary institution
and in the right of the people to work out
their own destiny. But the fact that we
are having these long adjournments is
creating a section of thought throughout
Northern Ireland which inclines to the
belief that Parliament is ineffective; that
it is negligible; that it is so insignificant
that it is not worth consideration. That
is what people are saying. Very often
you hear comparisons made between local
authorities, for example, and our Parliamentary institution, and anyone who has
had any experience will admit the truth of
these. If we are going to adjourn in this
way until March let us compare that
adjournment with the adjournment
of a local body. The local body is
doing a great deal more work than
our Parliamentary institution, and that is
not good for the reputation of the Parliamentary institution in this part of our
country.

there is nothing in that over which to bestow self-gratification on oneself. You

Adjournment of the House
[Mr. Midgley]
are bound by law to maintain the social
services. You entered into a contract with
the people and took contributions from
them, and you are just doing the same
thing in regard to the social services as
any commercial insurance company would
have to do if it entered into a contract
with a client. And this idea of telling the

we are going to pay out £90,000 in this
way or in that way, we require a special
vote of thanks from the community is in
my opinion most illogical. We are
governed by Acts of Parliament, and from
1912 right up to the present time, in some
form or other, insurance has been contributed to by employers and employees, and,
therefore, you are only returning to the
people a proportion of what they have
paid and to which they are entitled by
Act of Parliament.
But the hon. Member for Shankill indicated one very serious thing, and that is
that, even when you have made all allowances for the social services, there are vast
numbers of people in Northern Ireland
who are outside the scope of these social
services. There are men, for example,
who have been so long out of work that
they are disallowed their rights as unemployed people. There are people who have
never been brought within the scope of
the Acts. There are people, like domestic
servants and out-workers, who are not
going to be brought within the scope of
the new Act. Those people are all in some
way affected by the problem of unemployment to-day.
Take another aspect of the matter. The
Minister of Labour himself admitted yesterday that during the last twelve months
the figures for unemployment have been
reduced from a little over 70,000 to about
60,000. That is for the registered unemployed. But it must be remembered that
you have to add to that number dependants on the average of, say, three to each
person signing at the Labour Exchange.
You will find, if you like to make a calculation along those lines, that the percentage of the community of Northern Ireland, out of a population of 1,250,000,
who are directly or indirectly affected
by unemployment is very high indeed.
I do not claim a monopoly
virtue, of good intentions, or of kindheartedness. I have never suggested and
I do not suggest that these benches have
a monopoly of sympathy. That has never
been claimed. There are bound to be kind
of

and sympathetic hearts on the Government

the aspect or angle from which we approach
the problem that counts. The Members
on the Government benches proceed from
the point of view that, having fulfilled.
their obligations according to statute,
they are doing all they possibly can.
I say they are not. There is acute
destitution in Belfast at the present time. I rose with the conviction
that, no matter what might be said from
these benches, it would make no change
in the intended programme of the
Government, but, even believing that, I
am now going to make an appeal to the

distress. If the Prime Minister ever
wants to be disillusioned-and there are

to slums, with regard to decrepit homes,

sections of the Division I represent and
to bring him into touch with poverty and
destitution in a way in which he has
never been brought in touch before. As

sufficient reason why we should not

Over and above all that there is the
question of schemes of relief. The
Minister of Labour and the Prime
Minister will admit that when the
present situation in the Corporation in

Our local Chancellor said last week that

in the interests of the community and in

fifty per cent. of the taxable capacity of

Order read for resuming Adjourned Debate on Question (18th December).
"That an humble Address be presented to his Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland, as follows:
"Your Grace,
"We, His Majesty's most dutiful and

beg leave to offer our humble thanks to

Question again proposed.
Mr. GAMBLE: I rise to take part
in this debate, and at this late hour of
the day I wish to join with those right
hon. and hon. Members who have
tendered their congratulations to the
mover and seconder of the Address for
the able manner in which they have performed that duty. There are only two
or three things in the Gracious Speech
that I intend to deal with, and I hope
to do so very briefly. Some of the things
that are mentioned in it I do not profess
to understand. Therefore, I do not intend to weary the House with my views
on those subjects. I see that in the early
part of the Gracious Speech there is a
gratifying note of a substantial increase
in the volume of employment, especially
in the two staple industries of Northern
Ireland. I refer to the shipbuilding and
linen industries. As to shipbuilding, I
am not a Belfastman. I do not represent
a city constituency, nor do many of my
constituents know much about shipbuilding. I will pass that over.
In regard to the linen industry, I speak
to-day only from the agricultural point
of view, that is, from the point of view
of the flax grower. I have been interested
all my lifetime in the growth and handling of flax, fitting and preparing it to
go to the textile workers. Much money
was scattered about in employment in that
very useful trade, and I hope that the
Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture will do their utmost to put the
claims of Ulster linen before the whole
world, so that it will get its rightful
place, and that the time will speedily
come when we will be able to sell Ulster
linen grown on Ulster soil, and handled
by Ulster people.
of
I think, on that point, there is a sum
which from Northern Iremoney
goes
land to the Imperial Parliament under
the Wheat Act, which could be better
utilised to subsidise the growing of either
flax or oats, which are the two staple
crops in Northern Ireland, as it known
to most of the Members of this House
that wheat cannot be so well grown in
Northern Ireland owing to the dampness
of our climate. I should like our
Minister of Agriculture to put our case
before the British Minister of Agriculture,
with a view to utilising some of this money
for the furtherance of the growth of those
two crops at home.
In Northern Ireland I think it is well
known to everyone that the farming industry is at the bottom of nearly everything. It is carried on under the most
adverse circumstances, and I think that
the utmost sympathy of our Government
should be given to those employed under
those conditions. The Member for
Pottinger stated in his speech yesterday,
I think, that the interests of the consumer should be looked after, and that
the producers were quite capable of
looking after their own interests. I do
not agree with the hon. Member for
Pottinger. While agreeing that the interests of the consumer ought to be looked
after, I also think that the interests of
the producer are of as vital importance,
because there is too much of a margin
between the price paid to the producer
and the price charged to the consumer.
The hon. Member for Dock (Mr.
Midgley) pressed the point that industrial
workers were not often able to purchase
the articles which they manufacture owing
to the glut in the manufacture of those
articles, with the consequent closing down.
of the works until the glut should be removed. The same does not happen in
the case of the farming community, because in the agricultural industry we must
look months ahead. We cannot put in
a crop and expect to take it out and
market it in a month or two. We must
prepare for months, and sometimes years,
ahead, and when we do so in order to
put our stuff on the market in proper
condition we must market it at a certain
time. If we meet with an adverse market
and a glut from foreign competition, then
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
20 DECEMBER 1933
those who are engaged in the agricultural
industry do not receive an economic return
for their labours, and as the produce
which they put on the market is in
very many cases perishable it must be
marketed no matter what the conditions
are, with the result in that case that the
farmer and the agricultural labourer are
both very badly hit.
I take off my hat to the agricultural
labourer who has to work in all classes of
weather and under all conditions, and
sometimes at a very poor wage.
I see in
the Gracious Speech that under the Agricultural Marketing Act schemes are being
prepared by the Ministry of Agriculture
dealing with the marketing of potatoes and
milk. The mover of the Address, the
hon. and learned Member for Willowfield
(Mr. Black), spoke of the marketing of
milk, and said it was a local thing, but I
beg to differ with the hon. and learned
Gentleman, because there is much milk or
cream shipped to Scotland and England
from our local creameries. Now the price
of milk has never been anything like so
low as it is at present in the memory, I
think, of anybody alive. The price we
receive per gallon for milk at the local
creameries is as low on the average as 4d
plus 2d a gallon for the skim milk we receive. Now 6d a gallon is an uneconomic
price for the producer. Therefore, I fail
to see what is going to be the result of a
scheme for milk if it does not put it on a
more fortunate basis than that. I hope
and trust that the things learned from the
Pigs Marketing Board will be of use to
those engaged in the formation of the
boards to carry out the milk scheme which
is to be put before us in the near future.
The marketing of pigs scheme, although
it is granted it has given a much better
price than we would have had otherwise,
gave a good deal of people a lot of disappointment disappointment in more ways
than one. A lot of people in my constituency, which is largely agriculturalalmost purely agricultural-were dissatisfied with the lavish scale of salaries and
expenses to the members and officials of
the Pigs Marketing Board, and also with
the deviation from our local markets of
the weighing and other expenses that were
usually spent in the small villages and
provincial towns. The grading of pigs
which is to come into force in the early
spring I hope will not also be taken away
from the local markets and placed either
in the stores of the curers or in the large
centres of our cities. After all, these
things are the just returns of the small
villages and towns and the neighbourhood
where this stuff is purchased, and I hope
before any further appointments are made
that the registered producers will get an
opportunity of expressing an opinion as to
how these ought to be made.
There is one other thing in the Speech
to which I would draw attention, and that
is the number of road accidents a thing
we are always up against in the various
country towns; and we hear a good deal
of complaints about the state of the roads.
Now if the roads were like smooth footpaths I do not believe it would be in the
interests of safety, because I think on
these roads, especially where corners have
been taken away and wide corners made,
the tendency of motorists is to speed at
way
those corners, and with consequent danger
to life and property. And there is also
another thing I want to draw the attention of the Prime Minister to, and that
is that there are pedestrians and slowmoving traffic that ought to be guided
and educated to understand the rules of
the road, and to give ordinary motorists
a chance to go along the roads.
There is just one other thing I want to
mention, and that is: "A Measure will
also be laid before you dealing with the
qualifying period of residence governing
the registration of voters in Northern Ireland." I think that legislation on that
point is long overdue. I believe that this
thing ought to have been tackled
previously. However, it is better late
than never. I hope the qualifying period
will be made sufficiently long to prevent
those who are not our friends, in fact
very
often the open enemies of the Province,
from settling down and becoming registered
voters in a very short time. Unless I go
on to deal with insects and pests, I think
I will leave the rest of the King's Speech
and the debate to more able hands, lest
I myself might be classed as one of the
insects.

We shall find that unemployment has increased as the result of every new scientific invention applied to industry.
I, myself, am very glad to notice an

our object as legislators must be is not

the moral point of view-but to mitigate
the evils of unemployment.
I am perfectly satisfied that we can mitigate the

I agree with what the hon. Member for

produce. I believe that in agriculture
to-day the current is too swift for the
farmer to stand against it much longer. I
regret to have to say that the farming
population of Northern Ireland are in
a very bad position financially, and I am
delighted to think that after all we have
reached a new experimental stage in
these marketing schemes. I repeat what
I said on a former occasion, that the only
hope of salvation for the farmer is in
marketing schemes and quotas combined
with tariffs. It is impossible for a
farmer to go on producing his crops at
an economic loss. When you to-day consider the price of farm produce and put
against that the total cost of production,
it is a wonder the farmers have been able
to stem the tide so long.
I feel I should pay a compliment to the
Minister of Agriculture, and I sympathise
with him very much, because he is
stepping into harness at one of the most
momentous times in the history of the
farming industry. I think it is the duty
of the agricultural Members on both sides
of the House to give him all the help they
possibly can. The pigs marketing scheme
has come into operation, and I believe
has been successful. If that scheme had
not been in force I believe that the price
of pork to the farmer would be something
like 40s a cwt. I am delighted that it
has survived all the attacks made upon
it and is now on the way to prosperity.
If that scheme had failed it would
have been a disastrous thing for the
agriculturists.
The Ministry, I understand, have
issued a milk scheme and a potato scheme,
and we in Ulster are very much interested
in those schemes, because the figures
relating to potatoes are something like a
total crop of a million tons to a million
people in Ulster, and in England a total
crop of four million tons to forty million
people. The hon. Member for Shankill
said we ought to step in front of Britain.
In regard to these marketing schemes
any man with an ounce of sense knows
that we must depend upon Britain for
our market.
It is a great compliment to
Ulster that we are allowed a quota of
200,000 tons a year under this new
marketing scheme.
It will be a great
relief to the farmer to know that that
outlet is there. Further, I think it has
been announced that if any more are re-

Debate on the Address

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Fryar]
but the Member for North Antrim (Sir
Robert Lynn) has applied the acid test
to this dream as a solution of the problem
of unemployment. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) He told the House that
the Socialist Party went into power in
Great Britain and Northern Ireland in
1929 with a mandate to solve the problem
of unemployment. What was the result
of the acid test? Unemployment increased by leaps and bounds, and reached
the highest figure it has ever attained.
He told us it has failed everywhere it
has been tried. It failed in Italy, where
it only held the reins of power for a few
weeks. In the early 1920's the Socialist
Party in Italy took possession of all the
factories and workshops. It failed to pay
the wages of its workers, I think in the
third week. Chaos followed, and the
King had to call in Mussolini, a military
dictator, whose followers bludgeoned to
death all persons who attempted to speak
freely on any platform. It has failed in
Russia. The mass manufacture of steam
tractors closed down Ford's works in
Cork. The herding together of men and
women, boys and young girls in great
camps, with no respect for sacred family
ties, like cattle in the field, can only end
in disaster, and no right-minded man,
much less a Christian, can support it.
Another feature of the speeches from
the Opposition was the claim that the
Roman Catholics are not receiving fair
play. The greatest unfairness, they say,
is the way they have been treated with
regard to education. They say that the
Amending Act of 1930 only benefited
Protestants. That is not so; in a sense
it benefited Roman Catholics more.
Under it a transferred school must have
a management committee, 50 per cent. of
its members to be appointed by the
transferors of the school, and 25 per cent.
appointed by the parents of the pupils
attending the school. The Regional
Committee only appoints the remaining
25 per cent. So the Roman Catholics if
they transfer a school can have 75 per
cent. of the committee of management
Roman Catholics. The committee of
management can secure that the teacher
whom they appoint will be a Roman
Catholic, because the Regional Committee must appoint one of the three
teachers whose names the committee of
management sent forward to them, and
they can appoint all three Roman
Catholics. If they transfer, they get 100
per cent. of all repairs, lighting, heating
equipment. If they do not transfer
they can appoint a 4 and 2 Committee,
4 appointed by the owners of the school,
and 2 by the Regional Committee;
in this case they only get 50 per cent.
for repairs, etcetera.
A good deal of light on the attitude of
the Catholic clergy on this subject was
shown when the Parish Priest of Bangor
applied to the Regional Committee of
County Down for a grant to build a new
school in Bangor, and the committee
replied that they would make a grant of
about £4,000 if he appointed a 4 and 2
Committee. During the discussion a
certain Parish Priest was the only
member of the Down County Committee
who opposed the grant, and he said with
regard to the 4 and 2 Committee, "I
don't believe in committees.
The only
committee I believe in is a committee of
one, and that one the Parish Priest."
So you see the cause of the whole evil is
the Roman Catholic clergy will not trust
the Roman Catholic laity.

the Pigs Marketing Scheme, 1 believe
that the people of this Province are
absolutely satisfied that it is a scheme
which has benefited them already, and
which will benefit them to an enormous
extent in the future. My experience
must be different from his, because I can
say that farmers of all classes and of all
creeds in my constituency have come to
me and expressed to me their gratitude
for the scheme, in spite of all the difficulties which have undoubtedly been encountered, and of the chaotic conditions which prevailed for some time
and their belief that it would be of
enormous benefit for the future of agriculture. I believe that there is a misapprehension in the minds of the people,
and possibly of some hon. Members in this
House, and certainly in
certainly in the mind,
judging from his words, of the hon.
Member for South Tyrone. I do not
think that the Marketing Board was set
up merely to sell live pigs through that
board. I believe the Marketing Board
is there in order to carry out the necessary
steps to ensure that producers shall
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mrs. Parker]
market their produce to the best
advantage, whether in the live market
or in the dead market. There, it seems
to me, we differ in our conclusions, because I am absolutely satisfied that the
Pigs Marketing Board has done, under
great difficulties, everything in its power
to help producers throughout the country.
I think I can claim, though I am not
a farmer, to have been as much in touch
as most hon. Members representing farming constituencies with the markets and
with the farmers everywhere, and I am
confident, from what I saw of the working of the Pigs Marketing Board and of
the difficulties of all buyers and producers, that those who were responsible
-and I am referring to the chairman
of the Pigs Marketing Board-have had a
most difficult and harassing task, and one
which they have been carrying out in a
very remarkable way for the benefit of
the farming community. And I would
like to say that I do not believe that any
salary or acknowledgment is too great
for the Civil Service head of the Ministry of Agriculture, now the head of that
board. I am absolutely convinced that
his qualifications were the finest that
could possibly be found for the post, and
that he has carried out his duties in the
most remarkable manner.
I do want to go one step further
in speaking of this scheme promised in
the King's Speech. I hope very much
that the Minister of Agriculture will
bear in mind the representations that I
know have been made to him from all
over the country with regard to the carrying out of this scheme of grading, which
we hope will take place in the local
markets. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I believe it is absolutely essential for the
benefit of all classes of the community,
not just of the farmer, but for the benefit
of the local market authorities and of
the trade of these small towns, and
especially for the benefit of the small
farmers as distinct from the large farmers,
that there should not be this danger of
too much centralisation in large cities. I
beg that this matter will be considered,
and carefully considered, before we meet
again in March.
There are a great many things I would
like to say in connection with the King's
Speech, but I am not going to deal with
them to-night. Just in conclusion I would
like to say that I think I am representing
the views of my constituents when I say
that we are delighted to see that the
authorities are effectively maintaining law
and order in our midst, and that they
propose, if necessary, taking further steps
to maintain law and order. I would like
to say on behalf of those whom I represent
here that if any further steps are necessary in this connection I am confident
that the Minister of Home Affairs and
the Government will have the support of
every law-abiding citizen, and that we
hope that there will be no holding back
or delay in taking those necessary steps.
I would just, before sitting down, like to
say in connection with this matter of law
and order that I noticed some of the remarks made by the hon. Member for Mid
Derry in connection with my Colleague
the hon. Member for Derry City. The
hon. Member for Derry City is a British
citizen, and of that I am sure he is very
proud, and nothing would make him wish.
to give up that British citizenship or
state that he was glad he was no longer
a British citizen. That is the fundamental
difference between him and the hon.
Member for Mid Derry when he spoke
of the Free State and Northern Ireland.
It is a very different thing giving up
one's citizenship of Northern Ireland,
which means one's British citizenship, and
renouncing citizenship of a part of a
country which was formerly British, but
which perhaps may very soon be British
no longer. In any case I wish to join
with those who support this Address in
reply to the Speech from the Throne.
I am
Rev. Professor CORKEY: It is a great

feel that when Standing Orders are set

particularly glad to see that the Government is not going to have any delay in
adopting the Insurance Measure which has

existence at the present time, but I feel

that all these marketing schemes will be

I am also glad that the Government is going to take notice of the
tremendous number of motor accidents
that are occurring in our midst. It
will be very difficult indeed to prevent accidents of this kind from occurring, and yet I feel it is the duty of
every Government to do what it can to
reduce their number. Might I say that
I think those Members of this House who
are also members of the City Corporation,
might urge upon that body the desirability of modifying their tramway
system. I believe that a great number
of these accidents would be obviated if
the City Council would introduce the railless trolley tram system, which would
enable tramcars, on lifting passengers
and setting them down, to draw up alongside the footpath. But until that better
tram system is introduced I do not think
that this legislature would be going beyond its rights if it made a law requiring
all motorists to come to a stand behind a
tramcar which is also standing, with the
exception, perhaps, of the central part of
the city where all traffic moves very
slowly.
Might I bring also before the notice of
the Government the desirability of trying
to impress upon motor drivers the great
value of sobriety. Here is a matter in
which we in this House are all in absolute
There is no difference of
agreement.
opinion in regard to this matter, but the

filtered down to the great number of those

trying to impress upon motor drivers the

undertake should they in any way impair
their senses prior to taking charge of a

While I have made those few remarks I
am glad the Government is not going to
be inveigled during the present Parliament into any very contentious legislation.
I am surprised at some of the observations
that have been made in this connection. I
am greatly surprised that there are still a
considerable number of Members in this
House who would like to undo the happy
Sunday legislation we have enjoyed in
this country for the past fifty or sixty
years, and which was piloted through the
Imperial Parliament by a predecessor of
my own who left his work in the Theological College in order to champion Sunday
closing in the Imperial Parliament. Those
people have nothing to complain about.
Might I mention one or two facts
which I have got to-day from the Ulster
Tourist Development Association. They
have had a record year. Things are
booming with the tourist traffic. Under
the happy laws we owe to the Prime
Minister this country is becoming a very
popular resort for holiday-makers from
all parts of the world. The Bangor
Borough Council, for example, had a
most excellent season, a record season,
with an increase of 63 per cent. in
tourists over 1932. Donaghadee and
district enjoyed one of the best seasons
it has ever had. Newcastle Urban
Council had a record season, the number
of tourists exceeding that of any previous
year. Portrush and Portstewart had a
similar happy experience, and the same
testimony is given by the Belfast and
County Down Railway Co., whose traffic
shows an increase of approximately 30
per cent. over 1932, and the same experience was enjoyed by the Great Northern Railway Co., the Ulster Imperial
Line, Thomas Cook & Sons, and many
other tourist agencies. These facts were
received to-day from the secretary of the
Ulster Tourist Development Association,
who desires to be absolutely impartial in
this matter, and would not give me any
further facts than those which were
printed in his annual report.
