The Late Mr. Joseph Devlin, M.P.
I
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): With your permission, Mr.
Speaker, and the indulgence of the House,
I would like, first of all, to apologise for
not being in my place yesterday.
hurried home as fast as I possibly could.
I wish to take this opportunity, the first
I have had of paying a tribute to the
memory of Mr. Joseph Devlin. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I have already
done so in my private capacity, but I
think that it will meet the wishes of
every
Member in this House if some record is
placed upon Hansard, as we call it. I
think we should have some permanent
record expressive of our feelings during
the Parliamentary career of our late
colleague. He never claimed to be the
leader of the Opposition. He
diffident on that matter, but, nevertheless,
I think that we all recognised he was an
outstanding figure on the Opposition
benches. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It is in consequence of that that I feel
that this House should place upon the
records the appreciation that we had of
his memory.
was
I had some thirty years knowledge of
Mr. Joseph Devlin. I served with him
in the Imperial Parliament and in this
House, and throughout all those years,
although necessarily, from the political
point of view, we differed very severely,
I never met a man who advanced his
cause more ably or who, on the other hand,
showed so little vindictiveness and bore
less malice after our discussions were over.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) He was
an outstanding figure at Westminster in
his early days amongst a lot of men who
were working for what they thought was
the best interests of their countrymen,
and his eloquence, his outstanding ability
in presenting his case and, I may say, the
affection that everybody at Westminster
had for him, passed the record that could
be attributed to any other Nationalist
Member. He was also an outstanding
figure beyond politics in the way in which
he strove, unremittingly, for the underdog, not only in the City of Belfast, but
throughout the Ulster area. So far as
his private life is concerned, I think he
was absolutely beyond all reproach. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) He was kindly,
and a sportsman to the backbone. Those
of us who knew him in public and in
private life deplore the loss of a great
Ulsterman, and we pay this small tribute
to him here, and tender to his relatives
our sympathy and our grief.
a
Mr. HEALY: On these benches, my
Friends and I feel the difficulty of putting
into words our feelings on this occasion.
Though other sections of this House and
the community may keenly regret thepassing of one who occupied such
prominent part in public affairs for so
many years, yet ours is a greater and a
more personal sorrow. He was at once
our adviser, our leader and our friend.
Like many pioneers in national fields, he
did not live to see the flowering of his
ideals. To his country's service he gave
all his energies and time, his talents and,
finally, life itself. That he should have
been serving a lost cause with such an
enthusiasm as his, he hardly realised,
even at the end. His faith was amazing.
When he came into this House he hoped
he could serve, not only the interests of
his own people, but the wider interests of
democracy in Belfast.
He believed his influence would have
tended to moderate political passion and
pave the way to a better feeling of peace
281 Late Mr. Joseph Devlin

7 MARCH 1934
Supplementary Estimates
and goodwill amongst all creeds and
classes. He struggled hard to attain this
object. It would be foolish, on my part,
to pretend that he was not disappointed
at many recent happenings both North
and South. If he failed in the major
ideal to which he devoted all his talents
he succeeded in many of the minor
schemes for the betterment of the working
classes. The mill-workers in Belfast owe
to him the beginning of a series of Acts.
which gave them rights in the matter of
pay and hours of labour so different to
what they had known in early days. He
had a good deal to do with the Labourers
Acts, which enabled district councils to
give decent houses and plots of land to
working people at rents as low as 2s per
week. He had a passion for the service
of the poor. He could not keep money in
his pocket. He loved to give even when
he could ill afford it.
""
Those who talk critically in these days.
of politics and politicians must revise
their verdict when they consider the case
of Joseph Devlin, who served everyone
but himself. Indeed, he used to say it
was only in the years after 1918, when
he left politics, or when temporarily
politics had left him, that he had any
time to look after his own affairs. Widely
read, particularly in the biographies of
prominent men, he had few illusions as
to the public memory. He used to say
that Ireland killed many of her greatest
leaders. A little later I heard him say:
"This is a strange country! They fling
stones at you when you are alive and they
throw flowers at you when you are dead.'
It was the very irony of fate that there
should have met, across his grave, for the
first time in years, not merely the representatives of North and South, but the
leaders of the contending parties in both
areas. Some one has said: "For one day
we had a united Ireland." It was the
ideal which always drove him forward,
towards which his feet ever led.
He was
not destined to see it realised. His ship
went down almost in sight of port. Those
of us who walk, however haltingly, in
his footsteps, feel his life to be an inspiration on the rugged and rocky road that
all of us must travel who try to serve the
interests of a united Ireland.
Mr. BEATTIE: I wish to associate
myself with the remarks of the Prime
Minister. I feel that he has covered the
whole career of the deceased Member for
Central. I had not as long an experience
of the late Member as the Prime Minister,
but I remember very well some of the
great fights in our city. I always felt
that no matter how bitter they were as
soon as they were over the late Member
for Central was always the same jolly
fellow again. The Prime Minister has
only voiced the feelings of Ulster in the
very kindly references he has made to the
work of the late Member for Central, and
we on this side of the House associate
ourselves with those remarks fully. I as
a young Member of this House never had
the privilege of sitting in the Imperial
Parliament alongside the late Member,
but in this House I can say he was personally the best friend to me when I was
sitting in isolation that ever I found in
any assembly in which I have taken part.
He is a loss to this House and to Belfast,
while his loss to Ulster is greater than we
yet realise. Although he has gone he
will live long in the memory of the people
of Belfast and of Ulster as a whole.
wish to pay my personal tribute to the
memory of the late Member for Central.

Ministry of Agriculture
7 MARCH 1934
Sir BASIL BROOKE: This Supplementary Estimate is
is in respect of
additional expenditure incurred by the
Ministry during the present financial year
in connection with (1) the Agricultural

the quota schemes for regulation of
imports of agricultural produce, and (2)
services rendered by the veterinary staff
of the Ministry, under an agency arrangement with the Board of Trade in the
administration of the Cattle (Import
Regulation) Order, 1933. The Estimate
has been reduced to a token sum by

The first item is a sum of £360 for
temporary staff. Following the introduction last summer of schemes for the
marketing of pigs and bacon it became
the duty of the Ministry under the
Agricultural Marketing Act to compile
from its agricultural statistics a list of
pig producers, and to send to each producer on the list particulars of the Pigs
Marketing Scheme, together with a form.
of application for registration as a pig
producer. The Ministry has also, during
the last few weeks, acting under the
authority of Section 2 (4) of the Act,
conducted elections of members of the
Pigs Marketing Board and Bacon Marketing Board respectively. For this work
the Ministry's permanent staff had to be
supplemented for short periods,
required by the employment of a number
of temporary clerks, whose wages are provided under this heading. The cost,
including wages and other expenses, of
preparation of the list of producers and
of conducting the election, is recoverable
under the Act from the Pigs Marketing
Board, and the necessary provision is
included in this Estimate under Subhead G. Appropriation-in-Aid.
as
Under Subhead A (8) (Veterinary
Inspectorate) is provided the estimated
cost of salaries of veterinary and other
part-time staff employed in connection.
with the Cattle (Import Regulations)
Order, 1933, which came into operation
on 22nd December last. The Ministry,
at the request of the Board of Trade, has
agreed to undertake, as agent for the
Board, the duty of classification for the
purposes of the Order of the cattle
imported into Northern Ireland from the
Irish Free State, as it was considered
that this work could, most conveniently

and economically, be carried out by the
Ministry's veterinary inspectors, assisted
by a few expert advisers employed part
time as required. The entire cost of the
salaries and expenses of the staff, while
so employed, is recoverable from the
Board of Trade.
Under Subhead C, Collection of
Agricultural Statistics, provision is made
for the cost of the expenses of the police
in collecting information for a census of
live stock which was made in January
last. In former years the Ministry
collected statistics of live stock, together
with statistics as to crops, etc., once
annually, in the month of June. In
view, however, of the need for accurate
figures of home production to facilitate
the Imperial Government in deciding upon
the volume of meat imports to be admitted
from foreign countries, it has become
necessary to have information as to the
live stock population in mid-winter, as
it is found that, owing to seasonal
fluctuations, the summer figures are not,
in themselves, an entirely satisfactory
basis for such calculations.
The provision under Subhead E represents additional postage incurred by the
Ministry in sending particulars of the
Pigs Marketing Scheme with forms of
application for registration to over 30,000
pig producers. Allowance is also made
for cost of postage on the reply envelopes
enclosed with these communications.
Under G, Receipts Appropriated-in-
Aid, provision is made for the recovery
of £1,300 from the Imperial Government,
as the cost of the services of the Ministry's
staff for the purpose of the Cattle Import
Restrictions. This sum represents, in
addition to the cost of salaries, estimated
at £600, already referred to, the
travelling expenses of the veterinary staff,
estimated at £700. It was not necessary
to make a supplementary provision for
travelling expenses, as this cost is met
from savings on the travelling subhead.
The remaining item under Subhead G
is the estimated sum recoverable from the
Pigs Marketing Board in respect of the
cost of temporary staff and postage under
Subheads A (4) and E, already referred
to and, in addition, a sum representing
the salaries of the Ministry's established
officers employed on the compilation of
lists of producers and the conduct of
elections. Included also in this sum is

CLASS VI. No. 2.
AGRICULTURAL SERVICES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum, not exceeding £10, be granted to His Majesty for
the service of the year ending 31st March,
1934, to defray the expenses of the
Ministry of Agriculture in respect of
agricultural education and research,
improvement of live stock, agricultural
development and credit, afforestation and
diseases of animals, including sundry
grants-in-aid (16 Geo. V., c. 4 (N.I.) )."
Sir BASIL BROOKE: This Estimate
is to provide funds for the maintenance
of the poultry research work which is
being conducted by the Agricultural
Research Institute of Northern Ireland.
As stated in the printed Estimate, this
work was financed by grants from the
Empire Marketing Board until the dissolution of the Board on 30th September
last. In view of the great importance to
Northern Ireland of the poultry industry
and as research into poultry nutrition
constitutes a vital factor in the Ministry's
plan for development of this industry, it
was imperative that this work should continue and it was, accordingly, decided to
provide the necessary funds by grants
from the Vote for agricultural services.
It was arranged, with the consent of
H.M. Treasury, that the entire assets,
that is, poultry houses, equipment and
poultry, which were provided out of the
grants from the Empire Marketing Board,
should be left undisturbed at the disposal
of the Ministry, on the understanding
that the results of the work should continue to be available to the Empire
generally.
This Estimate provides for grants to
cover the cost of this work, for the halfyear from 1st October last to 31st March,
and has been reduced to a token sum by
savings on other services borne on this
Vote. It is the intention of the Ministry
that the cost of this service, estimated at
£1,350 per annum, will continue to be
met out of economies on other agricultural
services.
Question put, and agreed to.

The second item in the Supplementary
Estimate with which we are dealing
relates to a matter which is now coming
before the Committee for the first time.
Many hon. Members will recollect the
passing, in June, 1932, of the New
Industries (Development) Act, which gave
power to my Ministry, after consultation
with an Advisory Committee appointed
for the purpose, to make grants out of
public funds to undertakings established
subsequent to 31st October, 1931, for the
purpose of manufacturing or producing
goods or commodities of a kind not being
produced in Northern Ireland at that
date. The grants were to take the form
of annual payments over a stated period,
in respect of the cost of acquiring the
site of the premises in which any such
new undertaking was established.
I regret that the benefits authorised by
the Act have not hitherto attracted any
large-scale industries to the Province, but
I think that hon. Members will agree
that this was hardly to be expected in
view of the difficult economic conditions
which have prevailed everywhere since the
Act was passed. A number of small
industries have, however, been established
in the last couple of years, but it is, of
course, a matter of no small difficulty to
find industries which, by their originality
and newness, will come within the limited
scope of the Act. Three such concerns
have, however, established their claims to
grants, and the provision for which
sanction is now sought is in respect of the
payments which fall due to these firms
during the current financial year.

schemes at the present time in operation
promoted by the Belfast Corporation.
The estimated cost of carrying out these
schemes is £255,000, and engaged in
those schemes at the moment there are
no less than 1,060 persons. There are
six other schemes being promoted in Belfast by other authorities at a cost estimated at £462,000, and on these relief
schemes there are 237 persons working.
In other words, on relief schemes in
Belfast at the moment there are 1,297
persons working each week.

I got up to defend the position of the

duce legislation to restore bag nets in

Mr. ROBB: I have been asked by my
right hon. Friend to reply. I would
remind the hon. Member that the com-
Imittee to which he refers found itself
unable to support the claim of the fixed
draft net owners to have one bag net
substituted for each existing fixed draft
net, but recommended that an attempt be
made to devise a scheme whereby substitution could be effected on the basis of
one bag net for every three existing draft
nets. Such a scheme necessarily implies
agreement amongst the owners of the
fixed draft nets, and also an arrangement
whereby ownership of the existing nets.
could be so adjusted as to allow of the
one-to-three proportion being applied.
The possibilities of devising such a scheme
have formed the subject of correspondence
with the association which represents the
fixed draft net owners, and have also been
fully discussed by the Ministry's Fishery
Advisory Council. So far, however, the
necessary measure of agreement has not
been reached, only one owner, representing four out of the twenty-two draft nets
concerned, having definitely expressed his
willingness to accept substitution on the
basis suggested by the committee. As the
hon. Member will appreciate, it would be
inadvisable to attempt a piecemeal
solution of this difficult problem and,
whilst the Minister of Commerce is still
prepared to lend any assistance he can
towards procuring agreement amongst the
fixed draft net owners, he is unable to
consider the question of legislation until
such time as general agreement has been
reached.
Mr. LEEKE: Am I to take it from
that that the Government intend to
proceed no further with legislation recommended?
Mr. ROBB: I can only repeat that,
pending an agreement amongst the
owners of fixed draft nets, legislation will
not be introduced.

TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES TO
MINISTERS.
4. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state if any
allowance above the ordinary Cabinet
salary and remuneration is
is paid to
Ministers and Members of the Government visiting England, or other places,
on business in connection with their office
as Members of the Government, and, if
so, the amount of such allowance.
Mr. POLLOCK: Following the practice
that obtained in 1920 for certain British
Cabinet Ministers who had to travel from
their official headquarters in connection
with Departmental duties, Northern Irish
Ministers receive subsistence allowance at
the rate of two guineas per day when on
official duty in Great Britain; this rate
is fixed in excess of the Civil Service
rate, as it is intended to cover expenses
of entertainment and other outlay
incidental to the journeys of a Minister
of Cabinet rank.
Parliamentary Secretaries and other
Members of the Government only receive
the normal rate of 22s per day.
Mr. NIXON: Would a person occupying the position of Lord Mayor of Belfast
be entitled to as much subsistence allowance as a Cabinet Minister?
Mr. SPEAKER: That is a different
thing altogether.
PAYMENT OF SALARIES DURING
ELECTION.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state if the
salaries and remuneration of Cabinet
Ministers and Parliamentary Secretaries
are continued from date of dissolution to
election and from election to assembling
of Parliament.
Mr. POLLOCK: The reply is in the
affirmative, provided that His Grace the
Governor has not, in the meantime,
revoked the appointments of such persons
as Cabinet Ministers and Parliamentary
Secretaries.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the Minister
extend the same generosity to the Members of this House who have been returned
and carried out their official duties all
along?
Mr. POLLOCK: Ministers must attend
to their official duties. They are not
relieved at all by reason of the difference
in time between the dissolution of Parliament and starting again.
Mr. NIXON: Is this not controlled by
the old rule, "Unto him that hath shall
be given and unto him that hath not shall
be taken away even that which he seemeth
to have."
Mr. POLLOCK: This is not a place for
moralising.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of that unsatisfactory answer I will raise the matter
on the Adjournment.

STAMP DUTY.
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
Question proposed, "That it is expedient to amend the law relating to stamp
duty, so as to provide for the application
of the proceeds of certain stamp duties,
and to enable local authorities to pay the
stamp duty on certain instruments otherwise than by means of impressed or
adhesive stamps."
Mr. POLLOCK: The Resolution which
I am about to move is the preliminary to
a small Measure relating to stamp duties.
I may say at once that it has no reference
to any question of increasing taxation.
It has a two-fold purpose. The first
part is intended to give effect to an
arrangement which has been entered into
with the Incorporated Law Society of
Northern Ireland for the provision of
additional financial assistance to that
Society in connection with the machinery
for the education of young entrants into
the profession. The reason for the proposed inclusion of this provision in a Bill
relating to stamp duties is that this subvention or assistance is to be related to
the stamp duties payable upon the
indentures of solicitors' apprentices. The
second part of the resolution will enable
arrangements to be made with local
authorities for the payment of stamp
duties upon certain Local Government
documents upon a certified return basis
With regard to the first part of the
Resolution, it will be within the recollection of many Members of the House that
the principle of assistance to the Incorporated Law Society was admitted by our
Government so far back as the year 1923,
since which time an annual payment of
£200 has been made to the Society and
met out of the Ministry of Finance Vote.
I may, perhaps, remind the House that
this was on the analogy of a similar grant
paid to the Incorporated Law Society
of Ireland before our Government was
established.
It is proposed in the Bill to which this
Resolution relates to alter the character
of this grant by issuing it directly from
the Exchequer instead of voting it
annually, and increasing its amount substantially by making it equivalent to the
total amount yielded by the duties paid
in each financial year upon the Articles
of Clerkship entered into by solicitors'
apprentices, subject to an over-ruling
maximum of £1,200.
The main reason for this considerable
advance in the scale of Government
assistance to the Society is set out in
Clause 1 of the Bill. In effect, the
position is that the Society, which, as
has always been fully admitted, exists
for the purpose of exercising functions of
a public character in connection with
legal education and the general control of
the solicitors' profession, has satisfied the
Government that the funds at present at
its command, derived in the main from
annual subscriptions from the members of
the solicitors' profession, are insufficient
to enable it to carry out these duties
efficiently. It is at a great financial disadvantage as compared with the corresponding societies in England and the
Irish Free State, where the conditions
and traditions of 250 or 300 years have
given opportunities for the accumulation
of funds upon which they can draw. The
Society of Northern Ireland has in its
short life only succeeded in accumulating
a small working balance. Therefore, I
say, being at that disadvantage forms a
cogent argument in favour of a sufficient
grant to enable them to carry on the work
to which I have referred.
There is a further consideration which
has influenced me and the Government.
It is with regard to the functions of the
Ways and Means-
Stamp Duty
8 MARCH 1934
Society in connection with the provision
of law books. Such manuals are of use
not only to lawyers but to private persons.
Mr. BEATTIE: They would not get
nearer than a hundred yards of them.
Mr. POLLOCK: But their existence is
of the greatest convenience to public
Departments. It is clear that in an area
of the size of Northern Ireland, the production of such books without some form
of public assistance could never be
economically practicable. Such assistance
can from time to time be afforded by such
a society as the Incorporated Law Society
if only it has funds available for the purpose. I am, therefore, of the opinion that
the amounts now proposed to be paid to
the society, when added to the sums provided by the members themselves, will be
only sufficient to enable the society to
carry out its functions adequately. The
proposed grant is on a logical basis, for
it is related to the number of apprentices,
and obviously the educational costs of the
society rise or fall with this number also.
The second part of the Resolution arises
out of the passing of the Finance Act of
1933. It will be recalled that Section 3
of that Act provided for the repeal of
certain enactments exempting from stamp
duty various instruments made for Local
Government purposes. It has been represented to me that if the duty upon certain
of these instruments, especially rate
receipts, is to be paid by means of
impressed or adhesive stamps in the ordinary way, a considerable inconvenience to
local authorities would result. The
Clause, which is a permissive one, therefore provides that local authorities may
enter into an arrangement whereby they
will remit the duty directly to the
Exchequer instead of having to stamp
each document.
I am sure that the House will find no
difficulty in agreeing in principle to the
terms of this Resolution, which are general
in character, and do not bind the House
to details. It is only a formal preliminary
to the Bill itself, which will contain much
more detailed particulars of the proposals.
I commend the Resolution to the Committee. I beg to move.

1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state, in
respect to the past two years (1) the
total number of persons murdered in
cases where no person was made amenable; (2) the total number of cases of
attempted murder where no one was
made amenable.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The number of cases
of murder in which no person was made
amenable was two in 1932 and four in
1933. The number of cases of attempted
murder in which no person was made
amenable was nil in 1932 and three in
1933.

SMALL DWELLINGS ACQUISITION
ACT IN DERRY.
3. Mr. McCARROLL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether his attention
has been called to the grave distress and
hardship caused by the instalments payable by the
occupiers of subsidy
houses built under the Small Dwellings
Acquisition Act in Derry, and to the
appeal addressed to the Corporation
concerning this matter; whether it is a
fact that, with the addition of rates to
other charges in respect of these houses,
there is now imposed on the occupiers an
outlay wholly disproportionate to their
earnings; and whether owing to the
altered conditions arising from depression
and other causes, it is proposed to take
any steps by extension of the term for
repayment, or otherwise to alleviate the
position of these tenants.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware
that some time ago persons who had purchased their houses with the aid of loans
advanced by the Londonderry Corporation under the provisions of the Small
Dwellings Acquisition Acts approached
the Corporation for a revision of the
terms of repayment. The administration
of these Acts rests primarily with the
Londonderry Corporation, and the
functions of my Ministry under the
provisions of these Acts are confined to
seeing that the statutory conditions have
been complied with and that the loans are
advanced on adequate security.
It would appear from the minutes of
the meetings of the Corporation that the
Council have the matter under consideration, but there are obvious difficulties
of a financial character in altering the
terms of the advances at this stage.

the autumn of last year when the procarcases.
ducers in certain areas persisted in

In order to alleviate the hardship to producers, the Board, although

PIGS MARKETING BOARD
CHAIRMAN.
10. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state the
terms on which the Chairman of the
Pigs Marketing Board holds office, and
whether it will be in the power of the
newly-elected Pigs Marketing Board to
revise his salary.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Under the
provisions of Sub-section 3, of Section 2,
of the Agricultural Marketing Act, the
chairman of any Board is nominated by
the Minister of Agriculture and holds
office in the first instance for a period of
at least two years. The Chairman of the
Northern Ireland Pigs Marketing Board
holds a position which is not comparable
with that of the Chairman of the British
Pigs Marketing Board. In the case of
the Northern Ireland Board the Chairman is, in addition, the Chief Executive
Officer of the Board. This arrangement
was made by the Board in order to minimise the number of appointments and
keep expenditure at the lowest possible
level. In the interests of the scheme,
the Board felt that this arrangement
with regard to the dual function of the
chairman was essential in the initial
stages, and in the terms of the appointment reserved the right to review the
salary and the duties in the light of
experience.

AGRICULTURAL PRODUCE (MEAT
REGULATION) ACT, 1930.
11. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state the total amount paid by pig producers in 1933 under the Meat Inspection
Act, 1931, whereby the curers are
authorised to deduct the sum of 1s per
pig bought by them; and whether he can
state the total value of the pig carcases or
portions of carcases condemned by the
Ministry's veterinary inspectors under the
same Act.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: It is assumed
that the hon. and gallant Member's
question has reference to the deduction
from the price of pork carcases referred
to in Section 10 of the Agricultural Produce (Meat Regulation) Act (Northern
Ireland), 1930. That section reads as
follows:-
"Where the carcase of a pig is bought
by, or on behalf of a licensed bacon
curer, the buyer may deduct from the
price of the carcase such sum, not
exceeding one shilling, as may, from
time to time, be prescribed so as to
defray the expenses of the buyer and
to insure the buyer against loss in the
event of the carcase being subsequently
certified by an inspector, acting in the
exercise of his powers under this Act,
to be unfit for human consumption;
and if such deduction is made the seller
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Basil Brooke]
of the carcase shall not be liable in
respect of any loss arising in the aforesaid event."
It should be borne in mind that this
section was included in the Act expressly
for the purpose of protecting farmers who
sell pork carcases to curers. Before the
Act came into operation on the 1st May,
1931, the prevailing custom was that
each curer deducted a sum for porterage
of, usually, 6d per pig. Section 10 of the
Act simply permits this charge of 6d to
be increased to a charge not exceeding 1s,
and for the small extra fee of 6d the
farmer is fully protected against loss due
to condemnation. During the year 1933
the extra deduction of 6d per carcase
amounted
of

£9,234 17s. During the same year the
value of carcases and portions of carcases
condemned by the Ministry's veterinary
inspectors amounted to £2,127 9s 8d.
to an
In coming to this arrangement to secure

through condemnation the Ministry has

FLYING OF KITES OR BALLOONS.
12. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he has any knowledge
of a serious accident caused by a wire
attached to a kite coming in contact with
a live electricity cable; and whether, in
view of the great number of overhead
electric cables now in Northern Ireland,
the Government will take steps to prohibit
the sale of any dangerous wires for kites
or balloon attachment.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The unfortunate accident
to which the hon. Member refers has been
reported to my Ministry in accordance
with statutory requirements. With
regard to the second part of the question,
the hon. Member will appreciate the legal
and administrative difficulties involved in
the prohibition which he advocates, in
view of the fact that articles, such as wire
and string, are normally sold without
reference to the purposes for which they
are to serve. My information is that in
the present instance the accident was due
to the presence in the string of a number
of strands of fine copper wire, and it is
highly desirable that the public should be
warned not only of the danger of flying
kites in the vicinity of overhead electric
lines, but also of the very special danger
incurred where string of this type is used.

Trade with a view to having the examination centre in Belfast re-opened and

Resolution reported: "That it is
expedient to amend the law relating to
stamp duty, so as to provide for the
application of the proceeds of certain
stamp duties, and to enable local
authorities to pay the stamp duty on
certain instruments otherwise than by

Question proposed, "That the House do
agree with the Committee in the said
Resolution."
Mr. BEATTIE: I hope the House
will reject this Resolution, as it is built
upon class legislation. The House is
being asked to increase certain fees to a
particular class of persons in Northern
Ireland and also to provide for the local
authorities a simpler method than placing
stamps upon the several forms they use.
The latter part I do agree with, but the
former part I totally disagree with, and
as the two are combined in one I must
disagree with the whole. Now, for the
legal profession, as I have said may times.
in this House, I have very little gra."
If the laws of our country were properly
made and administered we would not
require them. They are a class which I
think the community could very well do
without. That being so, I think that
when the Minister comes into this House,
when finances are so low, to ask that the
amount of the grant should be increased
from £200 to £1,200, he is doing something for which he should be brought to
book.
Further, the Incorporated Law Society
of Northern Ireland could very well have
kept within the confines of the Irish
Incorporated Law Society. It was not
necessary for them to break away. But
breaks are often brought about by
political manoeuvres, and I think that
this is a break which was brought about
by a political manœuvre. What did this
society do to the Minister of Finance?
They told him that if they did not get
1,000 feet floor space their charter was
going to the King. And those are the
people who are going to be considered to
the extent of having their grant increased
from £200 to £1,200! What did they do
after they got established? If my son, or
the son of any working-class man, was
inclined to go in for the legal profession
there was a barrier erected, because one
of the qualifications is the possession of
an arts degree.
It was a struggle for a working man to
provide for his son during his period of
study under the old regime, but it is
impossible for a working man's son to
qualify under the new conditions laid
down by the Incorporated Law Society.
That is my reason for saying that this
profession is really a preserve of the rich
classes, who are quite competent to carry
on their affairs without assistance from
the poor.
I feel that if the Government
have money to throw away they could
throw it away in support of a cause which
is more deserving of our consideration
than that to which they wish to divert it
by this Resolution. One of the avenues

Mr. BLACK: I had not intended to
speak on this Motion, but the arguments
that have been offered in opposition to it
have been based on such gross misconceptions that there is some necessity to
endeavour to clear away those misconceptions. At the outset may I say that
this proposition to give £1,200 a year to
the Incorporated Law Society does not
effect the branch of the legal profession
to which I have the honour to belong.
It affects the solicitors' branch of the profession. The arguments which have been
addressed against this proposition are
two-fold. The first is that it is a grant
out of public moneys to one specific profession. The second argument is that it
is something in the way of class legislation on the ground that the persons
concerned in the control of that profession have imposed the necessity of
having a university degree in arts as a
condition of entering that profession.
Those are the two arguments that have
been used, and I hope to show the House
in a very few words that both those
arguments are entirely without foundation.
The first argument is that this is a
grant of £1,200 of public money, the
suggestion being that it is a grant out of
the pockets of the taxpayers to a particular profession or to individual members of that profession. It is nothing of
the sort. If hon. Members had taken
the trouble to read the Resolution they
would have found that the object of the
Bill to which the Resolution is the preliminary is designed to allocate certain
stamp duties. The Resolution deals
with stamp duties, and with stamp duties
only. What are these stamp duties?
They are duties paid by members of the
solicitors' profession. Before a young
man can be apprenticed as a solicitor he
has to pay a stamp duty of £80 on his
articles of indenture. He pays that into
the Exchequer of Northern Ireland.
Mr. MIDGLEY: And it becomes
public money.
Mr. BLACK: Before he is admitted as
a solicitor he has to pay a stamp duty of
£25. That also is paid into the
Exchequer of Northern Ireland, so that
before a person becomes a solicitor he has
paid one hundred guineas into the
Exchequer. I ask what other profession,
what trade is there which is required, as
a preliminary to qualifying in that trade,
to pay substantial amounts of that kind
to the Exchequer? I can only think of
Ways and Means-

a
one other, and that is my own branch of
the legal profession. Furthermore,
solicitor has to pay other stamp duties.
Every solicitor practising in Northern
Ireland, if he practises in Belfast, has to
pay £9 in stamp duty to the Exchequer,
and if he practises outside Belfast he has
to pay £6 a year stamp duty to the
Exchequer. What other profession or
what trade is there that is required to
contribute duties like that, and what profession contributes amounts like that?
Surely it is only right and proper that
part of those amounts should be allocated
for the benefit of the profession? The
total revenue from those stamp duties
amounts to in or about £5,000 a year, and
this proposition is that, of that sum of
£5,000 a year, there should be allocated
some £1,200, in or about a quarter of the
total sum received, for the necessary
duties of the Incorporated Law Society,
which are duties of a public nature, which
are duties of providing for the proper
education and training of the solicitors'
profession, and which are duties of providing for the necessary regulation and
discipline of the gentlemen of the profession.
If those duties were not undertaken by
that society a Government Department
would have to be set up to undertake
those duties, which are duties of a public
nature. I think this will not be cavilled
at, that out of the revenue of £5,000 a
year from members of the profession the
Government should at least return to
them the amount necessary to carry on
the organisation and discipline of the profession. So, instead of asking for money
out of public moneys the solicitors are
only getting back one-fourth of what they
contribute in the course of a year, a
contribution which no other profession or
trade is called upon to make. So much
for the first proposition, that it is public.
money they are asking for.
The second proposition is that this is
a body which has introduced class legislation by making the holding of a university
degree in arts a necessary preliminary to
entrance into the solicitors' profession.
My answer to that argument is that that
is entirely without foundation, for the
solicitors' profession in Northern Ireland
has made no such regulation. Apart
from the actual legal professional qualifications which are demanded, that everyone wishing to become a solicitor should
pass a preliminary examination somewhat
of the standard of the matriculation
examination, they have not made it a condition that a person entering the
profession should obtain a degree in arts.
Whoever has propagated that notion has
got into a state of muddle. He has
muddled up the solicitors' branch of the
profession with my branch, the ruling
body of which has made a regulation-
Mr. MIDGLEY: Certainly; it is your
body we are getting at.

form in legal documents. If a person
purports to be selling under a power given
to him, then for the protection of the
purchaser it is laid down in legal form
that the purchaser shall not be bound to
inquire whether the circumstances giving
rise to the power have or have not arisen.
If you had not got that protection you
might have a man paying a large sum of
money for a piece of land, and years
afterwards some person might come forward and say the person who sold that
piece of land had no right to sell it because the occasion of the exercise of his
powers had not, in fact, arisen. The object.
of putting this particular sub-section into
this Bill regarding the sale by railway
companies of unused land is to protect
the purchaser having to prove on some
subsequent occasion that the railway
company had no right to sell the land
because the circumstances under which
they had power to sell had not, in fact,
arisen. It is a common form of legal
document, and it is perfectly innocuous.

Widows' and Old Age Pensions.
Mr. NIXON: I have pleasure in
moving the Motion standing in my name.
I want to say at the outset that I am
satisfied there are people in this Chamber
now who will see this Motion become law
just the same as the people who opposed
the Old Age Pension Bills when they were
first introduced lived to see those Bills
become law in spite of their efforts. The
Motion reads:
"That in the opinion of this House
the Government should, in order to
make better provision for the happiness and comfort of aged people and
widows, and also in order to relieve
unemployment, proceed to increase all
Old Age Pensions, Insurance Pensions
and Widows' Pensions to £1 per week,
and also reduce the age limit by five
years in the case of both Insurance and
Old Age Pensions."
In order to keep myself right I beg to
move that Motion now. It appears to
me, and to a great many more people,
that there is a change an absolute
change in the conditions of employment,
not only in this country but all over the
world, and that you are always going to
have a substantial section of the population unemployed. That has been brought
about by science and the introduction and
application of machinery. Everyone in
this House knows-and hon. Gentlemen
who are manufacturers know better than
other people that by the introduction of
machinery a lot more can be produced
with fewer hands. If all the machinery
available and all the factories available
were used to the fullest capacity and
everyone was employed, the result would
be, and very soon be, that there would be
such a surplus of goods that they could
not be disposed of at an economic price.
The Minister of Labour, I think, assents
to that, and that being so we are never
going to have all the people employed
again. If you have to keep a section of
the people unemployed-and you will
have to do it I submit it is better to keep
the older people unemployed by giving
them something more than they are getting. No one could live, or attempt to
live, on 10s a week. I am not by any
means suggesting that a man could live
on £1 a week, and I do not want any hon.
Member later to-day to say that I did
suggest that.
One of the greatest proofs I can give
the House that there will always be a substantial section of the people unemployed
was the state of affairs ten years ago and
the state of affairs now. I do not want
to do it by way of casting up.
Some
times I do indulge in that. In November, 1923, there were over 42,000 people
unemployed in Northern Ireland, and the
Prime Minister, addressing an election
meeting in support of the hon. Member
(Sir Robert Lynn), who was then sitting
for a Belfast constituency, stated that if
the Imperial Parliament would not solve
the unemployment problem he would.
To-day we know things are better than
they were, and we are proud of it, but
the Minister of Labour is after telling me
that the number of unemployed is
65,000.
Mr. ANDREWS: 63,000 I said.
Mr. NIXON: The total has been
increased from 42,000 to 63,000 in ten
years,

Mr. NIXON: The Minister admitted
as much in this House in a debate in
regard to the position of single unemployed men. No, the figure of 63,000 is
not complete. Why waste time over it?
I am not blaming the Minister. I am
only showing, or proving the statement I
made at the outset, that owing to the
introduction of machinery for the purpose
of production all the people will never
again be employed. It is the same thing
across the water. If I may refer to it,
before the Labour Government came in
they promised they would do a lot for
unemployment, and it got worse. The
National Government promised that they
would do a lot for unemployment, and it
got worse. Under the National Government, presided over by Mr. Ramsay
MacDonald-and people are known by
the company they keep-there were in
Great Britain more unemployed than
ever before. This is not an attack on the
Minister. It is only showing that the
people will never all be employed again.
I remember the time if a man was a
shoemaker he would sit down in his house
in the City of Belfast. He might have
"Shoemaker" over his door or he might
not, but he could make a living. He had
a certain number of customers who went
to his house. He took a measure for a
pair of boots and made them and he was
able to live. There is practically no such
thing going on now. There are a lot of
people going out of business, even in the
boot repairing business, because the boots
are made so complete and perfect with
these new soles-uskide, I think they call
them that they never have to be soled
or half-soled again. They wear the boots
out. Even the stick-breakers in the
poorer class districts, who went to the
shipyards and got boxes and broke them
and sold them and so made an existence,
are being done out altogether, because
you can go into a shop now and buy firelighters at 5d and 6d a dozen, which are
far superior to anything the stickbreakers could put up. That has done
them out of a living.
I remember too, and most of the other
Members remember, that when a man got
it tight to live he would buy a horse and
hackney car and he could go on a stand
and make a living. There is practically
no such thing now. There are a few
people have cars in the summer time
when the tourists are here. I am only
referring to all this to show the changes
that have come about and also to show
that all the people will never be employed
again. One solution is for the Government to give the older people something
that would keep them in some sort of
decency through the evening of their lives.
It would be an inducement to the older
people if they had £1 a week or if a man
and his wife had £2 a week. They would
not be so likely to be at the gate of the
factory or engineering shop taking a job
from the younger man. The Minister is
not to suggest later on that I said that
when they got that £1 a week they would
not be considered for work again. I have
not stated that.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: That is what it
would mean.
Mr. NIXON: I say it would help in
that direction. I have stated, and I have
it from several people, that if they had
£1 a week they would not be going about
from gate to gate looking for a job and
getting turned down. I would not go the
length of prohibiting them by legislation
from working, but I would not allow the
employer to take the benefit of the £1 a
week, as some employers in County Down
have done. I do not refer to anyone
present, but at the present time there are
complaints about firms in County Down
that, when a man becomes 65 and gets
the 10s a week, his wages are reduced by
his firm by 10s a week. All present are
exempt from that charge. Circumstances
will compel this Government and also
compel the British Government to do
something, and that sooner than most
people anticipate, because every July
there are young men coming from school
who will never get jobs under present
circumstances. Recruiting or emigration
is finished during our time. The Richhill emigration factory is also closed down,
I understand. I know a number of the
emigrants produced there have been
deported and sent back. This Government and the British Government cannot sit and shut their eyes to the position
of affairs much longer, because if they do
they will be removed, as recent elections
across the water have proved, and people
for better or for worse will do this.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: For worse.

I remember as a boy coming in contact with one of the most magnificent
blazers of the trail that Great Britain has

Widows' and Old Age Pensions 438

Let us come to another aspect of the
question, the question of age. One of
the first things that happened when the
original Old Age Pensions Act was
passed was that those who took any interest in statistics found out why it
was that the Members on the Opposition
side of the House had been so careless
as not to examine this question and to
vote against the first old age pension. It
was because it was found that the bulk
of the working class died before they
reached the age at which they were entitled to the pension. There were old age
pensions at seventy-as there are still too
many at seventy-and the bulk of the
working classes passed away before they
reached that age, largely because of the
conditions under which they lived,
because of their inferior social status, and
because of the fact that in the majority
of cases they were kept down in degraded
and depressing conditions of home life.
They were shut off from those things
which provide health and culture, and
comfort; they were denied proper housing
accommodation, while they were asked to
work inordinately long hours for abnormally low wages. Those were the conditions under which the pension at 70
years of age was first brought in, and as
a consequence we find that the majority
of the working classes died before they
reached that age. Later on pioneers and
reformers began to agitate for a reduction
of the age.
I need not recapitulate the
facts which I mentioned in my first speech
in this House, but I see in the House today an hon. Member who owes a great deal
of his evolution, in social matters at any
rate, to the instruction and education
received during the elections in which I
participated with him. I believe he will
appreciate it when I say that even if it
were the only result of our work, we
demonstrated to the public at large that
it was necessary to reduce the age from
seventy to sixty-five.
Now the next step is from sixty-five
to sixty. That step we ask the House
to take here to-day on the ground of
common humanity, on the ground of
ensuring that the masses of the peopleand I speak here for the masses of the
people. I do not care how the House
likes that term. I speak for the working
classes, those who by hand or brain contribute to the upkeep of the community.
I am not concerned with the privileged,
aristocratic, or wealthy classes. In a
properly civilised community we would
not have them. I speak for the masses of
the people who contribute the wealth
whereby the community lives, and in the
name of those people I say that the next
step must be to introduce pensions at an
age which will permit them to retire from
industry on an amount which will assure
them some period of happiness before.
they pass from this planet altogether.
Those are the two grounds at the moment
-the amount by which the pension ought
to be increased and the age reduction.
As to the age reduction-and I want
to say this in advance in case any dismal
Jeremiah tells us in the subsequent
debate that this is a revolutionary proposal-I want to tell the House that in
the light of scientific advances there can
be no finality put upon the question of
the age reduction, just as there can be no
finality put upon the question, for example, of how you are going to absorb
people in employment on account of the
advances of science. Indeed it might
come to pass within the lifetime of some
people in this House that we will have
another Motion asking for a still further
reduction of the age from sixty to fiftyfive. And if it is necessary in the interests of the community at some later
date to ask for that it would only be the
sensible thing to do so.
The mover of the Motion has brought
in the question of employment. I want
to ask the House to put their prejudices
and their biases behind them, to face up
to the logic of this question from an industrial point of view. I sometimes
think that the Members of this House,
especially those Members who sit on the
other side-naturally I would say thatare living in a world of illusion and removed from reality. They seem to think
that the whole of existence in so far as
this civilised globe is concerned begins.
and ends with their journeys from their
homes to Stormont here each afternoon
for a certain number of weeks in the year.
They seem to take no cognisance of the
significance of great events throughout
the world; and the significance of these
events is that the world at the present
time is marching on, even though in some
places it be through rapine, disorder, and
reaction, to the achievement of a greater
and grander civilisation than it has yet
439 Widows' and Old Age Pensions HOUSE OF COMMONS
Widows' and Old Age Pensions 440
[Mr. Midgley]
known. There is no doubt whatever that
the old conditions are passing away and
are rapidly being destroyed, and hon.
Members on the other side of the House
who do not take cognisance of this, and
who do not realise the tremendous
changes that are taking place, would do.
well to ponder on some of the facts I am
going to put before them now.
To start with, America can be stated at
any rate to be symbolic of the most
civilised conditions under the present
order of society. We find, when we come
to examine the pensions question in relation to unemployment, that America has
provided one of the most overwhelming
reasons why this question of pensions
ought to be adjusted in the light of the
possibility of absorbing the physical fit
into industry and leaving the aged people.
free to have the leisure they ought to
have. Some years ago in the United
States of America a report was brought
out as a result of ten years' investigation
by the most scientific men in America.
And what do they claim? In their
report, which became known throughout
the world as "Technocracy"—and this
is about eighteen months old-they claim
that if it were possible for America to get
back to the year 1929, which was the
highest year from the point of view of
productivity, not only in America but in
the history of the civilised world, if they
could get back to that year they would be
able to produce the standard of wealth
and the total output of goods which they
actually did produce in 1929 on 55 per
cent. of the labour which they required
to do it in the year 1929. In other
words, in the intervening years the advance of science, the growth of invention,
and the application of new mechanical
processes in industry had resulted in the
creation of a surplus army amongst the
masses of the American population of
forty-five per cent.
What is true of America is true of
other countries throughout the world. It
is a strange thing that the only countries
in the world in which you do not get
destitution in the midst of plenty are
uncivilised communities, what are called
primitive communities. If you go to any
of the primitive communities you will
not find any such thing as destitution in
the midst of plenty. It is only when you
come to highly civilised countries that
you find that phenomenon. That is because all these new mechanical inventions
have been utilised, not to bring about a
higher standard for the masses of the
people but to allow a small section of the
community to arrogate to themselves the
fruits of industry.
That brings me up against the question
of what we are going to do with regard
to this developing science. How are we
going to apply it? Are we going to
realise that we are passing through a new
industrial era, that to-day we are not
only confronted with but right in the
midst of a new industrial revolution, far
greater than the industrial revolution of
the latter part of the eighteenth and the
early part of the nineteenth centuries,
only we are living so close to it to-day
that we cannot realise the significance of
it at the present time? I want to ask
the House how they are going to face up
to that, unless we are prepared as one
progressive step to accept the Motion
moved by the hon. Member for Woodvale.
The Motion says that in order to keep
pace with the changing economic and
social system under which we live it is
necessary to have the amenities of life
redrafted in such a way that there would
be employment available for the younger
members of the community and adequate
pensions provided for the aged members
of the community.
There are many Members in this House
on whose faces I can see unbelief. I can
see the incredulity, the unbelief, the
scepticism on the faces not only of right
hon. Gentlemen on the Front Bench but
on those of their meek and humble
followers on the back benches. I can see
all the profound signs of unbelief. They
believe in nothing except that they
represent certain constituencies by the
grace of God and the credulity of the
people. I realise that it is almost like
barking at the moon to try to convince
some people in this House of the necessity
for fundamental social change. But I
am convinced that what we on this side
are doing in this House to-day millions
of other people are doing throughout the
world. This is the transitional period
between the decline and downfall of the
old system and the birth of a new and
better system, and these are some of the
steps by which I hope, along with others,
in my day and generation to help to bring
about that better system.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Representation of the People Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The Bill which I
now have the honour of bringing before
this House is one designed with the object.
of remedying certain defects, and even
abuses, and further, of simplifying procedure in connection with the registration
of electors and the holding of our local
Parliamentary and local goverment
elections.
The Bill is a comparatively short one
and involves four Clauses only-one dealing with the residence qualification for
registration, another dealing with the
holding of elections to this Parliament,
the third dealing with the procedure at
elections in connection with blind voters,
and the fourth dealing with company
franchise for local government elections.
Taking the first Clause, which provides
that a period of residence of seven years
in Northern Ireland is in future to be a
condition precedent to registration for
purposes of our local Parliamentary and
local government elections, the House will
remember that this subject was debated
at very considerable length in Parliament
in October, 1928, at the time of the introduction of the Representation of the
People Act of that year.
I pointed out at that time that the
Government had been viewing with some
concern the growing tendency on the part
of persons coming into Northern Ireland
for short periods of stay and thereby
qualifying for registration. No doubt,
some of these persons were persons who
came to Northern Ireland to take up
seasonal or temporary employment, but
it would not be unreasonable to assume
that many of them had in their minds
the main object of enabling themselves to
qualify for votes at our elections.
During the course of those debates it
was obvious that the proposition which
was then for the first time enunciated,
of requiring a three years' residence
qualification was one that did not commend itself to a certain section of the
House. On the other hand, a reference
to the debates will show that it found
undoubted favour amongst the majority
of the Members of this House who represent the loyal sections of our community.
In fact, the only criticism that was
voiced at that time from the loyal section
of the inhabitants was the criticism that
the period of residence prescribed was all
too short and that the prescribed period
of residence should be seven years, corresponding to the period which in the
Free State is required for citizenship,
and, I presume, for qualification as a
voter.
473 Representation of People Bill-

14 MARCH 1934
Second Reading
Since the passing of that Act the Government has been carefully following the
trend of events, and, while it is impossible without the institution of the
lengthy and expensive course of inquiries.
to arrive at any accurate conception regarding the extent of the influx of persons into Northern Ireland, we at any
rate have sufficient information to justify
us in bringing forward the proposal
before this House, that the period of
qualification for registration should be
seven years.
The basis of any Constitution is sound
and equitable Parliamentary representation, and that principle depends on the
electorate embracing only those who have
a definite stake in the country and a
definite and permanent interest in the
good government of the country.
It cannot be said that this principle
would continue to exist in Northern Ireland if we continued to allow young men
and young women, who come into Northern Ireland for the purposes of seasonal
employment, or even of temporary employment, such as domestic servants, to
acquire for themselves the right to influence the conduct of our Parliamentary
and local government affairs. These
have
young people
no stake in our
country, and they have no interest in
our country other than, unfortunately
in many cases, perhaps a hostile interest,
and even a period of three years or five
years residence, and employment of the
kind which they can manage to secure, is
not, in the considered opinion of the Government, of a character to justify us in
allowing them to influence the destinies
of the Ulster people and our Parliamentary or local government institutions.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
In this connection I do not attempt
to quote any comparisons with other
countries or the principles of their
respective Governments and Pariiaments which they lay down for themselves. The affairs of Northern Ireland,
in the opinion of the Government-an
opinion which I hope will be endorsed
by this House-must be designed and
conducted according to our Own conditions and our own ideals-
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
we
Sir DAWSON BATES- -and
are satisfied that the period which is
specified in Clause 1 of the Bill is necessary, in the interest of the stability of
the State. Whilst we welcome all persons who come into Northern Ireland
prepared to obey our laws and assist in
building up our Province, we are determined to put every obstacle in the way
of those whose sole object in coming here
is the disruption of our Constitution.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I will now turn to the second Clause of
the Bill, which brings us to the question.
of the conduct of elections for this House.
Every Member of this House is familiar
with the incidents which took place at the
last Parliamentary election, and particularly to the cases of certain candidates who, whilst standing for election,
publicly announced that it was their
intention not to take their seats if elected.
I do not know if these acts of what I
may term bravado appeal to hon. Members opposite, but, speaking for the
Government, I can
only say with
emphasis, and I confidently believe it
is the opinion of the Members who sit
on this side of the House that such
conduct on the part of those candidates
can only be described as a deliberate
insult to this honourable House and to
this Parliament-(Hon. Members; Hear,
hear)—an insult which cannot be tolerated
and cannot be allowed to be repeated.
There is another aspect of the question
which must also be taken into consideration. By such acts of, what I may also
term folly, these candidates have deprived
the people of the constituencies concerned
of their civic rights and of the normal
right which belongs to every man of being
duly and properly represented in Parliament. I cannot use more appropriate
words in justifying my action in introducing this Measure than those used in
this House by the late hon. Member for
Belfast Central (Mr. Devlin):-
-
"We can hear a good deal about the
value of the vote and the privilege
which the vote affords. No man has a
right to ask a right or demand
privilege from the State unless he is
prepared to exercise that right and
privilege."
a
Those are the words of the late hon.
Member for Central, and I would commend them to hon. Members opposite.
475 Representation of People Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Sir Dawson Bates]
Accordingly, Clause 2 of the Bill has
been designed with the object of preventing the repetition of the state of affairs to
which I have just referred, and in future
when any person allows himself to be
nominated as a candidate for election to
this House his nomination will be
invalidated unless at the time he submits
his nomination to the returning officer
he hands to the returning officer a
declaration in writing, subscribed by
himself in the presence of a witness, that
he intends, if elected, to take his seat
in this House.
I will now turn to the third Clause in
the Bill, which also relates to the holding
of our local Parliamentary and our local
government elections. Under the existing law in Northern Ireland, a blind
person who wished to exercise his right
as a citizen to vote at any of the elections
concerned, had to secure the services of
the presiding officer at the appropriate
polling booth to assist him in marking his
paper in accordance with his wishes.
some time past it has been felt that this
was a rather undesirable mode of action,
as it cut across the principles of the
secrecy of the ballot by enabling the presiding officer to know how the blind
person in question had voted.
For
The Imperial Parliament, some months
ago, passed an Act altering the old procedure, under which the services of the
presiding officer, in connection with the
exercise of votes by blind persons, are
dispensed with, and enabling the blind
voter to take with him into the polling
booth a member of his family, or even a
friend, to assist him in exercising his
franchise. I should say, however, that in
a case where a blind person has not at his
disposal a member of his family of the
prescribed age, or does not wish to avail
himself of the services of a member of his
family, or a trusted friend, he will, as
heretofore, be entitled to avail himself of
the services of the presiding officer.
The last Clause in the Bill merely
deals with machinery in connection with
the arrangements for extending the local
government franchise to limited companies, which principle was adopted in
our 1928 Act. As hon. Members
who were present in the House in
1928 are aware, the principle of extending the local government franchise to
companies was first adopted in that year,
and certain machinery was prescribed
under which the companies entitled to the
companies' franchise would be enabled to
secure the inclusion of their nominees on
the register. The machinery provided at
that time was necessarily somewhat complicated, and the object of this Clause is
to remove certain difficulties which
experience has brought to light.
Under Section 3 of the 1928 Act it will
be observed that the actual claims for
registration submitted by companies,
which have to be made annually for each
new register, must be authenticated by
the seal of the company. This is a
cumbersome procedure and involves
difficulties in the case of companies whose
seals are not readily available and which
can be only used in certain limited circumstances. The whole object of the
original Act was to ensure that the registration of representatives of companies on
the local government franchise list was
effected with due care and responsibility
on the part of the company, and it is not
intended that there should be any
diffusion or weakening of their responsibility.
On the other hand, it is felt that the
necessity for sealing every document submitted to the registration officer as part
of a claim is cumbersome and unnecessary.
Accordingly, under the new arrangement,
as prescribed in Clause 4 of the Bill, it is
proposed to dispense with the authentication under seal of the documents concerned and to prescribe that in future the
claims will be authenticated by the
signature of a director, manager, secretary, or other officer of the company who
shall be specifically authorised by the
company for this purpose under seal of
the company.
Mr. BEATTIE: It will be done by
Unionist election agents.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Or by Labour
agents.
Mr. BEATTIE: No, by the Unionist

Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon.
Friend will have ample opportunity to
reply to me later on. In other words,
the company will delegate, under seal, to
a responsible representative of the firm,
the power and the duty of putting forward claims each year to the registration

of Labour whether he proposes to restore
the cuts in unemployment benefit.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I can assure the hon. Member
that there will be no departure from the
definite policy which the Government
initiated 12 years ago, and has upheld
ever since, of maintaining equal standards.
with the rest of the United Kingdom.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I would like
to ask whether it is a fact that the cuts
were less than those recommended by the
Socialist Government in Great Britain?
Mr. MIDGLEY: May I be permitted
to ask the Minister if he cannot tell this
House in advance whether or not the
policy of the Government is, in view of
the improved financial conditions, to
restore these cuts as it has been rumoured
from time to time they are to be restored
on the other side? What is the considered policy of the Government?
Mr. ANDREWS: With regard to the
question of the hon. Member (Sir Robert
Lynn) the position is simply this, in
my opinion, that the policy of the
Socialist Government has been disputed, and I am not prepared
to say what that policy was. What I
have said indicates the policy of this
Government.

Northern Ireland. I have always
preached economy, not through any spirit
of niggardliness, but because I have felt
that money would fructify more freely in
the pockets of individuals than in the
coffers of the State, and the more money
that fructifies in this Province the better
it will be for those seeking employment.
The policy of the Government, with all
its limitations, has been a wise policy. I
know the Opposition has got to oppose,
that that is its first duty, but apart from
that I do not think there can be any
legitimate grievance against the Government or against the policy that is being
pursued. I, as one who has always
preached economy, have no hesitation in
voting for this sum of money asked for
to-day. The Government have made any
necessary adjustments in the amount of
money spent in past years, and I think
we have now got very nearly down to rock
bottom as regards the amount of money
required for the administration of this
Province.

scheme, and, difficult though it is, I am
hoping that eventually a scheme will be
evolved which will prove satisfactory. But
unless one can see quite definitely that a
scheme which is to be introduced is not
going to fail it would be better to leave
it alone. Once a scheme is introduced
and the people of this country lose confidence in it, then it will be very difficult
to get other marketing schemes launched.
Let me assure the hon. Member that the
Ministry are examining this matter and
discussing it with all those interested to
see if a satisfactory and workable scheme
can be produced.
Own
I cannot give any authentic reply to the
hon. Member regarding the carrying of
meat and other goods, but, as I am sure
he understands, in many cases where a
small rate is charged on ships coming from
a big distance, and a large rate is charged
on ships going a short distance, the reason
can easily be exemplified by the transport
lorries that are working in our
country. I am sure he is aware that
lorries that go to Enniskillen loaded are
prepared to bring goods back to Belfast
for whatever you like to give them. The
same thing applies to ships going to South
America and South Africa. They are
prepared to take a load to act as ballast
and accept a small fee for it.
Then the Member for South Fermanagh
referred to the report of the Marks Committee. One of the statements contained
in this report was that the railway companies have already given sympathetic
consideration to several anomalies and
injustices, and stated they are prepared to
consider all such cases with a view to
modifying the treatment. I cannot give
the hon. Member any further information
as to that matter, because this report was
submitted before I took over the office of
Minister of Agriculture, and I should
have to study the report to explain it
further. The hon. Member urged me to
see that when any future boards or committees were appointed those interested in
the particular trade concerned should be
represented. I am sure the hon. Member
will appreciate that the Pigs Marketing
Board is a thoroughly representative body,
because, with the exception of three members appointed by myself, the members are
elected by the producers themselves. Any
boards that may be appointed in the
future will be constituted on the same
basis, although perhaps in the first year,
in order to get the scheme working, the
members may be appointed by the Minister
of Agriculture. It is quite obvious that,
whoever may be the Minister of Agriculture who makes the appointments, he
will only appoint those who have a
thorough knowledge of the particular
trade concerned.
The question of flax was also mentioned
by the Member for South Fermanagh.
Even when Northern Ireland was producing as much flax as she was able to grow
she produced only one-fifth of the requirements of our mills. Therefore, if a tariff
was put on foreign flax you would, in
effect, be putting a tariff on your raw
material. That would mean that the flax
spinners would not be in a position to
compete with other countries, and that
would result in more unemployment
amongst the people in Northern Ireland
who buy the produce of the farmers.
Although the growing of flax is to be
encouraged, and everything is being done
by the Ministry to encourage it, if the
farmers would grow the fine quality that
is required by the millers I think, judging
by the prices that have ruled this year,
they would get a satisfactory return.
It
is one of those cases where a tax put on
an article to help agriculture would
seriously injure the employers in the industry, and that would curtail the buying
power of the people.
Another matter the hon. Member
raised was the growing of sugar beet. I
expect he has cast his eyes to the South,
where sugar beet factories have been
established. Sugar factories are all very
well in a country which is suitable for
that purpose, but from reports I have
seen I am rather doubtful if the South
of Ireland is really suitable. If you try
to grow sugar beet in an unsuitable country your sugar content is
SO low that, rather like mining
gold out of dirt, you have only
a very small percentage of profit. The
result is that you have to grant an
extremely heavy subsidy in order to make
the industry a financial success. In the
case of the Free State, as a result of the
subsidy and the tariffs that have been
placed on sugar, the price of sugar in the
Free State is now £20 a ton as against a
world price of £7. I am very doubtful
if any person in Northern Ireland, even
Supply-

As well as I can remember one of the

In addition to what I have just

Ministry now have to collect is information.
concerning the population of pigs and
sheep in order to allow the Ministry on
the other side to know exactly how they
stand with regard to the quota. That

actual cost of issuing the report is very
small. I feel convinced that those people
who have read the report value it and

being devoted to what the weather was

Mr. ELLIOTT: While I do not agree
with all that the hon. Member (Mr.
Healy) has said, I rise to endorse the

where the right hon. Gentleman made a

meeting early and before a resolution was
put dealing with this important matter of
the dairying industry. Our creameries,
which are located in Tyrone and Fermanagh, are having a lean time, and that
is simply due to the uneconomic price
received for their products. It is due to
the unfair competition of butter from New
Zealand and the Colonies. I have every
sympathy with our Colonies, and I like to
see Colonial stuff coming in when our stuff
runs out, but it is unfair to allow a condition of affairs to arise which results in
New Zealand butter being sold in Belfast
at 7d per lb. Our creameries have to
compete against that. It has put many
of the creameries out of existence. That
is not fair competition, because the same
butter is being sold in New Zealand to-day
at 1/-, 1/2 and 1/3 per lb. It is allowed
to come in under, the abominable quota
system, and it is due to the arrangements
made at Ottawa which have ruined our
whole dairying industry.
I would appeal to the right hon. Gentleman to see if some pressure could not be
put on the Imperial Government as soon
as possible to end a condition of affairs
that is intolerable, and which is putting
our creameries out of existence. I would
appeal especially for the creameries in the
border counties of Tyrone and Fermanagh.
They occupy a prominent place in the
agricultural industry. I think if the
position was explained by the right hon.
Gentleman to the Imperial Government,
who alone have the power to act, surely
they would see to it that this condition
of affairs, which exists at the moment,
would be speedily brought to an end. I
hope that this appeal will not fall on deaf
ears.

With regard to butter, while I like

""
Made in Lisbellaw Creamery."
That
may be quite true, but at the same

There is not a single one of those creamery

£100 here is equal to £125 out there.

to me.
sure
With regard to the last part of the
question, I am
the hon. and

PURDYSBURN MENTAL HOSPITAL
-MENTALLY DEFECTIVE
CHILDREN.
5. Mr. MIDGLEY (for Mr. Henderson)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he is aware that the Belfast Corporation are erecting extensions to
the Purdysburn Mental Hospital, and
whether any provision is being made for
mentally defective children in order to
segregate them from adults..
Sir DAWSON BATES: There is a
small number of juvenile inmates in the
Mental Hospital. The plans for the extensions do not specifically provide for
special accommodation for these inmates,
but I understand that it is the intention
when the extensions are completed to rearrange the distribution of the inmates,
in order, so far as possible, to segregate
these juveniles from the adult patients.

Sir DAWSON BATES: Only one

cadets, two of whom were appointed in

I feel that the Government themselves
are deviating from the laws laid down
by the British Parliament for the government of this Six Counties area, and I
have read with horror the speeches of
