thought we would have got better things
from them, and if I were one of the
faith to which hon. Members on this
side belong I would feel very resentful
and would say that the time is now
opportune to get clear and unfettered
from the tyrannical Government which
rules the destinies of the Six Counties.
If the policy of the Government is to be
judged from the statements of the right
hon. Gentleman (Sir Basil Brooke) and
his colleagues in the Cabinet-and that
is the only way you can judge the policy
of the Government, by the statements of
responsible Ministers-I think we have in
the Minister of Agriculture something
we have not seen yet. I personally think
he will make a success of his job, but he
will not be very successful if he continues
in the strain of his Derry speech.
I say here that the Government have
no policy at all. The moment they get
away from the religious basis of
their political creed, that moment the
Government lose their position in
this House. Hence the reason for
the Prime Minister being so afraid
of the Socialist Party. He knows that
once the shibboleth about differences in
religion is wiped out he has to confront
real democracy, and when real democracy
presents him with its policy he will not
be competent to handle that policy and
will, therefore, have to go into retirement either at the back or outside. I
feel that the Government will have to
change, and that very soon.
Before I take my seat I want to tell
the Government this: You claim that
you represent the Protestant people of
Northern Ireland. My hon. Friends on
this side claim to represent the Catholic
people of Northern Ireland. I represent
the two classes. I am out for justice for
all and am not going to see any division
of the people made for the purpose of
keeping any privileged class in power,
which has been the customary method
employed by the Unionist Party in Northern Ireland for the last generation.
Now that we have this Six County Parliament the least the Government can do
is to be careful in their speech-making
outside this House and to give to the
citizens of Northern Ireland equal rights
and equal opportunities for any of the
jobs which are likely to be vacant in the
near future. I am sure if they do that
the time will not be long before we take
our proper places in this House and control the interests and destinies of the
people.

Widows' Pensions.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I rise to move the
Motion standing in my name.
It is:
"That in the opinion of this House
the time has now arrived when legislation should be introduced for the
purpose of granting pensions to all
widows."
I rise to move that Motion with a considerable amount of pleasure, because I
happen to be one of the persons-and
I do not say this egotistically-who
pioneered this question in Northern Ireland. I acted as champion of widows'
pensions when I was about fifteen years
of age, and when very few people could
be found either in Belfast or Northern
Ireland to come out on the side of widows'
pensions. At that particular time I
based my outlook on this question on my
personal experience in my own home. I
had experienced all the sordidness and
squalor associated with a mother left to
carry on a tremendous struggle against
great odds on behalf of her children, and
my home experience taught me to realise
the good foundations and the good ethics
behind the question of widows' pensions.
In company with other people throughout Northern Ireland, indeed throughout
the whole of Ireland and Great Britain,
we set out on the task of building up
public opinion to believe in the principle
of widows' pensions. It is comparatively
few years since I heard not only Members
of this House but very prominent
citizens outside say that this question of
widows' pensions was something far
beyond the dreams of practical things.
and far from realisation. However, we
have now seen the time when there is a
comprehensive Measure of widows' and
old-age pensions on the Statute Book.
Events have moved, public conscience
has been aroused, and we have to-day a
realisation of our social responsibilities
that did not exist a few years ago.
Some people might ask what is the
justification for this Motion. The justification for it is to be found in the fact
that, in reply to a question which I
addressed to the Minister of Labour
about a fortnight ago, the information
was elicited that in Northern Ireland
7,388 claims for widows' pensions have
been disallowed since the introduction of
the Act. The Minister on that occasion
was unable to give the House or the
public information to the exact
number of widows who have no pension.
He was, however, able to give us the
number of claims that had been
disallowed, and, whatever the final number of widows who have been disallowed
may be, we can assume that it was a
goodly number, even though we have not
precise information.

House to express the opinion that the
time has arrived when legislation ought
to be introduced for the purpose of giving
all widows pensions. Consequently I want
to deal for a moment with my reasons
for putting down the Motion in the form
in which it is on the Paper. A person
getting up in a House of Parliament to
discuss the question of widows' or any
other kind of pensions is circumscribed by
virtue of the fact that the administration
of pensions is subject to the statutory
conditions laid down in the Act of Parliament. Therefore, when you raise the
question as to the number of claims disallowed or turned down, you are conscious
all the time of the fact that the bulk,
if not all, of them have been turned
down under the statutory conditions laid
down in the Act, and you know in
advance that you are speaking against
the operation of an Act, the provisions
of which may go a certain length, but
not so far as you think they ought to go.
It is precisely because I think the provisions of the Act do not go as far as
they ought to go that I am asking the
House this afternoon to agree with me
in the principle that the time has arrived
when every widow ought to have a
pension.
I want to guard myself in advance.
against a form of argument which will
probably be used by a certain Member
of this House. There is a certain Member in this House and every time any
question of social legislation is raised
he seeks out the most ridiculous element
in the case and then builds up his case
on the basis of that ridiculous element.
I am not alluding to anybody on the
Front Bench at the moment, and the
hon. Gentleman to whom I am referring
is not in the House at the moment,
though I hope he will make his
appearance before a vote is taken on this
Question. We will be met, probably, by
the argument of what this Motion to give
all widows pensions means. We will be
asked are we going to give, for instance,
a pension to Mrs. So-and-So, the widow
of Mr. So-and-So who died a multimillionaire. Are we going to pass an
Act of Parliament to give a pension to
one who is in possession of millions? My
answer to that is "No." We are not
going to give Mrs. So-and-So, who is the
widow of a multi-millionaire, a pension,
although my Motion might read that
way. What we are going to do is to run
the risk of Mrs. So-and-So getting a pension in the hope that the 7,388 deserving
cases who have no pensions at the present
time will get pensions under the changed
conditions. I hope, therefore, I will not
be met this afternoon by some outstanding or abnormal cases which, if we
accepted them at their face value, would
prevent these other widows for whom I
speak from getting the pensions to which.
they are entitled.
I want the House to listen for a few
moments while I review some of the conditions under which widows are disallowed their pensions at the present time.
The most common disallowance under the
operation of the present Act is that which
says that the deceased person had not 104
contributions since his last entry into
insurance and that he had not an average
of 26 contributions for the three years
preceding his death. That is the most
common disqualification at the present
time. There are other disqualifications.
There is a disqualification which operates
in much the same way but which arises
from a different cause. During the
abnormally bad trade in the city of
Belfast and throughout Northern Ireland many people were encouraged by the
spokesmen of the Government to emigrate
to the Dominions and other parts of the
earth. In many cases these people
went expecting to find employment. In
a considerable number of cases they got
employment only for a limited period,
and had to return to the homeland. But
by the time they had come home and had
got into employment such a gap had
taken place between their leaving the
home country and their coming back that
they were never able to recover their first
position in respect of insurance. That
meant that when death took place, as
it did in a number of cases, their widows
were disallowed the pension because of
that particular circumstance.

I want to remind the House of something else at this juncture. We hear a
good deal, and we may hear a good deal

and commission of a certain Government,
a minority Government, that was in

the policy which made the social services
in their present form possible. It was
the political section of the community to
which I belong that acted as pioneers on
all these questions, and forced the hands
of
successive Governments. Then we
tried to bring about a condition of things.
in which widows' pensions would be

original old-age pensions; we were denied

The Government with which I was
indirectly associated as a friend was a
minority Government; it was not a
majority Government like the Northern
Government. After all, you have always
had a majority here, and you cannot
blame your defects upon some other body.
You have supreme authority in this
House, and have had since the inception.
of Parliament. But the Labour Government was in office in Great Britain without a majority. What did they do?
They took the Widows' Pension Act as it
appeared upon the Statute Book, and
they passed an Amending Act. That
Amending Act of 1929 admitted the right
to pensions of 500,000 widows who had
been deprived of their pensionable rights
under the Act of 1925.
And lest you people should think it
does not apply to Northern Ireland, let
me quote from the last Ulster Year Book
once again. In the last Ulster Year
Book, at page 146, you will get the following information:-In 1929 there were
2.615 widows receiving non-contributory
pensions, and 3,074 receiving contributory pensions. In 1930, the widows in
receipt of non-contributory pensions
numbered 2,593, and in receipt of contributory pensions 4,028. In 1931 the
number of non-contributory pensions payable to widows was 6,952, and the number
of contributory pensions to widows was
4,948. In 1932-the last year for which
figures are given in this book-6,928
widows were in receipt of non-contributory pensions, and 5,921 in receipt of
contributory pensions. That shows the
net effect of the Amending Act of 1929.
I want the Front Bench Members to
remember this, that although they poke
fun and wax sarcastic about the defects
of a minority Administration which had,
to a certain extent, to depend upon the
goodwill of another party, yet in
Northern Ireland, for the year 1932,
there were 6,928 widows getting pensions
who would not have had pensions but for
the Labour Government's Amending Act
of 1929. The total number of widows in
receipt of pensions at the present time in
Northern Ireland exceeds the number of
widows who are entitled to their pensions
through their late husbands' insurance.
It is not stressing the point too much to
say this, if it was possible for a minority

500,000 widows, apart altogether from
other types of pension, surely to goodness
it ought not to be beyond the wit of man,

for a majority Government to be able to

a fortnight ago.
My suggestion was this, that the

of pensions. In one of them he laid

Karl Marx, the author of Socialism,

afraid they would take away the driving
force which Socialism must have if it was

hon. Member for Dock does not make

There are a great many, and the number

The hon. Member towards the conclusion of his speech said that he was
going to make this House a sounding
board. That is truly characteristic of
Socialism. It never produces anything
else but sound and sounding boards. It
never produces anything practical to pay
for pensions for widows or for anybody
else. If this Motion of the hon. Member
for Dock were carried, one of the first
things it would do would be this-it
would lead to the breakdown of the whole
system of pensions. It would be so overloaded that it would not be able to exist.
It is just because of that that the
Socialists, when they were in office on
two occasions, did not go in for any of
these things. They had sense enough to
see that it was all very well to capture
votes in the country by offering pensions
to everyone from five years of age upwards, but they knew when it came to
practical business that there was a limit
to the amount of money available, and
that that limited amount had to go round
in many ways. Therefore, they had the
good sense to drop these things, and to
move step by step in a careful and useful
way.

I am
entirely dissatisfied with the policy of the

Gentleman travels a great deal. He goes
to France and America. The Government
of every other country has done something
to create new industries, but the Ministry

outside shoulders. That is not right. The
Minister should have got into close conjunction with the Minister of Labour in
his efforts to stem the tide of unemployment. We have seen the exhibition of
inaction on the other side a few minutes

against giving pensions to all widows.
That was the policy also of the Ministry
of Commerce regarding the creating of new
industries. This inaction is nothing more

rise to great heights with the idea of
establishing new industries that would
absorb 10,000 or 20,000 people.
Nothing is being done. The linen
industry is being gradually stolen from
us. Every country that we used to supply
with linen is now manufacturing linen
which is almost equal in quality to that
made in Northern Ireland. What is being

It is not my desire to break the record

make criticisms of a kind which I hope

The Bill asks

time.

situation in Northern Ireland is being

Acts since 1912. I continue to receive

Ireland umpire. In my leisure moments
I compare the decisions on similar

Britain, and I may say that it is a very

two agreeing on the principle under consideration. I often fail to agree with the
principle on which decisions are given in

where you have two or three people
acting, you get a broader mind and you

Decisions are given by four persons in
Great Britain, while in Northern Ireland the majority are given by one.
Let me take a case as an illustration.
We have in the Northern Ireland area
what we call a seasonal occupation. We
have in Great Britain the same occupation
followed at seaside resorts. We will take
the case of waitresses. Large numbers of
girls, who follow their normal occupation
as waitresses in the city of Belfast, go
to the seaside in the summer because of
the better wages and conditions, and because their surroudings are brighter
than they get at home. But when they
come back to Belfast and fail to get employment in the months of October and
March, if they fail for two seasons they
are challenged before the court of
referees and are disallowed benefit on the
ground that they have not had a reasonable period of work in the two seasons.
The same case in Great Britain is decided
in this way: Such a girl belongs to an
area in which the industry which she
follows is continuous the year round.
Although she goes to the seaside in the
summer it makes no material difference
to her position as a normally insurable
person. It is the condition of her employment in the district in which she
resides which is taken into consideration,
and the girl who is disallowed in Northern Ireland has been decided by the
British umpire to be a normally insurable
person within the meaning of the Act.
No seasonal qualification attaches to her
claim at all in Great Britain.

do not feel as sorry for the men sometimes

I feel that Regulation 4 should be
administered in the most humane way.
If the husband is working and in receipt
of 25s a week, is it right that she should
be deprived of her benefit? I say no.
That income is insufficient to maintain
the husband, the wife, and five children.
Hence she is compelled to go into industry
to augment the income of the home. She
requires the benefit to augment the
income of the home, and if she does not
get it then you are asking the husband
to keep himself, his wife, and five
children on 25s a week; you are asking
him, in addition, to keep himself
physically fit in order to give an honest
day's work to his employer. The harshness of that regulation could be alleviated
and effect given in the administration to
the real intention of the originators.
The unemployed are being starved.
Starving means slow death, and slow
death is the most horrible death that one
could be asked to face. Some claim that
capital punishment is the worst thing; it
may be very severe, but certainly it puts
the victim out of action very quickly. We
have thousands of unemployed roaming
the streets to-day endeavouring to get a
job at every turn, and at every turn they
are told "not required." Some of them
have given service to their King. Some
of them have taken over positions to the
detriment of their fellow workers, owing
to the slow death with which they are
faced by means of starvation. What is
that due to? The individual has a right
to a living so long as he is willing and
anxious to get employment. That condition of affairs is due to the curtailment
of relief work owing to the refusal of the
Northern Government to grant assistance,
and their refusal to find an outlet for the
surplus unemployed, who will never
again be restored to their normal
occupation.
I always look upon Northern Ireland
in the same light as Japan. Japan has a
very large population. She has no outlets, and she is endeavouring to get outlets by fair means or foul. We are a
small area, and we have no outlet.

Therefore I want to throw across the floor

only interest in the farm is his money,

not prosper. Although the Minister of

Nelson. The Nelson eye is turned on the

give the farmer that right. Why not

Why make a distinction?
Of course,

roads. This has become a grave menace
to our community, and is a proof that a
speed limit is required. We all know
that when a vehicle is travelling at a
speed far beyond the control of the driver
very little can be done to avert disaster if
an obstacle or person happens to get in
the way. We also know that if a
vehicle is going slowly or at a reasonable
speed, the car can generally avoid trouble.
I feel that legislation is required on this
matter. At one time the idea prevailed
that there should be a speed limit. Then
we got away from that view, and it was
considered quite a safe thing to rely on
the judgment of the driver. That has
proved a wholly fallacious safeguard, and
I think the circumstances clearly call for
a speed limit. I do not mean to suggest
that the local authorities should be permitted to impose their own varying speed
limits, but I believe that the Ministry
should take the matter in hand and fix a
speed limit for the entire Province.

it was the same Bill to all intents and
purposes except in one regard, and that
was that no financial provision was made
by the Parliamentary authority to assist
the local authorities in clearing slum
areas. That was a tremendous omission
which made all the difference in the world
to the importance of the Bill. We found
then that after passing that Act a
situation arose in Belfast and Northern
Ireland in which there was an increasing
demand for working-class houses produced under conditions which would enable the average working class person to
have the tenancy of a house. That was
the problem presented to Parliament and
the local authority. In face of that, and
of the propaganda carried on by sections
of the community in regard to better
housing, what happened? The Government which had some time previously
decided to do nothing, to stop all
financial support of any housing schemes
were prevailed on under certain very
restricted terms to grant a subsidy of
£25.
The Belfast Corporation added to that
another £25, but that does not matter at
the moment. I think that the people
who take an interest in housing will be
able to subscribe to this.
When you
compare the Housing Act in Northern
Ireland and housing conditions generally
at the present time with those across the
water we must be driven to the conclusion that the defect lies in our placing
the subsidy, or financial assistance, on
the basis of each house instead of on the
basis of the individuals who are likely to
be displaced or re-housed under new conditions and removed from the slum area.
That is what the British Act set out to
do. That Act has accomplished it in
part, and if the local authorities and the
Parliamentary authority would COordinate in Great Britain to make the
fullest possible use of that Act a tremendous amount of re-housing could be
carried out.
But in Northern Ireland, under our
very restricted scheme, there is no such
likelihood of the re-housing of the
masses of the people. God knows, they
need re-housing. In the division I
737 Consolidated Fund Bill-

represent in the City of Belfastalthough there are supposed to be no

permits the perpetuation of some of the

If we were actuated by as full a spirit
of Christian ethics, as we pretend to be, or
are supposed to be, we would go after this
housing question in the crusading spirit.
If we went out in the crusading spirit a
good deal could be done. For example,
there is nothing to prevent the Minister
of Home Affairs and the Minister of

in the spirit of co-operation to consider
the housing requirements, not only of

Northern Ireland to produce building
material. We have no need to take a

the nucleus of what might be used in

to provide a mobile army for five, ten,
fifteen, or twenty years for the mobilisation of all the industrial arts and crafts
in connection with housing.
A programme for a long term can be mapped
out. I submit that that can be done.
I am not stretching the imagination or
the intelligence. When you are
fronted with a national peril in days of
war and you have got to project your
vision into the future in order to meet
the national requirements in face of a
national menace, all the resources of the
country are co-ordinated and utilised to
the end that the national requirement
shall be met. If that can be done in time
of war in face of danger, it can be done
in days of peace.
con-
I wish to say that if that policy were
developed something of a substantial
character could be done for housing. I
want to let this House know what I try
to let the public know through the
Belfast Corporation, but apparently my
intellectual status as a Corporator is not
as good as it is going to be as a Parliamentarian, as some of the words of
wisdom I let fall in the Corporation never
see the light of day so far as the Press
are concerned, although I use them for
the purpose of safeguarding the public.
On the day it was announced in Belfast
that the Minister of Home Affairs had
granted a subsidy of £25 there was
movement started which became menacing and dangerous in character. It was
consummated, or reached its highest
point, on the day the Corporation decided
to pass a subsidy of £25 in collaboration
with the Minister of Home Affairs.
a
What was this movement? I was told
by a contractor in Belfast, who belongs
to the same political party as the Government a very decent man nevertheless
(Laughter) on that particular occasion
what was likely to happen in Belfast and
what history has proved to be correct.
He said that any time there was a coordinated effort on the part of the Parliamentary and the local authorities to bring
about any change in the housing policy
there were some people who proceeded to
hold the community up to ransom in
regard to prices and material. When the
meeting was over I had a longer talk with
him, and I asked him if he had any conclusive proof for this. He said, "Yes, I,
in my private capacity, went to buy
certain materials that were required for
the construction of houses and I was

them up for increased prices."
or
At the last meeting of the Belfast Corporation and this is a matter of public.
importance of which the Minister of
Home Affairs, or the Minister of Labour,
the Minister into whose province
it comes, should take cognisance-I drew

commodities in connection with housing
a tremendous increase in prices had taken
place, ranging in some cases as far as 25

up to the 1st of this month the average

and in his own case he was of the opinion

was not the worst feature. A worse

to have as a Parliamentary authority,

face up to this and answer it. There is
a conspiracy in Northern Ireland on the

of materials for housing to exploit the

I think a case is made out on the face
of that for Government action. The
Free State housing authority was compelled to take action. When they drew
up the conditions regulating the construction of houses they
got Parliamentary authority, if there was an upward
trend in prices or an attempt by the
market to create a monopoly, not only to
buy materials but to commandeer
materials and control the prices in the

going to construct the houses. That condition has been put into operation time
and again in the history of Great Britain,
particularly in the days of the war and
those immediately following. It is a well
established principle, and I would commend this thought to Cabinet Ministers
in this House.
to
Cabinet Ministers are talking about
what they are prepared to do in regard to
parallel lines of travel as compared with
Great Britain. Let them indicate to the
masses of the people in reference
some of these commercial highwaymen, who are holding this part
of the nation up to ransom at the
present time, that even if they are their

to cut across the amenities of the area
over which they have control. I believe
that if they do that they will be doing
something in their day and generation
which will contribute a very valuable
element to the rehousing of the people.
I feel strongly on this question of rehousing, because I can trace my own
intellectual and physical development
from the kitchen house to the attic house,
and from that house to the attic house
with a bath. If social development is to
be measured by development along those
lines I have developed at an alarming
pace. I can still go and look at the house
in which I was born in Belfast, and
although it was a well-kept house from
the point of view of cleanliness and
hygiene, there were no amenities there to
lighten the burden of a mother who had
to look after a family of children. I am
sorry to say there are many houses in the
City of Belfast at the present time in
which there are no amenities to help a
mother who is overburdened from day to
day, not only with the anxieties of the
home, but with the domestic duties of
the home. There ought to be no such
thing as a working-class house without
the fullest hygienic amenities for cooking
and all the rest of it.
-
You will find, if you take a census of
the houses in Belfast, that there are a
good number still-in fact, it runs into
some thousands that have not the
slightest pretence at a scientific or
hygienic amenity.
That is not a good
enough condition. We ought to do for
houses the same as we do for other things.
In fact, we ought to do for housing what

some members of the community have

We can produce more abundantly as
we have machinery at our disposal which
has revolutionised building. There is no
for the perpetuation of bad,

less the slum type of house. I am speaking for some of the thousands of people in
my constituency. They may not all on
this question be as progressive as I am.
Some may prefer to live where their forefathers lived and die in the home environment of their forefathers. But I am
representing them. I have been sent
here as their mouthpiece, and I am
voicing the aspirations of, I think, a
newer and better generation, when I say
it is the bounden duty of the Parliamentary authority to utilise every
resource it can possibly utilise to the end
that the community might be better
housed.
Remember that, apart altogether from
the material side of this question, there is
a spiritual side and a moral side.
Housing is inextricably interwined with
the ethical and moral and philosophical
consideration. If we bring children up
in a slum evironment they sometimes
turn out to be bright and shining lights,
nevertheless there are bound to be
thousands of children who get a distorted
outlook on life, who do not get the right
spiritual perspective, and who do not get
an opportunity of developing the physique
God intended them to enjoy, because of
the bad housing conditions under which
they were brought up.
It is against conditions like those that
I and my colleagues are speaking. It
ought to be the duty of the Government
to see if they cannot do something better
in the days which lie ahead along the line
of calling all the interests of Northern
Ireland together to evolve a scheme to
deal with this matter. Call the artisans
together, if you like; call the building
trade employers together, and
suppliers of commodities, and utilise your
Parliamentary authority to co-ordinate
all these interests into one great organised
the
plan with the object of re-housing the
people of Northern Ireland. If you do
that not only will you be fulfilling a
great function from the point of view of
employment, but you will be doing something greater than that, you will be transforming the lives of the people, and in
your day and generation, if you embark
upon ambitious schemes like that,
especially in regard to housing, you will
have the assurance that you, in so far as
lay in your power, did your best to fulfil
the words of the man who originally used
the term "the new Jerusalem."

SPAHLINGER TREATMENT
TUBERCULOSIS.
FOR
1. Mr. GAMBLE (for Dr. Wilson)
asked the Minister of Agriculture
whether any report has been published
regarding the treatment of tuberculosis
in cattle by means of the Spahlinger
method, and, if not, when a report can
be expected.
was
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): As
stated in an answer to a question
on 27th April last a preliminary report
on the experiments which are being
carried out by the Ministry's Veterinary
Research Division with the Spahlinger Bovine Anti-tubercular Vaccine was published in the "Veterinary
Record" for January, 1932. The work
is still in progress and I shall not be in
a position to issue a further report before
the end of the year.
In order to prevent any misunderstanding and in view of the wording of
the hon. Member's question, I think it
is desirable for me to emphasise that the
experiments do not deal with the treatment of tuberculosis, but with the
immunising efficacy of Spahlinger Vaccine.
DROMORE (COUNTY DOWN) NEW
P.E. SCHOOL-WAGES OF
LABOURERS.
2. Mr. GAMBLE (for Dr. Wilson)
asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the
Ministry of Education whether he has
now any information regarding the wages
being paid to the labourers on the site
of the new public elementary school at
Dromore, County Down, and whether
these wages are of the standard usually
paid for similar work in that neighbourhood.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): Inquiries
have now been made from the Down
County Regional Education Committee,
who state that some work is being carried
out by direct labour in connection with
clearing the site for the proposed new
public elementary school at Dromore and
that the rate of wages paid is sixpence
per hour, no deduction being made in
respect of employees' contribution
towards National Health Pensions and
Unemployment Insurance.
The Ministry has no information in
regard to the current rate of wages paid
in the locality for such work, but the
Regional Committee state that a similar
rate was paid by them in connection with
other direct labour schemes of a similar
character.

Act, 1932, empowers the use of the
"humane killer,' and, in view of

made by humane societies and others to
this end, he will extend the powers of
the Act to cover all animals.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have not received
any representations on this matter, and
I do not propose to introduce any legislation on the subject.
Major McCORMICK: Is the Minister.
aware that there is a precedent in this
matter in the fact that other countries
which have adopted the humane method
of killing have not exempted the Jewish
fraternity?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, on the
contrary, if my hon. and gallant Friend
looks up the English Act he will find
that is not so.
Major McCORMICK: I am referring
to other countries which have adopted
the humane method, not necessarily the
United Kingdom.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I feel that I
must apologise to the House for introducing a Bill of such a gloomy character

as this one. It carries one's thoughts
back to the pests of Egypt and the plague
of London when the prayer was offered up
to "Save us from those things that
happen in the night."
Mr. HEALY: And the Papists of
Fermanagh.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: We will come
to that later. There is, unfortunately,
an increasing risk of the appearance in
Northern Ireland of the Colorado beetle,
which constitutes one of the gravest
menaces to the potato crop. This beetle
happens to be a gentleman who wears
the orange and black. I know the hon.
Destructive Pests Bill
Railways Bill
22 MARCH 1934
Member (Mr. Healy) will be interested
in that. Perhaps it might be well to
pass on to what really might be a great
danger to agriculture in the future. This
particular insect we have in question
rapidly destroys all potato crops it comes
in contact with. The spraying of such
crops with various chemicals is a very
costly business. Not only that, but if
the Colorado beetle was introduced into
Northern Ireland there would inevitably
be an embargo on the export of all
potatoes from this country. It is most
necessary that we should have the necessary machinery here to deal with this
pest, which we all hope will never appear.
I may say that the potato exports from
France are entirely prohibited into the
British Isles owing to the possibility of
this beetle being introduced. It has
been suggested by a certain gentleman
in England that the Colorado beetle
really deserved a statute by itself in view
of the fact that a large importation of
potatoes from France had been thereby
prevented. The beetle was discovered
only some nine years ago in the Bordeaux
district and it has now travelled about
250 miles in a northerly direction.
might be well to read to the House an
extract from a recent French publication
which illustrates the seriousness of the
position:
It
"The situation of all branches of
French agriculture was discussed at the
annual meeting of the Agricultural
Federation of the Centre and
South. The first branch to be dealt
with was the potato industry.
The
districts infected with the Colorado
beetle are becoming more and more
numerous, all efforts to prevent its
spread have only delayed its progress
slightly."
The reason why the Bill is introduced
now is that last summer the Colorado
beetle was found, fortunately by a member of the Ministry of Agriculture, at the
Tilbury Docks. He was able to recognise
it and was able to take suitable action.
It did invade certain crops, but that has
now been dealt with. The British
powers to deal with the pest are very
much greater than ours. In view of the
rapid movement of the beetle there is a
possibility that it may eventually reach
this country. The British Act under
which the pest was attacked was the Act
of 1927. The only Act which so far
applies to Northern Ireland is the Act
of 1877. Though that minimises the risk
of importation of the beetle, it has no
power to destroy crops or pay compensation. Those powers are now sought for
in this Bill. As to the payment of compensation, it was considered that the
Ministry should bear the cost of compensation rather than the local
authorities, who were held responsible
under the Act of 1877. This Bill will
put Northern Ireland in exactly the same
position as Great Britain with regard to
powers and with regard to compensation,
the only difference being that in England
the amount of compensation to be paid
in one year without specific Treasury
consent is £2,000, while it is proposed to
insert the figure of £250 in the Northern
Ireland Bill. I beg to move.

NEW CLAUSE (Power to operate
signals and points by electricity)
A railway company may, with the
approval of the Ministry, operate its
signals and the railway points
associated with such signals by means
of electrical energy, and any authorised
undertakers within the meaning of the
Electricity (Supply) Acts (Northern
Ireland), 1882 to 1933, may, by agreement with a railway company and with
the approval of the Ministry, supply
electrical energy for that purpose for
use either within or without their area
of supply.
This section shall have effect notwithstanding the provisions of section
five of the Electric Lighting Act, 1909,
as amended by section forty-one of the
Electricity (Supply) Act (Northern
Ireland), 1931.
Brought up, and read a First time.
Question proposed, "That the Clause
be now read a Second time."
Mr. ROBB: This new Clause consists
of two parts. The first part enables a
railway company to work signals by
electrical power, and the second part
enables an electrical undertaking to
supply electricity for that purpose outside its own area. This is introduced for
two reasons. In the first place, there are
certain signals and points which are not,
in fact, within the area of any particular
undertaking supplying electricity. That
case is easily met, but in addition to that
the railway companies desire in order
that they may have an assurance that
electrical energy
will not fail them for
this particular purpose that they should
have power to contract for a supply from
two different undertakings so that if one
fails the other may be called upon. Take,
for instance, Greenisland. Greenisland

Clause 1, as will be borne in mind by
those who spoke on the Financial Resolution, deals with the grant that the House
is asked to make to the Incorporated Law
Society. The reason why it is essential
that the Government should make a contribution arises from the fact that,
whereas in other parts of the country,
both in Great Britain and in Dublin, the
old-established Law Societies had, by the
efflux of time, gradually accumulated a
considerable sum of money, when the
break took place and a new charter was
granted to the Incorporated Law Society
of Northern Ireland they had to begin
at the very bottom and had no funds
upon which to fall back to enable them
to carry on without assistance. The
justification for this House giving assistance of a modest character was that this
House imposed upon the society certain
public duties of an onerous nature and,
having done so, they considered it only
fair and proper that from the fees, or
rather duties, imposed upon new
entrants, and so on, there should be
deducted a sum sufficient to keep the
chartered association in such funds as
would enable it to carry on the duties
which Parliament had laid upon it.
The second part of the Bill, Clause 2,
deals entirely with the granting of
facilities to local authorities where stamps
upon certain documents are required by
law.

Seeing that you are now fathering the
lawyers to the extent of £1,200 a year,
I am justified in asking you to take this
Bill back, and bring in a Measure
making the same provision for the boilermakers, the shipwrights, the draughtsmen, and the linen workers. All those
organisations which cater for the industrial classes require assistance. They
have just the same right to be included
in this Bill as the Incorporated Law
Society. They pay their fees indirectly;
they also pay their fees to their trade
unions for the purpose of qualifying for
the occupation they have decided to
follow. It is no argument for the Prime
Minister to say that, because the Incorporated Law Society broke away from the
parent body, and because it has established its own organisation at the expense
of the taxpayers in the Law Courts in
Belfast, we should be asked to subsidise
the Society to the extent of £1,200 a
year. That is a privilege, and it is a
privilege that I am not going to agree
to, unless you extend the same privilege
all round.
I may say that we are justified in
asking for similar grants for educational
classes under trade union auspices in the
city of Belfast, the Farmers' Union included. The Farmers' Union is an
educative body-at least it is supposed
to be an educative body—and is as much
entitled to inclusion in this Measure as
the one privileged class with which the
Bill deals. I hope the Prime Minister
will see the error of his ways in allowing

the House at all. He has said time
after time that there is no class legislation passed by this Parliament. If he

because this is purely and simply a device

You do not return any of the money
that they pay in. Of course, that is a

true.
The industrial classes pay into the
Exchequer as well as the legal union.
They do not pay as much-I am quite
aware of that but indirectly they pay
more in the aggregate. It passes my
-
comprehension that the legal Members on

FAIR RENTS COURT.
1. Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is proposed to
introduce legislation this Session for the
purpose of setting up a fair rents court
for Belfast and the provincial towns in
Northern Ireland in order to allow
tenants of decontrolled dwelling houses
up to £26 valuation, and tenants of
licensed premises up to £52 valuation,
who were protected by the 1914 Rent
Restriction Act up to the 1st May, 1928,
and who are still tenants of their houses,
but whose leases have expired since 1925,
or are soon to expire, the opportunity
to appeal against harsh increases in
rent and fines; or whether he would
give facilities for the introduction of a
Private Member's Bill at an early date.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The reply is in the
negative.
Mr. BYRNE: I wish to give notice
that I will raise this matter on the
Adjournment, as it is very important.
Mr. SPEAKER: I am not sure that
the hon. Member will have the opportunity. However, I will let him know
later.
FISHERY RIGHTS ON RIVER BUSH.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he can state if Sir
Francis Macnaghten is permitted to fish
six unlicensed draft nets without certificates and with illegal meshes at
different weirs on the River Bush;
whether he is permitted to make illegal
weirs across the river to enable him to
catch salmon; whether he has been
allowed to erect a fixed draft net for the
past ten years on a site at the mouth of
the river where no certificate was ever
issued; whether he is allowed to have a
mill race at Bushmills without a proper
grating; whether the Clerk of the Ballycastle Conservators is allowed to act as
head water keeper on the river although
he has been convicted of illegal fishing;
and whether any prosecutions have been
taken against Sir Francis Macnaghten
when he was reported on several occasions
during 1932 and 1933 by the local police
the proper authorities for illegal
fishing on the river.
to
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I am informed that it
is the practice of Sir Francis Macnaghten
to fish the River Bush by means of
licensed draft nets and that these are
used in the pools and not at the weirs.
The only such net at present being
used has been inspected and found to be
of legal mesh, and I have no reason to
believe that an illegal mesh has ever
been employed.
The answer to the second part of the
question is in the negative. Certain
structures to which the hon. Member
presumably refers have come under the
notice of my Ministry, which is of opinion
that their erection does not constitute
any infringement of the statutes.
The position of the fixed draft net at
the mouth of the river has also come
under notice, and whilst it is true that,
in the interests of the safety of the men
employed in working it, the net. was
being fished from a position some short

Question proposed: That notwithstanding any Standing Order or Custom
of the House the Proceedings on Government business, if under discussion when
the said business is postponed at halfpast Four o'clock this day, be resumed
and proceeded with though opposed after

Six o'clock. (The Prime Minister.)
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the Prime Minister the reason for this
great hurry with Government business at
this very early period of the Session of
this Parliament. I cannot understand a
Government that clamours to love Ulster
so much wanting to be so little time in it.
That being so, I demand an explanation
from the Government as to why they
have the audacity to come forward on
this Tuesday afternoon and ask that all
these outstanding Measures which appear
on
the Order Paper should be put
through the House with the least possible
delay. Several of the Measures on the
Order Paper, which, I presume, will be
pushed through this afternoon, require
the serious attention and consideration
of Members on this side, but no
time for that purpose is going to
be given if this Motion is going
to be accepted. I think Members of this
House, between three o'clock and halfpast six, are not devoting too much time
to their Parliamentary duties. Perhaps
I may be charged with taking my Parliamentary work too seriously. If I
take it seriously, I must say that a large
percentage of Members do not take it
seriously.
The Prime Minister, who is the
greatest culprit of all, now comes forward
to prove what the outside public have
charged him with, that he does not care
for Ulster or Ulster's legislation. All
he desires is to spend as short a time in
Ulster as is possible and take as long a
time as possible elsewhere. I do not
stand for this class of Motion at all.
If it were necessary I would be the first
to accede to the request of the Prime
Minister, but I do not think the Motion
is necessary.
I believe we would do well
to be here each day of this week and
return early the following week to consider what is best to be done for the
starving multitudes outside. The Prime
Minister does not seem to realise that
this House controls the destinies of a
million and a quarter people. He depends greatly on the British Parliament
carrying through legislation on their
behalf. I have been reading in the
Business of the House.
Business of the House
27 MARCH 1934
papers about the legislation in the
British House of Commons, and the people
of Northern Ireland are by no means
concerned or interested in those Measures.
If it takes the British Parliament 250
days in the year to deal with legislation
for their area it is as little as we can do
to take six months to consider the Bills
brought forward here. I know I have
always opposed a Motion of this sort.
I oppose it quite sincerely, because
to-day I had representations made to me
as to the desperate plight of the unemployed in our city due to the action of
the Government, combined with the
action of the Belfast Corporation. I
have also got in my possession many
letters from deserving widows in Northern
Ireland as a result of the controversy
that took place last week. I feel that
if we get into matters of that kind and
spend our time here in one united effort
to do good towards those two classes our
services would be given in a way which
would be a credit to ourselves and a
benefit to the Province.
I know the outlook from the Government side is this: Let us get into
Parliament for a few days and let us pretend that we are doing an enormous
amount of work on behalf of the people,
but after we have worked about three
days let us get recreation likely to extend
for a month's duration. I do not know
any employers of labour throughout the
world who would pay the same wages for
services similar to those given by the
Members of the Government. Would we
not be well advised to sit down in this
assembly-it is not a horrible assembly
to remain in, it is about as pleasant as
any other assembly throughout the
world-
Mr. STEWART: Sometimes.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am not talking
about the Members, I am talking about
the atmospheric conditions inside and the
beauty of the surrounding conditions,
which are as pleasant as could be desired.
I feel that we ought to get down to bedrock and decide that the policy we are
pursuing for Northern Ireland will be in
accordance with the needs and requirements of the people. We might get
down to a shorter working week. May
I give an illustration of that? We have
to-day in the shipyards, which formerly
employed 20,000 workers, a a forward
movement towards the elimination of the
human element.
In 1934, at the highest peak, the shipyards could only employ 10,000, leaving
the remaining 10,000 shipyard workers
idle for all time. We could sit down and
consider ways and means for providing
employment for those 10,000 in a
direction not likely to run contrary to
any other industry. Whether the
Government like the idea or not, sooner
or
later they have got to meet this
position. They will not be able to find
employment for all those idle people who
are roaming the streets, because the
industries cannot absorb them.
Mr. SPEAKER: I hope the hon.
Member will not stretch his illustration
too widely.
Mr. BEATTIE: That would be one
useful
way in which we could work out a
policy for this Province if we sat here.
But the Government have neither the
desire nor the will to do anything which
would be likely to remove poverty and
distress and give little bits of comfort to
the people outside, whom they claim to
love, honour, and obey. Therefore, I
feel I am justified in asking this House
to reject this Motion and to continue to
sit, as in my opinion your Parliamentary
time is ample for the carrying out of a
bigger programme than you have at the
moment. In doing that I believe you
will not succeed in many directions, but
you will certainly raise yourselves in the
estimation of the people, because if you
do nothing you will at least attend Parliament and endeavour to go on the step-bystep policy. I hope the House will reject
the Motion. I certainly will divide it.

throughout the community in regard to
We felt, and we
this particular Bill.
still feel, that to oppose a Bill like this
in the House of Commons is going to
result at some time or other in people
being informed that we took up the
attitude on this Bill that we are taking up
because we do not appreciate the conditions
under which we live, and because we do not

I opposed each of the Clauses on the
last day with the exception of one, and,
generally speaking, those of us who spoke
against the Bill based our case on
the two main provisions in the Bill. One
is the seven years residential qualification
for voting, and the second is that a

can be deemed to be a candidate
must sign a declaration that he intends to take his seat. I may be
pardoned if to-day I again review our
attitude with regard to the Clause dealing
with the signing of the declaration, lest,
when I sit down some hon. Member on
the other side should unconsciously, or
consciously, misrepresent what we mean
by our opposition to that Clause.
I stated on the last day that I belonged
to an organisation and section of thought
in Northern Ireland which, up to the
present, believes that it is right to take
our seats in this House and try to mould,
as far as we possibly can, the policy to
be decided upon in this House. That is
our policy. We believe, no matter what
changes time may bring about in the constitution and development of the country,
that it is right and proper to take our
part in utilising the existing machinery to
the end that social problems may get the
consideration which they deserve. And
in furtherance of that policy my hon.
Friend, the Member for Pottinger, and
myself have been duly elected in pursuance of the elementary rights of
citizenship by the people in the parts of
the city to which we belong.
We are here to voice the point of view
of those who elected us; we are here to
put the point of view that received con-
781 Representation of People Bill-

27 MARCH 1934
Second Reading
firmation when we presented ourselves as
candidates. We, therefore, take up this
attitude with regard to the signing of the
declaration, not because it is part of our
policy at all, but because we do not
believe in imposing such a condition. We
believe you are cutting across the rights
and dictates of conscience in regard to
certain members of the community. I
am at pains to stress this point of view.
I believe in the right of conscience being
respected. The last war proved conclusively that you cannot crush effectively
the voice of conscience when it expresses
itself in opposition to a policy pursued in
any particular country.
Years have gone by and many of those
who could have been derided and degraded in the years of the war and
the years immediately following the war
for the manifestation of their consciences are to-day more respected, from
many points of view, than they were in
those particular years. At the same time,
there is some historical analogy between
the conditions then prevailing and the
conditions to-day. There are to-day
people in Northern Ireland and throughout the whole of Ireland, who believe,
conscientiously, that it is right to do a
certain thing or to pursue a certain
policy, and to impose conditions politically
or electorally upon those people which
would prevent them from giving expression to what they conscientiously believe,
is a negation of the spirit of liberty and
a denial of the rights of citizenship, and
because of that I am opposed to this
Clause.
When we come to the other Clause with
regard to the seven years qualification, I
wish that the whole public of Northern
Ireland were here to hear the flimsy pretexts put forward by hon. Members in
this House as a justification of that
Clause. One hon. Member said it was
to prevent people from entering our
territory and taking advantage of our
social services; another Member said it
was to prevent infiltration; another Member said there was a kind of propaganda
being carried on which rested upon the
basis of people coming over from an
inferior area into a superior one to
take advantage of the general standard
of living. Another Member said that, in
his opinion, the Clause did not go far
enough. He would not have it seven
years, he would have it seventy-seven
years. I interjected, "Why give them a
vote at all?" and he said, "Why, indeed,
give them a vote at all?" He added
these significant words that before any
person in Northern Ireland could be put
on the register of voters he ought to be
compelled to sign the Oath of Allegiance.
And several hon. Members on the
other side of the House who are more
renowned for their veracity than for
their thinking shouted "Hear, hear,"
not realising the significance of that. At
the same time we had a declaration by a
leading Front Bench Member that it
was not the desire of the Government to
impose any kind of dictatorship or
any denial of political rights upon any
section of the community. Yet on that
particular day the back benchers were
clamouring for a Clause which would
deny the right of any person even to
vote at an election, much less to be a
candidate, until he had signed an Oath
of Allegiance, the oath, of course, to be
an oath conceived and drawn up by hon.
Members on the opposite side of the
House.
All those points show the kind of confusion that exists in regard to what
is the purpose of this Bill. I demonstrated that in very devastating fashion
last day. I am sorry some of the back
benchers who are here to-day were not
present on that occasion, because I know
they will speak this afternoon with all
the
appearance of innocence of which they
are capable, entirely oblivious of the fact
that good, sensible, constructive arguments have already been used to destroy
the particular case they will try to make.
I am sorry they had not the advantage
of being present the last day this Bill was
debated, because they would have found

upon other people because they happen to

the principles of true religion or of

an
interests and dug themselves in to such

The point is this, if we are going to
continue to legislate and look out upon the
affairs of Ireland from the point of view
of Bills like this, we are going to get
nowhere. We are not going to bring
about the improvement in the conditions
of the people and of the country that
ultimately we hope will be brought about
for the good of every section of the community. Good gracious, I should not
like the people of Northern Ireland to
think that the Government have
monopoly of the desire to express their
spiritual identity or to enjoy spiritual
freedom. I claim-so do my colleagues
in the movement to which I belong
-that the people of Northern Ireland, the people of Southern Ireland,
the people of the world, have a right
to think theologically and every other
way what they like. We do not want
to see any conditions imposed which
would restrict that liberty. We are just
as jealous and proud of it as anybody
else. It is incompatible with our
ideals of liberty and of bringing
about a better state of feeling, to proceed upon the assumption that everybody
outside is our enemy and aiming at our
destruction, and that the right thing to
do is to put conditions into a Bill which
are a violation not only of British laws
and British traditions and British institutions, but are contrary to the spirit of
fair play and justice.
That is not the right way to bring about
a change of conditions. As I have said,
a business man told me some time ago
that it was possible to bring about
a better commercial relationship on the
basis of seeing that the rights of every
section of the people of Northern Ireland were defended and safeguarded. It
would be for the good of all the people
of Ireland to have some improvement in
their relationships. He told me that his
firm has lost £100,000 in one year as a
result of the conditions that prevail today, and he told me that other firms in
Belfast were in a similar position. He
also said that people were scared to
mention this, because if they gave expression to it, the political party presided over by the Prime Minister, with
its prostitution of economics to political
expediency, would turn round and, perhaps, use the weapon of public opinion
to do them further commercial injury.
And he belonged to the same faith as myself and the Members of the Government.
Further, he said, that the right policy
to be pursued by public men in Ireland is

It is for that spirit I plead here this

It makes me depressed. Nevertheless, I

worship and all the rest of it.
I can do all those things-and do them
-without impinging upon the liberty of
anyone else. I have found nobody

constituency, and I am thankful to say

although we have sacrificed none of our

House to listen to that. I have sacrificed

of the social and economic questions that

It is the duty of Members of this House

If
a man does not want to fight, I do not

some of the economic requirements of the

I do not intend to present figures to the
House, but I speak from actual knowledge when I say that over a period of
years, subsequent and I would like to
call the attention of the Member for Dock
to this subsequent to the last census of
1926, a considerable filtration has taken
place from the neighbouring County of
Donegal into the City of Londonderry.
Other Members can speak as to their own
constituencies, but with regard to my
own I speak with assurance. I do not
intend to follow the hon. Member for
Dock, whose speech has consisted
largely of references to religion, but I
wish to say that there has been a definite
filtration from the County of Donegal of
those whom I describe as disloyalists.
When I describe them as disloyalists I
would like to say that, in my opinion,
which of course will not be shared by
many hon. Members opposite, a disloyalist
is one who to-day would wish to see Ülster
thrown into the Free State. That is my
definition of a disloyalist and, in my
opinion, a man or woman who comes into
Ulster to-day from the Free State, having
as his or her object the intention of working for the destruction of our Constitution because that is involved-and the
merging of Northern Ireland or Ulster
into the Free State, that man or woman
is a disloyalist. Surely it is not very
much to expect that man or woman, holding those views and coming from the Free
State into Northern Ireland with that
intention and with the object of assisting
towards that consummation, should serve
a definite apprenticeship, and should, at
least, have a certain number of years
residence in Northern Ireland before he
or she qualifies for a vote.
In the course of the debate I have not
seen any suggestion by hon. Members
opposite that the period of years prescribed in the Act which we are now asked
to amend, namely, three years, was in
any way oppressive. Do hon. Members
opposite suggest that a person coming in
from the Free State should qualify for
a vote the moment he or she walks across
the frontier. If not, what is to be the
period. A three years' period was prescribed many years ago, and surely the

do so because one day last week I met

Mr. ROBB: There is nothing in the

employee of any employer, they are not

that they are prohibited from living in,

permitted to become candidates for
election either to Parliament or to local
boards.
Mr. BEATTIE: And why?
Mr. ROBB: Should a teacher, however, be selected as a co-opted member of
a rural or an urban district council he is
permitted to occupy that position so long,
of course, as it does not interfere with
his attendance at his school. I am asked
why they are not permitted to take an
active part in politics. I will put the
answer in the simplest way. In this area
teachers are directly paid by the State.
They are employees of the State to that
extent. The schools in which they teach
are schools which children of all creeds
and classes are bound to attend, and it
is not considered advisable, in the
interests of educational administration,
that teachers of the children of parents
who may hold differing views should be
allowed to take an active part in politics.
These rules apply only to elementary
school teachers, because we found that it
was not necessary to apply them to any
other class of teachers. Secondary school
teachers are under boards of governors,
and we found that the governors take
the same view as the Government, that
it is not advisable for teachers to take an
active part in politics.

Some of the biggest principles in life

way. We are supposed to stand for civil

a certain electoral division in Fermanagh

his vote he returned whence he came.
Hence the term "swallow."

I am now asking the Committee to provide.
of

There is one argument which the hon.

the whole of the solicitors' profession in

Law Society in Dublin. It has been
suggested that in some way the present
difficulty has been brought about by the
solicitors of Northern Ireland. Nothing
could be further from the truth. This
position was forced upon the solicitors of
Northern Ireland. There are many arguments why it would have been impossible
for them to have carried on under the
jurisdiction of the society, which meets in
Dublin. When they found themselves in
that position they necessarily lost their
share in participation of the large
accumulated funds which enabled that
society to carry on its duties, statutory or
otherwise, which it is bound to carry on
in the interests of the profession.
If I might put one point to the Committee to show that the present position
is inevitable it is this. The ultimate
tribunal which decided all matters connected with the Incorporated Law
Society and the solicitors' profession was
formerly the Lord Chancellor of Ireland.
After all disciplinary measures had been
discussed by the society and reported on
by them the matter came before the Lord
Chancellor, who gave his decision on the
merits of the particular case, and
appropriate cases solicitors were liable to
be struck off the roll by the Lord Chancellor. Since 1921 that jurisdiction has
been partitioned, and that was a matter
due to the legislative effect of various Acts
of Parliament and had nothing to say to
the Incorporated Law Society themselves.
in
The jurisdiction in the Irish Free State
is now vested in the Chief Justice of the
Irish Free State and the jurisdiction over
solicitors in Northern Ireland is vested in
the Lord Chief Justice of Northern
Ireland. It is obviously impossible that
the Lord Chief Justice of Northern
Ireland could exercise his jurisdiction
over the solicitors' profession upon the
advice of a body which is not amenable
to his jurisdiction but which sits in
Dublin and which looks after the interests
of the solicitors of the Irish Free State.
Therefore, the argument that the hon.
Member for Pottinger has advanced to
the Committee that in some way the
Incorporated Law Society were responsible for having precipitated the crisis
which has necessitated their being put in
funds to carry on this new jurisdiction
does not apply because it was not a matter
over which they had any control. It is
the result of the legislation which has
taken place and under which the Government of Northern Ireland has come into
being.

is it going to be possible for a registration.
agent to know when those people became

Mrs. PARKER: The Bill which I have
the honour of introducing here this afternoon has received the unanimous approval
of another House where it was piloted
by one whose name, I think, will always
be associated in Northern Ireland with
the welfare of animals (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). It has been entrusted to
me and I would feel that a considerable
responsibility rests on my shoulders were
I not confident that even if I only
formally moved the adoption of the Bill
hon. Members would give it most
sympathetic consideration. I know that
although we may differ on politics, and
even some of us may not see eye to eye
in the matter of history or even of art,
yet when it comes to a question of the

Mr. P. O'Neill.
interpretation of our duty towards those
whom Providence has placed at our mercy
and who look to us for protection, I am
confident we will all be of one mind.
man.
The dog has always been the friend of
It is only right to say that in
most cases he is the best and truest friend.
The dog has always given the most
unquestionable loyalty and unswerving
fidelity, and I am afraid we cannot say
that of all human beings. That loyalty
and fidelity have persisted in the face of
discouragement and I am afraid sometimes even of persecution. There is an
eastern legend which deals with the origin
of that devotion. The story is that in the
very beginning man went in friendship
with all the animals. Gradually as awakening and development came to his soul he
realised that he was spiritually apart and
towered immeasurably above the animals
and yet was immeasurably inferior to and
lower than God. His loneliness was
very great. He could find no longer
even satisfaction and contentment with
the animals and as this realisation of his
isolation came to him the story runs that
the sky darkened, the earth shook, and
a crack appeared in the surface of the
earth. It was a gradually widening
crack which separated man from his
former companions. As the crack
widened into a gulf the dog alone of all
the animals unable to endure separation
from the only being he had looked on as
his master and the only god he knew,
made his irrevocable choice and crossed
the gulf to stand beside the man, his
master, through all his loneliness and
sorrow. That is the legend.
I am sure hon. Members would like me
to get on with the Bill. Personally, in
some ways I would really rather remain

much to the care of human beings. Also,
from another point of view, I would like
to say that I think the two points of
view are inseparable and that cruelty is
certainly very bad for the perpetrator as
well as for the victim. Cruelty is an
infectious disease. It deadens the susceptibilities and coarsens the moral
fibres, and those who are cruel to
animals are also certain to be cruel in
their dealings with their fellow human
beings. Finally, I would like to quote.
some words which I quoted in 1926 in
connection with the Protection of
Animals Bill. These are the words:
Once we realise that cruelty is as
bad for the cruel as for the victim
it becomes clear that those who work
for the protection of animals against
man are working also for the protection of man against himself. And
since far more cruel things are done
through ignorance and insensibility
than through a morbid love of inflicting pain, the champions of animals
may be discerned as doing for man a
very valuable work of education.
When cruelty to animals has disappeared from earth cruelty to man
will have disappeared with it.-
(Official Report, 14th October, 1926,
vol. VII., col. 1689).
If the Second Reading of this Bill is
passed here this afternoon without any
opposition we will be doing something
for the animal kingdom and something
for the kingdom of man. I beg to move.

owning or keeping one, and it will prevent those people who allow their
passions and cruelties to be expended on
a defenceless animal from repeating the
offence.
The hon. Member in introducing the
Bill instanced two cases of cruelty which
occurred in England. I think that the
society which is doing such useful work
not only in Belfast but all over Ulster
is worthy of all praise. A memorandum
has been issued detailing the cases of
cruelty brought up at the various courts
here, and I am sure hon. Members are
astonished that there are people living
in our midst who could be guilty of
such offences. It is only right that they
should be properly dealt with.
I was pleased to observe that the hon.
and learned Senator (Mr. Campbell)
who introduced the Bill in the other
House, and whose love and thought for
dumb animals is a trait of his character,
saw fit to insert a Clause which would
get over the sham of the owners transferring the charge of the dog to someone
else in his house. That is a subterfuge
that could not be permitted. If we are
to deal with an inhumane owner we must
make every provision to prevent evasion,
and I feel certain that the Clause which
has been inserted will do that. The Bill
in the opinion of some of us may not go
far enough, but at any rate it is a step
in the right direction, and I trust it
will receive a unanimous vote.

Mr. HENDERSON: I beg to move:
"That in the opinion of this House the
time has now arrived when schemes of
public utility should be promoted by the
Government with the object of absorbing
married and single men into employment."
I know from past experience that this
Motion will not appeal to right hon. and
hon. Gentlemen opposite. I know that
the people who were talking about cruelty
to dogs will vote against the Motion which
I am now introducing and which would
be helpful to humanity. It horrifies me
to think that the Government, from the
time of its establishment, has done
absolutely nothing for the single men of
Northern Ireland. The plight of the unemployed worker in Northern Ireland
to-day is worse than it was twelve years
ago. I would have thought that, in view
of such an important Motion being on the
Order Paper, the Prime Minister, who is
paid the greatest salary of any Prime
Minister in the world, would have had the
ordinary courtesy to have come into the
House during the time the Motion was
being discussed. But the Prime Minister
is not interested in the unemployed.
There are very few of the Government
side interested in the unemployed of
Northern Ireland. Instead of doing
something useful for the people who were
responsible for sending them to this.
House, the people who made some of
them, the people who have made Ulster,
the people who built Belfast, the people
who, according to the Government, are
the backbone of the British Empire, they
have neglected them and done nothing for
them. The Minister of Labour is the
only Member of the most costly Cabinet
in the world who has seen fit to be present,
with the exception of the Minister of Commerce (Mr. Barbour). (Laughter.) It
is deplorable that they are not here,
because this concerns nearly every
Cabinet Minister. I am delighted to see
the Minister of Commerce here, because I
think he, himself, is partly responsible for
the thousands of people who are unemplayed in Northern Ireland. He will
have to share responsibility in regard to
the Government's neglect of those people.
I notice that an Amendment has been
put down by the hon. and gallant Member
for Clifton (Major Hall-Thompson). The
poor who live in his constituency are
almost the poorest people in Northern
Ireland. There is greater hardship, I
believe, in the hon. and gallant Member's
constituency than in any other constituency in Northern Ireland.
Of course
we all expected an Amendment, but when
it comes from the hon. and gallant Member for Clifton it amuses me. Seeing the
Prime Minister is not here, and is not
likely to be here during the time I am
speaking, the Minister of Labour has to
tell the House what is going to be done
for the married men who are unemployed
in Northern Ireland and also what is
going to be done for the single men who
are unemployed. (An hon. Member:
Marry them.) It is rather unusual that
one of the "big guns" should have made
that same very important statement
already and that it should now be
reiterated by a "machine gun" or a
"revolver." It horrifies me to think
that the Minister of Labour should have
stated that in order to get help the single
men should get married.

Motion made, and Question proposed:

Mr. NIXON: I was going to ask for
some information from the Prime Minister.
I did not give him notice, because the
Prime Minister has already been discussing in other places the matter about which
I was going to ask him. We will be
honoured in the near future by a visit
from the Earl of Ulster, and the Prime
Minister has been telling the guests at a
dinner in the Grand Central Hotel something about the arrangements which are
being made to give him a reception worthy
of his position and worthy of the occasion.
I cannot but regret that the Prime
Minister did not disclose that information
to the House in the first instance. However, that cannot be helped now, but there
is to be a ceremony, I believe from reading the papers, in this House. What I
would like to suggest, and I am sure
everyone on all sides of the House will
agree, is that that should be a national
reception; that everyone interested should
have an equal opportunity of participating
in it, and that it should not, under any
circumstances, be turned into a political
function or anything like that. I want in
my little way, as representing a great
loyal constituency, to do what I can to
make it a success.
The last time we had a Royal visitor
here I took serious objection to one room
of this House being put at the special
disposal of a political party. All I want
in this reception, or whatever it is to be-
I am sure it will be worthy of the occasion;
I have no doubt about that. There is no
one on that side of the House from the
Prime Minister down lacking in a sense of
duty is that everyone, even those who are
not subject to the Whip, and the supporters of those who are not subject to the
Whip, should have an equal opportunity
of showing their respect and appreciation
of the Throne on this occasion, and I hope
the very grave blunder of putting any part
of this House at the disposal of any
political party will not be repeated.
Mr. BEATTIE: I want to add my
voice of protest against any political party
using any part of this House for any
political purpose. I think we are justified
in making that protest. We know it has
been used for that purpose in the past,
but we are forgiving the past in the hope
that in the present and future no political
propaganda of any description will be
carried out in any room set aside for the
use of Members of this House.
I would like also to ask the Prime
Minister to tell the House the order of
business for to-morrow and the following
day, and also on what day the Minister
of Finance is likely to introduce the
Budget.

18 APRIL 1934
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 18th April, 1934.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
RAILWAYMEN AND POSSESSION
OF FIREARMS.
1. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he has received
a resolution from the Associated Society
of Locomotive Engineers and Firemen
protesting against certain men being retained in the railway service who are in
possession of firearms, one of whom was
recently fined for having a revolver in
his possession; and whether he proposes
to make representations to the railway
company for the removal of such persons
so as to ensure the safety of other railway men.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): In
the unavoidable absence of my right
hon. Friend I have been asked to reply.
I am aware of the resolution referred to
by the hon. Member. It would, however, be improper for me to make representations to the railway company with
the object of the removal by the company of any of their employees.
Any person who is found to be in
possession of firearms without proper
authority is liable to be proceeded
against under the Firearms Act.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Is the hon. and
learned Gentleman aware of the fact
that certain employees of this company
claim that they are working under conditions which are very serious to themselves, and that they really believe they
are in danger of losing their lives?
Mr. HANNA: No, I am not aware
that those conditions exist, but I would
imagine that the strength and power of
the law would be sufficient to deal with
the situation. If any person feels that
his life is in danger he can make a claim
in the proper way.
IRISH AMATEUR BOXING
ASSOCIATION AND BRITISH
EMPIRE GAMES.
aware
2. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is
that the Irish Amateur Boxing Association has decided not to send a team to
the British Empire Games this summer
on the pretext that the men would then
be out of training and that it has now.
been decided to pick a representative
Irish side to meet a team coming from
France in August; and, if so, whether
he will take the necessary steps to prevent any member of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary from taking part in this
tournament.
Mr. HANNA: With regard to the
first part of this question I am not in
a position to state what action may be
taken by the Irish Amateur Boxing
Association in regard to sending representatives to take part in the British
Empire Games.
I am informed that the Irish Civic
Guards hold a sports week in August
each year and that it has been the
custom to invite a continental boxing
team to compete at this meeting against
a team of the Civic Guards. This year
I understand a French team has been
so invited, and it is probably to this
team that the hon. Member refers. I
have no knowledge whether or not this
invitation has been accepted.
This is a purely Civic Guard function,
the organisation of which has nothing to
do with the Irish Amateur Boxing
Association and in no way affects the
question of the attendance of representatives of the Royal Ulster Constabulary at the British Empire Games.
