CLASS VII. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF COMMERCE.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £15,217 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge
which will come in course of payment
during the year ending 31st March,
1935, to defray the salaries and expenses
of the Ministry of Commerce (15 and 16
Geo. V., c. 3, s. 4 (N.I.); 16 Geo. V.,
c. 4 (N.I.))" (£5,000 has been voted on
account).
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The Estimate before the
Committee represents the anticipated
cost to the Exchequer of administering
, the various services performed by the
Ministry of Commerce during the financial year 1934-35. I face the Committee this year under happier auspices
than I have done for many years past.
The improvement which has taken place
in the position of our trade and industry
during the last eight or nine months is
undoubted and is in itself a reflection of
the improvement which has taken place
in the trade of the Kingdom as a whole
and even, despite many adverse factors,
in that of the world.
I am far from wishing to suggest to
the Committee that this is a time for
unbridled optimism. Whilst you are
all aware of the substantial fall in unemployment which has taken place in
the Kingdom as a whole, there are still
over 2,000,000 persons on the unemployed register in Great Britain and
64,500 in Northern Ireland, and there
is still a great deal of leeway to be
made up in our export and import
trade. But when all is said and done,
substantial improvement has set in and
there is every reason to hope that it may
be continued. The disastrous fall in
prices which has caused such havoc in
recent years has at last been checked
and, if in many directions there is not
as yet any marked upward tendency,
there is at least stability, which leads to
renewed confidence.
Whilst conditions abroad are still
difficult and obscure, the export section
of the linen trade has more than held
its own, and the quantity of linen piecegoods despatched overseas in 1933 was
the largest recorded for eight years.
Figures which I have had abstracted
from the trade returns show the increase
for the 12 months ended 31st March
last in the value of linen piece-goods to
be 22 per cent. over the similar preceding period, whereas in the value of yarns
exported it is as much as 51 per cent.
These are encouraging figures. The
position would, of course, be more satisfactory than it is, were weavers and
merchants able to obtain for the goods
produced an advance in prices commensurate with the rise which has taken
place in the price of flax. The lag in
the market prices obtainable for
finished goods still acts as a brake on
industrial activity. Nevertheless, there
is considerable satisfaction to be derived
from the fact that unemployment in the
linen industry which reached the high
level of some 24,000 persons in 1932,
has now been reduced to a figure of the
order of 10,000.
I think I may describe the change
which has taken place in the position
of the shipbuilding industry as dramatic.
When I faced the Committee last year,
there were only two vessels under construction in our yards, to-day there are
fifteen, with a considerable amount of
repair and reconditioning work, which
includes, or will shortly include, the
provision of new propelling machinery
for four large vessels.
The repeal of prohibition in the
United States has restored an important
outlet for our distilling industry. In
the harbour of Belfast one of the best
and most accessible docks in the Kingdom has been opened and on its quays,
already in operation, stands an important new
new flour milling enterprise.
The canning of fruit and vegetables and
other new manufacturing activities have
been started, albeit on a small scale,
but the tale of returning confidence and
reviving industry goes on, and I trust
that it may have an even happier sequel
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
18 APRIL 1934
when these Estimates are again presented to you in the next financial year.
As Members of the Committee will
be aware, the negotiation of trade
agreements with foreign countries, to
which I referred in my Estimates speech
last year, continues to occupy an important place in the external trade
policy of the United Kingdom. I wish
to assure the Committee that my Department is keeping in close touch with
these negotiations which it watches
constantly from the point of view of
Northern Ireland trade interests, ensuring that the appropriate trade organisations are given an effective opportunity
for the expression of their views, and
that no aspect of the negotiations of
direct interest to Northern Ireland is
neglected through inadequate presentation of the special case of the
Province.
When I addressed the Committee last
year the future of the Empire Marketing
Board was still in doubt. In the meantime, as the Committee will be aware, the
Empire Marketing Board has been dissolved, and this decision has necessarily
deprived my Ministry of many opportunities for the display of Northern Irish
produce in the provincial centres of Great
Britain under the exceptionally advantageous conditions which the Empire
Marketing Board exhibitions themselves
provided. Nevertheless, there is one
exhibition at which, in my judgment,
Northern Ireland should continue to be
represented so long as a corporate
exhibition of all the partners in the
British Commonwealth of Nations continues to be one of its most distinctive
features.
I refer, of course, to the British
Industries Fair. We are satisfied that
not only is this exhibition of solid commercial value to our Province, but I
would remind Members that, in addition,
it affords us an opportunity of demonstrating, not only to our fellow-countrymen across the water, but also to the
buyers who attend the fair from every
quarter of the globe, our unity with
England, Scotland and Wales.
The
exhibits of these countries are grouped
with ours at Olympia under the one
heading of United Kingdom. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Ever since I have been associated with
the Ministry of Commerce it has been my
settled policy to co-ordinate the supply
of electricity, so that, so far as possible,
the advantages which are derived, and
can only be derived, from bulk supplies
in the hands of large undertakers covering wide areas, might be afforded to
consumers, large and small, scattered over
our whole area. The past year has
witnessed a great step forward towards
the realisation of this ideal.
During the past year the sales of
current throughout the area increased
from 76 million units to approximately
88 million units, an increase of over 14
This has been due to a large
per cent.
extent to the rapid progress made in the
electrification of our rural and semirural areas, the greater part of which
are already covered by the high tension
net-works of the Electricity Board and
the Antrim Electricity Supply Company.
I have been particularly gratified to
note the eagerness. with which the small
consumer has been ready to avail himself
of the facilities offered, and the development in the use of electric power for
domestic purposes other than lighting has
been phenomenal over the countryside
and in the small towns, and has far
exceeded our expectations. We are by
no means at the top of the curve, and I
anticipate that the coming year will be
marked by further important developments, as our people come to realise that
electricity is no longer the luxury of the
town-man or the rich man, but a boon
and a
means of relief from drudgery
standing at the disposal of every citizen,
whatever his station in life may be, and
wherever he dwell.
may
Nor is this the whole of the story. We
have been aiming not merely at extending the domestic use of electricity, but
also at placing cheap supplies of power in
bulk at the disposal of industry, and the
progress in the direction of industrial
electrification can be gauged from the fact
that during 1933 over two million units
were sold for industrial power purposes
in rural districts as compared with
650,000 units in 1932. Hon. Members
will appreciate that my Ministry, as the
Ministry responsible for the administration of the Electricity Acts and for the
exercise of the statutory powers which
those Acts confer, is intimately associated
with this rapid development work.
Ministry of Commerce
Estimates-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
I may, perhaps, venture to say a word
in regard to our fisheries. Here we have
a field in which it is not within the power
of man to command success, since nature
can, and often does, make conditions that
will defeat the best efforts of fishermen
and governments combined. Unfortunately, 1933 witnessed such conditions in
our herring fishery, the returns from
which were amongst the poorest of recent
years. The absence of herring in any
quantity proved a bitter disappointment
to men whose main source of livelihood
is the summer herring fishing off our
County Down coast, and the disappointment was the harder to bear in that it
followed a succession of poor seasons.
In the hope that the gap thus left in
the men's earnings might in some
measure be filled up, the Ministry undertook a detailed survey of the sea bed
along the coast from Groomsport to Carlingford Lough on the one side, and on
the Antrim shore of Belfast Lough on
the other, with a view to determining
the extent of the known, and of locating
any hitherto undiscovered, escallop beds.
Escallop fishing, as hon. Members may
know, was at one time actively prosecuted
along the northern coast of Down, but,
owing to the exhaustion of the known
beds, had practically ceased to engage
attention in recent years.
The exploitation of an old bed near the
mouth of Strangford Lough a couple of
seasons ago suggested the possibility of a
general revival of this kind of fishing,
and the Ministry decided to test this
possibility by first finding out, through
dredging operations, the extent of the
resources actually available. The tests
were carried out last July, and, I am
glad to say, the information thus gained
has been speedily turned to good account
by our fishermen. Of the new beds discovered, one lying off Ballyquinton
Castle, near the mouth of Strangford
Lough, and another off Black Head in
County Antrim, have proved valuable,
and there is reason to hope that the
possibilities indicated at other places will
materialise when they have been more
fully explored by the fishermen themselves.
The year 1933 will be memorable in
the history of the British sea-fishing
industry, as marking the institution of
the system of controlling the landings of
foreign-caught fish in the United Kingdom. The system, of course, applies to
Northern Ireland equally with Great
Britain and, whilst our fishermen have
not hitherto been subjected to competition in our own local market from
fish landed in Northern Ireland by
foreign-owned vessels, they undoubtedly
stand to benefit equally with the English
and Scottish fishermen from the protection afforded in Great Britain.
We may
hope, too, that the outcome of the
investigations which the Sea-Fish Commission are now making into the whole
of the British sea-fishing industry will
result in improvement of the conditions
under which fishermen in Great Britain
and Northern Ireland are at present
working.
I would also refer to the continuance
of the Ministry's fishery loans scheme,
with the principles of which hon. Members are already familiar. During the
time that the Ministry has been responsible for Fishery Services up to the
end of December last, the number of
loans made was 210, representing a total
of £6,936. Whilst the magnitude of this
sum may not be impressive, the assistance actually given to the fishermen, as
measured in terms of boats and gear is,
I think, far from negligible. Altogether,
by means of fishery loans, Northern Irish
fishermen have acquired 600 nets, 43
boats and 10 engines. Some of the boats,
of course, included engines, whilst the 10
engines I have mentioned were purchases
made for installation in boats already in
use.
I now turn to industrial assurance.
Very extended use continues to be made
of the facilities which my Ministry provides for the settlement of disputes
between policyholders and companies or
societies. The number of such disputes
referred to the Industrial Assurance
Commissioner during the calendar year
1933 was 841. To deal with them it was
necessary to arrange sittings not only at
Belfast, but also at such centres as
Londonderry, Enniskillen, Dungannon,
Newry, and Strabane. Some increase is
shown in the figures for the current year,
and it is evident that the facilities already
well-known in Belfast are becoming
increasingly known to policyholders in
provincial towns, who are coming forward.
in rising numbers to take advantage of
them. Provision is made in the
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
18 APRIL 1934
Estimates for continuing to utilise the
services of a barrister, who acts for the
Commissioner in hearing and determining
cases of disputes.
The actual Estimates before the Committee differ but slightly from those which
I presented last year. Such variation as
there is, is in the direction of economy.
The number of staff in respect of which
provision has been made is 51, as compared with 52 in the last financial year,
and the amount required for salaries,
wages and so on, is £20,180, as compared
with £20,504 in 1933-1934. The provision under Sub-head C 1 (Collection of
Trade and Fishery Statistics) and D
(Postage, Telegrams, and Telephones)
also shows a slight reduction as compared
with the previous financial year, while
the Estimate of Appropriations-in-Aid of
the Vote has been increased by £179. I
beg to move.

seems to me a great pity that the Minister
should not have taken greater care to
encourage a new industry of that kind,
having regard to the fact that concrete
poles used local cement, local sand, local
gravel, and local labour, and resulted in
much money being circulated in this
Province, money that would otherwise go
at least to some foreign country, and
possibly to Russia.
It is admitted that on a contract
recently given out, amounting to something in the neighbourhood of £100,000,
concrete poles would have cost 5 per cent.
more, but having regard to the fact that,
with the approval of the Ministry of
Home Affairs, local authorities have given
contracts to local firms on the basis of an
advance of 16 per cent. over tenders from
the other side of the water, I think you
would have been justified in this case in
supporting a home industry to the extent
of 5 per cent. While I make that
criticism I none the less congratulate the
Minister on the progress he is making,
and I am sure we are all delighted to hear
him say that he looks to the future with
great confidence, and that he anticipates
the present improvement in trade will at
least continue, if not much improve,
during the next twelve months.

formerly. Thus a great deal of that

nowadays a great many

Major HALL-THOMPSON: I do not

criticism of the Electricity Board, but I
should like again to ask the Minister of

imported foreign wooden posts. I
admit that the Electricity Board of
Northern Ireland may be inclined to
regard concrete posts as an experiment,
and therefore feel that they are perfectly justified in going slowly and
carefully in this matter. But having
regard to the fact that these posts have
been used for over 20 years in France
and on the Continent generally, and for
over 20 years in America, it seems to be
apparent that they are beyond the stage
of experiment.
They have also been used between
three and four years in some parts of
England, and I may say that no public.
utility company in England has ever
ordered any without ordering more.
That shows, therefore, that with their
limited experience of these concrete
posts they are perfectly satisfied, and I
have no reason to doubt that any of the
experts who have been consulted in this
matter in Northern Ireland are also perfectly satisfied. I quite admit that the
Board may be reluctant to take what
they regard as an undue risk, but I feel
that the present unemployment situation is such that if there are any risks
-which I will not admit-we are justified in taking them. We would be justified at the present time in taking risks
that we would not normally take in
order to help to reduce unemployment throughout the Province.

When I interjected the remark about

so because I happened to know that 90
per cent. of the ships that come into
Belfast with timber are Ulster ships with
Ulster seamen in them. I have gone down
to see them. You know perfectly well
yourself, if you have any cognisance of

that in the vast majority of cases the
ships carrying timber belong to two wellknown firms in the city of Belfast, and
that any interference with the carrying
trade of those two firms means that anything you may try to remedy in the unemployment market would be adversely
balanced by what you disturb on the
other side.
The element of the dock labourers also
enters into this. I like to hear people
talking glibly about a little tinpot industry. I want the Minister to think of
this. My experience of some of the socalled industries of Northern Ireland and
Great Britain is simply that you have incompetence, impotence, and stupidity of
the worst kind sheltered behind tariff
barriers and protective walls. Those
things are very seldom conducive to the
development of scientific ideas in industry.
As to the unemployment aspect of this
question, I may say that the transport
workers form a very important section of
the working class community, and if you
try to remedy unemployment by destroying overseas trade remember that under
existing conditions, as your present social
system is operated, you can only do one
at the expense of the other.
It is very cheap and popular in Belfast
to sneer at timber which happens to come
from certain places. I have yet to learn
that any person in this House or outside
this House is not prepared to carry on
commerce because commodities come from
a certain country. The last person to talk so
sneeringly about any country should be the
hon. and gallant Member for Clifton, because he formerly belonged to an industry
that took 80 per cent. of its raw material
from the country that he is prepared to
sneer at now in regard to timber. I hope
that the Minister, when he is investigating these questions, will please keep in
mind that it is not simply a proposition
of scrapping timber and erecting concrete
posts.
If I were expressing my own personal
views upon this matter, I would say that
concrete is likely to be more durable than
timber, and on that ground I would probably select it, provided that tests had
been carried out. But to turn round and
base an argument in favour of concrete on
the statement that the timber is supposed
to come from a place that we do not wish
to develop relations with is altogether
ridiculous, coming from the hon. and gallant Member for Clifton, who has had
such an intimate and profitable connection
with Russia.

what the position is as regards the relationship of the Ministry of Commerce and the
Electricity Board. As I have already

the members of that Board. The Minister

The members of the Board, as well as the

Apart

is that the public safety must be conserved, and when you are distributing

question of concrete poles was considered,

Member on this side could say, would be

numerically smaller than it is in most

in the electorate as contemplated by this

quite well that their numbers here are

of their majority.
My view on this matter is that it will

I was rather surprised when the hon.
Lady (Mrs. Parker), who represents
South Derry, contributed what was, I

day, though it was not accepted. Her
suggestion was that the onus of proof
should be on the person making a claim.
I think the Ministry of Home Affairs have
probably been reconsidering the position.
in that respect. There are many Unionists

be to a Nationalist. I think that what
really occurred in this matter was not that
the people of Northern Ireland wanted
legislation on these lines at all, but rather
that in an unfortunate moment the hon.
and learned Member for Derry (Mr.
Murphy) during an electoral contest down.
there seemed to find it necessary, in order
to allay public feeling in that city within.
a very limited circle, to give a promise of
legislation in this House that he felt must
be implemented at the earliest possible
moment. And, of course, the hon. and
learned Member for Derry City is such an
important factor on the Government
benches that when he expresses a wish,
and certainly when he gives a promise, the
Government feel that they are bound in
honour to implement it.
Derry is a peculiar place. I sometimes
think that there is a sort of political
microbe in Derry, and that when normal
people, normal politicians, leave other
parts of the country where there is not the
same political feeling as there is in Derry
and go to that city, they receive a microbe
of some sort. My memory goes back a
considerable time. I well remember an
array of lawyers who left the Four Courts
long ago, and came down to Derry, and
completely changed their characteristics as
soon as they arrived there. It was
almost like one of those things of which
you read in the Arabian Nights entertainment, and sometimes the ending was
nearly as dramatic or as picturesque. A
lawyer left the Four Courts and came
down to Derry. He had been a constitutionalist before, but then we found him
defending stoutly, not merely as a lawyer
but as a politician, people who had been
breaking the law to such an extent, that
one or two Royal Commissions in that
city decided that they were the provokers
of very serious riots. The hon. and
learned Member who at present represents Derry in this House must have
passed through the same process. In some
way
he must have got hold of this germ.
His statements in Derry were so very
unlike
the calm, judicial statements one expects
to receive from him both in this House
and in this city that something abnormal
must have taken place in the interval.
The hon. and learned Member took
umbrage at my describing his followers
as a mob. I would like to point out to
the hon. and learned Member that I did
not invent the term "mob;" that it was
invented by a Royal Commission a good
many years ago, and that it was applied
not only to the Orange Order in Derry,
but to the Orange Order in Belfast in
connection with the successive riots which
they promoted or provoked from the year
1881 to 1886.

remain in closer touch with Great

I gave a reason in the beginning why
I thought the Measure was being introduced, and I still believe it is the only
motive behind this extraordinary procedure. It was that this was a series of
pin-pricks aimed at the Free State. The
speech of the Parliamentary Secretary,
if there was nothing else, makes it very

Crozier's, and reads of the type of loyalty

in the action of Ministers since 1914, or
in the men who went down to the Liverpool boat in that year and threatened
that if a warrant had been issued for
the arrest of Sir Edward Carson they
would shoot down the British police and
British soldiers. Yet they have the
audacity now in 1934 to talk of loyalty.
If the Parliamentary Secretary had
been more tactful he would have left out
the plea of loyalty altogether. You are
not loyal except in so far as loyalty suits
your own selfish ends. You do not care
a straw about the English connection. If
the Socialist Government comes in tomorrow you will just be as disloyal as
ever you were, and act in defiance of the
King's writ. You have no right to talk

humbugs with which you delude the
people from time to time. The only
people who are loyal in this area are the
people who sent their sons out to fight
for a dream, and were disillusioned. These
are the people you want to penalise to-day
if the power were given you to do it. It
may be that you will carry this Bill-I
think you will-and have it amended.

I stand here for democracy and I am
going to voice my opinion.

Mr. BEATTIE: I would like the
Prime Minister to reflect on the question
I put to him last night on the Adjournment of the House. It is the usual
custom and courtesy of the Government
Leader to reply when the business of the
House for the following day and the day
after is asked for. The Prime Minister
last night was asked that question on behalf of Members of the Opposition, and
he refused to answer. I regret he is not
present now to give an explanation as to
why he refused to answer a question
directed to him for the guidance of
Members on this side of the House. That
being so, I would ask the Deputy Prime
Minister would he mind paying that
respect to the Opposition and informing
them what is the order of business for tomorrow and also what is likely to be
taken next Tuesday.
Captain DIXON: I would like to reply
to the hon. Member for Pottinger. He
is quite incorrect regarding the Prime
Minister. He asked the Prime Minister
for the order of business, and the Prime
Minister turned round to me to get the
business. While I was about to hand
him the paper, you, Sir, got up.
You
were on your
feet and the House was
closed. The Prime Minister then, with

over with the paper in his hand to the
hon. Member for Pottinger, but the hon.
Member refused to take the paper.
Therefore if there was
any lack of
courtesy in this matter it was on the part
of the hon. Member for Pottinger. The
Prime Minister always shows his usual
courtesy to every Member of this House.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would be sorry if I
misunderstood what took place. I asked
a question last night and you handed the

He laid it down there on the Table. I
was walking out when my colleague here

was closed, "Thank you for your answer
about the order of business." He
immediately proceeded to that end of the

want to say if his attention was distracted

for order of business.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 19th April, 1934.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
HILLSBOROUGH WATER SUPPLY.
1. Dr. WILSON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether, following his communication with the Ministry of Finance,
he is now in a position to state whether
a supply of pure water can be made
available for the people of Hillsborough
Village.
The following question also stood on
the Order Paper in the name of Dr.
Wilson:
2. To ask the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he is aware that certain members
of the Hillsborough Rural District
Council recently visited the Agricultural
Research Farm at Hillsborough and that
it was admitted to them on that occasion
that some of the effluent from the byres
and piggeries had access to the stream
feeding the dam which in turn supplies
water to the village.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): With the hon.
Member's permission, I shall take this
and the next question together.
With regard to the second question,
as I informed the hon. Member on the
15th March last in answer to a question,
it is a fact that some of the effluent
from the byres and piggeries at the Agricultural Research Farm at Hillsborough
finds its way ultimately into the lake at
Hillsborough, but the position in this
respect is no worse than it was before
the Government took over this property,
and it must be borne in mind that the
water in the lake, owing to
tamination from this and other sources,
has never been suitable for drinking purposes.
con-
I am informed that the Ministry of
Finance is prepared, so far as concerns
water under the control of the Ministry,
to facilitate as far as possible the Rural
District Council, which is the responsible
authority, in any effort it may make to
provide a water supply for Hillsborough.

RAILWAY COMPANIES' BUS
ROUTES.
4. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he would state the
total number of bus routes acquired by
the railway companies in Northern Ireland up to the present.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Up to the
present the railway companies in Northern Ireland have acquired omnibus services operated by 42 owners on 92 routes.
ANTRIM PUBLIC ASSISTANCE
COMMITEE.
5. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour whether the Public Assistance
Committee of Antrim has laid down a
minimum scale of payment which is lower
than the statutory benefits; whether it is
the practice of this Committee to pay
considerably lower than the statutory
rates; whether this is contrary to the
practice prevailing in other places and
whether he can state if this policy is
the result of a meeting of the Ballymena,
Larne, and Antrim Committees of which
it was decided to pay higher rates in the
urban districts and lower rates in the
rural districts.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I have no control over the
rates of payment settled by public
assistance committees so long as they conform to certain conditions and do not
exceed the statutory limit. It is true
that the hon. Member for Antrim
brought to my notice some weeks ago
that the amounts determined by the
Antrim Committee appeared to be less
than those determined by some of the
adjoining committees, and, in view of his
representations, I arranged that a joint
conference would be held between the
committees mentioned in the question.
This conference took place, but no such
decision as is mentioned in the question
was arrived at.
Mr. MINFORD: May I be allowed to
thank the Minister for his kindness in
this matter.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I wish to give notice
that I intend to raise this matter on the
Adjournment.
LICENSING OF BULLS.
6. Dr. WILSON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he is prepared to
amend the regulations regarding the
licensing of bulls so that bulls can be
inspected on owners' premises, as is done.
in the case of boars.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): The reply is
in the negative, because the existing
arrangements for the licensing of bulls
are working smoothly and any change in
the direction suggested would involve not
only considerable expense, but inordinate
delay.
LONG-TERM LOANS FOR FARMERS
7. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Finance whether he is aware that British
farmers can now obtain long-term loans
from the Agricultural Mortgage Corporation at 4 per cent. and Improvement Loans at 4 per cent., and if he
will arrange similar accommodation for
Six-County farmers.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have not been able to verify
the figures quoted by the hon. Member,
but assuming that they are correct, he
will find, on considering the various
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
19 APRIL 1934
schemes of agricultural loans operating in
Northern Ireland, that the present rates
of interest payable by the farmers here
are, on the whole, more favourable than
those operating in Great Britain.
In the first place, there are five-year
loans issued under Government guarantee by banks at a subsidised rate of discount of 3 per cent.; next, there are the
loans for improvement of pedigree stock
and farm buildings, issued from the Government Loans Fund at 43 per cent.;
and, finally, there are the long-term
advances for land purchase under the
Northern Ireland Land Purchase Act of
1925, on which the farmer is paying a
rate of interest of 4 per cent.
I suggest, therefore, that the second
part of the hon. Member's question does
not arise.
Mr. HEALY: My question deals not
with land purchase, which is an entirely
different thing, but with the ordinary
purposes for which farmers require
money at the moment-restocking and
improving their land. Is the right hon.
Gentleman prepared to give the same
terms to Northern Ireland farmers as are
available to farmers across the water?
Mr. POLLOCK: I have just informed
the hon. Member that there are various
forms of Government loans for the benefit
of farmers. There is a form of loan by
which the farmer can get money for the
object which the hon. Member has
mentioned, and the rate of interest is
only 3 per cent.
Mr. HEALY: For short-term loans.
Mr. POLLOCK: Short-term loansfive-year loans.
Mr. HEALY: I wish to ask the
Minister if he has any objection to giving
long-term loans, not short-term loans,
that are now available to English
farmers?
Mr. POLLOCK: No, I am not prepared to follow something of which I have
no knowledge. I know there is a Government organisation which advances
money to farmers, but what the conditions
are I am not aware of at the present
moment. I certainly will not undertake
blindfold any form of lending money.
Mr. HEALY: When the Minister
obtains this information will he kindly
let the House know whether he is in a
position to follow suit?

CLASS V. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF EDUCATION.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a sum not exceeding £49,338 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum which will come in course of payment during the year ending 31st March,
1935, to defray the salaries and expenses
of the Ministry of Education (15 and 16
Geo. V., c. 3, s. 4 (N.I.) ). (Note—
£17,000 has been voted on account.)
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): Hon. Members will find these Estimates on page 104
of the book of Estimates. I propose, as
in former years, to present both these
Votes together to the Committee, as I
understand that course is
more conare
venient to Members. With regard to
Vote 1, that for the salaries and expenses
of the Ministry of Education, the amount
asked for, £66,338, is slightly more than
last year, the increase being due to the
automatic growth of increments in the
salary scales paid to the officials. The
net increase is £698. There
practically no changes of importance in
the details of the Vote since last year,
but the arrangement whereby a principal
officer of the Ministry was lent to the Air
Ministry at Westminster has come to an
end, the officer in question having now
been permanently transferred to the
Imperial Civil Service.
He
During the year the Ministry lost the
services of Mr. Thomas Rea, senior chief
inspector, Mr. Rea having died suddenly
last August after a short illness.
spent almost the whole of his 25 years'
service in the inspection of the secondary
schools of the Province, and his efforts
for the promotion of modern language
teaching were of great value. His loss is
much regretted by his colleagues and by
all engaged in educational work both
inside and outside the Ministry.
The amount required this year for the
educational services under Vote 2 is
£1,911,350, and it will be observed that
the two Votes together amount to
£1,977,688, very little short of, but still
less than, two millions. I might remark
that the sums voted for education in this
Committee, year after year, are very
much the same, notwithstanding the
great developments that have taken place
in our education system during the last
dozen years and the substantial increases
in the attendance of pupils at all classes
of schools. Just ten years ago, in
1924-25, the Votes for education were
nearly the same as in the current year,
namely, £1,971,278—a difference of
£6,410, less than a third of one per cent.
Whatever criticisms may be directed
against the Government for alleged
extravagance, it certainly cannot be said.
that this charge can be justified in regard
to educational expenditure, nor on the
other hand, when we consider the
progress made, one evidence of which
leaps to the eye all over the Province in
the shape of new and commodious school
buildings, can it be said that the needs of
the children have been unduly stinted.
But the Committee will recognise that
we have been enabled to keep our expenditure below the two-million mark only
because reductions have been made in the
salary scales of the teachers, following on
the great need for public economy, and I
willingly recognise the public spirit and
forbearance with which, in the main, the
teaching profession has submitted to these
"cuts.'
It would afford me pleasure to
be able to say that there was some prospect of the reductions, or any part of
them, being restored in the near future,
but this is a question on which I cannot
make any statement at present.
""
Coming back again to the amount of
the Vote, the Committee will observe that
there is a net decrease on last year of
£19,450. But this decrease is not due to
any decline in the number or amount of
the Ministry's grants, but entirely to the
adoption of a different method of financing the building grants payable for new
voluntary schools under the provisions of
Section 10 of the Education Act of 1930.
Up to the end of last month the Estimates

contained the actual amount of the
grants expected to become payable under
this head during the year, but in future
it has been decided to pay the grants out

Ministry of Finance, and the amounts.
appearing on the Education Estimates

while sums of £30,000 and £39,000

Committees in similar circumstances, and
it is quite fitting and sound finance to
spread the cost of permanent works, such
as school buildings, over a term of years,
instead of throwing it altogether on the
present taxpayer.
If this transaction in the Estimates be

are an additional £10,800 required for

a saving on the training colleges of over
£1,000.

I propose now to run over the chief
sub-heads of the Vote in turn with a few
comments. Taking first the cost of the
training colleges, there is, as I have said,
a decrease in the Estimate of £1,115 as
compared with the previous year. The
decline is due to a reduction in the
number of students in training which, at
present, is 322, as against 338 in the last
session. The Ministry endeavours to
regulate the numbers in training so as to
meet, but not to exceed, the probable
needs of the schools, which, as I have
frequently pointed out, it is not always.
easy to foretell accurately, owing to a
number of uncertain factors in the
calculation. The present number is
lower than for several years past, and is
expected to furnish a sufficient supply of
young teachers to fill all vacancies that
will take place in the 12 months after the
30th June next. Notwithstanding statements to the contrary in the Press, I can
assure the Committee that the number of
unemployed teachers in the Province is
comparatively insignificant at the present
time.
In this connection I may mention that
the Management Committee of Stranmillis College (which I am pleased to say
is working most harmoniously) has again
had under discussion the necessity of providing an efficient and properly equipped
demonstration school in which the
students may observe and practise the art
of teaching under the practical supervision and guidance of the teachers of
method. Before the Ministry of Education was established, twelve or thirteen
years ago, all Irish training colleges were
provided with practising schools under
the control of the college authorities and
in their immediate vicinity, and no training college was considered properly fitted
for its purpose which did not possess such
a necessary adjunct to the securing of a
practical knowledge of school-keeping.
When Stranmillis was started it was an
integral part of the scheme of training to
provide a practising school, and the
public elementary school at Stranmillis
Road was secured by the Ministry for the
purpose.
At the same time the system
of sending the students for practice of
teaching to selected elementary schools in
the city was adopted, but this was never
intended to take the place of the practising school at Stranmillis, which was in
intimate connection with the College, and
only needed some additional accommodation and the rearrangements of the
central schoolroom to fit it for the purpose for which it had been acquired by
the Ministry. Unfortunately, delays of
various kinds intervened to prevent the
work being done, but the Committee has
now, with the approval of the Ministry
and the Minister of Finance, set on foot
a scheme of improvement and rearrangement of the premises at moderate cost,
which will meet fairly adequately the
needs of the College.
Advantage has been taken of the fact
that the Belfast Education Authority is
planning to build two new schools within
a reasonable distance to refit the Stranmillis school for a smaller number of
pupils than its present attendance. This
scheme will save considerable money,
being estimated to cost, approximately,
£3,000, as against the £7,000 of the
earlier scheme, and it will prove of considerable advantage in enhancing the
efficiency of the training given to the
students. Some portion of this expenditure would, in any case, be necessary for

I am aware that many Members of the
Committee are much interested in the
question of the feeding of necessitous
school children, and I should like to say
that the Ministry heartily approves of
the action of those education authorities
who have taken steps to give effect to
their powers under this head. Unfortunately only three or four authorities
have so far taken such steps: still I like
to give honour where honour is due, and
I would commend particularly the action
of the education committees in Belfast,
County Down, and the Lisburn and
Belfast area of County Antrim, for the
arrangements they have made. In
Belfast about 4,000 children are fed daily
at a cost of £5,024 for the year. The
County Down Regional Education Committee is feeding 1,132 children spread
over 36 centres at a cost of £1,260, and
the Lisburn Committee has arranged for
134 children to be fed daily at a cost of
£93. In many of these centres committees of ladies have taken charge of
the arrangements and the services of
these voluntary helpers are very much
appreciated. I should like to refer also to
the valuable assistance that has been freely
given by the teachers, who are under no
statutory obligation to take part in this
work, but have in almost every case
readily co-operated for the good of their
pupils. Besides the three committees
mentioned who have shown so much skill
in the organisation of this service, there
are two or three other committees who
have made some tentative beginnings of
a system of providing soup or cocoa in
a few schools. I hope the good example
will be followed more generally throughout the Province.
Another matter in which the pupils can
receive substantial aid from the committees is the provision of school books,
stationery and school requisites. Eleven
out of the 18 education committees show
some activity in this respect, but the
amount of assistance given varies very
much. In one or two of the smaller areas
the expense of this service is less than £10
per annum, while in others substantial
sums are spent. Clothing and books are
also provided for necessitous children in
some of the less prosperous parts of the
country, in County
County Fermanagh for
example, where about £400 is spent on

Mr. HEALY: I beg to move a reduction of the Estimate by £1,000 in order
to call attention to the unfair discrimination that has been exercised in the matter
of Catholic schools. When I say
that unfair discrimination has been

like to point out
as a preliminary that
that Catholics are
in a majority over any other church in

Therefore when the Government in a

something which I submit is not
calculated to make the best type of

should be to prepare the citizens for their

per cent. of the cost of erecting the
school and again 50 per cent. of the cost
of heating, cleaning, and lighting. I say
that is a manifest injustice for which
there can be no defence and no plea
except the plea of sectarian bias.

That was on 16th March last year,
when the Parliamentary Secretary

teaching of Irish in words of which I
approve. On 25th April, after a threat
delivered to him by the Member for Duncairn (Mr. Grant), whose interest in
education must be very well known to
every Member of this Committee, he came
down to this House and asked for sanction
for this grant of £1,500 for the teaching

means by that, but he mentioned that
even a study of archæological Irish was

It is pretty well known that the

small grant were Catholic schools and, in
my opinion, it was not because the subject
was Irish, but because it constituted a
vulnerable point at which certain reactionary elements inside and outside this
House could strike at the Catholic
minority that this grant was discontinued.
The hon. Member who represents the
Department of Education came down to
this House and acquiesced in a disgraceful
policy of that kind. His excuse for discontinuing the grant was that it was on
the ground of economy. Fancy any
Government being reduced to the extreme
where £1,500 would make that much
difference to their expenditure in the
year.
I have heard the story of the mean
man who, on one occasion, rifled his
child's savings bank, but the action of
the Parliamentary Secretary in coming
here and stealing £1,500, which was distributed over the whole schools of the Six
Counties for the teaching of Irish, seems
to be almost as mean as that. There is
nothing political in the teaching of Irish,
and there is nothing sectarian, notwithstanding what the hon. and learned
Member for Armagh (Mr. Davison) says.
Mr. DAVISON: It was made both
political and sectarian.
Mr. HEALY: By you and your
followers, not by us. On one occasion
last year I was travelling from Holyhead
to London, and in the carriage with me
were a number of women and girls who
had been coming from Ardglass in
County Down and going to the East
Coast of England for the herring curing.
These people were talking Gaelic in the
train, and their conversation was about
ourselves. I discovered that these people
were Presbyterians and Irish speakers.
Surely there was nothing sectarian in
that, except from the point of view of the
Presbyterians, and I do not think any
education authority anywhere would
withdraw a grant because the majority of
the recipients happened to belong to a
particular denomination, if they took
into account its cultural and educational
value and did not allow themselves to be
driven by intolerant bigots who, I hope,
do not represent anything like a reasonable minority of the people outside.
I suppose it is all in pursuance of the
policy this Government has adopted
towards Catholics. You will not allow
Catholics to find work, and now you will
not allow them an opportunity of being
educated. You penalise them in the
matter of schools and in the matter of
Irish, in which a good many of them are
interested. Finally, I suppose the policy
of the Government will be to crush them
out of existence altogether. If that is
your real policy you might find a more
straightforward way of doing it than this
mean, mangy, and back-handed system
that has been adopted.
There are other things I had intended
speaking about, and one of them was the
question of school books. The school
books in a system of national education
ought, surely, to reflect national pride.
They ought to teach the child something
about his own country and, particularly,
the local places in which he moves and
Estimates-

lives and has his being. That ought to
tend to give him culture. At one time
the primary schools of this country were
of that character. There were a great
many books, the primary purpose of
which was to tell the child something of
his own country. Now, probably in pursuance of the same old anti-national
policy, school books are more about the
Empire. The majority of people are not
going to live in the Empire. (Hon.
Members: "They are.") They are
going to live in this country.
When you
appeal for support for Ulster industries
you do not appeal to Great Britain, you
appeal to the people of Ulster only,
Protestant, Presbyterian, and everyone
else. You appeal to their sense of
patriotism, but you first kill patriotism
by strangling it in the schools. You do
not give the children an opportunity of
knowing their own country. You do not
make them proud of their country. You
do not make them even proud of the Six
Counties, with the natural result that the
child loses its sense of citizenship and
becomes a citizen of the world, and of the
British Empire, if you like, with no pride
in its own part of the world.
You not only strike at one of the vital
characteristics of citizenship, but you
strike at the material prosperity of the
country. When the children grow into
manhood and womanhood, so long as they
buy Empire produce it does not matter,
but the industrialists want them to buy
the produce of this country.
If you
destroy national pride you have nothing
left. You can find the quays of Belfast
strewn with cheap foreign linen at a time
when you are manufacturing the finest
linen in the world. That is the final outcome of your policy. In conclusion, I
have very great pleasure in moving a
reduction in this Vote.

Our
Prior to 1923 every educationist was
agreed that the curse of our system here
was the multiplication of small schools
identified with each particular church.
The 1923 Act attempted to remedy that
by offering an inducement to those
churches and bodies which had control of
schools, to transfer them. It did not
penalise anybody who had control of
schools. It gave them the grants they
had before, but it put an obligation on
them to make some contribution towards
the education of the children if they
wanted to keep control of the schools. A
large number of schools have been transferred by their managers, and it would
be a most unfair thing to those managers
who have transferred schools if we should
turn round and provide for the non-

The nervous system has been imposed
upon to an extent which I do not think is
appreciated at the present time.
In dealing with the question of nervous
complaints amongst children I am mindful of the fact that we are dealing with
a generation of children who came after
the war, and you cannot dissociate the
war and the influence of the war from the
nervous condition of the children at the
present time. I can see that aspect of the
question in my own home very well and,
therefore, I make due allowance for it.
But having made all allowances, I still
think a great case has been made out for
an investigation by the Ministry into the
length of the school hours, and the
amount of home work. If I have the
opportunity of putting what I believe to
be right into operation I do so, and some
years ago I went to the Education Committee in Belfast and asked them to
abolish home lessons, especially for
children under a certain standard or a
certain age, whichever of the two distinctions they like to take. I was beaten
on that question.
Last year I attempted to get the school
hours revised, especially in the winter

to be the winter months, and I suggested
that if they could not see their way to
revise the school hours, especially the
commencing hour, for the whole of the

hour for at least six months. I suggested
10 o'clock as the starting hour during
those six months. I was again confronted with this peculiar mentality to
which I have already referred, and people

they went out into the field and gathered

always watch the percentage figures, and

They were not fed during the holiday

place where it is not true to make that

If you toured Great Britain at the
present time, if you toured the Continent
of Europe, if you toured the Dominion of
Canada, if you toured the United States

This is the part of the world with the
lowest percentage of the population enjoying opportunities of higher education.
Six per cent. of your school population!
It is a disgrace. Why is that so? I will
tell you why it is so. You may not like

to certain things, but I have only had
it as the result of intensive effort. I
want to see them recognised as socially
responsible. I want to see our people
not considering their education finished at
fourteen. Why should the education of
the working man's child finish at fourteen
and the child of the lord, or the duke, or
the duchess be regarded as not educated
until eighteen, nineteen, twenty,
twenty-one years of age? In the eyes of
God we are all supposed to be equal, and
it ought to be the duty of the State to see
to it that facilities are provided to make
the children of the community equal in
the eyes of man as regards opportunity.
or
Some person may say here I know
some "Smart Alec" in this Institution
may say that of course you may give

educational opportunity but you cannot
create intellect and you cannot create

give to those with ability, some of the

of that, I want to see the educational

along lines that will give our children

During the Great War when I was at
the Western Front, nearly every time I
met a German, that German could speak
the English language. Why? Because
it was part of the elementary school
curriculum in Germany before the war to
ensure that every child should be able to
speak at least one language in addition
to its own. That is a standard we have
not attained. I think that would be a
splendid thing from the point of view of
world relationship if we could bring about
a better cultural condition on the part of
the children. But it will not be done.
These educational changes will not be
carried out until we have a new educational perspective.

a
It is a new educational perspective I
am putting forward this afternoon. It
rests upon this basis, that every child of
the community should at least undergo a
period of secondary education in order to
collective spirit of goodwill
towards every section of the community,
without which the State can never

child to higher education, and as a preliminary towards that very desirable end
there ought to be abundant opportunities
for every child that is equipped mentally
in a way likely to benefit as a result of

at the present day.
I make no bones about saying this. I
believe in the right to secondary education.
for all. That is what I believe in
education. I do not see that any section

whilst another section is deprived of it.
It ought to be the aim of the educational
authority to give it to every section of
the community. That, again, comes back
to this. Why are our people not getting
it at the present time? They are not
getting it. That is frankly admitted.
When somebody to-day challenged the
authority of my statement that higher
education was regarded as the prerogative of the wealthy, I proved it by
statistics of society. Let us face up to
this. Is it not true to say that wealth
has been the passport to education, and
poverty has been a bar to education? We
ought not to recognise that educational
principle at all. I think a start has
been made towards giving certain children
a better chance than they had before. I
rejoice to believe that the educational
facilities are better than they were in my
day and generation.
Children are blest from the point of
view of being housed in better schools,
and from the point of view of scientific
equipment. To walk through some of the
new schools as compared with the kind
of school I was compelled to go to is a
sheer joy and inspiration. We are proud
of these schools from that point of view.
We want to carry on that work. Some
of those schools are so well built and so
splendidly equipped that they might very
possibly be used as municipal secondary
schools. The Parliamentary Secretary is
bound to admit this. The Education Act
as it stands to-day throws the onus on

to develop municipal secondary schools.
Do you know, I met a member of the City
Council who was so ignorant on one

said: "I wonld not support a municipal
secondary school, because I would not
support anything with the name municipal at it." He was so hopelessly
ignorant he did not know what a municipal secondary school was. He thought
it was some violently revolutionary thing
that was going, perhaps, to upset his

—

I have no control over the rates of

24 APRIL 1934
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 24th April, 1934.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
MOTORING OFFENCES-POLICE
TRAPS.
1. Dr. WILSON asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state the
names of the counties in Northern Ireland where police are specially employed
at dangerous bends on roads for purposes in connection with the detection of
motoring offences; the number of prosecutions in each county resulting from
the employment of such patrols during
the quarter ended 31st March, 1934;
whether it is within the scope of police
duties for a policeman to lie in wait
behind a hedge for several hours at a
stretch for the express purpose of detecting motoring offences; and whether
police so employed are entitled to special
remuneration to compensate them for
the hardships incurred in carrying out
such duties during the recent inclement
weather.
em-
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Police are
ployed throughout Northern Ireland at
dangerous bends and similar places in
connection with the detection of motoring
offences. It would be impossible to segregate accurately the number of prosecutions resulting from these special
measures during the quarter ended 31st
March, 1934, but the numbers approximately are as follows:-Antrim, 16;
Down, 16; Londonderry, 3; and for the
remainder of the area, nil.
It is within the scope of police duty
to remain in concealment as long as may
be necessary
for the detection of motoring offences, but this method of detecting
offences of this description is not resorted
to unless the circumstances render it desirable to do so. No special remuneration is paid to the police in connection
with duty of this description.
R.U.C. AND CUSTOMS DUTIES.
2. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Home Affairs the total number of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary who are engaged upon Customs Duties; the amount
of their salaries and allowance which are
defrayed by the Imperial Government;
and the total number of Special Constabulary who are engaged in like duties,
with the cost of same.
Sir DAWSON BATES: There are 15
sergeants and 85 constables of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary engaged upon
Customs Duties at the present time.
The amount of their salaries and
allowances defrayed by the Imperial Government is £31,048.
There are 8 members of the Special
Constabulary employed in protection
duty in connection with Customs Posts,
costing approximately £1,240, which is
also defrayed by the Imperial Government.
TOTAL COST OF SPECIAL
CONSTABULARY.
3. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he can state the total
cost of the Special Constabulary; how
much the officers and men receive, respectively, of this sum, and the total
numbers of officers and men.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The estimated
total cost of the Special Constabulary
for the financial year 1934/35, as the
hon. Member will see on reference to the
printed Estimates, now in his hands,
amounts to £51,698.
The officers of the Special Constabulary
receive by way of pay and allowances the
sum of £9,100 approximately, and the
men £28,000 approximately.
The total numbers of officers and men
in the Force on 31st March was 11,984.
DUNDONALD SEWERAGE SCHEME
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state
if the loan for the Dundonald sewerage
scheme has been granted; what are the
conditions of employment of the men to
be employed; whether single men as well
as married men are to be engaged; and
whether he can state the rate of wages
to be paid.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Sir DAWSON BATES: The loan was
sanctioned on the 26th January last, and
tenders for the work were accepted by
the Castlereagh Rural District Council
at its meeting on the 20th instant.
I am informed by my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Labour, that he
has sanctioned the payment of an unemployment relief grant towards the cost
of this scheme, subject to the usual conditions on which such grants are made.
These conditions stipulate that all
labour required shall be recruited
through the employment exchange, and
that the rate of wages to be paid shall
be that which the promoting authority
would normally pay for similar work in
the case of unskilled men, and the district rate in the case of skilled men.
The usual preference will be given to
married men,
and ex-Service men before
civilians, and it will only be after these
are employed that vacancies
offered to single men.
can be

DOWN REGIONAL EDUCATION
COMMITTEE'S ARCHITECT.
5. Dr. WILSON asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he can state the
amount of salary and other emoluments
paid for each of the last three years by
the Down County Regional Education
Committee to their architect; the amount
of the sum outstanding for which this
committee is liable to the architect by
reason of plans drawn up by him for the
erection and repair of school buildings,
but not yet put into operation; and
whether the Regional Committee is bound
by agreement to retain the services of
the architect for a further number of
years; and whether, in the event of his
removal from office, the Regional Committee are legally entitled to pay him
commission on all contracts based upon
plans drawn up by him previous to his
removal from office and subsequently put
into operation.
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): I am informed
that the amounts of salary and other
emoluments paid by the Down County
Regional Education Committee to their
architect for each of the last three years
are as follows:-Year ended 31st March,
1932, £2,513 15s 8d; year ended 31st
March, 1933, £2,082 13s 11d; year ended
31st March, 1934, £1,782 6s.
In reply to the second part of the
question, I understand that the total
estimated cost of outstanding works in
connection with the building, repair and
and maintenance of schools at 1st April,
1934, for which plans have been prepared
but have not yet been put into operation
is approximately £110,000, but I am not
in a position to estimate the liability, if
any, of the committee to their architect
in respect of this amount.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
24 APRIL 1934
An agreement between the committee
and their architect terminated on 31st
March, 1933. The question of a fresh
agreement is at present under consideration by the committee.
So far as I am aware there is no obligation on the committee, under the terms
of their agreement with the architect, to
retain his services for a further number
of years.
The past agreement with the architect
provided for the payment of a fee of 4
per cent., calculated on the total of the
net amounts of all certificates issued by
him on behalf of the committee, and 24
per cent. on the estimated cost of works
approved of by the committee, but not
carried out.
The legal liability of the committee
under the agreement in respect of plans
drawn up by the architect previous to
his ceasing to be employed by the committee is one upon which I do not express
any opinion, as that is a question of
legal interpretation.
Mr. FRYAR: Is it a fact that there
is only one architect for the whole of
County Down, the county with the
largest population in Northern Ireland,
and that Antrim, Derry and Tyrone employ from three to five architects to do
similar work; and is it a fact that the cost
of architectural services in County Down
is as low as the cost of such services in
any other education area in Northern
Ireland.
Mr. ROBB: I would like notice of that
question.
CHILDREN'S HOME PREPARED
LESSONS.
6. Major MCCORMICK asked the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry
of Education whether he is satisfied with
the answers indicated by parents to the
questionnaire about home prepared lessons
to be done by the children; and whether,
in view of the many complaints of harshness to backward or nervous children
through home lesson work, he will endeavour to see that children in this category are not subject to the same standard
in this respect.
Mr. ROBB: I have no information in regard to the questionnaire
referred to in the first part of
the question, but as regards the
amount of home work, the Ministry is in
general agreement with the recommendation made by the Departmental Committee of Inquiry on the programme of
instruction in public elementary schools.
That recommendation was that no
home work should be required from any
pupil below the third standard, and that,
whilst it is impossible to lay down a hard
and fast rule, for other pupils one hour's
home work should be sufficient for a
pupil of average ability.
Should the amount of home work be
found to press with undue severity upon
any child, the matter should, in the first
instance, be brought to the notice of the
principal teacher or the school manager;
should there then remain any cause of
complaint, the Ministry would, upon
application be willing to make inquiries.
into the case.
Major McCORMICK: Is the hon. and
learned Gentleman aware that many
children in the third standard are unable
to prepare home lessons?
Mr. ROBB: I am not aware.

Rights of the Minority.
MOTION BY NATIONALIST PARTY.
Mr. HEALY: I beg to move, That in
the opinion of this House the campaign
against the employment of Catholics promulgated by the Minister of Agriculture
and expressly sanctioned by the Prime
Minister is a grave violation of the rights
and liberties of the minority placed under
the rule of the Northern Government.
We have put down this Motion not to
elicit what the Government policy on the
matter is, because we know that already,
but rather to give supporters of the
Government in this House and outside an
opportunity of saying whether they
approve of the declaration of the Minister
of Agriculture who has advised audiences
on more than one occasion not to employ
Catholics. We have been told that these
statements, as well as the declaration of
the Prime Minister, have shocked many
Protestants both inside and outside this
House and they have failed to find any
justification for the practice either in the
New Testament or in present day conditions here. These statements are not
merely anti-Catholic, they are anti-
Christian. Some supporters of the
1073 Rights of the Minority

24 APRIL 1934
Rights of the Minority

Government in this House have told us
that they employ Catholics and that they
will continue to do so notwithstanding
the slogan of the Minister of Agriculture,
No Catholic need apply." Those hon.
Members live on terms of neighbourly
friendship with Catholics, and I trust
that despite the interference of the Prime
Minister they will continue to do so.
The
The policy is not a new one.
right hon. Member for Enniskillen (Sir
Edward Archdale) who was then Minister
of Agriculture, declared on the 31st

Mr. DONNELLY: What are the steps

government constituencies all over the Six

Let me give a case in point. Take
the County of Tyrone, one of the
divisions of which I have the honour to

55 per cent. Catholic and Nationalist,

divisions in that county, and, as a result,

minority on that Council. Since that

Catholics comprise two-thirds of the

The Government again gerrymandered

They ran one electoral

As a result, Catholics are in the minority

a majority in the population of 8,000.

It is charged against us in your Press

And in setting it up, avowedly for the

preservation and protection of the rights

rights would be treated with contempt
and that there would be instant disregard
of our liberties as citizens of this nation.
That is what brings us here to-day, to

laid down by His Majesty the King.

The effect of that will be this, taken in
context with the preliminary words it will
read :-
"That in the opinion of this House
the employment of citizens in Northern Ireland should be on the basis of
equality of opportunity and without
discrimination as to religion or politics,
this being the only basis on which full
civil and religious liberty can be preserved."
I want to state specially on behalf of
the party I represent that some of the
elements in the discussion here this afternoon must be deplored from the point of
view of public life. So long as there are
people in the community who are prepared
to subordinate all public questions and all
questions of policy and public life to the
interests of sectarianism, so long are we
going to be precluded from obtaining the
best we can obtain for the citizens under
our control. I want to state here and now
that in my opinion the form of words
employed on the Order Paper this afternoon is a form of words which would, if
allowed to remain as they are and be voted
upon as they are, be a gross misrepresentation-the Amendment I mean-of the
point of view of people like myself in this
House.
I have all along stated, and I repeat it
here, that it is a deplorable thing in the
House of Commons, or in any sphere of
life, to have to talk about one's religion,
and in Northern Ireland misrepresentation has become such a fine art that it is
absolutely essential that one should be
clear. In everything I may say this afternoon I hope the House will remember that
I speak as a Protestant, one who has been
trained in the tenets of Protestantism,
and has done his best to maintain the
aspirations and objects of his teaching.
My teaching taught me in honouring and
respecting my own religion to honour and
respect the religious observances and
points of view of others. That does not

worship or forms of religion practised by
others.
It simply means if you believe in a
higher power who brought you into existence, you must be prepared on that basis
to give equal rights and opportunities to
others to do the same. It is rather
unfortunate, but it is true, nevertheless,
that while the Government collectively
might disclaim responsibility as a Government for certain of the statements made
in public life, it remains true that certain
statesmen and politicians in Northern Ireland have from time to time given expression to sentiments which were certainly
not in keeping with the best interests and
the best perspective of the State. So as

in Northern Ireland to have represen-
