When presenting the Estimate last
year my distinguished predecessor (Sir
Edward Archdale) in reviewing the
position of the agricultural industry of
Northern Ireland, expressed the view
that bad though the conditions had been
for our farmers, the coming year (which
is now at an end) would show a substantial improvement. Events have justified him. I should like as the successor
to my right hon Friend to express my
appreciation of the work which he
carried out while he was in charge of
the Ministry. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) He laid the foundation on which
we have been able to build the various
marketing schemes, and I think it is an
acknowledged fact that the organisation
in my Ministry is not to be beaten in
any other country in the world. That
is entirely due to my right hon. Friend
(Sir Edward Archdale). (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
The right hon. Gentleman based this
opinion I have referred to on the results
which would steadily, if slowly, follow
the policy inaugurated at the Ottawa
Conference. I know that certain hon.
Members choose to think that this Conference was of no value to our agricultural industry.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I do say, on
the contrary, it did accomplish something, although perhaps the results have
not been all that we desired. The agreement arrived at Ottawa has, for the
first time, brought in the use of the
instrument of quantitative control of
imports, and under that control the
marketing schemes were inaugurated. If
it had not been for the fact that the
agreement had been arrived at, I venture to say that no marketing scheme
could possibly have been inaugurated.
I think, further, if no scheme had been
Ministry of Agriculture 1132
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Basil Brooke]
inaugurated the agreement would not
have worked satisfactorily, because there
would have been a lack of confidence on
the part of the producer. It is hoped by
these schemes that the producer will get
a larger share in the home market.
I am fully conscious of the fact that
the flaw in the Ottawa Agreements as
far as the home farmer is concerned is
that it tied the hands of the United
Kingdom Government with regard to the
limitation of the imports of Dominion
butter and eggs until 1935-a time limit
which is rapidly approaching its end.
But for the fact that agreement was
obtained as to the limitation of imports
of all meats and meat products, who can
doubt that the position of our cattle
trade to-day would closely resemble that
of our unfortunate neighbours in the
Irish Free State.
Perhaps the outstanding development
which has taken place during the past
year has been the launching of the Pigs
and Bacon Marketing Schemes. Initial
difficulties were inevitable, and I am
facing the fact that there are many
difficulties still to be overcome, but I am
confident that they will be solved.
The successful development of the
bacon industry is of such immense importance to our agricultural community
that I feel sure I need not apologise to
Members for occupying their time by dealing with some of the salient features.
That the Pigs and Bacon Marketing
Schemes have been an outstanding
success, and that our farmers, like true
Ulstermen, have grasped their opportunity no one will, I feel sure, deny.
The welfare of 40,000 farmers is involved in this scheme. It is my duty,
and I count it a great privilege, to further their interests and see that they
get fair treatment. As long as that
great trust is in my keeping I will not
allow any sectional interests to jeopardise
the future of this scheme, and, consequently, the welfare of our small
farmers. (Hon Members: Hear, hear.)
The census which we took in July of
last year showed an increase in our pig
breeding population of 33 per cent., and
of 24 per cent. in the total pig population. Members may be aware that
for the purpose of estimating our share
of the home output it was necessary to
take a further census of the pig population in January of this year, a period
of the year when the pig population is
at its lowest. The Ministry's census
shows not a decrease on the June figures,
but a further increase of 23 per cent.
above the June figures in our population
of breeding sows.
Let me illustrate the position in
another way.
In 1932 our Northern
Ireland farmers sold 280,000 pigs for
bacon purposes.
Our estimate, and it is
a conservative one, is that for the year
commencing on the 1st of this month, we
shall produce 480,000 pigs that is our
share of the home quota for this year. In
that short period we have increased our
output by the amazing figure of 70 per
cent. At the present standard price it
means an increase in the gross income of
our farmers of about £1,000,000 per
annum—and, if I may say so, we have
only started.
The very magnitude of the success has
intensified one or two major problems and
made their solution a matter of extreme
urgency. I refer, of course, to the
questions of Wiltshire cure and grading.
Apart altogether from the fact that a
definite obligation rests on the Pigs and
Bacon Marketing Boards established in
the United Kingdom to see that their
increased production takes the formnamely Wiltshire sides of the bacon.
which formerly was imported, the situation which we have to deal with is that
our Ulster roll and ham trade is a
specialised one. There is one outstanding
fact and that is that that particular trade
is not capable of expanding doubly or
trebly to correspond with the increase in
the pig population.
It is anticipated that there will be this
year at least 110,000 pigs surplus to the
requirements of our local curers, and for
these the Pigs Marketing Board will be
responsible. If these pigs are marketed
in England it will, owing to transport
charges and other obvious factors, mean
a loss of at least 15s per pig which, on
110,000 to 150,000 pigs means £80,000 to
£100,000. Apart from this fact alone I
am certain that on the grounds of
employment and the welfare of our
Province every hon. Member would like
to see all our pigs cured in Northern
Ireland factories. This will give employment, and the losses on transport charges
will not be so great.
Ministry of Agriculture 1134
Estimates-
25 APRIL 1934
That is the problem which the Pigs
Marketing Board is tackling. I understand that some months ago they drew the
attention of curers in Northern Ireland to
the situation and offered on behalf of the
producers to give our existing curers
secured loans should they require them
for the purpose of developing the Wiltshire cure. I mention this matter in
order to remind the Committee that it is
one which is no longer within my jurisdiction, and that full power was vested
in the Pig Producers' Board by the
Marketing Act. Before leaving this
aspect of the question I would remind the
Committee that my Ministry recently conducted an election of greater magnitude,
as far as votes are concerned, than the
General Election which constituted this
House.
Mr. NIXON: That is making very
little of the House.
Every regis-
Sir BASIL BROOKE:
tered producer of pigs was able to record
his vote in electing his Board by means
of a secret postal vote. Over 80 per
cent. of the producers voted, and the
present Pigs Marketing Board is as truly
and democratically representative of its
constituents as our Parliament.
The only power bearing on this matter
which is reserved to my Ministry, is the
final say with regard to the quota. I
have already made it abundantly clear
to both the Pigs and Bacon Marketing
Boards that our existing curers are fully
capable of dealing with the roll bacon
trade and its development. Further,
that new factories must be for the Wiltshire cure, and that their supplies must
come from the pigs which are surplus to
the requirements of our existing curers.
That is the policy which I have pursued
throughout and which I shall continue to
pursue. I have already made my intention to protect supplies to existing curers
perfectly clear by reducing the shipment
of live pigs from 2,500 a week to 500 per
week during a period when curers had
difficulty in securing adequate supplies.
I mention this to show that we in the
Ministry are trying to hold the balance
evenly, and I think we have succeeded in
doing so.
Now as to the problem of grading,
there is general agreement that effective
and real grading is vital to the success of
the whole scheme. Without it the whole
edifice will fail. The concern which the
market authorities, who have my
sympathy, are showing in the matter
arises, not from their desire for an
efficient grading system, but because they
fear that pigs will be deflected from the
markets and they will lose the tolls which
they levy on the farmers' pigs. I have
already made it clear that whatever
system of grading is adopted we propose
that no alteration will be made in the
marketing of pigs.
Some hon. Members were good enough
to meet me a short time ago to discuss this
question and, perhaps, I might be allowed
to remind them that the proposal was
that the grading for weight should take
place in the market. The farmer would
be paid 80 per cent. of the value of the
pig when it had been graded for weight.
The remaining operation of grading for
value would be carried out at the curer's
store. Subsequent to the grading for
value the farmer would receive the
remaining 20 per cent. due to him for the
value of the pig. I do not desire to
weary Members with the pros and cons of
the skewer system which is being
advocated by certain market representatives. I do not think that anybody responsible for grading can be satisfied with
a system whereby the driving in of a
skewer in one place would show a satisfactory result, while driving it in even
one-eighth of an inch from that recognised
place would give an entirely different
result. Of course, the error which the
skewer system would show might mean a
loss of £1 a pig to the small farmer.
the Ministry we have been able to get
only a 30 per cent. accuracy with the
skewer system, but even if the system was
successful, and was 100 per cent. accurate,
it would still not solve the difficulty of the
remaining stages of grading which we propose to go in for, namely, depth of belly,
and hardness or softness of back fat. The
only satisfactory way is to split the pig,
and if it is split in the open market on a
wet or rainy day or when dust is blowing, I do not think it is necessary for me
to explain to agricultural Members that
that carcase would not be in a very fit
condition to turn into bacon.
In
Whilst we are by no means finished
with our difficulties with regard to the
Pigs and Bacon Marketing Schemes, I
am sufficiently optimistic to believe that
Ministry of Agriculture 1136
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Basil Brooke].
if we will eschew agitation and keep clear
in our minds the goal of an output which
is to be doubled and trebled within a few
years, we shall succeed in establishing in
our small area a bacon industry which
will bring much needed wealth, not only
to our countryside, but to our small
towns. I think it is necessary that I
should remind hon. Members that this is
a big scheme. There are naturally bound
to be differences of opinion as to how the
smaller matters connected with the
scheme are to be carried out. Every
time the scheme is criticised or that difficulties are put in the way a lack of confidence is liable to be produced. It is
very difficult, perhaps, for the small
farmer living in backward districts to
understand the scheme and, therefore, I
would ask hon. Members before they
criticise these various points to go into
them most carefully to see that they
really understand the points at which the
Pigs Marketing Board are aiming before
they launch their criticism, which, as they
are aware and as I am aware, creates a
great deal of suspicion amongst some of
the smaller farmers.
I should like to touch, for a moment,
on the milk scheme. Hon. Members will
be aware that a milk marketing scheme
has been in operation in Great Britain
since October last and they will not be
unfamiliar with the difficulties which have
strewn its path. I should be sorry if the
producers of this country thought that
we did not produce a milk scheme because
we did not take the trouble to work one
out. That is not the reason. The reason
we have not produced a scheme is
because we realised the very great difficulties the English scheme was up against
where the liquid milk producer is carrying the manufactured milk producer on
his back. In England the output of
liquid milk is 70 per cent. and of manufactured milk 30 per cent. of the total.
In this country the opposite percentages
exist, that is to say, the total output of
milk in this country is 30 per cent. on the
liquid side and 70 per cent. on the manufactured side.
It will be obvious that if in England
their scheme cannot succeed without great
difficulties in keeping their Board in a
sound financial position, it would be
impossible for any Board, situated as we
are in this country, to be a financial
success.
Therefore, to work on the lines
Great Britain has inaugurated would only
spell disaster, and until we can see our
way clearly to produce a scheme where all
the chances are in favour of it being a
success I am convinced it would be a great
mistake to inaugurate such a scheme, but
I hope that within a comparatively short
time we shall discover something that will
be of assistance to the milk producers.
The portion of the milk trade which is
causing me the greatest anxiety is that
portion comprising the creameries and
manufacturing side. The price paid in
the creameries for milk is in the vicinity
of 2d per gallon, and I shall use all my
energies, and my Ministry will do the
same, to see if we can hammer out something that will help this very deserving
undertaking. We shall have to encourage the consumption of milk. The
consumption of milk per head of the
population in the United Kingdom is
rather less than half of what it is in any
other country in Europe.
If we can encourage the consumption of milk by
cleaning up our milk and making it of a
better keeping quality I think we may be
able to do something to help the milk producer. Let me assure all those interested
in milk production that I will do everythink I can to bring about a scheme that
I will be of real value and that will not
run the risk of proving a failure.
Now I should like to say something
about potatoes. The importation of main
crop varieties from abroad has practically
ceased, and the scheme which has been
introducd in England is one whereby the
home producer is limited to the acreage
which he can normally plant. He can
only increase that acreage by paying a
fine of £5 per acre. The crop which he
produces is again dealt with by the riddle
system. That is to say, that if in a
normal year he produced one hundred
tons per ten acres, and in a bumper year
he produced say 120 tons to the ten acres,
the riddle will be introduced to limit the
size of the potatoes that may be put on
the market. It will be quite obvious that
a system such as that would be inoperative in this country. We cannot
limit the acreage of potatoes which can
be grown here.
We have, however, agreed that we
shall confine our shipments to Great
Britain to 200,000 tons per annum, and
in case there should be any misunder-
Ministry of Agriculture 1138
Estimates-
25 APRIL 1934
standing, may I hasten to add that we
have never in the past ten years shipped
200,000 tons to Great Britain. Further,
this quantity does not include potatoes
shipped abroad, and the arrangement
only holds good so long as main crop
potatoes are not imported into the United
Kingdom.
The Potato Marketing
Scheme for Northern Ireland will, I
expect, be in operation by September and
will, I hope, in conjunction with the
action which has been taken in Great
Britain, secure for our growers an
economic return for this important crop.
Finally, I should like to refer to one or
two points which arise out of the census
returns for June of last year and January
of this year. Hon. Members will be glad
to note the substantial revival in flax
growing, an increase from 6,093 acres to
9,784 in 1933. A much larger acreage
has been sown this year and, I hope, the
revival in the linen industry will long
continue to make this crop a remunerative
one for our small farmers.
Perhaps the most gratifying feature of
the January returns is the substantial
increase which they show in our breeding
stock. I take this as an omen that
farmers are gradually regaining confidence in the future of their industry. I
am sure even the critics will agree that
the corner has been definitely turned.
There are still black spots, perhaps even
patches, but I hope that during the
present year we shall be able to illuminate two of these dark patches by carrying
through, in close collaboration with Great
Britain, plans for bringing much needed
relief to the milk and the stock producer.
I beg to move.

explained to the Committee the various

in keeping his eye on these schemes.
Regarding agriculture as a whole, the
chief difficulty under which it is now
suffering is lack of prices for livestock as
a whole. If you take the cattle trade
you will find that this time last year
we were getting on an average 34/- per

cwt., while the English average was 38/-

January, we are now back to the low
level.
This question of livestock has
recently been the subject of a very exhaustive report by the Fat Stock Commission in England. The chief point in
that report is the fact that they intend
to co-ordinate the marketing of all livestock, with the exception of pigs, which
are under contract under the Pigs Marketing Scheme. This, to my mind, will
involve a very large organisation and
will require very close co-ordination.
The whole point to my mind will be that
the organisation dealing with the livestock industry should deal with the subject as a whole, that is, cattle, sheep,
lambs. There is no use having a scheme
for one part of the livestock industry.
There must be a scheme embracing the
whole.
As regards the cattle industry reference
to the figures of export for the first three
months show that we exported 50,300
cattle through the ports of Northern
Ireland as against 37,700 for the same
period of last year. It looks to me as
if we were exporting more cattle but we
are not getting the same money for them.
The situation on the Border may be
responsible for this. I am not prepared

135,000 sheep and lambs.

In the bacon trade last year according

370,000 pigs were cured, and the visible.
pork population according to the Minister
was about 480,000 leaving a surplus of

that it is far better to deal with them here
on this side of the water than to send them

lose in weight. They get abused, the

deteriorates, but I cannot say exactly how

in Northern Ireland establish factories
the money is saved both to the farmer and
to the country insomuch that the manufacture here gives employment and so on.
In this respect this expansion-I know

To my mind it is a very strong point

dealing with it piecemeal. You ought to

The next thing will be a board for

The people whose cause I am supporting this afternoon are the least able to

The reason that they are unable to help

farmers are prepared to work hard and

Mr. McCARROLL: Although I represent what is more or less a city
constituency I have a certain amount of

Mr. McCARROLL: It is in two constituencies. I take a keen interest in it.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. McCarroll
He said that as a result of what happened
in Ottawa people here in the North were
not in the same position as their unfortunate neighbours in the Free State. Or
course, everyone knows that these socalled, or alleged, unfortunate neighbours
in the Free State occupy a totally different
position from us here. They are a
Dominion, and we here are in a totally
different relation to Great Britain, but
apart from anything else I suggest it is
not good taste for the Minister to express
anything in the nature of a disparagement concerning the position of that state
and what transpired at Ottawa.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: It was not in
any sense a disparagement of the Free
State. I was drawing attention to the
disparity in the actual prices.
Mr. McCARROLL: I am dealing with
the use of the word "unfortunate."
The people in the Free State have elected
to adopt a certain attitude. We all know
the conditions there in regard to tariffs,
and if you were fighting the nation they
are fighting you would be in exactly the
same position. You have the advantage
of having your annuities, which are part.
of your revenue. The Free State is fighting to retain their annuities as part of
their revenue, and as you are using your
annuities for the benefit of the people in
this area the Free State is at the present
time being hit severely. I think it is not
in good taste for any Minister here to
say anything which would throw any
reflection upon the Free State. I
candidly express the hope that they will
win in that fight. They have as much
right to the annuities as you have.
A reference has been made here to the
Wheat Commission. Having regard, to
the amount of money extracted from this
area for the purpose of subsidising wheat
growers, this area is not getting an
adequate return. It was said that something like £200,000 is taken out of
Northern Ireland annually, and I
venture to say that only a very small
fraction of that amount is returned by
way of subsidising wheat growers. It is
probably one of the functions of the
Ministry to see that a larger proportion
of the money extracted by way of a tax
on flour from the taxpayers of Northern
Ireland should return into this area to
subsidise wheat growing here.
There is one other matter to which I
wish to refer. A large amount of the
taxpayers' money in Great Britain is
being devoted to the subsidising of the
sugar beet industry. All of us who pay
taxes are contributing our proportion of
the money that is levied for the purpose
of subsidising the sugar beet industry
across the water. I would like to know
from the Minister of Agriculture what
provision, if any, is made to secure that
an adequate share of the money devoted
to subsidising the sugar beet industry is
returnable to this area, and if it is
possible to develop the sugar beet industry
in this area. That is a very pregnant
question on which I would like to have an
expression of opinion from the Minister.
I am also in agreement to some extent
with the hon. Gentleman who has just sat
down. I think one of the tragedies of
the whole industry in Northern Ireland
is the multiplication of officials and
boards and the making of regulations with
which the small farmer in this area will
never be able to keep pace. He does not
understand those regulations, and even if
he could get a much superior education
to the education he has got it would be
absolutely impossible to keep in touch
with the extraordinary network and
entanglement of regulations of one sort
or another. Can hon. Members conceive the
position of the small farmers? In Tyrone,
a county which I know intimately, the
greater proportion of the farmers have 40
or 50 acres of land. They all live within
themselves. They do not pay wages at
all, because very few of them are capable
of paying wages, and you cannot conceive
that type of farmer keeping pace with the
extraordinary output of regulations that
are issued in this area.
With all due respect to the Member for
Dock, I think you are absolutely socialising the whole agricultural industry. You
are creating in the industry, under
another guise, a Socialistic system. You
are taking charge of a man's whole
industry, and yet you are pretending all
the time that you are absolutely opposed
to the Socialisation of any industry. I
am familiar with all the aspects of the
life of the small farmer, and I know that
under the weight of all your regulations
he will ultimately get into as bad a
position as the farmer across the Border
who has to fill up so many forms to
comply with the Custom regulations.

Notwithstanding the advantages we

getting for our cattle a price that is at all
adequate. Some people are taunting
those across the Border with slaughtering

to rear them for the price you will ultimately get for them. That is due to the
conditions that have arisen under the
Ottawa agreements, and which could be
corrected if the Minister took the proper
steps. There is one other aspect of the
matter. I am not capable of inflicting
long speeches on the House, and I would
not do so if I could. But there is one
other matter I want to refer to, and it is
more of a personal matter.
I say, and I say advisedly, that it is
a particularly difficult thing for members.
of the farming community who are not of
the same political or religious outlook as
the right hon. Gentleman who now has
the honour to preside over this Ministry,
when they find that in his political

gravely hostile to their national aspirations. I say it is impossible to divorce
the position and the personality of the
Minister, and I submit, with all due
respect to this Committee, that it would
be much better if, instead of trying to
provoke bitterness and hatred and
rancour directed against the people in this
area who belong to our religious faith and
our political allegiance, and creating an

better feeling amongst the people instead
of carrying on that raging campaign
which is a disgrace to civilisation and to
Christianity in this area.

In connection with the milk scheme I

The potato scheme is also about to be
launched, and let us hope it will bring

At the present time potatoes are unsaleable, and in my own district the farmers

applied in the case of potatoes. Grading
will be applied as at present, but riddling
will not be applied. With regard to an
investigation into black scab that disease
has been in existence for some time, and
as the hon. and gallant Member knows it
has actually been found to be dormant in
the ground for twenty years. No remedy
has been found to stop it. As to the matter
of milk for children it has not been overlooked in the marketing scheme. Another
point that raises a certain amount of
interest is that of financing bacon
factories. I pointed out in my speech
that the Pigs Marketing Board have been
given power to take whatever action they
consider necessary.
In addition to that
the Pigs Marketing Board are a completely democratically elected body. I
have given them certain powers. As
Minister I am not going to restrict those
powers and say, "You cannot do this or
cannot do that; you have not considered
the whole position, and you are not in
a position to judge what would be in the
best interests of the producers."
This Board represents the producers,
and the lending of money to a company
cannot be called a Government subsidy
in any way. It is solely the representatives of a private concern lending
money to another concern who, they
think, can deal with their produce in the
most satisfactory way. I should like to
say that the money which is being lent
by the Pigs Marketing Board is amply
secured. The Pigs Marketing Board will
have two directors on the board of this
company, and in addition the great
advantage that Northern Ireland will
have from this particular company is that
they are, I suppose, the biggest firm in
the world dealing with this commodity.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I do not desire to
interrupt the right hon. Gentleman, but
I would like to ask him a definite question. Is it a fact that this money has
been lent by the Pigs Marketing Board?
I am merely
Sir BASIL BROOKE:
giving information that I am aware of.
The hon. Gentleman as a member of the

ment with other firms. There is no

With regard to agricultural wages,
referred to by the hon. Member for
Shankill and the hon. Member for Dock,
I have before me a return which, I think,
has been made out by the police, of the
wages of the various counties-
Mr. BEATTIE:
By the police?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Yes, the information was collected by them. In County
Antrim the actual wage of a ploughman
is 21s. and is made up to 29s. by various
allowances. The wages go down to as low
as 9s. for boys who are housed. Their
allowances bring them up to somewhere
about 16s. I do not think I can go into
all the details. The average for ploughmen in Northern Ireland is 25s. 6d., for
cattlemen 24s. 3d., for ordinary labourers
21s. 9d. and for boys 15s. 3d. Therefore,
the wages do not compare unfavourably
with those in some of the other industries
where a great deal of skill may be
required.
Mr. HENDERSON: Will the right
hon. Gentleman set up a Commission to
inquire into the wages?
Sir BASIL BROOKE:
This information is as nearly accurate as can be
obtained. The hon. Member for South
Derry (Mrs. Parker) said she had attended
a meeting at which Mr. McElderry was
present and she would have liked to have
seen an actual test as between what Mr.
McElderry calls his system of skewer
testing and the Ministry's system. The
Ministry's skewer system, as a matter of
fact, is the same as Mr. McElderry's
system. The system of testing for
quality has been going on for some time
by way of experiment. As I said in my
original speech, we at first got only 20
per cent. accuracy, but latterly we got
slightly over 30 per cent. accuracy. No
matter how accurate the skewer system
may be it
can only be a test at the
shoulder and we have got to go further
aз the scheme develops.
Even that system of securing a test is
open, I will not say to dishonesty, but to
inaccuracy, because if you put the skewer
in at a given spot it is supposed to give
the depth of the fat at the shoulder, but
it requires only a very slight movement to
miss the bone and give a higher percentage
of fat, which would work out very detrimentally to the small farmer. Therefore, that system would not be
satisfactory, and we could not entertain
it for a moment.
I have gone, I think hon. Members will
agree, as far as I can in helping the small
markets, and I sympathise with hon.
Members who naturally desire, as I do,
to get these small markets going. I think
they will agree that I have done nothing
that has made the position of the small
markets any worse than they were
before. They are in the same position.
I find it rather difficult to understand
why a certain market agitation has
arisen, when the interests of the markets
are identical and they are in the same
position as before.
May I repeat that the farmer still gets
his 80 per cent. of the value of the pig
when it is graded for weight and the
remaining 20 per cent. will be paid afterwards? I do not see how, without
interfering with the efficiency of the
scheme, I can make any alteration in that
arrangement. Any splitting of the carcase is obviously quite impossible. You
have only to take an ordinary wet day
and the pig would be in a most hopeless
condition.
Mr. CRAWFORD: The right hon.
Gentleman says that 80 per cent. will be
paid at the time and the remainder afterwards. That is a vague statement. Can
he put a time on it?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: It will be in a
week or ten days.
Mr. CRAWFORD:
Thank you.

course, a very much shorter time than it

creamery milk. The hon. Member for
Shankill affirmed that the Ministry were
responsible for any unhealthy tubercular
milk that came into Belfast.
Mr. BEATTIE:
Partly responsible.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: He may have

The Member for Foyle suggested that
a sugar beet factory should be set up in
this country. To be of any use at all,
an enormous subsidy would be required
to pay for the sugar beet in this country.
That sum would be spent very much better
in improving live stock, for which this is
a suitable country. The difficulty you
are met with in connection with
the growing of sugar beet is that
the further North
you go the less
sun you get, and the lower the sugar
content. It is exactly the same as if you
were working a low paying mine. You
have to remove a tremendous lot of dirt
before you get any gold, and in the case
of sugar
beet you
have a tremendous
amount of pith which is of no value, compared to the small amount of sugar you
are able to extract.
Mr. McCARROLL: I did not exactly
advocate the establishment of a sugar
beet factory. I asked if we could not get
a share of the money that is going to
subsidise the sugar beet industry in
England.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Through the
Colwyn Committee a population proportion is distributed, and that goes to
the central fund. I understood the hon.
Member to mean he wished to have a
sugar beet factory set up, which I think
would be most inadvisable. I think that
covers all the questions I was asked
during the debate.
Mr. BEATTIE: In the few minutes
at my disposal I would like to put forward one or two arguments to refute the
arguments used by Members of the
opposite side of the Committee. I will
deal with the last question first. The
Minister has read to the Committee a
schedule drawn up by the police throughout the country giving the average rate
of wages paid to agricultural labourers.
My colleague and I are prepared to go
round the farms in County Antrim with
any policeman and ascertain the rate of
wages paid from the men or boys who are
actually receiving them, and base our
average on the result. I am not prepared to accept the average of 21s. plus
extras, making a total of 29s. as the
wage paid to the agricultural labourer in
County Antrim. No such wage exists,
except perhaps in an isolated case such
as the Member for Mid Antrim who, I
understand, specialises in paying high
wages to agricultural labourers. I do
not accept that figure, and I hope the
Committee does not accept it, because
during the War period, when agriculture
was at its hey-day and prosperity was
flowing into the homes of the farmers,
they would not pay decent wages to the
labourers on the land. I want to say
quite candidly that the Minister's policy
is wrong, because what is good for the
farmer should be good. for the farm
labourer. I agree with the policy of the
Minister in regulating the sale of farm
produce for the benefit of the farmer, but
I cannot agree with his policy in refusing
to set up a board governing the wages in
that industry. How can you justify
boards for every unit of agriculture while
refusing to set up a board to regulate
wages.
The Member for South Tyrone has
drawn attention to the smuggling that is

Mr. BEATTIE: I contend that the

To-day we are getting a class which will
automatically find itself in the privileged
class. The Minister has been accused of

I am rather afraid his Socialistic
doctrine might develop into a system of
dictatorship. We have the practical
farmer and the talkative farmer. The

in this House, and does nothing in the
farming industry except talk about it. I
have met a practical farmer in this
House. We had the pleasure of having
a practical farmer here for a period of five

House, but I have yet to listen to a
practical farmer in this House saying to
me that the labourer is not worthy of his
hire. On the other hand, I have had
the talkative farmer telling me in this
House that the labourers are being well
paid for their work. When a man with
a wife and four children receives 9s. a
week for a sixty hour week, do you consider that is a fair return for his labour.
The Minister has started a system of
grading. We have two pork curing
industries in Ballymacarrett, and I agree
Iwith the Minister that it would be most

to the public who consume this pork to

KILKINAMURRAY P.E. SCHOOL.
6. Mr. FRYAR asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he can state the
reason why the Kilkinamurray Public
Elementary School was closed against the
wishes of parents and ratepayers of the
district; whether he can state why his
Department refused to open the school in
response to the resolution passed by the
Sub-Education Committee of Dromore
and the unanimous resolution of the
Regional Committee of the County of
Down in favour of the re-opening; and
whether the Minister of Education would
reconsider the matter.
Mr. ROBB: This school was closed

been justified either on grounds of expense or of educational efficiency.

occurred since the decision to close it.

Road Traffic Bill-
Second Reading
26 APRIL 1934
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Motor Vehicles and Road Traffic Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Modern legislation
of a comprehensive character with regard
to motor vehicle traffic on the roads was
initiated in this Parliament by the Motor
Vehicles (Traffic and Regulation) Act,
1926. This Act introduced penalties for
negligent or dangerous driving and for
drunkenness in charge of a motor-car, and
gave powers of suspension on conviction
of certain of these offences. It also introduced the new principle, which was subsequently extended to other countries, of
compulsory insurance as regards third
parties, but this only applied to public
service vehicles.
Since that time I have had the honour
of introducing two other important Acts,
amending and extending the original Act,
in the years 1929 and 1930, respectively.
The first of these was popularly known as
the Bus Act, and the second extended
still further the principle of compulsory
insurance by extending this principle to
all classes of motor vehicles.
In addition to these Measures, I also
submitted the important Roads Improvement Act of 1928, which has proved an
extremely useful piece of legislation by
facilitating the local authorities in their
efforts to make the roads safer. It would
not be out of place if I were to recall that
the 1926 Act was, in Great Britain and
Ireland at any rate, the pioneer legislation on this subject, and has served,
together with the Amending Act of 1929,
as the model for legislation both in Great
Britain and the Irish Free State.
While we may be accused of lagging
behind in adopting modern legislation,
this charge cannot be levelled against the
Northern Government in regard to motor
legislation, and it has been a source of
considerable satisfaction that the principles adopted by us have, in many
instances, been followed by the legislatures
of other countries.
At the outset, I would like to make
clear what this Bill aims at and what it
does not aim at. There are two distinct
problems in connection with this matter,
and in many respects they are very
different, although at some points they
impinge upon one another. Both of these
problems have recently been prominently
before the public mind. There is, first,
the problem of public safety on the roads,
and in using the word "public" I mean
to emphasise that it is the safety of all
classes of road users, pedestrians and
motorists, and to this aspect of the
problem I will refer at more length later.
The second problem is the problem of
transport, and I do not in any way limit
that expression to road transport,
because it includes rail transport. It is
a matter of great complexity and difficulty, and it is of paramount importance
to Northern Ireland that there should be
devised a sound and workable system of
transport. The Government have been
giving the matter earnest consideration
for some time, and investigation is being
actively pursued into the various aspects
of the problem.
As soon as our investigations are complete we shall put a scheme before the
House, and I can assure hon. Members
that we fully realise that the matter is
one of urgency and importance and that
there shall not be any avoidable delay
in dealing with it. I desire, however, in
order to prevent any confusion during the
debate, to make it clear that this Bill
does not purport to deal with the system
of transport, and that this matter is reserved for another occasion.
The Bill which I am now introducing
is directed to the problem of public
safety upon the roads, and to that alone.
I do not think that hon. Members will
expect me to make any apology for submitting legislation on this subject. It is
one which has continuously given the
Government and the public generally
grave concern.
During the year 1933 there were no
fewer than 1,633 accidents reported, in
which there was injury to persons, and in
these accidents 141 persons were killed,
and 1,757 people injured. This is an
appalling total for a small population
such as we have in Northern Ireland, and
even the fact that the number of
accidents and the number of people
injured show an appreciable reduction on
the numbers for the previous year, 1932,
it gives little cause for satisfaction, more
especially as the number of persons killed
shows an appreciable increase.
The statistics of these accidents are
collected by the police, and careful
inquiry is made as to the causes. This

The figures which I have given are more
than ample justification for examining
more closely our motor legislation, with
the view, if possible, of making such
amendments in our laws as may result in
a reduction in the toll of the road.
I wish, however, to emphasise one point.
I do not believe that any legislation, however perfect, can abolish road accidents,
nor do I believe that police activity alone.
can have that result. While legislation
can contribute much to greater safety, I
believe that the true solution must rest
with the public who use the roads. If
everyone who goes out in the morning,
whether as a pedestrian, cyclist, or
motorist, would make up his or her mind
not to run any risks, to consider other
road users, and to co-operate with the
police in bringing to justice those who
misuse the privilege of the public road,
the ratio of accidents would, in my
opinion, rapidly fall.
There are two classes of drivers who
contribute mainly to the toll of the road.
You have what is known as the road hog.
There is no use in appealing to his sense
of decency. His one aim is to make himself objectionable and, consequently,
dangerous to everyone else on the road.
He desires to drive faster than anyone

Turning now to the Bill itself, hon.
Members will observe that it is divided
into seven Parts. The first Part, consisting of twelve Clauses, deals principally
with road offences. The second Part proposes amendments with regard to the law
of third-party insurance. The third Part
relates to the licensing and regulation of
goods vehicles, and Part IV to the provisions as to the lighting of road vehicles.
Part V deals with some miscellaneous
matters, and Part VI with proceedings in
respect of offences. The last Part, consisting of four Clauses, is mainly formal.
Hon. Members will hardly expect or
desire that I should go through each
Clause of this rather long Bill. I am sure
that they would prefer that I should
direct their attention to the more salient
points, leaving the details until the Committee Stage of the Bill.
The first two Clauses rewrite in a more
convenient form with some amendment
Sections 1 and 2 of the Act of 1926 and
Section 2 of the Act of 1929. Hon.
Members will remember that under
Section 1 of the Act of 1926 a driver who
is convicted of driving recklessly or in a
dangerous manner is subject to a fine of
not less than £1 and not more than £10
for a first offence; for a second offence not
less than £2 and not more than £20; and
for a third offence not less than £5 and
not more than £50. In the last case the
court may also award imprisonment for
a term not exceeding three months. We
have re-enacted these penalties, but we
propose to enable the court to impose
imprisonment whether the offence is a
first, second, or third offence. This is in
no sense the minimum penalty, but there
are gross cases of negligent driving,
usually by "road hoggers," which cannot be adequately met by a fine, even
though it may be a first offence.
I feel certain that this House will agree
with me in giving adequate powers to the
court to suppress with ruthless severity
this gambling in human life. There is
a further alteration in that we propose
that the courts will have the power to
impose imprisonment on the first conviction for the offence of drunkenness in
charge of a motor-car. As the law now
stands, imprisonment can only be imposed
on the second conviction.
Clause 3 makes a somewhat important
amendment with regard to suspension of
licences. As the law now stands the
courts can order suspension in any case of
reckless or dangerous driving or drunkenness in charge of a motor-car. In the
latter case the minimum period is twelve
months, but in all cases it is open to the
delinquent to apply to the court at the
end of three months to have his or her
licence restored. The Bill provides that
the minimum period of suspension will
be six months, instead of three months as
it exists at present in regard to dangerous
driving, and in all cases the court will
not have authority to remove any suspension until a period of twelve months
has expired. I trust that the authorities
charged with the administration of the
law will make full use of the additional
powers proposed to be imposed on them.
The drunken driver of a motor-car is
one of the worst menaces to public safety.
The drunken driver of a horse-drawn
vehicle or the drunken driver of a pedal
cycle is also a menace to road users, and
deserves punishment. Cause 4 makes
such people subject to a fine not exceeding £5 for a first offence or not exceeding
£10 for a second or subsequent offence.
Clause 5 is one of very considerable
importance. It is taken from the
Imperial Road Traffic Act of 1930, and it
is intended to deal with the careless
motorist, who does acts upon the road
which are careless and inconsiderate, but
which it might be difficult to prove that
they came within the provisions of the
Clause dealing with reckless or dangerous.
driving. We think that this Clause
would be useful to the police in dealing
with this class of offender. The penalty
is a fine not exceeding £5 for the first
offence or not exceeding £10 for a second

Now I come to the question of inspection of vehicles. There can be no doubt
that many vehicles are used on the roads
to-day which are in an unfit condition.
From time to time cases of defective
brakes and such like come to light, but
they always come to light after an accident
has taken place, and it is beyond doubt
that there are far more cases than are
discovered. One would think that a sense
of responsibility and a sense of what is
due to other people on the roads would
prevent anyone taking out a vehicle which
is in a mechanical condition which renders
it unsafe, but such is not the case.
propose to try to check this practice by

to take power to stop vehicles on the road

competent, by reason of their knowledge

The proposed system of inspection is
in no sense a new principle. It was
brought into force, as regards public service vehicles, by the Act of 1926, and
has proved most efficacious in ensuring
that public service vehicles are not
allowed on the road unless they are in
proper mechanical condition, and I see
no reason why this principle should not
be applied to ordinary cars and lorries,
and that the police should have the
opportunity of detecting mechanically
defective machines before an accident
takes place, rather than after, when loss
of life may have occurred.
This provision will in no sense be a
hardship on motor owners who keep their
cars in good condition, but I will say
this, it will be most salutary with regard
to those motor owners, small in number,
who, for economy, are prepared to
gamble with human life. I understand
that a question has been raised as to
how the owner's insurance would be
affected in case of an accident during
inspection by the police. I am inquiring
into this point, and, if necessary, I shall
propose an Amendment to safeguard the
position.
In this connection I would like to draw
attention to one point-I regret to say
that it has been brought to my knowledge that drivers have been compelled
by their employers to take out lorries and
other motor vehicles which
are in a
defective condition. The driver has a
responsibility and he cannot escape it,
but an even greater responsibility rests
on the owner who sends the driver out.
It is his clear duty to see that his vehicles
are kept in proper condition, and if he
fails to do so we shall certainly pursue
him with all the rigour of the law. I
would like to call the attention of the
House particularly to Clause 12, in which
it is proposed to limit the time which
drivers of public service vehicles and
goods vehicles may remain continuously
on duty.
Mr. BEATTIE: Hear, hear. Restrict
the hours.
Sir DAWSON BATES: We are

it is essential in the interests of public

we were able in many cases by administrative action in regard to the withholding of licences to compel owners of public
service vehicles to treat their drivers in
a reasonable way as regards working

We have now had more experience,
and as a result of our investigations and

the Clause which is materially different

be more satisfactory to the public, to the

Mr. BEATTIE: Oh, no, it will not!

Now we come to the question of third
party insurance. Part II of the Bill
deals with that thorny and difficult subject, and it contains amendments to the
existing law which are important and
far-reaching.
When I spoke in this
House, introducing the Traffic Bill of
1930, which instituted the system of
compulsory insurance, I warned the
House that the scheme which I was then
submitting was not a water-tight scheme,
but that it went as far as at that time
had seemed practicable to go. I claim
that the provisions of the 1930 Act did
effect a considerable improvement in the
conditions, and that the number of cases
in which it was found that an injured
person was unable to get reasonable compensation was greatly reduced, but four
years' experience has undoubtedly shown
that there are gaps in the scheme.
I
have come to the conclusion that the
requirement on an insurance company to
deposit £15,000 with the Supreme Court,
either in Great Britain or Northern Ireland, is not a sufficient safeguard to ensure that this business will be handled
by companies of repute only. Certain
companies, some of which subsequently
became insolvent, were able to qualify
themselves and to issue policies, and not
only have their policy-holders suffered
from their insolvency, but whilst these
companies were operating they did not
deal with claims in the spirit in which
a reputable company would have done,
and, therefore, I propose to revert to the
system which obtained under our 1926
reason-
Act, namely, that we will only recognise
policies which are framed in a
able spirit and which are issued by an
insurance company which has made the
requisite deposit and also been approved
by the Ministry of Home Affairs. This
system worked well in the past, and
the House will be interested to know
that prior to the Act of 1930 certain
insurance companies, which afterwards
became insolvent, applied under our
1926 Act to be put on the Ministry's
approved list and were rejected.
The next point to which I wish to
draw the attention of hon. Members is
not an amendment of the law of compulsory insurance, but an amendment of
the common law of the land, which hon.
Members should appreciate in order to
understand the provisions relating to compulsory insurance. According to a rule
of the common law, if a person commits
a wrong against another, legally known
a tort, and dies before judgment is
obtained, the right of action falls to the
ground. For instance, if a motor driver
by his gross negligence injures another
person and is himself killed in the
accident no action can be brought against
his representatives, or if a motor driver
by his negligence injures another and an
action is brought, but in the meantime
before judgment is obtained the person
committing the wrong dies, there is no
remedy.
Therefore, Clause 15 sets aside this
rule of law and provides that all such
actions can be brought or continued
against the personal representative of the
deceased person, and I am sure that hon.
Members will appreciate that this is a
very important change in the law, but
I think it is one which will commend
itself to the House as eminently fair and
reasonable. In order to make this provision effective in practice, it is necessary
to provide that insurance policies shall
cover not only the drivers and owners of
motor-cars, but also their personal representatives.
A point that has caused considerable
difficulty is that the validity of insurance
policies under the existing law depends
to a very great extent upon there being
no material misrepresentation, whether
deliberate or unintentional, on the part
of the proposer of the policy. Hon.
Members, I think, will appreciate that
a contract is based on the facts disclosed
Road Traffic Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
in a proposal to the insurance company.
The law is that contracts of insurance
require the utmost good faith on the
part of both parties. It is a serious
thing to interfere with this very
salutary rule, and I should be very slow.
indeed to suggest to the House any modification of it where the only two parties
interested in the contract are the insurer
and the insured. If a man induces an
insurance company to insure his house
against fire by misrepresenting the facts.
to them, then he has only himself to
blame if when his house is burned down
the insurance company decline to pay,
but compulsory third-party insurance
with regard to motor-cars is entirely
different. There is another party interested, namely, the public, a member
of which may be injured by the insured,
and the insurance may be the only
practical guarantee that compensation
will be forthcoming if awarded by the
court. Parliament has recognised that
there should be such a guarantee, and
it is therefore the duty of Parliament to
see that the guarantee is reasonably
effective.
On the other hand, it would, I think,
be placing an entirely unreasonble burden upon insurance companies to say that
under all circumstances, no matter what
fraud they were subjected to or by what
trick a policy was obtained from them,
they must be liable. We have, therefore, to try to find some course which will
give adequate protection to the public
and, at the same time, give reasonable
safeguards to the insurers. What we,
therefore, propose to provide is that no
matter what fraud or misrepresentation
may have been committed in order to
obtain the insurance policy, the insurer
will not be permitted to repudiate liability
unless the offender has been prosecuted by
the company to conviction.
I admit that this may give rise to an
occasional hard case at first, but I submit to the House that our primary duty
is to ensure the suppression of fraud, and
thus to prevent the necessity of repudiation arising, rather than to require payment to be made by the defrauded party.
We must not lose sight of the fact that
whilst by recent legislation we have somewhat altered the character of third-party
insurance, still the fundamental principle
remains that it is a contract of indemnity
between the insurer and the insured.
The penalties for fraud or misrepresentation with regard to an insurance policy
are severe, and the provision which we
put forward should make sure that severe
punishment will follow in the case of fraud
or misrepresentation. I attach considerable importance to the certainty of
punishment in the suppression of this
offence.
The next point to which I wish to draw
the attention of the House is, that it is
a practice with all insurance companies
to some extent, and with certain insurance companies to a much greater extent,
to insert in their policies some provisions
of a restrictive character, a breach of
which enables them to repudiate liability
when an accident occurs. One example is
a condition that the vehicle must be in
proper mechanical order, and if, when an
accident occurs, it is found that the brakes
were defective, or something of that kind,
the insurer is in a position to repudiate
liability. Limitation on the power to
insert conditions is necessary, and we,
therefore, propose that the Ministry may
lay down conditions which may not be
inserted in a policy.
The final point to which, I think, it is
necessary to draw the attention of the
House in this Part of the Bill, is contained in Clause 16. Where the driver
of the car or the owner of the car is a man
of straw, there may be very considerable
difficulty on the part of a person injured
in obtaining redress. Judgment may be
got against him which cannot be realised,
as he has no goods to seize, and he may
not take the trouble to make a claim
against his insurance company. In some
cases direct remedy against the insurance
company may be secured by making the
judgment debtor bankrupt, but it is a
somewhat cumbersome procedure and,
accordingly, I suggest that where a judgment has been obtained in respect of the
liability for which such owner or driver
is insured and where that judgment has
not been fully satisfied, the person who
is entitled may apply to the court for
leave to execute the judgment against the
authorised insurer who issued the policy.
This procedure will give the injured party
an effective remedy, whilst, on the other
hand, the court will see that this power
is not abused.
Perhaps hon. Members would now turn
to Part III of the Bill, and in consider-

ing these provisions I would again ask.
hon. Members to bear in mind what I

This part of the Bill is designed to
ensure the safe and reasonable use of goods
vehicles upon the roads. It is not
designed to regulate goods traffic. That,
as I have pointed out, is reserved for
another and early occasion. Put shortly,
goods vehicles will not in future be allowed
to operate on the roads until a licence has
been obtained for them, and a condition
precedent to this licence will be that the
vehicles conform to a proper standard of
fitness. They will be examined annually
by inspectors, who will be members of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary, and who will
be recruited on the same lines as the
inspectors of public service vehicles.
I think the House will agree that this
is a reasonable and proper precaution to
ensure that safe and properly equipped
vehicles only are operated upon the
roads. It is essential that such vehicles,
especially having regard to the heavy
loads which they carry, should be in
proper mechanical condition and sufficiently well constructed to carry safely the
heavy weights which are put upon them,
and not only that, but it is reasonable
that the vehicles should be so equipped
as not to cause unnecessary inconvenience
to other road users. A common case is
for goods vehicles to have no mud guards,
and they go along the roads or through
the streets of the towns throwing mud
in all directions.
The House will realise that a scheme of
this kind cannot be carried out without
expense. There will be, not only the
annual inspections, but if the scheme is to
be effective there must also be test inspections from time to time. This involves
the employment of men in the constabulary of adequate motor mechanical experience. It is but reasonable that such
expense should be borne by the industry,
and we, therefore, propose to recoup the
expenses necessarily incurred by a licence
fee to be fixed by the Minister, but it is
proposed to limit the maximum amount
of such fee to £2. I do not suggest that
it will be necessary to charge all goods
vehicles £2, but within that limit we can
find a scale which will produce the funds
necessary to meet the expense, and it is
not intended that more should be raised
by means of licence fees than that which
is absolutely necessary to meet the cost.
It is common knowledge that many of
the goods vehicles upon the roads are
grossly overloaded. There are numerous
obvious objections to this practice. It is
unsafe to load a vehicle beyond the maximum capacity for which it is designed.
The engine, the brakes, and the various
mechanical parts of the vehicle are
designed to carry a certain load. If this
limit is habitually exceeded an undue
strain is placed upon the vehicle and its
equipment, and it is a potential source of
Overdanger to all other road users.
loaded vehicles cause extensive damage to
the roads, and continual overloading is
really an evasion of the taxes which are
necessary for the upkeep of the roads.
The owner who is continually exceeding
his proper load is placing an unfair
burden upon the other road users who
contribute to the upkeep, and also on the
ratepayers.
My Ministry has power to prescribe
maximum weights. Hitherto we have
only laid down the maximum weight
which may be carried upon any vehicle,
but we are engaged in devising a scale so
that maximum weights are prescribed for
different vehicles. To make this effective
it is necessary
to strengthen the
machinery of enforcement. Hitherto the
only persons who could require a vehicle
to be weighed, laden or unladen, were the
taxation officials of the various county
councils, and it is clear that having
regard to the very limited number of
these officials and to their other duties,
the supervision which they could exercise
in this respect was very limited. We now
propose that the police should have
be
authority to require vehicles to
weighed and, further, that it should be
competent for such officer to require the
vehicle to be taken to any weighbridge or
other machine which is situate not more
than 2 miles from the place where the
vehicle is when the requirement is made.
At present the limit of diversion is halfa-mile, which is quite useless.
Another source of danger, and one
which has been responsible for a very
considerable number of accidents, is the
practice of carrying passengers on goods
vehicles. Usually out of good nature
drivers give their friends lifts upon their
vehicles, and frequently passengers are
carried in such a way as to impede the

driver in carrying out his duties properly.
We think, and I am sure the House will
agree, that the right to carry passengers
on goods vehicles should be very strictly
limited, and Clause 22 sets out the people
who may be so carried. First, there is
the driver of the vehicle; secondly, the

may be carried on the vehicle, provided

would cover the case of a contractor who

to allow the carriage of not more than

go, and I am glad to observe that the

responsible lorry owners. As hon. Members have, no doubt, already seen, some
lorries going about have a notice prominently displayed stating that no passengers can be carried.
Clause 25 introduces an important departure from the existing law. Under
the provisions of the Act of 1926 the
Ministry has power to prescribe the maximum speed of goods vehicles of more
than 2 tons unladen weight, and speed
limits for the different classes of such
vehicles have been laid down. There is,
however, no power to prescribe any speed
limit for vehicles weighing less than 2
tons, but having regard to the modern
development of these vehicles and to the
loads which they now carry I have come
to the conclusion that some limitation is
necessary, and accordingly I propose that
the power which is already in existence
with regard to the vehicles over 2 tons
should be extended to vehicles under that
weight.
I need not detain the House very long
over Part IV of the Bill, which deals
with the law of lighting of vehicles on
public roads. It is in the main a consolidation of the existing law with some
amendments on the matters of detail,
and it brings the law in Northern Ireland into line with the law in Great
Britain. There are, however, two matters to which I think I should refer.
Clause 27 (3) proposes to give to the
Ministry somewhat unusual powers to
add to or vary by regulation the requirements of this part of the Bill. These
powers are similar to the powers given to
the Ministry of Transport in Great
Britain by the law in force there. This
part of the Bill deals rather with matters
of detail, and it may be desirable at any
time to alter the requirements as to
lighting, having regard to the changes
which may take place in vehicle design,
or as a result of new inventions, and
matters of that kind. Any such regulations that may be made will, of course,
be subject to the jurisdiction of Parliament, as laid down in Clause 47 of the
Bill, and I think that the House will
agree that, having regard to the subject
matter which would be dealt with by
such regulations, and the provisions for
supervision by Parliament, the power
which we propose to take is reasonable in
the special circumstances.

matter which has engaged public

good reflector which is properly attended

Clause 39 in Part V of the Bill is perhaps the most important matter in it.
It deals with the making of false statements and forgery, or the fradulent use
of licences, and matters of that kind, and
it collects, and to some extent amends,
the provisions relating to these matters
which are scattered throughout the motor
code. The matter to which I wish to
direct the special attention of the House
is contained in sub-clause (4). Hon.
Members are, no doubt, aware that
generally speaking, proceedings under
the Summary Jurisdiction Acts must be
brought within six months of the commission of the offence. This provision
which, with regard to the majority of
offences, is entirely reasonable, defeats
the ends of justice in some cases.
instance, a person may obtain a certificate of insurance by making fraudulent
misstatements to the insurance company.
Some considerable time afterwards he
may have an accident, gravely injuring
or killing some other person on the road,
and when a claim is made the fraud which
he committed to obtain his insurance
certificate may be discovered, and by
reason of this fraud the person whom he
has injured may find that no compensation can be obtained. Yet if the fraud
is not discovered until more than six
months after the commission of the
offence the offender goes scot free.
Accordingly, we propose that in the case
of offences under this Clause a prosecution may be brought at any time within
six months from the date on which it
came to the knowledge of the prosecutor
that the offence had been committed.
Clause 44, which is in Part VI of the
Bill, is designed to reduce the expenses
of motor prosecutions. As hon. Members are, no doubt, aware a person committing an offence can be prosecuted at
petty sessions either where the offence is
committed or where the defendant
resides. For instance, if a motorist residing in Fermanagh commits an offence
in County Down theoretically he may be
prosecuted in either place, but a summons issued by a County Down magistrate can only be served in that county
or in an adjoining county, and consequently cannot be served in County
Fermanagh, and, therefore, in practice
the prosecution must be brought in
County Fermanagh. This means that all
the witnesses must be taken down to
Fermanagh and the prosecution is put
to a great deal of expense. To get over
this difficulty we propose that, with regard to motoring offences, a summons
issued by a justice of one county may be
served in any other county in Northern
Ireland, so that the prosecution may take
place in the place where the offence is
committed and where it can be carried
out with the least possible inconvenience
and expense.
This would give rise to another difficulty. If a County Down summons is
served in County Fermanagh it is necessary to bring up the person who serves
the summons to prove that it has been
served, and this means incurring considerable
expense to carry out a necessary
formality. Accordingly, we propose that
service of a summons may be proved by
an affidavit which will avoid the necessity
of incurring the expense of bringing a
witness in person.
Clause 45 lays down a procedure for
giving evidence of previous convictions.
A motorist who is charged with an
offence may have convictions in a number
of different places, and under the present
procedure it is necessary to bring
witnesses from these different places to
prove the convictions although the
defendant may have no intention of disputing them. The Clause provides for
the service of a notice with the summons
setting out the particulars of the previous
convictions, and unless at least two days
before the hearing of the summons the
defendant informs the person having
charge of the prosecution that he disputes
the convictions, he will be deemed to have
admitted them. Of course, if the convictions are disputed they will have to be
proved in the ordinary way by the production of the necessary witnesses.
Under the existing law the costs which
the court can award against a person
convicted of an offence under these Acts
is limited to 20s. by the Summary
Jurisdiction Acts. In many cases the

serious, to lay down minimum penalties,

court.
These are all offences of gravity, and
offences which must be sternly suppressed
if we are to have any degree of safety
upon the roads. They are offences which
show a disregard for the safety of others,
and I feel, and I am sure the House will

such offences as these should be severely
punished and have no claim to the benefit.
of the Probation of Offenders Act, which

type of offender.
The next Clause in the Bill is directed
to deal adequately with offenders coming
from outside the United Kingdom who
misuse our roads and with whom we are
not now in a position to deal. Briefly,
where one of the more serious offences
has been committed by a person coming
from outside the United Kingdom, who
cannot be reached by our courts if he
escapes outside the jurisdiction, the
police are given power to arrest and
detain him until a summons has been
served and until he enters into a recognisance, with sureties or other security,
before a justice of the peace binding him
to appear on the hearing of the summons.
This is in no sense a punitive Clause. It
merely gives the police sufficient power to
enable them to secure that an offender
will appear to answer the charge against
him, and to prevent those to whom we
offer the hospitality of our roads from
abusing that hospitality and defying our
courts. Last summer a case came before
my notice in which an individual was
stopped for a serious offence. His name
was taken, but he went off that night to
England, and that was the last we heard
of him. These, then, are the main points
dealt with in the Bill, but before I sit
down perhaps I might add a word or two
on matters which are not in the Bill.
It is somewhat of a coincidence that
there should be Bills before the Imperial
House and this House at the same time,
dealing with this matter. The problems
which both houses have to consider are
fundamentally the same, but hon. Members will have noticed that we are dealing
with various matters in a different way
from that in which they are dealt with
in the Imperial Bill, and there are certain
provisions in the Imperial Bill which are.
not incorporated in the present Bill.
These divergencies are largely due to the
different conditions obtaining here and in
Great Britain. We have adopted the
expedients which we think are more
appropriate to our own local conditions
and circumstances, and without being
egotistical I think I can claim that taken
as a whole our motor legislation cannot
be regarded as unsuccessful.
I have carefully considered the matter
of speed limits and have come to the conclusion that the proposal to impose a
general speed limit in built-up areas
would not meet the situation here.
In

observance within any limits or places in

I fully admit that the trend of opinion

arrived at all the relevant circumstances

There are cogent arguments on both sides

Another matter which has engaged my
attention is the question of requiring all
new applicants for driving licences to
undergo a test. I would refer hon.
Members to the figures which I quoted.
at an early stage in my speech. Last year
out of 1,633 accidents, in only seven had

of
the figures have been
similar
character. I am not convinced that any
benefit which might be obtained would be
commensurate with the expense involved,
nor am I satisfied that it is possible to
devise a test which would obviate any

Apart altogether from this side of the
question it is impossible to devise a test
which will provide the condition of affairs
which arises prior to an accident. There
are two main classes of offenders-the
"road hogs" and those with no road
sense-both classes can pass with flying
colours any mechanical test that can be
provided. For the present, therefore, in
the light of the information at my
disposal, I cannot advise the House to
legislate in this direction.
As regards the question of carelessness
on the part of pedestrians, under the Act
of 1929 we have power to make regulations. The matter is one of great
difficulty, and before exercising these
powers I propose taking an opportunity
of consulting the various local authorities
with a view to making practical regulations in respect of towns for the
protection of pedestrians against their
own carelessness and folly.
The Bill, the Second Reading of which
I have now the honour to move, is the
result of a great deal of consideration and
care. I am putting forward provisions
which will, in my opinion, remedy the
defects which experience has shown exist
in present legislation. I do not suggest
that this is the last word in legislation for
securing safety on the public roads, but
I do commend it to the House as an
earnest effort to meet the situation as we
see it to-day. At the same time I would
like to emphasise what I have already
said. The dangers which exist on our
roads to-day cannot be abolished merely
by legislation. The real remedy lies in
the hands of the public themselves. It
lies in a higher sense of responsibility,
not merely on the part of the motorist,
but on the part of the cyclist and on the
part of the pedestrian, and the education
of the young.
There must also be more
co-operation on the part of all classes with
the police who are charged with protecting all sections of the public, and there
must not be, as at present, obstruction
to the police in the performance of their
duties. In these directions, rather than
in further repressive legislation, lies the
real hope of progress. I beg to move.

regard to the danger of crossing the road
and that his own dog looked up and
down the road before he crossed it. He
went on to make a comparison which I
am not going to follow. I might get
into trouble. I hope that seven generations of people will not be killed before
they learn the rules of the road.
I thought something should have been
done to compel foot passengers at least
to keep to the footpath. When I was
motoring some few years ago-I do not
know whether it is the same now or not
-when I happened to be coming into the
city-in fact at any time, but particularly on Sunday afternoons on any
road leading to the city, but particularly Balmoral, the whole road
was filled with people. Most of
them were walking on the road.
Only a few were on the footpath. I
submit that where there are footpaths
people should be made to walk on them.
Another thing which motorists experience
is the risks run when one overtakes three
or four people cycling on the road. This
applies particularly to ladies. Some go
to the right hand and some to the left,
and leave the motor-car to pass in the
centre, which is a most difficult thing
very often. You do not know exactly
what they are going to do, and that contributes largely to accidents. But the
most dangerous thing of all to my mind
is a cyclist in front of a motor-car at
night meeting another car with headlights. If the headlights are strong you
do not see the cyclist, and if you are
going anyway fast the danger is that he
will be run down. That is all I want to
say on the Bill. I hope that the next
time a Traffic Bill comes along we will
have no railway directors directing its
passage in this House.

Rev. Professor CORKEY: I have

Rev. Professor CORKEY: Thank you.

example set by the Imperial Government
in establishing a speed limit in built-up

limit in country districts, although even
there speeding occasionally leads to
accidents, but in built-up areas there are
special reasons which would justify the
application of a regulation of this
character. Inevitably there are a great
number of people in an area which is built
up, and so the liability to accidents is
greater.
Then there are children playing on the
sideways. In addition to that there are
a great many corners because a number
of roads lead on to a main road in a
built-up area, and nearly always they
are blind corners owing to the unfortunate habit of our forefathers building
houses flush with the footpath. The great
number of blind corners in built-up areas
seem to me to justify the imposition of
a speed limit in areas of that type.
It has been said that if you impose a
speed limit in any area that speed will
tend to be the normal speed at which
people will drive, regardless of the conditions. I fail to see that there is any
objection in that at all. Surely it would
be possible to frame an Act in such a
way that motor drivers would understand
that they could not in any circumstances
exceed the speed of, say, 30 miles an
hour in built-up areas, and in addition
to that, when circumstances were such
that even 30 miles an hour was a dangerous speed, they would be under an
obligation to drive at such lesser speed
as would be in keeping with the safety
of the public. I cannot myself see any
contradiction between those two methods
of regulating speed, and I think that in
built-up areas both those methods might
very well be in force. One would not
tend in any degree to militate against
the effectiveness of the other.

ought to be applied to individuals when
