Mr. POLLOCK: Doing what?
Mr. HENDERSON: Driving buses.
To my mind there is nothing that causes
accidents more than overworking people
of that sort.
Mr. ANDREWS: I agree with that.
Mr. HENDERSON: If you agree you
ought to use your influence with the
Minister of Home Affairs, and get into
the Bill the number of hours per week
or per day these motor drivers shall work.
Mr. ANDREWS: You will get it in
the regulations.
Mr. HENDERSON: The right hon.
Gentleman knows that in so far as the
regulations are concerned very little
attention is paid to them. The regulations are broken every day.
In any case,
I feel dissatisfied that the Minister of
Home Affairs did not put in the number
of hours particular motor drivers should
work per day. You are allowing
Northern Ireland men to do two men's
work per day. That is not fair.
Any
time I am in one of the omnibuses I am
asked by the drivers or conductors:
"When are you going to raise the
question of a reduction in our hours?"
They have told me they were working 20
hours a day, from very early in the
morning to late at night, and the drivers
of these omnibuses have on their
shoulders the lives of 32 persons.
But all the talking will not alter the
fact that even if an
Amendment is
moved from any side of the House to restrict the hours the drivers work the
right hon. Gentleman will not accept it.
The Minister should have put it in the
Bill. I would have thought also that
the Minister, in the interests of the safety
of the travelling public of Northern Ireland, would have insisted on the persons
who employ motor drivers paying these
men a decent wage. We have men who
are twenty years of age working for 10s
and 15s a week as drivers of motors.
Hunger is far more dangerous than
alcohol, and unless you pay these men
proper wages they cannot get food to
make them Al citizens. I am glad the
hon. Member for Woodvale referred to
one of the most important matters in this
Bill. I cannot for the life of me understand why this Government are always
passing their powers on to other persons
outside this House. The fact of the
matter is, in so far as the road transport
of Northern Ireland is concerned, you
have handed over the monopoly-
Mr. POLLOCK: They trust the
Government.
Mr. HENDERSON: You cannot trust
the Government.
Mr. POLLOCK: Why did they put
the Government in?
Mr. HENDERSON: I did not vote
for the right hon. Gentleman. I do not
know what I might do if he was in my
division. But in any case here is the
position. The Government has set up a
Bus Tribunal. As soon as that Tribunal
was set up the railway companies got,
practically speaking, a monopoly of the
roads throughout Northern Irelandoutside one or two companies. I think
it was 94 routes-eighty or ninety routes
according to the statement made by one

to a question by the hon. Member for

out in the country is receiving 9s or 10s
a week.
Mr. POLLOCK: You know that is
wrong.
Mr. HENDERSON: It is not wrong,
and the right hon. Gentleman cannot
dispute it, because he knows very little
about agriculture. There are two or
three Members on this side of the House
Road Traffic Bill-

who know something about agriculture,
and the facts are these. Since this Bus
Tribunal was set up you have given them
a monopoly of the roads. They have
raised the fares all over the country.
Quite recently there was an increase of
fares. One of these omnibus companies
was prepared to reduce fares so that the

Mr. ANDREWS: What about wages?
Mr. HENDERSON: The firm that was
prepared to reduce fares pays fairly good

this particular firm who are paying the

eight-hour day for the workers. The right
hon. Gentleman opposite does not travei
by omnibus. He travels in a Rolls Royce.
I am a bus traveller. Immediately this
Bill becomes an Act of Parliament, you
will allow this Bus Tribunal to control all
fares. I think that is a crying out shame.
When that is done Members of this Parliament will not be able to object to any huge
increase in fares imposed on the travelling
public. It is terrible thing. As the hon.
Member for Woodvale has said, you would
really think that this was being done
owing to the fact that many of the hon.
Members opposite are railway directors.
In fact, when this Bill is put on the
Statute Book, I am quite certain that the
taxpayers will say that you have done this

That is the reason why I have always
advocated in this House that in your own
interests it would be far better for you
not to hold any outside posts at all. You
should just hold your jobs as Cabinet
Ministers.
Mr. SPEAKER: I must point out that
it is not in order for the hon. Gentleman
to suggest that Ministers use their positions to help undertakings in which they
are personally interested. Another thing
to which I must call the attention of the
hon. Member is that he should address the
Chair.
Mr. HENDERSON: I will be delighted
to do that. When I address the Members
of this House through the Chair they pay
more attention to me. I would not for
the life of me suggest that right hon.
Gentlemen opposite were doing anything
to further their own businesses. I am
only saying that it would be in their own

any private companies. These firms would
still go on without them, just in the same
way as if the right hon. Gentlemen gave

order to look after their private business,
somebody else would come in to take their

time of the House unduly, for I see that
the hon. Lady wishes to speak.
It is most important that the Government should control the fares charged to
the travelling public of Northern Ireland.
Why should we not retain the power that
this Tribunal is going to exercise? They
could charge agricultural labourers 2/- for
a 1/- journey. and the matter would be
out of our hands. As soon as this
Tribunal was established the fare to
Bangor was increased from 1/- to 1/6.
The Bill states:
The Tribunal established under
section seven of the Act of 1929 shall
have power, and shall be deemed always
to have had power, to fix fares for all
classes, or any particular class of passengers, and when they fix any fares
under the powers conferred upon them
by that Section as amended by this
section, they may attach to the fixing of
such fares such terms and conditions as
they think fit.
Suppose that on a Saturday afternoon the
wife said to me, "Take the child out for
a motor drive, or for a run in the train."
If that child was going to be a nuisance
to the passengers, either in the bus or
train, the Tribunal could say they would
make certain reservations whereby one
could not bring a child into a bus or train.
That is very unfair. This power should
be kept in the hands of the people,
through their Government, and you are
deliberately passing it on to a Tribunal
which has already exploited the travelling
public. Some of the people in the agricultural areas, away in Derry and other
places, are being asked to pay exorbitant
fares. I think the charge per mile in
Northern Ireland is higher than in any
other country in the world. That is due
to the fact that the Government have
handed over their powers to a Tribunal.
I feel this very much.
I want to support the hon. Member
for the University (Professor Corkey),
who spoke about excessive speed. This is
rather a serious matter. The Minister of
Home Affairs ought to visit the Lisburn

that, owing to complaints from firms
which have local representatives that

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.

MAGISTRATES-JUDICIAL
FUNCTIONS.
3. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of
Home Affairs what the Government's
intentions are regarding the necessity for
amending the Summary Jurisdiction
Acts in Northern Ireland, and in this
event whether, in view of recent
incidents, an opportunity will be taken.
to alter the status of Justices of the
Peace.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The Government
have had brought to their notice the
unsatisfactory condition of affairs in
connection with the Summary Jurisdiction Acts, and the necessity of
bringing them up to meet modern requirements. As a result, a Measure has
been approved by the Cabinet having for
its object the reform of the whole system
of Summary Jurisdiction, which will
include a provision relieving Justices of
the Peace of their judicial functions.
It is not proposed to abolish the office
of Justice of the Peace as such, or of
depriving the Justice of the many other
functions which they now exercise, such
as:-
The signing of summonses;
The signing of warrants;
The administration of oaths and taking
of declarations, affirmations, informations, depositions and affidavits;
The signing of Reception Orders for
the admission of persons of unsound
mind to public and private mental
hospitals;
The power of visiting and reporting
on prisoners under the Prisons
(Ireland) Act, 1877; and
The power to remand and admit to
bail.
Mr. GRANT: I would like to ask the
right hon. Gentleman will there be any
compensation given to the five-shilling
magistrates?
Mr. McCARROLL: Will the right
hon. Gentleman say whether this is in
accordance with the step-by-step policy?
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is with
the idea of providing the best judicial
system, which we have not got at the
present time.
Mr. STEWART: Will the Minister
give an undertaking to the House that
in future he will not appoint any more
kill-joy magistrates as the country is overrun with thein?

NEWRY ELECTRICITY
UNDERTAKING.
5. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Labour whether he can state,
as regards the conditions of employment
in the electricity undertaking at Newry,
if the proportion of Roman Catholics
and Protestants is in accordance with
the population of the district; or whether
men are employed from the Labour Exchange under the rules of the Exchange.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply.
The Newry Electricity Undertaking
has now passed into, and forms part of,
the larger undertaking operated by the
Electricity Board for Northern Ireland.
I am informed that the Electricity
Board neither records particulars of the
religious denominations of its employees,
nor does it require them from applicants
for employment. I am, accordingly,
unable to furnish the statistics sought
by the hon. and gallant Member in the
first part of his question.
With regard to the second part of the
question, I understand that labouring
staff is recruited regularly from the
Newry Exchange, preference being given
to ex-Service men.

Road Traffic Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Motor Vehicles and Road Traffic Bill.
Order read for resuming the adjourned
Debate on Question (26th April), "That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
-(Sir Dawson Bates.)
Question again proposed.
Mr. BEATTIE: In resuming the
debate on this very important Measure
which is before the House, I feel
that an effort has been made to meet
the requirements of modern transport on
our roads. I feel also on reading
through the Measure that it is a Bill
of Spierism. Spierism is a sort of
policy which is guided mostly by the
railways, and if I find anything of that
description in the Bill it is my intention
to move Amendments.
In making my comments I hope I will
not be taken as opposing the Measure,
because I am not doing so. I want, if
possible, to give helpful criticism. In
some particulars I think the Bill is rather
too drastic, and in others is not
sufficiently strong enough to produce the
conditions on the road which we would
like to see. The Minister in his speech
outlined various Clauses of importance for
the guidance of the House, and in Clause
1 I find there are extreme Measures in
regard to penalties. I feel that that
Clause deviates from the practice followed
in all other Measures, both in the
Imperial House and in this House, in so
far as it creates a minimum fine for a
particular offence.
If you have magistrates on the Bench
trying a case it is quite within your
power to set out a maximum, but I do
feel the imposition of a minimum is
taking away a lot of discretionary powers
from the magistrates. We all know that
slight accidents occur on the roads, for
which a fine of £1 or £2 would be quite
sufficient. I think the discretionary
power which the magistrates at present
have should be sufficient guarantee that
the penalty imposed would fit the offence.
Therefore, I disagree with the policy
adopted in this Bill of fixing a minimum.
as well as a maximum. I believe it is the
only Bill of its kind that adopts a
minimum fine.
I find also in Clauses 1 and 2 of the
Measure
a very drastic and severe
penalty. We will assume, for a moment,
that a man is taken up on a charge of
manslaughter and that that charge is
dropped. Under this Bill there is power
given to prosecute under each of those
Clauses, that is, two prosecutions for the
one offence. I think that wants a little
bit of clearing up. If that is the case,
there is grave danger of a man being so
hard pressed that it would have been
better to have been charged with manslaughter, because to have two prosecutions on one charge is unfair under the
law.
The next point is this. I feel that the
power given to the police could be used in
a manner which would be dangerous to
decent motorists. We will take the case
of a lady motorist driving by night. A
policeman who is not in uniform presents
himself in the middle of the road and
holds up his hand. There should be
something to distinguish him. A policeman should be in uniform, so that the
motorist might know that she was being
stopped by an authorised officer of the
law and would not have any fear of being
insulted or robbed by a highwayman. I
feel there is a danger in allowing any
man in plain clothes to stop motorists at
night, because it might be discovered that
the man who stopped them was not a
constable at all.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It may save
time if I say that no policeman in plain
clothes will be permitted to exercise that
power.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am expressing what
I see in the Bill. I am doubtful whether
it carries the right hon. Gentleman's
expression of opinion.
Sir DAWSON BATES: You may take
my assurance.
Mr. BEATTIE: I hope this point will
be guarded. Then there is the medical
examination of the licence holders. The
Minister did not give me just the information I wanted. Does he mean to suggest
that the person applying for a licence will
have to be medically examined? Does
that examination apply to private
motorists, because I find in the speech of
the Minister that the greatest number of
accidents have been caused by private
motorists. During the year 1933 there
were 1,633 accidents reported, and of this
number 866 were ascribed to causes con-
Road Traffic Bill-
Second Reading
1 MAY 1934
nected with either the vehicle or the
driver of the vehicle. In 661 cases the
pedestrian was stated to have been at
fault, and 37 cases were due to other
causes. In looking down the various
grades of motor accidents I find that the
greatest number are caused by private
cars.
Therefore, we must concentrate on
what is the real reason for these accidents.
The statement which I am about to
make may not be popular, but I make ic
because I am very fond of motoring
myself, as I believe it is a very nice way
of passing an afternoon. I feel that the
speed must be regulated. I would
certainly fix a national speed limit for the
whole Six Counties, and I believe that
that would minimise to a certain extent
the number of accidents due to speed.
Of course, when I say I would fix a speed
limit I do not mean the old idea of 20
miles an hour. I know that modern cars
require a certain amount of speed so that
you may get sufficient service from your
engine. I would regulate speed in
accordance with the improvements to
motor engines and the requirements of
our modern age.
Children at school must be educated as
to their duties on the highway. You are
endeavouring to educate the motorist.
But their speed has gone far ahead of the
speed of the pedestrian's education.
Therefore, we must bring the two nearer
together. I say you must regulate one
mechanical process until such time as the
pedestrian is sufficiently educated to know
the p's and q's of road law. One notices
in London the great amount of traffic
handled and the small number of
accidents. If you compare London traffic
with our traffic you will agree that the
motorists in London have more road
manners and that pedestrians have more
respect for the road manners shown by
motorists than they have in Northern
Ireland. They wait and then pay strict
attention to their duty in crossing the
road, whilst the motorist also waits and
pays strict attention to his duties. That
is the reason for the curtailment of the
number of accidents in that area. We,
in Northern Ireland, have not reached
that state of perfection yet, and I hope
that this Measure will teach motorists
their duty as it will teach pedestrians.
The next thing I want to say is that I
fear if we restrict the motorist we are
going, perhaps, to do damage to the
motor industry. That is a point that
may not be grasped at the moment. The
more restrictions are put on motorists the
less motoring will be done, and the less
motoring is done the fewer cars will be
built. I would, as a consequence, be very
careful in going into this Measure to see
how far any legislation might affect the
output of cars, because I live in hope that
we in this part of the country will have
a motor factory yet. Therefore, a guard
should be put up against doing any
damage to the motor industry.
There is another matter to which I
want to refer in Part I. Clause 12 gives
me the right to claim a certain amount
of credit for the propounding of an idea
which is partly in the Clause, but the
most important part of it is left out. I
would like to ask the Minister, after all
the public declarations which have been
made by judges, magistrates, and responsible ministers, and by those who
understand industrial fatigue, why he has
not set down a definite law governing the
working hours of drivers of public service
vehicles. This has been included in the
British Measure, but the right hon.
Gentleman here stated in his speech that
he wanted to make the regulations elastic.
If he makes them elastic he will find some
time that the elastic will be stretched to
its fullest.
There are ways and means of getting
under laws that are elastic, and I want
a definite law laid down whereby, if I
get into a public bus I will know that the
driver has not been over-worked or underfed and is in a condition of health to drive
that bus. I feel a man should not drive
a motor for more than eight hours a day
without an interval. Any motorist in
the House can readily understand what
I mean if he sits at the wheel for 31
hours. I claim that no pubic service man
should be allowed to work more than
eight hours a day, those eight hours to
include a meal hour. I hope the Minister will remember my Amendments in
1926 and 1929 in regard to an eight-hour
day. That is necessary for the safe
carrying of the travelling public in
omnibuses and also in regard to lorries,
which are now being brought under
control.
The public service certificates have
given a certain amount of guarantee that
the bus is mechanically sound. They
have also eliminated to a great extent the

Coming to the question of lorries, I
feel we have been slow in adopting this

"rattling good cars." I have met

would have heard them. You did not

their own noise gave you all the warning
that was necessary. I am pleased, not
only that lorries are to be included, but
that the lorry driver will be in exactly the

I have known boys of sixteen, eighteen,
and twenty years of age to be employed
on lorries with very large loads for sixteen
hours a day, in some cases for eighteen
hours a day, and the physical condition
of some of those boys was not too good at
the best of times. I say that practice
constitutes a danger on the road for other
motorists, and I hope you will regulate

goods-carrying vehicles, and also include.
a test of physical fitness for lorry driver's
work.
Sir DAWSON BATES: If my hon.
Friend turns to Clause 12 he will see that

Mr. BEATTIE: I have Clause 12
before me, but many things which in the
past I have thought would happen have
not happened, and I now want to put

should happen. I hope these things will

I want it definitely laid down in law,
without any ambiguity at all, that these
men must not work more than eight hours
per day. If you lay that down as the
law there is a safeguard and a protection
for the public and also for the driver and

Another thing I want to point out is
that most of these lorries to-day are drawing trailers. There you have a condition
of affairs on the road of which you never
thought. A lorry with a trailer should
have at least two men on it. I have seen
these lorries with trailers and only one
man. That is unfair and is also a danger
to the travelling public. I say there
shoud be two men on those vehicles, and
I also say that certain carriers in
Northern Ireland, who carry very large
and bulky loads on their lorries, should
be compelled to have two men at least on
their vehicles. If it is necessary to have
two men on a passenger bus it is all the
more necessary to have two men on a
cargo lorry, because the driver cannot
always see what may fall from his lorry,
and if anything bulky falls from his lorry
at night another motorist may meet his
fate through that obstacle being on the
road. Therefore, I say it is necessary
and important that on all lorries carrying
heavy, bulky loads there should be two
men employed.
Another point is about the definition of
a drunken driver. I never have had the
experience of meeting one of these
drunken drivers, and I hope I never will
have. I heard a great repetition of
expert advice by the hon. Member for
Mid Antrim (Mr. Crawford) about how
long it was before one got free from the
effects of alcohol after one had taken it.
I could give the declaration of another
expert to the effect that the minds of some
men are clearer, more alert, and quicker
when they have had a half glass of whisky
than when they have had none. I could
give expert authority for that. I am not
advocating that any man should take a
half glass of whisky, but I have it on
authority, equal at least to those quoted
by the hon. Member for Mid-Antrim,
that the minds of some men are quicker
after that half glass of whisky than without it. If you work it out in practice
and take a company of men assembled
together at a meeting, you will find that
they are very quiet at first, but as the
hours go on and the beverages get more
into circulation you will find, if you
return to that quiet assembly, that they
are all jolly, hale and hearty. What is
the cause of that? Is it not the beverage?
However, those are things of which I
have no experience, nor am I advocating
them, but I have an authority here that
says that it is different in some cases from
others. There may be cases in which it
would be most dangerous for a man to
take a drink at all.

Professor JOHNSTONE: I should like
first of all to congratulate the Minister of
Home Affairs on the very exhaustive and
informing speech with which he introduced this Measure. Every Member who
was present must have felt after that
speech that, although he might not be
able to agree with all the points in it, he
certainly could not say that he did not
understand the Bill. There is another
point I should like to mention in that
connection. The Minister of Home
Affairs during his speech very frequently
referred to the return of road accidents
for 1933, which he held in his hand, and
of which I have been fortunate enough
to secure a copy. I must say this is really
one of the most informing documents I
have ever had, and it is a great pity that
it is not published. I would suggest to
the Ministry of Home Affairs that they
should take steps to publish this return
of accidents, specified and scheduled as
they are, and also to see that the return
is commented on in the motoring columns
of the various papers. I do believe that
a great deal of the careless and indifferent
driving that is done at the present time
is done as much from want of thought as
from want of knowledge or want of skill,
and if all motorists had before them these
lists of accidents as they appear in this
schedule I believe it would give them
seriously to think, and they would realise
that a very considerable liability rests
upon them to prevent accidents. I am
only throwing out that suggestion,
because I think this document is so
important, so interesting, and so valuable
that it is a pity that it should lie hidden
in the files of the Ministry of Home
Affairs. I hope it will be published every
year, so that motorists as well as other
users of the roads may understand exactly
the causes of a great many of the
accidents that occur.
Now I come to the Bill. I only propose to mention a few points that have
occurred to me as I have read over the
Measure. One of them is in respect of
Clause 2, When our first Motor Traffic
Bill was before the House, I think it was
in 1926, I brought this point forward,
and I wish to bring it forward again.
Clause 2 (1) reads:
"If any person is found when driving
or attempting to drive, or when in
charge of, a motor-car on any highway
or other public place to be under the
influence of drink or drugs . . .
I am not going to defend in any way those
who are in charge of motor-cars or who
drive motor-cars while under the influence
of drink, but I should like to put in a
plea that the man who realises that he is
too drunk to drive a motor-car and who
pulls his motor-car into the side of the
road, or who does not even attempt to
drive off in his motor-car, but who, to use
a vulgarism, decides to sleep it off before
he attempts to drive, that that man
should not be punished in the same way
as if he were driving a car when under the
influence of drink. That man has
realised that he is a danger to himself and
to other users of the road. He is adopting what I submit is the only possible way
in which he can get over that, and that is
by waiting until he is sober before he
attempts to drive his motor-car. But he
goes off to sleep in his car, a policeman
discovers him, gets him out, sees that he
is not completely compos mentis, and
promptly arrests him for being drunk in
charge of the car.
Road Traffic Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS

I submit that that is a very severe
penalty and is doing the exact opposite
to what the rest of this Bill is intended to
do. This Bill is intended to ensure, as
far as possible, that those who are driving
motor-cars shall adopt all possible precautions against accidents. I submit
that the man who feels that he is too
drunk to drive a motor-car in safety, and
who pulls into the side of the road, or
gets into his car and falls asleep so as to
sober up, is really doing his best to make
the roads safer as far as he is concerned.
It is a very hard thing under those
circumstances that that man should be
summarily arrested, taken to the police
office, detained over night, and then
brought up the next day and fined.
only so but a very heavy penalty is
imposed, for if he is convicted under this
Clause he is deprived of his licence and
cannot get a licence to drive for twelve
months.

I speak with some feeling about this
matter, because a good many years ago
I happened to be a member of the General
Medical Council, which has the duty of
seeing that the conduct of medical men is
such that they should remain on the
medical register. On one occasion we had
before us a man who had been to a race
meeting and who had dined afterwards
and was on his way home.
It was a
rather rainy night and he discovered that
he had taken a little more wine to dinner
than was wise. He pulled up his car at
the side of the road and promptly proceeded to fall asleep. He was investigated by a constable, taken back to the
town which he had left, detained for the
night, fined the next morning and, as a
result, lost a very excellent job which he
had held under the Corporation. He was
brought before us to see whether he
should be struck off the medical register.
We did not, however, decide to do that,
but put him on probation for a period.
But it did seem to me at that time that
really the law was too severe in such a
case. That man was really doing the best
he could in the interests of everybody as
well as himself, and I do not really see
why he should have been punished for it.
It is a matter rather of administration
than of legislation. Of course, the
obvious answer is that the policeman who
comes along and finds a man drunk in a
car does not know when that man will
start the car and drive off, and that he
cannot be expected to stand beside the
car until the man is sober. From his
point of view the only thing to do is to
arrest the man. But I do think that the
proper thing to do is to see that cases of
this kind are treated with the leniency
which everybody will admit they deserve.
Then I come to the next point, which is
in connection with Clause 9. Clause 9
starts as follows:-
"In any case where, owing to the
presence of a motor-car on a public
highway, any accident occurs . .
""
I submit that that is very wide, and I do
think we should have a definition of an
accident. After all, I may be taking my
car into my gate or into my garage and
may scratch my mudguard on the gates.
Accurately speaking, I presume that is
an accident. Am I to go round to the
nearest police office and report that
accident? I see the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs
(Mr. Hanna) is here and I think he
means to say "No." But where are we
to draw the line? We really should
have a definition of an accident; otherwise
conscientious motorists who wish to obey
the law will report things that do not
matter to anyone.
It is said that it takes
a policeman from half-an-hour to an hour
to take particulars of any accident, and
on that assumption we will have to
increase the number of the police if we
are going to have all accidents reported.
On the question of the power of a

think that defective brakes are more
responsible for accidents than any other
Those of us who do a great deal

Clause 27 deals with the obligatory
lights to be carried by vehicles at night.
Under Sub-Clause 2 (b) the Ministry of
Home Affairs may exempt vehicles when

perhaps very objectionable. On a dark

opposite direction. The Ministry may

I would point out that a handcart or a

is being pushed along the left hand side

if pedestrians or those in charge of these
things proceed on the right hand side of
the road, so as to face the oncoming
traffic. They are coming towards you,
and your lights illuminate them more or

up behind a handcart or perambulator.
The whole of the silhouette is black, and
does not show up against the road, and
there is very grave risk. I do suggest
that the Ministry should not exempt
vehicles of this kind.
That, I think, is all I have to say in

with hay. These loads project on both

accidents concern every type of vehicle.

of heavy
vehicles. Before the Local Government

with the heavy trailer behind. It has

The next point I come to is the question

i3 my experience in regard to accidents

I suggest that before a

not a case of earning the full £25. That

Twelfth of July.
I do not believe that the money which
this proposal would cost would be lost
money at all. Hon. Members on the
opposite side, after the laborious sitting
of this Parliament, like to go away for
a holiday. When they return they come

goes for a holiday and comes in here
strong and vigorous, and we are all very
glad to see him returning to this House
in good health and spirits. What is
good for higher-class people ought to be
good for the workers. I believe we
would get better value out of the
workers. They would come home after
a week or fortnight's holiday with renewed vigour, they would take a greater
interest in their work, and you would
get far better service out of them. They
would appreciate that holiday by the
seaside or elsewhere and would do their
work more efficiently. I do not believe
that this money would be lost. As for
the millions that we have heard it would
take to give this holiday I do not believe
in them at all. I believe it would be just
like the case of old-age pensions. The
country was going to be broke when 5/-
a week was proposed for old-age pensions.
To-day the pensioners are getting 10/- a
week, and all this money for the social
services has also been granted, and I do
not think any Member of this House
regrets what has been done. I hope even
to see increased pensions in the future.
I do not believe that this can be put
into operation at once, but the Government should give it serious consideration.
I believe that the employers would get
good value for their money, and that it
would be well worth a trial. I am not
frightened at all about the financial end.
The money could be found; the people
would have better conditions and would
do their work better and more earnestly,
and the little money spent on giving this
holiday would return tenfold to the employers. I heartily commend this motion
to the serious consideration of the Government. It may not come just at the present time, but it will come in somebody's
day, and those who live long enough will
see each worker getting fourteen days'
holiday with pay.

When I started to drive a car 35 miles

Another thing that I wish to say in

The farmers have sufficient restrictions

And I do not agree that we should

I also believe that, particularly near our

Mr. MURPHY: In rising to express

like to make certain comments, not so
much on the actual Clauses of the Bill

Bill and on some omissions which I think

make representations to the Imperial
Government for the purpose of abrogating
this old rule of law, which says that the
King can do no wrong. With some
experience of cases in our courts I cannot
see any justification for the continuance
of that old law. I cannot see any justification for the present state of affairs,
which says that when a person is driving,
say, a Post Office van and drives in a
negligent fashion-and even Post Office
vans, in the experience of many Members
of this House, are sometimes driven in a
negligent manner-and that when that
van knocks down and injuries a person in
the street, or collides with another vehicle
and causes damage, the only remedy for
the person who is damaged should be by
an action against the individual driver of
that Post Office van. While I fully
recognise that it is not a matter that can
be cured by legislation in this House, I
certainly join with the hon. Member for
Antrim in expressing the opinion that it
is a matter that should be remedied if
possible, and that, if necessary, representations should be made from our
Government.
There is another matter on which I wish
to comment. As the law now standsand the Minister of Home Affairs and the
Parliamentary Secretary will bear this
out if a person is injured in a motor
accident through the negligent driving
on the part of the driver of another
motor-car, for the purpose of establishing
liability against the owner of that motorcar, he is bound to prove that that motorcar was either being driven by the owner
of that car or by some person who was the
servant or agent of the owner of that
motor-car. In such cases the law
requires that the injured person should
discharge that onus of proof, and in my
experience in the courts it is sometimes
extremely difficult for the injured person
to establish that the actual driver of the
car was, in fact, the servant, or what the
law would describe as the agent, of the
owner of the car.
It seems to me that there, again, the
law definitely requires amendment.. I
would suggest to the Minister of Home
Affairs that that is a matter in which we
might take the lead of legislation in Great
Britain and provide that in the case of an
accident the owner of the motor-car
should, if negligence is established against
the driver of the motor-car, be liable
unless he is in a position to prove, to
the satisfaction of the judge or the jury,
that the person who was driving that
motor-car was not his servant or agent;
in other words that the onus, to use the
legal phrase, should not be upon the
person who is injured to establish that the
driver was the servant or agent of the
owner, but that the onus should rather be
cast upon the owner of the motor-car who,
at least presumably, has allowed that
motor-car to be driven by some other
person, to establish the proposition that
the person who was driving that motorcar was not his servant or agent. I would
suggest to the right hon. Gentleman that,
if necessary, on the Committee Stage
there should be included in this Bill a
Clause providing for what I consider to
be a very necessary amendment of the
law.

I am a pedestrian myself, and I fully

Road Traffic Bill-

is going to cure the number of road

be regulated by the lights.
I have some practical experience of
crossing where there are light signals, and
frequently I see that people have great
difficulty in getting across although they
wait until the signals definitely hold up
the traffic to one's left. While the traffic
to one's left is being held up the traffic
flowing to one's right is turning either to
right or left-trickling traffic-and that
is the traffic the pedestrian has to guard
against. That traffic can never be
efficiently regulated by light signals. I
merely mention this in view of the fact
that some hon. Members hold that
pedestrian traffic can be regulated in that
way. I quite recognise that there are
cases in which pedestrian traffic might be
regulated with some hope of success. I
quite recognise, for instance, that
pedestrain traffic might be confined to
certain defined crossings, especially crossings where policemen were in attendance
to hold up the motor traffic to enable the
pedestrians to cross. In some American
cities I understand there are notices
"Pedestrians cross here. You pay your
own funeral expenses." That is really
the position of pedestrians at large in
crossing our streets to-day. It is not confined to Belfast.
""
Last week I happened to be on the
Kingston Bypass, which many of you
know as possibly one of the busiest main
roads in the south of London, and the

desirable in these built-up areas.

Major McCORMICK: I think it is
indeed gratifying on this, the third day of
this debate, to find that a different tone
has come over the House so far as the
discussion of this Bill is concerned. We
are getting down to the fact that
unlimited speed is the main cause of
accidents on our roads. After all, the
object is to avoid these horrible accidents
that are daily occurring on our roads. As
one speaker to-day said, we are getting
hardened to them. We feel horrified for
five minutes and after that we get into
our cars and speed again.
I should like to say that, in spite of this
Bill, which I am in favour of, we will
have an increase of accidents at the end
of the year, because the Chancellor of the
British Exchequer is lessening the tax on
the horse power of cars. The craze will
be to get larger horse power motors and
thus increase the speed and go on in these
awful, distressing, tragic circumstances.
After all the very interesting explanatory
dissertation by the Minister on the
Clauses of the Bill I confess that I felt,
and do feel, disappointed that the very
essence of the things is missed. It does
not grapple with the main cause, which
is pace or speed.
The right hon. Gentleman said safety
lies with the people themselves. Does he
mean the pedestrians? Is it a case of
jump Jack or you will die on the road, or
stay at home and you will die in your
bed.
I
say it is the Government's duty to look
after the safety of the users of the road.
On the basis that prevention is better
than cure, I ask what good is it to punish
the motorist who is unfortunate enough
to kill anyone on the road, when, by
means of lessening the speed they could,
in a great measure, prevent an awful
affair like that. I feel that it all comes
down to speed. I think in these days,
when we are all speeders, except the
pedestrians, we have gone to unreasonable
lengths. Are we catering for the speed
merchant? The careful driver on the
road where there is unlimited speed is
at the mercy of the other fellow.
The days we are passing through of
violent deaths, both on the road and in the
air, make one think that wars will be unnecessary for killing off non-combatants.
I read in the Press only recently that the
number of killed and injured through
accidents was upwards of 500 in one week.
I believe that exceeds the casualties at the
famous Battle of the Boyne. That may
give some gratification to the adherents of
both sides to know that victory was
achieved at such small loss of life. Anyhow, it would seem as though we will not
require wars for killing off the surplus
population. I hasten to say I do not
blame the drivers in all these cases, certainly so far as the casualties are
concerned. Speed is the underlying cause.
It is almost wholly this insane craze for
speed. Motorists themselves, might I
say, have become responsible for their own
suicide and the killing of others.
This Measure before the House is really
forced upon us in order that some safeguard might be found to lessen these
awful fatalities. We are forced to protect ourselves against our neighbours'
racing propensities. We might say the
framers of this Bill going out to-day may
be the victims to-morrow of their own
speed. If one were to count these
accidents and to dwell upon them it might
bring one to realise that the regulations
are not drastic enough. If the underlying cause is still there, then the Bill
misses the point. In abolishing the speed
limit, I say, what were we thinking of?
When some experts came forward and
said speed limits were obsolete, did they
think our roads were to be turned into
racing tracks and pedestrians were to have
no rights? Did they believe that it was
only the fool who could not look up and
look out who could not avoid an accident
going at the rate of 50 miles an hour?
We listened to them and we adopted that
with very few dissentient voices.
I feel strongly that in reducing the
speed limit now we would be doing the
sensible thing in those areas that are
described as built up or congested. It is
all very well to say that an ordinary
motorist would pass a given test. When
that motorist is placed in a case of
emergency what about the test if he loses
his head? I know some of you will tell
me he might lose his head and meet with
an accident at 10 miles an hour. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I am not a killjoy. I suppose if I had a car I would go
out for speed and be a speeder. But not
having a car, and not being able to afford

So far as braking tests are concerned,
I think such tests are very important. I
feel that it is one of the most vital points
of the Bill, and I should like to give the
House some information with regard to
the matter. I say why should the regu
lations that will accompany this Bill allow

It is interesting, in connection with this,
to notice that in some European countries
they have what is known as a loading
braking limit. Such countries as
Sweden, Switzerland, Belgium, and
Rhodesia have got these tests, and the
means that are used are the Ferrodo brake
tester. It is made by the Ferrodo firm at
Chapel-en-le-Frith, and it is universally
used so far as Great Britain is concerned.
It is used by the Ministry of Transport
and by the M.O.T. officials. Until
definite limits are decided upon, however,
police action cannot be effectively taken.
In all these countries I have mentioned it
is the police authorities who make the
test, and the tests have to be undergone
under their supervision. Many countries
in Europe are now adopting this brake
test.

He referred to the return of accidents,

arresting return to the Press. That has

hon. Member professed a degree of

drunk in a motor-car and who had driven
in the car until he had become SO
exhausted that for his own and his
passengers' sake he stopped. That did not
move me in the way intended. I have no
sympathy with such a man at all, and I
cannot hold out any hope that we will
do anything to make things easier for
those who take control and charge of
motor-cars when they are so under the
influence of drink that they cannot be
other than a menace to themselves and
others, and I am sure the hon. Member
did not seriously suggest that we should.
There was some controversy about
Clause 9, and some hon. Members wanted
a definition of the word "accident." It
was never intended that if a man
accidentally scraped his mudguard he
should have to report it, but if it should
prove that the words in the Clause as now
drafted are too loose for our purpose the
matter can be made clear in Committee.
Our object is that all accidents should be
reported when third persons or their
property are involved, or where persons
were injured. Those are the accidents we
intended should be reported. It will be
appreciated by the House how important
that is, because the hon, and learned
Member for Derry City (Mr. Murphy)
pointed out the difficulty some plaintiffs
have in establishing their case. This will
be a step in the direction of making it
easier for them, because when all these
accidents are reported the parties involved
will be known and will appear.
Now I come to deal with Clause 10,
which gives a specially authorised officer
power to stop a car. The intention here
is that a specially qualified and authorised
police officer who suspects that a car he
sees being driven along a road does not
comply with our motor regulations, will
have power to stop and examine it. That
is really what we want to do. Hon. Members seem to interpret that Clause as being
an authority to any policeman at any
time and at any place to stop any driver
of any car and disport himself unreasonably in that car. That, of course, is
impossible, and it would be unreasonable.
If a policeman so abused the licence and
authority given by the law he would
become a trespasser from the very
beginning, because the law is that if a
man abuses an authority or licence given
by the law he becomes a trespasser.
Mr. MINFORD: But you give him
the authority.
Mr. HANNA: That is just where the hon.
Member is wrong. He has no power to do
anything but act within the authority of
that Clause, which is to stop and examine
a car to find out whether or not it is in
accordance with our regulations. That is
all. I quite admit that this is a big departure. I quite admit that this is something we would not do unless we felt we
were driven to it, but there is a type of
motorist who brings on to our roads
motor cars that are not mechanically fit
to be driven on the roads.
A great many accidents-and fatal
accidents- are directly attributable to
men of this kind, and we feel that the
only way by which we can catch these
men is by having a qualified policeman
specially authorised to stop a man and
examine his car. I know he would have
power to stop some of ourselves—a powerful annoyance, but I cannot imagine any
wise policeman stopping any car that is
moving properly. I do not think he will
want to undertake any more work than
there is need for. As I
say, if any hon.
Member can suggest a form of words that
will limit the Clause in a way that does
not interfere with the principle of giving
us the right to stop gentlemen who really
have been responsible for a great deal of
harm we shall be glad to consider it.
We know there are not many of these
gentlemen. I think, perhaps, if we could
only have this Clause in the way it is for
about a year we would then have the
opportunity of eliminating it at the end
of the year.
However, as I say, we
will take the greatest care in connection
with the Clause when we come to the
Committee stage.
Mr. MINFORD: I am quite prepared
not to oppose this Clause, but I think
that the test should only apply to the
steering and brakes.

Mr. HANNA: It is not a personal

Mr. MINFORD: Here is the Clause.

Exceptional Distress (Transitional

Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
an
Mr. HANNA: This Bill requires very
little explanation. It is really
extension of an Act which was passed in
1921 enabling local authorities to borrow
money temporarily for short periods to
meet exceptional circumstances.
As the House is aware, it is proposed at
a very early date to introduce a Bill dealing with the relief of able-bodied persons who are unable to obtain employment
and who are not eligible for unemployment
benefit. This will involve a
recasting of the whole administrative
arrangements in connection with such
relief.
Up to the present it has been the duty
of the local authorities concerned to make
the necessary provision for according
relief, and, accordingly, it may be
regarded that the administration of the
existing services is of a transitory nature,
and that the local authorities should be
enabled to take their places in the new
scheme, whatever it may be, without
undue hardship, and without having to
discharge immediately accumulations of
financial liability which they may have
incurred in recent years.
The Act of 1921, which is referred to
above and which enabled local authorities
to borrow temporarily for ordinary
expenditure under exceptional circumstances, required the local authorities
to discharge the liability within the
currency of the financial year concerned.
This Bill, as I have already said, is merely
an extension of that power and will enable
the local authorities to spread any liability
which they may have accumulated over a
period not exceeding five years, subject to
the approval of the Ministry. I beg to
move.
Mr. BEATTIE: I understand this is
the Exceptional Distress (Transitional
Provisions) Bill.
a
Mr. SPEAKER: This is purely
financial Measure extending the time from
one year to five years on temporary loans.
The debate is a very narrow one.
Mr. BEATTIE: I could not on those
grounds raise the question of the administration of this money.
Mr. HANNA: No.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the

Oral Answers to Questions.
CONDITION OF DROMORE LABOUR
EXCHANGE.
1. Dr. WILSON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is aware that grave
dissatisfaction exists among the unemployed of Dromore and district by reason
of the inadequate accommodation at the
local branch of the Labour Exchange;
whether he is aware that the staircase
and floors are considered unsafe and that
it is quite common for people to faint
from fatigue and the faulty ventilation of
these premises; whether any sanitary conveniences are provided; what the rent of
these premises is and the rent charged for
use of the Town Hall, which was formerly
used for this purpose; will he also say
whether the owner of these premises has
the right to prohibit people calling at
this Labour Exchange from leaving their
bicycles in the gateway through which
they must pass.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) I would point out to my hon.
Friend that the office referred to is not
an employment exchange, but simply a
paying office for the convenience of
Dromore claimants, at which they attend.
twice weekly. The premises are not as
good as we would like, but they are the
best that we have been able to obtain up
to the present. Sanitary conveniences
are provided at the premises for the staff,
and there is a public convenience about
100 yards distant. The rental is the
same as was paid for the use of the Town
Hall, namely, 6/3 for each day on which
the premises are used, and this charge.
includes lighting, heating and cleaning.
The gateway referred to leads to other
premises and this constitutes a difficulty
in the way of allowing the storing of
bicycles. Two persons, I regret to say,
were ill on the premises. I understand,
however, that this was due to the general
state of their health. Inquiries will be
continued in the hope of better accommodation being obtained.
Dr. WILSON: May I ask why the
accommodation which is available in the
Town Hall is not utilised for this purpose?
Mr. ANDREWS: I am informed that
the premises are not suitable, that they
are badly heated, and frequently required for other purposes.
CONDITION OF COLLIERS
ENTERING BELFAST.
2. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is aware that
strong dissatisfaction prevails because of
the conditions under which men are employed on the ships which carry coal into
Belfast and Northern Ireland also that
grave anxiety prevails as to the conditions
of these ships; and whether he is prepared
to have these matters investigated or
advise other authorities to investigate
them.
Mr. ANDREWS: Navigation, including merchant shipping, is a Service reserved to the United Kingdom Government, and I would suggest that the hon.
Member should address any representations he has to make to the local office
of the Board of Trade in Belfast. My
Department's responsibility is limited to
protecting dock workers engaged in
loading, unloading and coaling ships in
Northern Ireland ports. Regular inspections are carried out to enforce the
requirements of the Regulations, and,
when necessary, prosecutions have been
taken.

MOTOR ACCIDENTS.
5. Rev. Professor CORKEY asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether, in
view of the widely held opinion that
many motor accidents are due to faulty
judgment or impaired ability on the
part of the driver caused by quite small
quantities of intoxicants, he is prepared
to collect statistics which would show the
proportion of accidents that occurred
with drivers who had not partaken of
any intoxicants immediately prior to the
time of the accident as compared with
the number occurring with the drivers
who had intoxicants within a few hours
before.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I cannot
agree that the opinion referred to in the
first part of the hon. Member's question
is widely held, nor do I share it. If
the hon. Member can suggest to me any
practicable means of obtaining the information which he desires, I shall be most
happy to consider his suggestion.
Rev. Professor CORKEY: As the
Minister has, I think, misinterpreted the
question, may I ask if it would not be
possible in future, when an accident
occurs, to make a simple record of the
fact that drink had been taken, just as it
is possible to make a record of the fact
that brakes were defective, or the light
was dazzling, or the driver was drunk?
If it is possible to make a simple record
of that fact, would the Minister be willing to do it?
Sir DAWSON BATES: It may be
very simple to my hon. Friend, but I
never yet met a case where an accident
occurred in which a man accused of
being drunk did not claim that he was
sober and had not taken any drink at
all.
Rev. Professor CORKEY: The term
"drunk" is not now a legal term. May
I ask the right hon. Gentleman if it
would not be possible simply to make a
record of the fact that drink had been
taken ?
Sir DAWSON BATES Will my hon.
Friend undertake to examine the person
and determine whether he or she had
drink taken?
Mr. HENDERSON: It is a matter of
smelling his breath. (Laughter.)

Capital Fund No. 2 in respect of training

It has been decided to proceed with the

Enniskillen, which are intended to provide the accommodation required in connection with the scheme for establishing
the permanent R.U.C. depôt there. The

will be class-rooms for officers and men,
reading and recreation
and a
musketry room, as well as a covered rifle

rooms

£20,000, and provision has been inserted

will be undertaken later. These will consist of residences for the commandant and

centralise at Corporation Street the work
at present carried out at Corporation
Street and Frederick Street, and should
result in material economies in administration.
It has been agreed that it is an
essential part of the training of teachers
at Stranmillis College that they should be
given practical demonstrations of up-todate teaching methods. The facilities
hitherto available have been largely of
a make-shift character, and various
proposals for the adaptation of the Government-owned Stranmillis Public Elementary School for this purpose have
been under consideration for some time.
It has now been decided that a modified
scheme of reconstruction should be carried
out at a cost estimated at £3,000.
The Ministry is satisfied that the building, viewed merely as a public elementary
school, does not, in its present state, provide the up-to-date teaching facilities
which should be expected in a publiclyowned school, and the greater part of the
expenditure now proposed will merely
bring the building into closer conformity
with the standards of present-day
school design. The only special expenditure on the building over and above this
will be the equipping of the existing large
schoolroom, so as to enable students to
observe teaching demonstrations taking
place therein. The expenditure which it
is anticipated will be incurred during
1934-35, namely, £2,000, is recoverable
from Capital Fund No. 2.
The cottage occupied by the caretaker
at the Veterinary Research Division,
Stormont, is in such a dilapidated condition that it would be uneconomical to
carry out any further repairs to the building. There is, therefore, no alternative
but to erect a new cottage on a site in the
garden adjoining the present cottage, and
a provision of £360 has been provided to
meet the cost of the work, which will be
carried out during 1934-35.
Turning to the other sub-heads of the
Vote, I will first take together Sub-heads
B, C and D, which cover general maintenance expenses. There is an increase of
£4,952 in the total of these sub-heads.
The increase of £2,227 under Sub-head B
is made up of £700 in respect of the
Houses of Parliament and Administrative
Offices at Stormont, due partly to
internal repairs and re-decorative works
which it is essential to carry out during
the present financial year, at an estimated
cost of £350, and partly to an increase in
the general provision for maintenance to
cover additional maintenance services
which may arise during the year; £1,000
in respect of Administration Offices at
Belfast, partly for anticipated expenditure amounting to £600 on the provision of
additional plan-presses for the Ordnance
Survey Office, and partly for the maintenance and renewal of furniture and fittings
in the departmental portion of the new
Law Courts; and £400 in respect of
equipment for drainage works. The
increase of £2,000 odd under Sub-head C
is due mainly to the increase in the rates
in Belfast, and that of approximately
£550 under Sub-head D chiefly to the
rise as a result of increased taxation in
the cost of oil fuel used in the Administrative Buildings, offset, to a certain
extent, by savings in other directions.
I now come to Sub-head E-Lower
Bann Navigation: This year's figures
include provision for the completion of the
dredging work which is being carried out
on the Lower Bann. I may say that this
is in connection with navigation only. It
is anticipated that the dredging craft will
be engaged on this work for a period of
approximately five months in 1934-35.

Owing to unforeseen difficulties, it was
not found possible to commence the reconstruction of the four swivel bridges at
Toome, Portglenone, Kilrea and Agivey,
and provision for the execution of this
work has accordingly been included in the
figures for the current financial year.
The under-pinning of the Agivey
Bridge could not be carried out last year,
as this would have necessitated the closing
of the navigation under the bridge for a
lengthy period, and would have interfered with the passage of the contractors'
craft engaged on Bann drainage works.
Provision of £1,600 has, therefore, been
included in this year's Estimate as a revote.
The only other sub-head which, I think,
calls for comment is Sub-head F, covering
drainage schemes. This sub-head, which
shows a reduction of £2,835, is, of course,
related chiefly to the Bann Drainage
Scheme. The abnormally dry weather
conditions experienced during the past
twelve months have, on the whole, been
favourable to the progress of the scheme,
although dredging operations were
hampered for a time owing to lack of
navigation water in the lower reaches of
the Bann. On the other hand, the low
level of the river was exceptionally
favourable to rock excavation. The level
of Lough Neagh fell to statutory summer
level in March, 1933, and remained at or
below that level until 31st December. In
the early weeks of January this year, the
Lough rose somewhat, but summer level
was again reached at the end of February.
The item of £860 provided under this
sub-head for the control of lake levels and
flood-gates at Belleek represents the costs,
including the salary of an engineer, of
experimenting with the sluices, which are
in the charge of the Ministry's engineers,
for an experimental period of two years.
from January last.
The Exchequer contribution for the
Quoile River Drainage Scheme, namely,

Finance, the Down County Council, and
Downpatrick Urban District Council, as
confirmed by the Drainage Act (Northern
Ireland), 1933, and arises owing to the
revised estimate of the cost of the scheme
being in excess of the original estimate
of £11,000. Any excess over this figure
falls on the Exchequer. The appropriaall selftions-in-aid are, I think,

a week-making a sum of £222. I do not

these grounds at all. These men have to
look after acres and acres of land, and no
citizen of Ulster can get next or near the
grounds. In view of the handsome salary
the Prime Minister gets he should be able
to pay these two gardeners out of his own
pocket. Take the case of any civil
servant, or take the case of the Minister
of Labour. He has to pay his own
gardeners. Year after year thousands of
pounds are being spent on Stormont
Castle estate. I would not mind that so
much if the house was used to full advantage by the Prime Minister, but for

this huge upkeep for a residence for the

an old building, an old castle. There are

There is one important matter which
deserves very careful consideration. That
is the question of the Government purchasing at a cost of £16,000 land for the
extension of the prison on the Crumlin
Road. I think that was the Bruce
Estate. I consider that that policy is
wrong. In the first place it is not a suitable place for a prison. It could be very
usefully utilised as a housing site. The
proper system would be to do as other
countries are doing, and that is to take
their prisoners out into the country,
where better use can be made of their
services. To construct an addition to the
Crumlin Road Prison practically on the
verge of the Antrim Road and the
Cliftonville Road is an outrage. I do not
know who advised the right hon. Gentleman to purchase this land for the purpose
of housing prisoners, when the proper
thing was to have gone out into the
country, where he could have got a site
as large as the estate he has now purchased at about one quarter of the price.
It would have been far better not only for
the people in the vicinity of the prison
but in the interests of the prisoners themselves.
The right hon. Gentleman's Estimates

Is per hour, but the right hon. Gentleman

The PRIME MINISTER: The hon.
Member suffers under a misapprehension.
The positions to which he has referred
are positions attached to this House.
The Serjeant-at-Arms and Black Rod
are the servants of the House. They
are not Government appointments in the
sense of civil servants. The procedure
on the other side has always been that
the Serjeant-at-Arms and Black Rod are
positions which are given as rewards, to
a certain extent, to distinguished men.
In both cases they are filled in this
House by ex-Service men who have to
my own certain knowledge fully earned
the positions which they now hold.
With regard to pensions, I should point
out that pensions are matters entirely
for the War Office and should not be
taken into account by this House in
fixing salaries, because those pensions.
were earned in a different capacity. We
never inquire into what private means or
what pensions people may have when they
are appointed. I must say that from the
beginning these two gallant gentlemen
have filled their posts with credit in this
House, and it must not for a moment be
taken because when this House is

the hon. Member referred in rather

the context, it is perfectly in order.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I am approaching
this matter from the point of view of the
office and the size of our territory.
Northern Ireland is less than the size of
Yorkshire, and from an economic point
of view, these governmental problems
ought to be considered from the point of
view of the size of territory and population. To have modelled the Parliament
of Northern Ireland on the conception
of the Imperial Parliament, and to have
standards of salary and scales of
hospitality on the basis of the Imperial
Parliament is a luxury which the people
of Northern Ireland cannot afford.
At
this juncture I might say, lest some
economist would get up afterwards and
remind me, that I am under no misapprehension as to what any economies that
might accrue on a Vote like this would
mean to the people of Northern Ireland.
I know that if you wiped out these
salaries altogether it would not solve the
economic problems of Northern Ireland.
They did not come into existence because
of these high salaries, and they will not
be remedied by their reduction or abolition. But I want to put this point of
view; that, after all, the psychology of
our people, and their spiritual contentbe apment or unrest, whichever may
parent at the moment, must be considered
from the point of view of economics, and to
have such a condition of things in Northern
Ireland where the Prime Minister, either
the present Prime Minister or some other
Prime Minister, presides over the
political and administrative destinies of
1,250,000 people with an insurable population of 270,000, is altogether too
absurd.
If there were not other elements in the
political life of Northern Ireland this
condition of things would not be
tolerated for another year.
The back
benchers on the Government side of the
House may delude themselves into the belief that the rank and file of the workers
in their constituencies agree with these
things and their continuance, but they
can take it from me that they do not.
There is grave discontent, and if it were
not for the bogies the back benchers so
successfully resurrect at election and
other times these economic questions
would get the consideration they deserve
and do not get at the present time.
Leaving aside all that I have said with
regard to what can be done by a reduction or abolition of salaries, my opinion
is that the economic amount which should
be paid in Northern Ireland to the Prime
Minister is £2,000 a year, and the maximum amount that should be paid to any
Cabinet Minister is £1,000 a year.

BELFAST CITY MAGISTRACY.
1. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can furnish
particulars of the attendance of Justices of
the Peace, other than Resident Magistrates, at the sittings of the Belfast
Petty Sessions Courts during the year
1933.
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): In
the unavoidable absence of my right
hon. Friend I have been asked to answer
this and the other two questions. During
the year 1933, out of a total of some
181 magistrates, 119, or almost twothirds of the total, did not attend any
of the 311 sittings of the Courts.
29 attended less than 5 times.
10 attended more than 5 and less than
10 times.
8 attended more than 10 and less than
25 times; and only 15, or less than 10
per cent., attended more than 25 times.
Mr. GRANT: I would like to ask

2. Mr. MCCARROLL asked the

state the number of Justices of the Peace
who held the commission at the time

the number who have died or resigned
in the same period.
Mr. HANNA: At the date of the
transfer of services in connection with
the administration of Justice, there were
1,544 Justices of the Peace exercising
jurisdiction in Northern Ireland.
Since that date, 690 appointments to
the Commission have been made, and
768 magistrates have died, resigned, or
have been removed or have otherwise
vacated office.
The present number of Justices of the
Peace in Northern Ireland is 1,466.

The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): The object
of this new Clause 7 which has been
inserted in another place is to extend
the powers which have already been given
to the Ministry of Agriculture under
Section 14 of the Agricultural Marketing Act, 1933. Under that Section the
Ministry of Agriculture is enabled to
make regulations for regulating the
removal from Northern Ireland to Great
Britain of
of any agricultural product
which is the subject of a marketing
scheme either in Northern Ireland or in
Great Britain.
It is in the exercise of these powers
that the Ministry has recently restricted
the quantity of pigs removed from
Northern Ireland to Great Britain so as
to prevent the supplies of pigs available
for curers in Northern Ireland being
unduly depleted by large exports of live
pigs to Great Britain.
Similarly, it was by virtue of this
Section that the Ministry was able some
months ago to enter into an agreement
with the provisional Potato Marketing
Board for Great Britain to the effect
that Northern Ireland would, under
certain conditions, accept a quota of
200,000 tons as representing the Northern Ireland quota of potatoes shipped
from Northern Ireland to Great Britain.
This latter quantity was, I may mention,
1419 Agricultural Marketing Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Senate's Amendments
[Sir Basil Brooke]
very substantially in excess of any shipments of potatoes to Great Britain in
recent years.
It has been found, however, that
Clause 14, of the Agricultural Marketing
Act, 1933, is defective in one important
respect. It does not enable the Ministry to make any charge in respect of
registration under the Section. From
an administrative point of view this is
clearly an undesirable omission. The
Ministry is placed in the position that
it must either register every person who
comes forward and seeks registration as
a shipper of agricultural produce to
Great Britain or else it must arbitrarily
decide as to who shall, or shall not, be
registered.
This House will agree that it is far
better that this matter should be decided
automatically by the imposition of a
registration fee, which will ensure that
unsuitable persons do not seek to register
as exporters of agricultural produce and
upset the market by occasionally shipping
small quantities or by undercutting
prices. It is essential, if we are to keep
faith with the marketing boards which
are being set up in Great Britain, that
our export trade in agricultural produce
should be well organised. The object of
these marketing schemes in Great
Britain is to secure a higher price for
the produce there. It would be fatal if
Northern Ireland produce were allowed
to be exported to Great Britain and used
to undercut prices there.
The new Clause will enable the
Ministry of Agriculture to secure the
payment of fees by registered dealers as
follows:-Either (a) an annual fee which
will not exceed £10; or (b) a fee not
exceeding 3 per cent. of the value of
the regulated product removed by the
registered dealer to Great Britain; or
(c) both an annual charge not exceeding
£10 and a fee not exceeding 3 per cent.
of the value of the regulated product
removed by the registered dealer to
Great Britain.
The figures mentioned in the Clause
are maximum figures, and normally it
will not be necessary to charge large fees
for registration. It will be appreciated,
however, that since the Clause may cover
a wide range of agricultural produce
varying appreciably in value, a certain
margin for the variation of the fee must
be allowed in the Bill. I may also
point out to the House that the essential
object of this Clause is to simplify, as
far as our producers are concerned, cooperation with marketing boards
Great Britain. It will enable us to
regulate the quantity of our produce
shipped to Great Britain, and thus to
co-operate with whatever marketing
schemes are framed there.
It may be necessary to secure that this
produce is graded according to the
standards which have been adopted in
Great Britain, and also a certain expenditure may be incurred in connection
with the distribution of market intelligence. The proceeds from the fees will
cover these expenses, and this Clause,
taken in conjunction with Section 14 of
the Agricultural Marketing Act, 1933,
will enable us to give the fullest cooperation with marketing boards in
Great Britain without imposing on our
producers the restrictive regulations and
levies
somewhat heavy
which are
operative on producers under the marketing schemes in Great Britain. I beg to
move, "That the House do agree with
the Senate in the said Amendment."

In rising to move the Motion which
stands in my name I wish to remind the
House that it is now more than four years
since the question of fair rents was raised
in this House. I myself have asked
about six questions on this matter, and
the reason is that I come across many of
the people who have been suffering so
severely from these high rents. I am
glad to say that the Act of 1932 brought
very great relief to some tenants.
It put
an end to the system known as the hirepurchase system. Many tenants at that
time had suffered very grievous losses
owing to that hire-purchase system. But
what I wish to deal with to-day are those
houses between £8 and £26 valuation
which have become decontrolled when
they have come into the possession of the
landlord or agent under the 1925 Act. I
am sorry that those houses were not
brought back under control, because from
that time until now very large rents have
been charged for them and the people are
suffering very severely. The tenants of
these two classes of houses have a special
claim on the sympathy of this House, and
if the Government cannot see their way to
amend the 1932 Act they should at least
establish a fair rents court to which
oppressed tenants could have resort, just
as oppressed workers can get a court of
arbitration to settle disputes regarding
fair wages and conditions of employment.
In the case of tenants of houses of £26
valuation and under there is no protection
the
whatever against the rent being raised as
high and as often as the owner chooses,
and the owner may distrain on
tenant's furniture as is done by one agent
weekly in subsidy houses without the consent of any Court as there is no law to
stop him. I want to give the House an
instance. In a case which came before the
Recorder three months
ago the particulars made known were that the house,
in Parkmount Street, became vacant in
1927. The owner made the tenant pay
him £10 key money, and gave him a
receipt for the money, as for key and contents. The tenant's case was that the
house was not legally let, and though the
owner admitted taking the money as key
money, the case was dismissed. Had the
owner done the same in the case of his
controlled house next door, he would have
been liable to a penalty of £100, or six
months' imprisonment.
The report of the Select Committee
stated that the rents of houses becoming

If there is sympathy for the widow owner

"Mr. Byrne: What is your opinion.

Mr. McConnell: I would be in

born and reared in the country in
County Antrim, and I am very fond of
my own county. I remember when I
was a young lad, in 1881 and 1883, the
tenants were very hard pushed, and
under the Gladstone administration a
fair rents court was set up. That was
the salvation of the farmers. They got
a fair rent fixed by having a valuer
from each side who went into the question of the value of the land and
buildings and the amount of money
invested in the property. As a result
a just rent was fixed, and that saved
the farmers of that day."
I know I will have the support of hon.
Members on the opposite side of the
House. Many of them, like myself,
remember the great land agitation when
we had unfair and unjust landlords in
this country, and I am sure they will give
credit for the great work which the Irish
Parliamentary Party did in those days
for the tenant farmers of Ireland. I am
one of those who belonged to that Party.
I have been a supporter of the Irish
Parliamentary Party all my life. They
continued their agitation under the
leadership of Davitt, Redmond, Dillon,
and other great men, and I think it is
largely due to that Party that the tenant
farmers of Ireland are to-day the owners
of their land, that they have no landlords, and no rack rents.
I could occupy a long time with the

the

That Resolution was carried on a Division.
For the Resolution were:-Mr. Beattie,
Mr. Byrne, Mr. Collins, Rev. Professor
Corkey, Mr. Grant, Major Hall-Thompson, Mr. Minford, and Mr. M'Carroll.
Against the Resolution were:-Mr. Davison, Lieut.-Colonel Gordon, Major
Blakiston-Houston, and Mr. Murphy. I
think my proposal to-day is a very reasonable one. I could quote you many
instances of hardship from this Report,
cases in which 100 per cent. was added to
the amount of the rent. I may say that a
