their rents. When a man with a wife
Fair Rents Court
Fair Rents Court
8 MAY 1934
and family starts a business the rent is
sometimes doubled on the expiration of his
lease, and if the tenant does not wish to
pay he is ordered out.
In the case of licensed premises, the
necessity for a fair-rent tribunal will be
evident from a few actual cases that have
arisen on the expiration of leases. The
hardship is greater in the case of licensed
houses, because the tenant cannot carry
his business away, but must leave it
behind in the landlord's hands, if he cannot buy it back on the landlord's terms.
John Murray, Peter's Hill, was leaseholder of his public-house and a shop next
door at £122 10s rent. On expiration of
the lease he offered £100 rent for the
public-house alone, which the landlord
would not entertain, and he was forced to
leave. D. J. Bowen, Grosvenor Road,
obtained in 1917 licensed premises on
Grosvenor Road, for the residue of a
lease made for 20 years, at £70 rent.
On expiration of the lease, the owners
demanded £200 rent, subsequently they
reduced the demand to £175, and finally
an agreement was reached at £150, an
increase of about 115 per cent.
I think I have fully convinced the
House that these are very sad cases, and
that they require attention. I do not see
any better way of enabling them to have
their grievances remedied than to set up a
fair rent court. We all have confidence
in the courts of law and, while it may be
said that this course would involve a good
deal of time and expense, I do not think
it would take too much of either. When
a few cases had been decided the other
would agree to the reductions, and fair
rents would be fixed, just as was done
under the Land Acts. Under the Land
Acts the half of the cases did not go before
the courts. The landlords and
tenants found out the reductions that
were being made, and 25 or 30 per cent.
was allowed off. That saved time and
expense.
the
I should also like to draw the attention
of the House to the fact that some of us
have been hoping for the introduction of
a Landlord and Tenant Bill in this Parliament, but somehow or other there has
been great delay, and again people are
suffering serious grievances. In 1927 the
Imperial Parliament passed an Act which
granted power to the county courts of
England and Wales, as follows:--
1. To award compensation to a tenant
in respect of any improvement on his holding which adds to the letting value of the
holding.
2. If the lease is renewed the court can
fix the rent payable by the tenant,
irrespective of the value attributable to
the improvement in respect of which compensation would have been payable.
3. If the tenant proves that by reason
of the carrying on of a trade or business
for a period of not less than 5 years, goodwill has become attached to the premises
whereby the premises could be let at a
higher rent than they would in the
absence of such goodwill, he may be
awarded compensation for such goodwill.
4. The court may grant a new lease for
a term not exceeding 14 years where the
tenant alleges that the amount of compensation which could be alloted to him
under the Act would not compensate him
for the loss of goodwill he would suffer
if he is compelled to remove to other
premises.
5. In certain well defined circumstances
the landlord may be given possession of
the premises, notwithstanding the proved
claims of the tenant.
This Act became law on 22nd December,
1927, or over six years ago, and during
that period tenants in Northern Ireland
have been at the mercy of their landlords, although English tenants were protected. Many cases are well-known where
the terms for new leases could only be
described as harsh, and also cases where
the goodwill created by the tenant has
been used as a lever to extort an increased
rent.
There has been other legislation on this
matter. In 1931 a Landlord and Tenant
Act was passed in the Irish Free State
even more far-reaching than the English
Act. It provides that improvements were
to be paid for by the landlord. It enacts
that, on the termination of his tenancy, the
tenant shall, subject to certain reasonable
restrictions, be entitled to a new tenancy
on terms to be agreed on between him and
the landlord, or in default of such agreement, on terms to be fixed by the court.
Where the landlord requires the premises
for re-building or estate scheming, the
tenant is entitled to compensation for
disturbance.
Notwithstanding the example shown by
the two neighbouring Governments, the

Mr. BLACK A Motion of this sort
naturally analyses itself into two proposals first, the suggestion that certain
difficulties and certain hardships exist and,
second, that the method proposed by the
Motion is the proper method to deal with
such difficulties and hardships. The
speeches of practically every hon. Member who has addressed the House in
support of the Motion have been almost
entirely devoted to what I would call the
first element in the analysis of the Motion,
and nine-tenths of the time taken up by
hon. Members in addressing the House
have been devoted to pointing out the
difficulties which have arisen in regard to
housing and hardships which have been
caused to tenants within the last twenty
years. But very little of their speeches
has been devoted to what I think is the
crucial part of this Motion, that is, the
attempt to establish that the proposed
fair rent court would be the proper and
the best method of dealing with these
hardships.
The hardships of which hon. Members
have spoken are obvious; they are known
to everybody. They arose because of the
lack of housing due to the war, they arose
largely during the war and the boom
period immediately after the war, and of
course the result was what one would
expect. Very early in the war period, as
early as 1915, it was observed that owing
to the shortage of houses the landlords
were increasing rents unduly, and increasing them to amounts which tenants found
it hard to pay, and which it would not be
fair or just to expect tenants to bear. It
was necessary to deal with the matter,
and as early as 1915 the Legislature
attempted to deal with it by passing the
first of the Rent Restriction Acts. Now
that Act was probably the only way in
which the matter could be dealt with at
that juncture. The ideal way of dealing
with the lack of houses, of course, is to
get more houses built, but it was obvious
during the war period that the energies of
the nation could not be diverted to the
building of houses.
After the war period there was a great
leeway to make up, and it was recognised
that we could not hope, within a reasonably short time, to have a sufficiency of
houses. Accordingly, it became necessary
to continue the fixing of rents which had
come into operation during the war.
Broadly speaking, I think the Rent
Restriction Acts have operated reasonably
well. There is a great deal in them that
can be criticised. In some ways they
were not very well drafted at the beginning, and in the course of their administration in the courts it was observed that
there were a great number of anomalies
and hardships. If anyone started now
to draft a new code it might be possible to
draft a good deal better code, but taking
them by and large the Rent Restriction
Acts have worked reasonably well and
have given reasonable protection for the
classes which they were designed to
protect.

that

It was,
of course, said by the Attorney-General

rent would be is the fair value fixed in

has the house to let and the man who
wants to take it. That is obviously
what is not wanted here. The whole
difficulty is that the law of supply and
demand in its operations enables a landlord to charge whatever rent he likes so
long as there is a shortage of small houses,
which there continues to be up to the
present. If you leave it to the law of
supply and demand in order to get the
fair value which the tenant would give
in the open market, you get a rent which
is far in excess of any of the rents
charged now. If the criterion is not to
be what you get in the open market,
what is it to be?
It was suggested by another speaker-I
take it that it was a suggestion that the
fair rent should be based in some way
on the amount of money invested in the
building of the house. Take a man that
builds a house to-day for £250 or £300
or £400. I am dealing with the small
houses. He goes to the court and gets a
fair rent fixed on that sum. But then
you have the case of the man who built
a house in 1920 or 1921 and had to
expend twice as much on that house
which was in every way superior to the
house built by the man to-day. Would
not this man have a real and genuine
cause of complaint if the person with the
inferior house is to be allowed by the

amount allowed to be charged by him
for his superior house? That must be
the result if you are going to base your

the house. Then it is suggested that the
fair rent might be based on the cost of
investment in the house. Again, is the
man who made a good investment, and
a fortunate one, and made with foresight, to be penalised and allowed to get
a smaller return because some other
person goes to a much higher price to
get his house?

With regard to the smaller houses, we

longer period, unless some miracle

The local authority have built houses of

is not purely that, but it is very largely

twenty years.
As I say, the one way to deal with it

builder. The only way I can see is the
way adopted by the Government and the
local authority-to give subsidies which
will encourage the building of houses.
One thing may be said about the subsidy
houses is that the Government or Legislature has shown itself willing to impose
fetters on the selling of subsidy houses
so that they should not be sold or rented
at an excessive amount. The point of
that is that when the public puts any
money into an enterprise the public is

not advance money and where the private
person builds out of his own pocket, I
think that the State has no right at the

sympathising with the class which have

Motion would not be a remedy, and
instead of doing any good in the way it is
said it would it would only do harm.

I believe that if you set up a fair rent

houses who will be applying for adjustment, but it will also be those many house
owners who consider that the rents they

Restrictions Acts were not getting a fair

practically all the houses that are subject
to the Rent Restrictions Acts would apply
to have the rents adjusted, and the adjustment in practically every case would be
bound to be upwards and not downward,
so that the final result would be that, in
the case of many thousands of houses, not
only in Belfast but throughout the whole
of Northern Ireland, you would find that
house rents would go up. I would be
surprised to find that the hon. Member
for Falls, the hon. Member for Dock, or
any of those who have spoken from the
Therefore, I think we are justified in
coming to the conclusion that if we
interfere with house property at the

MINISTRY OF LABOUR.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) To-day I propose frankly to
state the policy of the Ministry of Labour
in connection with its many branches, and
if I occupy a little longer time than I am
accustomed to do my excuse and justification is that it is the one occasion in the
year when I have an opportunity of referring to some of the activities of the
Department and justifying its large
expenditure. I feel in a very much
happier position to-day than I have done
on several former occasions when asking
hon. Members to approve of the Estimates
of my Department, because on those
occasions to which I have referred we were
passing through a period of industrial
depression, word-wide in its ramifications,
unparalleled in severity, and unequalled
in duration.
A little over a year ago we saw signs
on the horizon of an improvement, and
I am sure we all rejoice that that improvement has developed and has been maintained. Each month since January,
1933, there has been a steady increase in
employment except for seasonal fluctuations at Christmas. The improvement
has been revealed not only in our linen
but
and shipbuilding industries
in
practically every other trade group. In
this House, if I may say so, we are
frequently focussing our minds entirely
on problems of unemployment, and we
fail to look at the other side of the
account to see how many of our people
are, day after day and year after year,
About
engaged in useful employment.
189,000 persons were employed at the end
of April in those industries covered by
the unemployment insurance scheme. If
we add those engaged in the agricultural
industry, et cetera, we find that approximately half a million of our people are
working.
The number registered for employment
has fallen by over 16,000 since January,
1933, and the fall has been specially
marked in February, March, and April
of this year. The aggregate fall during
those months amounted to 7,667 persons.
We are largely dependent for our prosperity and employment on world conditions, and it is gratifying to know that
the return of the International Labour
Office, which is associated with the League
of Nations, shows that there has been an
improvement in every industrial country
with the exception of France, Poland, and
the Irish Free State; and we can only
hope that the improvement will extend to
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
9 MAY 1934
those three countries before long, so that
we may feel that the conditions are
world-wide.
Now, may I venture to say to hon. Members opposite that they should not to-day
say anything of a despondent nature?
They must know, as we on this side of the
Committee know, that prosperity, in fact,
industry, largely rests upon confidence,
and anyone who, in existing conditions,
says anything to damp down that returning confidence, which has become very
general of late, is accepting, in my
opinion, a very grave responsibility. I
therefore ask, if I may, hon. Members
opposite to join with us on this side of the
Committee in rejoicing that there has
been a substantial improvement and in
the hope that that improvement may continue and extend.
As Minister of Labour I have been
frequently criticised during the past few
years from two different points of view.
One body of critics has attacked the
Government for having consistently pursued equality in connection with the four
social services which my Department
administers on the ground that it cannot
be afforded, and the other body of opinion
very vocally maintains that British standards are not good enough for the people
of Northern Ireland, that we ought to
have higher standards here. I am sure
we would all be very glad if that was
possible, but I venture to think that the
policy of preserving equal social standards throughout the United Kingdom has
been reasonable, just, and wise-(Hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-better cannot be
afforded, if the truth is to be told, and
less in the opinion of my colleagues and
myself would be indefensible.
In dealing with the work of my Department to-day I desire to refer to it under
two heads, first, what we are doing in
connection with furthering employment,
and, secondly, our duty to our working
people when unemployed, sick, bereaved,
and aged. As regards employment, we
try to help employers to obtain suitable
workers and we help workers to obtain
suitable employment, and our success in
that respect is to be gauged by the fact
that since this improvement to which I
have referred began the Employment
Exchanges have placed in employment.
33,000 persons. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) In many directions the Government have stimulated employment,
as hon. Members know, but it would
not be in order for me to refer
to-day to what other Departments
have done in this connection. One of the
means which has been taken by the
Ministry of Labour has been to encourage
public bodies and local authorities to
undertake schemes of public utility,
which, without the Government grants,
they would not have been willing to
undertake for several years at any rate.
As examples of the excellent work which
has been done in this connection I may
refer to the Herdman Dock and Pollock
Basin, which were declared open by Her
Royal Highness Princess Alice a few
months ago, and also to the new
Exhibition Hall in connection with the
Royal Ulster Agricultural Society, which
His Majesty has been graciously pleased
to consent shall be called The King's Hall,
and which is to be opened by H.R.H. the
Earl of Ulster in a few weeks time.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Again, many schemes have been
carried out by the local authorities in
Londonderry, the most important being
their great Banagher water scheme,
which has given a vast amount of employment and which has proved to have
been very necessary. Dock improvements have also been carried out. Again,
I would refer to the excellent work that
has been done through these relief schemes
in rebuilding, enlarging, and improving
nearly all our hospitals throughout
Northern Ireland. Many buildings,
which formerly were poor-houses, and
which, I am glad to say, are no longer
required for that purpose, have been
turned into very excellent district hospitals. These schemes, and a great many
other schemes too numerous to mention,
have given a vast amount of employment,
and, in addition, have added to the
capital assets of our country, and will,
I feel confident, confer perennial benefit
not only upon this generation but upon
succeeding generations.
The Ministry's work in smoothing out
the differences that inevitably arise in
adjusting wage relationships between employers and employees has, I think I can
claim, been of rather an important
nature. I am glad to think that, except in
one instance, no strike of importance has
occurred in Northern Ireland for a great
many years. This is largely due to the
evident desire of employers and em-
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
ployees to accommodate each other and
also to the help that the Ministry have
been able to give, in certain cases.
There is another matter in this connection to which I would like to refer.
Since our Trade Boards Act was passed
in 1923, Trade Boards, as hon. Members
opposite know, have become much more
popular than they were in our midst.
There are now eighteen Trade Boards,
covering 3,000 establishments and 50,000
workers, and they are looked upon now
both by employers and employees as a
means of maintaining industrial peace,
preventing unfair competition where competition is largely local, and of preventing
unfair wage cutting. The inspection work
in connection with this branch of the Department's activities requires to be considerable, but I am glad to be able to
say that the employers very generally
conform willingly to the statutory rates.
that are fixed; on occasions where it is
found that employers are not conforming,
then the Ministry insists on the workers
who have been deprived of what they
should have received being recouped, and
last year payments in this connection
were made to the extent of £750.
Our Factory Code is rather a complicated one. It covers twenty Acts of Parliament, some dating back for 100 years.
Everyone recognises how necessary it is
that employment should be made as safe
and as healthy as possible, and everyone.
also recognises the benefit of well-lighted,
suitably heated, and ventilated workrooms and factories. I feel that the provision of efficient dust removing exhaust and inlet ventilation in our textile
factories is essential, and in recent
years employers in Northern Ireland have
spent large sums in order to bring their
factories up to a reasonable standard in
this connection. Many, I am glad to be
able to say further, have gone beyond
what I may call the statutory measured
mile and have willingly embarked upon
schemes of even greater benefit.
There have been too many accidents of
late in our mills, factories, and workshops, and I regret to say accidents have
been increasing. There were eleven fatal
accidents in 1932 and twenty in 1933;
in 1932 there were 216 non-fatal accidents
sufficiently serious to require investigation, while in 1933, the year with which
I am dealing, there were 343 non-fatal
conaccidents. From the human point of view
this is a very sad story, and it is also
very expensive because employers are
paying at the present time no less a sum
than £1,000 per week in the form of
compensation. The vast majority of
these accidents have not been the result
of the machinery being insufficiently
guarded. They have simply been the
result of what I may call a psychological
circumstance. Persons who are
tinually working in the neighbourhood
of machinery which may be dangerous if
improperly used become somewhat
accustomed to it, and, therefore, take
risks and possibly become somewhat careless, and before they know an accident
occurs. I think some educational work is
necessary in this connection, as I am
sure it is the wish of every Member of
the Committee that everything possible
should be done to prevent the continuation of these accidents to the degree to
which they have taken place during the
year under review.
In Northern Ireland at the moment we
have still, I regret to say, 60,472 persons
unemployed-far too many if it could be.
avoided. It is the lowest figure, however, since 1932, and that is something
to be thankful for. It has to be understood that these figures do not represent
a solid body of people permanently unemployed. Approximately 15,900 have
been out of work for less than three
months, whilst 6,780 of the total are
those who are temporarily stopped or who
follow only casual employment. I am
correct in saying that, while it is only
too true that some people have been
unemployed perhaps for years, speaking
generally, we turn over our unemployed
three times in the year.
Some years ago it was recognised that
young people in particular should have
the advantage of instruction whilst
unemployed and drawing benefit. Twelve
thousand young people have been
admitted to our Juvenile Training
Centre. These young people, as some
hon. Members no doubt know, are given
what may be called a continuation
education; the girls are taught domestic
science, cooking, needle work, laundry
work, and the care of children, while the
young men are taught handicraft, physics,
and other very desirable subjects. I would
like in passing to pay a tribute to Mr.
Williams, chairman of the juvenile
Training Centre, and his committee for
Ministry of Labour 1474
Estimates-
9 MAY 1934
the splendid work they have done in
having this Centre established and carried
on. Outside Belfast tuition has been
provided in similar subjects during the
past year with the co-operation of
education authorities
at twenty-three
different centres, and 117 classes have
been held.
Our local employment committees continue to give great help to the Department in many directions. I especially
desire to compliment, if I may, the
Carrickfergus Committee, the Newtownards Committee, and the Lurgan Committee on the work which they have done
in establishing occupational and recreational schemes for the unemployed in
their districts.
Our Health Insurance scheme works
along smoothly and satisfactorily. Our
policy from the very beginning has
been to keep linked up inseparably with
the British Health Insurance scheme.
We have a reciprocity arrangement with
Great Britain. We are represented on
the Joint Committee. We receive
advantages from the central fund. The
scheme is worked in Northern Ireland
by nineteen approved societies with their
headquarters here and by fifty-six
approved societies with their headquarters
in Great Britain, and cash payments and
additional medical benefits have been
paid to our sick and insured persons to
the extent of the large sum of half a
million during the past year.
We are
budgeting for the same figure this year.
I wish to say just a few words in connection with our medical benefits scheme.
Hon. Members will recollect that when
this scheme was talked about there was a
great deal of criticism. We were told it
would not be worth the money it would
cost. We were told it had not been
entirely satisfactory in Great Britain. We
were told that there was no great demand
for it. I am glad to say to-day that it
has worked here quite satisfactorily from
the very beginning, and that it is appreciated, not only by the workers who benefit,
but, I think, by our whole community,
with the exception of a few-a very few—
who object to paying their contributions.
The scheme is worked by 489 doctors,
and I appreciate more than I can say the
way they have co-operated with my
Department in this connection. The
scheme covers 370,000 persons, or one,
third of our total population, and this I
can say to be a fact beyond doubt that
our doctors do not discriminate in the
least as between their panel patients and
those whom they treat as private patients.
I have not heard during the whole of the
year of a single complaint from an insured
person as regards the scheme not working
satisfactorily or as to patients not
receiving from their panel doctors the
attention to which they are entitled.
On previous occasions the Parliamentary Secetary and I have referred to
our pension schemes at considerable
length, and I do not intend to do more
to-day than mention them. It will
interest the Committee, however, to know
that there are now 15,368 widows
receiving pensions, 629 more than during
the year previous; that there are 536
orphans obtaining pensions, 14 more than
in the year previous, that we have now
31,900 pensioners under our contributory
scheme at 65, and that that number is
2,293 more than in the year previous.
Under our non-contributory scheme we
have 36,088 pensioners, and the total
number of those who are receiving weekly
pensions in Northern Ireland amounts to
83,892, certainly, I think, a goodly
number. As an example of the immense
amount of work which has to be done in
this connection, I may mention that
10,000 claims for pensions were received
last year, all of which had to be investigated.
I would point to another part of the
Ministry's activities, and that is the
collection of contributions from employers
and employed, the income from which this
year will amount to one million and threequarters. I am very glad to say that
there is really very little non-compliance
now-there was a good deal some years
ago and that where non-compliance is
discovered my Department does not
hesitate to prosecute the wrongdoers and
bring them to justice.
If hon. Members will now turn to
the summary table on page 85 of the Book
of Estimates they will see that the total
Estimate of the Department amounts to
£3,616,044, showing a decrease on the
previous year of £477,179. Under all
heads, except contributory pensions, there
is a decrease, the most important being in
respect of unemployment insurance. Last
year unemployment turned out to be at
the rate of 25.7 per cent. It has now

I happened just a few days ago to be
reading one of John Stuart Mill's works,
the Principles of Political Economy, and
I wrote out a short sentence which I
thought might illuminate a speech on
these Estimates if I felt inclined to make
one. He wrote his Principles of Political
Economy about the year 1850, and he
says it is a very remarkable statement-
"Hitherto it is questionable if all
the mechanical inventions yet made
have lightened the day's toil of any
human being. They had enabled a
greater population to live the same life
of drudgery and imprisonment, and
they have enabled an increased number of manufacturers and others to
make fortunes. They have increased
the comforts of the middle classes, but
they have not yet begun to effect those
great changes in human destiny which
it is in their nature and in their
futurity to accomplish."
That is a very striking sentence, and
that sentence was actually true at the

The rules by which the distribution

The rules by which the distribution

I am of opinion, having surveyed the

attaching to the courts of referees, that
this is a branch of the Ministry's activity
which is open to abuse and which can be
utilised on the basis of political patronage.
I say that advisedly. I say that because

accepted without question within the
ambit of their profession, men whose

have good public standing, and they were
never invited by the Minister to participate in the administration of the courts
of referees. On the other hand, I come
across lawyers who, if they had to exist
by having successful cases at the courts
would starve to death, and these people

. I agree there should be the best

quently of late the practice has been

There is another point, and that is the
question of reciprocity in regard to men
who leave this area and go to work in
the Free State. While on this point I
should like to say that there is no truth

Free State are losing their right to insurance and all the benefits they would
get if they remained here. I know a
case of a widow whose husband had a
very good insurance record. He was insured from 1912 until 1927, and he went
to work in Cork. He remained in Cork
so long that he was deprived of the right
of insurance in Northern Ireland. Then
he returned to the North and was insured
for a short period when he died. Now
the poor widow, notwithstanding the fact.
that her husband had such an excellent
insurance record, is deprived of a pension. That is one example of how men
who have left this area and taken work
in the Free State have been penalised.
I am not referring to a person of my own
particular political faith, because he did
not belong to my side at all.

I think it is a great hardship to deprive people of a pension under those

Mr. GORDON: When the Minister

One or two points have been raised by

He proceeded to discuss some of the

that branch of the work did not justify

speaking in this House he is not speaking

I know I am not speaking to the narrow

I wish to point out that during the last
twelve months we had 1,124 inspections
of the several firms connected with the
trade boards, and if we found any firm
evading its responsibility in the paying of
the proper trade board rate of wages we
took action, and as the Minister has said
we were able during the past twelve,
months to get the workers recouped in
wages to the extent of almost £800 that
had not been paid. Firms who had not
complied with the trade board rate we
compelled by the action we took to pay
the proper trade board rate of wages.
Another point raised by the hon. Member was with reference to the panel
system. He said there should be a fairer
apportionment on the panel. He referred
to the number of doctors, and in making
a calculation showed that the insured persons averaged 700 on a panel. Every
panel is not the same. Every insured
person has the right to select his own
doctor, and we have no right to make an
apportionment of any doctor's panel. It
is for each insured person to make his own
choice, and if he is not satisfied with a
doctor he need not select him. The doctor
is in a similar position. If he is
not satisfied with a panel patient he has
the right to say,
No, I do not desire
you for a panel patient, you may go
elsewhere." Consequently, we have no
right to say to any insured person that
he must go to a particular doctor in order
to receive medical treatment. Every
insured person receives treatment from
the doctor he desires should attend him.

I think the only charge levelled to-day
by any speaker was levelled by the hon.
Member for Dock against our referees.
He was of the opinion that all the referees
had been appointed from a political
standpoint. I must repudiate that with
all the power and force I am possessed of.
I know of no man who has been appointed
from a political standpoint. Every man
has been appointed by virtue of his
ability to adjudicate and of the necessity
of being required to act as chairman of a
court of referees.
The hon. and gallant Member for East

I have read of those areas referred to on

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gordon]
the other side as derelict areas. He refers
to them as pocket areas. He referred to
the fact that there are certain little
pockets where there has been a once
prosperous industry, which has fallen on
depressing times and consequently the
people in that area are out of employment. He wants to know what can be
done or what has been done for the people
of that particular area. He referred to
a mill at Shrigley that had closed down.
That mill closed down some few years
ago, and while that industry has been
closed down the only method that was at
the disposal of the Government was to try
if possible to influence the local
authorities to bring into being some
public works of utility, with a view to
giving employment to those men in the
distressed area. We have got the local
authorities to bring in a scheme known
as the Killyleagh water supply scheme,
which at the moment is giving employment to sixteen men. There is another
scheme under consideration, and we hope
that it will be brought into operation at
an early date, that is likely to give
employment to fifty men over a period of
thirty-five weeks. Then, of course, there is
what is known as the Quoile River drainage scheme.
This scheme is being carried
out by the Ministry of Finance, and is
giving employment at the present moment
to thirty-eight men. Then the Down
County Council are carrying out the
Blackwater River drainage scheme, and
at the moment forty-eight men are being
employed on that work. So that in that
particular area there are 113 men
receiving employment through relief
schemes, and we expect that in a very
short time there will be about 120 men
employed on schemes of a similar
character.
It is difficult to say, but I think the
note of optimism struck by the Minister
at the beginning of his speech, and
maintained by the hon. Gentlemen who
have addressed the Committee, has
indicated that the trend of trade is
upward, and we are hoping that better
times and better conditions will soon
arrive in the particular locality referred.
to. When there is a depressing time in

rather more than other parts of the
country.

PEDIGREE FLAX SEED SUPPLY.
1. Mr. FRYAR (for Dr. Wilson) asked
the Minister of Agriculture whether he
will take steps to ensure that flax growers
in Northern Ireland will have at their
disposal next year an adequate supply of
pedigree flax seed at a reasonable price.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The question which the hon. Member
raises has already been under consideration, and steps have been taken which
will, it is hoped, lead to increased
supplies of pedigree flax seed for our
growers being available from Canada next
year at more reasonable prices.
Mr. HEALY: Is it not the policy of
the Ulster linen merchants to buy
Russian flax?
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: That does
not arise on this question.

10 MAY 1934
Mr. GORDON: As a consequence of
the fall in unemployment, my Department has been obliged to dispense with
the services of a number of temporary
clerks, both men and women. In view
of the Government's policy to give a
predominating preference to ex-Service
men in recruiting its temporary staff, it
inevitably follows that when retrenchments become necessary ex-Service men
must be discharged.
It is true that a few of the men
referred to had been in the Department's
service for a number of years, and no
one regrets more than the Minister and
myself the necessity for discharging them.
No men have been brought into the
Ministry of Labour service within the
past few months and placed on the permanent list.

or more men have been brought into the

who never worked for
for the Ministry
before and are deemed to be permanent
men? If they are not permanent, they
are temporary at the moment, with the
likelihood of being made permanent.
The fact is-

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): In presenting the Estimate for the administrative expenses of
the Ministry of Finance, I would, in the
first instance, remind the Committee that
the Vote includes the cost of administration of several services which are common to all Departments, namely, duplicating and machine figure work, telephone
service, and cleaners.
One change of importance has been
made in the constitution of the Vote.
This is the transfer of the expenses of
the Valuation Division, which in the
Estimates for former years have appeared
in this Vote, to a separate Vote-Class
II, No. 2 of which I shall speak at a
Estimates-
Ministry of Finance
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
later stage. The net increase of £3,151
on the total of the Vote is, of course,
exclusive of the cost of the Valuation
Division as shown in the Estimate for
last year.
Under Salaries, Wages and Allowances
in Sub-head A, it will be seen that there
is only a slight variation as regards
numbers, namely, an increase of four in
the Works Division staff, the increased
cost of which (£1,959) is to a large extent offset by increased receipts for
agency work as a whole. Greater activity
on Agency Services performed on behalf
of the Imperial Government-in the
main in connection with the Telephone
Exchange programme-and for Local
Authorities' Drainage Schemes, has
brought about increased appropriationsin-aid, whereas decreased activity in the
use of the Ministry's architects as agents
for the building of schools is reflected in
the smaller amount shown as a receipt
from Regional Education Committees.
As regards drainage schemes, the bulk
of the sum of £1,600 credited to the Vote
is in respect of the Quoile River Drainage
Scheme, which is being carried out
jointly on behalf of the Down County
Council, the Downpatrick Urban District
Council and the Land Purchase Trustee.
I should like to emphasise that expenditure on the temporary professional
staff is closely watched, and the Ministry is
satisfied that it is not more than sufficient
to cope with the volume of architectural
and engineering work in hand. Under
Sub-head D additional provision has been
made to meet anticipated legal expenses.
in connection with important estate duty
appeals and similar legal work.
The increase shown for the cost of stock
management expenses under Sub-head E
is only an apparent one. As was
explained in connection with the Supplementary Estimate for this Vote in the
year 1933-34, an unforeseen and nonrecurrent saving was made last year with
regard to this item, owing to the first
management fee payable in respect of
the keeping of the register of Ulster 31
per cent. stock not falling due until the
current year.
It will be observed that the cost of
Ulster Savings Certificates administration shown under Sub-head H shows a
slight decrease. This is on page 17. In
this connection I should, perhaps,
explain that the cost shown under the
sub-head only includes the salaries of
such officers as are employed upon this
branch of the work in a whole-time
capacity and expenses directly attributable to this particular service. To arrive
at the total cost of administration, that is
taking into account an apportionment of
the expenses of superannuation, higher
administration and allied services, a
further sum of approximately £1,000
should be added. Let us assume, therefore, a total annual cost of administration of £4,400. During the year 1933-4
493,450 certificates were issued, representing a cash investment of £394,760.
Investments and repayments amounted
to £720,000, and the cost of administration thus works out at only .6 per cent.,
or one penny per sixteen shilling certificate handled.
On page 17 an increase appears under
Sub-head F, for incidental expenses, the
largest single increase being for fees paid
to auctioneers and the like, which are
necessary in connection with casual services rendered to the Works and Legal
Divisions of the Ministry. These
expenses and the £75 for the courier
service were formerly charged against the
first item in the sub-head, and have now
been segregated for greater clearness.
The small increase on page 18, under
Sub-head K1, for the expenses of the
Registrar-General's Office, is almost
entirely due to normal salary increments,
and there is no new factor which calls
for comment. I think, however, that
some remarks as to the work which this
Department is doing will be found to be
of general interest. There has been a
steady improvement in the registration
services since they first began to operate
separately for Northern Ireland, that is
to say, as from 1st January, 1922.
this connection it is, perhaps, not always
realised that for the successful operation
of the systems for the registration of

of all denominations is required, and in

In
During the calendar year 1933 it was
necessary to register, upon special
authority, 104 births and 13 deaths which
had escaped registration for a year or
more (in some cases, many years), but it
is apparent that omissions to register are
now decreasing in number. Certain
Estimates-
Ministry of Finance
10 MAY 1934
improvements in the state of registration
to some extent connote an improvement
in the social conditions of the people of
Northern Ireland. For example, whereas
in 1922 the deaths registered in cases
where there had been no doctor in attendance during the last illness represented
on in eight of the total deaths, in the
year which has just elapsed this proportion had fallen to one in sixteen.
The births registered during 1933
(24,607) were again the lowest on record
and showed a drop of nearly 17 per cent.
from the 1922 figure (29,531).
The
marriages registered (7,644) were the
highest since 1925, and the deaths registered (18,154) during 1933 were somewhat higher than usual, largely owing
to the influenza epidemic during the
early part of the year.
a
There is still a natural increase of
population due to excess of births over
deaths, and now that emigration to the
Colonies and foreign countries has ceased,
it appears that migration is responsible
for a net inward movement. The total
population of Northern Ireland is now
estimated to be 1,280,000 persons,
figure which is in excess of that which
existed at the time the Government of
Northern Ireland was set up. No precise records are available of the movements of population between the various
parts of the British Isles and, in the
circumstances, the difficulties of estimating are considerable. The question as to
whether a further census of population
shall be taken in Northern Ireland may,
therefore, become a matter of importance
at no very distant date.
Re-registration of births under the
Legitimacy Act following the marriage of
the parents after the original registration
of the birth numbered 61 during 1933,
and 72 adoptions, effected under orders
of the courts, were also registered during
the year. Copies of births, deaths and
marriage certificates, issued by
by the
General Register Office during 1933, only
number 205, chiefly owing to the fact
that central office copies of records relating to periods prior to 1922 are still
held in the General Register Office,
Dublin. Many thousands of certificates
were, however, issued by local registration officers in Northern Ireland, who
possess the originals of these records.
Steps will be taken during the current
year with a view to the production of
another issue of the Ulster Year Book in
1935. The sales of the past issues of this
publication suggest that it satisfies a real
need. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Two further items of increased expenditure appear in the Estimate, to which I
should, perhaps, refer. One is shown
under Sub-head I, on page 17, a sum
of £130, representing cost of plates for
a new design of entertainment duty
stamps. Hitherto we have been using
the Imperial stamps overprinted for use
in Northern Ireland. It is thought that
the time has now come when Northern
Ireland should have its own stamp. This
is especially desirable because the rates of
entertainments duty in Northern Ireland
are not the same as those operating in
Great Britain, so that the demand for
stamps of certain denominations varies
considerably in the two countries.
The second item is the somewhat larger
one, amounting to £900, for the cost of
actuarial investigation of the Teachers'
Superannuation Fund, shown under Subhead M on page 18. I should explain
that under the Teachers' Superannuation
Act, 1926, the Ministry is required to
carry out this actuarial investigation at
least once in every five years. The first
such investigation took place in 1928-29,
and the second is now in progress and will
be completed shortly. The work is
carried out by the Government Actuary's
Department of the Imperial Government.
Turning to the appropriations-in-aid,
there is one further item which calls for
comment, apart from those to which I
have already referred. This is the recoupment made from the Government
Loans Fund in respect of staff engaged
on the administration of loans services,
under which there is an increase of £400.
The amount is in the nature of an estimate and it is thought that this year's
figure corresponds sufficiently closely to
the facts.
The receipts and issues of the Government Loans Fund, together with those in
connection with British local loans
collected by the Ministry's staff, now
total nearly two and a half million
pounds per annum, and the cost of
administration in the Ministry thus works
out at less than one-tenth of one per cent.
on the sums handled annually.

These are the only variations in expenditure upon which I desire to remark,
but I feel that hon. Members may be
glad to have some further information
as to the work which is done by this
Department as a whole, for I doubt
whether even the public of Ulster, much
less the world at large, is aware of the
interest and variety of the monuments in
the Ministry's charge. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Besides Carrickfergus Castle itself, we
have at Dunluce a Castle which, so far as
its situation is concerned, is one of the
most romantic and picturesque in the
British Isles. Jordan's Castle at Ardglass, which was presented to the Minis-
Estimates
Public Records
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
try by the executors of the late Francis
Joseph Bigger and is filled with a
collection of antiquities which he had
deposited there, is a good specimen of a
small castle or defensible house probably
owned by a merchant in the port.
Amongst the monuments which the
Ministry has been able to accept from
the Land Commission, under a provision
in the Irish Land Act of 1903, are Harry
Avery's Castle and Mountjoy Castle in
County Tyrone, the former a Norman
stronghold and the latter containing,
what is a rarity in Ulster, some Tudor
brickwork.
These are the most interesting specimens of this type of architecture.
Northern Ireland is still more rich in
ecclesiastical remains, of which the most
notable are the Cistercian Abbeys of
Greyabbey and Inch, one lying on the
Ards Peninsula, between the sea and
Strangford Lough, and the other by the
waters of the Quoile. At Loughinisland,
County Down, there is a little sanctuary
island in a lake, crowned by three
successive churches, all of which are in
the Ministry's charge, and the Island
of Devenish, in Lower Lough Erne, contains a whole succession of ecclesiastical
buildings, beginning with the remains of
an oratory, built, perhaps, as early as
600 A.D., and closing with a small
mediaeval abbey. Here there is also a
round tower, built in the time of the
Danish invasions, one of the only two
complete round towers within Northern
Ireland, in which the Ministry has built
a
circular staircase supported by a
central pole without being attached in
any way to the walls, with the intention
of affording visitors an opportunity of
ascending to the top of the tower and
studying its remarkable construction.
We are also responsible for several
highly interesting prehistoric antiquities,
as, for instance, the Giant's Ring, close
to Belfast, which is believed to be a
sepulchral monument of as early as
2000 B.C. Coming to later times, we
have at Navan, outside Armagh, that
town of Emania, which was so celebrated
by the exploits of the Craobh Ruadh, or
Red Branch Knights, while in County
Down, a county exceptionally rich in
antiquities, there are a number of monuments in our charge, of which I may
mention the stone fort at Drumena, near
Newcastle, which contains one of those
curious underground chambers called
souterrains, and a stone circle at Ballynoe, near Downpatrick, which is one of
the largest and best in Ireland.
All these are monuments which attract
large numbers of visitors both from
Northern Ireland and from places outside. It would, of course, be impossible
to enumerate the number of dolmens,
stone crosses, and other antiquities cf
various kind of which Northern Ireland
possesses a particularly large number. It
may be said, in short, that Northern
Ireland, as a field for the antiquarian,
has a considerable claim to fame, and
that we, as a Government, are more than
justified in paying very great attention
to the preservation of a feature which is
of more value to the reputation of the
Province than perhaps many of us
appreciate. I beg to move.

preservation, I refer to the Irish
language.
Estimates-
Public Records
HOUSE OF COMMONS
The CHAIRMAN: It is the most
notable description I have ever heard
applied to the Irish language, to put it
in the category of an ancient monument.
We really must have some limit to this.
Mr. HEALY: Surely the most ancient
monument in this or any other country is
a language.
The CHAIRMAN: We are really
dealing with monuments in this Estimate
and not with the apocalyptic descriptions.
of the hon. Gentleman.
Mr. HEALY: The right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Barbour) referred a moment
or two ago to Craobh Ruadh. What
meaning has Craobh Ruadh for any
Member of this Committee? The
language is the key to the successful understanding of the ancient monuments of
the country.
The CHAIRMAN: Surely the hon.
Gentleman realises that a monument,
which is supposed to have associations
with a particular Order, does not entitle
him to embark on a disquisition on the
merits of that Order.
Mr. HEALY: You are taking over
monuments without taking over the key
which will open them to your understanding. A monument in these circumstances is like a locked house, and cannot
be used even by an antiquary. Antiquarianism again is associated with a
knowledge of the Irish language.
The CHAIRMAN: I really cannot
allow this to go on. We are dealing with
quite a definite question, and not a dead
language. I cannot allow the hon.
Gentleman to develop this argument.
Mr. HEALY: I am not speaking of a
dead language at all. I am speaking of
a language that is still living, the
language of a vast number of people
throughout the country. It is not a dead.
language.
The CHAIRMAN: Even if that be so,
the hon. Gentleman must agree with me
that he cannot develop the point on this
Estimate. He advanced his views upon
it, within my own recollection, a few
weeks ago.
Mr. HEALY: As I said at the beginning, I am not objecting to the amount
in this Estimate, but what I am suggesting is this, that the Government are not
sincere. If they were sincere they would
not have taken the action that they have
taken in regard to this language. If you
really meant to preserve these ancient
monuments as part of the national
traditions you would not have taken away
the paltry sum of £1,500 which had been
devoted to the teaching of the Irish
language.
The CHAIRMAN: The hon. Gentleman developed that point on the Education Estimates, and he cannot repeat his
statements.
Mr. HEALY: I am only doing this by
way of illustration. On this Estimate a
certain sum of money is being devoted to
what is described as antiquities-the
preservation of ancient monuments. The
more the Ministers look into the history
of this Castle of Dunluce and of Devenish
in Lough Erne, the more their minds will
be driven back towards national unity.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: No, no.
Question put, and agreed to.
CLASS II. No. 10.
MISCELLANEOUS EXPENSES.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a sum not exceeding £1,020 be
granted to His Majesty to defray the
charge which will come in course of payment during the year ending on the 31st
March, 1935, to pay certain Miscellaneous
Expenses, including certain Grants-in-
Aid. (Note.-£350 has been voted on
account.)
Mr. BARBOUR: This Vote, from its
nature, is liable to vary appreciably from
year to year. In the current year there
is a net decrease of £1,895, but I should,
perhaps, say that this represents a real
decrease of only £695, when we take into
account the fact that under the Finance
(Stamp Duties) Bill, recently considered.
by this House, it is proposed that the
grants payable to the Incorporated Law
Society of Northern Ireland, which
appeared as part of this Estimate for the
last financial year, shall, in future, be
charged upon the Consolidated Fund.
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
10 MAY 1934
The true saving of £695 is accounted
for by reduced provision under two items:
for the fee payable in respect of the preparation of an Index to the Statutory
Rules and Orders, under Sub-head A,
and for Turbary Schemes, under Sub-head
F. The fee for the preparation of the
Index is a re-vote of a part of the monies
provided in the last year's Estimate,
which is necessary because the expectation
that this work would be completed during
that year has not been realised. As to
the Turbary Schemes, there are no
specific schemes at present under consideration, and the provision of £300 is
made simply to cover contingencies; the
amount is, to that extent, speculative. I
beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.

report Progress and ask leave to sit
again." (Mr. Pollock.)

Motor Taxation.
Major SHILLINGTON: I beg to
present a Petition on behalf of the
Ulster Automobile Club. It is a
Petition from the motorists of Northern
Ireland and has over seven thousand
signatures. It stresses the necessity for
motor taxation in Northern Ireland
being kept on parallel lines with that of
Great Britain and it ends with the following prayer :-
on
Your petitioners, therefore, humbly
pray that the horse-power tax
motor-cars should be identical with
that in Great Britain.

upon the Table of the House.

Estimates, 1934-35.
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
CLASS III. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £39,881 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in the course of payment
during the year ending 31st March, 1935,
for the salaries and expenses of the
Ministry of Home Affairs (15 and 16
Geo. V., c. 3, s. 4 (N.I.); 16 and 17
Geo. V., c. 31 (N.I.); 20 Geo. V., c. 21,
s. 7 (N.I.), etc.)."-(Note.-£13,000
has been voted on account).
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In presenting the
Estimates for the Ministry of Home
Affairs for the current year, I would
point out, in the first instance, that it
involves a very slight increase over the
sum budgeted for last year. We are
asking for £52,881, as against £52,225
-an increase of £656.
we
The principal cause of this increase is
that
have found it necessary to
increase our local government audit staff
by the addition of one auditor, one assistant auditor, and two audit clerks. For
many years past our audit staff have
found it increasingly impossible to keep
their audits up to date, owing to the
increased responsibilities imposed
them by recent legislation. I refer, in
particular, to the establishment of
regional education committees, whose
accounts are proving more comprehensive and complex each year.
on
The introduction of the principle of
derating has also added immeasurably to
the work of the local government audit
staff, as upon their examination of the
local government authorities' accounts
and the certificates given as a result of
such examination, depends the payment
of the derating grants to local authorities.
The result of this increased work has
in recent years delayed to an embarrasing extent the completion of the
various audits of the accounts of the
local authorities, and consequently it has
delayed the payments by us of the
various grants to which the local
authorities are entitled on the basis of
the certificates of the local government
auditors.
Complaints have been made by the
local authorities regarding the delay in
payments to them, and we realise that
these complaints are largely justifiable
and, accordingly, have felt it necessary
to take steps to bring the audits up to
date and so hasten the date of payment
of the various grants to the local
authorities.
Another item in the Estimates, which
appears for the first time, will be found
under Sub-head G, an item of £150,
provided for the expenses of the Departmental Committee which has been set up
to inquire into the difficult and complicated question of markets and market
tolls.
Taking the Home Office side of the
Ministry first, it is appropriate that I
should deal generally with the question
of law and order. During the past
year the various judges of assize have
found it possible to make references of
a more or less satisfactory character as
to the peaceful conditions which they
Ministry of Home Affairs 1574
Estimates-
15 MAY 1934
-
found prevailing in the various counties.
This state of affairs is due, as I have
stated on previous occasions before this
Committee, to various causes the first
and most important, the good sense of
the law-abiding population (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-secondly, the
efficiency of our Constabulary forces;
and thirdly, and perhaps more important
still, the good feeling which exists between the people as a whole and the
members of the two Forces. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
At the same time, I cannot but refer with
regret to the attempts which were made
last autumn by what I hope is a small and
isolated section of the community to
foment disorder and strife in our midst,
and to institute a recrudescence of outrage and crime in what is, after all, one
of the most peaceful communities in the
social system to-day.
Members of the Committee are aware
of the two dastardly murders which took
place in the city of Belfast, and for
which, I am sorry to say, no persons
have as yet been made amenable in
spite of the large rewards offered for information which would lead to their
convictions.
case,
I must also refer to another case
of attempted murder, associated with
the same movement, in which
fortunately, no serious damage was done
and the persons implicated were brought
to justice.
That a member of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary should. be assassinated
while quietly and efficiently carrying out
his duties is a matter of regret to me,
as Minister responsible for the Force,
and that a respectable citizen should a
few days later meet with a similar fate,
is a matter which must be deplored by
every one of us.
These outbreaks, coupled with other
information which we had at our disposal,
satisfied me that a determined effort was
being made by certain misguided
individuals to recreate the spirit of outrage and disorder which, unfortunately,
marked the beginning of our Government
here, and I felt it necessary to avail myself to the fullest extent of the powers
which Parliament had accorded to me
under the Civil Authorities Acts and to
take drastic and stringent measures,
which we can all only hope had, and will
have, a cautionary and salutary effect
on all persons who feel disposed to dis
obey the law in Northern Ireland, or to
attempt in any way to interfere with or
disrupt our Constitution.
At the same time, I feel it necessary
to place on public record my sense of deep
appreciation, and the deep appreciation
of the Government, of the cordial support
and sympathy extended to my Department and to the police forces during the
very trying times which we were called
upon to endure, and I feel it appropriate
also to pay tribute to the able and
efficient manner in which every member
of the Royal Ulster Constabulary and the
Special Constabulary have carried out
their duties during the past year. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
With regard to prison administration,
there is not much to say which has not
been said before. The numbers in our
various prisons, unfortunately, show a
slight increase, as I find that during the
year in question 2,804 persons were committed to prison as against 2,622 in 1932.
This increase is due mainly to the
organised disturbances which took place
in the City of Belfast last year and,
incidentally, to the increased number of
persons made amenable for crimes.
Similarly, in the case of the Borstal
Institution, we have to record an increase
of from 70 to 100, although I am glad to
say there has been a drop from 30 to 18
in the numbers of youthful offenders
committed to the reformatory. These
figures indicate the value which the courts
attach to the system of training and reformation afforded to youthful offenders
by our Borstal Institution. Incidentally,
I may mention, that we are experiencing
difficulty in the provision of the necessary
accommodation for Borstal inmates. The
Malone Training School was originally
designed to accommodate 50 Borstal and
50 Reformatory boys. As I have
already mentioned, the number of Borstal
boys has increased to nearly 100, while
the number of Reformatory boys, I am
glad to say, has dwindled to 18.
In the interest of training and discipline it is essential to keep the two
classes apart as far as possible, and we
are at present considering ways and
means of dealing with this somewhat troublesome problem. We have
approached the Belfast Corporation with
the object of eliciting their co-operation
Estimates-
Ministry of Home Affairs
IlOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
in regard to taking over the Reformatory
boys from us and accommodating them
in the Balmoral Training School, but
certain difficulties have arisen in this connection which have not yet been cleared
away. If a solution on these lines could
be obtained it would enable us to devote
the Malone Training School wholly and
solely for the purpose of the training of
Borstal boys, an expedient which would
possess undoubted advantages.
Turning to local government administration, the past year has been one of
steady progress. The question of distress
and outdoor relief has been one of the
utmost concern and gravity. As I
explained last year, the position in
Belfast became so acute and the burden
on the ratepayers so accentuated, that I
deemed it necessary and essential to give
my approval to a scheme worked jointly
by the Board of Guardians and the
Belfast Corporation, under which certain
road works would be allocated to persons
applying for special outdoor relief, and
involving a contribution from the Road
Fund of 50 per cent. of the cost of nine
specially approved schemes.
schemes involved in all a charge on the
Road Fund of approximately £250,000,
and in order to enable the Fund to meet
this charge it was found necessary to
obtain Parliamentary authority for a loan
of £350,000 from the Exchequer to cover
the £250,000 already referred to, and a
further sum of £100,000 falling on the
Road Fund in respect of unemployment
relief schemes, the money to be repaid in
seven equal instalments of £50,000.
These
As the whole question of providing for
able-bodied unemployed is in the meltingpot at present, it is not necessary for
me to deal with this subject further, and
I am glad that the Government and
Parliament have been able to facilitate
the Corporation in connection with their
financial operations by enabling them
and other local authorities similarly
affected to fund over a period of five
years their outstanding commitments in
respect of special outdoor relief, pending
the adoption of the new principle which
may be introduced by the Unemployment
Bill.
Turning to the question of road
administration, I think we have reason to
be appreciative of the efforts of the
various road authorities in the Province
-county councils, urban district councils,
etc. to maintain their road systems at
a proper standard of efficiency. As the
result of our policy, I think we may claim
that our road systems compare more than
favourably with those in other countries
similarly situated.
The question of road traffic generally
does not, at the moment, call for special
comment from me, having regard to the
discussions which have taken place and
are taking place on the subject of the
Motor Traffic Bill. With regard to the
wider problem of rail and road traffic,
however, it is only due that I should give
expression at this stage to the appreciation of the Government of Northern
Ireland of the public-spirited action of
Sir Felix Pole-one of the greatest
experts in transport-in placing his
services voluntarily at our disposal for the
purpose of investigating the various
systems of transport and of reporting to us what, if any, change should be
made with the object of making the
system and its various elements as
efficient and as economic as possible. His
report will be awaited with the greatest
possible interest.
With regard to public health services,
there is nothing of outstanding interest
to be referred to at the moment, except,
perhaps, the urge that is apparent in
certain localities to have their existing
workhouse infirmaries abolished and to
institute instead up-to-date district
hospitals. The beautiful hospitals which
have been provided at Newtownards,
Banbridge, Lisburn and other places,
have, I am glad to say, acted as an
incentive to other areas, and we have, at
the moment, before us proposals from
various quarters designed with the above
object. In some cases these proposals
have met with unanimous support from
the whole community, who apparently
realise the necessity of good hospital
services. In other cases this unanimity
is not so apparent, and protests are
received from various quarters against
the possibility of an increase in rates. It
is not possible always to answer these
protests pending formal inquiry and
investigation, but I think it no harm to
say at this stage that I will not be a party
to any proposal of this or any other
character, which, after careful examination, would appear to me to tend to an
excessive imposition on the ratepayers.
Ministry of Home Affairs

15 MAY 1934
I would point out, however, that to a
very considerable extent an increase in
local expenditure involves an increase in
the Government derating grant, and it
is, therefore, apparent that from the
Government, as well as from the local
point of view, it is essential that extravagant expenditure on any service should.
be avoided.
Before concluding, I would like to turn
to the question of housing. As hon.
Members are aware, during the past year
a subsidy of £25 was available to private
builders and local authorities, subject to
the usual conditions, while local authorities themselves were empowered to grant
an additional sum not exceeding £25, or a
remission in rates in lieu. The number
of houses approved for erection during
that year was 805, while the number
completed was 466.
For the current year, under the
Housing Act, the Government grant is,
as the Committee is aware, contingent on
the local authority paying a corresponding grant of £25 or an equivalent in the
shape of remission of rates. As was
explained at the time, the conception
underlying the recent Bill is that the
local authorities are the best judges of the
needs of their particular areas, and that
this factor constitutes a justification for
the Government refusing to pay a grant
in any area in which the local authority
does not consider it necessary that houses
should be built.
Up to the present, out of thirty-four
urban and
and thirty-two rural areas in
Northern Ireland, only nineteen have
emphasised their need for houses by
agreeing to give a subsidy or rate exemption in
in lieu, but, nevertheless,
anticipate from information at present
before us that during the current year
at least one
thousand houses will be
erected by private builders and about one
hundred by local authorities.
we
It may be of interest to note that since
the question of Government assistance in
aid of housing was first instituted in
Northern Ireland by the Housing Act of
1923, no less than 1,933 houses have been
erected by local authorities and 22,798 by
private builders, the total commitments
of the Government being £2,141,005.
With regard to the question of the
provision of labourers' cottages in rural
districts, I regret that for financial
reasons it has not yet been possible for
us to remove the embargo on schemes by
local authorities, but the local authorities
themselves have power under the Housing
Acts to encourage the provision of
subsidy houses, and it must be borne in
mind that in addition to the 6,310
cottages which have been provided in
Northern Ireland since 1883 and prior
to 1921, we have, since the transfer of
Services, confirmed schemes for the
further erection of 1,902 cottages, of
which 1,858 have been actually erected.
I have endeavoured in this short statement to outline the principal points of
the Estimates, and I beg to move.

require a certain amount of force and

With regard to the housing policy in

been done. The Government can well
congratulate itself on the fact that it has
encouraged since 1920 the building of
some 20,000 houses. The only criticism
I would make is that their ideals have
not been daring enough. I observed in a
newspaper yesterday that in Germany the
leaders of the Nazis have decided that
1,000 small towns and villages shall be
built in the country districts for the
express purpose of relieving congestion in
overgrown cities. That is a wise policy,
and I would like to see our Government
taking to themselves something of the
power of a dictator in this matter of the
housing of the people.
I suggested some time ago to an

community are given positions of power

people may be able to live under con-

have no doubt that the hon. Member for

Ulster Constabulary fully

May I refer in a word to the prisons?

A
One matter in connection with this
Estimate has already caused a great deal
of adverse argument and that is the sum
devoted to the Special Constabulary. I
have heard with great astonishment some
of the statements made by hon. Members
on the opposite benches, particularly the
statement by the hon. Member for East
Tyrone. I was somewhat surprised to
hear him say that the vast majority in
this area I took it he referred to the Six
County area-considered that the Special
Constabulary should be abolished.
little further in his speech he said that
the elected representatives of the people
well knew that that was the opinion of
the electorate. Well, as one of the elected
representatives of the people, I say that I
most emphatically dissent from that now
and most emphatically assert that the
loyal members of the community in the
Six Counties are definitely of opinion that
the continuance of the Special Constabulary makes for the peace and good
government of the Six-County area. And
speaking as an elected representative I
would view with very considerable
apprehension any reduction in the Special
Constabulary, and I congratulate the
Government on increasing it, although it
is a small increase.
Some of the remarks made by the hon.
Member for East Tyrone are obviously
founded on a misapprehension as to the
situation. Amongst other references to
the Special Constabulary he spoke of the
magnificent sums paid to them.
As anyone who troubles to look at the figures
knows in the best sense of the word the
Special Constabulary is a volunteer
force. It is a volunteer force that
requires as any organised and disciplined
force does require, a permanent organisation, and the only possible justification
for the assertion that magnificent sums
are paid at least the only justification I
have heard advanced is that one most
efficient officer receives £820 a year. Well,
as it appears from the details into which
1 am not going at the moment, the actual
sum paid to the 12,000 men who represent the Special Constabulary is purely
negligible. No doubt a sum is expended
on musketry training and other training
of that character, but so far as the
individual members of the force are
concerned I assert without fear of contradiction that in the best sense of the
word it is a volunteer force.
I have listened in this House for a good
many years to the successive debates on
the Special Constabulary, and I suppose
we should be almost surprised if we did
not hear hon. Members opposite repeat
the arguments advanced from time to
time against the force. But when I
heard the hon. Member for South
Fermanagh asserting in the same breath
that the Special Constabulary should be
abolished and that he and others who
think with him are as interested as we
are in the preservation of peace in this
part of the country it seemed to me
almost a contradiction in terms. In our
opinion, however much we may differ in
this matter from hon. Members opposite,
the continuance of the Special Constabulary definitely makes for peace. The
hon. Member for East Tyrone made
suggestions with regard to the body of
persons who are responsible for the latest
outrage, the attack on the Armagh War
Memorial. The Hon. Member will forgive
me if I say I hardly thought he was
serious in his assertion that that
deplorable outrage was to be attributed

Mr. MINFORD: I would like to congratulate the Ministry on the peace and
law and order in Ulster. The only fault
I find with the Ministry is on the question
of housing. Some few months ago
we passed what is known here as
the Housing Act. This Act has,
in my opinion, only one flaw, and
that flaw is that it refuses to give
authority to the local authorities to build.
I am quite sure that hon. Members agree
that housing in Northern Ireland is not
what it should be. If you want to make
people content and happy you must give
them good houses. Speaking generally
for every constituency, the houses are not
what they should be.
This last Housing Act gave power to
individuals to get a subsidy of £25 or
exemption from rates for ten years from
the rural authorities, or they could
borrow from the local authorities at per
cent. under the rate which the local
authorities borrowed and the Government
would make up the difference. In the
third schedule there was a clause under
which they could build houses and borrow
from a building society up to 70 per cent.,
and the building society would have the
security of the house. The builder of
that house or the owner could borrow 20
per cent. of the cost of building and that
20 per cent. would be guaranteed to the
building society by the local authority.
Therefore, it gave the working man or any
man the chance of building a house and
borrowing 90 per cent. of the money.
The defect has arisen that a number of
persons want to build houses and go to
the local authorities and nobody seems to
know where they are.
Under the Labourers and Small
Dwellings Act the local authorities were
enabled to build houses but, unfortunately,
that has not been a success. The appeal
I want to make to the Minister is to
allow the local authorities to take
advantage of the last Housing Act,
because I believe if the local authorities
could borrow 70 per cent. of the money
from building societies and 20 per cent.
more to be guaranteed by the Government we would get on to what I consider
a right plan of curing the housing situation. It is all very well to say that any
man can start and build but we all know
it requires money. It is all very well to
say that the local authorities know local
conditions better. That can be argued in
other ways. There are times when the
Ministry of Home Affairs exercises
authority in spite of the local authorities.
I feel that if the Ministry see that the
local authorities are not carrying out the
building of houses to their satisfaction it
is the duty of the Ministry to tell the
local authorities that our people must
have houses. The Housing Act in the
rural areas seems to be a dead letter so
far as the local authorities are
concerned. Four or five years ago we in
Antrim had about 190 applications for
houses. While we must not forget the
great housing schemes for which the
Government has been responsible
through its subsidies to builders and
owners, the agricultural and industrial
workers require something to be done to
help them out of their difficulty, and,
therefore, I suggest that the Minister of
Home Affairs should amend the Housing
Acts so as to empower local authorities to
build houses, and, if necessary, to sell them
to the tenants. I think I am disclosing
no secret when I say that quite a number
of industries are contemplating launching
housing schemes whereby they can build
houses and transfer them to their
workers.
I feel that good housing is essential
to health and happiness in every country,
and, therefore, I appeal to the Minister
to amend the Housing Acts in the
direction T have indicated, and if he does
SO it will clear the way for better
housing. Some of the rural authorities
have done very little in regard to housing,
but the Antrim Rural District Council
has offered ten years free from rates to
any one who builds a house within its
area. I do not think it is fair that
because a rural authority does not under-

surely it is not pretended that the Government are unaware up to this moment
Ministry of Home Affairs 1620
Estimates--
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. McCarroll]
of its existence. They are not going to
get out of the gravity of this charge by
saying, as the Attorney-General has said,
that the Opposition did not go through
the form of handing it over to the Government. I think that is a contemptible
way to get out of a grave situation of
this sort.
Mr. HANNA: It may seem strange to
Members on the other side, but I have
to confess that I have never seen and
never heard of this paper. Our
attention has now been drawn to it and
the statements made in it will be carefully considered. It is not suggested
that anybody wants to put an onus on
the hon. Gentleman that he is unwilling
to bear. Having drawn our attention
to this, the hon. Member may rest
assured that this matter will, as the
Attorney-General said, be taken into
consideration and dealt with if it is
thought desirable.
Mr. HEALY: I think the Parliamentary Secretary is riding off too
lightly, especially as the concern of the
Home Office is the peace of the city and
Six Counties. This is a deliberate
menace to the peace of the Six Counties.
The police force have, no doubt, their
copies of this paper, and the Home
Office, I have not the least doubt, have
copies. If they have not got copies they
are remiss in their duties. This is an
incitement to breaking the peace. I can
assure the Parliamentary Secretary that
if the incitement had come from the
Nationalist side he would have had the
paper prosecuted just as he did some time
ago when he got one of his servile resident
magistrates to fine a Nationalist paper
£100 for an offence comparatively trifling
to this. If you mean to carry out the law
impartially you will have to deal with
that publication, and we shall know the
measure of your honesty and sincerity
when we see what you are going to do.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: It is
not a question of the Government's
honesty and sincerity. It will be a question of the sincerity and honesty of the
Attorney-General. I will deal with the
case.
Mr. McALEER: It is a humiliating
thing to see the Attorney-General and
the Cabinet saying they never heard of
the publication of this infamous journal,
the statements in which are an incitement
to crime. I hope the Attorney-General
and the Parliamentary Secretary will, as
they say, consider this thing and see that
the proprietors do not get off.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: The
hon. Member may not take me as
assenting that it is an incitement to
crime. I will decide that when I see the
paper.
Question put, and agreed to.
