HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 16th May, 1934.
The House met at Three of the Clock.
The Clerk, at the Table, informed the
House of the unavoidable absence of Mr.
SPEAKER from this day's sitting.
Whereupon Mr. MOLES, the Chairman of Ways and Means, proceeded to
the Table, and, after Prayers, took the
Chair as Deputy-Speaker, pursuant to
the Standing Order.
LOCAL BILLS.
Ministry of Home Affairs Provisional

Gasworks) Bill.

reported from the Joint Unopposed Committee on the Bill as follows:-That
they had considered the said Bill, and
examined the allegations thereof, which
were found to be true, and that the
Committee had gone through the Bill,
and directed the same to be reported
without Amendment to the House.

Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
Financial Statement, 1934-35.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): Before I
on the
presentation of our estimated revenue
and expenditure for the coming year, I
would like very briefly to report on the
results of the year which closed on the
31st March last. Hon. Members will,
doubtless, recall that a year ago, owing
to the extraordinary fall in our revenues
from customs and excise, and especially
in income tax, as estimated by the
British Treasury, I was placed in a
position of some difficulty and embarrass-
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
16 MAY 1934
ment
in
the endeavour to discover
revenue to bridge the gulf thus created.
To impose additional taxation in the very
limited area of Services to which our
powers of taxation extend was very repugnant to me. But it was essential that
the Budget should be balanced, and
balanced from our own resources. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). Thus, I was
forced to re-examine previous years'
accounts to discover revenues which had
not been brought into account. In this
we succeeded, and I am happy to say
that when the year ended we closed our
accounts with a small surplus of £29,000.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Looking back on the financial year of
1933-34, it is gratifying to find that the
trade and commerce of the Kingdom
showed a decided improvement compared
with its two predecessors. This gratifying change in the internal business conditions of the country can be traced to
the new fiscal policy, which had the effect
of reducing the enormous volume of unnecessary and unwanted foreign goods
dumped on our markets and which our
free trade institutions had invited and
encouraged. In the year which lies
ahead conditions are not greatly dissimilar. Trade has undoubtedly shown.
signs of improvement. In the
two
staple trades of the Province, linen and
shipbuilding, there are encouraging
features of a reassuring character-unemployment is slowly but steadily falling,
but the full reactions of all these encouraging features on the finances of the
Province can only appear later on.
I am proud to say that the credit of
Ulster to-day stands high-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)—and I have no doubt
in my mind that this is largely due to
the fact that it has been possible each
year since the establishment of the Government of Northern Ireland to show a
balanced Budget. That, undoubtedly, is
the result, as I judge it, of careful financial accountancy.
If hon. Members will turn to the
upper portion of Table I of the White
Paper which has been circulated, they
will find statements comparing the estimuated with the actual outturn of last
year's finance. My first duty will be
mainly directed to that table, but if hon.
Members wish to see the items in greater
detail, they may do so if they turn to
Table II for the outgoings and Table
III for the income.
Expenditure, 1933-34.
Dealing first of all with the expenditure, we find that Consolidated Fund
Services, apart from the Road Fund,
accounted for £407,000, or £4,000 above
the Estimate.
The Road Fund payment of £591,000
represents the corresponding receipt from.
motor taxation. The Budget estimate of
£570,000 was exceeded by £21,000,
which is a useful addition to the revenues
of the Fund.
SUPPLY SERVICES.
The Budget Estimate for Supply Services was £8,803,000, to which should be
added £182,000 for supplementaries,
making a total estimated expenditure on
our Departmental Services of £8,985,000.
The actual expenditure for the year
was £8,761,000, a gross saving of
£224,000, so that I was able not only to
pay for the supplementaries but also
make a saving of £42,000 on the original
Estimate.
DEDUCTIONS FROM RESIDUARY SHARE.
We repaid to the Imperial Government
sums collected by us from the local
authorities in repayment of loans made
before we took over control (£68,000)
and also collections of "new" land purchase annuities (£299,000), a total
sum of £367,000.
The expenditure of the Imperial Government on the reserved services which
they control, such as the cost of collecting
income tax, Post Office, Customs, etc.,
was £1,758,000.
The total expenditure, therefore, of
the Province last year amounted to
£11,901,000, and if hon. Members will
keep that sum in their minds when I come
to speak of revenue they will be able to
judge of the difference involved. I shall
now refer briefly to the sources of revenue
for meeting this expenditure.
Revenue, 1933-34.
TRANSFERRED TAXES.
The revenue from transferred taxes
imposed by our Government produced
£863,000, that is £36,000 less than the
Budget Estimate. The amount of the
Estate Duties has continued to drop,
which is disappointing in view of the
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
appreciation of about 15 per cent. in
capital values, but there is a welcome
increase in the yield of Stamp Duties,
which have produced £29,000 more than
estimated, due to an increase of activities
on the Stock Exchange-a sign of
improved conditions of trade.
Motor taxation, as I have stated above,
produced £591,000, which, of course,
went to the Road Fund and appeared on
the other side of the account.
RESERVED TAXES.
I come to revenue from reserved taxes.
The Budget Estimate for reserved taxes,
collected by the Imperial Government,
was £7,190,000. The receipts shown are
£100,000 higher than the Estimate, but
this figure is provisional in a sense, and I
cannot, at the moment, say whether there
will be any substantial amount still to
accrue to our Exchequer in respect of
these reserved taxes of last year. I
hope that it may be found that this will
be so, but, as hon. Members know, the
Joint Exchequer Board has to make
intricate calculations in order to arrive
at the reserved revenues properly attributable to Northern Ireland as distinct from
the pure collection of revenue, and it is
inevitable that every year there should
be a lag before the final true revenue is
ascertained.
The transferred and reserved taxes
together, therefore, as actually received
on 31st March last, provided us with
£8,744,000.
There
NON-TAX REVENUE.
are other revenues accruing
which do not come under the heading of
taxation but still form a very important
part of the income of the Province.
Amongst the items of non-tax revenue,
the adjustments of residuary share for
prior years have exceeded the Estimate
by £30,000. The appropriations from
the various funds, to which I had to have
recourse in order to balance my Budget
last year,
amount to £404,000,
£404,000, an
additional £42,000 having been available
in the Reserve Fund.
Other items of non-tax revenue are set
out in Table I in the White Paper and
are so close to the Estimates that it is
unnecessary for me to weary the Committee by quoting items and figures in
detail.
In all, the non-tax revenue (including
the self-balancing items in respect of
public buildings, local loans repayments,
"new" land purchase annuities, and
residuary share adjustment, and appropriations from various funds) amounted
to £3,186,000, bringing the total revenue
available from all sources last year to
£11,930,000.
If we deduct from this the total expenditure for the year, already mentioned
by me, of £11,901,000, we are left with
a balance of £29,000 as the provisional
amount available for surplus and Imperial
contribution. This may not be regarded
as a very large surplus, but having regard
to the unusual depression of trade which
has obtained during the last few years,
I think the position may not be regarded
as entirely unfavourable.
Expenditure, 1934-35.
I now pass from the year that is
finished and come to deal with something
which, I have no doubt, is a great deal
more interesting to the Members of the
Committee than the matters which have
disappeared, that is the accounts of
revenue and expenditure for the year that
lies ahead of us. I shall first take the
expenditure side of the accounts. The
figures will be found in the last column of
Tables II and III of the White Paper.
CONSOLIDATED FUND SERVICES.
The first category of expenditure is that
of our Consolidated Fund.
The interest on Exchequer borrowings,
£85,000, shows an increase of £43,000,
which is chiefly due to the necessity for
providing for a full year instead of a halfyear's interest on our 31 per cent. Ulster
stock.
The Sinking Funds take £219,000
instead of £124,000, as last year. Hon.
Members will remember that last year I
made no provision for the Land Purchase
Sinking Fund, but I do not feel justified
in omitting provision again this year. I
have, therefore, included £91,000 for this
purpose. The Sinking Fund for the
extension of land purchase annuities
amounted, on 31st March last, to
£1,540,000, and if we add the £91,000
for which I am now making provision, we
find that during this year the Fund will
be fully maintained. The amount will be
£1,631,000.
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
16 MAY 1934
The other Consolidated Fund Services
take £174,000, of which £168,000 is the
estimated amount of our payments in
respect of prospective amounts falling to
be met under the Loans Guarantee Acts.
The last item is £615,000 to be paid over
to the Road Fund, an anticipated
increase of £24,000 over last year. There
is, of course, a corresponding Exchequer
receipt on the other side from motor
taxation.
At this point I should like to comment
on the wonderful resiliency of motor
taxation. In 1925 the revenue from this
source was £284,000, while this present
year of 1934 the receipts are estimated at
£615,000-an increase of £330,000. Hon.
Members can draw any conclusion they
please from this extraordinary development, as it affords an indication of the
increasing wealth of the Province, on the
assumption that the possession of a motorcar necessarily means increased wealth.
The total Consolidated Fund expenditure is £1,093,000.
SUPPLY.
The Estimates for the expenditure on
Supply Services total £8,500,000, which
is half-a-million less than last year.
I am glad to state that the improvement in employment, which is expected
and which has already partially taken
place, is largely responsible for this
reduction.
The full details of this principal figure
of expenditure are, of course, set out in
the Book of Estimates, which have
already been discussed and passed by this
House, and which, therefore, need not be
recapitulated.
RESERVED SERVICES.
The last category of expenditure
is that relating to the cost of Reserved Services, the total of which is
£1,794,000, which is £36,000 more than
last year. The increase is mainly
accounted for by the Post Office expenditure, which is higher than last year by
£33,000. This increase is partly due to
the expenditure on our new telephone.
exchange, which is met by means of an
annuity, and partly, I am glad to say, to
an anticipated further improvement in
trade and business, which, though it
increases the Post Office activities and so
its expenditure, also involves a corresponding growth on the revenue side.
The "new" land purchase annuities are
£300,000, the property of the Imperial
Government, and the pre-transfer local
loans £69,000, making a total of
£369,000. Therefore, the total estimated
expenditure of the Province for the year
is £11,756,000.
Revenue, 1934-35.
I now turn to the revenue for the
current year, showing how I propose to
provide for this very considerable expenditure-which will be found in the last
column of Table III-and I may say that,
while my difficulties are not as serious as
last year, they are still serious enough to
cause me anxiety in producing a balanced
The figures in the table are
those which existing rates of taxation
would produce.
account.
On the transferred revenue side on the
present basis of taxation estate duties are
expected to produce £525,000. I have
already mentioned that these duties are
very uncertain, but, so far as any human
calculation can make them accurate, I
think we are moderately safe in assuming
that the revenue from that source will be
£525,000. Last year it was £503,000,
one of the lowest amounts on record-
Stamp duties estimated to yield
£240,000, excise duties £125,000, motor
vehicles duties £615,000, giving a total
revenue of £1,505,000.
are
Mr. NIXON: Will it be reduced?
Mr. POLLOCK: The hon. Member
will hear something later. I now come
to reserved revenue, which is collected by
the Imerial Government and imposed by
that authority.
Customs receipts amount to £4,800,000,
an expected increase of £310,000 over the
provisional figure for last year, and but
for the resiliency of these revenues, it
would indeed be difficult to show a
balanced Budget for the year.
The chief increases over last year's
Estimate are: -Tobacco £130,000, oil
duties £140,000, import duties-the
result of the new import duties recently
imposed by the Imperial Government-
£118,000, while there is an estimated
decrease in beer and spirits of £130,000.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The uninterrupted decline in the consumption of beer and spirits is one of the
most astonishing features of our modern
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
social life. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It may interest the Committee to learn
that the revenue from this source in 1924
amounted to £2,435,000. This year we
will receive only £1,422,000, a decline of
more than £1,000,000 in that period.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Temperance theorists claim that loss of revenue
from alcohol would be made good by an
increase in other sources of revenue. I
am sorry to say that this is not my
experience. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
INLAND REVENUE.
Coming now to income tax, the remission of 6d in the standard rate in the
British Budget will entail a loss to
Northern Ireland revenue of £220,000
this year. Against that there is the disappearance of the concession to income
tax payers last year, by which only threequarters of the tax was payable, owing to
the smaller proportion falling due in
January. This was estimated to cost
Northern Ireland last year £170,000.
Taking these factors, among others, into
consideration, the British Treasury inform
me that I may expect a reduction of
£100,000 on the provisional receipt for
last year, making an estimated revenue
from that source of £2,695,000.
This figure is some £614,000 less than
the receipts for 1932-33, and £1,058,000
less than those for 1931-32. If think
you
of what I have just mentioned in respect
of the revenue from alcohol being less by
over £1,000,000 and the drop in our
income tax revenue of over £1,000,000that is to
say, considerably over
£2,000,000 of a loss in revenue in a comparatively recent period-you will understand that my position was not entirely
enviable in trying to find sources of
revenue to balance such a heavy loss. Such
a huge drop in our small revenue is a
very disquieting factor and, but for the
increase in Customs and Excise over the
same period, due chiefly to the British
tariff policy, the difficulties in making at
balanced Budget in this period would
have been well-nigh insuperable.
POST OFFICE.
The Post Office revenue is estimated at
£945,000, an increase of £25,000 on last
year. But, as I have already indicated,
the expenditure is estimated to increase to
£955,000, because of the cost of the new
telephone exchange, so that there is a
deficit of £10,000 on this service. It is to
be hoped that through the additional
vigour and enterprise of the Post Office
this loss will be recovered in future years.
I have no doubt it will.
Another item of revenue is £75,000 in
respect of miscellaneous receipts from
other reserved departments, namely, Post
Office Savings Bank, etc. The total of all
these reserved revenues is £8,520,000.
We also received adjustments of residuary
share due to us for the year 1932-33 of
£200,000, an amount which has been
determined in the last few weeks by the
Joint Exchequer Board.
NON-TAX REVENUE.
Under the head of non-tax revenue we
expect to receive from :-

Now I can arrive at a balance sheet for
the year.
If hon. Members will look back
and recall the expenditure of £11,756,000
and the revenue £11,512,000, it will not
be difficult to realise that the deficit is
£244,000.
When the British Chancellor of the
Exchequer arrived at this point in his
Budget speech he had the good fortune
to be able to disclose a substantial
balance on the right side, and he then
proceeded to indicate how he proposed to
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
16 MAY 1934
reduce this balance by increased expenditure or reduced taxation. I am, however, in the less enviable position of finding a deficit at the same point, though
this is in part due to the income tax
reliefs which we, in common with Great
Britain, will enjoy.
My task, therefore, is not to dispose
of a surplus, but to reduce a deficit-a
much less congenial operation. My first
step in effecting this may seem to the
Committee rather a curious one, for I propose to increase this deficit of £244,000
by a further £45,000. As, however, the
policy which renders this necessary will,
I am sure, have the sympathy of this
Committee, I have had no hesitation in
the matter.
Having regard to our partnership with
Britain in respect of Unemployment
Insurance matters, we are bound to maintain similar standards of unemployment
benefits, and indeed, in every respect,
conform to British arrangements. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Hon. Members
will have seen that the British Chancellor
in his Budget Statement provided for a
return to the scales of unemployment
relief obtaining in 1931. We must,
therefore, adopt a similar course, and this
restoration will, as I have said, involve
us in an expenditure of £45,000, which
increases my Budget deficit to a sum of
£289,000.
Beyond this, I regret that I am unable
to follow the British Chancellor. It will
be recollected that he has used his surplus
in part to make a partial restoration of
the various cuts in salaries in Great
Britain, made in the year 1931, in respect
of teachers, police and civil servants, and
others. Similar cuts were made here, but
at a date six months in advance to the
cuts in Great Britain. So that in this
case we cut ourselves off entirely from
the British methods of tackling the
troubles which existed at that time. We
were six months ahead of them.
While I am sorry that I am unable, in
principle, to restore the portion of the
cuts made in 1931, representations have
been made to me regarding the desirability of using the present opportunity
of assimilating to that in operation in
Great Britain the percentage contribution
to pension made by the Royal Ulster
Constabulary. There are considerable
advantages in this and I have, therefore,
concurred in its being effected as from 1st
July next. This will cost me £13,000 in
the present year. Now, I can readily
realise being cross-questioned in the
House and outside its walls regarding the
future of a question which touches so
many interests. I will only go so far as
to say that the door is not shut, but that
nothing more definite can be said until
next year, when the whole matter will be
brought under careful review by the
Government in the light of the circumstances obtaining at that time.
MOTOR DUTIES.
I now come to the question of motor
duties. Hon. Members will have noticed
-everybody will have noticed that the
Chancellor's Budget Statement embodied
a provision for a reduction of 25 per
cent. of the horse-power duty on private
motor-cars and motor-cycles. I feel sure
that the House will experience no sense
of surprise or disappointment when I say
it is quite impossible for us to follow the
British decision.
Mr. NIXON: Shame.
Mr. POLLOCK: The arguments in
favour of this course hardly admit of any
controversy. The Chancellor made it
clear in his Budget Statement that his
concession was not concerned so much
with the interests of home motor-car
users, but rather to encourage them
to purchase higher-powered cars, which
would enable manufacturers to develop a
greater export trade with which, unfortunately, we in Ulster are not concerned.
But, apart from this point, there are
overwhelming local reasons for maintaining our present revenue from motor
vehicles of all kinds which do not apply to
Britain. Our mileage of roads is
relatively enormously greater in Ulster,
as compared with Britain, and this
entails a much heavier maintenance expense.
If we made any change involving a
reduction in revenue, the grants to local
authorities for road
purposes would
necessarily be proportionately lower.
This would impose an additional burden
on the ratepayers, which would be very
unfair and which I am not prepared to
face. It will have been observed that
the Chancellor of the Exchequer
is in the normal course appropriating
£5,000,000 from the British Road Fund
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
and treating it as an ordinary source of
revenue; although I am refraining from
similar action in regard to our Road
Fund this year, I wish to make it clear
that I am not surrendering my rights to
do so on any occasion when the necessity
may arise in the general interests of the
Province.
Road authorities have for the past
three years willingly co-operated with the
Government in reducing their expenditure on roads, especially on maintenance
work, with a view to ensuring that the
total amount paid in percentage grants
from the Road Fund would be on the
average 10 per cent. less than they were
in the year ended 31st March, 1931. I
am aware, and, indeed, my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Home Affairs,
has more than once stressed this point,
that road authorities have been uneasy
at this curtailment, and they will be
relieved to hear that I can give an
assurance that some measure of relaxation ought to be possible next year.
DUTIES ON MECHANICALLY-PROPELLED
VEHICLES.
I have, however, had under examination for some time, in consultation
with my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Home Affairs, certain aspects of motor
taxation where some minor adjustments
are desirable. These will be set out in
detail in the Resolution which will be
formally tabled at the close of the
Debate, but I will briefly describe what
is proposed.
The main change is one which is
already in operation in Great Britain,
namely, increasing the rates of taxation
on vehicles which are propelled by heavy
oils. These vehicles are in an unduly
favoured position, and in Great Britain
the necessary corrective has already been
applied. The duty levied by the Imperial
Government on heavy oils is, as hon.
Members are aware, considerably lighter
than that on petrol. In fact the tax on
petrol is 8d a gallon. The tax on oil is.
only one penny a gallon, and I am given
to understand that 50 per cent. greater
mileage is obtained from oil than from
petrol. Therefore, while petrol pays 8d,
an oil vehicle pays only equal to twothirds of a penny for its motor power.
Accordingly, if the motor vehicle duty is
the same on both types of vehicle, that
added to the excise duty gives an unfair
advantage to the vehicle run on heavy
oil. This I propose to remedy as
in Great Britain-not because it has been
done in Great Britain but because I
think it is an equitable procedure-by
increasing the motor vehicle duty on this
class of hackney carriage (which includes
omnibuses) or motor lorry by approximately 33 per cent. As I have stated,
the full scale will be set out in the
Resolution itself.
At the same time, I find that in Great
Britain, under last year's Budget, the
motor vehicle duty paid by heavy lorries.
exceeding five tons in weight was substantially increased. In order to preserve, therefore, the proper ratio of
advance in the higher categories here, I
propose that for each ton in excess of five
tons, the scale should be increased by
£20 per ton. At the present time no
heavy lorry in Northern Ireland is taxed
to a higher figure than £100-an arrangement which, in view of the serious
damage that these monsters do to the
roads, is obviously inequitable. For the
same reason, I am proposing to increase
somewhat the rates chargeable on vehicles
used for haulage purposes and trailers.
It is not easy to estimate the increased
revenue to the Road Fund from the
above changes, but it may be put tentatively at £5,000. The changes will not
operate until 1st January next.
I also have viewed with some concern
the damage which is done by solid tyre
motor lorries, more particularly to the
less elaborately surfaced roads. In
Great Britain there has for some years
past been a distinction between the tax
on the pneumatic tyre vehicle and the
solid tyre.
To introduce such a distinction in Northern Ireland at short
notice might be held to be inequitable,
but in order that ample notice may be
given, I propose to seek power to increase
the rate of tax on such vehicles by 25
per cent. as from the 1st January, 1936.
This gives eighteen months' notice of the
operation of the change.
MOTOR-CYCLES.
Having now referred to certain items
of increase in motor taxation, I am
about to announce a concession, namely,
the taxation of motor-cycles. Consequent on representations which have
been made to me, I now propose
to alter the taxation of these
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
16 MAY 1934
machines from a weight basis to the basis
of cylinder capacity. From 1st January
next, therefore, where the cylinder
capacity does not exceed 150 cubic centimetres, the rate will be 15s. Between
150 and 250 cubic centimetres it will be
£1 10s, and thereafter £3.
VEHICLE REGISTRATION.
Hon. Members may allege that the
result of failing to keep taxation of
private cars on the same basis as in
Great Britain will lead to loss of revenue
here, on the ground that cars may, at
any rate for the first year, be taxed in
Great Britain. If any hope to evade the
difference in tax by this method, they
may at once disabuse their minds.
be
Apart from tourists and visitors, for
whom there are special arrangements
already in existence, any car owned by
a person domiciled in Northern Ireland
must, even at the present time,
licensed here. The ordinary arrangement is that even though the tax has
been paid to a local authority in Great
Britain—and I may say that such
authority will not accept money tendered
to it by a person whose residence is known
to be in Northern Ireland-a Northern
Ireland resident is required by the police
and the local authority to pay tax afresh
in Northern Ireland, although he can in
the course of a few days receive from the
Ministry of Home Affairs a refund of the
tax which he shows that he had paid in
Great Britain. The Ministry of Home
Affairs, in turn, take steps to recover
from the British Road Fund the amount
refunded to the Northern Ireland resident. Such adjustments between the two
Road Funds are, even at the present time
a matter of ordinary administration.
EDUCATION RATING.
Now I come to a subject which is of
far more importance than these matters
which affect only a small part of the
population. For some considerable time
past, my colleagues and I have been
gravely perturbed by the heavy burden.
thrown upon the Government in providing practically the whole cost of
education, amounting to £2,000,000
annually. There are two important
aspects of this question involving the
relation of taxes to rates, to which I
desire to draw special attention.
In the first place, we have established
an education system under which very
wide powers of control and administration
have been conferred upon local authorities, yet their contribution towards the
service has been almost negligible; and,
in the second place, throughout other
parts of the United Kingdom the ratepayers bear 50 per cent. of the cost of
education, and the State is consequently
only called upon to bear a corresponding
burden.
I propose, therefore, to ask Parliament
to require the local authorities to provide for the remainder of this year a
sum equivalent to a rate of 6d in the
pound towards the cost of educational
services. For a full year in future, the
rate will be one shilling. It is
interesting to note that, whereas the
British Government's expenditure on
education since 1924-when the Colwyn
Committee made its award-has decreased by about 12 per cent., our own
Government's expenditure has increased
by 12 per cent. during the same period,
above the Colwyn allowance.
Death Duties.
There are only two small matters to
which I wish to refer before bringing my statement to a conclusion,
and they are not perhaps of particular
interest to the Committee. As regards
death duties, I propose that legislation
should be introduced in order to provide
a small concession to charities, which
has been pressed on me from various
quarters. Section 38 of the Stamp
Duties (Ireland) Act, 1842, made provision for exemption in Ireland from
legacy and succession duty of money left
for the education or maintenance of poor
children in Ireland or to be applied in
support of any charitable institution or
purpose in Ireland. It has, however,
been held in law that if the will of the
deceased person does not explicitly indicate the Irish charities to which the
money is to be applied, but gives a
discretion to trustees or executors, the
fact that such a discretion exists prevents
the application of the exemption provisions. Moreover, it also has the effect
of imposing duty in a case where the
activities of the charitable body to whom
the legacy is left extend both to Great
Britain and Ireland, even though they
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
might be willing to earmark the legacy
to the Irish end of their activities. A
typical case is the Royal National Lifeboat Institution.
One, at least, of such cases came under
my personal notice in Northern Ireland
some years ago, and it appeared to me
at the time that the Act, as interpreted,
worked somewhat harshly and should be
amended. I have ascertained that a
similar viewpoint has been taken in the
Irish Free State, and they legislated so as
to remedy this evident hardship in the
year 1932. I propose to follow a similar
course. The opportunity will also
taken to stop a very wide interpretation
of this charity concession in the 1842 Act,
which has been given in a recent judgment in the Free State Courts and which,
I note, that Government itself is taking
steps to remedy.
Entertainments Tax.
be
Representations have also been made to
me that the theatres in Belfast are being
financially crippled owing to the
incidence of entertainments duty, more
particularly because picture theatres,
which cater for the public merely by
mechanical means, are able to undercut
the theatre prices owing, in the main,
to the fact that they can run continuous
performances during the afternoon and
evening, and have not the expense of
employing the large number of stage
hands and orchestra which the ordinary
dramatic performance entails.
I may say that I have considerable
sympathy with this presentation of the
facts, more particularly as I am aware
that in the Irish Free State dramatic
performances of all kinds were freed from
tax in the year 1931. My difficulty,
therefore, in meeting the request that
tax should be remitted in this case, is
purely one of finance, and I would ask
those who are affected to accept the
assurance that if in the future we find
that they can be assisted, either by an
adjustment of the existing rates of tax
by completely relieving dramatic
performances of entertainments duty, they
will find us sympathetic.
or
SUMMARY.
Now that I have finished these explanatory statements, I have merely to
summarise their financial implications
and submit the method by which our
financial accounts for the year can be
balanced, and the deficit bridged.
I have already explained the deficit
to be £289,000. The produce of Education Rate which I have mentioned is
expected for this year to be £72,000; the
withdrawal from our reserves is
£150,000; and the anticipated savings
on Estimates of £80,000 will bring into
existence a total of £302,000, leaving a
surplus of £13,000, which I propose to
dispose of by allocating as our Imperial
contribution £10,000, and bringing
down an actual surplus of £3,000.
----
I have endeavoured to submit to the
Committee a clear statement of the
financial position of the Province.
Doubtless, some will be disappointed,
and others may be aggrieved. But I
think it will be agreed by all who have
the welfare of our Province at heart that
our accounts should be balanced from
year to year, and balanced out of our
own revenues. Any other course is unthinkable, from my point of view, for
a self-respecting people such as ours.
And if we cast our survey over the
world, whose deplorable conditions fill
our newspapers from day to day, and
compare the comforts we enjoy in Ulster
as a constituent Province of a Kingdom,
whose progress and prosperity are the
envy of every nation, we have good
grounds for thankfulness for the blessings we enjoy. And now I am in a
position to make an announcement,
which will bring this home in a very
tangible form. Hon. Members are aware
that the position of the milk and butter
industry in Northern Ireland is one that
has been giving the Government great
concern. As this is in the main due to
excessive imports of butter and cheese
into the United Kingdom,
United Kingdom, including
Ulster, my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Agriculture, and myself,
have been in touch with British Ministers
on the subject, and I am empowered by
the Chancellor to announce that in the
forthcoming Bill in the British House of
Commons, which will give statutory
sanction to final arrangements which
have already been announced in order to
assist milk producers in Great Britain,
provision will be made for a sum not
exceeding £200,000 this year for the
purpose of assisting milk producers in
Northern Ireland.
The Budget-
Resolutions
16 MAY 1934
In conclusion, I would like to ask
those who feel aggrieved, and urge
either a reduction of taxation or a restoration of the economy cuts, to
suggest any alternative measures by
which the obligations of the Province
can be met. This would be vastly more
constructive than simply inveighing
against the Government, who exist for
one object, and one alone, that is the
welfare of our common country.
Mr. NIXON: And ourselves.
Mr. POLLOCK: I beg to move.

should read the details of the three

Legacy Duty and Succession Duty.
II. That it is expedient to amend the
law relating to legacy duty and succession
duty by providing that-
(a) The enactments relating to the exemption from legacy duty of charitable bequests shall extend only to such of those
bequests as may be given for charitable purposes in Ireland, but so that,
where the Ministry of Finance is
satisfied that the whole or part of a
legacy given for charitable purposes
has been or will be applied to charitable purposes in Ireland, such legacy
or portion thereof (as the case may
be) shall be exempt from legacy duty;
(b) Any succession or part of a succession
which, if it were a legacy or part of
a legacy given by the will of the predecessor, would be exempt under this
resolution from legacy duty shall be
exempt from succession duty;
(c) The said exemptions shall apply only
where the charity becomes entitled in
possession to the legacy or succession
on, or with reference to, the death of
a person dying on or after the date on
which the aforesaid amendments of
law come into operation.
Payments to Exchequer by Local Authorities.
III. That it is expedient to provide
for the payment into the Exchequer of
Northern Ireland of sums of the following
amounts, to be levied and raised by local
authorities, in respect of the cost to the
said Exchequer of educational services for
each financial year, namely, such amounts
as are equivalent to the produce of a local
rate on all rateable hereditaments of sixpence in the pound for the financial year
ending the thirty-first day of March,
nineteen hundred and thirty-five, and one
shilling in the pound for each financial
year thereafter.
Mr. HEALY: I think the first duty
the Committee will expect me to discharge
on rising will be to congratulate the
Minister of Finance on the clearness with
which he was able to present this Budget,
notwithstanding the many years that
have passed over his head. However we
may view the Government-and I think
there can be no doubt in the minds of
many people about that-it does not
extend to our personal feelings and
relations towards the right hon. Gentleman. Indeed, I think the most satisfactory feature of this Budget is that the
right hon. Gentleman is here himself to
present it. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It is unfortunate for him, I am afraid,
and for the Government, that this is the
thirteenth Budget that has been presented
to the Parliament of Northern Ireland,
and I think by universal consent it will be
admitted to be the unlucky one.
It is a
Budget that will cause the first wave of
depression to spread amongst the various
classes in Northern Ireland who are going
to be affected by it. This Government
made a good deal of capital out of the
fact that it walked step by step with

Great Britain in matters of taxation. But
whatever claim they may have made in
the past in that connection has gone today. You have come to the cross roads,
and now you are walking down an avenue
that probably leads to——
Mr. ELLIOTT: The Free State.
Mr. HEALY: a more perilous position
than you have been in for a considerable
time. The amount shown in this Budget
is merely spectacular. We are discussing
a
budget involving eight-and-a-half
million pounds, but the real taxation over
which we have control amounts to only a
million and a half. Some hon. Members
of this House know that in passing
through the streets of the city they see
certain shops decorated with wares that
are really dummies. I think this Parliament is very much in that position today. We are talking about five, six and
eight millions of pounds, but in reality
this flouse has control over only one and
a half millions. A Belfast newspaper, a
Government organ, recently criticised the
Finance Minister of the Free State for
the method he had adopted in balancing
his Budget, and they quoted the case of
Oliver Goldsmith, who on a very notable
occasion thanked God he had paid off all
his creditors, when in fact all he had
done was to give them I.O.U.'s. I think
people who live in glass houses ought not
to throw stones.
Mr. ELLIOTT: You keep doing it all
the same.
Mr. HEALY: That Belfast newspaper
ought not to raise the cry of victory until
they had at least got their feet out of the
bog. There are two matters which I
think will strike the public of Northern
Ireland particularly. The first is the
recent revaluation of Belfast and the Six
Counties. Great Britain may have been
very generous with you up to now, but
it is perfectly clear to anybody who
studies the situation that the time is
coming when Great Britain is going to
exact her pound of flesh. She is going to
get it off you in the form of extra taxation,
and she is going to get it off you in the
withdrawal of many of the grants upon
which you have been relying from the
beginning until now. But the most disquieting feature, or at all events one of
the most disquieting features of the
Budget, will be the throwing on the local
rates of the cost of education. From the
Nationalist point of view this has a more
serious side than is apparent. If we must
go to the local administration in futurebecause I am afraid the tendency is going
to be in that direction-we are going to
have to go to local administrations that
are politically hostile to us, and however it
may have been with the Government in
the past, I think we are not likely to fare
any better with the County Councils in
the future.
The Minister of Finance, speaking of
motor taxation, almost indicated that the
possession of a motor-car was regarded as
wealth. I think he is not going to
appreciably add to that wealth in future.
Motor owners, the majority of whom use
their cars for business purposes, will feel
keen disappointment to-day at the refusal
of the Minister of Finance to follow the
course that has been pursued in Great
Britain. I also think there will be
particular disappointment in Belfast,
where the only crude oil factory in the
Six Counties exists, that this additional
taxation is going to be imposed upon
them, and at a time, I suppose, when the
output is increasing far more than will be
possible in the future.
The Chancellor has already raided the
Road Fund, and I think that is not in
the interests of the maintenance of the
roads. In Great Britain the road area
is far smaller in proportion to the
taxation than in Northern Ireland, and
therefore there was less justification for
taking out of the Road Fund moneys
that were intended clearly by Statute
to be for the maintenance of the roads.
The fact that the roads in Northern
Ireland are not being kept up to the
standard that one would expect from
the additional taxation derived from
motors is, I think, rather deplorable.
I have not much fault to find with the
additional taxation on heavy lorries,
because for
a long time the local
authorities have felt that these vehicles,

a great deal more injury to the roads
than anything which could possibly be
derived by way of taxation. They have
been competing with the railway services
and working long hours-working hours.
it is not possible for the railway companies to ask their servants to work.

the Budget, by which the Minister draws
£150,000 out of reserve, is an indication,
to a great extent, that he has come to the
end of his tether. He first raided the
Road Fund; then he raided the reserve of
the Land Purchase Fund, and now he
has raided the Reserve Fund.
Mr. POLLOCK: I did not do anything
of the kind. I did not attempt to raid
any sinking fund.
Mr. HEALY: You have taken
£150,000 out of reserve here in order to
balance your Budget.
Mr. POLLOCK: Reserves are for that
purpose.
Mr. HEALY: When a firm begins to
draw on its reserves to balance its
accounts, where has it come to? I suggest
that it is beginning to slide down the slippery slope. That is exactly the position
of the Government, however they may try
to disguise it. Every hen roost has been
robbed and pillaged, and now you have
come to the point of throwing on the local
authorities the cost of education. That
is a very serious question. The local
authorities are not able to bear that, and
the end of the thing will be that you will
throw the cost of the whole of the educational services on to the local authorities.
That will mean that this time next year
the rate will not be 1/- but 2/-; and so
the progress will continue, and this
institution will begin to slip further and
further away from that stability on which
it prided itself in its earlier years.
First Resolution agreed to.
Second Resolution agreed to.
Third Resolution agreed to.
Resolutions to be reported to-morrow;
Committee to sit again to-morrow.

SENATE'S AMENDMENT.
Order for consideration of Senate's
Amendment read.
CLAUSE 1 (Extension of Period of
Residence in the United Kingdom required by s. 9 of 7 and 8 Geo. 5, c. 64,
and s. 4 of 18 and 19 Geo. 5, c. 24).
Senate Amendment:
Clause 1, page 1, line 11, at end add
"Provided that a person who is registered
as a parliamentary or local government
elector in the register which is in force
or
at the passing of this Act shall not be
disqualified from being registered
voting as such elector by reason only of
the provisions of this section."
(Mr.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL
Babington): I beg to move "That this
House do agree with the Senate in
the said Amendment."
When the Bill left this House it was
in doubt whether this Clause, which provides that a voter shall not be qualified
until he has had seven years' residence,
applied to persons who were already
on the register or not. When the matter
was considered in another place it was
felt that it would be better to put in
this Amendment in order to make it
clear that persons who have been on the
register, and are entitled to vote under
the law as it stands at present, should
have their rights preserved, and that
this inhibition should extend only to persons coming on to the register in future.
There is also another minor reason
other than the equitable one why this
Amendment should be accepted. If it
were not it might cause complications in
the register, because names on the
register might have to be taken off.
Accordingly, the Government, having
considered this, ask the House to accept
the Amendment proposed by the Senate.
When the matter is looked at from the
point of view of equity the House will
probably consider that when the Bill left
this House it was not intended that persons who, under the law as it stands at
present, had acquired the right to vote
should be prohibited from voting in
future. Accordingly I beg to move.
Mr. MCCARROLL: I think the
intention of the House in the first instance
was quite clear. This seven years'
exclusion period was meant to applyand I have no doubt that in the minds of
the Government when they introduced the
Bill it was meant so to apply to all
persons resident in Northern Ireland.
With all due respect to the Attorney-
General may I suggest that the reasons
he has advanced for this House now
accepting the Amendment proposed by
the Senate are not correct reasons. I think
I should go not to the Senate but to the
Unionist headquarters in order to find the
genuine reason for the insertion of this
Amendment. I suggest that it is not the
1669 Representation of People Bill

16 MAY 1934
Adjournment
[Mr. McCarroll]
Amendment of the Senate at all but the
Amendment of the political party that
brought in this Bill for their own political
interests in this area.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: It must be
borne in mind that this House has already
given the Third Reading to this Bill, and
that the Bill itself cannot now be discussed. The only matter open to debate
is the Amendment made by the Senate.
Mr. McCARROLL: I do not propose
to go outside the present Clause at all.
I merely wish to state that so far as I am
concerned, and so far as the party I
am associated with is concerned, we are
not interested in the least at this stage as
to whether this Amendment is accepted
or not. What I do want to point out is
this, that the Amendment is the result of
the discovery that the operation of the
Clause as it stood when it left this House
would seriously affect the political interests
of the party that introduced this Bill. I
know this as an actual fact from those who
have investigated the register, and have
pursued a house-to-house investigation,
that the operation of the Clause as it left
this House would have seriously prejudiced the interests of the Government
party. For that reason, and for no other
reason, has this Amendment been introduced. There is no doubt whatever about
it. It is simply a question of playing the
game of politics throughout.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 17th May, 1934.
The House met at Three of the clock.
The Clerk, at the Table, informed the
House of the unavoidable absence of Mr.
SPEAKER from this day's sitting.
Whereupon Mr. MOLES, the Chairman of Ways and Means, proceeded to
the Table, and, after Prayers, took the
Chair as Deputy-Speaker, pursuant to
the Standing Order.

Ministry of Education:
Public
Elementary Schools Regulations, 1934. (By Act.)
Oral Answers to Questions.
LIVE PIG EXPORT SCHEME.
1. Mrs. PARKER asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state if
any representations have been made by
his Department to the Pigs Marketing
Board, as to the necessity of using the
local markets, with their existing weighing facilities, as depots in the various
collecting centres which are to be set up
in connection with the live pig export
scheme.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The answer is in the negative. It is
understood, however, that the Pigs
Marketing Board is fully alive to the
desirability of making use of the local
markets and of the weighing facilities
provided by them when this can be done
in connection with the assembly of live
pigs for export.
LOANS GUARANTEE ACTS.
2. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the total
amount of Government guarantees
issued under the Loans Guarantee Acts
up to 31st March, 1934, the amount of
loans repaid up to the same date and
the total amount of the guarantees outstanding.
that
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): In reply, I would refer the hon.
Member to the last published quarterly
return for the quarter ended 31st March,
1934, from which it will be noted
guarantees issued up to that
date amounted in the aggregate to
£15,118,307. The total repayments to
that date amounted to £4,015,669,
leaving the total amount of guarantees
outstanding at £11,102,638.

The following Amendment stood in the
name of Mr. Nixon:-First Resolution,
to move to insert, "The duty on private
motor-cars shall be fifteen shillings for
every unit of horse power."
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: There is
an Amendment standing in the name of
the hon. Member for Woodvale. If he
will look at paragraph 6 under the heading, "Other Vehicles," he will find the
words, "Exceeding 6 horse power, £1 for
each unit or part of a unit of horse
power." The technical Amendment
that he will move will be to delete those
words in order to insert the words which
appear on the Order Paper under his
name. That is clearly the technical
form.
Mr. NIXON: I beg to move, that
"The duty on private motor-cars shall
be 15s for every unit of horse power." I
hope hon. Members opposite will be careful how they vote, because if they vote
and lose their seats the Government will
convert them into resident magistrates or
judges, or something like that. I would
like, at the outset, to congratulate the
Minister of Finance on still retaining his
personality and good health. That
really is a personal compliment to the
Minister which I mean. I also want to
congratulate him on his nerve, because it
takes some nerve to stand at this Table
and impose on the loyal people of Ulster
the highest taxes in the world. That is
where we stand to-day. I noticed as I was
coming up here that the very flags over
this House are drooping. I would also
like to congratulate him on the way he
can manipulate the Press-
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: Will the
hon. Gentleman allow me to explain to
him the procedure? For the moment we
are discussing a particular Amendment
which stands in his name. Until that
has been disposed of one way or other by
the House we cannot debate the Budget
as a whole. When the Amendment is
disposed of and I put
I put the general
question the whole matter will be open.
For the moment we must stand on the
Amendment.
Mr. NIXON: I quite appreciate that,
and I do not intend to go outside the
Amendment, but I wanted just to pay a
few compliments before I started. My
Amendment deals with private motorcars. That, of course, is not saying that
I do not take exception to other parts
of the Budget. Usually a Budget is a
secret, but this was no secret since the
Prime Minister attended the dinner of
the Water Board, because he made it
quite plain, after he had something complimentary to say about myself, that
there were going to be no remissions as
far as he was concerned.
Now, the Minister of Finance, in
introducing the Budget, and by the way
of apologising for not taking off or reducing those duties, threw out this
challenge, what would we do if we were
in his shoes and found ourselves up
against a deficit? The reply to that is
that there would be no deficit if the
Minister had taken the advice he got
from both sides of the House during the
last twelve years.
: That

Ways and Means-
Report Stage
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
I thought it was the policy of the
Government to encourage new industries,
but according to this Budget and according to the statement of the Minister, it
appears to be the policy of the Government to put on a tax that will deter
manufacturers from starting the industry
of manufacturing motor-cars in Northern
Ireland. Someone may say that is not
likely to happen, but I remember reading not so long ago in the "News-
Letter" that such a thing was contemplated. If the Imperial Government
reduce taxes to encourage industry are
we to be told by this step-by-step Government here that they will not reduce them
because they do not want to encourage
industry? Is that the way Northern
Ireland is going to be treated? If it is
I, as one person who loves this city,
regret it very much indeed. We are
often told that there is nothing tells as
much against industry as taxation, and
I agree with that. But this Budget, and
this Clause with which I am dealing
now, in particular, is calculated to drive
out, for all time, any notion that any
manufacturer might have of starting the
industry of manufacturing motor-cars in
Northern Ireland.
A few days ago the hon. and gallant
Member for Central Armagh (Major
Shillington) presented to this House a
Petition signed by 7,000 people asking for
a rebate of this taxation. I hope to-day
that the hon. and gallant Member will
support that Petition with his vote in
this House. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) But I am very much afraid that
the Ulster Motor Union that got up that
Petition, as it is at present controlled, is
like the Ulster Farmers' Union, and that
it is only a branch of the official Ulster
Unionist Party. I am very much afraid
that it was not taxation that was
troubling the Minister so much as a desire
to assist the railway companies. I am
very suspicious of the Northern Government in that respect. They are always
leaning in that direction for reasons that
we know.
I have little doubt that if this rebate
were granted-and the Minister admitted
something like this on a former occasion
-the Minister would probably get more
duties than he will get without the rebate.
Northern Ireland is full of old cars that
are lying up because people cannot afford
to take them out. Before a man takes
out his car now he wants to be a wealthy
man in order to pay the pound per horse
power and insurance, and the result is
that he allows it to lie up. But if this
taxation were taken off thousands of old
cars would go out. The lower duty would
be paid. The duty on petrol for those
old cars would be paid and would be
another source of income. In addition
the ranks of unemployed motor mechanics
would be greatly relieved, because if you
take out an old car it is not long out till
you have to put it into a garage, and some
man gets a job repairing it. But the
Government do not want that. They do
not want the old cars out. They want
the people to travel on the railways. I
do not intend to take up a long time on
this. I want to test the vote of the
House, and, having regard to the fact that
we are out of step, I want to reiterate
what I stated here before that the only
remedy is to get back to the good honourable Imperial Parliament.

pose of helping the Exchequer on one

a ratepayers' question, that, notwithstanding what the hon. Member claims as

Ireland, and that the ratepayers must pay
the balance. Therefore, had I agreed

that we would have denuded the Road
Fund to the extent at any rate that the
local authorities, and therefore the ratepayers, would have had to provide the
difference. In the interests of whom?
Of the motor users. It has always been
held as an axiom in this House and elsewhere that is was those who used the roads
who were entitled to maintain the roads.
If that theory be correct then obviously
it would have been a fatal policy for us
to have reduced the taxation upon those
who really use the roads, the main portion
of whom are really luxury owners, if I
may put it that way. As I have said the
ratepayers would have had to pay twothirds as against one-third from the Road
Fund.
In reply to the hon. Member's suggestion that in this instance we have departed

(2) Legacy Duty and Succession Duty.
Resolution reported: That it is
expedient to amend the law relating to
Legacy Duty and Succession Duty by
providing that
(a) The enactments relating to the
exemption from Legacy Duty of charitable bequests shall extend only to such
of those bequests as may be given for
charitable purposes in Ireland, but so
that, where the Ministry of Finance is
satisfied that the whole or part of a
legacy given for charitable purposes
has been or will be applied to charitable purposes in Ireland, such legacy
or portion thereof (as the case may
be) shall be exempt from Legacy Duty.
(b) Any succession or part of a
succession which, if it were a legacy or
part of a legacy given by the will of
the predecessor, would be exempt
under this resolution from Legacy
Duty shall be exempt from Succession
Duty;
(c) The said exemptions shall apply
only where the charity becomes
entitled in possession to the legacy or
succession on, or with reference to, the
death of a person dying on or after the
date on which the aforesaid amendments of law come into operation.
Mr. MURPHY: I want to express my
entire opposition to this Resolution.
Before doing so I would like to join with

spoken in this debate, in congratulating

As the Minister stated in opening his

passed as far back as the year 1842
certain charitable legacies were exempted
from the payment of legacy duty.
Whether that policy is right or wrong,
it was adopted in the year 1842. But
the House should remember, and those
Ways and Means-

enhon. Members who were not aware of it

towards

charity during his lifetime when he is

a
"And defer not charities till death.

It seems to me that those words of Lord

It also seems to me that, so far from
increasing the abatement given to certain
charities in Ireland, the policy of the
Government should rather be to decrease

Resolution is to increase the scope of

know that, while under this Statuto
passed in 1842 certain charitable
legacies were exempted from the payment of legacy duty, that exemption
was confined to charities which were
applied to charitable purposes in Ireland,
and the question of whether the exemption could be more generally applied
was finally determined as far back as
1868. Since the year 1868 the law has
been quite clearly stated, and adopted
and acquiesced in by everyone, that that
exemption from the payment of legacy
duty should be so confined. But now it
is proposed by this Resolution that the
enactments relating to the exemption
from legacy duty should extend only to
such bequests as may be given for
charitable purposes in Ireland. It seems
more or less an innocuous Resolution, but

"but so that, where the Ministry of
Finance is satisfied that the whole or
part of a legacy given for charitable
purposes has been or will be applied to
charitable purposes in Ireland, such
legacy or portion thereof (as the case
may be) shall be exempt from legacy
duty."
Under this Resolution it is now suggested
that the Ministry of Finance should determine what part of a charitable legacy,
which under the existing law would be
subject to legacy duty, should be declared
exempt from legacy duty, and that the
Ministry of Finance should also determine
what portion of that legacy should be
treated as applicable to charitable
purposes
in Ireland. It seems to me that that is
objectionable on a great many grounds. I
cannot see why this exemption should
have been extended. I cannot see why

exempt. I cannot see why that matter
should be left to the determination of the
Ministry of Finance. Personally, I cannot understand what has induced our

POLLOCK: The position in
respect of the present arrangements in

unchanged and will not be affected by

to remind the House that this question of
assuming local responsibility for education is not by any means a new one.
the year 1918 I was responsible for the
preparation of a Bill on behalf of the
local authority in Belfast-the Corporation to enable them to provide school
accommodation and to carry on a system
of education under practically the same
conditions as were provided in the Bill
which ultimately found its way to the

But now, when a comparatively small
burden is thrown upon them in regard to
Ways and Means

it, and when the State takes over the
whole of the education system, which for
Belfast they themselves were prepared to
do at that time, you would think that an
avalanche has burst upon them or that,
as some hon. Member has said, a bombshell had been thrown amongst them.
This levy will naturally be made upon
the underated portions of the country,
but I would remind hon. Members that,
although our farmers are derated, their
farm houses are not derated and will have
to bear their proportion of this levy. I
am sorry the hon. Member for Mid-
Antrim (Mr. Crawford) is not here at
the moment. I think the figures which
he suggested as representing the
unexpected burden upon the authorities
in County Antrim were greatly enlarged.
However, I need not go into that now,
because the fact is that it is a rate and
not an amount. But provision will be
made to relieve public authorities of any
great disturbance they think may occur
in regard to their finances, either by
giving them the necessary authority to
supplement the rates, just as we submit
supplementary estimates here, or,
alternatively, to borrow money to carry
them over to the following year. No
difficulty can arise on that point, and it
is really nothing to interfere with the
character of the general arrangement.
Let me suggest that, as the county
councils are responsible for the finance of
all this matter, and as they have control
of the local education authorities, it will
be their duty, if they consider it right to
do so in the interests of economy, to
curtail the enterprises of the local education authorities if they think they are
too expansive or, as some hon. Members
have said, too grandiose. I do not suggest
they are, but I would point out that this
whole matter rests in the hands of the
county councils.
I can assure the House that it is not a
very pleasant task which I have to perform in connection with this subject. It
really has, to use a common expression,
been boiling up for some years. We have
been reminded over and over again that
we are not living up to our responsibilities, and that if we were not prepared to take over the education of our
own children some other arrangement
would have to be made. After all, if we
are getting and taking all the advantages
of British citizenship in respect of all the
social services, which claim such an
enormous amount of money, and are
helped by the British Government in that
respect, I do not think it is unreasonable,
when you bring the matter down to hard
argument, that the British Government
should expect that we would endeavour to
live up to our responsibilities. And if
the fathers and mothers of families are
interested in the education of their
children surely the small imposition that
will be made upon them in respect of this
matter should not be regarded as a dreadful burden. Remember that in the city
of Glasgow, which is an industrial centre
corresponding to our own, the education rate is something like 4s 9d or 5s in
the pound. We are not going to the local
authorities to say we want 5s, or 4s, or
even 3s in the pound.
I have resisted this for a considerable
time, but if we establish the principle
that we are willing to assume local responsibility for the education of our children,
and that we are willing to pay for that
principle, then I think we may take it for
granted that the local authorities are not
likely, at any rate in the immediate
future, to be called upon to bear any
heavier burden than is now suggested by
this levy as it is called. In the general
interests of the Province there is no via
media. We have either to say that we
are willing to acccept partial responsibility for the education of our children,
or upset our whole relations with the
Imperial Government. I need not
remind the House that those relations
have been of the pleasantest kind, and
that this is the only disturbing factor we
have had in the settlement of the
multitudinous affairs and accounts with
which we have had to deal on the other
side. I think, therefore, although we
may squirm a little, although it may be an
unpleasant duty for me to stand at this
Table and say I am the head of the
Department responsible for the execution
of this it is a Government responsibility
deliberately undertaken by the Government still I hope and believe that the
ratepayers of the Province will recognise
their responsibility to their children of
giving them a good education, and the
advantage of having control of education,
to such an extent that they will not
object to what, after all, is a comparative
moiety of the cost that is imposed upon

22 MAY 1934
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 22nd May, 1934.
The House met at Three of the Clock.
The Clerk, at the Table, informed the
House of the unavoidable absence of Mr.
SPEAKER from this day's sitting.
Whereupon Mr. MOLES, the Chairman of Ways and Means, proceeded to
the Table, and, after Prayers, took the
Chair as Deputy-Speaker, pursuant to
the Standing Order.
Oral Answers to Questions.
EQUIPMENT OF PUBLIC SERVICE
VEHICLES.
are
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether any precautions
are taken to see that all public service
vehicles
provided with adequate
emergency exits; whether a sufficient
and suitable number of instruments are
available in all buses for the purpose of
forcing windows or doors in the event
of an accident; and whether the windows
of buses are so fixed as to be capable
of being adjusted to regulate the ventilation as circumstances may require.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): It is provided by
the Regulations that
every omnibus
must be provided with an emergency exit
unless it was in use before June, 1932,
and had the entrance behind the rear
axle.
All omnibuses must carry two hatchets
similar to those used by the fire brigades.
One is carried inside the vehicle and the
other outside. These Regulations are
rigidly enforced.
With regard to the last part of the
question, the Regulations provide that
there must be adequate ventilation without the necessity for opening the main
windows. Where a window of a public
service vehicle has been constructed so as
to be capable of being adjusted and is
found not to be capable of being
so adjusted, the owner is required to have
the defect remedied. If the defect is
not put right the licence for the vehicle
is withdrawn.
PLANNING AND HOUSING ACT,
1931.
2. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether it is obligatory
upon local authorities to operate Part II
of the Planning and Housing Act
(Northern Ireland), 1931.
Sir DAWSON BATES: While Part
II of the Planning and Housing Act,
1931, imposes certain obligations on
local authorities in connection with the
clearance and improvement of unhealthy
areas, these obligations are subject to
certain conditions and to the proviso
that the resources of the authority concerned are sufficient to enable them to
be carried into effect.
THE "ULSTER PROTESTANT."
3. Mr. HEALY asked the Attorney-
General whether he is
now in a
position to deal with the incitements to
crime contained in the May issue of the
Ulster Protestant League, with which
a well-known clergyman is prominently
connected; whether the placards in red
advertising it are pasted on hoardings
on the Newtownards Road; whether it is
the duty, both of the Ministry of Home
Affairs and the Detective Branch of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary, to file
copies of such publications; and whether
he can state if this duty was neglected in
this instance.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Babington): I have dealt with the
matter referred to by the hon. Member.
The article referred to is most inproper, but does not, in my opinion,
constitute a criminal offence. Accordingly, I have directed that no action be
taken.
My only knowledge of this publication
is derived from one copy which has been
submitted to me.
The answer to the last part of the
question is in the negative.
Mr. HEALY: Is the right hon.
Gentleman going to wait until this incitement to crime is implemented before
he takes action?

Motor Vehicles and Road Traffic Bill.
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
The CHAIRMAN: In addition to the
Amendments that appear on the Order
Paper that has been circulated, a considerable number of manuscript Amendments were handed in to-day. For the
moment they are not available to hon.
Members, but we hope to have them.
shortly. In the meantime, as we reach
them I will indicate where they come
in on the Bill.
CLAUSE 1 (Penalties for reckless or
dangerous driving).
*
* *
*
*
*
(1) If any person drives a motorcar on a public highway recklessly or
at a speed or in a manner which is
dangerous to the public, having
regard to all the circumstances of the
case, including the nature, condition
and use of the highway, and the
amount of traffic which is actually at
the time, or which might reasonably
be expected to be, on the highway,
he shall be liable-
(a) on summary conviction to a fine of
one pound or any greater sum not
exceeding ten pounds, or in the
case of a second conviction to a
fine of two pounds or any greater
sum not exceeding twenty pounds,
or in the case of a third or subsequent conviction to a fine of
five pounds or any greater sum
not exceeding fifty pounds, or, in
the discretion of the court, in the
case of any conviction under this
section to imprisonment for a
period not exceeding three months
in addition to or in lieu of any
such fine as aforesaid;
indictment to
imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, or to a fine, or
to both such imprisonment and
fine.
(b) on conviction on
On the trial of any indictment for
manslaughter in connection with the
driving of a motor-car, the jury may
acquit the defendant of manslaughter
and find him guilty of an offence
under this section.
Mr. MINFORD: I beg to move, in
page 2, line 6, to leave out "case" ("circumstances of the case") to "he" ("he
shall be liable") in line 10.
This Amendment stands in the name
of the hon. Member (Professor Johnstone) and myself. We consider these
words should be omitted in the Bill.
This Clause particularly refers to cars
coming from a side road, and we feel
that if these words were deleted it would
be very much fairer.
Sir DAWSON BATES: This Amendment cannot be accepted by the Government. It seems to me to be most
unreasonable. Surely when a motorist
is using the public road the matters
which it is proposed to leave out are
the very things which a reasonable and
careful driver should take into account,
such as, whether it is a narrow road or
a wide road, whether it is greasy, and,
above all, he should take into consideration what traffic he would expect to meet
on that road. I would ask my hon.
Friend behind me is it to be an excuse
for driving fast out of a side road on
to a normally busy road that there did
not happen to be traffic on that road at
the time he drove out.
In 99 cases out of 100 that individual
might get away with it, but that would
not be due to any care on the part of
the motorist, but only, might I say, by
the mercy of Providence. If it is
correct that these matters are to be
taken into account by an ordinary
prudent motorist, why should we not
state that in the Bill, as we have done?
After all, this Bill is brought forward
for the purpose of trying to reduce
accidents. I am glad to think that the
vast majority of motorists are careful
drivers, but there is a minority who are
absolutely reckless, and it is with that
minority this Bill proposes to deal. For
these reasons the Government cannot
accept this Amendment.
Professor JOHNSTONE: I should
like to correct the right hon. Gentleman. There is no intention on the
part of the mover of the Amendment or
myself to exclude from the purview of
magistrates persons who do not take into
consideration the amount of traffic on the
highway at the time. Personally, I put
my name to this Amendment because I

Mr. MINFORD: I beg to move, in
page 2, lines 11 and 12, to leave out

The reason I move that these words
be deleted is that I do not think there
should be a minimum fine. The last
Amendment I did not press to a

Amendment.
Professor JOHNSTONE: I would
like to support what has been said by
the hon. Member for Antrim. It is in
the recollection of most Members of this
Committee that when the Motor Bill of
1930 was before the House the Minister
of Home Affairs and the House were
quite satisfied that they could not
altogether rely on unpaid magistrates to

by this Clause, which the Ministry ask
us to accept, that they do not quite
believe in the resident magistrates either.
I suggest that the Ministry have power

acted.
I would like to point out also that it
is a great pity minimum penalties should
be put on.
I am quite in favour of
putting on maximum penalties so that

CLAUSE 2 (Penalties for driving
motor-car when under the influence of
drink or drugs).
(1) The following section shall be substituted for section two of the principal
Act:
2. (1) If any person is found when
driving or attempting to drive, or when
in charge of, a motor-car on any highway or other public place to be under
the influence of drink or drugs to such
an extent as to be incapable of having
proper control of the vehicle, he shall
be liable-
(a)
on summary conviction to a fine
of five pounds or any greater sum
not exceeding fifty pounds, or in
the case of a second or subsequent
conviction to a fine of ten pounds
or any greater sum not exceeding
one hundred pounds, or, in the
discretion of the court, in the case
of any conviction under this section
to imprisonment for a period not
exceeding six months in addition
to or in lieu of any such fine as
aforesaid.
(b) on conviction on indictment to
imprisonment for a term not
exceeding two years, or to a fine,
or to both such imprisonment and
fine.
On the trial of any indictment for
manslaughter in connection with the
driving of a motor-car, the jury may
acquit the defendant of manslaughter
and find him guilty of an offence under
this section.
(2) Any person liable to be charged
with an offence under this section shall
not be liable to be charged under
section twelve of the Licensing Act,
1872, with the offence of being drunk
while in charge on a highway or other
public place, of a carriage.
(3) A police constable may apprehend
without warrant any person who he
has reason to believe is committing an
offence under this section.
(2) Sections two and three of the Act
of 1929 are hereby repealed.

Mr. CRAWFORD: I beg to move, in
Clause 2, page 2, line 38, to leave out
from "drugs" ("influence of drink or
drugs") to "he" in line 40.
I want to move to delete these lines. I
wish to say in doing so that I am in full
sympathy with the objects of this Bill.
I realise that the Government are making
an honest effort to try to reduce the
number of accidents that take place on
the roads. I really feel that as this
Clause stands at present the wording is
not satisfactory. It gives drivers absolute
freedom up to the point of being incapable. I do not think that has been
satisfactory in the past, I do not think it
is satisfactory in this Bill, and I do not
think it will work satisfactorily in time to
come. How is it to be decided that a
driver is incapable? The person charged
has the right to call in his own doctor. The
doctor may not be at home; he may not
be available for an hour. Then he is
obliged to come to give evidence that in
his opinion the driver was capable two
hours after the accident. I think
altogether that is a very unsatisfactory
thing. The police doctor and the doctor
called in may not agree. And the result
is it is a very difficult thing to find out the
exact quantity. I would like to point out
what has been very clearly stated in correspondence that took place in the "London
Times" in the month of January. The
correspondence was carried on by several
eminent members of the medical profession and others. They pointed out in a
way that would have convinced me if I
had not thought they were perfectly right
in saying that a person under the influence of drink or drugs might be very
dangerous, although he could not be said
to be drunk or incapable. That is where
the difficulty comes in. It is a most
important thing for this Committee to
know that a person may be dangerous
under the influence of drink while no
person could say he was incapable. Every
drunk person is under the influence of
drink. Any observer can tell that, but
every person under the influence of drink
cannot be said to be drunk, although he
may be dangerous. That is what the
Minister of Home Affairs has failed to
realise, and in this Bill, which is admirable, it is not made suufficiently clear.
A great man Dr. Eccles, of London,
states postively that alcohol in all its
stages of influence on the nervous system,
is a narcotic. A narcotic is any substance
which, reaching the cells of the brain,
causes it to function less quickly than is
normal for that person. I looked up the
best dictionary I could find and the meaning of narcotic is any substance which
produces stupor or drowsiness. It is not
the amount swallowed. We hear people
saying we only had one bottle of stout or
two half-ones. But this eminent doctor
says it is not the amount swallowed; it
is the amount that circulates in the blood.
I would like to emphasise that. He goes
