The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: I was
rather surprised at this Amendent,
especially having regard to the quarter
from which it comes. I think it right
the Committee should really understand
what the Amendment involves.
Prior to the last Act that was passed
by this House the test was whether a man
was drunk or not. If he was drunk in
charge of a car he was convicted and
there was no definition of drunkenness
other than under the old common law
where a policeman was the judge of
whether a man was drunk or sober. When
that Act was before the House the Member for the University (Rev. Professor
Corkey) referred to the Commission which
sat on the other side of the water, and
he quoted a speech of one of the Ministers
at Westminster when he dealt with this
question as to the uncertainty of the
meaning of the word "drunk." He pressed
upon the House that there should be a
further definition of the word "drunk."
and accordingly he moved an Amendment
to the Bill then before the House to the
effect that any person found when driving
or attempting to drive a mechanically
propelled vehicle to be so under the
influence of drink or drugs as to be
incapable of having proper control of such
vehicle shall be liable, etcetera. Those
are the very words in this Clause.
They are not the Government's words,
they are the words of the Member for
the University, whose name is associated
with this Amendment, and in order to
make it clear what the meaning of the
word "drunk" is the Government
accepted that Amendment and it is now
part of our law. But they are not
satisfied with that. The words now in
the Clause having been substituted for the
word drunk," hon. Members now want
to get rid of the words, "to such an
extent as to be incapable of having proper
control of the vehicle." Previously it
was "drunk," and then, "so under the
influence of drink as to be incapable of
having proper control," and now hon.
Members ask that the qualification of
being incapable of having proper control
is to be left out, and the test is merely
to be whether or not a man is under the
influence of drink or drugs.
I look upon this matter entirely from a
practical point of view, having been
engaged for a great number of years in
the administration of the law. How and
when is a policeman to say when a man
is under the influence of drink. It is left
entirely to him. Is he to say that a man
is under the influence of drink when he
has had one drink or when he has had
two drinks of beer. And what test is the
doctor to apply? I think the Committee
will agree that to use the words "under
the influence of drink" without some
qualification or definition will leave the
law in a most absurd state and make it
impossible to administer it. The Constabulary know what "being under the
influence of drink or drugs to such an
extent as to be incapable of having proper
control of the vehicle " means, but I defy
anyone, whether he is a policeman or a
doctor or anyone else, to say what “ being
under the influence of drink or drugs
means, because it is incapable of
definition.
There is a regular formula by which
doctors give a certificate that a man is or
is not under the influence of drink to such
an extent as to be incapable of having
proper control of his car, and unless some
definition is kept in the Bill I think the
Committee will agree that it would be
almost impossible either for the police or

Professor JOHNSTONE: I support

in connection with this Clause on the
Second Reading, and I am afraid I must
have failed to make myself thoroughly

Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Hanna). I
have been accused, generally, of trying
to minimise the offence of being drunk in
charge of a motor-car. I have done
nothing of the sort. I do not wish to

an offence against the law, and the person
found guilty should be punished. What
I did suggest at that time was that if a
man does become drunk and gets into a
motor-car and starts to drive it he has
aggravated the offence. But a distinction
ought to be made between such a man and
the man who is found drunk and lying
asleep in his motor-car. I am putting
this from a practical point of view. The
object of this Bill, as it is the object of
everyone who is interested in it, is to
minimise the number of accidents that
occur on the road. Let me take the case of
a man who brings out his car and puts it
into a public car park. He then proceeds
to spend the evening with friends and gets
too much drink. That man gets into his
car and he is too drunk to drive, and he
falls asleep in the car.
He knows perfectly well that if the policeman on beat
duty sees him he will be convicted. On
the other hand, if that man takes his
courage in both hands and drives the car
he may arrive home without being met by
a policeman. On the way home, however,
he has been a danger to the public on the
public highway, while the man who fell
asleep in his car in a public park was not
a danger to anybody. He may be a
nuisance, but not a danger.

CLAUSE 9 (Duty to furnish reports.
and give information in cases of motor
accidents).
(1) In any case where, owing to the
presence of a motor-car on a public
highway, any accident occurs, the
driver of the motor-car shall as soon as
possible, and in any case within twentyfour hours of the occurrence of the
accident, report the accident at a police
station or to a police constable, and
thereupon give his name and address
and the name and address of the owner
of the motor-car, and if he fails to do
so, he shall be guilty of an offence under
the principal Act.
(2) In any case where, owing to the
presence of a motor-car on a public
highway, any accident occurs, it shall
be the duty of the driver of the car, so
far as it is within his power to do so, to
give to any police officer or constable
who demands the information, the
names and addresses of all persons who
were in the car at the time the accident
occurred, and if such driver fails or
refuses to give such information, or
gives any such information which is to
his knowledge false or misleading, he
shall be guilty of an offence under the
principal Act.
(3) If, in any case where, owing to
the presence of a motor-car on the
public highway, any accident occurs,
the car was being driven by some person
other than the owner, it shall be the
duty of the owner to give to any police
officer or constable who demands it, all
such information in his possession or
procurement as shall be demanded of
him by such officer or constable for the
purposes of ascertaining the names and
addresses of the driver of the car and
of all other persons who were in the

and if any such owner fails or refuses

CLAUSE 12 (Limitation of time for
which drivers of certain vehicles may remain continuously on duty).
(1) With a view to protecting the
public against the risks which arise in
cases where the drivers of motor vehicles
are suffering from excessive fatigue, it
is hereby enacted that it shall not be
lawful, in the case of any public service
vehicle or any goods vehicle, for any
person to drive or cause or permit any
person employed by him or subject to
his orders to drive-
(a) for any continuous period longer
than the number of hours which
may be prescribed for a continuous
period of driving; or
(b) for continuous periods in any period.
of twenty-four hours amounting in
the aggregate to more than the
number of hours which may be prescribed for such continuous periods
of driving; or
(c) so that the driver has not at least
the prescribed period for rest in any
period of twenty-four hours calculated from the commencement of
any period of driving.
(2) For the purposes of this section
and of any regulations made thereunder:
(a) any two or more periods of time
shall be deemed to be a continuous
period unless separated by an interval of not less than half an hour
in which the driver is able to obtain
rest and refreshment;
(b) any time spent by a driver on other
work in connection with a vehicle
or the load carried thereby, including in the case of a public service
vehicle any time spent on a vehicle
while on a journey in any other
capacity than as a passenger, shall
be reckoned as time spent in driving.
(3) If any person acts in contravention
of this section he shall be guilty of an
offence under the principal Act:
Provided that a person shall not
be liable to be convicted under this
section if he proves to the court that
the contravention was due to unavoidable
delay in the completion of any journey
arising out of circumstances which he
could not reasonably have foreseen.
(4) This section shall not apply to
motor vehicles used for fire brigade or
ambulance purposes.

(5) Regulations for the purposes
this section may prescribe periods of

classes of vehicles and for vehicles of the
same class operating under different
conditions, and such prescribed periods
may be varied from time to time.

view of efficiency and safety.

Mr. BEATTIE: I regret that the
Government cannot see their way to

Road Traffic Bill-

on the road. On that occasion I think the
Government agreed that when an appropriate Bill was introduced consideration
would be given to this question. You
may make whatever regulations you like,
but if you neglect to provide for the
limitation of hours of drivers and conductors and others engaged in the transport service you have neglected the
essential factor in safeguarding the roads.
for the users of the roads. The highest
authorities in the land were consulted
before the British Bill was introduced,
and the British Parliament decided that
a limitation of hours was necessary by Act
of Parliament.
It is all very well to say you will make
regulations in accordance with the needs
and requirements of those engaged in the
industry, but it is most important that
an Act of Parliament should define absoiutely the number of hours during which
each man may be employed.
If you
refuse to do that you are omitting from
the Bill the most essential factor in safeguarding the public and users of the road.
I hope the Government will reconsider
their decision and bring in an amendment
on the lines set out in Section 17 of the
British Act. While the British Act lays
down that a driver may be employed for
eleven hours, it does not permit him to
be employed for that period continuously.
The continuous period of duty is restricted
to five-and-a-half hours, and I am going
to argue that five-and-a-half-hours is too
long to allow fair competition on the roads
and the railways. The only way in which
we can ensure that fair competition is to
limit the hours on the roads similarly to
the way they are limited on the railways.
It may seem strange that I should act as
an advocate for the railways, but I do so
in the interests of the employees, who for
many years have been fighting hard to get
a fixed standard of hours and conditions.
That standard is being carried out on the
railways at the present time, and it is
unfair to railway employees that you
should omit from this Bill any similar
limitations of hours for those engaged in
road transport.
The moment you let it become known
that you are about to make regulations to
deal with this question, you will have representations coming from Londonderry,
Coleraine, Ballymena, Armagh, and elsewhere putting forward a case in favour of
fourteen hours at a stretch, with perhaps
six hours continuous duty. You will
have Belfast asking for an eight-hour day
and a six-day week, and you will have a
variety of suggestions and representations
which will create a terrible number of
anomalies in respective districts in regard
to transport rates. Therefore if you
want to have the matter dealt with
properly you must centralise it in an Act
of Parliament and set out quite definitely
what the hours of work are to be.
I think we in this Committee realise that
the travelling public is an asset which we
have to cater for. In the past the railways had a monopoly of that travelling
public, hence the reason for their being
compelled to observe reasonable and fair
working hours and conditions. Road
transport has now taken a portion of that
traffic, and I ask you to regulate the hours
and conditions of the workers engaged in
that industry in the same way as you have
dealt with the railways, and thus give the
same opportunity for both classes of
workers to enjoy equal conditions of
labour. To-day you have the drivers and
conductors employed on buses operated by
the railway companies working longer
hours than the employees on the railways. That is the thin end of the wedge
to lengthen the hours of railway workers,
a thing which we on this side of the Committee will not stand for.

Professor JOHNSTONE: I am sorry,

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: Ambulance drivers and fire brigade drivers are
in a very special class. Sometimes they
do not drive for days. When they do
drive they may be taken to be on active
service just like a soldier, and the
exigencies of their occupation may require
them to drive for very many more hours
or to be at their job for many more hours
than an ordinary person. You cannot say
in the case of an emergency when an
ambulance is out exactly what the period
of that emergency will be. It is almost
impossible very often to make arrangements to have the man relieved. The same
applies to the fire brigade. The fire
brigade in Belfast may be called out
sometimes to a fire at the end of the
Province. The driver may be driving
for the whole night, and, perhaps, next
day on the way back again. These are
two very special classes of employment,
and the Government thought it was only
right they should be excluded from the
general application which can be properly
made in the case of the ordinary employe,
but cannot be in the case of special servants.
Question, "That the Clause stand part

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: I beg
to move, in Clause 16, page 12, line 14,
to leave out from the word "court" ("has
in any court") to the end of line 29, and

"In proceedings of which the insurer

mentioned had notice, obtained judgment against the owner or the driver
of a motor car for a sum in respect of
the liability for which such owner or
driver is insured by a policy issued, or
secured by a security given, for the
purposes of Part II of the Act of 1930,
as amended by this Act, and the
claimant has not recovered from such
owner or driver the whole amount of
such judgment, the claimant may,
within such time as may be prescribed
by rules of court, apply to the court in

an order against the insurer or the

be, to pay to the claimant any sum
payable under the said judgment, including any sum payable thereunder
in respect of costs, and thereupon such
court may, if it thinks proper, grant

whole amount of such judgment and
costs, or in respect of any specified part
of such amount.
(2) The notice mentioned in the last
preceding sub-section shall be in such
form as may be prescribed by rules of
court, and shall be given to the insurer
or the giver of the security, as the case
may be, before or within seven days
after the commencement of the proceedings in which the judgment is sought."
The object of this Clause which it is
proposed to amend is to enable persons
who have obtained judgment for damages.
in respect of injuries in motor accidents
and have failed to recover the damages
to resort to the insurance company. This
is a new principle. It is obvious that if
any person is to be bound by the proceedings he should have notice of the
proceedings. That is a fundamental proposition of our law. It is difficult for
the person who is to benefit under this
Clause that is the insured party-to
obtain the necessary information to enable
him to ascertain what is the insurance
company concerned, so that he may give
them notice, and under the provisions of
Clause 18 of the Bill the person doing
the injury is bound to furnish the information as to his insurance. If he refuses
to do so he is guilty of an offence, and
can be punished.
In order to make it certain that the
necessary information will be available
the Ministry of Home Affairs will make
orders administratively that, when the
certificate of insurance has to be presented
to the local taxation officer for the purpose of licensing the vehicle, a note will
be taken of the insurance company, and
that note by arrangement will be available to any person requiring it. The
result of this will be that when persons
want to bring proceedings under the
circumstances contemplated by this Clause.
they will be able to find out what the
insurance company is which indemnified
the person responsible to them, and they
will be able to have recourse against
them. That is the main portion of this
Clause.
The second matter in the Clause is a
more technical one. Hon. Members will
see that the Clause as it stood prescribed
that a person could apply to the court
in which he recovered judgment for leave
to execute judgment against the authorised insurer who issued the policy. That
is to say, that having failed to recover
against the person who had injured him,
the injured party might take out judgment against the insurance company. The
insurance companies represented to the
Minister of Home Affairs when this Bill
was in draft that this was not a matter
that they looked upon with favour. They
do not want to have judgments issued
against them, and consequently the
Minister has proposed this new Clause,
in which you will see that the claimant
may within such time as may be prescribed by rules of court apply to the
court in which he recovered damages for
an order against the insurance company,
so that instead of taking out judgment
he will apply for an order which will be
granted. And as all the insurance companies under the Bill have to give substantial security and have to be approved
before they are allowed to insure persons,
there will never be any question but that

The court is not to take the fraud or
misrepresentation into consideration unless the claimant has been a party to it or
unless the person making the false statement or misrepresentation has been
prosecuted to conviction under Clause 39
of the Bill.
The Committee will agree that it would
be entirely wrong to allow a claimant to
take advantage of fraud or misrepresentation to which he has been a party. This
principle is universally applied in the
courts.
Our aim in this Clause is not so much
to make an innocent party who has been
induced to enter into a contract by fraud
or misrepresentation, pay, as to suppress
fraud and misrepresentation of this
character. We want to ensure in the first
place that every case of fraud and misrepresentation will come to light, and in
the second place that the person guilty of
such fraud and misrepresentation will be
adequately punished. By this means we
hope to put an end to fraud and misrepresentation, which I am afraid is
rather common to-day, and taking the
longer view I am convinced that this is
a sounder policy and will give much more
satisfactory results than the policy of
compelling a person who has been
defrauded to pay in
every case.
Amendment agreed to.

not
If the driver of any goods vehicle

The persons authorised by
section are

this
(c) any person in the employment of the

Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move
in Clause 24, page 18, line 11, after the
word "vehicle" ("carried on the vehicle")
to insert the words "in connection with
such employment and."
This Clause limits the number of persons who may be carried upon a goods
vehicle. First of all, there is the driver
of the vehicle, then there is the owner
of the vehicle. Then the Clause as it
stands at the present time permits any
person in the employment of the owner
to be carried on a vehicle with the consent of the owner. We think that is too
wide, because it would really permit the
use of the vehicle for purposes for which
it was not intended, and we think that the
use in such cases should be limited to the
carriage of persons in the employment of
the person and in connection with such
employment.
In other words, we propose that the owner of the vehicle should
be allowed to carry his employees for
purposes in connection with their employment, and not for other purposes.
They will not be allowed to use his goods
vehicle as a passenger carrying vehicle
except to this limited extent.
Amendment agreed to.

Mr. BEATTIE: I notice that this
Clause refers to the Fares and Rates
Tribunal, and I want to ask that something should be done to meet the
enormous amount of public opinion that
is gathering against the operations of this
tribunal which the public think is a
means of keeping up the high rates of
travelling that prevail at the present
time. When application is made to this
tribunal for reasonable facilities for
summer residents at the seaside and for
workmen and other classes of persons
who use the road transport they will not
give way. They seem to be subject to
some control from another source, and
might I say that that control is the railways.
I am not saying that that is
correct, but it is what the public think,
and it is what is in the minds of some
persons who have had recourse to this
tribunal in an attempt to obtain reasonable facilities for travelling at the weekends. Their opinion, and the opinion of
working class people, is that some amendment of this Clause is necessary so that
when a reasonable request is made by a

to outlying districts where people go for

I beg to
Professor JOHNSTONE:
move to delete this Clause. Again it is
purely on general grounds that I move
the deletion of this Clause. I think
everybody is agreed that the application
of the Probation of Offenders Act has
been very successful in a great many
cases, and I do not see why motorists
should be deprived of the benefit of this
Act. I do not suppose that many of the
cases dealt with in this Bill would get the
benefit of that Act, but it should be left
to the discretion of the court to give the
benefit of the Act in cases where there
might be a doubt in the mind of the court,
or where there were sufficient extenuating
circumstances. I realise, of course, that
the cases enumerated in the Second
Schedule could not possibly come within
of
the provisions of the Probation
Offenders Act, but there are other classes
of cases which might be dealt with under
that Act.
I
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: I am
not surprised at this point having been
raised, because for some time past this
Probation of Offenders Act has been
applied to cases to which personally I
think it should not have applied, and to
cases to which it was never intended to
apply when it was passed in 1907.
would like to say a word to the Committee
about that Act, because I do not want
there to be any misapprehension as to why
the Government have adopted this Clause.
The Act says that where any person is
charged before a court of summary jurisdiction with an offence, and the charge is
proved, but the court is of the opinion
that having regard to the character,
antecedents, age, health, or mental condition of the person charged, or the trivial
nature of the offence, or the extenuating
circumstances under which the offence was
committed, and that it is inexpedient to
inflict any punishment, or that it is
expedient to release the offender on probation, the court may either make an
order dismissing the charge, or discharge
the offender on a rule of bail to come up
for conviction and sentence if called upon.
That Act was originally passed mainly
to deal with juvenile offenders. To deal
first with the question of character, I
think the Committee will agree that the
character of the accused does not enter
into the case of an offence against the
motoring laws. Whether a man has a
good character or a bad character, if he
commits a motoring offence he is equally
liable to punishment in the eyes of the
law. The antecedents of such defendant
are also an immaterial matter. Neither
does the age of the delinquent apply,
because if a person is so old as to be
incapable of managing a car he should not
be on the road, and he cannot complain
if he is convicted of an offence.
other hand, if he is so young as to be
incapable of looking after himself he is.
not entitled to have a licence. Again, if
a man is not in proper health and able
to control his car efficiently he cannot
complain if he is convicted. The same
applies to his mental condition. If his
mentality is so poor that he is not capable
of looking after himself on the road he
should not be there.
On the
With regard to the trivial nature of the
offence, as the Member for the University
(Professor Johnstone) has pointed out,
the cases mentioned in the Second
Schedule are offences which cannot be
considered trivial. They comprise reckless
or dangerous driving, being under the
influence of drink or drugs while in
charge of a motor-car, using a motor-car
in contravention of section six of the Act
of 1930, offences under sub-section (1) of
section three of the principal Act of-
(a) driving a motor-car during a period
of suspension of licence; or (b) driving a
motor-car while disqualified for obtaining
a licence; or (c) obtaining a licence while
disqualified for obtaining such licence.
All these are deliberate offences. The
motoring public enjoy a great privilege in
being allowed to use the roads, and a
regular code is laid down for their
behaviour. They are all supposed to
know this code because they have to pay
a licence before they are entitled to go on
the road, and they also have to pay a
licence in respect of their car. None of
these offences can be committed through
inadvertence, and when all these matters
are taken into consideration, and looking
at the object of the Probation of Offenders
Act, there is nothing hard or unconscion-
Road Traffic Bill-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Attorney-General]
able in the Government saying that in
these serious matters the Probation of
Offenders Act should no longer apply.
The motoring public should not complain,
nor do I think they will complain.
I think it will relieve the magistrates
who administer the law of a very great
burden, because they are pressed day
after day in cases in which it should not
be pressed upon them, to put the Probation of Offenders Act into force, and very
often against their better judgment they
yield to the application made to them.
The Government propose to relieve them
of that embarrassment, and to say that
the Probation of Offenders Act, which was
never intended to apply to these cases,
should no longer be put into force. If in
future a person is brought up and fined
for an offence he must have known he was
committing, and which was not done
through inadvertence, I do not think he
can complain. The Probation of
Offenders Act was never intended to
relieve persons of their responsibilities
under a Bill such as the one now before
the Committee. It was intended to
prevent young persons gravitating into a
life of crime, or being committed either
to a Borstal institution or an industrial
school. Therefore, I do not think
motorists can complain if in the future
they are not to have the protection which
in the past this Act sometimes threw
around them.
The CHAIRMAN: Does the hon.
Member press his Amendment?
Professor JOHNSTONE: No.
Amendment by leave withdrawn.

NEW CLAUSE (Highway code to be
issued by local authorities).
A local authority shall issue with
every driver's licence a highway code
which shall include, amongst other
things, (a) Directions as to signalling,
(b) Precautions to be taken when entering a main road, (c) A warning as to
the danger of partaking of intoxicants
either immediately before driving or
when in charge of a motor-car.
All such codes shall be submitted to
and approved of by the Ministry.
Brought up and read a First time.

There should also be precautions taken.
when entering main roads. The various

NEW CLAUSE (Speed limit in builtup areas).
In built up areas (that is, areas in
which there is in existence a system of
street lighting) motor vehicles shall not
exceed a speed of twenty-five miles an
hour between the hours of eight a.m.
and twelve midnight. This section
shall not apply to motor vehicles used
for fire brigade or ambulance purposes.
Brought up, and read a First time.
Road Traffic Bill-

fixed at 30 miles an hour. The speed

was imposed there had been no fatal
accidents, while the number in the
previous year was four. He said, "The
murderous high speeds of the preregulation era have virtually
appeared."
dis-

our young people from accident. I hope
the Government will accept this New
Clause.

NEW CLAUSE (Driver of car presumed to be servant or agent of owner).
If, in any case where proceedings
are taken against the owner of a motorcar for damages for the negligent
driving, control or management of the
car, it is shown that at the time of the
accident the car was being driven, or
in charge of, some person other than
the owner, that person shall, until the
contrary is proved, be deemed to have
been acting as servant or agent of such
owner at the time the accident occurred.
Brought up and read a First time.
"That
This
Mr. BLACK: I beg to move,
the Clause be read a Second time."
New Clause stands in the name of the hon.
and learned Member for the City of Derry
(Mr. Murphy). The object of the New
Clause is this, when an action is brought
by a person who has been injured through
negligence in the driving of the motor-car,
the action is almost invariably brought
against the owner of the car.
The owner
of the car is responsible for any injuries.
caused in the driving of the car by his
servant or agent, and accordingly the
plaintiff in the action is concerned to show
that the car at the time of the accident
was being driven by a servant of the
owner. That is a matter which lies within
the knowledge of the owner of the car.
The unfortunate man who has been run
over can know nothing about that, and
the result is that in the actual practice of
the law the plaintiff in such an action is
driven to all sorts of expedients in order
to endeavour to get an admission from
the owner of the car that the person
driving it was his servant.
The object of this Clause is that when
an accident happens, the person driving
the car will prima facie be presumed to
be the servant of the owner,
as he
is in 99 cases out of 100. In the
hundredth case, which may be concerned
with a stolen car, all that is required is
that the owner should come forward and
establish that fact. In the one case. I
think the onus ought to be thrown upon
the owner of the car. The matter has
very little legal authority upon it. There
was a decision in a Divisional Court in
England a few years ago to the effect that
in such cases the onus ought to be
regarded as being on the owner of the
car. But that is not looked upon as
beyond question. There has been no
decision on the point in the Court of
Appeal either of England or Ireland, and
it is very desirable that this Clause should
be passed.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think this is
an entirely reasonable Amendment, and I
accept it.
Question put, and agreed to.
Clause accordingly read a Second time,
and added to the Bill.

NEW CLAUSE (Bankruptcy, etc., of
insured persons not to affect certain
claims by third parties).
Where a certificate of insurance has
been delivered under sub-section (4) of
section seven of the Act of 1930, as
amended by this Act, to the person by
whom a policy has been effected, the
happening in relation to any person.
insured by the policy of any such event
as is mentioned in sub-section (1) of
section one of the Third Parties
(Rights Against Insurers) Act (Northern Ireland), 1930, shall, notwithstanding anything in that Act, not affect
any such liability of that person as is,
by virtue of paragraph (b) of subsection (1) of section seven of the Act
of 1930 as so amended, required to be
covered by a policy, but nothing in this
section shall affect any rights against the
insurer conferred by the Third Parties
(Rights Against Insurers) Act (Northern Ireland), 1930, on the person to
whom the liability was incurred.
Brought up and read a First time.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: This is
a technical matter. Under the Third
Parties (Rights Against Insurers) Act of
Northern Ireland, 1930, if an insured
person becomes bankrupt the injured
person ceases to have any right and is
restricted to his right of action against
the insurers direct. Consequently, if the
injured person goes bankrupt before the
injured third party obtains judgment, the
third party would be unable to avail himself of the provisions of Clause 16 which,
it will be observed, may be availed of
when the third party has obtained judgment against the insured person, but has
not been successful in recovering the
amount of the judgment. This Clause
provides that the liability of the insured
in respect of third party risks is to be
unaffected by bankruptcy, so proceedings
against him may be taken or continued
after bankruptcy. It is another Clause
to ensure that in all cases a person who
is injured shall have the right of action
against some solvent body. I beg to
move.
Clause read a Second time and added
to the Bill.
The following New Clauses stood on the
Order Paper in the name of Mr. Beattie :
NEW CLAUSE (Regulations classifying roads).
Regulations shall be made by the
Ministry of Home Affairs to provide
that where one road intersects another,
one of the roads shall be defined as a
"major road" and the other a "minor
road" and traffic on the major road
shall have preference. In the event of
a collision at any road junction the
person who was immediately before the
accident on the minor road shall be held
to be at fault, unless he proves to the
contrary.
NEW CLAUSE (Overhanging loads).
If on any public highway any person
drives a vehicle on which the load over-
Road Traffic Bill-
Committee
22 MAY 1934
hangs the rear of the vehicle by more
than three feet he shall indicate the
overhanging load by an unobscured and
easily visible signal as prescribed by
regulations made under this Act, and
if he fails to do so he shall be guilty
of an offence under this Act.
NEW CLAUSE (Driving animals on
public highways).
Any person driving animals on a public highway during the hours of darkness shall, unless such animals are being
led, provide efficient lights which shall
be carried before and after such
animals at a prescribed distance, and
if he fails to do so he shall be guilty
of an offence under this Act.
NEW CLAUSE (Pedestrians on the
public highway).
Every person proceeding on foot
along a public highway shall, if a footpath be provided, remain on such footpath. If he desires to cross the road
he shall do so at right angles to its
length. If no footpath be provided he
shall keep within a reasonable distance
of the side of the road having regard
to the circumstances of the case and to
the amount of vehicular traffic on the
road at the time. Any person failing
to do shall be guilty of an offence under
this Act.

of the existing arrangements under which

£25,000 was established, the period of

seven years ended the 31st March, 1933.
On the 5th October last I explained
the position to the House and pointed
out that it was necessary to have Par-

Oral Answers to Questions.
STORMONT CIVIL SERVICE CLUB.
1. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state if goods
are sold in the North of Ireland Civil
Service Club, House of Commons, Stormont, for consumption outside the Parliamentary premises.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I have been asked by my
right hon. Friend to reply to this
question.
For the convenience of its Members,
the Stormont Civil Service Refreshment
Club stocks a number of small portable
articles in frequent or urgent demand,
such as tobacco, cigarettes, chocolates,
etc.
The main business of the club is and
will be to cater for its members in the
matter of meals during the official day.
Members of Parliament have similar
facilities in their dining-room.
CIVIL SERVANTS' SALARY AND
BONUS.
2. Major SHILLINGTON asked the
Minister of Finance whether the salary
and bonus of Northern Ireland civil
servants will be consolidated, and, if so,
whether they will be prejudiced in
respect of their remuneration in comparison with their colleagues in the Imperial Service by reason of his inability
to restore the portion of cuts restored
to Imperial civil servants; and whether
he is prepared to accord to the Northern
Ireland civil servants terms equivalent
to those obtained by their colleagues in
the Imperial Service on consolidation.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Mr. Pollock): As hon. Members are
aware, the remuneration of civil servants has for many years included a
bonus element which has varied with the
cost of living. The British Government
is at present engaged in discussions with
its staff in order to reach a settlement
for consolidating salaries and bonus.
Should a decision be arrived at, our
Government will consider the whole
matter in respect of our Civil Service,
as there are many advantages in making
a fixed scale of salaries. The restoration
of half cuts made by the Chancellor in
respect of the salaries of the Imperial
Civil Service will not become operative
until 1st July and I am hopeful that an
agreement may be reached before that
date to determine a fixed scale of
salaries.
At the moment, I do not propose to
anticipate our Government's policy on
this subject further than to say that
the position of Northern Ireland civil
servants will not be prejudiced by the
delay.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Unemployment Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr.
ANDREWS: I beg to move,
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
It is a sad truth that "the poor are
always with us." It has ever been so;
it is true of every country in the world,
apart altogether from its constitution, its
social system, and the personnel of those.
who govern and are governed. Poverty is
the result of many causes. In the
majority of cases it is beyond the control
of those who suffer; in other instances it
is the result of their actions or inactions,
as the case may be. Earnest people have,
for generations, been dealing with this
problem. In the United Kingdom
charitable institutions have played a
noble part; our churches of all denominations have done a great deal; we have had
distress committees and many Measures
under the Poor Law Acts, but it was not
Unemployment Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
until 1908, when the first Old Age
Pensions Act was passed-with which the
name of Mr. Joseph Chamberlain will
always be honourably identified-that
the State recognised its direct and permanent responsibility.
Our first Health Insurance and Unemployment Insurance Acts followed in
quick succession, and in 1925 an addition
of great value was made to our social
code, as it may be called, when our
Widows', Orphans' and Contributory Old
Age Pensions Act was passed.
It was in April, 1922, that I first had
the honour of moving the Second Reading
of an Unemployment Insurance Bill.
Since then the Parliamentary Secretary
and I have been responsible for no fewer
than seventeen such Measures. They
have all been Measures of considerable
importance. These Bills have reflected
conclusions that have been drawn from
time to time from the varying experiences
of the last twelve years. They have
represented the differing ideas of many
schools of thought; they have been stages
along the road that we of the United
Kingdom have been travelling towards our
goal of a just, humane, and practicable
provision for our fellow country men when
involuntarily unemployed.
I have been the target for some
criticism at times for advocating each of
these Measures-the creation of each
party at Westminster in succession, but
I am proud to say the Government has
never varied the policy I told the House
we had decided to pursue when I introduced my first Unemployment Bill in
1922. I said then :
This Bill is drafted on parallel lines
to the Bill which has just passed the
Imperial House of Commons. It is in
conformity with the decision of the
Cabinet of Northern Ireland, of which
I am sure hon. Members will approve,
viz., that our unemployed persons
should be dealt with similarly to, those
who are unemployed in Great Britain."
(Official Report, 11th April, 1922, Vol.
II, Col. 413.)
To-day, twelve years later, I repeat
that this remains our policy, and that this
Bill is in complete accord with it. There
are those who say we should do better.
To them I answer that it is impossible for
this little part of the United Kingdom to
do better than has been done by that
greater and wealthier part which lies
across the Channel. On the other hand,
there are those who say we cannot afford
to do so much. To them I answer that
the Government will not agree that, with
regard to our social and industrial code,
what is considered right and reasonable
and fair for the working people of
England, Scotland and Wales is too good
or unnecessary, for their fellow countrymen in Northern Ireland.
We are members of one family, all
citizens and taxpayers of one United
Kingdom, and we are determined to
maintain the heritage of uniform social
standards which the Imperial Parliament
passed on to us when they asked us to
accept a Parliament of our own for certain services, including labour matters.
It should not be forgotten that this policy
of equality has enabled us to continue reciprocity, to bring about the re-insurance
of financial liability, and to preserve unrestricted freedom of movement for our
people in the common employment field of
the United Kingdom.
I cannot claim to be the author of this
great Measure; the credit must be given
to the Imperial Minister of Labour, who,
in my opinion, has richly earned the
gratitude of the industrial classes, both
in Great Britain and Northern Ireland,
for his exertions in its creation. I can,
therefore, with more freedom, because it
is the work of another, declare it to be
beyond all doubt a much greater, more
beneficent and widespread Measure than
any of its predecessors.
I think it will be agreed that short
spells of unemployment present a very
different problem, both for the individual
and the State, to long spells of unemployment, and all who have studied the two
types, including the Royal Commission
on Unemployment, believe that different
methods for dealing with them should be
followed. That course is being taken in
this Bill. I cannot see how any reasonable person can criticise unfavourably a
scheme which places insurance on a
sound actuarial basis, and which provides for its being kept in that position
in order that our insured workers shall
receive that which they have contracted
to obtain or a Measure which, in its
second part, establishes an Unemployment Assistance Fund for all able-bodied
workers, whether insured or not, who
need assistance.
Unemployment Bill-
Second Reading
29 MAY 1934
Now, I do not intend to-day to weary the
House by referring to many of the fiftyeight Clauses and six Schedules contained
in the Bill. The White Paper, which
hon. Members have, no doubt, studied,
explains each Clause very clearly, but I
should like hon. Members to appreciate
very definitely what is contained in its
main provisions, and I shall take them
in their order in my opinion — of
importance.
-
Clause 5 provides that the cuts in rates
of unemployment benefit, introduced in
October, 1931, under the Economy Act,
will be restored as from the 1st July next.
This means that a single man will receive
17s per week instead of 15s 3d, and a
single woman 15s instead of 13s 6d, with
corresponding increases in respect of other
beneficiaries. Adult dependent benefit
will be 9s instead of 8s.
In view of the fall which has taken
place in the cost of living the restoration
of the cuts will mean that in purchasing
power the benefit will be considerably
greater in value than before the cuts were
made; in fact, 17s a week now will be
equal to what 20s would have been in
1930-1931.
Clause 3 increases the period during
which benefit may be drawn in a benefit
year in such a
manner as to enable
insured persons with good records to draw
considerably more benefit than is possible
at present. The existing maximum
period in a benefit year is 26 weeks. It
is proposed to introduce a sliding scale
for persons who have been upwards of
five years in insurance, and the effect of
this scale will be that where a person has
a good employment record the 26 weeks
will be increased in accordance with the
record of contributions and benefits up to
a maximum of fifty-two weeks in a benefit
year. Therefore, in such cases
the
exhaustion of the title to unemployment
benefit, and the necessity of applying for
unemployment assistance will be largely
avoided.
Clause 1 lowers the insurance age to the
school leaving age. The present gap
between the compulsory school attendance
age of 14, and the insurance age of 16,
will be closed, and all the young people
entering insured employment after
leaving school at 14 will become insured.
When these young people have no work
their parents, if unemployed, will be entitled to dependants' benefit for them,
and the weekly contributions which will
be paid in respect of their employment
will qualify them, subject to the statutory
conditions, for benefit at 16, instead of
not less than 30 weeks after 16, as at
present.
The contributions to be paid by these
young persons will be 2d per week, to
which their employers and the State will
add 2d each. In order to encourage
young people reaching the school leaving
age to continue at school it is proposed to
allow a credit of contributions, if attendance at school is continued for at least
twelve months. The number of credits
allowed will be from ten for twelve
months to twenty for two years, and these
contributions will be of use in establishing
title to benefit if young persons become
unemployed after 16.
The parents of these young people will
be entitled to dependants' benefit if unemployed in respect of periods during
which the young people continue at a day
school. I think these provisions will
meet with the approval of all hon. Members, because they are intended to assist
young persons in several ways, and their
parents in certain circumstances.
It is further intended, as recommended
by the Royal Commission, to place on the
education authorities the duty of providing courses of instruction for persons
between the minimum insurance age and
18, who are capable of and available for
work, but who have no work, or only
part-time or intermittent work. These
courses will require my approval, and must
be conducted in accordance with a scheme
made by my Department, with the consent of the Ministry of Finance, and in
consultation with the Ministry of Education. Only one quarter of the cost of
these juvenile courses will be carried on
the rates; three-quarters will be borne on
the Vote of the Ministry of Labour, and
a grant not exceeding half of this may be
charged to the Unemployment Fund.
I have already had a helpful conference
with the representatives of the Association of Education Committees, and I am
glad to know that this new development
meets with general approval. Before
steps are taken to put these powers into
force I hope to set up a committee on
which the educational authorities and the
Local Employment Committees will be
represented, and I shall ask for their

advice regarding the lines on which we

There are only two other matters in
connection with Part I of the Bill to
which I feel it is necessary that I should
refer. Under the re-insurance agreement, as hon. Members know, statutory
arrangements that are in operation
ensure that our Unemployment Fund is
kept in parity with the Fund in Great
Britain, the level of that Fund being the
governing factor. The new scheme has
been designed to secure that the
expenditure from the Great Britain Fund
shall be Lalanced by income, and the new
instrument for affecting this will be
the standing statutory Committee, of
which one of the members will be
appointed after consultation with me.
For this concession my colleagues and I
feel deeply indebted to Sir Henry
Betterton and his colleagues.
It will be the duty of this Committee
to report from time to time on the
financial position of the Fund, and to
recommend any changes in the financial
clauses of the scheme that may be necessary to preserve its equilibrium. To
have a separate Committee in Northern
Ireland would obviously be unnecessary,
objectionable, and very probably
embarrassing for obvious reasons.
If, as a result of the Committee's
investigations, a change is effected in the
financial balance of the scheme in Great
Britain, whether, for example, by
altering rates of contribution up or down,
or by increasing or reducing rates of
benefit, a corresponding change will be
made here by Order in Council, and it is
proposed that the Order shall be laid
before each House of our Parliament,
whose approval will be required within
twelve months.
Existing borrowing powers will be
cancelled, and the present current debt
will be liquidated by the payment of halfyearly instalments of approximately
£62.000, which will be in proportion to
the instalments to be paid in connection
with the corresponding debt of the British
Fund.
Further, I may add that contributions
remain unaltered in this Bill, and conditions for insurance benefit are substantially
similar, except that it is proposed to
extend the residence qualification enacted
in our 1928 Act from three to five years.
This is not proposed in any vindictive
spirit, but simply for the purpose of protecting our workpeople from the possible
penetration of labour from outside the
United Kingdom (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear)—and also for the purpose of
protecting our social funds from a burden
which they ought not to be called upon
to bear.
I shall now turn to Part II of the Bill,
and I must ask for the indulgence of the
House for a little longer whilst I try to
outline the many provisions of the proposed new Unemployment Assistance
Scheme. It has long been recognised
that the Poor Law is not an appropriate
medium of relief for able-bodied
industrial workers (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear) who are unemployed
through causes quite outside their own
control, and who are anxious to work,
as I know the overwhelming majority of
them are. In future, when insured persons continue to be out of work for longer
than a normal spell and have exhausted
their right to unemployment insurance
benefit, it is proposed that such aid as
they may need shall come from their
fellow-countrymen as taxpayers and ratepayers. A new non-contributory Unemployment Assistance Fund is to be
established, to which the general public
will pay at the present estimated level of
unemployment approximately 95 per
cent. as taxpayers, and only 5 per cent.
as ratepayers. This Fund will be available for the support of all able-bodied
unemployed persons resident for five years
in the United Kingdom who ordinarily
obtain their livelihood from employment
within the industrial field, whether they
are within or outside the scope of the
Unemployment insurance scheme, such as
agricultural workers, domestic servants,
etcetera.
It is obviously desirable that some test
that can be easily applied should be
adopted to identify those
those who are
intended to be brought within the scope
of the scheme. Accordingly, it is proposed to make its scope coincide with that

of the contributory pensions schemeapproximately this will bring in about
100,000 more of our working peoplewith the addition that those who have not
been able to obtain any substantial

insurable under the contributory pensions
scheme, owing to industrial depression,
will also be included-a most generous
arrangement and, I think hon. Members
will admit, a very proper one.
The age
limits will be 16 to 65. The scheme will
take the place of the transitional payments scheme administered by the public
assistance committees, and of the existing
arrangements for the relief of the ablebodied unemployed by the Boards of
Guardians. As I have pointed out, it
will, therefore, be widespread in its scope.
In passing, I desire to express my
appreciation of the unselfish and difficult
public service which these Committees
have rendered for more than two years.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
I feel that I should stress at this point
that the condition of need is considered
fundamental in connection with this
service. Personally, I have too high an
opinion of our people to believe that any
man or woman would wish to live at the
expense of his or her neighbours if their
help was not required. The general
standards to be applied will be laid down
by regulations, which will require the
approval of both Houses of Parliament.
Briefly, the amount of an allowance
will be determined by reference to the
unemployed person's needs, including
those of any members of his household
dependent on or generally supported by
him. Just as the needs of all members
of the household will be considered, so
the resources of all members of the household will be taken into account, except
certain sources of income which in part
will be disregarded. Normally
Normally the
assistance given will be a cash allowance.
In cases, however, which the Board may
consider to present special difficulty
assistance may be given in one or other
of the forms set out in Clause 35 of the
Bill. These powers will only be exercised
where the Board is of opinion that such
action is necessary to protect the interests
of the applicant or of persons dependent
on him. In all these cases the decision
will be subject to a right of appeal to the
appeal tribunal to be established under
the Bill.
It is much more difficult to administer
a scheme of discretionary relief, such as
this unemployment assistance scheme will
be, than an insurance scheme. The latter
is concerned with the administration of
prescribed conditions laid down by statute,
on the fulfilment of which definite rights
to fixed benefits emerge to persons falling
within an equally well defined category,
viz: contributors. On the other hand,
this unemployment assistance scheme is
largely on a discretionary footing, providing for the assistance of the unemployed on a basis necessarily flexible,
because it has to be adjusted to the great
variety of needs which the differing circumstances of individuals and householders may be expected to disclose.
Undoubtedly it is a great experiment; it
represents an advance into an area of
country which is to a large extent unexplored and unmapped.
The administration of the scheme will
raise many questions which will involve
personal, social and economic considerations. For these reasons, therefore, I
think we are well advised to provide, after
securing full Parliamentary control of the
policy and finance of the scheme, for a
closer identification of the public in its
administration than would be possible if
the whole work were left entirely to my
Department. An Unemployment Assistance Board will, therefore, be set up,
consisting of a chairman, together with
not less than one or more than four
members, to be appointed by His
Majesty's Representative, His Grace the
Governor, and the Board will have power
to establish advisory committees for such
areas as may be considered suitable, so
that it may secure the advice and assistance of persons having local knowledge
and experience. Both the National Confederation of Employers' Organisations
and the Trades Union Congress General
Council gave evidence before the Royal
Commission in support of the principle of
the Board system of administration, and
the Royal Commission pointed out that
the working of an assistance scheme would
be so experimental that it would be of
great advantage to have the advice of an
impartial body outside the field of
politics.
Discretionary and flexible though the
functions of the Board must be, if justice
is to be done between the members of the

general public finding the money for
assistance and the persons obtaining help,
some central guidance and direction must
be given to those responsible for day-today work of determination.
In particular, regulations will have to be laid
down for assessing needs and resources,
and Parliament must be the final
authority for approving the general standards to be observed. Accordingly, the
Bill provides that the Board must first
submit to the Minister of Labour draft
regulations for this purpose. The Minister must then consider the draft and, if
he proposes to vary it, he must consult
the Board, and give them an opportunity
of considering the proposed regulations.
The regulations, when made by the
Minister, must be laid before each House
of Parliament, and will cease to be operative unless they are approved by both
Houses within twelve months.
The Board will be responsible for
establishing its Own administrative
machinery but, SO far as possible,
arrangements will be made to use the
Ministry of Labour premises and staff,
for registering applicants, for assisting or
receiving their applications, for paying
them and, so far as may be found
practicable in the course of time, for
training and helping to place them in
employment. As a general rule, the
Board's own staff will carry out all
investigations, and determine the allowance to be granted.
I should like, at this point, to emphasise
two new main features of the scheme.
First, the lack of uniformity of standards.
in circumstances approximately similar,
which has, unfortunately, characterised
the administration both of transitional
payments and outdoor relief, will be
eliminated by the power reserved to
approve the regulations under which
applications for assistance will be decided.
secondly, where the question arises whether
a particular decision is not in conformity
with regulations of which Parliament has
approved, the person aggrieved may ask
for leave to appeal to an appeal tribunal,
consisting of three persons, one being the
chairman appointed by the Minister of
Labour, the other two members being a
representative of the Board and a representative of the workpeople drawn from a
panel nominated by the Minister.
Another provision important to our
workers is that the two Unemployment
Assistance Boards of Great Britain and
Northern Ireland are to be empowered to
enter into reciprocal arrangements for
dealing with persons moving between the
two areas of the United Kingdom. The
control of Parliament over the policy and
expenditure of the Board, and of the
actions of its officers, and of the procedure of the appeals tribunal, will be
complete. Matters of details, however,
requiring individual decision will be
removed from what the Trades Union
Congress General Council described before
the Royal Commission as
"the arena of
party politics."
Part III of the Bill provides for the
transition from the present arrangements
for insurance benefits to the new conditions, and ensures that claimants will
not suffer. Clause 56 provides that if
amendments to the British Bill, which has
only recently passed the House of Commons, are made in the House of Lords
and are incorporated in the Bill, such
amendments may be adopted by Order in
Council here, but such Orders will require
confirmation by Parliament within twelve
months.
The financial effect of the provisions of
this Measure is really very hard to forecast. The factors that have to be taken
into account have been set out as correctly
as possible in the financial memorandum
which is now in the hands of hon. Members, and the effect on the Exchequer will
be outlined in some detail when the Bill
reaches the stage of financial resolution.
The two main items arising out of the
amendments of the insurance scheme are,
first, the extension of the minimum
period of benefit, which, it is estimated,
will cost about £70,000 in a full year,
involving a consequential saving of about
£56,000 in the cost of the arrangements
under part 2 and, secondly, the restoration of the cuts in insurance benefit,
which, it is estimated, will cost the Insurance Fund in a full year about £90,000.
These estimates are related to a figure of
21 per cent. unemployment, and will, of
course, be affected if that figure is not
realised.
With regard to the new unemployment
assistance scheme, we are really dealing
with factors that are almost unascertainable at the moment, but, after taking
1909 Unemployment Bill-

29 MAY 1934
Second Reading
into consideration the many factors which
will operate, I venture to offer, as a very
rough figure of additional cost in a full
year of this scheme, the sum of £300,000.
I am sorry it has taken me so long to
explain the outlines of this Bill, but it
is a rather complicated and comprehensive
Measure. No country outside the United
Kingdom has ever gone so far in the
direction of abolishing poverty. It represents a great step forward. The contributors, whether employers or employees,
to the Insurance Fund, will feel a new
confidence that their contributions are
going to be preserved for their proper
object to insure against all ordinary unemployment risks. They will not be
swallowed up in relieving the needs of
those who have already drawn from the
Fund much more than their contributions
possibly warranted. Those unemployed
workers who, through no fault of their
own, find their insurance benefit
exhausted, or who earned their living in
occupations not covered by the unemployment insurance will, in future, find their
needs met fairly, and free from all association with the poor-law system, which
exists for other persons than able-bodied
industrial workers.
I have purposely refrained carefully
from saying anything to-day of a political
or party nature, for, as I have often
previously said, I feel that these social
schemes, of a purely domestic nature,
should be lifted on to a higher level, and
I am glad to think that this Bill aims
in that direction. It would gratify us
immensely to-day if we could agree that
the benefits which this Measure undoubtedly confers should be passed on to
our entire community-all of whom are
affected in one way or another-with our
united approval and support. It only
remains for me to thank hon. Members on
both sides of the House for the kind,
patient, and uninterrupted hearing which
they have been good enough to give me.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be

of this Bill. The peculiar thing about the

The Minister referred to what he conceived to be the most important Clause

for my own particular information. With

say it is a Socialist principle. I say that

we have always with us. Human history

This Bill when stripped, and it must be

insurance. It perpetuates the vicious

The hon. Member (Mr. Johnston)

It means, in the last analysis that you

and on those who are associated with the

the machinery and operation of the whole.
community and not by a particular

Accordingly, this Bill does not do what

not achieve that object. I took "making

number of unemployed were to be lifted

shoulders the only shoulders capable of
bearing the burden. I took it that unemployment would be met in some well
organised fashion along national lines
from national taxation. The original
proposal in the British Bill in regard to
able-bodied unemployed who were not in

that their upkeep should be a charge on

per cent. That has been changed here to
a rate of 11d in the £ in the case of

and 1d in the £ in some rural districts.
Is there any Member in this House will

In regard to Clause 1, I am opposed to

of age in insurance or out of it I would

of age.
We ought to aim at keeping

Then these children can remain in

he stays one year at an educational

very highly appreciated by the unemployed themselves. I am very pleased
that the scheme has now been placed on
a sound financial footing, because I was
in the United States of America in 1929,
a short time before the events which led
up to the crisis of 1931, and I have no
hesitation in saying that the financial
crisis was largely attributed to the fact
that it was the opinion of most people
on the Continent and of the majority of
those in the United States of America,
that we were squandering money right
and left on our unemployed, and that we
were jeopardising the financial stability
of the country with very serious results.
1945 Unemployment Bill-

Second Reading
Therefore, I feel it will have a farreaching effect upon the credit of the
country that the general public of the
world should know that our finances are
on a sound footing, and that this Unemployment Fund must look after its own
liabilities. Reference was made by the hon.
Member for Dock to the fact that interest
at the rate of 32 per cent. was being
charged on the outstanding debt of the
Unemployment Fund. I would like to
remind the House that this money was
originally borrowed not at 33 per cent. but
at 4 per cent. and 5 per cent., and the
loss of something over 1 per cent. has
been met by the Chancellor of the
Exchequer.
Those who to-day benefit, or anticipate
that they may benefit in the future from
this Bill, must be very pleased to realise
that it will be possible in the future for
good lives to receive full benefit for
twelve months instead of six. It has
been stated by the Opposition that very
few will ever benefit by this change. I
cannot agree. If this statement is
correct, it means that those who have
been good lives up to the present will
continue to be good lives in future and
will benefit in employment.
The hon. Member for Dock has cast a
reflection upon a suggestion made in one
of the local papers that trade was improving. He said he saw a reference to that
in to-day's paper. If he had turned to
another page of that same paper he would
have found that unemployment in Northern Ireland had been reduced during the
last twelve months by 12,900 persons.
That figure speaks for itself, and, I think,
confirms the article which suggests that
trade is improving. Therefore, I believe
the Minister is perfectly justified, and I
sincerely hope he is, in taking his percentage of unemployment at 21 instead of 25.
No credit has been given to that part of
the Bill, which restores the cuts, but this,
of course, is simply confirming what was
already promised. It is a very necessary
confirmation, and one which must give
great satisfaction both to the employed
and unemployed. I think the provision
in the Bill for reducing the entry into
employment from 16 to 14, and making
certain provision for contributions to be
credited to children remaining at school
to 16 is a step in the right direction. The
Member for Dock has suggested that the
leaving age should be raised from 14 to 16,
but that has absolutely nothing to do with
the Minister of Labour, and is a question
that can only be dealt with by the
Minister of Education. The Minister of
Labour is to be thanked for the great interest he has taken in this question, and
also for the facilities he has placed at the
disposal of the children for continuing
instruction after they have left school.
If I have one complaint to make in that
direction it is that the local authorities
will have to contribute some of the cost of
the education which will be given to the
children under 18. I would not consider
that anything but reasonable but for the
fact that the other day the Minister of
Finance promised the local authorities the
privilege of paying another 1/- in the £
towards the education rate, in addition to
any liability they may have at present.
Therefore, I feel the local authorities are
ill-fitted at the present moment to meet
any additional contribution though it
naturally is small compared with what it
would be if they had to maintain the
children at school until they were 16 years
of age.
I would like to ask the Minister of
Labour what the position will be when
the 11d rate, which will now produce in
the city of Belfast about £83,000, will be
found to produce a great deal in excess of
that. If, for example, we find that the
valuation of Belfast is increased by 50 per
cent. and the 11d produces 50 per cent.
more than it does at present, is he going
to reduce that rate from 11d to a figure
which will give the present sum of
£83,000?
I am sorry the Minister has not seen his
way to include agricultural labourers and
the black-coated profession, whose remuneration is under £500. I hope the
Statutory Committee, which has been set
up on the other side, and on which presumably there will be a representative
from Northern Ireland, will take this
matter into very serious consideration,
because if unemployment insurance is
necessary for what is spoken of as the
working man it is also necessary for the
lower-paid type of brain workers.
conclusion, I would like to thank the
Minister for the memorandum which he
sent out as a White Paper with this Bill.
I only wish that practice were more often
followed. If it was it would enable back
benchers like myself to take a more intelligent interest in the discussion when
Bills were introduced.

The means test has been discussed by

for

Dock (Mr.
Midgley), and I agree that it involves a

not one of those who stand for public
moneys being given out to anyone who is

few, but the means test, as applied, say,
to a family where the son is earning and
the other members of the family are not,
seems to me to be rather cruel. It has a
tendency if pushed to its logical conclusion, as it has been in England, to
drive members of the family who are
earning away from their homes, either to
go into lodgings or probably to get
married. That is the effect of the means
test in England, and anybody who has
been reading the Debates in the Imperial
House will have seen the many instances
given of the hardship caused by this
means test. I would have thought in the
circumstances that, when other Clauses
of the 1926 and other Acts were being
amended, the Government would have
taken the opportunity of wiping away
this very objectionable Clause as well.
I know it can be claimed that the
Socialists agreed to the means test. That
is perfectly true, but if they did it must
be said for them in extenuation that they
did it under the threat of the bankers and
financial houses and with the financial
stringency of the times hanging over their
heads, and they could have done practically nothing else except to have resigned.
That was the reason why this means test
was introduced, and there were amongst
the Socialist leaders of that time people
who vehemently protested against its introduction. And I have no doubt, too,
that the Socialists realise to-day the great
error they made in incorporating the
means test in their Report. But, whatever
may have been the original intention of

those who introduced it, it has been used

at the time. Why should there be a

You do not ask an Army officer to come

As well as that no Member of this
House who seriously considers the

of 2/- for children again introduced. It
is deplorable that in a so-called Christian
age we should set down as sufficient for
the maintenance of a child a sum of 2/-
a week or 4d a day-it is not 4d a day.
How is a parent to clothe, feed, educate,
and train a child on 2/- a week? Anybody who has children of his own, and
those who have no children of their own,
must know how impossible it is. Even
if you multiply it by five and assume that
there are five children in the home it is

Mr. MIDGLEY: They had not enough
Members.

I agree with the hon. and gallant

But I would go a little further and say

but they are going to have no control

administration. I hold that such a step
is neither democratic nor modern. After

all employment is a national charge and a

The present insolvent Insurance Fund

administration of the last few years, and

burden
SO heavy as approximately
£6,000,000 between No. 1 Unemployment

changed the intention of the original

You still retain the poor-law. Piece
by piece you have legislated with regard
to the poor-law introduced away back as
far as 1834. Of course I suppose most
Members of this House know that the
poor-law is really survival of the
monastic system in this country. The

the road. When the poor-law was introduced they sought to give that some kind
of legislative order, but the poor-law has
been repealed, amended, and altered time.
and again until I suppose this last alteration is prior to its complete extinction.
A few years ago you had a report from

in Northern Ireland. I certainly thought

to implement it before now. I certainly

was the case in a good many instances
under the legislation we have known
recently.
If these public assistance committees
enter into the spirit of the time with
decency and generosity I believe they can
go a good way to restore the confidence of

reading of a case in County Down

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 31st May, 1934.
The House met at Three of the Clock.
The Clerk, at the Table, informed the
House of the unavoidable absence of Mr.
SPEAKER from this day's sitting.
Whereupon Mr. MOLES, the chairman of Ways and Means, proceeded to

Standing Order.
Oral Answers to Questions.

BALNAGRAVEY.
1. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he is aware that a
schoolboy, ten years of age, died at Balnagravey, near Ballymoney, on Tuesday,
the 17th April, 1934, through weakness,
the outcome of malnutrition; and what
steps the Minister proposes to take to
compel education authorities to exercise
their powers for the feeding of necessitous school children.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): I have no
information respecting the death of the
schoolboy referred to in the question.
In reply to the second part, I would
refer the hon. Member to the answer
given to a similar question on 26th April
last.
RETIRED TEACHERS AND
PENSIONS.
2. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he can state the number of retired teachers who had, on the
31st March, 1934, pensions less than £52
a year, and the number on that date who
had pensions of £52 a year and more.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): On 31st March, 1934, there
were 1,138 pensioners in receipt of £52
or more per annum, and 193 who had
pensions of less than £52 per annum.

EDUCATION 1932-33.

emoluments of teachers; also the amount
of headquarters expenses for that period.
was
Mr. ROBB: I would refer the hon.
Member to my answer to his question on
Tuesday last, in which I stated that the
cost of public elementary education for
1932-33, apart from the salaries of
teachers and headquarters expenses,
£146,024. So far as the headquarters
expenses of the Ministry for that period.
are concerned, full details of the expenditure are given on page 99 of the Appropriation and Consolidated Fund Services
Accounts, 1932-33, the net total for that

These headquarters expenses include

and give information in cases of motor

(1) In any case where, owing to the

the

Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move,

9, to add:

motor-car shall not be guilty of an

I put down this Amendment in
accordance with the undertaking which I
gave to the hon. Member for Antrim
(Mr. Minford) and the hon. Member
for the University (Professor Johnstone)
during the Committee Stage of the Bill.
They raised objections to the Clause on
the ground that there was no clear
definition of what was an accident, and
that the expression contained in the Bill
was vague, the consequence being that
motorists might be compelled, in order
to comply strictly with the law, to report
every accident, no matter how trivial.
Personally, I can quite see the force of
the objections raised by the hon. Members. We have found it rather difficult
to arrive at a definition of an accident,
but I think the words we propose to
insert will meet all reasonable objections.
Amendment agreed to.
CLAUSE 16 (Extension of personal
liability for negligent driving).
(1) The liability of any person for
injury occasioned by the negligent
driving, control or management of a
motor-car by himself or by his servant
after the commencement of this Act
shall not be limited to such person himself or be terminated by his death, but
shall continue after his death and be
a liability of his real and personal
estate in like manner and with
the like priority as a debt or other
liability under a simple contract.
(2) Proceedings (including proceedings
under the Fatal Accidents Acts, 1846
to 1908) instituted against any person
for damages for negligent driving, control or management of a motor-car by
such person or by his servant after the
commencement of this Act shall not
abate on the death of such person but
may be continued against his personal
representative.
(3) Proceedings (including proceedings under the Fatal Accidents Acts,
1846 to 1908) for damages for negligent driving, control or management of
a motor-car by any person or by the
servant of any person after the commencement of this Act may, after the
death of such person, be instituted and
prosecuted against the personal representative of such person.
