The
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): Hon. Members will realise that
in moving the Second Reading of this
Bill it will not be necessary for me to
enter into any elaborate explanation as
it is a necessary corollary to the changes
in taxation which were embodied in the
Resolutions recently passed by the House
in connection with my Budget.
two main items deal with motor taxation
and the contribution of local authorities
to central educational expenditure. The
principle of these has been fully debated
when the Budget was discussed, and so
it will not be necessary for me to go
meticulously or exhaustively into these
two points.
Clause 1 deals with the change in
duties on mechanically-propelled vehicles.
It has been thought better to reproduce in the Schedule the duties which
have not been changed, as well as those
which have been changed, in order that
reference may now be easily made to
this Schedule, which is comprehensive of
all duties on motors.
were
The chief changes are, firstly, the
classification of motor-cycles. This has
hitherto been determined by weight, but
representations
made by motor
manufacturers and users that a change
should be made to the cubic centimetre
system, and embodied in this Clause will
be found the provision for this change.
The duty on motor-cycles will suffer a
slight reduction, but while the finance
involved is not of much consideration
this change will remove a hardship which
was creating dissatisfaction.
Secondly, the various haulage vehicles.
described in Sub-clause (3) of paragraph
4 of the Schedule are brought up to the
British scale to a maximum of eight tons.
The previous scale was entirely inadequate.
Il
Finance Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
Thirdly, it has been necessary for me
to have regard to the fact that certain
vehicles, both for the conveyance of passengers and of goods are being run on
oil fuel. It is not within my province
to attempt to equalise the costs as between petrol-driven vehicles and oildriven vehicles, except so far as the
incidence of tax is concerned, but in view
of the fact that petrol pays eight pence per
gallon and oil only one penny, it is obvious
that some equalisation in this direction
is very necessary. Accordingly, the oildriven vehicle is to pay approximately
one-third more tax than the petrol-driven
vehicle. I cannot pretend that this will
necessarily bring about a nice balance
between the two types of fuel as regards
tax, but it will, at least, remove the
This proanomaly to a large extent.
vision will be found in Sub-clause two
of paragraph 5 of the Schedule.
Fourthly, I have deemed it advisable,
with the concurrence of my right hon.
Friend (Sir Dawson Bates), to make the
vehicles fitted with solid tyres pay a
higher rate of tax than those fitted with
pneumatic tyres, because of the excessive
damage done to the roads by solid tyres.
I night just make this one observation.
I have been informed that in the United
States exhaustive tests were carried out
as to the relative damage done to roads
by pneumatic and solid tyres, and it was.
found that the solid-tyre vehicle did three
times the amount of damage to roads
that was done by the pneumatic-tyre
vehicle. This fact, in itself, brooks no
answer. The provision will be found in
the last column of Sub-clauses one and
two of paragraph 5 of the Schedule. It
will be observed that the proviso to the
first Clause of the Bill makes this duty
operate twelve months later than the
other changes. This will allow those who
have solid tyres on their vehicles to exhaust or get rid of them.
Fifthly, the tax in the case of lorries
in excess of five tons weight has been
increased by gradations and will no
longer remain stationary at the five-ton
point, as has been the case hitherto.
Sixthly, in Sub-clause (3) of paragraph
5 and in paragraph 6, the tax on trailers
attached to goods vehicles and private
cars has been increased with a view to
securing a proper ratio between
the
vehicle accompanied by a trailer and the
vehicle running alone.
Clause 2 clears up a point of law. By
a decision given in the British Courts
two years ago, it was held that a passenger vehicle which was used for carrying
goods temporarily, even although it had
not undergone any constructional change,
incurred the higher rate of duty, that is
to say, the duty payable on a goods
vehicle. Up to that time, it was always
thought that the goods duty was only
payable if the vehicle were constructed
or adapted solely for the purpose.
Great Britain, the hardship which this
brought about was corrected by a Section
in their 1932 Finance Act, and it is proposed to make a similar provision now in
this Bill. The small trader or farmer,
therefore, who owns a motor-car for his
own private use but uses it temporarily,
without structural alteration, for the
carriage of his wares, will not have to
pay the higher rate of tax payable on
goods vehicles.
In
Clause 3 deals with an entirely
different subject. It is concerned with
the charge to be made against local rates
for centralised educational services, in
order to relieve the Exchequer of this
amount of expenditure. I need not go
into all the arguments again in regard
to this matter, because they were discussed very
fully on the Budget
Resolution.
I might state, however,
quite definitely that this charge only
applies to hereditaments which are not
derated and, furthermore, it has no
relation whatever to the grants made by
the Government under Section 76 of the
Education Act of 1923 towards the expenditure of local authorities on education, and it will not itself rank for a
contribution under that Section; it is
simply a flat charge of sixpence for the
present year and one shilling for subsequent years. Hon. Members will note
that facilities have been given in the
Clause for temporary borrowing of the
charge in respect of the current year in
order to relieve the Councils of any
embarrassment in respect of the 6d rate
in the middle of their financial
year.
It will be noted that urban councils will
not deal direct with the Ministry of
Finance in regard to their share, but the
county councils will make the demand on
the urban areas. The dates of payment
within the financial year will be arranged

Mr. POLLOCK: I think it is better
that I should be perfectly honest and let
hon. Members and our people know what

The hon. Member who spoke last referred

attempt is being made at this moment to

a basis very much lower than the British
basis in respect of our educational
system. I cannot think that there is any
family in this community that can
reasonably object to contribute something to the education of their children.
That is the whole principle on which
education is carried on in Great Britain.
Grants from the Imperial Government
are given to the local authorities there,
and these grants happen to be equal to
about 50 per cent. of the cost of education, but apart from that the people
themselves must bear the burden of the
cost of education in Great Britain.
When hon. Members talk of Great
Britain receiving a surplus from Northern Ireland and draining the resources
of Ulster they do not seem to remember
that every penny of revenue raised in
Northern Ireland, or practically every
penny of revenue raised, is spent in Northern Ireland. It is spent for Northern
Ireland purposes and, while the money
may be distributed in a different way to
that which obtained twenty years ago,
still it is all spent here, and it goes into
the various businesses carried on in the
Province. That being so, I cannot see
that we have any ground of complaint
when the British Government expect us,
in regard to such local questions as
education, to pay something for our
children's education, not on the same
standard as in Great Britain, but, up to
the present, on a very much lower
standard than in Great Britain.

With regard to other matters raised,
the Member for Dock (Mr. Midgley) used
some rather fantastic language with

He raised matters which were not

we have advantages which they do not get.
For instance, the land annuities which are
the property of investors and are guaranteed by the British Government, were
handed over to us free. That is something
that is a gift, and gifts, somehow or other
-perhaps it is common to humanity—are
not very much appreciated after they are
received. Statutorily we have this gift
which cannot be taken from us,
and now
we apparently forget that that was a very

The hon.
The PRIME MINISTER:
Member does not, I think, appreciate
what my right hon. Friend has just told
the House, that naturally we could not
expect to get a contribution from Great
Britain if we ourselves were not living on
parallel lines to what they are on the other
side. I think we will be able to manage
in years to come on our own taxation in
our own area, and pay our way like an
honourable country and not have to fall
back on the alternative to which I refer.
Mr. McCARROLL: But you are putting it on the ratepayers.
The PRIME MINISTER: The hon.
Member does not quite grasp the matter.
Instead of scolding my right hon. Friend
and appearing ungrateful to him for what
he is doing, he and other Members ought
to be passing a hearty vote of thanks to
him for having postponed for the last 14
years imposing the taxation which we are
now forced to impose in order to live within our own means.
Mr. McCARROLL: I say we should
not have had to pay at any time.
The PRIME MINISTER: I think that
would be a rather pious wish.

Tuesday, 5th June, 1934.
The House met at Three of the Clock.
The Clerk, at the Table, informed the
House of the unavoidable absence of Mr.
SPEAKER from this day's sitting.
Whereupon Mr. MOLES, the Chairman of Ways and Means, proceeded to

Oral Answer to Question.
REPRESENTATION OF THE
PEOPLE BILL.
Mrs. PARKER asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state what
action the Government are prepared to
take towards establishing compulsory
registration in connection with the new
Representation of the People Bill, and
what steps they are taking to put the
onus of proof of residential qualification
upon all claimants for votes.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The matter which
the hon. Lady has raised is already receiving the attention of the Government.
It raises many difficult questions of a
constitutional nature, all of which have
to be carefully considered in their
various aspects before any legislation to
give effect to it can be introduced.
Mrs. PARKER: I am not sure that I
understood the right hon. Gentleman to
say that the matter was engaging the
attention of the Government. Will he
give me an assurance that something
s definitely going to be done towards.
establishing compulsory registration?
Sir DAWSON BATES: As I have
already explained to the hon. Lady, the
matter is engaging the attention of the
Government. It is a very difficult subject, but I can assure the hon. Lady
that we are anxious to do everything we
can in the direction indicated.

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): In a Bill of the size and
character of the Unemployment Bill there
are, inevitably, a number of scattered
financial Clauses dealing with more or less
distinct matters. The Resolution which I
2013 Unemployment (Money)-

5 JUNE 1934
Committee
now bring before the Committee is so
designed as to Cover them all. The
Resolution relates only to those parts of
the Bill which deal with its finances so
far as the Exchequer is concerned, and
only with new payments out of the
Exchequer. The full financial effect as it
concerns also the Unemployment Fund
and payments into the Exchequer is set
out in the White Paper, which is in the
hands of hon. Members, and possibly
that paper will be clearer than the more
technical explanation which it is now my
task to give.
Paragraph A (1) of the Resolution
refers to the financial provision in Subclause (3) of Clause 19 of the Bill. The
earlier parts of that Clause provide for the
repayment by half-yearly instalments of
the existing debt of the fund on current
account, and repeal any future power of
long-term borrowing. It is, however,
necessary to ensure that the fund shall not
be short of ready cash at any time out of
which to meet its current liabilities, and
for this purpose Sub-clause (3) provides.
for the making of temporary advances out
of the Consolidated Fund to the Unemployment Fund. Such advances are not,
however, to exceed the parity proportion.
of any similar temporary advances to the
Unemployment Fund of Great Britain
which may be provided for in the British
Bill. If any hon. Member is desirous of
knowing in detail in what circumstances
temporary advances may be made in Great
Britain I can supply the information at a
later stage in the debate. But it will
probably suffice for me to say that such
advances are carefully restricted in order
that there may be no question of the
accumulation of any additional permanent debt. The interest upon the advances
will, of course, vary from time to time,
according to the market and will be fixed
by the Ministry of Finance.
Paragraph A 2 (a), (b) and (c) and
paragraph B of the Resolution relate to
Clause 26 of the Bill, which provides for
the payment by the Exchequer of moneys
for several purposes. Firstly, under 2
(a) there is the increase in the State contribution to the Unemployment Fund,
which will arise as a consequence of the
lowering of the minimum age for entry
into insurance effected by Clause 1 of the
Bill. As will be seen from the Financial
Memorandum, this additional liability is
not expected to amount to more than
about £5,000 per annum.
Any increase which may be necessary
in the equalisation payment made under
the agreement known as the Reinsurance
Agreement, which was confirmed by the
Act of 1926, entered into for the purpose
of keeping the Northern Ireland Unemployment Fund in parity with the British
Fund is also covered by this part of the
Resolution. It cannot, of course, be foreseen whether, in fact, an increase, or a
decrease, in the equalisation payment will
result, as the amount which may require
to be paid in this way will continue to
depend upon the same factor as heretofore, that is to say, upon the comparative
of unemployment in the two
state
countries.
The provision for a possible increase in
grants within the control of the Ministry
of Education, referred to in Clause 2 (b)
of the Resolution, is necessary in the event
of any contribution of this nature arising
towards expenditure which does not
qualify for grants out of the fund under
Clause 16.
Paragraph 2 (c) of the Resolution
relates to any increased expenditure
attributable to the provisions of any
Order in Council made under Clauses 18
or 56 of the Bill, that is to say, an Order
applying to Northern Ireland, any part
of an Order made by the British Statutory
Committee relating to rates of contribution and benefit, or an Order modifying
the Bill so as to give effect to any Amendment made in the British Bill before it
reaches the Statute Book.
What any
such Orders may contain cannot, of course,
be foreseen at the present stage. As, however, the powers of the British Statutory
Committee to make Orders are related
chiefly to matters that concern the Unemployment Fund rather than the
Exchequer, any change in Exchequer
expenditure in this connection would probably affect mainly the equalisation payment under the Reinsurance Agreement.
Paragraph 2 (d) refers to the interim.
provision, contained in Sub-clause (5) of
Clause 54 of the Bill, which continues in
effect the present system of transitional
payments until such time as the new
system of allowances administered by the
Unemployment Assistance Board is
brought into operation.
2015 Unemployment (Money)—

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Committee
[Mr. Barbour]
The paragraph of the Resolution headed
B relates to that part of Clause 26 which
provides for the administrative expenses
of the Ministry of Labour in carrying this
part of the Act into effect, including costs
arising from providing or contributing
towards the courses of training and
instruction dealt with in Clauses 14 to 17
of the Bill. The initial cost of the latter
item to the Exchequer is estimated at
£30,000, of which, under Clause 16 (2),
either 50 per cent. or 75 per cent., according to the type, of course, will be recouped
to the Ministry by the Unemployment
Fund.
The last part, C, of the Resolution
relates to the expenses of setting up and
operating the new unemployment assistance scheme and the relevant financial
provisions are contained in Clause 42 and
paragraph 6 of the Fourth Schedule.
The salaries of the members of the new
Board will be charged upon the Consolidated Fund, and thus they will secure
the same independent position as, for
example, the Speaker of this House or the
Comptroller and Auditor-General, whose
remuneration is not borne on Votes. The
aggregate amount of the salaries is
specified at a maximum of £2,000.
The Resolution also makes provision for
the whole cost of the unemployment
assistance scheme and for the payment to
the fund of the contributions by local
authorities under Clause 40 of the Bill.
It is only possible to give a very
speculative estimate, but the total net
cost payable under this head may, in all,
amount to approximately £1,176,000, as
compared with the present cost of
£870,000 for the making of transitional
payments—an increased expenditure of,
say, £300,000. Sub-clause (2) (e) of this
part of the Resolution provides for any
expenses attributable to the provisions of
any Order in Council made under Clause
54, embodying any Amendments in the
British Bill made at a later stage.
In conclusion, I should like to make it
clear that the contributions of local
authorities are related to the valuations of
the year preceding that in which they
strike the rate and that, consequently, the
revaluation lists, which cannot take effect
till 1st April, 1936, will have no effect on
the contributions payable under this Bill
up to 31st March, 1937. I beg to move.

Mr. BEATTIE: I have not had time to
put in any amendment to Clause 1 but I
feel that some general comment should be
made on the Clause seeing it is so very
important to the whole Bill as it stands
and as it affects our present system. I
feel that the fixing of the age of fourteen
for the entry of children into insurance
is something to which we in the present
age should not agree. It would have been
different if the Minister had made the
insurable age eighteen, and during the
transitional period between the ages of
fourteen and eighteen he had given
financial grants to the parents of those
children for the purpose of equipping
them for the battle of life. But, instead
of giving a grant for the better education
of the child and keeping it on at school
till it is sixteen or eighteen years of age,
we are now putting in a provision to allow
a boy or a girl of fourteen years of age to
pay 2d
a week. It is outside all the
bounds of decency to treat a child in that
fashion.
We are compelled to accept the principle involved in this first Clause because
of the arrangement which we have with
Great Britain, but, nevertheless, I think
we should have a general discussion on the
principle involved in this Clause, which
we in our day and generation should not
feel justified in accepting except under
protest. That was the line on which I
had intended to draw up my amendment,
but, considering the connection of this
Bill with the British Bill, I found that
it would be futile to do so and that it
would only be lost time on my part to
propound that idea in an amendment.
But I think an expression of opinion
should go out from this House that we
thought the age for insurability was too
low and that, instead of classifying
children of that age in the insurable
grade, it would have been better to have
classified them in what we might call the
educational grade with a financial grant
towards providing that education, and
the same time bringing the school
leaving age up to a decent standard.
at
I can see the irony of this Clause in its
reaction in working-class homes. I feel,
as I am sure many Members on the
Government side feel, that we are dealing
with the potential product of the State.
We are dealing with the young people,
and I have here the opinion of an expert
on modern industry to the effect that the
school leaving age is too low. Our difficulty at the moment is to find work for
those of mature age, and as we go on the
finding of that work will become more
difficult because the elimination of labour
in industry is proceeding so fast that
in the near future we will be able to have
the same amount of production by
employing 30 per cent. of the industrial
population.
If we are going to retain in industry
children between fourteen and sixteen,
and if we endorse it in this Clause, we are
going to perpetrate a grave injustice on
the rising generation. I feel that if the
Minister could give us some consolation to
the effect that consideration will be given
to the youth of our Province, that an
educational policy will be drawn up with
the object of keeping them at school, say,
till they are sixteen years of age, and that
at the same time financial assistance will
be given to the parents of those children
who are unable to bear any of the
financial responsibility involved in that
education-if I got that assurance from
the Minister then, for the meantime at
any rate, owing to our connection with
Great Britain, it might meet our present
position to an extent which would give

able, through circumstances over which he
has no control, to have anything like the
insurable record of the other man. One
man has statutory rights and is safeguarded for a certain number of weeks,
but the other man is thrown to the shelter
of the Public Assistance Committee or to
the new Unemployment Insurance Board,
which means that his case is going to be
measured from a different angle altogether
to that of the other man who did not,
of his own volition, create his insurable
record. The one is probably as guiltless
as the other.
Some men may make greater efforts to
find employment than others. My experience during the past five veare is that I
have known married men with families who
have offered their services to employers
in the city of Belfast-this is a striking
statement to make-in return for exactly
the same amount in wages as they would
have got at a labour exchange had they
been entitled to benefit. Yet these men
have been unable to find employment.
Under this Clause these men
are discriminated against. The net effect of
discrimination will mean
additional payment of £14,000. That is
all there is in it from the point of view
of the insured population in Northern
Ireland.

[Mr. Midgley]
To ask that this Unemployment Fund

interest is to do somethng which is the

of world-conditions. The members of the

:he

population
I think I heard the Minister of Finance
ask, almost under his breath, "How is
it to be paid?" If a legitimate debt has
been contracted it ought to be paid by
the whole Consolidated Fund of Northern
Ireland.
Mr. POLLOCK: That is how it is going
to be paid.
Mr. MIDGLEY: It is not. The people
who are the contributors to this Fund
are in the end going to be held responsible
for this debt. It is a wrong policy. In
Great Britain the people who accept the
point of view I am expressing protested
against this principle being carried out in
Great Britain, and I would ask the Members on the Government side of the House
to face up to this question, and to be
logical and consistent about it. At various
times I have heard them recommend that
debts ought to be cancelled, and they have
gone dangerously near repudiating one at
the present time. I saw this morning
something on the placards about the debt
of Great Britain to another country being
repudiated, and for some time past only
token payments have been made, which
is very near repudiation. The whole
argument has been that this debt to
another country ought to be extinguished.
Why should you apply this philosophy
to international debts and not to a
national debt? Why try to saddle a fund
with a debt which accumulated as a result
of the very acute depression through
which we passed from 1924 to 1932-33.
I think the whole thing is wrong, and it
is only elementary justice to protest
against it. When you are bringing about
a new set of conditions and trying to deal
with unemployment from an entirely
different angle to that from which it has
been dealt with before, I suggest the time
is opportune to deal with the debt in one
or two ways.
This is an inter-departmental debt,
and could have been met out of
surpluses in the ordinary way, instead
of fixing the debt on the Unemployment Fund. The Unemployment
Fund was a good Fund under anything like normal conditions. Speaking
from memory, when the Unemployment
Insurance Fund first came into existence
in 1912, as a result of the contributions
made to the Imperial Fund, there were
savings of about £19,000,000 by the
year 1918 or 1919, and it was only
subsequent to that that the fund began
to get into a precarious condition, because

(1) Subject to the provisions of this

Part of this Act applies, if he proves

allowance in the prescribed
manner; and

part-time or intermittent work as
not to enable him to earn sufficient
for his needs; and

be granted under this Part of this Act

reference to his needs, including the
needs of any members of the household
of which he is a member who are
dependent on, or ordinarily supported
by, him, not being persons in whose
case the qualifications set out in sub-

That means, working it out in conjunction.
with the Clause mentioned over-leaf, that
the individual position of each member
of the family is taken into consideration,
and people are having their needs ascertained by how much can be brought in by
other members of the family. To the

a man or woman's position should be faced
up to by virtue of the fact that they are
unemployed people, and they should be
dealt with on the basis of what would be
their status under the Unemployment
Insurance Act. This business of introducing consideration of the family and
reference to the resources of each
individual simply means that a man
who has been 30 or 40 years in a
firm like the Queen's Island and has
contributed his best to the upkeep of
industry and the upkeep of the community is going to have his right to
benefit dependent upon the attitude the
authorities take with regard to the
earnings of his son or daughter.
If he has an adult daughter earning
£1 a week or 25/- his right to benefit
is going to be determined upon that
basis. I protest against that. I think
it is wrong. It is degrading and
humiliating to the man. I have come
across many cases in the city of Belfast
of people whose right to benefit was.
determined by the position of the other
members of the family. I have known
skilled artisans who have worked all their
lives being denied benefit, although they
were insured workers from 1912 up to
the time of the trade depression set in.
It is to prevent a recurrence of that,
which is alien to the best sense of decency
and alien to the principles of insurance
that I move this Amendment.

(a) By the council of the county

Major HALL-THOMPSON: I beg to
move in page 36, line 2, to leave out the
words "the amount of a rate of elevenpence
in the pound on the rateable value of the
said county borough," and insert the
words "sixty per cent. of the estimated
cost of the year 1932-33.”
This Clause, as it stands at present,
throws a certain responsibility on the
local authorities. As far as the County
Borough of Belfast is concerned it proposes a levy of 11d in the £ on the rateable value of the city. The present value
is estimated to produce about £83,000
per year. It has been the boast of the
Minister of Labour that he has gone
practically step by step with the British
Parliament in all social services, and that
in this particular Bill he has practically
copied word for word the Westminster
Act, but I cannot understand why he has
not, in Clause 40, used the same words as
appear in the British Act, namely, that
the charge on the local authorities should
be 60 per cent of the estimated cost of the
year 1932-33. Whether that produces
more or whether it produces less, that is
what the citizens of Belfast-I can only
speak for them; the representatives of
other local authorities can speak for them
-prefer should be done in this Clause, if
for no other reason than the fact that
during the last few weeks this House has
taken advantage of its majority to vote
already two additional charges on local
authorities, that is, a charge of £25,000
on Belfast for police, and a charge which
will work out at £90,000 on the city of
Belfast for education.
Therefore, I personally protest against
a charge being made under this Clause
which will be an ever increasing charge,
as long as the figure of 11d in the £
stands. That is regardless of the huge
increase that would take place if the rateable value of the city were increased. I
observe, with pleasure, that the Minister
of Commerce stated that the contribution
for the last financial year will be on the
basis of the year 1935-36 and, therefore,
not be subject to an increase due to revaluation. I do not, therefore, attribute
to the Minister any desire to get a larger
sum under this 11d in the £ than he
would get from taking 60 per cent., but
I object to the principle being introduced.
I must ask the Minister to seriously consider whether he will not, in this Clause,
as in the other Clauses, copy the English
Act, which assesses the local authorities
with 60 per cent. That is regardless of
whether the 60 per cent. produces more or
less. I understand, as far as the city of
Belfast is concerned, that the 60 per cent.
at present would produce £86,000 against
the 11d in the £ producing £83,000. I
am quite satisfied that the city should pay
an additional £3,000 per year for the
privilege of sticking to a principle. The
principle is that we should keep step by
step with the Imperial Parliament as far
as this Clause, like most of the others, is
concerned.

I have to take a choice as between the

Obviously the fairest basis is the percentage basis.
There is only one point
I am a little perturbed about. Despite
all that has been said by some Members
we have no guarantee that conditions

The proportion of 60 per cent. and 40
per cent. is not fair in Northern Ireland. I mentioned on a previous
occasion in this House that 60 per cent.
in England was a different proposition
from what it is in Northern Ireland,
although I have an objection to the

Great Britain. In Belfast, if you take
the derated areas away and exempt them
-the biggest part of derating falls on
the rural areas- -it works out that Belfast pays considerably more than 60 per
cent. of any arrangement that might be
come to. Similarly an 11d impost is
going to be a big one. I see, according
to the Clause, this is only supposed to
operate until March, 1937. What are
we going to do after March, 1937? We
will have to bring forward a new principle altogether, because the conditions
that this was meant to meet will have
passed away for good in the year 1937.
The 11d rate is based upon what the
parties were called upon to pay at the
peak period. That is what I have been
informed and I think it is correct. It
is calculated on the expenses for the year
1932-33, and I think, therefore, that
the mover of the Amendment ought to
have made the rate as between State
and city 50-50. That is obviously fairer
than 60 per cent. and 40 per cent.,
because Belfast comprises almost 50 per
cent. of the textile population of Northern Ireland, and in regard to education.
it is going to pay a great deal more than
its quota. I think the Government
ought to have thought the whole thing
well out and come forward with a policy
more in keeping with the position Belfast occupies as compared with large industrial cities across the water.
To all intents and purposes you have
only one industrial centre in Northern
Ireland. Belfast stands out pre-eminently
in Northern Ireland. The other places
are not worth serious consideration from
a first-class industrial point of view. If
I am driven into the position of having
to vote for either basis, although I
think the correct stand for me to take
up at the present time is to continue
my revolt against the introduction of a
principle which I think is wrong, as it
is going to place on a local community
portion of a burden which ought to be
maintained from State resources, I am
going to support the Amendment.

A similar Clause appeared in the Unemployment Bill we are after dealing
with, and I ventured to move an Amendment. The Minister gave an assurance
that the new valuation would not come

period fixed in that Unemployment Bill,

to help the Government to specify the
amount of contribution, and so prevent
the recurrence of gross anomalies which
the Government will be anxious to prevent. These anomalies would occur on a
great increase in the valuation and,
accordingly, my proposal is that when a
new valuation does come instead of the
contribution being calculated on the new
valuation it should be calculated on the
last year of the old valuation. I commend
my Amendment to the Committee.

The PRIME MINISTER: I really
think it is necessary, before winding up
a debate on such a serious subject as this,
that some reply should be made to the
extraordinary statements which the hon.
Member has just made. He has accused
the Government of retarding the progress
of the great city of Belfast. A charge
of that sort is foolish, in the first instance,
coming as it does from a member of the
Belfast Corporation, and it can be
repudiated in the strongest terms. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I would ask
hon. Members of this Committee to cast
their minds back over the past fourteen
years and
to follow the long line of
difficulties through which the country,
including the great city of Belfast, has
been passing. No Government anywhere
has been more generous in helping any
municipality over its difficulties than the
Government of Northern Ireland have
been to the city of Belfast. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) If we look back
to 1920, if we compare the serious
financial difficulties that have arisen since
then, if we remember that, in spite of all
that has occurred in those years, the
Government have contributed very
generously to the housing of the working
classes, to education, and to practically
every case of hardship that was brought
to our notice, hon. Members will realise
the truth of that statement. Certainly
if we analyse the accounts dealing with
Unemployment Insurance we will find
that my right hon. Friend the Minister
of Finance and my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Labour have secured for the
people of Belfast out of Government
funds a much larger contribution than
any Government has given to any other
municipality throughout the world.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I defy
contradiction of that statement from any
quarter.
Finance Bill-
Committee
5 JUNE 1934
Then, Sir, to take last year alone-
I cannot quote figures at the moment-
I venture to say that the assistance of
the grants for those special schemes in
order to occupy the unemployed were
the envy of every municipality across the
Channel. Far more has been done by
this Government than has been done by
any other Government that I know of.
Therefore, these loose, vague charges fall
far too frequently from hon. Members
representing the municipality. I agree
that the municipality has a great responsibility, but I do not think their responsibility is so great as that which falls
upon the Members of this House, which
covers the whole area of Ulster, a responsibility which is placed upon Members as well as upon my colleagues in
the Government.
The hon. Member says that the 6d for
this year and the 1s in a full year that
will be imposed for educational purposes
will retard education. The people of
Ulster now have what they have been
crying out for since I was in the Imperial Parliament, beginning in 1906.
They cried out for more liberty in the
local areas to manage their own educational affairs. They wanted education
placed upon a thoroughly democratic
basis. That has been carried out, and
for the past 14 years my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Pollock) has been able to
shelter the local authorities, including
the Belfast Corporation. He has stood
abuse in this House from people who
should have known better, and also from
those who do not know a single thing
about it. He has stood abuse night
after night, and day after day, whilst
he himself was actually sheltering the
local authorities, including the Corporation, from having this shilling, or,
indeed, any sum of money, placed upon
them for the service of education.
as
Then the time came when the loss of
revenue on the one hand and the increase of social services on the other
brought him, as the Minister in charge.
of the finances of the Province, to the
point when, if we were to carry on
honourable persons in an honourable
part of the United Kingdom, if we were
to carry on with clean finances, with,
I hope, a balance on the right side each
year in the future as in the past, he had
no alternative but to ask the local
authorities to help to bear some of the
weight of education, and he has placed
upon them, in my opinion, a very modest
sum.
The truth of the matter is that, having
reached that point, the Corporation and
other local authorities may say, "Well,
what of the future?" With regard to that,
I have had no time, of course, to consult my right hon. Friend, but I would
say to the House, generally speaking,
that I believe as we stand here to-night
we are at the bottom of the trough. I
think that certainly 1933-34 and 1934-35
should see us at the very bottom of the
consequences of the extraordinary,
the phenomenal depression through which
we have been passing, and that once
again, when we move in the upward
direction towards another peak of prosperity which always succeeds low depression, I hope it will never be necessary
again to deviate from any of the principles laid down by the British Government.
In the meantime, my hon. Friend can go
back to the Belfast Corporation and tell
them in all seriousness that, although I
have been attacked, although my right hon.
Friend has been attacked, and although
the Government generally have been
attacked by local authorities, and even
by members of the Belfast Corporation,
I think we have always held our hand.
We have always been very cautious in our
criticism of what they are doing, and
through it all I cannot remember one
single bitter sentence falling from my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance, against any one of those who
spend their time in passing these
resolutions of condemnation or of demand.
I also venture to say in this connection, in closing, that I do think that
much more good would be done in Ulster
here if there were a better feeling, which
I have endeavoured constantly to promote. I would ask the hon. Member in
future, if he does not wish to do harm
to his own native country, to be kind
enough not to throw out these charges
which are made, and not to say that
above all people in the world the Government here would attempt to hamper
in any way the progress of our common
country.

Milk and Milk Products Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): In submitting this
Bill to the House I am very conscious of
the fact that it represents the most
important piece of legislation which has
yet been attempted by my Ministry. I
feel confident that there are contained in
the Bill provisions which will commend
themselves to every section of the House.
Towards the end of last year the Prime
Minister and my predecessor gave to the
farming community an assurance that a
scheme for the better organisation of the
milk and dairying industry would be
introduced at the earliest possible
moment. I should here like to thank all
those whose livelihood depends on the production of milk and who have been going
through hard times for not pressing me
unduly to rush this Bill. I have stated
on previous occasions that in my opinion
one of the greatest disasters that could
accrue would be the introduction of any
Bill which had the element of failure
in it.
After the most careful consideration of
the Marketing Schemes for milk which
are operating in England and in Scotland, we came to the conclusion that a
scheme on identical lines had no prospect
of success in Northern Ireland, and it
seemed to us that if we were to succeed
in our efforts we must follow much more
closely than it has been possible to do in
Great Britain the recommendations of
what is known as the Grigg Commission
for the marketing of milk. I should like
in passing to pay a tribute to the exceedingly valuable and helpful character of
this report. Some of the
of the principal
recommendations of the report are outside the scope of the Marketing Act and
that is one reason why it has been necessary to proceed by specific legislation
instead of by means of the Agricultural
Marketing Act.
In certain of its aspects the milk
problem in Northern Ireland presents
much more difficult features than in
England and Scotland. In Great Britain
70 per cent. of the milk produced is consumed in liquid form and only 30 per
cent. is utilised for manufacturing
purposes. Here the position is exactly
reversed and 70 per cent. of our milk is
used for manufacturing purposes. In the
old days a producer who was 30 or 40
miles from a city like Belfast had little
hope of placing his milk supply on the
Milk Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
more
[Sir Basil Brooke]
liquid market. It was a much
difficult matter to the farmer unless he
was living close to a railway.
At the present time with improved
transport that milk can be brought into
the towns, and the consequence of that
is that the producer who merely produces
summer milk is tempted to introduce his
milk into the liquid market, such as Belfast, where he may during the summer
period obtain a higher price than at the
creamery. The final result of such action
is that the man engaged in the liquid
market trade for a city such as Belfast
would be handicapped during the summer.
He would not have sufficient reserves to
feed his cows in such a manner that they
would keep up a sufficient supply of milk
during the winter. It will be obvious to
hon. Members that if you flood the liquid
market with cheaply produced milk during
the summer and endanger the financial
position of the genuine milk producer
who has to produce during the winter the
whole milk supply of a town may
be seriously jeopardised. It must be
remembered, as I have already said,
that some 70 per cent. of our
milk is manufactured into butter or
cream. The creameries at the present
moment are in a very serious financial
position. They are competing against
bounty fed butter, and the entrance of
that butter into Northern Ireland has
forced the price of milk down to somewhere between 2d and 3d a gallon.
A milk scheme for Northern Ireland
must, therefore, be primarily one for
assisting the producer of manufacturing
milk, which represents as I have already
said 70 per cent. of our production. One
of the great difficulties we were faced with
before we were included in the financial
assistance given to the milk industry in
Great Britain was that we were unable to
finance such a large percentage of the milk
that went into the manufactured side. If
we were not in a position to help in this
direction I think a great deal of the milk
which used to go the creameries would
have been diverted into the towns, and
any scheme that would have been
started purely for the local market
would have been seriously affected
by the surplus milk coming in
from the country.
By this assistance it
will be possible to pay those who are
supplying milk to registered creameries at
price of 5d per gallon in summer and 6d
per gallon in winter.
If during the period 1936 to 1938 the
price of creamery milk rises above 6d. per
gallon in summer and 7d. per gallon in
winter, then there will be a contingent
liability upon creameries to pay into the
fund a levy per gallon equal to the amount
by which the average price paid by all
creameries exceeds 6d. in summer and 7d.
in winter. Perhaps I might explain that
more clearly. If through economic reasons
the prices rise in the creamery so that 6d.
is paid in the summer and 7d. in the
winter then taking the average of all the
creameries whatever sum is above that will
be paid as a levy for the repayment of the
£200,000 which has made made available
for this milk scheme. That is the only
liability placed on the creameries, and,
as I have said, it is contingent upon a
measure of real prosperity.
My right hon. Friend the Minister of
Finance has already informed the House
that for this purpose we shall receive
from the British Exchequer a contribution not exceeding £200,000 per
annum. This sum will be paid into the
Milk Fund, whch is provided for in this
Bill. I think we should express our
gratitude to the Chancellor for that
action. My Ministry is responsible for
the repayment of this sum in the event
I foreshadowed a moment ago, and it is
therefore incumbent upon the Ministry
that it should have perhaps a larger control over this industry than has existed
in other marketing schemes.
It may be that certain classes of our
farming community would like to see a
scheme which was controlled only by the
producers of milk for the liquid market.
If so, I would ask them to reflect carefully
and to bear in mind that a scheme which
failed to do real justice to the producers of
manufacturing milk, and they produce 70
per cent. of the total supply, has no
chance of success.
Now I should like to turn for a few
minutes to the main item of policy which
underlies this Bill. If a scheme of reorganisation is to be successful it must be
of benefit and of real service to all the
parties concerned. In the case of milk
the consumer is an important factor. The
consumption of liquid milk in this
country is lamentably low: it represents
Milk Bill-
Second Reading
6 JUNE 1934
only a fraction of the per capita consumption of the United States and
Scandinavian countries.
That can be partly traced to the fact
that perhaps the dairying trade in Great
Britain is not up to the standard of some
other countries. The result, I think, is
that many who would otherwise buy
fresh milk are afraid of its keeping
qualities and in consequence buy tinned
milk instead. If we are to increase our
consumption of liquid milk, a most desirable thing from the point of view of
the future of the race, we must do everything possible to give a continuously improving service to the consuming public.
That can best be done by steadily improving our milk supply from the cleanliness
point of view.
In order to facilitate Members in getting
a grasp of this intricate Bill I caused a
memorandum to be circulated. As hon.
Members will see from it we propose to
license three grades of milk, Grade A,
Grade B, and Grade C. All producers
supplying the liquid milk market must
be licensed, and producers who fail to
reach the standard of purity which will
be laid down for Grade C will be unable
to sell their milk for liquid consumption.
Gradually, I hope, the standards for
Grades B and C will be raised. There
is a financial inducement to the farmers
to produce the better grades and although
I do not want to anticipate the policy of
the Milk Council the scheme makes it
possible to supply Grade B, a much
superior grade of milk to C, to the consumer at the same price as Grade C.
Grade A and Grade B milk must be sold
to the consumer in bottles or other
suitable containers.
It is obvious to those with practical
knowledge of the milk industry that a
number of producers of Grade B and of
Grade C milk will not be able to secure
a liquid market for their supplies. Such
producers will have, as at present, to take
their milk to the creamery. There they
will receive not only the guaranteed price
of 5d. per gallon in summer and 6d. per
gallon in winter but, in addition, a bonus
in respect of purity of 1d. per gallon for
Grade C milk and 24 per gallon for
Grade B milk. That will be a further inducement for cleaning up the milk which
may not be all that is desired when sent
to the creamery.
There will thus be a
direct incentive for producers of manufacturing milk to improve their supplies
from the cleanliness point of view. It is
quite obvious that butter in consequence
will be of much better quality.
The Bill also empowers the Ministry
to license all distributors. The fee for a
distributor's licence will be £1, and the
proceeds will, as in the case of other
licence fees, go into the Milk Fund. The
Ministry is also empowered to make
regulations with regard to the premises,
equipment and appliances for handling
and distributing the milk. This it would
not have been possible to do under the
Agricultural Marketing Act. I should
like to explain why that power has been
taken. It will be manifest to all hon.
Members that there would be little value
in cleaning up the herds and the byres
and forcing the producer to produce better
milk if between the producer and the consumer there was any organisation which
possibly might let that milk deteriorate.
We are taking steps to see that the milk
from the cow reaches the consumer in a
clean and healthy condition.
In order to secure the smooth working
of the Scheme the Bill proposes to set up
a Joint Milk Council, representative of
producers, distributors and consumers,
and with three independent representatives with no financial connection with the
industry who will be nominated by my
Ministry. It will be the function of the
Joint Milk Council to determine the price
which is to be paid to the producer for the
three grades of milk, and if the Council
cannot come to a unanimous decision on
this matter the three independent Members have the power to arbitrate and make
the determination.
consumer.
The Joint Milk Council may also fix the
retail price subject to the concurrence of
the Ministry. The reason for that is that
it would be possible for the producer to
cover, perhaps, disorganised distribution.
by placing the full financial burden on the
The result would be detrimental to the producer because an enhanced price would mean a reduction in
quantity. Therefore, this has been placed
in the Bill to allow the Ministry to give
their assent to the price fixed. The Joint
Milk Council is also given power to require
that all contracts for the supply of liquid
milk shall be registered with the Council
and it will advise the Ministry on all
matters relating to the standards for the
Milk Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Basil Brooke]
three grades of milk which may come on
the liquid milk market.
One other item of the Bill calls for
special mention, and that is the power
which is taken to license all merchants
who deal wholesale in butter and margarine and to charge a fee of 5s per cwt.,
which works out roughly at d. a lb. In
passing I may say just to show that the
wholesale dealers do not consider that an
exorbitant sum that a wire was received
in my office this morning from one of the
biggest dealers in margarine requesting
that the licence should be increased to
somewhere in the vicinity of 9s. However, I think 5s. will cover all we require.
This charge will also apply to our
creameries but not to butter made on our
farms, and the money raised thereby,
together with the contribution from the
Imperial Exchequer and the levies from
the three grades of milk, will go into the
Milk Fund. It will also include the
£200,000 contribution from the Imperial
Exchequer. It is from this fund that the
5d. and 6d. per gallon in summer and
winter respectively will be guaranteed to
producers who send their milk to the
creamery.
We also propose to carry out a tuberculosis inspection of animals, and the cost
will be defrayed in part or in whole from
this fund. Our own veterninary officers
will carry out their inspections twice a
year. So that it is quite clear that an
effort will be made to clean up the herds.
It will be quite clear that that effort will
start very soon, indeed it will probably
start as soon as the producer realises
where the money is going to come from to
clean up his herds. There is no better
inducement-it is better than any legislation, it is better than any Order that could
be made if a man is told that by cleaning
up his herd he will get a better price for
his milk, and it will be realised that that
big financial help-and it is a big financial
help will achieve more than has ever
been achieved before. We intend also to
assist in providing milk for school children
if any scheme of that sort is started in the
future.
I am sure that Members of the House
will appreciate the heavy and difficult
problems which we are endeavouring to
solve. Our production of milk is approximately 100 million gallons per annum and
its value approximately £3,000,000. But
If
that is not the whole story. A matter
that has been exercising my mind and
that has given me a very great deal of
anxiety is the very serious position of the
creameries. Many have been contemplating closing down. If they were to
close down it would be one of the most
disastrous things that have ever happened
to agriculture in this country, because it
will be admitted that with the creameries
goes the improvement of our herds.
the creameries go down fewer cows will be
kept, fewer store cattle will be the result
and it will be difficult to feed the pigs
which we hope are coming forward under
the Pigs Marketing Scheme, while in
addition poultry feeding would also suffer.
But it will take some weeks of intensive
work before the quality of grading can be
brought into operation. As far as I am
concerned I do not mean to spare myself
in any effort to get the scheme working as
quickly as possible. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). I do not want to disguise
the fact that I am anxious to get this Bill
through as quickly as the House will allow
me, because so soon as this Bill is passed
through its various stages so soon shall I
be able to pay the farmers in this country,
retrospectively as from April 1st, 5d. per
gallon for their milk. I beg to move.
Mr. McCARROLL: I think we are justified in congratulating the Minister on the
very lucid statement he has made in introducing this measure and in saying that,
as far as we are concerned, and I am sure
as far as the entire House is concerned,
there will be nothing done to delay the

community. I happen to know something
about the condition of the creameries and
of the farmers who have been supplying
milk to them. To me it has been amazing
that they have been able to carry on all
these years under such conditions.
various parts of the country, particularly
in County Tyrone, I have often said to
farmers I have met that it was quite uneconomic for them to continue keeping ten
or twelve cows and to cart their milk
every morning to the creameries at the
prices they were able to obtain. If this

and if it is going to bring some hope of
prosperity to those farmers who carry on
that milk trade-farmers having from six
to a dozen cows and depending on the
creameries for the sale of their milk and
In

then on the cattle for another branch of

section of the House will cordially support.

But there is another aspect of the
question. What I feel about it is that
there is no element of permanency. There
is just the difficulty that there is being
reared here, under this method of artificial
assistance to industry, an edifice which
may not be permanent, and that the prosperity, which we are told it is likely to
bring to the farming community in the
immediate future may, under governmental changes elsewhere, prove not to be
lasting. That is an element which has to
be borne in mind. There is the possibility
that, with changes elsewhere, the measure
of prosperity which this Bill is bound to
bring to the farming community may not
continue, and that the farmers, who are
crying out for assistance now, and who
under this measure are going to get that
assistance, will not enjoy permanent prosperity under it. That is a very likely
possibility and one to which the Minister
should face up.
I feel that all the assistance that is given to industry in this
artificial way has no element of permanency and is questionable. Of course
it is only a matter of pure speculation,
but the farming community should
seriously consider whether the measure of
prosperity which this measure is going to
bring will be enduring.
I should have thought that in explaining the measure the Minister would have
given us some details in regard to the
cattle population in the North, that is the
number of milk cows in the Six Counties.
Information of that sort is, I assume, in
the hands of the Ministry. The Minister
could also have told us what the health of
that population is, what percentage of
that cattle population is estimated to be
suffering from disease. I think in England the percentage is thirty, but in Northern Ireland it is said to be much larger.
One man, who is in a big way in the industry, told me the other day that he estimated that one in every five cows in Northern Ireland was suffering from some
form of tuberculosis. I do not know
whether that is so or not, but it seemed to
me to be a startling statement. It would
mean that a very large percentage, at any
rate, was suffering from the disease, and
that is a very serious matter.
There is one other side of this question,
and I wonder has the Minister considered
it. I refer now to the effect of the measure
on border towns. The Bill provides that
all milk producers and sellers shall be
licensed. If we take the city of Derry,
which depends very largely for its milk
supply on cross-border farms, has the
Minister considered the position that may
easily arise when this Bill receives legislative sanction? I am sure thirty or forty
milk carts cross the border daily into
Derry, and under present circumstances
you could not exercise supervision over
them. How can those people be licensed,
and is any provision being made in regard
to them? Derry depends very largely
for its milk supply on Donegal, and I
should like to hear from the Minister what
provision, if any, is being made in respect
of those people and the people who depend
on those producers for their milk supply.
Nothing, as far as I can recollect, was
said by the Minister in regard to any propaganda with the view to increasing the
demand for milk in this area. Part of
the English legislation provides that there
is to be a propaganda in favour of the
No
greater consumption of milk.
reference has been made here to that. In

Mrs. PARKER: I should like to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture
upon the introduction of this Bill, and to
say that, at any rate on reflection, most

that we are dealing with a Measure of
major importance to the whole of the Six

have been in urgent need of the assistance

is a Measure which affects not only the

consumers as well as to the producers, and
I consider that the Government and the

with the outcry, the clamour, which was

Bill until they were in a position to do so

They have not allowed themselves to be

I should also like to take this opportunity of saying that I doubt very much
whether the people of the Six Counties
quite realise the gratitude which they owe

We hear a great deal about the various

When 1 came to Clause 5 I
astonished to find that notwithstanding
the appointment of a Joint Milk Council
of 17 members, representing producers,
consumers and distributors, the actual
powers of that Council were to be wielded
by three representatives chosen by the
Ministry of Agriculture. I say that this
is a principle which is open to very grave
suspicion. Many hon. Members of this
House have read a remarkable book,
written two or three years ago by a very
distinguished Lord Chief Justice of
England, protesting against the growing
tendency to hand over powers for all time
to bodies which are altogether removed
from the jurisdiction of Parliament. Here
we have a position in which, failing
unanimity in this Board, three members
appointed by the Ministry of Agriculture
can determine every question upon which
the Board is competent to express an
opinion or to give a ruling.
Now, the questions that will arise in
connection with such a Board are questions of the very utmost importance with
regard to agriculture. One of the
questions that will be dealt with by the
Board is the regulation of the price of
milk, and if this Bill passes without any
amendment in the Committee stage it
will mean this, that three members representing the Ministry of Agriculture will
have power to arrange for the price of
milk irrespective of the views of this
great community of Northern Ireland
and, furthermore, there are other things
with which the Board is competent to
deal. I find on looking at Clause 6,

power to prescribe the terms and form
in which the contracts shall be made
between suppliers of milk and distributors
of milk, and that power, too, instead of
being exercised by this Board, which this

in effect simply by three members
nominated by the Ministry of Agriculture.
In introducing this Bill the Minister
of Agriculture stated that these three
Members were three independent Members, and I was astonished, I may say,
to find that independent Members, three
in number, could exercise such power.
There are three independent Members
in this House, and up to the present they
have never yet been able to make their
power felt, and this autocratic principle.
seems to me to interpenetrate the whole
framework of the Bill. Why, if hon.
Members will turn with me to Clause 2,
sub-clause (3) they will find not merely
that all milk vendors and milk
distributors are to be licensed. That is
a
very fit and proper provision in the

find that the licence may be refused for

desire to sell milk here in the neighbourhood of Belfast, and apply for a licence,
then, though I comply with all the demands which are now rendered necessary
owing to the progress in bacteriological

an oligarchy from

the corresponding English

Marketing of Potatoes Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:

This Bill is
The
Sir BASIL BROOKE:
virtually an amending Bill. Hon. Members will recollect that the Marketing of
Potatoes Act, 1928, gives the Ministry
power to enforce the grading of all
potatoes shipped to Great Britain.
1928 Act has been of immense assistance
to the producers and the shipping trade
during these depressed times. For some
years the production of potatoes in Great
Britain has been greater than the consumers' demands. Even a small surplus
depresses prices and renders the production of potatoes for sale an unremunerative proposition. It is a great
tribute to the success of the 1928 Act
that with a surplus of potatoes in Great
Britain it has enabled Northern Ireland
to maintain its position in the British
market.
in
The reason, of course, is obvious.
The Northern Ireland farmer has exported graded potatoes, whereas
Great Britain the potatoes are not
graded. Consequently, there has been a
very natural demand for potatoes which
the merchants realised were the same
from top to bottom. If evidence is
necessary that grading has been a
success, it is afforded by the fact that
the graders have requested the Ministry
to extend the period of inspection and
grading from the 31st May to the end
of June. New developments are, however, now taking place across Channel
requiring a tightening up of our regulations if our favoured position is to be
preserved and developed. The Act of
1928 provides that each exporter shall
pay a licence fee of £1 and the licence
received for this fee remains in force so
long as the holder complies with the
prescribed conditions; therefore for all
practical purposes the licence fee covers
the lifetime of the licensee. In addition
to the licence fee, each exporter pays
to the Ministry an inspection fee at the
rate of 6d a ton on all potatoes exported
by him. It is now proposed to make
the following changes:-(i) The licence fee
to be an annual one of five pounds;
(ii) The inspection charge of 6d a ton
to remain unchanged, but each merchant
to pay in each season a minimum sum
not exceeding fifteen pounds towards
inspection fees on potatoes exported.
This minimum sum would be payable in
advance at the commencement of the
season.
2173 Marketing of Potatoes Bill-

6 JUNE 1934
Second Reading.
It will be realised by hon. Members
that with a possible increase in prices in
Engiand under the new marketing
schemes certain shippers may try to take
advantage of rising prices. These men
have no very great responsibility. They
place the potatoes on the English market
and crush the prices over here. It is
because of this that we propose to introduce a higher licence and deposit of £15.
Actually any shipper who exports 600
tons or over will be at no loss. The idea
is to prevent a man who is not really
serious in the business of shipping from
handling potatoes by which he may hope
to get a temporary gain, but who in fact
is spoiling the trade from the shippers'
and producers' point of view. It is
hoped by this extra licence fee and
deposit that a definite check will be placed
on these gentlemen. I should say in case
hon. Members think that my methods are
savouring of Hitler and Mussolini that
the shippers themselves have requested us
to carry out these changes which have
found approval. I think what we must
do is not to cut out competition, but to
prevent the man who is not shipping
seriously from injuring the trade.
Hon. Members are probably aware that
with a view to limiting the supply of
potatoes coming into the English market
stringent regulations are made with
regard to the acreage of potatoes that
can be planted there. Any infringement
of that excess of acreage planted by the
farmer is subject to a fine of £5 an acre.
It is quite obvious to everybody that any
scheme of that sort would be completely
unworkable here, because in Northern
Ireland approximately one million tons
of potatoes are grown. As we export
200,000 tons it is obvious that between
700,000 and 800,000 tons are consumed
in this country either on the farms for
personal consumption for feeding
animals. To attempt to restrict in any
way the acreage of potatoes grown would
effect the whole routine of the farm and
the feeding of these animals. What we
must do is to place ourselves in a position
to co-operate with the English Potato
Board when they bring their scheme into
force. It is with this object that this
Amending Bill is placed before the
House. Under the Agricultural Marketing Act passed by this Parliament we
have power to regulate the removal of
potatoes from Northern Ireland to Great
or
Britain. This power will, however, only
be used when necessary and the
machinery will be as simple and inexpensive as possible.
I should say that under the Act of
1928 we had power to grade for the
export market, but we had no power to
grade potatoes for internal consumption
and sale in the home market. I think
both consumers and producers will agree
that if you place ungraded potatoes on a
market such as Beltast there will be a
natural tendency to sink potato prices in
this country.
Especiany will that be
emphasised when grading is taking place
for export. There will be a temptation
for merchants to place on the Belfast
market, where no grading takes place,
those inferior articles which they were unwilling to ship abroad. There is no
doubt that a low potato price in the city
will be reflected right through the
country. I want to assure Members that
so far as the producers are concerned
there will be no change whatever. The
position remains as at present. A free
permit is granted to every farmer who
desires to ship his potatoes, there is no
licence or licence charge and no deposit
is required in respect of inspection fees.
I beg to move.

Mr. HENDERSON: Often in this
House Cabinet Ministers have not been
very relevant in many things they have
put before the House. I feel that this
is another injustice that is being forced
on the farmer. I was speaking to an
agricultural expert outside the House but
who had not the "guts" to come inside,
and he told me that he did not agree with
this Bill. I thought the proper thing to
do was to come inside the House and to
protest against this Bill. The introduction of this Measure will again mean an
increased number of inspectors. Under
this Bill it will be the duty of the
Ministry of Agriculture to see that every
one of the 200,000 small farmers in
Northern Ireland complies with its provisions and grades his potatoes in the
manner suggested by the Ministry. Is
that not so? It is definitely stated here.
Clause 1 states:-
Any person who sells or offers or
exposes for sale any potatoes in contravention of any provision in this Act or
rule made thereunder shall be guilty of
an offence against the Marketing of
Potatoes Act . . .
That goes to show that the Ministry will
be compelled to appoint additional
inspectors. Goodness knows, we have
enough inspectors. When the farmer is
grading his potatoes he will have an
official in attendance, and there will be
another official to see that they are of
proper quality. I feel that that is an
imposition on the taxpayer. If the right
hon. Gentleman tells the House that no
additional inspectors will be required, I
shall be satisfied. I should also like the
right hon. Gentleman to tell the House
whether this will enable the farmer to get
a better price for his potatoes, and
whether it will increase the consumption
of potatoes. I feel that instead of assisting the farmers you are putting obstacles
in his way. These Marketing Bills are
not doing anything to help agriculture
at all. By the introduction of Measures
of this sort you are meddling too much
with the farmer. Give the farmer a
chance. Do not interfere with him as
much as you are doing. There is too
much officialdom. Less interference by
the Government would be to the
advantage of the farming community and
to the citizens of Belfast. Some of these
officials would not know the difference
between a turnip and a carrot. I protest
against the appointment of another horde
of officials.

1. Mrs. PARKER asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state the
total amount contributed by the Government of Northern Ireland since its
inception towards assisting the Belfast
Corporation in respect of roads, housing,
unemployment relief schemes, education,
derating and other services, and the
amount which sixpence in the pound,
imposed by the Finance Bill for educational purposes, will produce this year.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The total sums contributed by the Government of Northern
Ireland since its inception up to the 31st
March, 1934, towards assisting the
Belfast Corporation in respect of roads,
housing, unemployment relief schemes,
education, derating and other services,
amount approximately to £5,542,150.
As regards the 6d rate referred to, I
understand that it will produce approximately £39,545 this year.

having been contributed to the Belfast
Corporation has, during the same period,
been drawn from Belfast in taxation and
distributed amongst the country districts
in Northern Ireland? (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)

McELDERRY SYSTEM OF PORK
GRADING.
8. Sir ROBERT LYNN asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether his
officials have carried out grading tests
under the McElderry system on 100 or
200 pigs and under the system which
prevails in public abattoirs; and whether
he can say which system produced the
best results.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Officers of my
Ministry have carried out a number of
tests at curers' establishments with a
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
7 JUNE 1934
view to comparing what is known as
"the McElderry system of grading" with
the system adopted in Great Britain and
elsewhere. These tests showed conclusively that the McElderry method
would be quite unsuitable, whereas the
recognised method proved satisfactory.
It must be remembered
in this
connection that the McElderry system
attempts only to measure the back fat and
that at a particular, and not necessarily
the most suitable point in every case;
whereas by the recognised system under
which grading takes place after the carcass is split fat can be measured at the
point which gives a fair reading of its
distribution on the carcass as a whole.
Further, as a grading system is developed
quality as well as depth and distribution.
of fat will have to be taken into account
and on this aspect of the matter the
McElderry system can never be a guide.
THE
EDUCATION
RATE-NEWS-
PAPER COMMENT.
Mr. YOUNG (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Finance whether
the statement which appeared in a
leading article of the "Northern Whig"
to-day accurately represents the Government's viewpoint regarding the reasons
which have led up to the proposal to
levy a shilling rate for Educational Services.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I am obliged to the hon. Member for affording me an early opportunity
of expressing my profound regret that
the writer of the editorial in question
should impugn the good faith of the
Prime Minister and myself by the suggestion that the proposed levy on local
authorities is merely a pretext, and thus
conveying the implication that it is to
be used for other than educational purposes. Clause 3 of the Finance Bill
clearly states in unambiguous language:
"There shall be paid to the Exchequer
of Northern Ireland by the council of
every county and county borough an
annual contribution towards the cost to
the said Exchequer of educational services," and, consequently, the Estimates
for Education will in future show a
reduction by the exact amount so levied.
It is not the first occasion on which
this journal has published statements
gravely misrepresenting the Northern
Government in its financial negotiations
with the British Treasury, and I cannot
deprecate too strongly the dissemination
of unfounded statements of this kind
with so much at stake. It is particularly
disheartening when I am at the moment
actively engaged in an
an endeavour to
reach an agreement on matters of farreaching importance to the future of
Ulster, involving immensely larger issues
affecting local authorities, I hope advantageously, than the modest contribution
they are now being asked to bear for
educational purposes.
Mr. McCARROLL: Is it not a fact
that the Chairman of the Finance Committee of the Belfast Corporation stated
exactly what is in to-day's "Whig,"
and has there been any repudiation of
his statement?
Mrs. PARKER: Yes, in this House.
Mr. POLLOCK: It was repudiated
by myself and by the Prime Minister.
Mr. NIXON: It is absolutely correct.
And a thousand times more.

Member knows, having been a Member

that I myself have nominated Mr.
Glendinning, of Derry, to take his place
in the Senate once again. I should not
like to leave the hon. and learned Member under the impression that action had
not already been taken in that direction.
Of course, it is open to any hon. Member of this House to nominate anybody
for that Assembly.

several years in another place. This is
the first day on which I have taken part
in the debates here. Now I find that having come here to discharge a public duty,
and to do that in the best way I can, I
am asked to disappear for about four
months. It is a rather startling position
to find oneself in. At a time like this
when all over the world faith in Parliamentary institutions has been shaken and
Parliamentary Government has fallen into
disrepute it does seem a remarkable feature
2211 Adjournment of the House HOUSE OF COMMONS
Adjournment of the House 2212
[Mr. Campbell]
that this House, under the conditions prevailing in Northern Ireland, should be
asked to break up and disappear for a
period of one-third of the year. Is there
any necessity for the continued existence
of this House? Is there no public urgency
or demand for the House sitting at least
once a week or fortnight? Those familiar
with the conditions in Northern Ireland
know, and know well-those who know
anything about the working classes of the
city and other urban areas-that there is
very acute I do not say general-distress
among large sections of our people. That
question has to be left in abeyance for four
months. I do not propose to discuss the
Unemployment Bill. That is beyond our
province at the moment, but it is only
nibbling at the problem of unemployment.
I say to the House that the impression.
may go abroad amongst the people of all
classes in Northern Ireland that Parliament has come to the condition that it is
really of no use to the people at large.
They will put a sinister construction on
our disappearance. They will say “If you
are no good for four months then you are
no good for twelve months." In Ulster
at the present time there is a rising and
powerful volume of public opinion
amongst the local authorities with regard
to the impositions that are gradually being
taken from the central authority and
placed on the county councils and urban
councils. The ratepayers in nearly every
area are feeling the matter acutely and
are protesting against it. Perhaps it is
to avoid that storm and take shelter that
the Government propose to take this prolonged summer holiday. I do most
strongly protest against this. I do not
see that there is any reason for the
Government taking this prolonged, unnecessary, and, as I think, vexatious
holiday time.

I would remind those hon. Members of

under Gresham's law it is said that a
debased currency is always apt to drive

Grade B will drive Grade A out of circulation. The object of this should be not

Sir BASIL BROOKE: By leave of the

limit of 200,000 tons only holds good
