THE SENATE VACANCY.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn.".
(Sir Wilson Hungerford.)
Mr. CAMPBELL: I mentioned earlier
in the day a question which I think is
one for every Member of this House
individually, that is the question of the
election of a Member by the majority of
this House to fill the vacancy now existing in the Senate. This is a matter of
deep concern to our people. Steps have
already been taken during the past fortnight which have caused very deep feeling
amongst the masses of the people whom
we on these benches represent. What is
the position at the present time? The
nominations for the Senate will be made
next week, and the election of the new
Member will take place a few days afterwards.
What is the state of the parties in the
Senate? The majority in this House is
represented in the Senate by twenty
Members, while the Nationalist minority
in this House is represented by only five
Members. The pro rata basis is four to
one. One vote more or less cannot affect
the preponderance of the Unionist
majority in the second Chamber, but one
vote more or less is of value to the
minority having regard to the fact that
the utmost they can command there is five
Members. Now, if the step contemplated
by the Prime Minister is taken next week
the door will be slammed against the
admission of a Nationalist to the second
Chamber in succession to a Nationalist. I
do appeal to Members of the House to
consider if in all the circumstances of the
situation here that is a fair or a chivalrous
gesture.
The hurry-scurry over this business has
been remarkable. After the issue of the
writ for the Central Division of Belfast,
and before the polling day, a meeting was
called and was reported in the public
Press, and the name of the candidate to
be put forward by the majority in this
House was publicly announced. At that
time the issue of the election could not be
known with any certainty and it can not
be contradicted that manoeuvring of the
kind I have described meant in the case
of my own defeat in the Central Division
that my return to the Senate would have
been cut off. I do not know whether the
intention was that I should be marked
down for proscription. Perhaps I should
rejoice at this proscription; perhaps 1
should wish no higher tribute. I did my
duty in the Senate, and I did it without
any regrets.
I would appeal to hon. Members
of this House. I think that if I
could appeal to them individually
I would appeal to some effect, because I fain hope that a good few of the
Members here have a sense of fair play
and toleration. This Parliament was set
up thirteen years ago, almost to a day,
but the majority, a great many of whom
have now passed away from these benches,
allowed, I understand, five seats to be filled
by the Nationalist minority. To-day the
majority are receding from that position.
They are not willing to deal by our people
as they dealt by them in 1921. I do not
know why that should be so. It may be that
if they had their chance they would keep
all the seats. That may be the case, but it
would hardly appeal to one as an argument of statesmanship. If the answer
given by the Prime Minister to-day can
be correctly interpreted it means that if
the majority in this House had their way
there would not be even one representative of the Nationalists of Northern Ireland in the Senate.
7 JUNE 1934
Adjournment--

The Senate Vacancy
We
have a discussion of this, because in
reality it is not a matter of administration for which any Minister could be
made responsible. The hon. and learned
Gentleman dealt with it by way of personal appeal to the individual Members
of the House, and in that sense only
could the hon. Gentleman (Mr. Grant)
reply.
Is the slogan in future to be that there
is to be no quarter for the Nationalists as
a party? We do not seek for mercy.
do not ask for any favour, but we do ask
for something in the nature of elementary
fair play, and the policy indicated in the
regrettable answer of the Prime Minister
to-day is, to my mind, an indication that
in this matter the rules of fair play will
not be followed. Our people are discontented about many things, and actions
of this kind intensify the discontent.
You have no eyes to see, no ears to
hear, when it is a question of toleration.
and fair play. I do appeal to hon.
Members who constitute the majority in
this House, if it is not too late now, to
reconsider this matter and to recognise
what the impression of the step that is
now contemplated will be upon so many
people in our area and upon far
larger numbers outside our area. I
submit that it is a harsh step, that it is
an abuse of power, and that it is neither
wise nor generous statesmanship. I
sincerely appeal to hon. Members to see
whether at this late stage the position
cannot be reconsidered with a view to a
more generous gesture to our people.

GRADING OF APPLES.
Mr. CAMPBELL (for Mr.
McCarroll) asked the Minister of Agriculture whether he can state if it is a
fact that in a circular, dated September,
1933, issued early in October, 1933, to
fruit growers and exporters in Northern
Ireland intimation was given of a
decision to raise from 2 inches to 21
inches the minimum diameter of "C"
grade apples for export whether, in
accordance with the terms of this circular, exporters were prohibited from
shipping graded apples under 2 inches
in
diameter; whether subsequently
permits were issued to certain exporters
to ship to British markets apples between the sizes of 2 inches and 24 inches
and to how many exporters were these
permits issued.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): It is a fact
that the circular referred to in the
question was issued by the Ministry.
The regulation referred to in the circular raising the minimum diameter of
apples for the "C" grade was made
after consultation with the Ministry's
Fruit Advisory Committee and it prohibited the export of graded apples of
less than 2 inches in diameter. No
export permits specifying apples from
2 inches to 21 inches diameter were
issued.

In drawing any inferences from these
figures regard should be had to the
following facts:-Exports of apples in
the 1933-34 season were seriously
diminished owing to a severe frost
towards the end of April, 1933, which
reduced the Northern Ireland crop by
more than half. Furthermore, owing
to exceptionally heavy consignments of
Australian and Canadian apples the
prices during the season in cross-
Channel markets were so depressed as
to offer little inducement to Northern
Ireland shippers and the bulk of the
Northern Ireland apple crop was
marketed in Belfast.
In 1930-31 season Northern Ireland
was fortunate in having an apple crop
above the average, while crops in Great
Britain and other apple producing
countries were below normal, consequently Northern Ireland shipments to
Great Britain in that season
were well
above the average, and, in addition, substantial shipments were made to Continental countries where normally our
apples are not required.

SINN FEIN TRICOLOUR IN DERRY.
12. Mr. MURPHY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware that
the Sinn Fein tricolour was extensively
flown in Londonderry on Sunday, 17th
June, and that such display has caused
indignation among the Londonderry
loyalists, and whether steps will be taken
to prevent such provocative displays in
future.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am informed
that on Sunday, the 17th instant, a large
number of persons, accompanied by five
bands, travelled from Londonderry to
Letterkenny to take part in a meeting.
On the outward journey no flags were
openly displayed, but on the return
journey to Derry, while the main body
proceeded in an orderly manner to the
bandroom at about 1 a.m. on the 18th
instant, the last contingent, with a band,
marched from the Lough Swilly Railway
Station to the bandroom. Whilst the
band played the followers indulged in
singing songs, using expressions of a party
nature and waving tricolour flags.
As such conduct was calculated to lead
to a breach of the peace five persons who
were identified were summoned to
Londonderry Petty Sessions on the 25th
instant, to show cause why they should
not be bound to the peace and to be of
good behaviour. They were bound over
by the court for two years, or in default,
one month's imprisonment.
I can assure the hon. and learned
Member that the police will continue to
take all the necessary steps to prevent a
recurrence of any such incidents.

The Senate agree to the Motor Vehicles

They agree to the Motor Vehicles and

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Motor Vehicles and Road Traffic Bill.
Order for consideration of Senate's
Amendments read.
Resolved, "That this House do forthwith take into consideration the Senate's
Amendments."-(Sir Dawson Bates.)
CLAUSE 1 (Penalties for reckless or
dangerous driving.)
Senate Amendment :
Clause 1,
page 2, line 38, after
"offence" insert "sub-section (4) of
section twenty-one and."
Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move,
"That this House do agree with the
Senate in the said Amendment."
Under sub-section (4) of Section 21 of
the Motor Vehicles and Road Traffic Act,
1926, the police can appeal against any
order made by a Court of Summary
Jurisdiction under the Act. The present
Amendment is designed to make it clear
that the police should not have a right
of appeal against the decision of a court
deciding to treat an offence as a first
offence under this Clause where there has
been no conviction for a similar offence
for a period of three years. This appears
to be a reasonable provision, and I beg to
move.

Road Traffic Bill-
Senate's Amendments
26 JUNE 1934
Senate Amendment:
Clause 4, page 4, after line 18 insert-
"provided that any person liable to be
charged with an offence under this
section shall not be liable to be charged
under section twelve of the Licensing Act,
1872, with the offence of being drunk
while in charge on a highway or other
public place of an animal or carriage."
Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move,
"That this House do agree with the
Senate in the said Amendment."
Clause 4 provides that if any person is
found, when driving in charge of a
vehicle drawn by a horse or other animal
on any highway or other public place, to
be under the influence of drink or drugs
to such an extent as to be incapable of
having control of the vehicle, he shall be
guilty of an offence under the Motor
Acts. Such a person would be liable to
be charged under Section 12 of the
Licensing Act of 1872, and it is considered undesirable that he should be
liable to be charged under two separate
Acts and, accordingly, it is proposed to
provide that he shall not have this
double liability, but shall only be liable
under the Motor Vehicle Acts and not
under the Act of 1872. I, therefore, beg
to move.
CLAUSE 7 (Obstruction of traffic on
public highway).
Senate Amendment:
Clause 7, page 4, line 32, leave out "an
obstruction" and insert "any obstruction
or danger."
Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move,
"That this House do agree with the
Senate in the said Amendment."
It is possible that a person might leave
a motor vehicle on the road in such a
position that it would not be an obstruction but it might be a source of danger
to the public. A case in point would be
if the driver of a car left it on a hill without taking reasonable precautions to see
that the vehicle would not start to move.
Cases have occurred of this kind where
proper precautions were not taken, with
the result that there has been injury to
persons and property. I think it is
reasonable to impose upon motorists the
responsibility of seeing that, under ordinary
circumstances, their vehicles are not a
source of danger to other people and,
accordingly, I beg to move.
Mr. MINFORD: I would like some
information as to this Amendment. It
would be very serious if a man was to
be charged for having caused a danger
when he left his car on the roadside.
Sir DAWSON BATES: We retain the
word "obstruction" and bring in the
question of danger. A car might be an
obstruction but not necessarily a danger,
while it might be in a dangerous position
but not necessarily be an obstruction.
This Amendment is to cover those two
points.
Mr. MINFORD: Am I to understand
the word "obstruction" to mean that it
must be proved to be dangerous?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No. If my
hon. Friend looks at the Amendment he

Mr. CAMPBELL: I should like to

have cars. That feeling exists at the

ought to consider carefully if we are

What are we proposing to do by this
Amendment? For the first time in the
history of the law of British or Irish community, we are proposing to make.
absent-mindedness-carelessness, if you
like on the part of pedestrians a crime.
Many people are absent-minded; I
think the benches over there are proof
of that. It is, of course, from force
of habit that many people are absentminded. As far back as the days of
Adam and Eve, people walking the highways of the country have been accustomed to wander more or less on their
feet. It is a habit that is engrained;
it is a habit that has never been checked.
You will find it exceedingly hard to kill
that habit, which is the result of
generations of inherited feeling and
instinct. It will die hard.
Instead of making it a penal offence
for a person to leave the footpath in a
moment of heedlessness, instead of
running a poor man into jail because
he cannot afford to pay the fine-it may
be only 5s or 10s-for a mere act of
incaution, I think we ought to trust to
the education of the people. We all
learn lessons from the past. I understand that in Paris there was an increase
of 50 per cent. in the number of motorcars from 1929 to 1932. During those
three years there was a gradual development going on in the way of providing
safe crossings for pedestrians, marking
places at which they could cross the road
in perfect safety, and the result was that
during those years casualties went down
to 27 per cent. That was a very remarkable result of the process of education and of the provision of safe crossings for the people.
In Germany they have just concluded what they call an "Education
Week," during which people were
instructed as to how to guide and guard
themselves on the highways. Germany
is a highly developed and progressive
country, and they are trusting there,
as in France, to the gradual process of
education. We are now trying to
educate the people by making it a crime
to be absent-minded or careless on the
roads. Last September the Automobile
Association held an investigation in over
100 areas in Great Britain into the dangers
of the roads. That Association applied
certain tests to ascertain the ages at
which the dangers are at their greatest,
and the result of the experiment was
this, that the most dangerous ages in
regard to the use of the highways are
from 5 to 6 and 60 to 70. Those are
two remarkable facts. I do not say that
children will be caught by this Amendment, but the older people may be
caught by it. They found that the most
dangerous day of the week so far as the
public was concerned was Saturday, and
the most dangerous hour of the day so
far as the general public was concerned
was between five and six o'clock, the
rush home hour. They found that the
most dangerous occupation in life in
Great Britain at the present day is walking the highways.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: This Amendment makes it clear that the Joint Milk
Council will have power to fix differential prices in different areas of Northern
Ireland. In view of the great difference
of conditions as between urban and rural
districts in Northern Ireland it is clearly
desirable that such a power should rest
with the Joint Milk Council. The
Amendment has the effect of making it
quite definite that the powers of the Joint
Milk Council in regard to the fixation of
prices may be exercised in this way. I
beg to move, "That this House do agree
with the Senate in the said Amendment."
Question put and agreed to.
Senate Amendment:
Page 9, line 12, at end add the following new sub-section:
:-
"(3) If, at a meeting of the Council
held for determining the price at, below
or above which, or the terms on which,
milk of Grade A, Grade B, or Grade
C may be sold as aforesaid, the members present, other than those
appointed by the Minister of Agriculture, are not unanimous upon the
question of the price or terms to be
so determined, then the three members
of the Council appointed by the said
Minister shall decide the question and
communicate their decision to the other
members of the Council and to the said
Minister, and the decision so communicated shall have effect as if it were a
decision of the whole Council.
The Ministry of Agriculture may by
regulations provide for carrying this
sub-section into effect, and in particular may prescribe the procedure to
be observed thereunder."
Sir BASIL BROOKE: During the
passage of the Bill through this House a
certain amount of discussion took place
with regard to the exact functions of the
three members of the Joint Milk Council
to be nominated by me. This Amendment has been put down with the object
of removing any misunderstanding which
may have existed with regard to the
functions of these three members of the
Council. In the event of the fourteen
members of the Council representing producers, distributors, and consumers being
unanimous in regard to a question of the
price or the contract terms on which
Grade A, Grade B and Grade C milk may
be sold, then there can be no interference
with their unanimous decision on the
part of the three members nominated by
me.
In view of the divergent interests represented by the producers, distributors, and
consumers it is clearly essential that there
should be provision for arbitration in the
event of these representatives on the
Council being unable to agree. This
function will be performed by my
nominees who, in addition to being
present on the Council as potential arbitrators, will also, I hope, frequently be in
a position to act as mediators in the discussions. In any case it is clearly desirable that the persons who are to act as

Mr. BEATTIE: The question put by
the hon. Member for Falls contained a
matter concerning the Ministry of Home
Affairs in regard to the law affecting
tenants. Thousands of people
living in controlled houses in Northern
Ireland, and they have recently been
subjected to an increase for rates. The
law governing the increase of rates is
very definite, and it is also very definite
in regard to the decrease of rates. I
understand that rents have been increased from 3d to 9d a week over and
above the actual amount allowed by law.
That is owing to the decrease not being
taken off at the proper time. The hon.
Member for Falls, when I was speaking
to him, had this in mind; hence the
latter part of his question.
I should like the Minister of Home
Affairs to take action and to ask all
local authorities to comply with the
request that all controlled houses from
£8 to £26 valuation should be clearly
set out at net rents, plus the increase
of rates which is due in the year 1934.
If that is done a great relief will be
given to many thousands of tenants in
Northern Ireland. I feel that the law is
sufficiently strong as it stands for the
Minister to act, and to compel the local
authorities to set out in a schedule the
net rents, plus the valuation, plus the
increase of rates over the year 1914. I
could quote many cases in which I have
been responsible for bringing down the
increase of rents from 9d to 3d. In
my own division I found that in one
street alone there were 20 controlled
houses, and that the landlord had
actually charged 6d over the controlled
rents.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Fisheries Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I think before entering
on the introduction of this Bill I might,
on behalf of every section of this House,
express the great gratification and
pleasure we all feel at seeing you, Mr.
Speaker, once more in the Chair. We
trust you are restored to the enjoyment
and blessing of good health and hope
that you may be long spared to preside
over our deliberations here. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
This is the third occasion on which
the House has been asked to legislate
on fishery matters. The first was in 1928
when Parliament gave its assent to the
Government's proposals to control the
sale of salmon, trout and eels by means
of a licensing system whereunder any
person dealing in such fish was obliged
to obtain a dealer's licence and to keep
certain records of his transactions. The
second occasion was towards the end of
last year when the Sea Fishing Industry
Act was passed. That Measure, as hon.
Members will recollect, empowered the
Ministry of Commerce to prescribe the
minimum sizes of sea fish which may be
sold in Northern Ireland in the same
way as the corresponding Measure, passed
only a few weeks before, had empowered
the English Ministry to prescribe for
Great Britain. The present Measure,
which, in its effects, will concern fresh
water fisheries mainly, deals with the
local machinery which the legislature has
provided for the protection and conservation of our fisheries and for the
enforcement of the fishery laws.
When speaking of fresh-water fishing
one is apt, I find, to think only of
angling and to overlook the much more
important commercial aspect of the subject. Northern Ireland is fortunate in
the possession of exceptionally valuable
salmon and eel fisheries, and whilst our
trout fisheries are not, for obvious
reasons, commercially exploited to the
same extent as either salmon or eels they
Fisheries Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbourj
do constitute a distinct asset to the
Province. As I am sure the House is
aware, there exists no public right of
fishing in any inland waters in Northern
Ireland. The fishing rights in such
waters, with the exception of those in
Lough Erne, belong either to private
The impersons or corporate bodies.
portant salmon fisheries in the Rivers
Foyle and Bann belong to the Irish
Society and are exploited under lease by
the Foyle and Bann Fisheries Company.
There is also the
the important. salmon
fishery in the River Bush, which, like
those in the Foyle and Bann, is fished
on commercial lines. Where there is no
several or exclusive fishery in the whole
of a river belonging to one person or
body, the fishing rights are owned by the
riparian owners who, it is pleasing to be
able to state, are usually most willing to
allow trout anglers to fish without
charge.
The importance of our salmon, trout
and eel fisheries has, of course, been long
recognised by Parliament, and legislation
dating back to 1842 is to be found providing for the protection and development of these fisheries in the national
interest. Whilst the entire responsibility for protecting and developing a
fishery has not been placed upon the
Government or upon the local bodies
appointed to administer the fishery laws,
it will be obvious to the House that Government control, within certain limits, is
essential to avoid the danger of over exploitation or neglect by any particular
owner. In the existing fishery laws,
therefore, we have a system whereunder
protection of the fisheries is secured by
the employment of water bailiffs by the
local conservancy boards and through the
assistance of the police force. Over and
above the protection secured in this way
the law has enjoined the observance of
certain rules and regulations such as, for
instance, the cessation of fishing during
the annual and weekly close seasons, the
prohibition of certain types of fishing
engine and the maintenance of a free
gap in the weirs in rivers frequented by
salmon. The Measure now before the
House is directed principally towards the
improvement of this system, and therefore to the development of a valuable
national asset.
The Bill has been designed principally
to give effect to the recommendations
made by the Committee on Local Fishery
Administration which I appointed in
1932, the Report of which has, no doubt,
come under the notice of hon. Members.
The administration of fishery services
in Northern Ireland rests with the Ministry of Commerce and the immediate responsibility for the enforcement of the
fishery laws with the four local bodies,
known as Boards of Conservators. The
conservancy districts are:-
(a) The Londonderry district covering
the sea along the coast from the
boundary of Northern Ireland at
Lough Foyle eastward to Downhill and the whole of the rivers,
lakes and their tributaries flowing
to this coast, being mainly those
in the Counties of Londonderry
and Tyrone;
(b) the Coleraine district covering the
sea along the coast from Downhill
to Portrush and from Larne southwards to the Northern Ireland
boundary at Carlingford Lough
with the rivers, lakes and their
tributaries flowing to these coasts;
(c) the Ballycastle district covering
the sea along the coast of Antrim
from Portrush to Larne with the
rivers, lakes and tributaries flowing to that coast;
(d) the Enniskillen district, which includes Upper and Lower Lough
Erne, and the rivers, lakes and
tributaries flowing to these loughs.
The boards of conservators, as I shall
presently explain, are representative of
the licence holders and the fishery owners
in the respective districts, the members
holding office for a period of five years.
Although changes in the geographical
divisions of the districts and in the tenure
of office of the boards have been made
from time to time, the machinery in its
present form dates as far back as the
Act of Parliament passed in the year
1848, which provided for the election of
boards of conservators for each fishery
district by the licence holders in that
district. The number of conservators to
be elected for each district was left for
the determination of the Central
Fisheries Authority-at that time the
Commissioners of Fisheries.
Fisheries Bill-
Second Reading
2 OCTOBER 1934
As hon. Members may well imagine, an
interval of almost ninety years has been
more than sufficient to allow of changes
taking place in the general conditions
surrounding local fishery administration,
and in 1932, after six years' experience
of the working of the machinery created
in 1848, I was convinced that however
satisfactorily the system may have worked
in the past and however ungrudgingly the
members of the various boards may have
given and are still giving their services
and time to the performance of the
important duties assigned to them, the
time had come when a thorough examination of the system was called for. The
examination, as I have said, was carried
out by a committee and, in so far as the
present Bill touches upon the constitution
and method of electing boards of conservators, as well as on the amount of
licence duties payable on certain classes
of fishing engines, the provisions I am
now submitting to the House embody the
recommendations of that committee.
As at present constituted, membership.
of a board falls into three categories:-
year,
(I) Members elected by the votes of
the persons who have paid licence duty.
during the the number of votes to
which the licence-holder is entitled
varying with the amount of licence.
duty paid;
(II) Ex-officio members, comprising
those persons
who own a several or
exclusive fishery in the district carrying a poor-law valuation of £100 a year
or upwards, and
(III) Ex-officio members comprising
magistrates paying licence duty and
being the owners of land abutting on a
river or lake within the district.
It was clearly the intention of the
Legislature that all interests should be
represented on each board, but experience
has shown that this intention is liable to
be frustrated. After careful consideration it has been decided that a more
effective method of achieving this object
would be to allow the holders of salmon
rod licences to elect their own representatives, and the holders of all other
licences who are, broadly speaking, professional fishermen, to elect theirs.
The
committee recommended that no alteration
in the geographical divisions of the existing districts was necessary or desirable,
and in this view the Government concurs.
The circumstances of the four districts
vary so greatly, however, that the committee considered it impracticable to
devise a uniform scheme of representation
in all districts. The Government has
adopted the committee's recommendations, and the details of the scheme are
set forth in the First Schedule to the Bill.
The procedure laid down in the earlier
Acts for the holding of elections has been
entirely recast, and the new procedure,
which is set out in the Second Schedule
to the Bill, will render voting by proxy
unnecessary.
With regard to the qualifications for
ex-officio membership of the boards,
experience has shown that certain
modifications are necessary. As I have
already stated, the owner of a several
fishery rated at £100 a year and upwards
is at present entitled to act as an ex-officio
member of the board of the district in
which the fishery is situated. The
Government concurs in the view of the
committee that the £100 minimum is too
high, and the Bill accordingly proposes
to lower the minimum to £30 per year.
It is felt that at the same time additional
representation should be given to the
proprietor of a large fishery, and provision is
is accordingly made that the
proprietor of a fishery rated at £300 a
year and over should be allowed to
nominate a second representative as
ex-officio member of the board.
an
As regards the second class of ex-officio
member, that is magistrates owning land.
abutting on any river or lake in the
district, the view of the committee was
that the possession of such qualifications
was not in itself adequate justification for
membership under present conditions.
The committee accordingly recommended.
that the Section of the 1863 Act which
conferred ex-officio membership upon this
particular class of licence-holder should be
repealed and that, in place of such
persons, owners of lands in the district
carrying a valuation of £50 per year or
more, and having a frontage to fresh
waters in the district of not less than half
a mile, should be admitted to ex-officio
membership.
Part II of the Bill prohibits the sale
of salmon and trout between 16th
September and 31st January following,
and makes it an offence to sell salmon or
trout of a size less than eight inches in
length. There is, of course, a saving
clause for any act done for the purpose of
ol
Second Reading
Fisheries Pill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
artificial propagation of fish or the stocking or re-stocking of waters under a
certificate granted by the
the Ministry.
These, I think the House will agree, are
desirable restrictions in the interests of
the preservation of our fishery resources.
Part III provides for certain alterations
in the licence duties chargeable under the
Fisheries Acts. The House will observe
that no change is proposed in the existing
salmon rod licence duty of £1 10s per
annum, which was fixed by the Act of
1928, but provision is made, largely in
the interests of tourist development, to
meet the case of anglers who may be able
to fish for only a few days in the year.
Boards of conservators are empowered to
issue a licence for angling with a single
salmon rod within their district during
the limited period of seven days on payment of a reduced licence duty of 10s.
Hitherto trout fishers have not been
required by law to take out a licence, and
no general provision requiring them to do
so has been included in the Bill. There
are, however, localities in Northern
Ireland where an angler for trout might
fairly be required to procure a licence,
and provision is accordingly made in
Clause 15 for the Ministry, after consultation with the board of conservators and
after holding a public inquiry, to fix by
by-law the amount of the duty to be paid
for a licence to fish with a trout rod and
line in any particular area.
The committee further recommended that
the owners of certain fishing engines
should be required to make a somewhat
larger contribution than they do at
present to the expenses of conservation
and, accordingly, provision is made in the
Bill for moderate increases in the existing
duties on these engines, all of which, it
will be observed, are used in salmon fishing. In order to ensure the necessary
measure of elasticity in the fixing of
duties, the Bill proposes to authorise the
Ministry, after consultation with the
board of conservators and after holding
a public inquiry, to vary any particular
rate of duty within the maximum laid
down by statute.
The matters to which I have so far referred all come within the scope of the
recommendations of the committee. The
opportunity presented by the Bill has
been taken to effect certain other improvements in the law which have either
recommended themselves in the ordinary
course of administration or have been suggested to the Ministry by advisory and
other bodies. The most important of
these is probably the provision in Part V
of the Bill for ensuring satisfactory cleanliness in the packing of fish and in fishhandling establishments other than retail
premises. The provision is one which, I
am sure, will commend itself to hon.
Members.
Clause 16 of the Bill might also be
mentioned. As the law now stands, the
positions of fixed salmon nets around our
coast were specificially fixed by certificates
granted by the Commissioners appointed
by the Fisheries Act of 1863. Experience has shown, however, that in certain
instances some slight variation in the
position of the net might with advantage
be made, and the Bill, therefore, proposes
to empower the Ministry to make such an
alteration, provided that the removal and
re-erection of the net in the new position
is in the interests of the fishery, and that
it will not conflict with the reasonable
and legitimate interests of any other
person.
It is also proposed to modify the provisions in the 1863 Act relating to the
maintenance of a free gap in any fishing
weir where immediately adjoining such
weir there is a navigation gap which conforms in form and dimensions with the
requirements of the statute, and thus
secures the free passage of fish up and
down the river.
I may say, in conclusion, that the
proposals which I have outlined have
received the unanimous approval of the
Fisheries' Advisory Committee of my
Ministry, a body representative not only
of the four boards of conservators, but
also of fishery owners and fishermen
throughout Northern Ireland, and it is
with confidence, therefore, that I ask the
House to give the Bill a Second Reading.
I beg to move.
Question proposed: "That the Bill be
now read a Second time.'
Mr. LEEKE: In the first place I
would like to join with the Minister in
saying how glad we are to see you, Mr.
Speaker, here again and enjoying good
health. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
A long time ago we were promised that
we would get a Bill which would help
the fisheries of Northern Ireland. The
Fisheries Bill-
Second Reading
2 OCTOBER 1934
Minister has rightly said to-day that our
fishing industry is a valuable national
asset. Indeed, so far as the Minister has
led us to believe, it is second only to
agriculture. It is an industry which
should be capable of very great development, but, unfortunately, if there is one
industry in Northern Ireland which the
Government have neglected it is the
fishing industry. I have advocated again
and again that something should be done
to develop our fisheries in a way that
would give employment in our rural
areas, but, instead of doing that,
the Government have ignored our fisheries
to such an extent that the fishermen on
our coasts-I refer now to the poorer
ones and not to the wealthy monopolies
which, as the Minister has said, control
practically the whole of the fisheries in
Northern Ireland-are more or less
starving. There is no question that the
big English monopolies control the
fisheries in Northern Ireland, and all the
legislation in regard to fisheries in this
House has been so shaped as to assist
them to the detriment of the poorer
classes of fishermen.
I would just like to remind the Minister
of one thing in this Bill. He has raised
the licence duty on draft nets in tidal
waters on the coast from £2 to £3. What
has been the most disastrous of all nets so
far as the fisheries of Northern Ireland are
concerned? The river draft net in fresh
waters. Has anything been done to raise
the licence duty on those nets? That
duty I believe at the moment is about
£3. If you raised it to £10 it would
still be too low, and those nets would
still show a huge margin of profit. But
the poor man in the outside waters finds
his licence duty is going to be increased.
Is there any fair play in that? I leave
it to this House, and particularly to those
Members who come from around
County Derry, to say if there is.
The Minister also told us that a Committee has been set up. By the way that
Committee did not include any representative of the coastal fishermen. It was
representative largely of the inside waters
and of the big interests, but there were
no representatives from the democratic
parts of the country. Was there not also
a Committee which reported about three
years ago on the question of the alteration
of the fisheries on the coast? Did the
Government accept any of the recommendations of that Committee? Not one
was accepted, although they pointed out
that the fisheries could be improved all
round the coast if their recommendations
were put into operation. The Government did not accept those recommendations, but they now accept the recommendations of this Committee because
they will protect the big interests and the
monopolies, which are mostly English.
That is why I say this Bill is really a
disadvantage to Northern Ireland.
The Minister has explained the
Measure very clearly and has certainly
shown a knowledge of our fisheries which,
I must say, has amazed me. But he did
not tell us that the system of election
of these conservators is the most
undemocratic in the world. There is no
other body elected in the same way.
Practically all our fisheries are controlled
by elected representatives nominated by
these monopolies. I say that should not
be the case.
I thought also that the Bill would have
been of such a comprehensive character
that it would have embraced some provisions for dealing with the grievances of
the Lough Neagh fishermen, who have
been fighting for years to have those
grievances removed. There is not one
word in the Bill in the interests of those
poor men. It is only for the people who
have the control of fishing in Northern
Ireland. If the Minister gives me a
promise that he will drop this Bill for the
present and bring in a new Bill next
Session I will agree to go no further in
opposition to it, but if not I must move
its rejection. Such a poor attempt to
improve the fisheries of Northern Ireland,
or of any other country for that matter,
I have never seen. There is not one thing
in it to help the coastal fishermen, the
poor men who have to go out to sea in
their small boats. Instead their licence
duties are to be increased, while the big
associations like the Foyle and Bann
Fisheries are to be protected and their
licence duties, instead of being increased,
are to be kept at the same level. If there
were any opportunity to amend this Bill I
would not oppose it at this stage, but I
realise that we cannot amend this Bill,
and consequently in the interests of the
fishing people of Northern Ireland I move
that it be read a Second time upon this
day six months.
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I as a fresh
Member of this House join in the welcome

home which has been extended to you,

This Bill is only one of a long succession

this very
Bill, which one would have

Measure and purely self-explanatory

both our fresh water and deep sea fishing
into one codifying and consolidating Bill.
One reason why I find fault with this
Bill is that it is an attempt to keep up
the undemocratic conditions under these
boards of conservators. The Minister of
Commerce calls the conservators. He
prefers that to what I call them,
conservators. The qualifications for these
conservators are of such a character
that the ordinary poor fisherman or
licensee is practically excluded from
election. The elected element under the
Bill consists of thirty-four members
elected to the four different boards.
There are thirty-four elected members and
three nominated members. Then there is
the ex-officio element. That element is
to be appointed on a basis which is
certainly the negation of democracy at
the present day. When a Bill of this kind
was being brought in in the year 1934 an
effort surely should have been made to
secure the representation of the entire
fisheries of Northern Ireland on something like a popular basis. But how does
it stand under the Bill? We find the
qualifications set forth in Clause 5. The
ex-officio members of the boards must
satisfy these qualifications. If they are
owners, lessees, or occupiers of a several
or exclusive fishery this must have a rateable value of at least £30. If they are in
the happy position of being nominated by
a gentleman who is the owner, lessee, or
occupier of a fishery of a rateable value
of at least £300 they can become members
of these boards of conservators. If they
are owners of lands of a rateable value
of at least £50 abutting on fresh waters,
and have the right to fish those waters,
and pay a licence duty for fishing then
again they can become members of these
boards of conservators. Those are all
high qualifications, far too high to give
ordinary men representation on these
boards. What peculiar or special qualification for this work have these gentlemen
with these high property qualifications!
Does the mere fact that they are men of
wealth and extensive property give them
any peculiar right to have the power of
handling these fishery laws? I cannot
see for one moment that it does. I am
not sure of the ratio which the elected
element bears to the ex-officio element.
I know the elected element is thirty-four
strong. I know there can be three members nominated by the Ministry making
thirty-seven, but at present I am in the

CLASS VII. No. 2.
FISHERIES, HARBOURS, RAIL-
WAYS AND COMMERCIAL
SERVICES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £811 be granted to His Majesty for
the service of the year ending 31st
March, 1935, to defray the expenses of
the Ministry of Commerce in respect of
Harbours (1 Geo. IV., c. 113; 39 and 40
Vic., c. 236), Railway Fishery and
Commercial Services, including certain
Grants in Aid (16 Geo. V., c. 4 (N.I.));
payments under Section 6 of 13 and 14
Geo. V., c. 6 (N.I.), and under 46-47
Vic., c. 43, s. 9, and 52-53 Vic., c. 66;
Section 10 of 13 and 14 Geo. V., c. 31."
Mr. BARBOUR: This supplementary
estimate of £811, for which I am seeking the Committee's approval, is for the
purpose of defraying the expenses of a
scheme promoted by my Ministry to
meet the very serious situation which
resulted from the almost
complete
failure of the herring fishing off our
coast this season.
As hon. Members are aware herring
fishing is one of the most important
branches of the fishing
the fishing industry in
Northern Ireland and gives employment
to some 40 boats, manned by about 215
men, operating from the ports of Portavogie, Ardglass and Kilkeel. Altogether, therefore, it may be said that
something like 1,000 of our people are
directly dependent on herring fishing
during four or five months in the year.
The herring fishing season for these
boats commences in the beginning of
May and normally lasts to about the
third week in September. From the
1st May to about the middle of July
the herrings are landed at Portavogie,
Ardglass and Kilkeel, and sold locally
in their fresh state. From mid
July onwards the landing takes place
mainly at Ardglass, but to some extent
also at Kilkeel, at both of which places
the fish are cured for export to continental markets. During the curing
portion of a normal season Scottish and
English drifters augment the local fleet
and land their catches at Ardglass.
At
The majority of the Northern Ireland
boats engaged in herring fishing are
of the nobby type, which carry a skipper
and a crew of four, but there are also
a number of larger boats of the lugger
type, mainly working from Kilkeel,
which carry seven men in all, as well
as a few smaller boats manned by a
skipper and a crew of three men.
the beginning of the season the skipper
of each boat, who in most cases is also
the owner or part owner, is responsible
for fitting out the boat for the season
as well as for the supply of the boat's
share of the gear. The members of the
crew supplement the gear supplied by
the skipper by the addition of nets purchased on their own account. The expenses of fitting out and the purchase of
gear at the beginning of the season are
usually repaid from earnings during the
course of the season. The boats are
run on paraffin, supplemented to a small
2365 Supplementary Estimate-

3 OCTOBER 1934
Committee
extent by petrol, and the average
running expenses, including food for the
crew, vary from £3 to £7 per week,
according to the size of the vessel.
This year the herring fishing season
started as usual at the beginning
of May, but fish were very scarce and,
by the end of June, it was evident that
matters had reached a state of crisis.
By that time the total catch had
amounted to only 1,290 cwts.,
which
sold for £1,238, whereas the average
catch for this period over the previous
seven years was 7,920 cwts., valued at
£5,169. The sum of £1,238 realised up
to the end of June this year represented
the total earnings of some 35 boats over
a period of nine weeks, or, in other
words, an average of rather less than £4
a week per boat.
As I have already mentioned, the
average running expenses vary from £3
to £7 per week, and these sums cover
only the cost of fuel and food, so that
not only were the earnings insufficient
to cover running expenses, but there was
no margin to meet the bare necessities
of the men's homes. The fishermen, as
I have said, were working on credit and
were dependent on the profits of the
herring fishing not only to repay the
cost of fitting out, but also to assist them
over the winter months, when earnings
are much smaller. Moreover, it was
evident that the merchants who had supplied the boats with oil, fuel and food
on credit were not prepared and could
not be expected to continue to provide
these necessities indefinitely, and, in the
absence of assistance from some outside
source, the inevitable consequence would
have been the cessation of fishing
operations and the laying up of the boats
for the season.
The position was laid before my
Ministry by the fishermen at the end of
June, and I was convinced that in the
wholly exceptional circumstances which
had arisen the Ministry was called upon
to take such steps as would enable the
boats to continue fishing in the hope that
conditions would improve as the season
advanced. My object, therefore, was
to devise some means by which the
skippers could be indemnified against
loss, in so far as running expenses were
concerned, in order to give them and their
crews the chance of reaping the benefit
of any improvement in fishing conditions
that might occur at a later stage in the
season.
Obviously it was not desirable that
the Government should undertake to pay
the running expenses irrespective of
earnings, and the scheme adopted by my
Ministry was framed on the principle of
making good the running expenses to the
skipper in respect of any week in which
the earnings fell below a certain figure,
such figure being fixed by reference to
the type of boat and the number of the
crew. The scheme, which operated in
respect of the nine weeks in July and
August, applied to all Northern Irish
herring fishing boats which fished regularly and industriously during that
period. To all such boats the Ministry
undertook to make weekly payments on
the following scale: To luggers, £7, or
difference between the sum of £11 and
the amount realised on the sale of the
week's catches, whichever is the lesser; to
nobbies, £5, or difference between the
sum of £2 15s and the amount realised
on the sale of the week's catches, whichever is the lesser, and to smaller boats,
£3, or difference between the sum of £6
and the amount realised on the sale of
the week's catches, whichever is the
lesser.
Payments were made on the condition
that the skipper would undertake to use
the money to defray week by week the
running expenses of his boat; and receipts for the payments made by the
skipper in respect of the previous week's
expenses were called for and produced to
the Ministry throughout the entire
period.
In all, 39 boats were found eligible
under the scheme, but of these only 35
actually qualified for assistance. The
hoped for improvement unfortunately
did not take place, and the season of
1934 must, accordingly, be regarded
as a failure. In fact, I am informed
that it has been the worst for almost
forty years. The total amount expended
was £810 5s 6d, which is the amount
of the Estimate before the Committee.
During the period covered by the scheme
the total value of the herrings landed
was £1,888, which includes those landed
by Northern Ireland boats in the Isle of
Man, so that by a Government expenditure of £811 the fishermen were enabled
to earn a sum of £1,888. I think,
Supplementary Estimate-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
therefore, that the Committee will agree
that the effort to encourage the fishermen to persevere was distinctly worth
while, in view of the importance of this
branch of the industry in normal times.
I beg to move.
Mr. CRAWFORD: I do not rise to

look upon the fishing industry as second
in importance only to agriculture.
Consequently anything to help
help the
fishing industry will have my strong
support. I noticed in the Press this
morning that the industry, which was

£4,000 up to 1st October this year. I
believe it is deserving of support, and
I congratulate the Minister in bringing
forward this supplementary estimate.
I would like to ask the right hon.
Gentleman if he has confined his inquiries entirely to County Down and if
he has not taken County Antrim into

respect County Antrim is not nearly so
well situated. From Portrush round to

stations, and I would like to know if
the Minister has taken steps to get

there might possibly be places in County
Antrim as well as in County Down where
help would be needed in this connection.
In my own constituency there is one
place where there used to be a most successful fishery, but for some reason
unexplained the fish have gone elsewhere, with the result that last year was
a complete failure. In County Antrim.
the same thing applies that applies in
County Down.
Another thing I would like to ask the

Kingdoms which happens to be in
County Antrim. (Hon. Members:
Question.) Well, County Antrim
touches it at a great many points. A
large proportion of the fish caught in
Lough Neagh are landed in County
Antrim and shipped from County
Antrim. One hundred years ago, I
noticed in a paper recently, there were
over a thousand people engaged in fishing
there, but now the fishing industry has
died
away to a very great extent. I
ask the Minister if he has given his consideration also to this question and that
other places which are suffering will be
dealt with in the same way
as those
places in County Down. There has been
a good deal of suffering there, and I am
glad to see they are getting help, but I
would like an understanding from him
that if it can be shown that other places
are suffering also they will likewise be

I cannot move that this Supplementary
Estimate be increased. For once in my
life I would like to do so. I would suggest that the Minister should adjourn
this Vote until he makes inquiries, and
if he finds that need of a similar nature
exists in other places, he should help the
fishermen in those places because they
are engaged in producing food and are a
most useful set of men. I feel he should
consider other places as well as County
Down. He should adjourn this Vote to
find out whether the same conditions
exist in other places as exist in County

Mr. CAMPBELL: Were it not for
the fact that it is not competent for me
to move an increase in this Estimate I
would do so. I have some experience
of the fishery at Ardglass, and I do think
that that fishery is in danger of
extinction. It is
It is a melancholy sight,
morning after morning, to see those
boats coming in from the Irish Sea with
practically no fish. There is a very
large population in County Down round
Ardglass, and they are a fine, honest,
industrious race of people. I am glad

boats are each manned by a crew of four
and some by a crew of seven, and the

We find that in the season of nine
weeks the expenses of the smallest boat
setting out from Ardglass is about £27,
and in the case of the larger boats about
£63. If hon. Members take the average

which will fall to each boat under the

Mr. BARBOUR: In reply to the hon.
Member for Mid Antrim (Mr. Crawford), I do not think he would expect
the Government to make it their special

the plight of our herring fisheries in
County Down was so outstanding that it
obviously was a case to which Government assistance, if available, should be
devoted. Of course hon. Members will
realise that the fishing done in normal
seasons from our great herring port of
Ardglass is mainly done by trawlers
which come from England and Scotland
following the shoals of fish around the
coast. But we have a certain number
of local fishermen who make it their main

in order to keep these men interested in

scheme was started this year. In the
year 1926, I believe, the total value
of the herrings landed at Ardglass
amounted to the very large sum of
£72,000. In the year 1933 the value of
herrings landed there was £17,000.
But of course hon. Members will be
aware that, owing to the restrictions
placed on the import of herrings in
foreign countries to which our herrings
are usually exported after curing, the
whole character of the business has
changed very materially from what it
was before the war, and so we have to
face conditions as they exist to-day
rather than have regard to figures that
may have obtained some years ago.
My hon. Friend, the Member for Mid
Antrim, was particularly anxious to
know how the fisheries round about
Antrim had fared. Naturally I, myself,
would take a particular interest in
Antrim, but I do not know whether he
has brought forward this question with
any knowledge on his part of the conditions as they may exist round Antrim,
or merely with the idea that if Government plunder is going it would be a
great pity if Antrim did not secure its
share. It may interest him to know
that from the figures which I have received as to the landings of fish-other
than herrings, I may say-round Antrim
and the Northern Ireland coast, from
Torr Head to Warrenpoint, I find that
the values were as follow:-In the year
1931 the value of fish landed was £1,860;
in the year 1932, £2,932; in the year
1933, £1,589; and in the year 1934
£2,428; in other words, the past year
was, with one exception, the best of four
years. That is for the area of coast
from Torr Head to Warrenpoint. In
so far as the landings for the area from
Londonderry to Torr Head are concerned, I find that the figures are:-
1931, £2,369; 1932, £2,418; 1933,
£3,943; 1934, £3,606. So that, having
regard to the conditions that have prevailed in the fishing industry not only
in Northern Ireland but all round the
British coasts, the fishermen in these

Expiring Laws Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Expiring Laws Continuance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Babington): This is a Bill to continue
certain expiring laws as regards Northern Ireland. The details of those
respective Acts it is not competent for
me to go into now, because, as I understand the rules of the House, if hon.
Members object to any of those Acts they
can be challenged and taken out of the
Schedule when the Committee stage of
the Bill comes on.
The Bill continues
certain temporary Measures, some of
them old Measures of the Imperial Parliament and some of them Measures of
this Parliament, and there is a single
date fixed for their continuance-31st
December, 1935.
The Bill has been framed so as to fit
in with the corresponding Imperial Bill,
which applies to Northern Ireland in so
far as it deals with enactments relating
to subjects with respect to which the
Parliament of Northern Ireland has not
power to make laws. The present Bill
supplements this provision by dealing
with enactments relating to subjects
with respect to which the Northern Ireland Parliament has legislative power.
Accordingly the Schedule is in two
Parts, the first relating to enactments of
the United Kingdom Parliament continued in their duration, and the second
containing the enactments of this Parliament continued also in their duration
for the same period of time, namely to
the 31st December, 1935. Hon. Members will realise that, whether they
object to any of these Measures or not,
there is necessity for continuing, at any
rate, certain portions of this legislation.
Accordingly, I beg to move.
Question proposed: "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."
Mr. CAMPBELL: There is one Act
of Parliament in this Schedule which
deserves more than merely
merely passing
notice. That is the Local Government
(Emergency Powers) Act, which it is
proposed to continue. That Act was
passed in the year 1921, and it was used
by the Executive for the purpose of
suppressing the County Councils of
Tyrone and Fermanagh. Those Councils
were Nationalist. That was the head
and front of their offence, and under the
powers conferred on the Executive by
this Act those Councils were suppressed
and paid Commissioners put in place of
the elected representatives of the people.
That use of the Act elicited a memorable
remonstrance from Lord Birkenhead,
who was then a Member of the British
Cabinet. He said that the Cabinet
would have to take steps to guard
against a recurrence of tactics of that
kind by which a political majority could
penalise and victimise its political
opponents. Evidently what he had in
mind was the transfer of those two great
Counties of Tyrone and Fermanagh from
the jurisdiction of Northern Ireland.
Nothing came of that remonstrance,
however, and it became a mere scrap of
paper. Our people still exist in those areas,
and, no matter how this Act is worked
by the Executive, it will not deflect the
Nationalists of those areas one hair's
breadth from their settled convictions.
The people in that massive hinterland
of Tyrone and Fermanagh will remain
impregnably Nationalist and a permanent
factor in Irish politics.
Is it a coincidence that under this Act
of Parliament every Council on which
the axe has fallen, with one exception I
think, has been a Nationalist Council?
Tyrone had a Nationalist majority in its
Council. That majority is gone. Fermanagh had a Nationalist majority in
its Council. That majority is gone.
Armagh was a Nationalist Council, and
that Council is gone. The Armagh
Urban Council is no longer operating.
I do protest against this Act being perpetuated. It is capable of being used
harshly, vindictively, and
crupulously. It has been so used in the
past, and it will be so used in the future
when the pretext arises. I do submit to
this House that it is being kept on the
Statute Book for one purpose and for
one purpose alone, namely, as a means
of proscribing the political opponents of
the Government.

JOINT MILK COUNCIL.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state the
names and addresses of the members of
the Milk Marketing Board.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): I presume
that the hon. Member refers to the
Joint Milk Council which is to be constituted for the purposes of the Milk
and Milk Products Act (Northern Ireland), 1934. No appointments to this
Council have yet been made nor have
any members been elected. I regret,
therefore, that I am not in a position to
supply the information which the hon.
Member desires.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the Minister
give the House the assurance that when
the appointments of the consumers'
representatives are being considered he
will have credentials that they are
genuine consumers of milk?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: That does
not come under my Ministry. It is a
question that should be addressed to the
Minister of Home Affairs.
ALLOCATION OF MEMBERS OF
MILK MARKETING BOARD TO
COUNTIES.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL (for Mr. Healy)
asked the Minister of Agriculture
whether he can state why he has allocated only one member of the Milk
Marketing Board to Fermanagh and
Tyrone and two to Down in view of the
relative importance of the industry in
these areas.
the
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I presume
that the hon. Member refers to
Joint Milk Council which is to be constituted for the purposes of the Milk
and Milk Products Act (Northern Ireland), 1934.
The Joint Milk Council (First
Election of Members) Regulations which
have been made by my Department
provide that of the members to
elected by holders of licences for the
production of milk for the liquid milk
market, two shall be elected by persons
licensed in respect of premises situated
in the Counties of Armagh, Fermanagh
and Tyrone.
I would point out to the hon. Member that the Joint Milk Council will be
entirely concerned with the milk sold in
liquid form for human consumption,
and the elected members will, therefore,
be representative of the producers and
distributors of such milk. Since it is
evident that the bulk of the milk sold in
liquid form is produced in the areas
adjacent to the principal consuming
centres, I think that the hon. Member
will agree that the producers in these
areas are entitled to a relatively larger
representation on the Council than producers in other areas, such as Counties
Fermanagh and Tyrone, where most of
the milk is used for manufacturing purposes. The hon. Member will appreciate that the majority of farmers in
Counties Fermanagh and Tyrone send
the milk they sell to the creameries and
that the price they receive for this milk
has already been fixed by statute.
ACREAGE OF OATS CROP.
3. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state the acreage under oats in Northern Ireland for the twelve months
ending 30th June, 1934; and whether
this is the smallest acreage under the
crop ever recorded in this area.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The area
planted under oats as at the 1st June,
1934, was 279,759 acres, which is the
smallest acreage recorded in Northern
Ireland under this crop.
There was, however, a substantial increase in the area under other cereals,
and, as a consequence, the total area
under cereals in 1934 does not vary
greatly from that in 1933 or 1932.

Mrs. PARKER: I want to ask the
Minister if he will, perhaps, say something more on the subject of what is
definitely an innovation in this Clause.
It is one which I fear will hit some of

before this is carried into effect. At the

for that inquiry, and it is a great innovation and, in my opinion, opens up a very
wide field. I would like to hear just a
little more as to what is in the mind of
the Ministry on this subject. Fishermen
in the country, the men for whom I am
speaking now, naturally will feel very
strongly indeed if, in any district, this
inquiry is held and turns out in such a
way that they have in future to pay a
licence to fish for trout. I would like
to know a little more about it.

Clause is, for an Act of Parliament, very
self-explanatory and clear, and the hon.
Member has really stated in as plain
language as could be stated the exact
intention of this particular Clause. At
present no licence duty is charged for
fishing for trout in Northern Ireland.
As I said in reply to the first question,
the whole object of this Bill is to try to
improve and develop the sport of fishing
in Northern Ireland, to help those who
are interested in the capture of fish
to preserve them, and to afford a supply
of fish so that they may indulge in the
sport in which they find pleasure. That
is the whole object of the Bill. It was
thought that there are certain rivers in
Northern Ireland which might be capable
of better development and better protection in the interests of trout angling, and
so, under the Clause, if it were considered that it would be worth while to
schedule any particular river to be preserved for trout fishing, and if the conservators, who are elected more or less by '
the anglers and by those who are
interested in fishing in Northern Ireland,
would recommend that such a course
should be followed, then the Ministry of
Commerce would give very sympathetic
consideration to their recommendation.

hold a public inquiry.
Mr. BARBOUR: Yes, as stated in the
Clause, and at that inquiry every consideration would be given to all representations made. This is to help the
fishermen, not to restrict them.

that the hon. Member for Woodvale (Mr.

Mr. BLACK: There is a point to
which I think attention should be called
in connection with this Clause 16 as it is
drafted. It is with regard to the words
"adjacent thereto." The object of the
Clause is to give the owner of a fixed net
power, when given permission by the
Ministry of Commerce, to remove that
net and to erect it at some other place
adjacent thereto. What does the phrase
"adjacent thereto" mean? I take it
that it does not mean immediately adjoining or contiguous, or you would have
used the words "immediately adjoining
or contiguous" or some such words. If
it does not mean immediately adjoining
or contiguous it does not mean anything
precise. It is a peculiarly vague term,
and it errs very much against what ought
to be one of the first principles in the
drafting of any statutory provision,
namely, that it should be precise and
clear. If there were many cases to
which this Clause might apply one could
see that the Clause in its present form
might be the cause of a considerable
amount of litigation as to the precise
meaning of the words "adjacent
thereto. For example, suppose there
""
were a net at Donaghadee and it were
proposed to remove it to the Copeland
Islands. Would the Copeland Islands
be a place adjacent thereto ?
Mr. LEEKE: No.
Mr. BLACK: The hon. Member for
Mid Derry says No." Someone else
might say "Yes." What is to determine the question? There is nothing
here. There is no criterion given to
determine it. I cannot, myself, suggest
any alternative phrase which has the
same meaning-(laughter)-but I think
I can suggest how the difficulty could be
removed from the Clause. That is by
omitting the words "adjacent thereto"
altogether, by simply enabling the
Ministry of Commerce to give permission.
to remove nets, and then proviso (b) at
the top of page 10 provides that before

must be satisfied that such removal or

other person. Now, if before any

not interfere with the reasonable and
legitimate interests of any other person,
would it not be sufficient merely to give
a general power of removal in the beginning of the Clause? If it is protected
by that proviso would that not be quite
sufficient? I suggest that for better
draughtsmanship and for clearer definition the Minister should omit the words
"adjacent thereto" from the Clause, and
that the Clause would be quite workable

2397 Adoption of Children Bill-
4 OCTOBER 1934

Second Reading
Adoption of Children (Workmen's Compensation) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. ANDREWS: The majority of the
Measures that I have had the honour of
bringing before the House have been
more or less of a controversial kind, but
my lot is a happier one to-day, because I
feel this is a Measure which will meet
with the approval not only of the Members of this House but also of those whom
we represent. The object of the Bill can
be very briefly stated. It is to provide.
that in cases arising under the Workmen's Compensation Act legally adopted
children shall be treated in exactly the
same way as if they were children in the
ordinary sense of the adopters.
workman is killed in circumstances that
give rise to a claim under the Workmen's
Compensation Act those members of his
family who are totally or partially
dependent upon his earnings become entitled, subject to certain conditions, to
compensation.
If a
The expression, members of his family,
is defined in the Act of 1927 and
includes the wife or husband as the case
may be and the other relatives who are
named in the first Clause of this Bill.
The definition, while including children,
contains no reference to adopted
children. What view our courts here
would take I am not in a position to say,
because no test case has as yet
been brought before them. There was,
however, a case in Great Britain
Known as Ward v. Dorman, Long,
Limited, and the county court judge
decided in favour of the adopted
child, but on appeal the Court of
Appeal held differently. The Imperial
Parliament, recognising the injustice to
the adopted child and desiring to right a
wrong, introduced a Measure which is
the counterpart of this Bill, and which
received the Royal Assent on the 12th
of July-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-
which, if I may say so, has a familiar
sound and historic interest to the people
of Northern Ireland. But, however, that
may be, I was able to arrange, when
the Bill was passing through the
Imperial House, that entries in a
Northern Ireland register would be
receivable in the British courts. I
undertook to introduce a Measure here
and to arrange that there would be
reciprocity in this connection.
Clause 1 simply sets out that an
adopted child should rank as an ordinary
child of the adopting parents or parent,
and sub-section (2) of this Clause provides a simple method of giving proof of
adoption. Sub-clause (3) includes
children adopted under the English and
Scottish law. I think it is sufficient that
I should say that when this Bill becomes
law a legally adopted child, even though
its parents by adoption may cross the
Channel, will rank equally for compensation with the other members of the family
in the event of a fatal accident to the
breadwinner. I feel that this Bill will
have the approval of the whole House,
and I am very pleased to move "That the
Bill be now read a Second time."
Mr. BEATTIE: I am sure
every
Member of this House will welcome a
Bill of this kind, a Bill that sets out
to right a wrong, a wrong that has been
inflicted on those who had no responsibility for it.
Mr. ANDREWS: Unintentionally.
Mr. BEATTIE: I give the Minister
of Labour credit for keeping step by
step with Great Britain in this matter
and having this reciprocity arrangement
with Great Britain, but I want him to
go a step further. I want to know why
the Minister has not made a reciprocity
arrangement with the House of Keys,
and why he has failed to recognise the
Isle of Man as being part of the British
Empire. I do not think he will be
doing full justice to the people of this
country if he does not apply this Bill to
those people from Northern Ireland who
may go to live in the Isle of Man. If the
parents of adopted children go to live in
the Isle of Man and the breadwinner is
killed in an accident they will be denied
the right to claim for those adopted
children under the Workmen's Compensation Act because this Government had
failed to make a reciprocity arrangement
with the House of Keys. But if they
broke up their home in the Isle of Man
-they might have had to start a boarding house there to earn a living-and
transferred their home to Liverpool they
would be entitled to the benefits conferred by this Measure. Therefore, by
not approaching the House of Keys to
make a reciprocity arrangement in respect
of this matter you are doing a possible
injury to North of Ireland people who
2399 Adoption of Children Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Mr. Beattie]
may be compelled to go to the Isle of
Man to earn their living.
In this Bill you have sought to right
one wrong, but there are many wrongs
in this Province you have got to right.
This is only one of many, and I hope you
will soon right the wrong I referred to
at the sitting of the House to-day. When
you right that wrong we will ask you to
go a step further and right another
wrong, and then, perhaps, by these

in connection with this Bill. He does not

a similar thing to happen in connection

Mr. CRAWFORD: I am sorry the

admirable thing,
thing, and the Minister

Mr. BYRNE: While agreeing with

Mr. CAMPBELL: This is admittedly

Imperial Bill
