Oral Answer to Question.
DUNDONALD SEWERAGE
SCHEME.
1. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is aware of the
fact that men employed on the Dundonald sewerage scheme, under the
Castlereagh Rural District Council, are
employed at a nominal wage of 9d per
hour; whereas their actual earnings
through stoppages due to wet weather
amount on an average to approximately
28s per week; whether it is a fact that
watchmen employed on this scheme are
paid 4d per hour; whether, in view of
these conditions, he will take steps to
ensure that a shelter is erected so that
men may lose the minimum of time
through inclement weather; and whether
he will make representation to have the
rate of wages increased.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The conditions under which
a relief grant is paid by my Department include a requirement that the rate
of wages to be paid to all men employed
on unskilled work shall be the rate which
northe promoting authority would
mally pay for similar work. My information is that the figure of 28s a week
quoted by the hon. Member applied only
to one gang for one week in which the
work was impeded by abnormally bad
weather, and that the average weekly
earnings of the workmen are about
32s 6d. In a week in which the weather
permits of the work being carried on
without stoppages, their earnings would
be 35s.
As regards the night watchmen, I
understand that at the outset the contractors, in accordance with their normal
practice, employed one watchman at each
watching post for all watching duties other
than the week-end duty, which was provided for separately. As a result of representations made on behalf of the men,
the watching duties at each post were
divided in more equal proportions, but
further consideration is being given to
the matter.
I am informed that it has been the
practice to provide a shelter for the men
during bad weather where there is a
substantial volume of work to be done at
one place; where, however, the work is
scattered, there is more difficulty, but
the contractors are quite willing to do all
that is possible to provide shelters.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I beg to give notice
that I will raise this matter on the
Adjournment.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the Minister in view of the answer he
has now given will he give instructions
to the labour exchange authority to continue paying benefits to all those ex-
Service men from the city of Belfast who
have refused to accept the conditions
attached to this occupation on the Dundonald sewerage scheme? I would ask
the Minister to give those instructions.
Mr. ANDREWS: No, I cannot
answer in the affirmative. This scheme
was promoted for the purpose of finding
work for persons who were unemployed.
I hope that it will do so. It is doing
so at the present time.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of that
answer I will certainly put my point forward on the Adjournment.
2405 Local Government Bill-

9 OCTOBER 1934
Second Reading
BILL PRESENTED.
Public Rights of Way Bill,
"to amend the law relating to public
rights of way, and for purposes connected therewith," presented by Mr.
Campbell, supported by Mr. Byrne, Mr.
Beattie and Mr. Leeke; to be read a
Second time on Tuesday next, and to be
printed. (Bill 27).
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Local Government Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The Bill I present
to the House this afternoon for Second
Reading is of considerable importance
and covers in its forty-four clauses a
great deal of ground. I wish to make it
clear, however, that it is not designed to
effect any comprehensive change in the
structure of local government. As hon.
Members will recollect, the whole field of
local government
was reviewed some
years ago by a Commission which
recommended a number of very drastic
changes in the whole system. With
most, if not all of the Commission's
recommendations the Government has
been and is in sympathy. At the same
time, I should like to make it clear that
many of the matters dealt with by the
Local Government Commission have
already been given effect to by legislation
or by administrative action. Further, a
close study of this Bill, with the recommendations of this Commission, will show
that wherever possible we have adopted
the lines suggested by the Commission.
It appears to us, however, that a time
when local authorities all over
the
country are battling with great financial difficulties is not one at which to
embark upon any scheme which would
involve the reorganisation of the whole.
system of local government, and which,
however likely to lead to increased
efficiency of administration in the future,
could scarcely fail, during a transitional
period of longer or shorter duration, to
add temporarily to existing difficulties,
and, quite possibly, to increase financial
burdens already approaching the bearable
limit.
At the same time, we felt that it
would not be advisable to uproot old
institutions until we could be perfectly
satisfied that the new arrangement proposed would not add to the difficulties or
cost of local government administration.
Unfortunately the time of stress is not
yet past, but, in the meantime, it has
become clear that, quite apart from any
need for a remodelling of the system,
something must be done to improve the
existing administrative machine if the
best use of it is to be made. The Bill
now before the House is designed to
effect such improvements and no more.
Hon. Members will be glad to know
that throughout the preparation of the
Bill my Ministry has been careful to
ascertain the views of local authorities,
either through their respective associations or directly, in regard to those
clauses of the Bill which materially affect
their powers or procedure, and I
am happy to be able to claim that there is
a general measure of approval of the
Government's proposals.
I cannot hope in the compass of a
Second Reading speech to deal in detail
with each of the many clauses of the Bill,
and I propose, therefore, at this
stage merely to explain as briefly as possible the general intention and effect of
the more important clauses, leaving fuller
examination for a later stage.
The Bill as a whole comprises six
parts and two schedules. Part VI and
the Second Schedule deal with those
matters such as Interpretation, Repeals,
etc., incidental to all enactments, and I
need make no further reference to them.
Part I deals with matters affecting
boroughs, urban districts and towns.
Part II comprises provisions relating to
local government generally, but mainly
to counties and rural districts. Part III
relates to the public health code; Part
IV to poor relief, and Part V deals with
some points of a miscellaneous nature.
The First Schedule relates to one of the
matters dealt with in Part II.
I come to the first two Clauses of
the Bill. Under existing enactments
municipal elections take place in January.
Representations have reached me from a
variety of sources that the short hours of
daylight and frequently inclement
weather at that period of the year are
definite handicaps in the holding of the
elections, and in response to these representations it is now proposed that the
Local Government Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
municipal elections should be held simultaneously with other local government
elections in May. It is also proposed to
introduce a measure of elasticity into the
dates of meetings of these municipal
councils, the present rigid statutory requirements having not infrequently
caused needless inconvenience.
It is also proposed to synchronise still
further the elections in municipal areas
with those in county and rural areas by
having the dates of triennial elections in
the urban areas in the same years as the
triennial elections in rural areas. The
next triennial elections in county and
rural areas will be held in 1936, and it
is accordingly proposed, under Subclause (7) of Clause 1, to postpone all
municipal elections until that year.
Clause 3 provides for uniformity of
practice in the different kinds of
municipal authorities in regard to a
number of points of procedure. The
points covered are the method of recording and counting votes at meetings; the
signature of minutes; and the participation in votes or debates of members
financially interested in the questions at
issue. The next three Clauses are designed
to remove several anomalies in regard to
the financial aspect of local administration.
As hon. Members are aware, the
foundation of all local government revenue
is a direct levy on occupiers of property
known as the poor rate. At its inception this levy was certainly intended to
provide funds for the relief of the poor,
but as local government becomes more
complex and more public services involving expenditure were entrusted to local
authorities the machinery of collection of
the poor rate
utilised to collect
revenue for these additional purposes, and
all sorts of charges were collected
together as items of poor rate. In county
was
and rural districts this principle has persisted consistently, so that the machinery
set up for the collection of the poor rate
covers all purposes, and the only anomaly
is in the name which is, after all, of no
practical moment.
In towns other than county boroughs
the situation is rather different. Poor
rate is, indeed, levied, but as a welldefined charge to meet the demand
annually presented to the municipal
council by the board of guardians of
whose union the town forms part. For
the numerous other purposes for which
the municipal authority requires revenue,

We, therefore, have two distinct parts.
in the rates levied in towns, each

Clause 6 deals with a somewhat

Clause 13, which relates to the audit of

Government

abolishes the restriction imposed by
Section 64 of the Local Government
(Ireland) Act, 1898, which limited the

whose accounts are subject to separate
audit. It is obvious that a charge of
£100 is completely uneconomic in the
case of Belfast Corporation, the audit of
whose various accounts occupies not one
but several local government auditors for
a period of from four to six months each

mention that this provision already exists.
in the case of road contracts and it is selfevidently desirable that the principle
should apply universally.
Clause 14 contains a number of somewhat technical provisions which I need
not attempt to cover in detail at this
stage. Briefly, however, it is designed
with the object of simplifying and harmonising the procedure in connection
with abatements and allowances to be
made to persons who have been rated in
respect of premises, but who did not
occupy those premises for the full period
in respect of which they were rated. It
abolishes at the same time the inequitable
arrangement which has hitherto existed
of making the subsequent occupier liable
for the arrears of rate due by the

Clause 15 relates to the appointment,
tenure, remuneration, and dismissal of
officers of local authorities. At present,
as many hon. Members are aware, the
practice is somewhat varied. In certain
cases appointments are subject to the
approval of my Ministry; in other cases.
the discretion of the local authority concerned is complete. For example, the
appointment of a clerk to a rural district
council requires the Ministry's approval,
whereas an urban district council can
appoint any person they wish as town
clerk without reference to the Ministry
of Home Affairs, even though his appointment as executive sanitary officer and his
salary as such requires the Ministry's
approval. This matter is one to which
we have given a great deal of thought.
Taken as a whole I have nothing but
praise for the general standard of ability
and integrity of the personnel of the
local government service, and to that
extent it might be held that the existing
system works well enough. At the same
time, although it is neither necessary nor
desirable for me to quote examples, hon.
Members are as well aware as I am that
cases come to light from time to time
which suggest that due and proper regard
has not been had by local authorities to
the suitability of officers appointed by
them. The Government has reached the
conclusion, therefore, that it would be
well to extend its control over the staffing
of the local government service. Consideration was given to the possibility of
restricting this control to certain key
positions, but the difficulty of determining which positions should be thus
regarded appeared to make successful
action along these lines unlikely. It has,
therefore, been decided, since something,
and something effective must obviously
be done, to ask the House to give to the
Ministry power to prescribe the qualifications to be required of those appointed to
different posts and to exercise a general
control over the appointment, removal,
and remuneration of local government
officers. This does not mean that the
Ministry is intended to consider every
appointment made by a local body. Hon.
Members will note from the wording of
the Clause that the Ministry is to have
discretion as to the kinds of officers to be
covered by its regulations and that its
approval will be required only in respect
of such officers. In view of this I do not
think that any practical difficulty need
be anticipated in the smooth working of
the arrangement now proposed.
The remaining sub-clauses are intended
to put an end to the undesirable practice
of paid officers of one local authority
being members of another local authority.
This is not a new principle. Members
will doubtless recollect that the 1898 Act
incorporated a provision prohibiting full
time employees of a local authority from
becoming Members of Parliament. The
Clause, however, will not affect existing
cases.

Second Reading
[Sir Dawson Bates]
Clause 22 has a formidable appearance,
but I can deal with it very briefly. In
certain cases the salaries of local government officials were subjected to temporary cuts in order to tide over a time
of crisis. It would be inequitable that
the pensions of those who retired during
the currency of these temporary reductions should be affected for all time,
and the Clause enables the authority to
grant pensions based on the full salary
in the cases of officers in whose salaries
a temporary abatement has, for economy
reasons, been made. Clause 23 has been
designed to ensure that solicitors will
furnish their bills of costs within reasonable time.
a
Part III of the Bill, to which I now
turn, relates to public health matters.
Clause 24 is designed to remove
difficulty which has been experienced in
connection with the making of bylaws by sanitary authorities. The
present position is governed by Section
221 of the Public Health (Ireland) Act,
1878, which provides that by-laws made
by sanitary authorities under that Act
become operative only on confirmation
by the Local Government Board, that is,
of course, now the Ministry of Home
Affairs. Before applying for confirmation of the by-laws the sanitary
authority must, one month in advance,
give notice by Press advertisement of
their intention to apply and during that
month must keep the by-laws available
for inspection in their office. The Ministry has power to confirm or to disallow
but not to modify the by-laws. As might
be expected cases occur in which the
Ministry is disinclined to confirm bylaws exactly as submitted, but would be
prepared to confirm them if modified.
Even should the required modifications be
merely of a drafting nature without
material effect upon the general sense of
the by-laws, the terms of Section 221 require the disallowance of the by-laws and
a fresh start.
The object of all this is of course to
give everyone concerned an opportunity
of considering the modifications, but it
seems a somewhat ponderous method of
dealing with a drafting amendment.
The Government feel that more flexible
machinery is both desirable and possible
and the Clause now in question is designed to provide that flexibility.
The
initial steps will be the same, but if
modifications are found desirable the
Ministry, instead of disallowing the bylaws in toto, will notify the proposed
modifications to the sanitary authority.
If the authority decline to consent to
the modifications disallowance follows.
If the authority agree to the modifications the Ministry will have discretion
in the use of two lines of procedure.
Should the modifications be of a minor
or drafting nature the by-laws, as modified, may be confirmed without further
ado. Should, however, the modifications
be material, the Ministry will suspend
confirmation for a month and direct the
sanitary authority to advertise and hold
available for inspection the modified bylaws during that period as under the old
procedure. In this way unnecessary
delays will be avoided and at the same
time, when essential, those affected will
have full opportunity of considering the
by-laws.
Clause 25 amends Section 28 of the
Public Health (Ireland) Act, 1878.
That section empowers an urban sanitary
authority to require the owners and
occupiers of premises adjoining private
streets to sewer, level, pave, etc., and
light such streets and failing compliance
by them to carry out the necessary
works, afterwards recovering the cost from
the defaulting owners and occupiers.
The effect of the Clause is to empower
the sanitary authority to collect the estimated cost from those concerned before
carrying out the work, and subsequently
make any necessary adjustments arising
out of any discrepancy between the estimated and actual cost.
The effect of Clause 26 is simply to
bring up to date the provisions of
Section 1 of the Public Health (Ireland)
Act, 1896. Under that section rural
authorities could be invested with urban
powers in relation to public health
matters dealt with in the Public Health
(Ireland) Acts up to 1890, but not in regard to matters dealt with in Public
Health Acts passed since that year.
I now come to another apparently formidable Clause, number 27, comprising
eleven sub-sections, but as nine of these
sub-sections are concerned with details of
administrative procedure I need at this
stage deal only with the first two subsections, upon which all the others are
consequential. The present position in

The section does not apply to rural areas

control everywhere and not merely in

The special case of theatres and music

is comparatively small and the existing

accordingly, proposes to make these miscellaneous entertainments everywhere
subject to licence by the local sanitary

the like. As the desired situation has
for all practical purposes already been
attained by the 1909 Act it is, of course,
not proposed to alter the existing
arrangement about picture houses.
Clause 28 makes an important change
in the sense of Section 71 of the Public
Health Act of 1878 by empowering any
sanitary authority supplying water in its
own area to supply water to any other
district instead of only to an adjoining
district. This will, for example, enable
one urban district to come to the aid of
another, which has hitherto not been
possible owing to the intervention of a
rural district between their respective
boundaries.
With regard to Clause 29, hitherto
Part I of the Tuberculosis Prevention
(Ireland) Act, 1908, which relates to the
notification of cases of infectious tuberculosis and the disinfection of premises
which have been in contact with such
cases, has been operative only in sanitary
districts whose councils have adopted the
Act. I need hardly point out that this
constitutes a serious weakness in the
struggle against this terrible disease, and
I have no doubt that the House will
heartily endorse the Government proposal in Clause 29 that the provisions of
the 1908 Act shall in future be operative
everywhere without exception.
Hon. Members who are familiar with
the Local Government (Ireland) Act of
1898 will recollect that Section 90 of that
Act dealt in somewhat general terms with
the conversion by boards of guardians of
their workhouse hospitals into district

the basis of the section a number of
district hospitals have, in fact, been
established. As I have indicated, the
terms of Section 90 of the 1898 Act
scarcely cover all possible eventualities,
and there has been some doubt as to the
strict legality of what has hitherto been

30 of the present Bill has been drafted

improvement of workhouse infirmaries;

Mr. BEATTIE: Why not abolish the

five deal with the management of district

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Sir Dawson Bates]
Clause 31 enables boards of guardians
to provide special medical and surgical
treatment for poor persons without requiring such poor persons to incur the
ignominy of being admitted to the workhouse as pauper patients. Since 1862 it
has been possible for boards of guardians.
to send poor patients from their
infirmaries to extern hospitals for special
treatment and to bear the cost, but this
applies only to persons who are bona-fide
inmates of the workhouse and not to
persons admitted to the infirmary simply
for the purpose of being sent for special
treatment. In other words, a person
must become an inmate of the workhouse
before becoming eligible for this benefit,
and this, of course, cuts out the large
class of dispensary patients who are poor
enough to require State medical assistance but who have not sunk to the pauper
level. The present Clause removes this
disability by making eligible for special
treatment any person who is in receipt of
medical assistance under the Poor Relief
(Ireland) Act of 1851.
Clause 32 extends the powers of poorlaw authorities in connection with the
granting of outdoor relief. Hitherto a
destitute, poor widow, with two or more
legitimate children dependent upon her,
has been eligible for outdoor relief,
whereas an equally destitute widow with
only one child has not been eligible.
This Clause makes her eigible. The
Clause also amends the provisions of the
Poor Relief (Ireland) Act, 1862, in
regard to the granting of outdoor relief
to occupiers of land. The attitude
adopted by the legislators then was that
an occupier of land was not prima facie
a person who should require poor relief
at the expense of the ratepayers. We
feel that the limit of one quarter of an
acre arbitrarily chosen in 1862 is not
really satisfactory, and it is proposed to
substitute in the application of the 1862
Act a reference to the net annual value
of the land instead of to its area, and we
have fixed the limiting valuation at £5
per annum.
The necessity for Clause 33 may come
as a surprise to some hon. Members, and
as the reasons underlying the Clause are
not apparent from its text I shall explain.
It has become the practice of a substantial number of paupers to seek
admission to, for example, Belfast Workhouse at night, to secure a night's
lodging and a meal the following morning, and then, without doing any work in
repayment for their shelter, or even, in
many cases, doing their share of the
essential cleaning up of their refuge, to
quit the workhouse. During the day
they follow their own devices and, if not
able to secure other accommodation,
return next evening to the workhouse for
another night's shelter. In other words,
a substantial number of people of this
kind has come to regard the workhouse as
a sort of free hotel provided for their
convenience. This is obviously very far
from the intention of the poor relief
system, and the remedy proposed in the
Clause is the only way to meet the
situation.
With regard to Clause 34, hon. Members will recollect that to meet the situation arising out of the abnormal extent of
unemployment an Act was passed in 1928
empowering the Ministry of Home
Affairs, if satisfied as to the existence of
exceptional distress in any union
electoral division, to authorise the board
of guardians to administer relief out of
the workhouse during any prescribed
period to poor persons of any description
resident in the union or electoral division.
or
The 1928 Act is general in its terms in
that it does not specify the particular
manner in which this special relief is to
be given. Accordingly, whilst in some
cases it has proved necessary simply to
give outdoor relief to individuals, in other
cases the Act has enabled guardians to
administer the relief in the form of wages
to workers employed in specially undertaken relief schemes of permanent utility.
Although to administer relief in the last
mentioned manner is obviously the better
method, when possible, it inevitably
means that the immediate cost of affording a given amount of relief to a given
number of people is much greater than it
would be were the same number of people
given equal relief in the ordinary way.
Against that, however, there is at the end
something to show for the money expended. The adoption of this method of
affording relief introduces, however, a
difficult financial problem, since it is
scarcely practical to ask ratepayers to pay
in once year, as part of an already swollen
poor rate, the whole cost of works of permament utility kind, which, had the
works been undertaken in the ordinary
2421 Local Government Bill-

9 OCTOBER 1934
Second Reading
course, could have been financed over a
term of years with relief to ratepayers.
As the law stands at the moment, however, there is no alternative to meeting
the whole cost out of the current year's
poor rate. The Government are satisfied
that provision should be made for the
spreading of the cost of these emergency
relief schemes over a period of years, and
Clause 34 of the Bill is designed to that
effect.
Mr. BEATTIE: Over the county?
Sir DAWSON BATES: It will be
applied so that ratepayers who would
otherwise have to pay in one year will
have it spread over a period of 20, 30, or
40 years as the case may be.
Clause 35 stiffens up the procedure in
relation to the calling in of a medical
practitioner by a midwife in case of
emergency, as defined in rules made under
Section 5 of the Midwives (Ireland) Act,
1918. It has been brought to the notice
of my Ministry that a practice has
developed on the part of certain midwives
of calling in the dispensary doctor or some
other medical practitioner to attend as
private patients women who are really.
entitled to free medical attention as dispensary patients. Under the terms of
the 1918 Act, as amended by the Midwives and Nursing Home Act (Northern
Ireland), 1929, unless the patient has
actually obtained a ticket for medical
attendance under Section 9 of the Poor
Relief (Ireland) Act, 1851, the county
council are obliged to pay the doctor a fee
and to recover the cost from the husband
or guardian of the patient as best they
may, subject to the condition that if it be
shown to their satisfaction that such
husband or guardian is unable, by reason
of poverty, to pay such fee they cannot
proceed for recovery. The net effect of
this practice has been that county councils
have been out of pocket in respect of
numerous fees paid to dispensary doctors
for attending cases which should have
been attended without fee in the ordinary
course of dispensary duties.
The Clause now proposed alters the procedure in several important respects. The
midwife must first ask the patient or her
husband or guardian to call in a doctor;
if they do not do so the midwife must
obtain medical assistance, but before
actually calling in a doctor she must ask
the patient or her husband or guardian
whether they are prepared to bear the
cost. If the answer is in the affirmative
any doctor can be called in and the board
of guardians have no liability for the fee.
If, on the other hand, the family decline
to accept responsibility the midwife must
first call upon the dispensary doctor, who
is bound to act unless prevented by some
reasonable cause, and only if he is not
available may any other doctor be called
in. Responsibility for any fee payable
has been transferred from the county
council to the board of guardians, and the
latter are relieved of liability to pay any
fee to a dispensary doctor if they decide
that the patient was one to whom medical
relief might lawfully have been afforded
under Section 9 of the Poor Relief

Clause 38 is drafted to meet
emergency for which, although it is not
likely to be of frequent occurrence, the
Government feel that provision should be
made. As hon. Members are aware, borough
councils have fairly wide powers of

It consequently may happen that a
2423 Local Government Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Sir Dawson Bates]
borough council may have an opportunity
of acquiring certain property either
inside or outside their area, the possession
and development of which would clearly
be of definite benefit to the inhabitants
of the borough, but find themselves
unable to seize the opportunity by reason
of the fact that some point in connection
with the nature of the property or the
terms upon which it may be acquired
conflicts with or is not covered by the
ordinary statutory authority. The present Clause is designed to provide a way
out of the impasse by empowering the
Ministry of Home Affairs, on being
satisfied regarding the desirability of the
acquisition, to make an order authorising
the borough council to carry through the
transaction.
Clause 39 makes provision for an
emergency which I know that all hon.
Members and the members of all local
bodies will join me in hoping will be of
very infrequent occurrence. Even in the
dignified atmosphere of Parliaments it
occasionally happens that some member
deliberately sets out to obstruct business
and succeeds to such an extent that his
continued or repeated presence means the
cessation of all rational proceedings.
Should this occur in Parliament a remedy
exists and the offending member disappears from the Chamber for a shorter
or longer period, as the case demands,
but an unfortunate local council has no
such remedy and must struggle on with
its business despite the handicap. This
Clause of the Bill provides a remedy by
empowering councils to remove obstructive
members from office by resolution.
The last Clause to which it is necessary
to make reference empowers the Ministry
of Home Affairs to hold a plebiscite in
any local government area should it have
to make a decision on any question of
general principle or policy affecting the
ratepayers in that area and not be
satisfied that the ordinary sources of
information have sufficiently acquainted
it with public opinion. The procedure
outlined in the Clause provides that the
power to hold a plebiscite is to be
exercised only following an application
by the local authority, representations
from a substantial body of ratepayers, or
a report by one of the Ministry's
Inspectors.
These are the main points of the Bill,
and I apologise to the House for the time
I have taken up in explaining them, while
thanking the House for the patient hearing they have given me. I beg to move.

way that must be involved in services

radium treatment the radium should, as
far as possible, be consolidated at one

have a large quantity of radium, as large
a quantity as you can reasonably get.
It ought to be at one centre, and

should be sent to that centre. There
are several reasons for that. One reason
is that if you have one centre people who
are dealing with radium treatment there
have much greater experience and are
much more likely to have good results
than people who are only giving treatment once a week or at even less frequent
intervals. Another very important
reason is that radium is an extremely expensive substance to buy; it is one of the
most expensive substances in the world.
Radium is not a substance which you
use and set aside and leave it there for
a while, then use it again, because the
essential and the important part of
radium is the emanation which is
coming from it all the time, and if you
are only using radium for one day out
of seven you are losing six-sevenths of
your radium emanation, whereas if you
have a large centre the radium is
practically in constant use all the time.
You are really wasting radium unless it
is being kept in constant use.

any Commission could well have been,

Government could receive. He sees, as
anybody who looks at this matter dispassionately must see, that the Government have failed to seize a great
opportunity and that they are, in reality,
evading the issue of poor law reform.
This is nothing else than an evasive Bill.
It in no way co-ordinates our social
services. It in no way puts an end to the
stigma of the poor law. It in no way
relieves the poor man, who is forced by
circumstances to enter an infirmary in
Northern Ireland, of the knowledge that
he can only do so on the one condition of
pauperism. That is a circumstance that
has always deeply touched and hurt the
conscience of our people in Northern
Ireland. I have no hesitation, after the

no doubt that at the present moment this

Government's opinion on this reform.

man may be unpopular, but he may be

disappointment and surprise. In fact I
think that that disappointment and surprise is felt not only inside the House by
al! Members but by the general population outside. We have waited ten years
for this Measure and it seems a very long
time more than necessary to deal with
the recommendations of a Commission
which reported in 1927. There is a saying that it is a wise parent who knows
his own child. I feel it is very difficult
for members of that Commission to find
very many resemblances to their report
contained in the provisions of this Bill.
We sat for three years and gave every
point of local government our closest consideration.
The Report I think contains 242 pages,
and it contained 75 clauses and in
addition many miscellaneous provisions in
connection with the county boroughs.
These provisions were, I am quite sure,
by no means hurtful, and they represented our considered opinion.
During
these seven years two Parliaments have
passed away and another is already well.
on its course, and I think it is very
natural that we who have looked forward
to this Bill with much of expectation

intervening period I know that one

completely disregarded. It was a majority
recommendation, and it was one with
reference to medical benefit. The
Government in their wisdom disregarded
the finding of the Commission and
brought in a provision for medical benefit.
When we came to that conclusion we did
so honestly because we thought that the
dispensary system was suited to this
country and the dispensary system was
working well. We were probably wrong,
but that is not, I submit, the question.
It does seem a pity when a Commission
is set up that the first act of the Government should be to act directly contrary
to the advice of the Commission and then
with regard to other matters not carry
out their recommendations.
However, when this Bill came it was
so long since the Commission sat that—
I think I am not unique in this respect-
I had forgotten many of our recommendations. I re-read the Report and I must
confess I came to the conclusion that we
as a Commission visualised a sort of Local
Government Utopia. Our ideals were
unobtainably high. Perhaps there are
many reasons why this was so. For one
thing at that time conditions were very
different from what they unfortunately
are now-I mean financial conditions.
We reported in what I think may be
called a boom period. It is a very
different matter to go into these questions
light-heartedly to-day. I admit that.
think it is also quite obvious when we
stepped so lightly to our task our hearts
were light and our hopes were higher.

submitted. I agree with him. We have
been told that the Minister objected or

Committee submitting their minutes for

very little confidence, dismissed a clerk

to give us the power to upset that
decision. The gentleman's name is Twist
and this whole transaction is twist. These
little irregularities occur from time to
time, but there is no minute of the proceedings so that they can be properly discussed in public.
In July, 1933, I brought under the
notice of the Minister of Labour the fact
that old age pensioners were being robbed
in a certain district hospital in Northern
Ireland, and the right hon. Gentleman
gave me great sympathy and support.
He laid it down that none of these
hospitals had any right whatever to stop
any part of an old age pension without
the written consent of the pensioner, but
this particular district hospital got that
written consent by fraud and duress-by
threatening the pensioners that they
would be put into the body of the house
if they did not put their names to the
document. The Minister of Labour sent
me a letter for publication in the Press to
show these people what their rights were.
He also sent an official to this particular
institution to say that these people were
not to be imposed on, but this district
authority was a very powerful body,
which consisted of a great many members
who were all under the thumb of one
man, and the Minister of Home Affairs
did not support the Minister of Labour.
There was a debate on the subject in
this House in which I took part, also the
hon. Member (Mr. Beattie) and the
Minister of Labour, but it did not bear

There is another good Clause in the

a local authority does not accept a tender
which is the lowest it should state in the
minutes why it is not accepted. That is
right, but sometimes it is very hard to
do that, because one cannot state the
reasons without reflecting on the firm
putting in the tender. It is hardly fair
to reject their tender and at the same
time reflect on them. We have had
some experience of that recently, and
what we did was to mark it confidential
and put it in the hands of every member
of the Council. If we put a minute to
it it would be public property; it might

good firms who, however, do not come
up to our standard. We cannot run
down a
tender without giving good

of age,

What is true of milk in respect of the

who have endeavoured to get us to depart

that we as a public health authority

that the Bill is a very minor attempt to
reorganise our local government services.
Coming directly to the Bill itself I
notice that practically the first proposal
in the Bill is that to extend the tenure of
office of certain people in the local
authorities. It is an ill wind that blows
nobody good, and for the first time in my
political life I find myself in the position
of getting an extension of my term of
office without having to fight an election.
But because the Government has inadvertently bestowed that boon upon me,
and because they have bestowed that
blessing upon my constituents, is no

reactionaries, who contribute no useful

has
borne with them as patiently as possible,

the matter about which I gave notice this
afternoon, that is the matter of the
workers employed in the Dundonald
sewerage scheme. I have studied the
reply of the Minister this afternoon, and
I propose for two or three minutes to
try to deal effectively with some of the
points in that reply. The Minister in
his reply stated:-
:-
The conditions under which a relief
grant is paid by my Department include a requirement that the rate of
wages to be paid to all men employed
on unskilled work shall be the rate
which the promoting authority would
normally pay for similar work.
I have made inquiries out in this district with regard to that.
I have gone
into the district personally. I have inspected the job and investigated the complaints, and what do I find? I find
that the only two jobs comparable in
magnitude to the one which is being done
at the present time were the erection of
a school and the erection of the Houses
of Parliament themselves. On both of
those jobs in this area I understand that
the minimum rate paid to similar men
was
as a
ls per hour, instead of 8d as
originally paid by this firm, a figure which
was afterwards
result of representations raised to 9d per hour. But
even with the 9d an hour I want to suggest that the information upon which the
Minister of Labour based his reply is not
strictly accurate. I have made inquiries,
and I find that out of a total of 16 weeks
during which the unskilled workers have
been employed on this job, for only two
weeks have they received the normal rate
of wages, the other 14 weeks showing
substantial reductions owing to the inclemency of the weather.
With regard to night watchmen, I
understand that the Minister is correct
in stating that originally they were
working on the principle of one night
watchman. I can say this without any
fear of the victimisation of the workmen
concerned, because no workman employed
on that job is afraid of victimisation;
he is more afraid of being kept on the
job permanently than of being victimised, owing to the intolerable conditions in which he has to work. I have
examined the pay dockets and the hours
of some of the people employed, and I
find that one watchman for the major
portion of his time had to work over 100
hours a week at a rate of wages which
worked out at 41d per hour. Against
a condition of things like that, every
right-thinking Member of this House
must protest and protest most emphatically, and something will have to
be done about it.
Take the question of shelter for these
men referred to in the Minister's reply.
I emphatically state that it is not the
practice of this firm to provide shelter
for these men. I have gone out there
in bad weather, examined the job, and
watched the men standing at the side of
the road drenched to the skin, hoping
that the weather would turn to normal
again, or rather that fair conditions
would return, in order that they might
resume their work. These men are
bowed down with the low rate of wages
and the arduous nature of their toil.
Even on the worst kind of day, when the
rain is coming down in torrents, these men
are knocked off on the side of the road.
They have to stand there until they are
absolutely drenched, hoping against hope
that the weather will take up in the
afternoon and that they will be able to
resume their work. It sometimes happens that in this climate the weather does
take up in the afternoon. It is not
very often that that happens, but
occasionally you have a wet morning and
a fine afternoon. The result of these
men having no shelter is that they are
in such a pitiable condition in the afternoon that they are in no fit condition to
resume work at all.
I want to protest against the continuance under such conditions of a job
which is financed by the Government.
No matter what the local authority may
say, and in spite of the local opinion that
the standard rate of wages in this district
is 8d an hour, and that that has since
been increased to 9d, I want to protest,
with all the emphasis at my command
against the subsidising of a job in which
men are compelled to work for 9d an
hour less reductions in respect of the
inclemency of the weather, bringing their
average wages to 28s or 30s a week.
notice that my average of 28s a week is
disputed. I made full investigations
before I arrived at that average, and I
base it on 14 weeks out of 16. I was
assured that the average would be from
28s to 30s a week at the most.
I protest against that.

Oral Answers to Questions.
BALLYMENA MODEL SCHOOL
CONTRACT.
1. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether labourers employed
on the Ballymena Model School contract
under the control of the Regional
Education Committee have been paid at
the rate of 61d per hour, instead of at the
rate of 8d per hour paid by good employers in Ballymena; and if so, what
steps he proposes to take in dealing with
the contractor for his flagrant evasion of
the fair wages clause governing this contract.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): I
have been asked to reply to this
question.
The Ballymena Regional Education
Committee obtained an undertaking from
the contractors that all workmen, skilled
and unskilled, engaged upon the work connected with the contract at the Ballymena
Model School would be paid the trade union
rate of wages prevailing in the Ballymena district. No complaint in respect
of this matter has been received from the
labourers concerned and the Ministry
has not been furnished with any evidence
that any breach of this undertaking by
the contractors has occurred.
At a deputation from the National
Federation of Building Trades Operatives, which was received in the
Ministry last August, the facts implied
in the first part of the question were
alleged, but no proof was furnished in
support of them.
Although the matter is primarily one
for the Ballymena Regional Education
Committee, the Ministry promised the
deputation to consider what action
could be taken if the Federation
would forward complete proof that rates
under the accepted standard rates for
the district were being paid. These
particulars have not been furnished and
the Ministry in their absence, does not
consider further action necessary.

Sir DAWSON BATES: A man named

arrested in Armagh by the Customs
authorities on the 7th instant on three

place in the execution of the warrants and

Mr. MIDGLEY: When speaking on
this Bill last evening I had not time to
refer to what I consider the very meagre
proposals put forward by the Minister
under the name of reorganisation of the
poor law services. Late last night I again
perused some documents in regard to local
government in Northern Ireland and
elsewhere, and the result of that study
has convinced me that those who complain
that this is a very narrow and very
incomplete Measure are thoroughly
justified in their views. I would like to
take this opportunity, if I am in order,
to protest against the method which
has been adopted by those who submit
Bills to this House. The time has
certainly arrived in the twentieth century
when Bills ought to be presented in some
intelligible form instead of presenting
them in the form of legislation by
reference. This is a Bill which purports
to reorganise branches of local government
in Northern Ireland, and about 80 per
cent. of it consists of reference to other
Acts of Parliament. It would take one
to have a whole library of Acts of Parliament in order to get the proper connection. I think it is not beyond the wit of
mankind and not beyond the capacity of
the draughtsman associated with the
Government to bring forward or devise a
Bill which could be presented to the
House in an intelligible form-in a form
at any rate that would not make it necessary for one to go to a lawyer every time
one wants a Clause interpreted.
Years ago when I was serving my
apprenticeship I heard the allegation
made that Houses of Commons existed
mainly in order to give security to lawyers
and to have Bills drawn up in phraseology
that only a lawyer could understand, and
in that way perpetuate their stranglehold
on the rest of humanity. I am inclined
to agree that there is a great deal of
truth in that. Though I have been
serving as a representative myself in local
government assemblies for the past ten
years, and am thoroughly familiar with
some of the Acts referred to in this Bill,
nevertheless, I think for the purpose of
simplicity and easy understanding it
might be possible in devising Bills like this
either to employ a more moderate form
of English, or to put down the section of
the previous Act which it is proposed to
amend, so that Members could at a glance
see what it is proposed to amend instead
of having to go to consult the references
made or get a pile of Acts of Parliament
down which I have no house room for
whatever. I have so much intellectual
literature that I have not room to store
Acts of Parliament, nor do I possess conditions conducive to a heavy study of
Acts of Parliament. I commend the
thought to the Minister of Home Affairs
and the Parliamentary Secretary, that in
future for the guidance of this House
some better method be devised so that
previous Acts spreading over 60 or 70
years may be more easily followed.

Before I refer to the results of previous

I want to refer to some Clauses of the

A member of the council of an urban

or take part in the discussion of any
matter before the council
or commissioners (or a committee of the

or his partner, any pecuniary interest.
I take from the reading of that that the
borough or the commissioner is exempted
from the operations of that section, and
that this restrictive legislation will only
operate in the case of a member of a
district other than a borough and commissioner, and that outside these every
person who may be directly or indirectly
interested in any question will not be
debarred from expressing an opinion or
voting. If my interpretation of that is
correct I would like to ask the Minister
what exactly is the purpose behind that.
Whom is it aimed at? What do they
hope to achieve by it?
I have often been accused in Belfast of
attacking employers and of not being perhaps as tolerant of the employers' point
of view as some other people would desire,
but I certainly would be tolerant enough
of the point of view of any employer in
the North of Ireland to give him the right
to express an opinion if he happened to
be an elected person. But here it says
he shall neither express an opinion nor
vote.
I think the restriction should be
confined to voting, but any member of an
elected authority who has gained the confidence of the people should be permitted
to express his point of view as long as
he has not a deciding vote or the right to
influence the decision by a casting vote.
I hope that when he comes to reply the
Minister will unravel this point which is
to me a little mystery, because I want to
know why it should be good morality to
impose certain restrictions upon members
of one local body and not good morality
to impose those restrictions on members
of other local bodies.
I should like at this juncture to express my congratulations to the Minister
on including in the Bill one of the most
intelligent things that have ever been
included in any Bill, that is Clause 4,
Sub-clause (2), which removes the limitation of expenditure on public parks.
Heretofore in the city of Belfast those of
us who are members of the Parks and
Playgrounds Committee have been

which limited our expenditure to 3d in
the £, despite the fact that the growth
and development of Belfast has been
phenomenal, especially during the last
quarter of a century. I welcome this
Clause, which removes the restriction on

of sixpence. I hope that local authorities, taking their cue from the Minister,
will be inspired by the desire which

I cannot allow this opportunity to pass
without identifying myself with those
who stand for the abolition of the poor
law altogether. The poor law is an
anachronism. It is something which
ought not to exist in 1934. In Great
Britain we have seen the overthrow of
the workhouses. The boards of guardians
have passed into the limbo of things forgotten. Their functions are being controlled and administered by civic representatives elected by the people for that
purpose. The line of demarcation
separating one section of the community,
the submerged tenth, from the other has
'been taken away for ever in Great
Britain. As long as we perpetuate it
here we are sticking to an unchristian
anomaly in 1934. We have one law for
the rich and another for the poor. To
talk of a poor law implies that there is a
rich law. I would like to see the thing
reorganised and overhauled in such a
way that the sting would be taken away
altogether.

three separate occasions three important
commissions put forward
forward this point
of view. The Viceregal Commission

depriving Catholic majorities of legitimate rights we would have under the
British Constitution.
That sort of thing is being done at this
moment in Omagh. A most scandalous
proceeding is being carried out there, and
it is being carried out by people who profess devotion to democratic principles and
who flout them and ignore them in their
daily actions and conduct. In Fermanagh there is a glaring example of it.
Tyrone is another, and Derry City is an
absolutely classic example of gerrymandering an area for the purpose of depriving
the majority of the citizens of the right

any say whatever or any control in the

describing as an absolutely farcical form

On the whole, as I have already said,

Government have made a mistake.
the whole, I should say the Bill will do

Mr. CRAWFORD: I took the liberty
yesterday evening to move the adjournment of the debate for the express
purpose of getting an opportunity of
saying a few words on this Local
Government Bill. I have taken a great
interest in local government administration for the last number of years and
have devoted a considerable portion of
my time to endeavouring to carry out
various things in connection with local
government. I happened to be vice-chairman of the Commission that sat some
years ago, and I attended its meetings.
regularly. We heard evidence from a
great many sources. I would like to
take this opportunity, with your permission, of saying that I think the
House can scarcely realise, and, indeed,
the public generally have not realised the
indebtedness they are under to the hon.
Member for the University (Professor
Johnstone) for presiding over that Commission. He certainly did a great
amount of work. He attended the meetings very regularly; he was of the
greatest service, and got out a magnificent
report. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
There were a great number of witnesses
summoned from various organisations
throughout the cities and county and
urban areas, and as I said before very
careful consideration was given to the
evidence, while great care was taken in
framing the report.
As a result of that evidence 161 recommendations were made to the Government, and certainly out of those 161
recommendations the Government might
have been able to frame a Bill or Bills
which would have revolutionised local
government throughout the area. Ten
or twelve of the recommendations required no legislation and could have
I
been carried into effect by the people as
time went along. Whole or partial effect
has been given by legislation since the
Report was issued to seven or eight of
these recommendations, but so far as I
can see from the Bill before the House
at present the Measure will only give
whole or partial effect to five or six of
the recommendations. The remainder of
the Bill, as far as I can judge, deals with
other things not recommended by the
Commission. I must say that these are
important matters and will be useful in
carrying out local government throughout
the country, but they do not form part
of the recommendations of the Commission. While approving of the Bill for
the Second Reading of which I intend to
vote, I am sorry that it leaves out the
most important of the recommendations made by this Commission.
regret that very much. I have a sort
of sympathy with the Minister of Home.
Affairs, who said that to bring in a Bill
containing all these recommendations
would revolutionise the whole thing and
add considerably to the already heavy
burden the ratepayers have to bear. I
do not mind saying that if the Minister
had brought in a Bill which would add
to the expense the ratepayers have to
bear I would have been one to oppose it.
At the same time, I think we might
have had more of the recommendations,
and certainly some of the major recommendations brought into this Bill. I am
sorry that he took no notice of the reorganisation of the medical services,
because I believe that nothing of any importance will be done in this area until
these services are reorganised. The reorganisation I refer to will prevent overlapping, and, in the long run, will work
more efficiently and less expensively.
I am sorry the right hon. Gentleman
did not abolish workhouses, root and
branch. I have been interested in that
question for the past five and twenty
years, and I believe it would be an
advantage to have workhouses abolished
entirely. In the county in which I have
the honour of being a representative of
one of the Divisions, we have now only
one, whereas we had six, so that we are
progressing in some degree in getting rid
of them, and I do hope the time is coming
when we shall not have a workhouse in
our whole area. While I say that I
recognise it cannot be done as easily as
some Members of the Opposition think.

HOUSE OF COMMONS

There are great difficulties in doing away
with workhouses. I know there are, unfortunately, great numbers of people
tramping through the country who have
not money to pay for lodgings. I have
advocated, and the Commission decided,
that these casual tramps should be dealt
with in a different way from being put
in the workhouse. I hold that the Constabulary should be utilised in giving
them tickets to recognised boardinghouses where they would get bed and
breakfast. This could be done at less
expense than keeping them in a workhouse, and is the way in which I believe
casual tramps should be dealt with.
I have not so much sympathy with
these people that I would object to keeping them in a workhouse for 72 hours.
I would keep them longer than that if
they were unruly, and if they were most
undesirable people I would keep them as
long as I could rather than let them
tramp through the country working mischief and spreading crime. I have no
sympathy with nonsensical talk of the
kind that was indulged in, such as that
it was interfering with the liberty of the
subject to keep persons in the workhouse.
If they do not behave themselves and do
duties allocated to them I see nothing
wrong in keeping them.

with. I have no sympathy with the

There were in this excellent Report those
two notes of warning as to the possible
cost. And what were the circumstances?
In 1925, when the Commission sat, the
total amount expended in respect of poor
relief for the year 1925 was £409,769.
In 1927, when the report was handed to
us, the expenditure had risen from that
figure to £448,240, and in 1933 that expenditure had mounted to no less a sum
than £608,957. How could the Government, in face of the circumstnces in
which we found ourselves with this exceptional distress, have dared to propose
to alter the machinery that had to handle
these amounts for public services?
Why, if the Government had come into
the House with a Bill to adopt any such
suggestion, as my hon. Friend says, they
would immediately have been asked to
justify their action and to say what the
probable cost would be.
We were not prepared with an answer
to that. All we knew was that burdens
were being imposed and super-imposed
upon our ratepayers that were almost
impossible for them to bear. How could
we in those circumstances do what the
recommendations asked? What did we
do? I share, as every Member of the
Government shares, the greatest admiration for those members of county councils
and local councils who devote a lot of
their time in an honest and upright
attempt to discharge their affairs within
the law. We yield to no man in our
respect for them. Therefore, what did
we do? We sent out from the Ministry
a circular letter to each and all of those
associations indicating to them the
recommendations that had been made by
the Commission and asking for their
advice as to what action we should take
in regard to the matter, having regard to
the abnormal times through which we
were passing. And the answer we got
from the Ulster Association of County
Councils was this:

street corner oratory. I hope that on
reflection he will, to a certain extent, be
sorry for that reference.
I do not present myself at street corners where I am
not wanted. I have had the honour to
preside at meetings at street corners and
to speak to the working-class people.
The reason was that there were no halls
in the division big enough to accommodate the audiences.
The hon. Member (Mr. Midgley) has
condemned the non-contributory pensions
scheme as far as local government officers
are concerned. It is a surprising thing
to me that condemnation of noncontributory pensions should come from
a Labour Member. I have from the
beginning of my public life always stood
for non-contributory pensions for all
classes. Under this Bill local government officers will be paid non-contributory pensions. My only regret is that
this particular Clause does not apply to
the working people within the local government area. I am also sorry it does
not apply to the police and teachers. If
it is at all possible for the Government
to bring in a non-contributory scheme of
pensions for all workers they will have
me with them. I fully agree with the
non-contributory scheme, but I do not
agree with pensions on a contributory
basis. If a pension is worthy of being
given, then it should be given without
contribution.

I next want to refer to the period of
years when I was associated with the
workhouse. As a member of the board,
I attended the workhouse three days a
week. I went round the wards constantly. I found out about all the conditions operating under the daily
routine that is applied by the workhouse authority, and if hon. Members
had the same experience-I know some
Members have-I think they would
agree that the time is long overdue for
the abolition of an institution of that
kind. I say to keep a man and woman
in the workhouse is more costly than to
keep them in their own little home.
When we went into the figures we found
that the cost was not just as put down
at 9s and 11s per head, but averaged
11s 73d in one building and 13s 24d in
another building. If it takes that to
keep these old people in
in collective
fashion in a place where you are buying
in large quantities and where a service.
is given that tends to economise, you
would, in my opinion, effect a very considerable saving if the aged and infirm
were transferred from the workhouse
into a home. I wish the Government
would only realise the great saving and
greater security there would be if they
said to Mrs. Jones or Mrs. Brown,
"Remain in your own cottage and we
will give you an enhanced amount every
week to provide the necessaries of life,
and we will see that it is paid when due."
That is the only solution-cottage
homes for the aged and infirm. If such
a thing is brought forward at
at the
earliest possible date the aged will give
you a blessing that will last for years
to come.
The part dealing with public services
was passed over by the Parliamentary
Secretary. I do not know whether it
was intentional or not. The hon. Member (Professor Johnstone) knocked all
the arguments by the board. Medical
service is not a thing that should be
tainted with pauperism. The taint of
pauperism is at the moment attached
to the medical service under the poor
law. Ι can see no earthly reason
why the Government should not apply
itself to the centralisation
the
public services in Northern Ireland.
Is there any great difficulty or
any financial liability in connection
with this system? We have the
of
infirmary and union, we have departments attending to women, we have the
public health authority in Belfast, we
have child welfare schemes, and we have
a committee looking after the insane.
Is there anything to prevent the Governmen bringing all these different units
under one central authority, to be
governed by one central committee?
I believe the whole thing would
tend towards economy
and better
services. I would have no workhouses, but I would provide a dwelling
for the tramp or vagrant class. That is
the class that you require housing for.
The figures that were given in respect to
exceptional distress were given for an
exceptional year and are not normal.
What was required was to set up a
modern system for the benefit of the
aged and infirm in our area.
It is said that the finances will not
permit it. Your heart is with us, but
your pocket will not allow you. I would
like to try to take something out of
the pocket of the Minister of Finance.
When the Minister is called on for a
subsidy for milk, for wheat, and for
many other things he can get the money,
but when a call is made for a subsidy
to assist and alleviate the declining years
of old people, the reply is: "We have
not got the money." When you are
passing along the street and see an old
person who asks for a copper, the first
thing you do is to put your hand in
your pocket and give it. You feel for
that old person, but in the house of
politics the human element seems to be
like the marble walls. Everything else
comes first. There does not seem to be
any human feeling within the house of
politics. I was not going to say anything about the auditors. I agree with
the Member for Mid Antrim. Sometimes I am guilty of many offences, but
having had experience of both local
government auditors and the auditors in
this House, I know that they carry out
their duty fearlessly. I have nothing but
the highest praise for the auditors I have
come in contact with.
I am sure all
Members of the House regret that the
Report of the Commission was not
accepted in full, and if the Bill is put
back for six months a better Measure
could then be introduced. In any case, I
must say that the Minister and the Parliamentary Secretary have done their
work pretty well.

1. Mr. CAMPBELL (for Mr. Beattie)

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I assume that the hon. Member is not suggesting that Members
should have telephone facilities gratis
from their private residences, and that
what he is suggesting is that there should
be a free telephone service for all Members from this building.
The hon. Member is, no doubt, aware
of the arrangement by which the cost of
all local calls within the Belfast area is
met by the Exchequer, which makes the
necessary payments to the Post Office,
but the cost of trunk calls is recovered
from hon. Members. The concession
already granted is the utmost which the
Government can, in reason, be asked to
make.

that point.

(a) to charge on and issue out of the

and

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The Resolution which is
on the Order Paper to-day is of a simple
nature and may be described in two parts.
The first part is the necessary preliminary
to the italicised Sub-clause (2) of Clause
18 of the Bill which was before the House
last week. Any fines paid in respect of
contraventions of any Order made by the
Ministry of Home Affairs closing roads
to public traffic will be paid into the
Exchequer, and the purpose of this
Resolution is to enable an equivalent sum
to be paid by the Exchequer into the
Road Fund, which is the ultimate
destination of all penalties for traffic
offences.
The second part of the Resolution deals
with the expenses of prosecutors and
witnesses at assizes, quarter sessions and
petty sessions which are under certain
statutes chargeable on the rates. For
many years prior to the setting up of
this Government it was the practice to
repay the cost of these charges to the
local authorities by means of extrastatutory grants covered by the Appropriation Acts from year to year, and this
practice was continued by this Government. The Select Committee on Public
Accounts has, from time to time, commented on the desirability of regularising by categorical legislation any grants
of this kind which are met by the Government as an act of grace, and not by
specific statutory provision, and it is to
meet this view that the opportunity
afforded by the present Bill is being
utilised to give definite sanction to this
long-standing practice. The amount of
these grants paid in the financial year
1933-34 was £2,186. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move

Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move
in Clause 3, page 3, line 30, at end of
paragraph (a) to add the following
paragraph:-
(b) if at any meeting there is an
equal division of votes upon any
question, the mayor, chairman, or

acting as chairman of the meeting
shall, in addition to his own vote

This is also a drafting Amendment.
The object of it is to make clear that the
chairman of a municipal authority will
still have the right, which he has had up
to the present, of having a second or
a casting vote if there is an equality of
votes.
Mr. O'NEILL: When the Bill was
before the House on Second Reading I
mentioned in connection with this Clause
the difficulties councils sometimes had. I
feel that the Government have not gone
the full length in this Amendment to
meet those difficulties. The Bill gives
power to councils to decide matters when
there is a quorum present, and whether
the majority of those present vote or not.
But there is still the question of the
appointment of a chairman. The
difficulty is still there even though you
give the temporary chairman and such
like persons a casting vote. What I
suggested was and I cannot understand
why the Government have not accepted
the suggestion that the town clerk
should have the right to determine by lot
any question on which the council were
equally divided. If twelve members meet
to-morrow and there are six on each side
no one can have a casting vote, because
no one can be appointed chairman,
whereas if you gave the town clerk power
to decide this thing by lot the matter
would be ended and it would put things
right. I say the Government should
even yet accept my suggestion, because
there is no doubt that great difficulties do
arise at council meetings over this matter.
I think the Government are right in
introducing legislation to amend these
things, but they have stopped short of
what would put them right. The
Government should accept the suggestion
I have made that the town clerk be
empowered to decide any matter on which
the council are equally divided by casting
lots.
Sir DAWSON BATES: In connection
with the election of a chairman, with
which, I think, the hon. Member for
Mourne is particularly dealing, I would
point out that under Section 38 of the
Act of 1847 there is power to cast lots
as to who shall be chairman in the event
of the two sides not being able to get a
decisive vote. We do not propose to
abolish that right, which is inherent in
any council.
Mr. O'NEILL: I know the council
actually have that right at present, but
I say you should make it obligatory on the
town clerk to decide the matter there and
then. It would make it much easier for
everyone in connection with the council.
It may not only be in connection with the
election of a chairman. The chairman
may not always want to give a casting
vote or to take the responsibility of
deciding an important matter. Therefore, I say the clerk should not only have
the right but should be compelled to
decide the matter by casting lots instead
of holding things up for weeks and
months and disturbing the business of
the council.
Mr. NIXON: I am sorry that I cannot
agree with the hon. Member for Mourne.
I do not think that would be a very
dignified way to elect a chairman, and
people opposed to him might say "You
were never elected. You were taken out
of the hat." I do not think it would be
dignified at all and in addition it would,
in a way, be giving official recognition to
a lottery. I think the first time we heard

was crucified the people cast lots as to
who would get His garments. They did
not want to tear them and they cast lots.
I believe that is the first record we have
of that. I really do not think it would
be a dignified way to elect a chairman of
any assembly. If the candidates on each
side have equal votes and they decide on

in the exercise of any of their powers
accept a tender for the execution of
any work which is not the lowest tender
received for that work, a minute shall

the Ministry of Home Affairs may
prescribe, stating the reasons for the
non-acceptance of the tender, or, in
case of more than one, of each tender,
which is lower than the accepted
tender.
There are the additional powers with
which the Minister will be armed in the
future. Supposing the Public Health,
the Tramways, the Gas, or the Electricity
Committee of the Belfast Corporation,
acting under that Section, accepted a
tender which was not the lowest. All
the actions of nearly every committee of
a local authority are subject to the confirmation of the appropriate Government
Department, and that Department could
withhold its sanction of the committee's
action, or send a communication drawing
attention to the fact that the explanation
forwarded was inadequate. All I am
asking for at the present time is this.
After you have imposed this regulation,
no surcharge in respect of any such
accepted tender may be imposed by a
local government auditor until an inquiry
has been held at which the body concerned is present. I know there is an
inquiry held at the present time, but it is
held after the surcharge has been
imposed. The auditor comes across a
contract which has been accepted at a
rate which he deems to be outside the
scope of the allowance of 5 per cent.
allowed by the Ministry of Home Affairs.
In pursuance of his constitutional rights
and his professional practice, the auditor
sends a communication to the people concerned that he is going to impose a surcharge, but if those persons have anything to say in defence of themselves they
shall attend on a certain date at the City
Hall, where he will hear them.
What I want to point out is that the
surcharge has already been imposed, and
the persons concerned are to a certain
extent pilloried before the inquiry is
held. The Press in Belfast publish the
information, not that that is a good argument in favour of my Amendment,
because all that the Press succeed in
doing is to make a kind of hero of the
person who has been surcharged. I have
heard of members who have become so
popular in consequence of being surcharged that they have actually increased
their poll, and we do not want polls
increased by that means.
There ought to be the fullest possible
inquiry before, and not after, a surcharge is made. I am with the Minister
and the Parliamentary Secretary when
they say they must stand for the adequate
defence of the rights of the ratepayers in
the matter of accepting tenders. I do
not want to try to besmirch a local
authority that I have any connection
with, but I am sufficiently familiar with
local government in Northern Ireland to
know that tenders have not always been

by a committee, and the

The Parliamentary Secretary says that

Ministry of Home Affairs. It is right
he should be up to a point. I am going
to state what I will prove. The most
illogical and unjust thing that could be
done by any auditor was done in Belfast
by a local government auditor. The

but an outside firm of auditors found
them incorrect. What do you think that
auditor did then? He surcharged the

could not know they were incorrect how
could the councillors know? I think I
can prove that statement up to the hilt.
He passed accounts as correct which an

comes back and, instead of surcharging

There could be nothing more illogical

independent of the Ministry of Home

No councillor, not if he spent all his

thousands and thousands of pounds and
if I were there night and day I could not

stand surcharged-a scapegoat in the

and the system is continued. I was
wondering if some means could be

buy a lot of stores for their respective

years had refrained from doing, although
they had permissive powers. The Education Act compelled them to do certain
things. Nearly every other Act of
Parliament at some stage or another
compels the local authority to carry out
certain services which were formerly
optional on the part of the local
authority. Therefore, it is not a good
refuge for a Member of the Front Bench
to hide behind to say "Why should we
try to force this upon the local
authority?" when the whole history of
legislation is in the direction of
compelling recalcitrant local authorities
to do what they ought to have done.
That is point number one. Number
two is in regard to the cost.
It is easy
enough for the Parliamentary Secretary
to get up in this Committee and say
none of the three hon. Members has referred to the cost of this.
No person
could tell you the cost of it unless it was
worked out on an actuarial basis. But
I can tell you that superannuation
implies that you can have various kinds
of schemes, and if one scheme is too dear,
you can try by actuarial calculation the
working of another scheme on a lower
basis than the one you have previously
considered, SO that in the end the
collective wisdom might begin with small
beginnings and rise afterwards according
to changing circumstances.

is abroad. Some Members on the

whole administration of the Province-
The CHAIRMAN: Might I remind
the hon. Gentleman that at the moment
we are not dealing with spiritual inspiration, but with superannuation ?
Mr. MIDGLEY: That is right. I am
trying to harness the two together. I
am trying to demonstrate to the people
on the opposite side of the Committee
that, having got this new spiritual
inspiration, they must translate it into
their everyday affairs if it is to be of
any value at all, and one way in which
they can do that is by seeing that the
legislation which they put upon the
Statute Book is of a higher moral and
ethical standard than it has been heretofore. I do not say it is low, but I want
to see it even higher. Therefore, I am
going to appeal again and again on this
matter. I appeal to the Government to
take off the Whip and let us have a free
vote on this question. In a community
which, perhaps, is a bit hard up,
the Parliamentary Secretary says, having
regard to the economic conditions under
which we are living, what do I say and
what ought we all to say? Having
regard to the conditions under which we
live it ought to be the duty of the State
to spread any blessings or assistance they
can as equitably as they possibly can.
Under existing conditions that is not
being done. What do you think of
certain people sitting in this Committee
along with myself having to go to the
Corporation week after week, and then
suddenly getting a letter of resignation
as
from an officer of one of the departments
and finding, when we come to consider the terms on which he is retiring,
that he is going to retire on a pension
of £25 or £26 a week? That would do
a great deal to finance a superannuation
scheme from the point of view of
what you are going to give to the men
on a contributory basis. That has
happened in our time. If you had the
history of the Belfast local authority
for the last ten years before you to-night
you would
would find that, through the
whirligig of time and the vicissitude of
circumstances, we have made so many
changes in the Belfast Corporation that
we have already amassed a tremendous
annual bill in respect of pension allowances alone. And those pension
allowances have not been given to those
people in return for any superannuation
contributions. They were given because
they were deemed to be pensionable
officers, and we have faithfully discharged
our responsibility to those officers.
But is it too much to suggest that as long
as you allow the present system to continue you are creating a very bad perspective in the minds of the masses of
the people? When the masses of our
people who are permanently living under
the spectre of insecurity see one body
of workmen, who have earned 50/- or
60/- a week for the past thirty or thirtyfive years, who have brought up their
families in decency, and who have faced
life on that wage and have emerged
triumphantly, being ruthlessly thrown
upon the scrap heap without any provision, while other men, who for twentyfive or thirty years have been in receipt
of salaries of from £1,000 up to £2,000
a year, retire on two-thirds of their
salaries as pensions-with £16, £17, £18,
£19, or even £20 a week, some of which
were referred to the other day in the
House-when they see all that do you
not think they begin to ask questions,
do you not think they begin to feel dissatisfied, do you not think they believe
that is unjust? I tell you they do. They
believe it is unjust. They believe it is
immoral, that it is lob-sided, and bad
treatment of the masses of the people.

The Parliamentary Secretary or the
Minister may now say, Why do the
people not return elected representatives
to the City Council who support.
superannuation scheme?" They do not

do so for this reason: When you stand for
