standing on a multitude of issues, and,

and so you have a number of men returned
to our local authorities who have got no
instructions on the matter.
In many
country districts superannuation has never

give outdoor relief).
(1) Outdoor relief may be given to a
destitute poor widow having one legitimate child dependent upon her, and
accordingly in section one of the Poor
Relief (Ireland) Act, 1847, the words
"two or more" shall be omitted.

(Ireland) Act, 1862 (which excludes an
occupier of more than a quarter of an
acre from being relieved otherwise than
in the workhouse) for the words "land
of greater extent than a quarter of a
statute acre' there shall be substituted
the words "land of a net annual value
greater than five pounds as shown in the
valuation lists for the time being in
force under the Valuation Acts
(Northern Ireland), 1852 to 1932
(whether any person is liable to pay
rates in respect of such land or not)."
Mrs. PARKER: I beg to move in
Sub-clause (2) to leave out "five"
("greater than five pounds") and insert
two." I would like to say that I endorse the suggestion that valuation should
be taken into consideration instead of
area of land, as was the case formerly. In
the Committee's Report we said that we
thought to fix any area of land was a bad
principle, owing to the great difference in
the value. We accordingly recommend
that a rateable valuation of £3 should be
substituted for a quarter of a statute
acre. The Minister of Home Affairs has
inserted instead of the recommendation
of the Committee £5. I do think that
would be a very great mistake, because in
certain areas it will be found that £5
would give an acreage of 261. Every
pound is equal to 51 acres and £5 makes
261 acres. I could give several other
instances of about 20 acres and 141 and
so forth. I do hope the Government will
agree that £5 is too high. I think, after
great deliberation, that £2 would be fair.
Mr. BLACK: I do not know a great
deal about land, but it occurred to me
that land value for only 4s an acre must
be very poor and unprofitable, and the
people with 26 acres of land of that type
would be people in a very poor and
wretched way. As far as I am concerned
£5 could not be said to be too high.
Mr. MINFORD: I endorse what has
been said by the hon. and learned Member for Willowfield, I agree that £5 is
a very fair figure. If you take a man
with 26 acres at 4s an acre I think he
would be far better if he never saw the
land at all. The majority of people who
own land are not even getting the wages
of a labourer, and it would be unfair to
debar a £5 valuation.
Mrs. PARKER: I would like to remind hon. Members that this was formerly
a quarter of a statute acre, and now hon.
Members are viewing the possibility of

realise the enormous difference and agree

Sir DAWSON BATES: The Government cannot accept the Amendment.
The provisions as they stand in the Bill
are designed with the object of apportioning to the board of guardians as a poor
rate charge all expenses in connection
with distress relief works. If the Amendment were accepted it would destroy the
whole principle of chargeability, and it
would be impossible for the Government,
or the local authorities, or the ratepayers
themselves, to see at any time what the
expenses in respect of poor relief are in
any particular area.
It is possible that it may be suggested
that the Clause in its present form may
involve some slight book-keeping transactions, but the trivial trouble caused by
such transactions would not outweigh the
value of having the expenses charged to
the proper account.
Amendment by leave withdrawn.

that this Clause hands over to boards of
guardians certain powers and duties which
have hitherto reposed in the county
councils? The change arises in connection with the provisions of the Midwives
Act as to nurses calling in medical assistance in cases of emergency. These cases
have been exploited in the interests of
the medical profession, particularly in
certain districts in County Down. What
has happened hitherto has been that poor
law relief tickets, which are commonly
known red lines, for particular
medical service by dispensary doctors,
have not only been asked for in maternity
as
cases but in respect of medical assistance,
and those doctors have been paid two
guineas a case. The fact is that the Down
County Council is concerned in 95 per
cent. of these cases in which the patient
would have been entitled to free poor law
medical service by the dispensary doctor.
In a large number of cases-I have the
list here the person called in in an
emergency was the local dispensary
doctor who, if he had got a red line,
would have been obliged to treat the
patient free. In County Down we have
during the last four years been called upon

officers, which would have been provided

for Dock raised the question of the taint
of pauperism. Apparently there is no

doctor is called in and paid £2 for doing
what he had got to do free for the ratepayers under the poor law. This Clause,
as it stands, has the full support of the
county councils of Northern Ireland.
Professor JOHNSTONE : I have
listened very carefully to both speeches
made on the subject and I really think
they show that we have not got a satisfactory Clause. We find that in County
Down the county council have been paying £80 a year for the last four years,
which, of course, is a very large charge
on a poor county like Down. (Laughter.)
Naturally, this Committee would like to
relieve them of it. It does seem to me
that this Clause tries to cure one injustice
by creating another. County Down has
lost £80 a year for the last four years,

the money the dispensary doctor has got

of ensuring that £80 a year will not be
paid into the hands of the dispensary
doctors of County Down. I do not know

less one likes it. It definitely lays down

NEW CLAUSE (Power to appoint
deputy town clerk).
(1) The Council of a County Borough
may appoint a deputy town clerk to
hold office during the pleasure of the
Council, with authority, during such
time as the Town Clerk shall be incapable of acting owing to illness,
2669 Local Government Bill-

16 OCTOBER 1931
Committee
absence or otherwise to act for the
Town Clerk, and, in the case of his
death, to act as Town Clerk until the
appointment of his successor.
(2) All things required or authorised
by law to be done by or to the Town
Clerk may be done by or to the Deputy
Town Clerk.
Brought up and read a First time.
Mr. BYRNE: I beg to move, "That
this Clause be now read a Second time."
This is a new Clause. There is at present
no power to appoint a deputy town clerk
to act during the illness or absence of
the existing town clerk. As the duties of
a town clerk under modern Acts of Parliament are voluminous any interruption
by sickness or otherwise in the carrying
out of his duties might be attended with
very great inconvenience to the public. It
is therefore considered that a Clause of
this kind is very desirable, especially as
there is precedent for it in one of the
English Acts.
Mr. HANNA: I am prepared to
accept this Amendment.

.NEW CLAUSE (Supplementary borrowing powers of county and urban
district councils).
(1) The council of any county or
urban district may, with the consent
of the Ministry of Home Affairs, borrow
by way of temporary loan or overdraft
from a bank or otherwise any sums
which such council may temporarily
require for the purposes of defraying,
pending the raising of a loan which the
council have been authorised to raise,
expenses intended to be defrayed by
means of the loan.
(2) Where money is borrowed in pursuance of sub-section (1) of this section,
and subsequently such a loan as is
mentioned in that sub-section is raised,
then for the purposes of the provisions
of any enactment or order regulating
the repayment of that loan the loan
shall, to the extent of the sum
borrowed under the said sub-section, be
deemed to have been raised at the time
when the borrowing under the said
sub-section took place.
Brought up and read a First time.
Mr. HANNA: I beg to move, "That
this Clause be now read a Second time."
This is a new Clause which has been
inserted at the request of local authorities
enabling them to pay interest on overdrafts pending the raising of authorised
loans. It is often found that considerable periods elapse between the date of

Mr. POLLOCK: This small Bill refers
to certain adjustments of finance of a very
simple character. They are adjustments of
the residuary share of reserved taxes paid
over to the Ministry of Finance by the
Treasury during the last financial year
that were treated
They
represent amounts that were successfully
held to be due in respect of previous
years. It was provided by the Exchequer and Financial Provisions Act of
1927 that all such adjustments should
pass into the Reserve Fund, and in order
to regularise the retention of the money
this little Measure is necessary. The
matter applies to certain receipts of
revenue in the current year.
The second Clause in the Bill deals
with the extension by £1,500,000 of the
statutory £7,000,000 limit to the issues
from the Government Loans Fund. In
addition to meeting the requirements of
local authorities the Fund makes advances
to the Exchequer for the purposes of the
Bann drainage, police barracks reconstruction, and several other matters.
The limit is a cumulative one, that is to
say, the instalments are repaid by the
local authorities and others, but the reissue of the money must still be added to
the previous total. In actual fact, on
the 31st August last the gross amount
outstanding was £5,900,000, though the
cumulative total was in excess of seven
millions.

Mr. MIDGLEY: In conformity with
the notice which I gave I raise the matter
referred to by question and answer in
this House on last Thursday, that is with
regard to the appointment of an officer
who had been retired from one Ministry
and had been appointed under the jurisdiction of another. I was at pains to
watch very carefully the different points
in the reply given by the Minister of
Labour to a series of questions which I
put forward. The answers to some were
in the affirmative, particularly one with
reference to the fact that this official was
an official who for twelve months had
been on extended leave. He had been
paid for the greater portion of that time.
by the Department, and for the remaining portion he was paid out of the Civil
Contingencies Fund, which I understand
is a violation of the principles of finance
So
far as this House is concerned. I
demand an explanation as to why that
procedure was followed in this case.
Furthermore, I should like to know
why an official who was paid his salary
for a longer period than a year had not
his services utilised to the fullest possible
extent by the Department concerned.
The Minister of Labour on Thursday
last intimated in reply to my query that
the amount of time given by this gentleman to the Department was very small
indeed. I should like to know what
justification existed for such a protracted
period of extended leave on full salary.
Then at the end of that time, as if the
imposition were not sufficiently heavy,
what do we find? We find that after a
period of over a year on full salary this
official is pensioned off at £600 a year.
Immediately he is pensioned off from one
Department at £600 a
year he is
appointed to a new Department at £700
a year, making a total of £1,300 a year,
or almost the
same salary he
receiving in his original position. The
Minister defended that on these grounds.
He said:
was
"Advantage has been taken of the
opportunity of securing the services, in
a temporary capacity, on the staff of
the Unemployment Assistance Board,
of an experienced officer who, before.
his retirement from the Civil Service,
had been Principal Establishment
Officer in the Ministry of Finance, and
subsequently an assistant secretary in
the Ministry of Agriculture."-(Official
Report-11th October, 1934, vol. 16,
col. 2527.)
I should like to ask the Minister this
question: Is the Province or the area of
Northern Ireland so deficient in constructive or administrative ability that it
was absolutely essential to wait for over
twelve months while this gentleman drew
his salary in order to get his services at
a cheaper rate ? Would not the correct
policy for the Government have been to
appoint someone else and so open up the
way to promotion amongst the junior
officers in the Civil Service and give them
some incentive to give of their best to
the servce of Northern Ireland?
I understand-I have heard, and in
saying this I say it with all respectthat the gentleman concerned belongs to
that section of the community which
takes no interest in this world's affairs;
that he is only concerned with the mansions above. But I notice not infrequently that when you come to deal with
this type of person you generally find
them ensconced in the best paid jobs
throughout the community. I think it
is an outrage, and there is a growing
tendency in Northern Ireland to carry
out this policy. I want to protest
against the growing tendency, not only
in the Government but in the municipality, to appoint to new jobs people who
have retired from old ones. When a
man reaches the pensionable age in the
Appointment of an Official 2684
Adjournment-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
a
service of the State and is rewarded for
those services to the extent of £600 a
year, I say, in view of the abnormality
of the unemployment problem, the very
least we can expect is that, when a new
appointment is to be made, it should be
made from the ranks of those available
for promotion, and so open up fresh
avenues of employment for those we have
to absorb. That we should allow
man to serve for a generation, then to
retire on an adequate pension, and then
proceed to appoint him to a new position
at £700 a year constitutes a burden
which I believe this Province should not
be called upon to bear, and in my opinion.
also constitutes an infamy in public life.
I want to protest with all the emphasis
at my command against this appointment and the methods by which it was
brought about.
I should like to ask the Minister to deal
with this aspect of the matter. What
pull has this man over the Government
that he was able to do this for over
twelve months? Here is a man who to all
intents and purposes, was suspended by
the chief officers of the Department to
which he belonged. What was the pull
or influence, of a sinister character
or otherwise, that he had over the Government by which he was enabled to
enjoy his full salary for over twelve
months, while for about three months of
that period his salary was paid from a
source from which it ought not to have
been paid at all? Where is the hidden
hand behind this, or what is the hidden
purpose? What kind of sinister influence
is at work which permits such an infamy
to be inflicted on our people here? And
then at the end of it all, as if it were
not bad enough, we have this man receiving a fresh appointment at £700 a year.
If that were the only action of this
kind associated with the Government one
might say some kind of misunderstanding had taken place, although it would
be very difficult to believe it. But this
is not the first or second case of this kind
in the history of the Government. There
have been several cases in the history of
the Government of people who have
drawn their full salaries, who have then
been placed on pension, and soon after
appointed to other positions. This one
comes directly under the Government.
In one or two other cases the Government
were able successfully-as far as the
masses of the people were concerned at
any rate-to plead that the salaries were
going to be paid by authorities outside
the Government. But in this case no
such plea can be put forward. It is a
very bad example to local authorities
throughout Northern Ireland when you
have the Government giving way to
influences like this, when you have the
Government perpetrating an economic injustice like this, and inflicting further
handicaps on a long-suffering community.
All these things combined are a bad
influence for local authorities, and there
is every reason to believe that, as a result of certain events recently, local
authorities are likely to take their cue
from the Government and embark upon
the same policy of appointing people who
have retired to new positions. That is
something nobody ought to defend. We
have an efficient civil service in
Northern Ireland. We have hundreds
of junior officers who are serving the
State faithfully and well and who are
waiting for their opportunity. They are
hammering all the time at the door of
opportunity, but the door is being closed.
against them by the policy carried out
by the Government.
I should like the right hon. Gentleman
in replying to this also to reply to the
other points raised last Thursday and to
define what is the policy of the Government in regard to promotion in the
civil service. It is alleged-I am not in
a position to verify this completely, but
it is alleged that, in Northern Ireland,
when it comes to making promotions and
appointments in connection with the
Government, the thing that counts most
is not what you know, not what
capacity you have, but whom you know
and how you happen to be related to that
particular person. Some of the appointments in recent days in connection with
the Government would seem to bear out
that construction to a great extent.
There is a feeling abroad, not only
throughout the population but amongst the
civil servants, a feeling of dissatisfaction,
that things are not as they ought to be,
that people are not getting the opportunities they ought to get in return for
faithful service to the State. Those are
various aspects of the question with which
I should like the Minister to deal.

I want now to say that at the first

if a plebiscite or a referendum were taken
there would be an overwhelming vote of

opportunity I have of protesting against
this financial imposition upon the people.
I say it is an outrage in face of the condition of things, in which you have 61,000

face of that continued abnormal situation
the idea of taking people out of jobs,
pensioning them on full pension, and
then putting them into other positions at
high rates of salary, is detrimental to the
best interests of the community, constitutes a grave injustice to those serving,
and definitely closes the door of opportunity against those seeking an outlet for
their labour at the present time.

Oral Answers to Questions.
MARKETING OF FRUIT ACT-NUM-
BER OF INSPECTORS AND
PRICES OF APPLES.
1. Mr. McCARROLL (for Mr. Healy)
asked the Minister of Agriculture whether
he can state how many fruit inspectors
there are, their total salaries and allowances, including travelling, and if the
Government are still providing police at
Annaghmore and other stations for their
protection; if he can give the price of
best cooking apples per barrel in Belfast
when the Fruit Marketing Act was introduced as compared with the prices to-day.
The
MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): The Ministry
employs three horticultural inspectors.
Since the Marketing of Fruit Act came
into force only one additional horticultural inspector has been employed.
The cost of this extra inspector, including
travelling expenses, was £420 in the
financial year ending 31st March, 1934.
The Government are not providing
police protection for these inspectors at
Annaghmore, because such protection is
quite unnecessary, and the Ministry has
the support of the growers in its policy.
Immediately before the Marketing of
Fruit Act came into force the price of
the best cooking apples on Belfast market
was 17s a barrel, the price now is about
8s a barrel. It should, however, be
borne in mind that this drop in price has
no connection whatever with the Act and
is due entirely to world conditions. For
example, in the same period the average
price in Great Britain has dropped by
about 50 per cent. which, roughly speaking, corresponds to the drop in Belfast.
It should also be remembered that the
provisions of the Act, with regard to
grading, do not apply in Belfast market.
They apply only to apples for shipment,
so that, by no stretch of the imagination,
can present low prices at Belfast be
associated with the operation of the Act.
I must also emphasise that, but for the
Act there would, in the present glutted
condition of the British market, be no
exports whatever of Ulster apples to
Great Britain, whereas, at the moment,
our graded apples are being exported
freely.

ARREST OF MR. T. GEEHAN.
3. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state if
Mr. T. Geehan, who was arrested on the
12th instant in Belfast whilst addressing
a meeting, is being held in custody without a charge being preferred against him;
whether he will grant facilities to his
relatives to pay visits; and whether he
will consider the advisability of releasing
the arrested man on bail.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Mr. Thomas
Geehan was arrested on the 12th instant,
and a prosecution under Section 2 (2) of
the Civil Authorities (Special Powers)
Act has been directed against him, and
it is understood that he was brought
before the Court to-day.
Permission has already been given to
his wife, Mrs. Geehan, to visit him in
prison.
Under the circumstances indicated
above, the question of the granting of
bail does not arise.
Mr. GRANT: I beg to ask the right
hon. Gentleman a question arising out
of his reply. Is it not a fact that on a
former occasion this gentleman asked the
Ministry to protect him from his own.
organisation?
LABOURERS' COTTAGES IN ENNIS-
KILLEN RURAL DISTRICT.
4. Mr. McCARROLL (for Mr. Healy)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether his attention has been called to
the refusal of the Enniskillen Rural
Council since 1921 to consider the repeated representations which have been
made to them by agricultural labourers
for the provision of cottages under the
Agricultural Labourers Act; and whether,
in view of the urgency of the matter,
some of the people being housed in oneroomed, unsanitary cabins, families, residing in two-roomed, tumble-down
houses, he will cause a sworn enquiry to
be held into the failure of this council to
discharge its obligations.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As the hon.
Member is aware, the Government has
felt it necessary to
to suspend for the
present the operation of the Labourers
Acts owing to financial stringency, and
under the circumstances, therefore, the
question of the attitude of the Enniskillen Rural District Council does not
arise.
It is hoped that it will be possible to
review the situation during the course of
the next year.

Where the medical officer of a dispensary district has been called to the

(Ireland) Act, 1918, as amended by
section two of the Midwives and
Nursing Homes Act (Northern Ireland), 1929, then, notwithstanding

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): I beg
to move, "That the Clause be read a
Second time."
Hon. Members will remember the full
discussion which this Clause had as
it originally stood in the Bill on the
Committee stage, and I want on behalf
of the Government to acknowledge the
help that we have got from all sides of
the House in regard to it. They will
notice that it removes all the matters
that divided us in reference to the form
of the questions to be put by a midwife
to the family concerned. The effect of
this new Clause is that the midwife will
be free to call in any medical practitioner, but no fee is to be paid to him

meet the objections made by hon. Members to the Clause at present standing

the Members of the House who spoke on

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I beg to

It was felt in County Down by the

whole.
a
Mr. HANNA: I am afraid the hon.
and gallant Member is under some misapprehension in regard to this matter.
Under the law, the county councils are
obliged to find courthouses for the conduct of petty sessions courts, but when
they do enter into an arrangement of
this kind it is a yearly tenancy. They
take the court not for so many days
per month or so many days in the year.
The courthouse must always be available for the magistrates who hold the
courts. Therefore it does not appear to
me or to my colleagues in the Government that any useful purpose would be
served by the insertion of these words in
the Clause. The courthouse is taken for
a year irrespective of the number of
courts held in it. May I point out that
the Clause as it stands is not mandatory?
Councils have found difficulty in the past
in finding suitable premises at a rent of
£10. This will enable them to go a
little further to secure proper premises,
but it does not necessarily follow that
the rents of all courthouses now £10 or
under will be raised to £15. For those
reasons I ask the House not to accept
the Amendment.
Mr. CRAWFORD: I would press the
right hon. Gentleman to accept this
Amendment. The result of the Clause
will be that in a great many cases the
rent will be raised to £15. It does not
apply to one courthouse, but to many
throughout the country, in spite of what
the Parliamentary Secretary has said.
These courthouses as a rule are in the
possession of a landlord, and they are
used for other purposes nearly every time
he can get them let. A great many
courts are held only once a month, and
this is certainly a temptation put in the

put additional expense upon the county
councils. As I said, I protest against it.
I think £10 is quite sufficient. Arrangements could be made in cities and towns

little more, but throughout the country
I think it is a great mistake to do so.

CLAUSE 21 (Public roads).
(1) Any county council may purchase or otherwise acquire from any
person any drain, or any right of
making or of user or other right in or

trusts (if any) as the drain, right or

this sub-section, has acquired a right
to use such drain shall be entitled to
use the same, or any drain substituted
in lieu thereof, to the same extent as
such person would or might have done
if the purchase had not been made.

This Amendment is introduced to meet
the wishes of local authorities. This
time, in case there should be any misunderstanding, may I say that the hon.
and gallant Member for East Down
(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon) was responsible
for bringing the matter to our notice. I
have discussed the matter with him and
with others, and we are now in agreement that this will do exactly what he
wants. It only differs from what we
were prepared to do in one respect, and
that is that we had refused arbitrary
power of entry upon any person's land.
Entry will now be governed entirely by
the provisions we have made for the
acquisition of rights and portions of land.
Mr. MINFORD: I would like the
Minister to explain to us exactly what
this means, because we seem to be in
something of a fog. I want to ask him.
does he now give a council power to take
surface water from the road and turn it
into a man's field at any part they desire
without having properly acquired the
drain?
Sir DAWSON BATES: In order to
meet the wishes of local authorities we
have put in a Clause similar to that which
applies in regard to roads, that is to say,
that if a county council wish to put water
into a man's land they have first of all
to apply to the Ministry of Home Affairs
for a vesting order. The matter is
inquired into and, if the drain is suitable, a vesting order is granted. Following on that the person into whose lands
the water goes is entitled to claim compensation for any damage that may
result. I do not think we could have
devised any better means of protecting
the interests of the land owner than what
we now propose. It has worked very
satisfactorily in regard to the taking of
land for roads, and I do not see any
reason why it should not work equally
satisfactorily with regard to putting surface water into a man's land.

When the Amendment was proposed
by the hon. and gallant Member for East
Down 1 ventured to suggest to the
Government that it was one that should
have careful consideration. It was an
elaborate Amendment, and was designed
to meet the difficulty that certainly had
occurred to me in connection with the
Clause as it originally stood in the Bill.
No compulsory power was included in the
Clause, and if adjoining owners did not
see their way to grant permission to the
county council to drain the surface water
off the roads, then the county council and
the adjoining owners might come to a
position of impasse, and the surface
water would be left on the roads. From
my point of view, as one who supported
the hon. and gallant Member, it seems
that the Amendment now proposed by the
Ministry exactly meets the case in a way
that cannot prejudice the rights of
adjoining owners but will undoubtedly be
beneficial to the county councils.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I desire to
support what the hon. and learned Member for Derry has said. This Amendment is simply to facilitate the county
councils to get rid of surface water on to
adjoining land when their roads are
flooded. As the law at present exists,
they have no right to go in on those lands
without the leave of the owner, and unless
that leave is given they cannot get rid
of the water. All this Amendment does
is to give the county council leave to go
to arbitration, just as if they wanted to
round off a corner of a road under the
existing law. They can go to arbitration,
and compensation is paid to the owner
of the land on the decision of the
arbitrator. This simply gives the county
councils power to keep their roads free of
water, not at the expense of the men
whose lands they drain them into, but by
arbitration. It is an Amendment which
should be fully supported in the interests
both of the county councils and of the
people who own the land.
Amendment agreed to.

Sir ROBERT LYNN: I rise, on the
Third Reading, to draw the attention of
the Minister of Home Affairs to some
remarks that were made regarding the
Bill in Portrush last night. I would like
the Minister to consider whether the claim
made by the Portrush Urban Council to
be allowed to continue to collect their
rates in the same way as at present should
not be granted in another place, which,
of course, he can do if it is necessary.
Then there were two other questions
raised, one with regard to the extension
of boundaries, especially if you have to
get portions of land out of another
county, which would be the case as far as
Portrush is concerned if they were proceeding in the direction of Portstewart.
Secondly, it has been suggested that the
Minister, before he finally parts with this
Bill, should give powers to the local
authorities to deal with camps and things
like that.
Those are the three points I want to

with regard to the question of rating,
secondly, with regard to the extension of
urban boundaries, and, thirdly, with

He will notice that

these have been dealt with fully and more

ought to be met. I hope the right hon.

Sir DAWSON BATES: Perhaps, by
leave of the House, I may reply to the
hon. Member for North Antrim. With
regard to the extension of boundaries, I
think there is a great deal of misapprehension in the minds of the Urban
District Council of Portrush. After all,
the law as it stood before this Bill was
introduced, was that if an urban council
wished to extend their boundary they had
first of all to go to the county council and
request them to make an order allowing
them to extend their boundary.
The
county council held an inquiry, and if
they turned the application down there
was no remedy left in the hands of the
urban district. If, on the other hand,
the county council approved of the extension of the boundary, the urban
district was increased accordingly. Hon.
Members will appreciate that there was
an active prejudice on the part of the
county councils to increasing any urban
area, because it took away so much from
their own county area.
I really cannot understand how an
elected body of representatives like the
Portrush Urban Council could have misunderstood what the purport of this Bill
is. The effect of the Bill now is that if
the county council refuse to accede to the
urban council's application to extend
their boundary then the urban council
can come to the Ministry of Home Affairs
as an appeal court against the county
council. That arrangement was arrived
at after consultation with the Association of Municipal Authorities, of which
the Portrush Urban Council was and is a
member, and I really fail to see how it
was possible for the Government to go
further than inserting the Clause which
stands in the Bill. It has received the
entire approval of the municipal authorities of Ulster, and I only wish to say that
if the municipal authorities in Portrush
would study the Bill first and criticise us
afterwards it would be very much more
satisfactory.
2705 Local Government Bill-

18 OCTOBER 1934
Third Reading
In regard to the question of camps, I
only wish that the Portrush Urban
Council would put into practice what
they preach, because under the Town
Planning Act, which was passed some
time ago, they could have taken these
powers and exercised them. But because
they are too weak-kneed to put into
practice the powers which the Government have given them, they come back
to the Government on the principle that
is known in America as passing the buck,
instead of doing their own job.
In regard to the question of rates, that
particular Clause was inserted by the
Government to prevent many injustices.
Take for example the case of a man who
pays his rates for the ensuing year and
then dies and his house becomes vacant.
I think it is only right that during the
time the house is vacant his successors
should be relieved of rates. What
happens in Portrush apparently is that
people live there for two months and
then leave the area. I think, on
the whole, it is only right that the people
who enjoy the benefits of the town should
pay only for the period during which they
enjoy those benefits.
Really I am rather shocked to think that
any urban council should put forward
statements such as appeared in the Press
to-day, statements which are without the
slightest foundation. I had the pleasure
to-day of attending a meeting of the
General Council of Urban Authorities,
and on all sides I found that those
authorities entirely approved of this Bill,
and, when I say that, I want to pay a
tribute to the local authorities for the
great help they gave to the Government
in framing this particular Measure.

MOTOR CAR TAXES AND
LICENCES.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the
figures for the past year for Northern
Ireland giving (1) the number of motor
drivers' licences issued and the sum
derived therefrom; (2) the number of
private motor cars taxed and the sum
derived therefrom; (3) the number of
motor commercial vehicles taxed and the
sum derived therefrom; (4) the charge
for a motor driver's licence in Northern
Ireland and in England; (5) the rate of
licence duty on motor commercial lorries
in Northern Ireland and in England;
and if he can state whether after 1st
January next private motor car owners
in England will get a reduction of 25
per cent.; and whether he can hold out
any hope of a reduction in Northern
Ireland.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to answer this
question. With regard to motor drivers'
licences, the number granted in the year
ended 31st March, 1934, was 54,186,
the receipts accruing therefrom being
£25,770 15s Od.
During the same year, in connection
with private motor cars, the number of
licences issued was as follows:-
-
Annual, 15,916. Quarterly, 36,597.
involving total receipts of £271,928 14s 8d.
The figures for goods vehicles licences.
were as follows:-
Annual, 4,318. Quarterly, 13,684.
with total receipts of £207,488 4s 3d.
With regard to the fourth part of the
question, the fee charged for a motor
driver's licence in Northern Ireland is
10s per annum, except where the licence
is so limited that the holder can drive
only an invalid carriage, a public service
vehicle or a goods vehicle. In such cases
the charge is 5s per annum.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
The fee for a motor driver's licence
in Great Britain is 5s per annum.
It would not be possible within the
limit of a Parliamentary question and
reply to indicate in full the comparative
rates of licence duty on goods vehicles
in Northern Ireland and in England, as
the scales are of a somewhat complicated
nature, and do not coincide in certain
respects.
With regard to the rates in Northern
Ireland, I would refer the hon. and
learned Member to the Schedule to the
Finance Act (N.I.), 1934. The corresponding rates in Great Britain will be
found in the Schedule to the Imperial
Finance Act of 1933.
It is a fact that in pursuance of the
Imperial Finance Act, 1934, there is a
rebate of 25 per cent. on the Excise duty
payable as from the 1st January next on
private motor cars, but in view of the
growing demands on the Road Fund of
Northern Ireland to meet
necessary
road services I am unable to hold out
any hope of a corresponding abatement
in the licence duties payable on these
types of vehicles in Northern Ireland.
AMALGAMATION OF ROMAN
CATHOLIC SCHOOLS.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education if he can state whether the
Ministry have had under consideration
the resolutions of the clergy of Down and
Connor at three conferences in October,
under the presidency of the Catholic
Bishop, protesting against the action of
the Ministry in amalgamating, or attempting to amalgamate, separate Catholic
Bays' and Catholic Girls' elementary
schools; and whether the Ministry will
have regard to the conscientious convictions of Catholic parents on COeducation?
The Ministry is always prepared to
consider the wishes of parents in educational matters, so long as those wishes
are consistent with educational efficiency
and have due regard to economy of
administration. The Ministry, however,
holds strongly that small, adjoining,
boys' and girls' schools, under the
same management, can be much better
organized and taught and more economically staffed when treated as one
establishment.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I beg to give
notice that I will raise this question on
the Motion for Adjournment.

4. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister

Mr. Stanley C. Ferguson, Edenderry
House, Banbridge, was on the 12th July
last, while driving his motor car
Trummery Cross Roads on the Belfast-
Lurgan Road, brutally beaten and his
motor car maliciously damaged by members of a passing procession; whether the
outrage was reported immediately to the
Lurgan police; whether the police investigated promptly and found the number of
the lodge and the names of the assailants;
and whether any of these assailants have

on
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is a fact
that Mr. Ferguson, in endeavouring to
drive through the ranks of a procession
the 12th July last, was forcibly
stopped by members of the procession,
and as a result his car sustained injuries,
in respect of which he was awarded the
sum of £6 14s 5d at Belfast Quarter
Sessions on the 15th ultimo as compensation for malicious damage.
The matter was promptly investigated
by the police, who submitted all the
evidence available to the Attorney-
General for instructions.
Having considered the evidence, the
Attorney-General decided that the case
was not one in which prosecution should
be instituted either against Mr. Ferguson
for dangerous driving or against the
parties who were alleged to have taken
part in the malicious damage.

CLAUSE 15 (Power of the Ministry
of Commerce to fix licence duty for trout
rods).
Senate Amendment:
Leave out Clause 15.
Mr. BARBOUR: This Clause proposed
to authorise the Ministry of Commerce,
after consultation with a Board of
Conservators and after holding a public
inquiry, to impose a licence duty on trout.
rod fishing either throughout the whole
or in any part of a conservancy district.
The Clause, as hon. Members may recollect, was intended to give effect to the
recommendation made by the Committee
on Local Fishery Administration, whose
report, to a very considerable extent,
forms the ground-work of the present
Bill. In making this particular recommendation the Committee was influenced
by two considerations, namely, the need
of providing additional funds for the
Boards of Conservators for the protection
of the spawning grounds in the upper
reaches of the rivers, and the fact that
the principal of requiring trout anglers
to make some contribution, however
moderate, to the funds of the various
Boards had found a considerable measure
of support amongst the witnesses who had
appeared before the Committee.
The Committee's recommendation was
endorsed by the Fishery Advisory Committee of the Ministry of Commerce and
by the Ulster Angling Federation. With
such support to recommend it the Government felt justified in including in the Bill
a Clause designed to give effect to the
recommendation. When, however, the
Clause came under consideration in the
other House arguments were advanced
that the maximum amount of additional
revenue which could be expected to accrue
from the imposition of a duty on trout.
rod fishing would be insufficient to provide
the additional staff essential to secure
effectual enforcement. A further objection to the proposal was made on the
ground that it would be invidious to
require payment of a licence duty by a
certain class of angler in one locality
whilst the same class was not required
to pay duty in another locality. Whilst
the Government opposed the proposal to
delete the Clause, and the Amendment
was carried only after a division, the
Government does not now desire to offer
further resistance to the deletion of the
Clause.
The view we have taken is that, whilst
in deference to the express wishes of the
trout fisheries who appeared before the
Committee, and to the views of the Ulster
Angling Federation, the Government
was in a sense morally obliged to insert
the Clause in the present Bill, the
position is now altered by what has taken
place in the other Chamber. Accordingly
the Government recommends that the
Amendment deleting Clause 15 be
accepted by this House.
I beg to move, "That this House do
agree with the Senate in the said Amendment."
Question put, and agreed to.
CLAUSE 21 (Publication and Proof
of By-laws).
Senate Amendment :
Clause 21, page 11, line 34, after the
second "the" insert "Crown and".
Mr. BARBOUR: This is purely a
drafting Amendment. Section 93 of the
Fisheries Act, 1842, which Clause 20 of the
present Bill reproduces and amends, required the deposit of by-laws with the
Clerk of the Peace. The office of the
Clerk of the Peace, however, is now
combined with the office of the Clerk of
the Crown, and the official holding it is
known as the Clerk of the Crown and
Peace. The Amendment, therefore,
merely provides for the correct designation of the official concerned.
"I beg to move, "That this House do

(Mr. Gordon).
Mr. CAMPBELL: I wish to raise a
matter of administration by the Ministry
of Education which is causing very deep
concern to a large section of people in
Northern Ireland. At the present time
under an order issued by the Ministry,
of recent date, where the Ministry think
it convenient that several boys' and girls'
schools should be amalgamated, they are
taking power to affect that purpose.
In the case of two schools in which the
average daily attendance for the past
preceding year falls under 50, as a matter
of course, the Ministry has already proceeded or are proceeding, where a vacancy
falls in, in either of the schools, to
amalgamate these separate boys' and girls'
schools. This is a matter of urgent concern to many of the people in whose
interests I speak here to-day. It is a
drastic order and affects the voluntary
schools, more especially the Catholic
voluntary schools, which are, I think,
now the sole upholders of the voluntary
system of education in Northern Ireland.
The answer given to-day arouses considerable perturbation in our community.
The Parliamentary Secretary knows that
these schools are close on 700 in number.
I refer particularly to the schools not under
four-and-two committees, because the
Parliamentary Secretary is well aware
there cannot be more than 4 per cent.
under four-and-two committees, and there
is not the least prospect in the world of
the remainder going under four-and-two
committees. We believe that this new
rule has been engineered by gentlemen
who are not friendly to the voluntary
Adjournment-
Roman Catholic Schools
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Campbell]
school system for which we stand. The
minority here in the North of Ireland
are doing their best to keep these schools
going. It means a very heavy sacrifice
out of their own pockets. They cannot
dip their hands into that apparently
bottomless purse, to which they in common
with other denominations in Northern
Ireland contribute. They have no power
to do that. The Parliamentary Secretary
should realise the danger of needlessly
provoking conflict on this point, because
a conflict on this point where conscience
is touched is a matter on which the
Ministry should not dare unless after
careful consideration.
It is officially said that the amalgamation of these schools is prompted by
reasons of economy. Well, I do submit
that the Government have economised on
these schools almost to starvation point.
We know from the reply of the Minister
here to-day that over £1,000,000 has been
spent on new schools and the reconditioning of transferred schools, and now they
proceed to cheesepare on the salaries of
a few teachers, a matter of a few hundred
pounds each year. You are doing that
by a method which has given the gravest

I do say to the Parliamentary Secretary

You are, I say, rashly and recklessly

You may ask what is our objection. I
may put it in a sentence. These Catholic
parents do object to the promiscuous

and delicate period of their lives as evil
and pernicious; and if you proceed with
the enforcement of this order the Catholic
parents will have to consult their consciences. It is a matter of saving a few
hundred pounds to proceed with this concentration of these children in larger
school units. It may be said you are not

that that is not your aim. It may be
